en: The Sātvata-saṃhitā,
together with the commentary composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa;
the first section.
On Mount Malaya, which is frequented by siddhas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas, sages remained devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
We worship the deity named Yogānanda-Nṛsiṃha, the crest-jewel upon the peak of the illustrious Yādava mountain and a mine of excellent virtues.
May the glorious Nārāyaṇa, who dwells on the Yugiri mountain, protect us— he who possesses the supreme divine form and this fourfold nature consisting of the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking;
he who bears the form of the Vaiśākha pillar and his manifold majesty.
Richly adorned with divine ornaments and weapons, and having the king of birds as his vehicle, he protects all the worlds.

May the Lion among Men, the protector of the universe, who eternally bestows upon his devotees enjoyments both perishable and imperishable, and who is the perpetual giver of all goals, be victorious everywhere.
Having bowed my head to the teachers who have established the Sātvata doctrine,
the meaning of the Sātvata is now elucidated according to the path they have prescribed.
Regarding the arrival of Nārada on Mount Malaya:

here, first of all, the venerable great sage Nārada, an expert in the scriptures of the Blessed One, having been instructed by Vāsudeva himself regarding Saṃkarṣaṇa, and having received from Saṃkarṣaṇa the *Ekāyana-śruti*—known as the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*) and existing in the form of aphorisms (*sūtra*) which serves as the sole means for attaining the Blessed One—instructed [Saṃkarṣaṇa] at the outset in the *Sātvata-tantra*, consisting of twenty-five chapters and encompassing investigations into the rites of approaching, acquiring, worshipping, studying, and yoga, as well as investigations into the Supreme Brahman in its forms as the Parā-vyūha and Vibhava.
He shows the sequence of its introduction with the words "of Viṣṇu.

Here, by employing the word *Viṣṇu* at the outset, an infinite auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is performed, which serves as the means for the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose. "Frequented by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas" means that because it is a place to be resorted to even by the gods, it is exceedingly pure. "On the Malaya mountain" refers to the Malaya range. "Sages" (*munayaḥ*) are the seers (*ṛṣi*) whose nature is the meditation upon the Blessed One. "Of Viṣṇu" refers to the Blessed One whose nature is to pervade the universe.

The meaning is that, being intent on propitiation, they remained with their minds fixed solely on [the Lord], wondering: "Where should the propitiation of the all-pervading Blessed One be performed? What is its procedure? And who will instruct us? By the prefix *sam* in the word *saṃsthitāḥ*, a state of persistence over a long period of time is indicated. || 1 ||
At a certain time, the divine sage Nārada, who is identical with the Blessed Lord, descended there from heaven, longing for a vision of Rāma.

"Nārada’s vision of Paraśurāma after some time": while the sages were situated there in that manner, "after some time"—meaning after a certain period had passed—the divine sage named Nārada, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas), being eager for a vision of Rāma and intent on serving Paraśurāma, descended from heaven and appeared there on Mount Malaya. || 2 ||
Having recognized his unwavering devotion, the Lord whose emblem is the axe appeared before him in person with a heart full of compassion.

"Know this": here is the speech of Paraśurāma to Nārada, [saying] "Instruct the sages in the Sātvata doctrine. The god Paraśurāma, whose insignia is the axe—having known the unshakable devotion (the firm resolve regarding himself) of that divine sage—with a compassionate mind, endowed with causeless mercy, he "came into direct perception," meaning he became an object of his vision. || 3 ||
Then, with a joyful countenance and his hair standing on end from rapture, the sage worshipped that god by prostrating himself with all eight limbs and other such acts.

"Then" means for that reason. The sage Nārada, with a joyful countenance—his face blossoming with delight—and with his hair standing on end from horripilation, worshipped that Lord Rāma with services such as prostration with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma), circumambulation, praise, and inquiry. || 4 ||
Then the Blessed Lord Rāma spoke with words of sweet syllables:
"Your devotion is unwavering and brings about the destruction of the seed of rebirth."
This, however, is the pure Sātvatī [path], which is eternal and unswerving;
for sages dwell here, seeking the station of Hari.

"Now" (atha) means: after the tumultuous cheering that encouraged the sage, the Blessed Lord Rāma spoke with a voice of sweet syllables—a composition of enchanting phonemes. The meaning is that he replied to Nārada. He describes the manner of his speech with the words beginning "of you" (tava). "But this devotion of yours" means that such devotion alone exists [in you]; the sense is that there is no other means to be obtained from us. He qualifies that devotion with five words beginning with "unwavering" (acala): it is unwavering, being free from fickleness.

It is that which destroys the seed of birth, annihilates the suffering of saṃsāra, is characterized by the Sātvatas, and is proclaimed in the Sātvata scriptures; that is to say, it has the attainment of the Blessed Lord as its sole means and consists of the constituent parts of ritual action such as *abhigamana* (approaching) and so forth. For that very reason, it is "pure," meaning unmixed. It is "constant," meaning uninterrupted. It is "unswerving," meaning it does not have other deities as its object. Since you possess such devotion, you have no further purpose other than seeing us; rather, the meaning is that you should instruct even these sages in the means to liberation.

"They remain" means: for this reason, on this mountain, the sages who desire liberation remain seeking the foot of Hari; therefore, engage those sages in the path of action proclaimed by the Sātvata teachings—the pure path consisting of approaching, collecting materials, worship, and study. "By my word, join them": go forth even upon the most secret path out of respect for our command and set the sages in motion; the sense is that you should go quickly for that purpose. (5–6)
"Go and, at my command, employ them in the path of action belonging to the Sātvatas. Having spoken thus to him out of a desire for the welfare of the sages, [he departed]. (7)

"Thus. Lord Paraśurāma, having spoken thus to that brahmin Nārada in the manner previously described out of a desire for the welfare of the sages, vanished from that place on the mountain peak in a mere instant, like a flash of lightning; the meaning is that he became invisible. || 7 ||
The god vanished from that place like a flash of lightning;
he, however, with a joyful mind, bowed his head to that speech.

"He" refers to Nārada. "Then," meaning immediately after the Lord had vanished; "he," that is Nārada, being delighted in mind, having saluted those words with his head—that is to say, having accepted that command with his head—worshipped that excellent place, the site of the Lord's manifestation, solely with flowers, and departed from that place. || 8 ||
Having worshipped that excellent place with flowers,
he then went forth and beheld another hermitage frequented by various birds.
"He saw" means he beheld the hermitage, the dwelling place of the sages. By the three qualifiers beginning with "various," the extreme loveliness of the hermitage is expressed. || 9 ||
Abounding with the flowers and fruits of *taru* trees and provided with ponds, wells, and lakes,
he was then joyfully greeted by the best of the twice-born residing there.

"Exceedingly joyful": then, because of seeing that hermitage, Nārada was exceedingly joyful; he was saluted—that is, paid homage—by the best of the twice-born residing there, and being honored with the *arghya* and *pādya* offerings, he was seated upon a mat (*viṣṭara*). The meaning is that he was placed upon a seat. || 10 ||
Honored with water for the guest and water for the feet, and having been seated upon a mat,
they all then stood with palms joined in reverence, their lotus-like eyes wide open in wonder.

Regarding the word *atha*: after the ritual reception (*upacaraṇa*), all the sages, with their lotus-eyes fully blossomed—meaning their lotus-eyes opened with joy—said, "By reason of seeing you, the fruitfulness of our birth has been achieved," the words "has been achieved" being understood as the ellipsis; thus they spoke, and one must accept the past tense (*bhūtārtha*) for the verb. || 11 ||
"Today our birth has attained its fulfillment by the sight of you," they said, having heard those words of his which were affectionate and full of joy. 12.24.

Having heard this, the sage Nārada, having bowed down and prostrated before Hṛṣīkeśa—here it should be understood that the prostration is for the purpose of beginning the instruction of the scripture—spoke words that were tender with affection and sweet with compassion; therefore, they were pleasing to Him and produced satisfaction in those sages. "Spoke" means he uttered [these words]. || 12 ||
Having paid homage to Hṛṣīkeśa, the sage Nārada also said:
"I truly consider myself to have achieved my life's purpose; indeed, I am now the best among the brahmins."

"I consider myself... [He says: "O best of sages, O munis! I consider myself to have achieved my life's purpose; the meaning is, 'I am one whose goal is fulfilled. The word *nūnam* means certainly; *hi* is used here to indicate what is well-known. The sense is that for me, in this auspicious hermitage—which is conducive to welfare because it is a place of the Lord’s manifestation and a refuge for many devotees—a connection with you has arisen (this is the ellipsis). The underlying thought is: 'Through this association with you, who are supreme devotees, I have become one who has achieved his purpose. || 13 ||
"Since I have a connection with you all in this auspicious hermitage, I was spoken to for your sake by Rāma, whose actions are effortless. (14)

Regarding the word "ukta" (spoken): since I have been spoken to—that is, appointed—by Rāma of unblemished deeds for your sake, meaning for the purpose of setting forth the Sātvata path for you, therefore, all of you now, being of one mind (note that the word *manas* is understood here as ending in 'a' due to its divine nature), listen—meaning hear—their words; this is the sense, with "their speech" being the implied object. || 14 ||
Listen now all with one mind to that which [I shall say]:
from this day forward, worship Keśava, the Lord of Gods.

"From this day forward, you must constantly worship and honor Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, the best among all gods, and the master even of Brahmā and Rudra, according to the procedure of the secret tradition (rahasyāmnāya) which grants eternal liberation and yields the fruit of perpetual mokṣa, following the sequence prescribed for the Sāttvatas. || 15 ||
"By means of the secret tradition (rahasyāmnāya) which eternally bestows liberation.
The sages said:
"O Sage, you are the refuge for us who have long sought protection and are most excellent. (16)

The sages' prayer to Nārada: Having been addressed in this way, the sages pray, "O Sage! [They say: "Even though we are distinguished—meaning those who have achieved the fruits of various well-known forms of austerity—and even though we have long since taken refuge in you, being intent on the practice of the means (upāya), [the word] 'of us' is to be supplied as the ellipsis; you, having become our teacher, are our goal (gati)—both the destination to be reached and the one who causes us to reach it. They say, "For the attainment of the state of Nārāyaṇa," implying that one should not wonder, "What is the use of searching for means for those whose fruit is already established by itself?"

"Neither by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing is this Self attained"—thus [it is said that] it cannot be attained through austerity and the like; yet, "He alone whom this [Self] chooses, by him is He attainable"—thus [it is said that] the fruit of liberation is attainable through the compassion of the perfected means. Therefore, reveal that action which is the means to the highest good, which generates delight for the Blessed Lord. 16.
"Reveal that which is the highest good for the attainment of Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
"That which was previously spoken by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) when urged by Balarāma."

"Yat" means: O twice-born ones, listen—that which was spoken and taught by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus, when impelled by Saṃkarṣaṇa, the plow-bearer, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga; that Sātvata doctrine, which has come down through tradition and reached you via the succession of gurus, hear it from me as I speak it. || 17 ||
O twice-born ones, listen as I relate that which has come down through tradition:
long ago, when the Kṛta age had passed and the subsequent age called Tretā had arrived.

"Pure" means: when the previous [age]—the Kṛta—had been made, passed, and transcended, and when another age-division called Tretā had arrived, while the Supporter of the World (jagaddhātṛ), the Immutable (acyuta) Vāsudeva, had attained a slight reddishness; the meaning is that his body was red, according to the sequence to be stated later: "In the Kṛta age he assumes fourfold forms such as white, etc.; indeed, O Great-minded One, in the Tretā age he is red in name and established in white. || 18 ||
When the infallible Sustainer of the World had become slightly reddened,
Saṅkarṣaṇa, though full of humility, spoke to Viṣṇu, recognizing him as he was.
"O Lord, what is this that I see—a transformation of your form?
Laughing, the Blessed One spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: (20)

He said: Saṃkarṣaṇa, although he already knew and understood the cause of the change in his complexion, being humble and possessed of the discipline that one must learn from the instruction of a teacher, spoke to Viṣṇu Vāsudeva. What did he say? "O Lord, I perceive a transformation in your form—a change in your color. The meaning is: "From what has this come? Then, "having laughed," the Blessed One Vāsudeva, laughing, [spoke] with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, possessing a depth like the roar of a cloud.
Here, the figure of speech is *upamānaluptā* (the elision of the standard of comparison). The meaning is that he replied to Saṃkarṣaṇa with his speech, that is, with his voice. || 19-20 ||
This is not the time when people were predominantly full of spiritual essence;
today the world is intent on passion, yet I preserve that former conduct.

"Not this": the meaning is that this present time is not that time when people were predominantly composed of *sattva*, being purely *sāttvika*. "Now": at this present time, the world—meaning the people—is intent on passion (*rāga*), characterized by attachment. Like those people of that time, I too maintain that same passion. || 21 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
By what action is such passion born of time and nature, which does not overwhelm the worlds, and especially those who are your devotees? (22)

Thus addressed, Saṃkarṣaṇa replies: "O Kālī! This passion, born of the nature of Time—that is, produced by the nature of the Tretā Yuga—is caused by what specific karma? [The word 'lokānām' is used in the accusative sense] 'of the worlds who are Your devotees'; it does not shroud or obscure those devoted people. || 22 ||
The Blessed Lord said: For those who worship the supreme, eternal Brahman in a threefold manner, passion remains far away.

Thus urged, the Blessed One replied: "In three ways. Those people who worship the eternal, supreme Brahman, Śrīmannārāyaṇa, through the threefold manner—namely, the distinctions of the Paravyūha, Vibhava, and [Vilāsa] forms—for them, passion remains at a distance. || 23 ||
Śaṅkarṣaṇa said:
"O Blessed One, for the benefit of those who have sought refuge and for the removal of their delusion, please explain the threefold goal characterized by Brahman."

Again Saṃkarṣaṇa said, "O Blessed One": O Blessed One, please speak—explain—for the sake of removing the delusion of those who have taken refuge in the threefold, three-pronged goal characterized as Brahman, which is the nature of that which is to be attained, and for the sake of their welfare, namely, for the removal of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable. || 24 ||

The Blessed Lord said: [I salute] the God whose body is the sixfold policy, who possesses the blazing splendor of the sun and fire, whose hands and feet are everywhere, and who has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides. (25)

Thus questioned, Nārada describes the characteristics of transcendence and so forth with the word "ṣāḍguṇya. "Possessing a body of the six qualities" means having a body composed of knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor; "having the brilliance of blazing fire" means possessing a radiance equal to the sun and fire; and "having hands and feet everywhere" means having eyes, heads, and faces on all sides—the sense being that he is all-pervading. Thus, the Lord's possession of hands, feet, and so forth on all sides is accessible through inference. And so it is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "For everything has been projected by the Supreme Self."
Therefore, the state of being all-pervasive is indeed inferred for that which is omnipresent;
for it is neither limited by space nor separated by time.
Therefore, because it is all-pervading, the Lord is remembered as being present everywhere;
just as the sun shines intensely, reaching upwards, across, and downwards.
In the same way, because its nature is luminosity, it is therefore the eye of all; for it is unborn.
Just as among all the limbs, the head is proclaimed to be the foremost.
But in this world, O best of beings, he is not like ordinary people;
because of his equanimity and purity, the Lord is established as the one whose head is everything.
Since all [flavors] are indeed always present within him who is of peaceful form everywhere, he is therefore remembered as being "all-faced."

"Know that the mass of sentient beings is indeed the Supreme Lord; He possesses hearing everywhere, just as He possesses sight, hearing, and movement. [This means] one, without a second—that is, having no equal or superior. The "refuge of all" is the support of the entire universe; the "Lord" is the master of the world, the God known as the Supreme Vāsudeva, who is designated as "Supreme" (param). The syntactical connection is: "know that this very Brahman, characterized by such supremacy, is the Existent (sat). (25)
This has been fully declared as the one Lord, the support of all;
this and another triad preceded by it are differentiated by qualities such as knowledge and the rest. || 26 ||

Having thus stated the characteristic of the Supreme (para), he describes the characteristic of the manifestation (vyūha) with the words "this" (etat). This refers to that which was previously mentioned: this Para-Vāsudeva is the first (pūrva) of which [the others] are subsequent; it is thus described. It exists on the east, differentiated by qualities such as knowledge (jñāna) and the rest, and then on the south, associated with power (bala) and knowledge (jñāna).
By means of his sovereignty and vigor, the Supreme Lord abides in the state of inwardness;
through the nature of his radiant power, he is established in the serene.

Thus, in the manner to be described, know that the other triad—namely the triad of Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, distinguished by their respective qualities—and likewise the fourfold group consisting of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, which is designated as the *vyūha*, is that very Brahman; know it to be the bestower of the fruit of supreme beatitude and the fruit of liberation. 26.

Know that to be the one designated as the *vyūha*, which eternally bestows the fruit of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); know it to possess various forms through its primary and secondary manifestations, endowed with qualities such as knowledge and the rest, and capable of granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (27)

Now, he describes the characteristic of the *vibhava* [manifestation] with the words "by the primary... and so forth. It means that [the *vibhava*] is endowed with qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*) through the distinction between the primary and the subordinate. Since this entire collection of *vibhava* incarnations is produced from Aniruddha, just as power (*śakti*) and splendor (*tejas*) possess primacy in their own cause, Aniruddha, while the fourfold qualities beginning with knowledge are subordinate, so too it is endowed with both the primary powers and splendors and the subordinate qualities such as knowledge. Regarding the fact that the *vibhava* deities are produced from Aniruddha, it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"The *vibhava*, which possesses infinite forms, has Padmanābha as its chief face, O All-pervading One."
The detailed exposition of Aniruddha is shown in that *Sātvata* [Tantra]:

"The Supreme Lord, by means of His pervasive power (*śakti*), resides in the gentle [Aniruddha]. Thus, it is stated that Aniruddha possesses the qualities of splendor (*tejas*) and power (*śakti*). If it is asked what is the proof for the persistence of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the other qualities within Him, [the author] will state "by the power of the Pervasive One" in the third chapter. It is also clearly stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Even though there is the manifestation of only one quality at a time, these six qualities are indeed present."
"All are neither deficient nor superior to the eternal Vāsudeva.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the phrase "endowed with qualities such as knowledge" connects only with the preceding [verse], while the distinction between the primary [form] and its manifestations is implied. Know that the Lord—who possesses various forms through the distinctions of Padmanābha and others, and who is of manifold appearances—is that very Brahman; know him as the truly existent (sat) who bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. Thus, the characteristics of the Supreme (para), the Manifested (vyūha), and the Expansive (vibhava) have been stated.

And likewise, these very characteristics of the *para* (transcendent) and so forth are embraced in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "The established doctrine of the Bhāgavatas is that the Supreme Brahman is threefold, by way of the *para*, *vyūha*, and *vibhava*. Among these, the *para* is the uncaused state, the ocean of the six perfections (*ṣāḍguṇya*) in their fullness, undivided from the effect; it possesses the sovereign umbrella of the eternally blissful manifestation (*vibhūti*), is the goal to be approached by the liberated, and is free from all limiting adjuncts (*anupādhika*)."

The manifestation (*vyūha*) consists of the fourfold station that effects liberation, comprising: the desire to emit [the world] (*sisṛkṣā*), the emanation, maintenance, and dissolution to be bestowed; the scripture, its meaning, and its fruits; and the play (*līlā*) consisting of meditation and worship. This [manifestation] is characterized by the playful sovereignty (*līlāvibhūti*) brought about by the arraying (*vyūha*) of droplets of activity in the form of the distinct supreme qualities suitable for such tasks. Furthermore, the manifestation of power (*vibhava*) is the class of intentional appearances (*prādurbhāva*) similar to its own sovereign power, belonging to the same genus as itself, such as gods, humans, animals, and so forth. ...

"In that regard, some manifestations (*prādurbhāva*) are direct, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others; others, however, are through the presiding over a distinguished personage such as a *ṛṣi*, such as Paraśurāma, Kṛṣṇa, Dvaipāyana, and others; others occur at a specific time through the descent of power (*śaktyāveśa*), such as in the case of Purañjaya and others; and still others descend themselves into individual forms, such as the *arcāvatāra* (incarnation in an image)—thus they are fourfold.
Now, one might object: "The *arcāvatāra* must also be included within the [other] manifestations. Or rather:
"The *vibhava* (manifestation) is of infinite forms, with Padmanābha as its foremost, belonging to the All-pervading Lord."
The detailed expansion of Aniruddha has been shown in that Sātvata [Purāṇa];
even the worldly worship is for those whose selves are permeated by the Blessed One.
Through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra and the Lord of Mantras, she too possesses a body composed of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
Within these four forms of mine, there is the descent of the supreme (parā) and other modes of worship.

If it is argued that the first mention of the *arcāvatāra* (the incarnate form) should be made according to the method stated in the *Lakṣmītantra* and other texts—namely, "The states beginning with the fourth (*turyā*) are to be known; this is the pure path"—we reply as follows: There is no dispute regarding those places where the first mention of the *arcāvatāra* has already been made. However, since the *Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā* expounds only the threefold division known as *para*, *vyūha*, and *vibhava*, the venerable Parāśara Bhaṭṭāraka has demonstrated the *arcāvatāra* in accordance with that [text].

How is this established? Because it is possible for all three—the supreme manifestation (*paravyūha*), the majestic manifestation (*vibhava*), and the iconic manifestation (*arcā*)—to exist in the form of icons; thus, it has been stated that the iconic manifestation is included within the supreme manifestation and the other two manifestations.

In reality, however, the intention of the Bhaṭṭārakas is as follows: although the manifestations known as the Vyūhas—Vāsudeva (Saṃkarṣaṇa), Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—descend in the forms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Balabhadra, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, they remain *vibhavas* (manifestations) rather than *vyūhas* (manifestations of the essential nature). Likewise, although the *paravyūhas* and *vibhavas* descend in the form of *arcāvatāras* (incarnations for worship), they are included only within the category of *vibhavas*, and not within the two categories of *paravyūhas*. For it is said:

"This wonderful path is threefold: that which is superimposed through the conceptualization of qualities (*guṇa-kalpanā*), that which proceeds from the manifestation of qualities (*guṇonmeṣa-kṛta-krama*), and that which consists of qualities incarnate (*mūrtībhūta-guṇa*)."

Thus, the state of being a manifestation (*vibhavatva*), characterized by the qualities having become embodied as described in the *Lakṣmītantra*, is common to both the manifestation (*vibhava*) and the incarnation (*avatāra*). || 27 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Question and Answer," in the Śrī Sātvata Saṃhitā of the Śrī Pañcarātra.

Thus ends the first chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśvara.
The Second Chapter.
Nārada said:
Having heard this from the mouth of Acyuta, the god of gods, Halāyudha—
O best of the twice-born, he spoke again for the benefit of those who fear worldly existence.
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord, by what kind of procedure indeed is worship prescribed here? Tell me in brief, O All-pervading One, regarding the devotees who are practitioners of worship.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen attentively; I shall explain that which you have requested, by knowing which a person shall never again undergo rebirth. (3)

Now the second chapter will be explained. Here, at the outset, he sets forth the sequence of questions and answers concerning the manner of worshipping the Lord Vāsudeva and Saṃkarṣaṇa through three verses beginning with "Having heard" (śrutvā). 1–3.
And for those Brahmins who perform sacrifices to the True Brahman known as Vāsudeva,
he has been the objective from the beginning of creation, residing within the hearts of those who possess the requisite qualification.
This great scripture, the Upaniṣad of Brahman, bestows supreme discernment;
it is endowed with a sequence of divine mantras and has liberation as its sole defining fruit.
Therefore, for the sake of uplifting the world,
I shall teach that primordial [scripture] which has spread in such a manner and exists in many diverse forms.

With the three and a half verses beginning with "of the Brāhmaṇas," he says that he will teach the Sātvata-tantra, which is the essence of the *ekāyana-śruti*. The meaning is: for those Brāhmaṇas who sacrifice to "Sat" (the Good), namely Brahman, and to Vāsudeva; that is, those who are intent upon worshipping the Reality alone, which is denoted by the words Sat, Brahman, and Vāsudeva. The sense is that it is not to be shown to Brāhmaṇas who sacrifice to other deities. For this very reason, it resides in the hearts of qualified practitioners who sacrifice purely, and is thus to be kept strictly secret.

It bestows discernment (*viveka*), providing the discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted; it is the supreme, most excellent *Brahmopaniṣad*, so named because it "sits near" (*upa-ni-ṣad*) [the Supreme]. Although all *Upaniṣads* abide in the proximity of the Blessed One, by the term *Brahmopaniṣad*, its status as being in immediate proximity to Brahman is indicated. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is the *Upaniṣad* which expounds Brahman alone. It is endowed with divine mantra-practices—that is, with divine mantras such as those for attaining power (*bala*) and so forth, which directly expound that [Brahman].
It is adorned, free from doubt, and dispels the darkness of ignorance.

In the manner described above, the scripture consisting of the *Ekāyana-śruti*—which, accompanied by mantras such as the *Bala-mantra*, bestows the fruit of liberation alone—has emerged from that root Veda for the sake of uplifting the world.
[It is intended] for those who, having abandoned the supreme Dharma, have resorted to a mixed Dharma;
yet who, longing once more for that state, have attained faith and devotion.
For the sake of favoring the social classes and for the purpose of bringing about their fitness,
as well as for the attainment of the desired fruits by all people.
In accordance with the root Vedas and in the Anuṣṭubh meter,
[the scriptures] such as the Sātvata, the Pauṣkara, and the Jayākhyā were revealed.
Having spoken that divine collection of true scriptures, he caused it to be promulgated on earth by Saṃkarṣaṇa and others who desired the welfare of all the worlds.

Because it has been stated thus: "The sequence (*krama*) is such as to resemble the root Veda; it bestows success and liberation (*siddhi-mokṣa-pradam*), granting both worldly enjoyment and the ultimate release (*bhoga-apavarga-dam*). Even though it grants desired fruits, its object is the Lord alone. It is perfectly pure (*pariśuddham*), accompanied by secrets (*sarahasyam*), containing various secret mantras, and unconfused (*asaṃkulam*), being unmixed with other deities. That divine scripture (*divya-śāstram*) exists in many divisions, distinguished by various *saṃhitā* differences; [I shall teach] that which is the first (*ādyaṃ*)—meaning the very first (*prathamam*) within that divine scripture—namely, the *Sātvata-tantra*. The words 'I shall teach to you' are to be supplied. (Verses 4–6)
It bestows both spiritual accomplishment and liberation; it is pure, esoteric, and unconfused, for those who have perfected the eightfold yoga and whose souls are devoted to the current sacrifice.

Demonstrating the distinctions among those qualified for that [practice] through the different manifestations of the supreme array, he first states the qualification of yogis for the worship of the Supreme Lord with the verse beginning "With eight limbs" (7).
The authority of yogins would reside in the one Lord of the Heart,
as well as that of the Brahmins who recite the Vedas and are engaged in the practice of mixed sacrifices.

He states that even among those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, only those who are free from delusion regarding other deities mentioned therein have the entitlement to perform the worship of the Supreme Vyūha with mantras, whereas for those who sacrifice in a mixed manner, there is no such entitlement; this he declares in the verse beginning with "vyāmiśra. (8)
However, the authority [to perform this] belongs only to one who possesses the mantra within the fourfold assembly (caturvyūha), and not otherwise;
nor does it belong to the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, even if they have truly taken refuge.

Then, [the author] states "of the three" (trayāṇām) to declare that those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes who are solely devoted to surrender to the Blessed One have the right to perform the worship of the Vyūha without mantras. || 9 ||
But for those who lack discernment, there is no authority over the mantra-less [state] in the sequence of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha-kriyā),
nor indeed over the empowered wheel of mantras (vaibhavīya-mantracakra) that involves ritual action.
For those who have completely cast off the sense of "mine," whose souls are devoted to their own duties, and who are properly devoted to the Supreme Lord through action, speech, and mind; 11.

With the two verses beginning with "sakriyaḥ," [the author] declares that even those who are devoid of discrimination because they are seized by the notions of "I" and "mine," yet are devoted to their own duties, dedicated devotees of the Lord, and initiated Brāhmaṇas and others—all four classes—possess the right to worship the Vaibhava [form] accompanied by mantras. Here, in the phrase "vaibhavīyevivekinām," the word division is *avivekinām* (of those lacking discrimination). One should not suspect a depreciation of the various Vaibhava forms on the grounds that they are said to be worshipable by those lacking discrimination; rather, through their exceptional accessibility, their excellence is indeed established. This very point is corroborated in the Lakṣmītantra as well:
The authority over the principles of the well-perfected yoga belongs to the Supreme Self;
for those of middling capacity who are engaged in the practice of mixed sacrifice, it concerns the meditation on the cosmic array (vyūha).

In the forms of Vaibhava and the others, for those devotees who are devoid of discrimination regarding the Self and who are afflicted by the notions of "I" and "mine," [there exists] devotion toward the Supreme Lord.
"Observing the diversity of the capacities of his devotees, he assumes various forms designated as the supreme, the manifest, and so forth. (10–11)
Indeed, there is the authority of four [classes] when the sequence of initiation has been attained;
thus it remains for those who have correctly entered [the path], preceded by mantra, according to their station. (12)

Thus, he says "evam" (thus) [in verse 12], meaning: "First, listen to the method of directly worshipping the Supreme, which is most beneficial for those who have reached this state in accordance with their respective offices."
Now listen to this single method for the one-formed [rite]:
on a praiseworthy, secluded, and protected patch of ground smeared with fragrant paste. (13)
He states the construction of the wheel for the purpose of extracting that mantra, beginning with the words "praśasta" (excellent). || 13 ||
Having prepared the wheel of colors in a well-perfumed place enriched with water for honor (arghya) and flowers—
[the wheel] upon which the entire universe, from the world of Brahmā downwards, is established.
By whose arising the origin of the world occurs immediately thereafter, and upon whose ceasing within itself dissolution comes about. (15)

"Because the wheel of phonemes (varṇacakra) is directly the body of the Blessed One, consisting of sound, and is the mother of mantras—as expressed in the verse, 'She is the manifest mother of mantras, my very body composed of sound'—the author states with two verses beginning with 'In which... that it is the support of the entire universe and the cause of creation and so forth. (14–15)
That which impels both the moon and the sun, both externally and internally,
which is eternally risen, situated within the eye, and is the phoneme that expresses the Lord (Īśvara).
In that regard, he explains the sequence of the arrangement of the phonemes beginning with the *praṇava* by means of the verses starting with "nityodita" (eternally arisen). || 16 ||
In that place, the Lord whose essence is speech resides according to the division of locations;
he consists of the collection of phonemes beginning with 'A' and ending with the Visarga, as well as the groups of digits belonging to the Sun and the Moon.

In the navel, according to the division of short and long [vowels], where the collection of principles (tattvasañcaya) consisting of the eighteen [consonants] beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', situated within the spokes, is the primordial (prākṛta). || 18 ||
From earth up to primordial nature (prakṛti), O wielder of the plow, through the union of pairs;
Time, the sustainer of the body, is the rim-mover characterized by nine aspects. (19)
In that Pradhigaṇa, there is the syllable beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'ha',
which is Time-Vaiśvānara himself, appearing like ten thousand suns.
The Blessed One, abiding at the end of the phonemes, is enriched by ten thousand times ten thousand flames;
[he perceives] the continuous stream of phonemes from the middle up to the head, ending with the mind.

Regarding the statement "beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga," it is taught in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* that the eight short vowels beginning with 'a' possess the nature of light and so forth because they belong to the solar [principle], while the eight long vowels beginning with 'ā' possess the nature of fluidity and so forth because they belong to the lunar [principle]:
"Light, sharpness, pervasion, grasping, casting away, and motion."
Indeed, ripening (pāka) and attainment (prāpti)— these eight are established within the solar portion,
sequentially within these short vowels beginning with 'a'.
Fluidity, coolness, satisfaction, luster, clarity,
essence, taste, and bliss— these eight are considered the lunar qualities.
Established in the long vowels beginning with *ā* as the essence of the Mātṛkā,
they indeed always exist in a state of mutual inseparability.
And of the eight [circles], there are eight [deities] situated both outside and inside.
Thus [ends the section]. (17–21)
Having uttered [the seed-syllable] and worshipped the King of Mandalas (cakrarāj) with the arghya and other offerings,
one should then extract the mantra that denotes the Supreme Self.

One should first extract the most excellent [syllable] resembling nectar, which grants the attainment of liberation in no time; it resides in the axle (akṣa). Immediately thereafter, one should extract the sixth [syllable] of the rim (nemi). 23.

He says that one should extract the mantra preceded by the worship of the wheel of letters (varṇacakra) in two verses beginning with "āmadhyāt. "The king of wheels" means the wheel of letters; the change in case-ending is Vedic.

And thus, the application here is as follows: on a ground that is auspicious, secluded, protected, smeared with fragrant paste, enriched with *arghya* flowers, and well-perfumed, one should draw a twelve-spoked wheel. In its center, at the position of the axle, one should write the *praṇava* (Oṃ); in the hub (*nābhi*), the sixteen vowels from *a* to *visarga*; on the twelve spokes, in pairs of syllables for each spoke, the twenty-four consonants from *ka* to *bha*; on the rim (*nemibhāga*), the nine letters from *ma* to *ha*; and in the outer circle (*pradhigaṇa*), the letter *kṣa*. Having written these, [one should proceed].

Having recited the sequence of syllables from the beginning to the end, starting with "Oṃ Oṃ Namaḥ" and "Oṃ Aṃ Namaḥ" in that order, and having worshipped it with water for offerings (arghya) and other substances, one should extract the mantra. || 22-23 ||
This second syllable is not stepped upon by the second [letter] from the navel;
it is the second from the tenth, and further below, beyond the eighth.
This second syllable is endowed with the thirteenth [consonant] from the navel;
then the second [syllable] is joined with the ninth from the navel and the fourth vowel.
Know that the second [syllable] consists solely of the fifth letter from the eighth;
then, immediately following that, take the three-syllabled word for consciousness (vijñāna). || 26 ||
The first letter, distinct from the eleventh, is not [separated] by what follows the navel;
then one should place that above the third letter of the rim (nemi). || 27 ||
This is indeed the ninth of the mantras; now learn from me the tenth: the first letter, preceded by the second [vowel], joined with the eighth row. (28)
Following that, having taken eight [units] from the circumference (nemi), the third [circle] is established;
it is situated above the fifth.
Know this to be the thirteenth, following after the ninth;
one should place that triad above the sixth, which is the color of the rim (nemi).
The sixteenth [vowel] is indeed joined with the third from the navel (the letter *u*);
the second [consonant] is joined with the tenth letter from the navel (the letter *ṭ*) and the eleventh (the letter *tha*). (31)
One should then offer the word "caitanyāya" along with "namaḥ";
this twenty-two-syllable mantra is thus adorned with six words.

He states that method with the words beginning "Then he should extract [the one] situated in the axle" (*tataḥ sa... akṣastham uddharet*). First, one should extract the *praṇava* situated in the axle. Immediately after, one should extract the sixth consonant of the rim, the letter *śa*, which is conjoined with the second vowel of the navel, namely the letter *ā*.

Then, having extracted the second *na* from the two *dha*s situated in the tenth enclosure among the ten [syllables], one should join beneath it the letter *ta*, which is the second letter following the eighth [from the end] and is endowed with the thirteenth [vowel] *o*. Then, one should join the second letter from the ninth, the letter *da*, with the fourth vowel from the "navel," which is *i*. Next, one should extract only the letter *ta*, the second letter from the eighth. Then, one should extract the three letters beginning with *vi-jñā-na*.

Then, having joined the first letter from the eleventh [group], the letter *pa*, with the vowel *ā* following the navel [the letter *ya*] to form *yā*, one should place it above the third letter of the rim, the letter *ra*. Next, one should extract the letter *ṇa*, which is the eighth letter in its row and is preceded by the aforementioned letter, being conjoined with the second letter of the navel and possessed of the vowel *ā*. Thereafter, one should extract the second letter of the rim, the letter *ya*. Then, one should extract the eighth letter of the rim, the letter *sa*. Finally, one should extract the third letter, the letter *ra*, situated above the letter *va* which stands upon the fifth letter of that [rim].

Then one should extract the letter *da* following the ninth; then, above the letter *śa*, which is the color of the rim of the sixth [wheel], one should place its third [vowel], the letter *ra*. One should join that with the third vowel of its own navel, the letter *i*. Then, one should take the second letter from the tenth, the letter *na*, and join it with the eleventh of its own navel, the letter *e*. Then, one should extract the four-syllabled word *caitanyāya*, together with the salutation—that is, preceded by the word of obeisance (*namaḥ*).

And thus, the twenty-two-syllable mantra, adorned with six words, is extracted as follows: "Oṃ, salutation to the Consciousness that is both the tranquil and the arisen, the Life-force, the All-seeing, the Pure Awareness. (24–32)
In that regard, knowledge is a word of one syllable, power is a word of four syllables, sovereignty is a word of six syllables, and supreme vigor is a word of five syllables. (33)
The four-syllabled word is the splendor of Śakti, as is that which consists of two syllables;
it is splendor, heroism, strength, power, sovereignty, and indeed knowledge itself. (34)

Regarding those same six categories, he states their status as denoters of qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*) by first specifying the number of syllables in each, using one and a half verses beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*). Now, since strength (*bala*) is subordinate to knowledge, it was mentioned immediately after that. In the same way, it should be understood that valor (*vīrya*) is subordinate to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and splendor (*tejas*) is subordinate to the power of valor (*vīrya-śakti*). That strength and the others are subordinate to knowledge and the rest is very clearly corroborated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"I have three inherent natures known as the powers of knowledge, sovereignty, and [will]."
The non-blinking ones are proclaimed separately by means of the three principles;
strength, heroism, and likewise splendor—this indeed is the triad of qualities.
"Fatigue and so forth—consisting of the states of ignorance—are subordinate to knowledge and the rest.
In reality, however, it should be understood that even the pentad beginning with sovereignty (aiśvarya) is an attribute of knowledge;
for the supreme form of both Brahmā and myself is of the nature of knowledge.

"The remainder—sovereignty, valor, and so forth—is the eternal quality of knowledge," according to the statement in the *Lakṣmītantra*. Knowledge and the other qualities are also explained in that very same work: "The internal form 'I' is declared to be the form of knowledge."
The nature of luminosity and so forth is characterized by qualities such as those of a crystal;
therefore, the nature of that knowledge belongs to both me and Nārāyaṇa.
"That which is the unimpeded state of my arising is my supreme sovereignty;
it is called 'Icchā' (Will) by the learned in the treatises on the principles."
That state of mine which consists of the world and so forth is declared to be my Śakti;
that state of mine which consists of the void while creating is held to be my Bala.
The support of an effect is declared to be its power;
those skilled in the true nature of things say that this support consists of a portion of [the cause's] capacity.
Even though I am the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), I am always free from modification;
for water quickly abandons its own nature when it arises as curd.
Even while the world exists, that transformation does not belong to me at any time;
the absence of modification is my power—this is the opinion of those who know reality.
Vikrama is said to be valor, and it is traditionally held to be a portion of sovereignty;
for it is my lack of dependence on assistance in the performance of all undertakings.
Those who know the truth declare that *tejas* (splendor) is the sixth quality;
some describe *tejas* as the capacity for overcoming others.
"Some who are experts in the reality of that splendor employ it in sovereignty.

Thus, these five qualities are considered praises of knowledge. Now, the meaning of the mantra is stated: here at the beginning, by means of the *praṇava*, the Supreme Vāsudeva residing in the sky at the end of its resonance (*nāda*) is intended to be expressed, because he is the subject under discussion now. And so it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
This syllable *om* has arisen first as the star-like point (*bindu*);
one should subsequently adorn it with the point (*bindu*), and immediately thereafter with the resonance (*nāda*).
One should meditate upon the continuous resonance that ends in silence, which is like a stream of oil;
this indeed is that Vaiṣṇava form, the three-syllabled eternal Brahman.
Aniruddha is the letter *a* here, Pradyumna is the fifth vowel (*u*),
Saṃkarṣaṇa is the letter *m*, and Vāsudeva is the fifth [syllable].
O Lord of the Gods, that which is the undivided form of the four is the nature of Nāda;
the supreme limit of Nāda is the Supreme Goddess Ahaṃtā.
That supreme Śakti is of the nature of form, called the sky at the end of sound;
consisting of the Śabdabrahman, subtle, she is "I," pervading all.
When the resonance ceases, that which certainly becomes manifest is the light,
the supreme Brahman, whose essence is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.

"Thus has been described this supreme Vaiṣṇava abode, the Pauruṣa. Here, "quiescent-emergent" refers to the subtle form characterized by quiescent-emergent consciousness, which is to say, it is distinguished by the state of experiencing one's own self alone. For it is well known that the Lord possesses two states: the quiescent-emergent and the eternally emergent. Among these, the state called "quiescent-emergent" is the state of experiencing one's own self alone, whereas the "eternally emergent" state is the state of experiencing one's own sovereign power (*svabhūti*).

And likewise, in the *Śrīguṇaratnakośavyākhyāna*, regarding the verse "taistaiḥ kāntena śāntoditaguṇavibhavaiḥ," the two states (*daśā*) are explained [in their proper order]. However, in the *Gargakulīnarāmānujīya* commentary on the *Śrīraṅgarājastava*, regarding the verse "prathante so'nantaḥ svavaśaghanaśāntoditadaśaḥ," it is stated—in reverse order—that the state consisting of the experience of one's own manifestations and qualities is the "state of the tranquil and the emergent" (*śāntoditadaśā*), while the state consisting of the experience of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the "eternally emergent state" (*nityoditadaśā*). That [reversal] is due to negligence.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Varadarājastava*, the author himself explained as follows: "The state known as 'the tranquil and the eternally arisen' (*śāntoditadaśā*) refers respectively to the state of experiencing only one's own self, and the other [state] to the eternally arisen state. This means that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the manifestation of the fourth state (*turyavyūha*).

Just as in the passage “Consciousness performs the sacrifice” (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*), the word *vijñāna* denotes the substratum (*dharmī*), so too here it should be understood that the term denotes the Blessed Lord. He is described as such because he is the life-force of that [Vāsudeva]. The sense is that the Supreme Vāsudeva, known as the "Eternally Manifest" (*nityodita*), is the cause of the Supreme Form known as the "Peaceful-Arisen" (*śāntodita*); thus, He is its life-force. Accordingly, in the *Tattvatrayavyākhyāna*:
"From the Eternally Manifest arose Hari, who is the Peaceful-Arisen...
and this fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) is likewise due to the grace of the Supreme Lord."
That which is proclaimed as "and another" is for the sake of favoring the lay followers (upāsakas).
O Seneśa, that triad of Cāturātmyas likewise proceeds from the quiescent and the emergent; tell me that again for the sake of favoring my devotees.

"That which is designated as deep sleep (suṣupti) and dream (svapna), as well as the waking expansion (jāgrad-vyūha) and the supreme—O fortunate one, this is the fourfold nature, with the Supreme Lord as the fifth.

This refers to the All-Seeing, the Omniscient, the Consciousness, whose form is knowledge, the Vāsudeva who is higher than the highest. As stated in the Lakṣmī-tantra: "The supreme form consisting of knowledge belongs to both me and Brahmā. The meaning of the word *namaḥ* is well known: "I shall perform all kinds of service for him; I shall not perform [service] for my own sake. (33-34)

The mantra for the eye-weapon, the armor, the conch, the head, and the heart— these six are applied respectively in the sphere of meditative absorption and in the various victories over the stages [of yoga].

He explains the sequence for joining the previously mentioned qualities, such as knowledge (*jñāna*), with the limbs beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*) for the sake of accomplishing the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), starting with the words "Teja" and so forth. And thus the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Oṃ oṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Oṃ oṃ, salutation to the heart, which is knowledge). *Oṃ vijñānaprāṇāya aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā* (Oṃ, svāhā to the head, which is sovereignty, the life-force of higher knowledge). *Oṃ namaḥ śaktyai śikhāyai vauṣaṭ* (Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock, which is power). *Oṃ śāntoditabalāya kavacāya huṃ* (Oṃ, huṃ to the armor, which is the strength of the quiescent and the emergent). *Oṃ sarvadarśine vīryāya astrāya phaṭ* (Oṃ, phaṭ to the weapon, which is valor, the all-seeing one). *Oṃ caitanyāya tejase netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ* (Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes, which are splendor, the consciousness).
Thus, the fact that these mantras begin with the *praṇava* (Om) and end with the suffixes such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth, will be explained in the section on the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*:
"The *praṇava* comes first for all; then one's own name should be applied at the end. Furthermore, one's own specific suffixes (*jāti*) follow in sequence, ending with *vauṣaṭ*. (35)
Brahman, characterized by suchness, should be remembered as formless and partless;
however, regarding the first means for attaining that—namely, sacrifice, oblation, and so forth—[it is otherwise]. 36.
One should recollect [the Lord] with his form, his limbs, and surrounded by his retinue—he by whom the qualities such as knowledge have themselves been brought to manifestation. (37)

With two verses beginning with "The mantra is the object of samādhi," he explains how this aforementioned root mantra possesses both form and formlessness according to the distinction of its objects. In the context of sacrifice, oblation, and so forth—"sacrifice" (yāga) refers to the worship of the Lord through images and other media; "oblation" (homa) refers to the satiation of the fire; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the general five-fold daily ritual (pañcakālika-karma) is indicated. "In the first" means in the first among the fourfold means for attaining the Lord—namely those called karma, jñāna, bhakti, and prapatti—which is to say, in the yoga of action (karmayoga).

Out of compassion for those performing ritual acts, that mantra—though bodiless—was remembered by him for the sake of the perpetual completion of sacrifices, through the power of devotion and faith. (38)
Indeed, it certainly bestows the fruit eternally upon those whose selves are purified by that [practice];
for while the stability of the sacrifice is primary, liberation follows as a secondary consequence. (39)

For those established in *karmayoga*, since it is impossible to perform the worship of the Lord and so forth without the recollection of His form (*sākārasmarana*), the Lord Himself, out of His extraordinary compassion toward them, manifests His own form consisting of the six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). However, for yogis—according to the manner stated in the verse "those who know the Self everywhere"—He grants the fruit even when remembered without form (*nirākāra*), being satisfied by the excellence of their devotion despite that independence [from form]. This he says in the two verses beginning with "ānītāḥ" (38–39).
In that regard, know that for the purpose of pacifying those obstacles, there is the mantra-form;
however, O Mahāmati, in the case of the opposite, the mantra ends with *netra*.

Where can there be obstacles for those whose vision and sight are purified by the Path and whose minds are stilled? Their own internal splendor has been brought forth externally through their own sovereignty. (41)

With the two verses beginning with "prādhānyena," he explains that for this mantra, when the ritual action (karman) has sovereignty (aiśvarya) as its primary goal, there is the sequence ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) in the ritual applications such as the placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa), whereas when liberation (mokṣa) is the primary goal, the sequence ends with the eye-mantra (netra). Therein, in that ritual action, the meaning is: "for the sake of pacifying those obstacles which may arise"—namely, obstacles to that ritual action, to the sovereignty produced by it, and to the liberation that is its incidental consequence. Conversely, however, the meaning is: when liberation is primary and sovereignty is incidental.

For those whose path has been purified by the vision of the Netra-mantra—where "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the *Netra*-mantra, and "purified" means made holy by that vision—their path is so described. The fact that the vision of the *Netra*-mantra brings about complete purification is clearly stated in both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]: "The Lord, abiding in the form of light within the space of the heart-lotus, should be brought from that place and placed in the center of the eyes."
One should take refuge in that which was previously described as being named Vāsudeva; then, O best of sages, with a pair of fixed eyes, one should proceed.
"One should perceive the *locana-mantra* as being useful for the sacrifice;
by that, the entire collection of materials and the assembly of substances are purified. (40–41)
For by whichever mantra that [deity] is remembered as being endowed with the eyes, he is self-luminous and peerless within the heart by means of that very [mantra]. (42)
That which is white and black is to be drawn together; it arises from the designator of that.
Now, listen to the method of propitiation for this supreme mantra.

With the two verses beginning with *svakam*, [the author] explains that mantras whose power is manifest externally are accompanied by words denoting that power, whereas those whose power is hidden within are devoid of such words. Thus, it should be understood that mantras lacking words denoting power possess only five limbs (*pañcāṅga*). As it is said in the section on the worship of Garuḍa in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*:
"O best of sages, the Gāruḍa mantra is known as 'five-syllabled' (*pañcākṣara*);
its five limbs are formed by the syllables together with the nasal bindu, according to the preceding [prescribed order]."

However, in the *Pārameśvaravyākhyāna*, on the occasion of commenting upon this verse, it is stated: "In this context, this five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) mantra is established for the *Pādma* and *Sātvata* [tantras], while the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are [established] by themselves; furthermore, regarding the function of the eyes, the heart-seed (*hṛdbīja*) is prescribed for the five limbs. This is inconsistent, because in the *Śrīsātvata*, neither this five-syllable *Garuḍa* mantra nor any discussion of its limbs is found.

Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of an explicit examination of the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Garuḍa-mantra, its sixfold nature (*ṣaḍaṅgatva*) is established because it is stated there—"The heart-seed (*hṛdbīja*) is prescribed for the rite of the eyes among the five limbs"—and thus, by joining the heart-seed to the general five-limbed mantra, its sixfold nature is proven. For if a sixfold nature were possible through the addition of the heart-seed, the statement in the *Sātvata*—namely, "of the five limbs"—would not be tenable at all.

Furthermore, in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, the statement that the Garuḍa-mantra possesses only five ancillaries (*pañcāṅga*) without mentioning its sixfold nature (*ṣaḍaṅgatva*) would not be consistent. Therefore, listen attentively to this for that purpose: [the application] "of the five ancillary mantras" (the word "in initiation and so forth" is understood as the remainder). Regarding the "eye-rite" (*netrakarma*), which is the rite to be performed with the Eye-mantra: "one should cook [it], having looked [at it] with the Root-mantra and consecrated it with the Eye-mantra.
Thus, one should also remember the attainment of its fruit through the Armor-mantra (*varman*) and its state of dissolution (*layatva*).
"Then one should bring about complete satisfaction for the eye by means of that very [mantra] and its placement.

In such passages as these, the *hṛdbīja* (heart-seed syllable) is prescribed. The sense is that because there is no *netrabīja* (eye-seed syllable) for the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*), one should employ the *hṛdbīja* in its place. In exactly the same way, since there is an absence of general limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) for mantras that lack limbs (*niraṅga*), it is stated in the *Sātvata* that the *praṇava* (syllable Om) should be employed in the rites to be accomplished by them: "But for mantras lacking limbs, [one should use the *praṇava*] in the rites prescribed for the limb-mantras."
"The Praṇava should be employed together with the word 'karma'.
It should be understood that by this much alone, it is not established that those [mantras] with five limbs possess six limbs, nor that those without limbs possess limbs. (42-43)
O one with stainless eyes, having attained the state that exists both externally and internally,
he is bathed, his impurities removed, wearing pure garments, and his senses conquered.

Having thus stated the nature of the mantra up to this point, he says "Now" (atha) to indicate: "Listen hereafter to the method of worship. This means the mental worship as well as both external and internal worship, which exist in their outer and inner states. || 44 ||

Restraining his speech, having first worshipped the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) together with the Discus (Cakra) standing at the entrance with flowers, darbha grass, and other offerings, he should enter the abode of the Blessed One.

First, he states the rules for the worshiper’s bathing and so forth with the verse beginning "paricyuta-": "One whose internal impurities have been removed" means one who has eliminated inner stains through rising during the *brāhmamuhūrta*, meditating on the Lord, chanting His names, and so on; "one whose external impurities have been removed" means one who has eliminated outer stains through purification, ritual sipping (*ācamana*), brushing the teeth, and so forth. "Bathed" means having performed purification—either individually or by combining all of these—to the best of one's ability: namely, the divine (*divya*), the aqueous (*āpya*), the mantra-born (*māntra*), the aerial (*vāyavya*), the earthly (*bhauma*), the fiery (*taijasa*), and the mental (*mānasa*) baths.

Having performed the bath according to the method thus described—the specific modes of performing these [rituals] should be consulted in the *Pārameśvara* and other such texts—although the water-bath (*audakas-nāna*) mentioned in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and elaborated upon in the *Pārameśvara* is indeed acceptable, nevertheless, it has been determined in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* that as long as there exists a tradition for performing the bath and other rites according to one's own *sūtra*, one must not abandon that and adopt another. By the phrase "having bathed" (*atra snātaḥ*), the application of the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), which is of the nature of an earthen bath (*pārthivas-nāna*), is also included; furthermore, the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and so forth are implied by this. By the phrase "wearing clean garments" (*śuddhavāsāḥ*)...
Adorned with perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and upper garments,
as well as with earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and rings.
Thus the meaning of these [verses] has been summarized. By the phrase "one who has conquered the senses" (*jitendriya*), "approaching" (*abhigamana*) is indicated; for [it is said]:
"By means of recitation, meditation, worship, and hymns, conjoined with action, speech, and mind..."

"One should approach the source of the world; that is known as *abhigamana* (approaching). By this statement regarding *abhigamana*, the conquest of the senses (*indriyajaya*) is accomplished. By the phrase "with flowers, darbha grass, etc.," the act of taking up the materials (*upādāna*) is indicated. By the statement "having first worshipped the Lord of Birds together with the Discus standing at the front of the gate," the preeminence of these two as the chief guardians of all the gates is signaled. For this very reason, even while Caṇḍa and the others are vigilant, it is said in both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]: "Having stationed there for the sake of protection the Discus and the Lord of Birds."

Furthermore, even in the section concerning the worship at the door of the sacrificial hall, it is stated regarding the inability to worship Caṇḍa and the others: "Or he may worship the Lord, the protector of birds, together with them at all the doors. And the location for worship is clearly stated in that very same place, beginning with: "One should meditate upon Garuḍa, radiant as gold, at the front of the door," and continuing:

"One should contemplate him, who is the presiding deity of the vital breath, situated within the circle of offerings (balimaṇḍala) in the center of the wheel, possessing the form of Puruṣa with all his limbs."

In a place where there is no *balimaṇḍala*, worship is said to be performed with cow-dung and other materials prepared immediately; or, if one remains in that very spot, one should worship there in a mentally constructed *balimaṇḍala*.
Indeed, one should worship the entire retinue, beginning with Khageśa (Garuḍa), along with Acyuta (Viṣṇu). Thus it is said.
At this juncture, the worship of the door-keepers of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should also be performed. This will be stated right here in the section of the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*:

"Having bathed, with his hair tied, observing silence, wearing clean garments, and holding the arghya and flowers, he should perform the worship of the door-keepers and so forth, and then sit upon his seat."

This very point is further elaborated regarding the Lord (Īśvara) as well: "Having worshipped the Vāstupuruṣa and the others in due order," and "one should enter the abode of the Blessed One. In this context, the division of the door for the Lord is stated for the purpose of entering the interior of the temple: "Then, having mentally divided the door into three parts, one should again divide that middle part into two."
"Then, having distinguished [the space] with the left side and the right foot, one should enter within very slowly... Thus it is said.

Furthermore, many other specific details required here and there have been collected in the *Īśvara-pratyabhijñā* and the *Parameśvara-tantra*, which serve as supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to this [text], and these should be adopted. (44–45)
Having placed all that great sacrificial equipment which was previously acquired on the right side, one should place the water-pot on the left.
One should place a *bhadrāsana* in the center of [the vessel] filled with strained water;
it may be made of clay, wood, or stone, and should have one, two, or three joints.
It may be four-cornered, or eight-cornered, or perhaps ten-thousand-cornered;
it is endowed with four legs and marked by four enclosures.
The water-spout with a crocodile mouth is characterized by its specific proportions;
it should be situated below that, either on the north side or fixed upon the surface of the earth. (49)
One should prepare a well-characterized water-vessel marked with the conch and the discus;
then, having sat down upon a seat made of darbha grass, wood, or an animal skin.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the supreme mantra;
first, one should place it undivided upon the head like the heat of the sun.
Thereafter, one should assign [the mudrās] according to their distinct characteristics by way of pervasion,
from the two thumbs up to the two little fingers.

One should assign the five limbs, beginning with knowledge (jñāna) and ending with vigor (vīrya), as pervasive [throughout the body] like the root-mantra; and the eye [mantra] should be placed on the upward-pointing fingers.
Then, one should contemplate the mantra within the body from the aperture of Brahmā down to the feet;
thereafter, knowledge resides in the heart, for it is there that [the mantra] is manifested.
O lotus-eyed one, whether it be worldly or pertaining to the ultimate reality, sovereignty resides everywhere above the region of the head. (55)
The king of mantras, Śakti, resides in the upward-pointing flame of the fire within the heart;
likewise, the strength of all the limbs is situated there along with the vital air (vāyu).

One should place that vigor which pervades all limbs into the two hands—that which is the nature of internal consciousness and which brings about the cessation of the darkness of material nature. (57)
At the time of ritual placement (nyāsa), the fire element is merged into the fiery locus;
[this occurs] within the body, which is like an ancient temple of the gods, possessing four wheels and nine gates.

It should be understood that this instruction on the placement of the *bhadrāsana* is intended either for the purpose of placing mobile icons (*bimba*) and the like upon it, or for the purpose of performing worship there even without such icons. As for fixed icons, their pedestal (*pīṭha*) is installed at the very time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

He describes the procedure for the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), preceded by sitting upon one’s own seat, with the words beginning "Then, having sat down" (*athopaviśya*). Although the performance of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) prior to this placement, as well as the placement of ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth after the mantra-placement, are not explicitly mentioned here, they are to be understood according to the method that will be described in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. (50–58)
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and relying upon that which is called the mantra, one should cause the group of senses situated externally to become stilled within the mind. (59)

Having first deposited the mantras in one's own body—which is endowed with the four wheels (cakras) of the foundation, navel, heart, and throat, and possessed of nine gates—with the realization that it is a temple of the Lord, one should also maintain the conceit of divinity within oneself according to the maxim: "One who is not a god should not worship a god. Thus he says, "the four wheels. The meaning is that one should assume the pride of being the Lord of Mantras (*mantranātha*) within oneself; as it will be stated later: "One should contemplate, 'I am the God. This has also been clearly stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "I am that Blessed Viṣṇu; I am Nārāyaṇa, Hari."
For I am Vāsudeva, the all-pervading, the abode of beings, and the stainless one.
"O Sage, having thus acquired such a very firm ego-sense," so it is said. || 59 ||
Having cast the mind into the intellect, and that intellect into the sphere of knowledge,
one should indeed perform action through the cultivation of knowledge for the sake of the ultimate truth.

Now, while teaching the mental sacrifice (*mānasika-yāga*), he describes the internal restraint of the external senses and so forth for the sake of accomplishing the uninterrupted cultivation of the Lord’s wisdom, using the verse beginning with *manasi* (along with a half-verse). Thus, it has been stated in the *Lakṣmītantra* that action performed through such cultivation of wisdom possesses the nature of pure being (*śuddhasattvamayatva*), whereas external action—being composed of the three qualities (*triguṇamaya*)—requires purification:
"One should perform all rites mentally, through the meditative absorption of wisdom (*jñānasamādhi*)."
Whatever action is performed with knowledge through absorption in Brahman,
that becomes composed of pure being, inexhaustible, and eternal.
Since external defects— those of the *rajas* and *tamas* qualities— are dependent upon material objects,
their purification must likewise be accomplished through action, mind, and speech.
Therefore,
having firmly established that pure knowledge which is entirely free from defect, permeated by meditative cultivation, and arisen from consciousness;
"One should indeed perform action that is ultimate through the cultivation of knowledge. (59-60)

In ancient times, within this divine abode of the body—possessing four wheels and nine gates—the lotus situated at the base of the throat-pit was indeed mounted upon its stalk and facing downwards. (61)
In the center of that forest of pericarp-roots, there is that which has grown with its face upward;
above that, however, resides the manifestation of sound, characterized by the sun, the moon, and fire.

In order to determine the location within one's own heart where the Lord is manifested, he first describes the abode of the Śabdabrahman with two verses beginning with "catuḥ-". The phrase "that which has grown upon the hollow of the throat" refers to the heart-lotus that arises from the region of the throat-hollow and faces downward; it is understood that this heart-lotus has grown and arisen in the middle of the forest of its pericarp. "Above that" means in the middle of the cavity formed by those two lotuses, specifically above the lower lotus.
The manifestation of sound, characterized by the sun, moon, and fire, and having the nature of light, exists as the Śabdabrahman; this is the meaning. || 61-62 ||
O Mahāmati, that channel which is radiant with three lights and whose form is unmanifest sound exists clearly above the triad of wheels.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), she went beyond the path of the sun;
then, piercing the netherworld (pātāla) by way of the gateway of the wind, she reached her proper domain.
Every relationship whose object is volition is established within it, just as a cluster of gems is strung upon a thread; therefore, it is known as the central channel (madhyamā nāḍī). 65.
But within that aforementioned locus of the target, indeed inside that very [space],
there is a casket known as the Moon and the Sun, characterized by closing and opening.
There, resting upon the sun and the lotus, dwells the supreme Vāgbhramarī,
who is the power (śakti) that gives birth to all mantras, belonging to the pervasive Lord whose nature is peace.
Resounding with a sound born of its own color, that which is remembered as the Śabdabrahman begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *ha*,
assuming the form of a continuous stream of syllables.

Having thus described the state of Śabdabrahman in brief, he further elucidates that very same point through six verses beginning with "tridīpti," preceded by a description of the nature of the Suṣumnā channel. Its luminosity consisting of three lights is due to its being the substratum of Śabdabrahman, which consists of the three-fold fire (tejas). Having the unmanifest sound as its body—unmanifest sound being Śabdabrahman—it is said: "Indeed, by my own power, in the form of Śabdabrahman, I myself arise from the Supreme Lord for the liberation of all living beings."

"Know that to be the unmanifest syllable (avyaktākṣara), like an indistinct sound on a lute string"—thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*. She whose form is such [is described as] "tathoktā. Above the three wheels—shining above the triad of the *ādhāra*, *nābhi*, and *kaṇṭha* wheels—she has emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and gone beyond the path of the sun; having pierced the netherworld (*pātāla*) by way of the gate of the vital air (*vāyu*), she has reached her own domain. The meaning is that she pervades from the root to the tip, reaching to the very end.

For this very reason, everything that is the object of the Lord’s volition becomes established in connection with the *suṣumnā* channel, like a cluster of jewels on a string; therefore, it is known and celebrated as the "Middle Channel" (*madhyamā nāḍī*). Within that, at the aforementioned focal point—meaning, at the location of the heart-lotus—it [is situated].

The two known as the Moon and the Sun are characterized by closing and opening—that is, distinguished by the acts of closing and opening. When the upper lotus is closed, it is designated as the "Moon"; when [the lower lotus] is distinguished by the act of opening, it is designated as the "Sun. In that "casket" (saṃpuṭa)—meaning the casket formed by the two lotuses—the term "solar" (ārkam) refers to the lower lotus associated with the Sun.

Having taken as an object and having resorted to [it], there is another, subtle *vāgbhramarī*—the bee that is speech itself, which abides. He qualifies her: that *vāgbhramarī* is the mother of all mantras; by the phrase "of the tranquil-souled, subtle, supreme one," it means she is the power (*śakti*) of the all-pervading Lord (*vibhu*), and thus she too is likewise subtle. That which begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *ha*—from *a* to *ha*—which bears the form of a continuous stream, like an unbroken stream of oil, is the *nāda* known as Śabdabrahman; they sound forth that *nāda* born of the phonemes (*varṇaja*). In this very way, the nature of *nāda* is also described in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
But it proceeds in many ways for the sake of stability through the nature of distinct colors.
This [Self], whose nature is the subtle phonemes, assumes the form of a continuous stream [of sound] for the discerning one who is established in Me and liberated from the sheath of the five paths.
"He attains the state of direct experience through the grace of the Supreme Self.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the nature of the power of speech (*vākśakti*) as she utters such a sound is described in that very same place:
"I am the Supreme (*parā*), whose essence is light and bliss, and the progenitor of all mantras."
Power is the mother of all sounds, free from rising and setting.
"That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, known by the name Nārāyaṇa—my state called 'quiescence' (śāntatā) is that very quiescence from which the entire universe is born. (Verses 63–68)
In the sky at the end of the sound (nāda), the Lord, accompanied by Ananta, is peaceful, consisting of the nature of pure consciousness, and desirous of bestowing grace upon his devotees. (69)
Indeed, with a body beyond compare, he who was formless attained a physical form;
nourishing the entire universe with a splendor equal to ten million full moons.
He is endowed with two hands that grant boons and fearlessness, marked by the conch and the discus, and skilled in uplifting the three worlds.
Just as the sun is accompanied by its rays and the ocean by its waves,
so too [the Lord] is accompanied by his own forms, both with form and without form, such as Acyuta and the others.
His limbs and body were changeless, yet he was filled with all kinds of radiant ornaments that were formless and abounding in waves of nectar.

Having thus described the abiding of the Śabdabrahman within the heart-lotus, he describes the nature of the radiant Supreme Brahman at its conclusion with five verses beginning with *nādāvasāne*.
