The phrase "at the end of sound in the void" (*nādāvasānagagane*) means as follows: among the four states of the Śabdabrahman—known as Nāda, Bindu, Madhyamā, and Vaikhari—the first state is characterized by the previously mentioned definition. Its "end" (*avasāna*) is its ultimate limit; the "void" (*gagana*) therein refers to the Power whose nature is the void (*gaganātmikā śaktiḥ*). Thus, it is said in the Lakṣmītantra: "That which is the supreme limit of Sound is the Supreme Goddess Ahaṃtā."
That power is supreme and subtle, called the sky at the end of sound;
composed of the Word-Brahman, subtle, and all-pervading, she is I.
"When the resonance (nāda) comes to rest, that which certainly becomes manifest is the Light, the Supreme Brahman, whose essence is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.

Regarding the phrase "marked with the conch and discus," it should be understood here that the two hands are marked by the mere lines in the form of the conch and discus; for otherwise, even the possession of the Varada and Abhaya mudrās by the two hands alone would not be possible. Thus it is further elaborated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
The Lord God is all-pervading, out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
He possesses a supreme form that is incomparable and indescribable,
which nourishes the entire universe with a splendor equal to ten million full moons.
With two arms, lotus-like eyes, and hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
he holds a discus and a conch shell formed of lines upon his two palms.
It is marked [with the signs], situated upon feet free from change, supremely beautiful,
and adorned with its own six qualities, neither deficient nor excessive.
He was symmetrical with well-proportioned limbs, beautiful in every part,
and adorned with brilliant ornaments that resembled the surging waves of nectar.
This single divine form, known as the Supreme Vaiṣṇavī, is indeed the highest; it is immutable, consisting of its own formless rays [of light] such as Acyuta and others.

"Those perfected in yoga worship Her, who is established in the heart as the state of the Fourth (turyapada). Regarding the phrase "accompanied by His own forms beginning with Acyuta," it should be understood that there are three forms beginning with Acyuta. This is stated in the *Pārameśvara-tantra*, in the chapter on installation (*pratiṣṭhādhyāya*):
"And likewise [of Him] who is the single seed-nature of the entire universe..."
"Of the all-pervading Vāsudeva, whose essential nature is eternally risen, and likewise of his three manifestations, Acyuta and the others. Thus it is said.
And in this way, it should be understood that Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha themselves have the alternative names Acyuta, Satya, and Puruṣa. Now, [one might object]:...
And then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [he beheld] the Puruṣa, who is Truth and the Infallible.
Those who know the Vaikhānasa scriptures call me Aniruddha;
but others, O King, the followers of the Pāñcarātra, understand me in this way.
O king of kings, they declare Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha to be the fourfold form.

Thus, it is observed that Vāsudeva and the others are denoted by such terms as *puruṣa*. If it is asked, "How have you explained the denotation of Aniruddha and the others by terms such as *puruṣa* in reverse order?", [the answer is: True; there is no contradiction with our own explanation because we have stated that such usage exists among the Vaikhānasas. Furthermore, the fact that Aniruddha and the others are denoted by terms such as *puruṣa* will be stated right here in the fifth chapter, in the section on the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*), in the passage beginning with "on the occasion of dissolution" (*apyayāvasare*).

Thus, even though in this supreme state (parātparadaśā) there is the presence of [the forms] beginning with Acyuta, it should be understood that Vāsudeva alone holds primacy, because of the predominance of that single form therein.

If it is asked, "In that case, why is there not a predominance of the fourfold manifestation (caturmūrti) of the Fourth Array (turyavyūha), which has the alternative names 'the Tranquil' (śānta) and 'the Arisen' (udita)?"—the answer is no; for, according to what will be stated later, "The primordial form exists non-differently, like the seed of a banyan tree," that array known as the Supreme (para) is non-different from Vāsudeva and the others who are beyond the supreme (parātpara).

For this very reason, just as in the case of the groupings such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, since no specific mantras denoting those groupings are mentioned individually, and because its purpose is fulfilled by the mantra of the "beyond-the-beyond" (*parātpara*) alone, one should understand that even in the state of "the beyond" (*para*), Vāsudeva alone is primary, just as he is in the state of "beyond-the-beyond. If it is then asked: "If they are thus non-different, by what means is there a distinction between the two?"—it should be understood that the distinction lies in their being "eternally arisen" (*nityodita*). "Being eternally arisen" means being characterized by the state of experiencing one's own manifestation (*vibhūti*). "Being [merely] tranquil yet arisen" (*śāntodita*) means being characterized by the state of experiencing only one's own self.

If it is objected that, in this way, even when there is a predominance of a single form within the arrangement of the quiescent and the arisen, the natural fitness (*svārasya*) of the term "manifestation" (*vyūha*) is not possible, it is replied: must the predominance of all four be accepted merely because of the word "manifestation"? If that were so, the term "manifestation" would indeed remain applicable even in the state of being higher than the highest (*parātparatva*).

For instance, in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras], within the section on the worship of Garuḍa, it says: "Of the eternally manifest (*nityodita*) manifestation (*vyūha*), as well as of the tranquil-and-manifest (*śāntodita*). Furthermore, in the section defining the characteristics of the Siddhānta, it says: "Wherein the most tranquil manifestation is immediately followed by the tranquil-and-manifest. And in the *Pratiṣṭhā* chapter of the *Pārameśvara*: "Of the Supreme Fourfold Self, who is higher than the highest;
of the manifestations such as the Tranquil-and-Manifest; and of the entire [pantheon] beginning with Keśava..."
And likewise, [it is the cause] of the entire world, which has the nature of a single seed.
Of the all-pervading Vāsudeva, whose nature is eternally manifest,
and likewise of his three manifestations, Acyuta and the others.
Regarding the Supreme One who possesses four aspects (*caturātman*) and whose nature is both quiescent (*śānta*) and emergent (*udita*):

thus, wherever there is the designation "higher than the highest" (*parātparatva*), in the state of being eternally emergent (*nityoditatva*) there is the designation "supremacy" (*paratva*), and in the state of being both quiescent and emergent there is the presence of the fourfold self consisting of Vāsudeva and the others; therefore, the terms "manifestation" (*vyūha*) and "fourfold self" (*cāturātmya*) are quite natural [in this context]. However, even in the two states of supremacy, Vāsudeva alone holds primacy; there is only one mantra, and by its worship alone, the worship of the others—who are subordinate—is accomplished. This and other such points should be understood. (Verses 69–73)
Then, one should visualize Gaṅgā descending from the center of the lotus in the sky situated above, onto the head of the Blessed One, by means of that nectar-water.
One should indeed perform the auspicious visualization of all enjoyments, beginning with the *arghya*;
by means of these, one should gradually gratify the Primordial God who abides in the Fourth State (*turyapada*). (75)

He explains the method of meditating on the descent of the Gaṅgā for the purpose of preparing the *arghya* and other offerings with the verse beginning "Then" (tataḥ), which consists of one and a half lines. The phrase "situated above the sun-lotus" (*ūrdhvasthādityabja*) is a qualification; it means [the Gaṅgā is situated] within the cavity of the two heart-lotuses, specifically the upper lotus. In the reading "situated above" (*ūrdhvasthitām*), it is quite clear that this is a qualification of the Gaṅgā. He will explain this matter in detail in the section on the *nṛsiṃhakalpa*, in the chapter concerning the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*). Regarding the preparation of the seat (*pīṭhakalpana*) required here, he will explain it in the *nṛsiṃhakalpa*: "Then, preceded by the *praṇava*, together with one's own name and a salutation..."

One should first arrange the seat ending with fire (vahni) according to the remaining [prescribed] order; then, having thus ascended, one should perform the mental visualization of that very [seat] within one's own heart. Thus [ends verses 74–75].
Having uttered the two *praṇavas*, [one should say]: "May the Supreme Lord be pleased with me.
Then, when the principle of the *karmātman* has fulfilled its purpose, the Lord remains, having dissolved his own form—that which is eternally manifest.

Regarding the propitiation of the Blessed One with *arghya* and other offerings, he states the mantra for each with the words "by those" (*taih*). The meaning is that [the mantra] is established in the first of the three forms known as Paravyūha, Vibhava, and Āvibhava; it is situated in the fourth state (*turyapada*) for the sake of purifying the four states known as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth. The definition of the objects of the waking and other states is clearly explained in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth—this is the tetrad."
The nature of the path of the waking state is to be known as the sequence of the external senses,
occurring when the power of the external senses has been overcome by *tamas*.
That modification of the internal organ which remains as a residual impression is to be known as dream; in the absence of that [modification], there is deep sleep.
When the activity of the external and internal organs has ceased for the wise man who abides in *sattva* and is not overcome by *tamas*, [the state of liberation is attained].
The continuum of one whose nature is pure being is designated as the "Fourth";
thus has this fourfold path been explained in these words.
"Excluding the fourth [state], one resorts to the impure states beginning with deep sleep.

In this context, because it occurs in the section on the worship of the Supreme Lord (Para-Bhagavān), this mantra contains the word *para*: "Oṃ Oṃ, may the Supreme Lord be pleased with me. However, in the sections on the worship of the Vyūhas and so forth, the word *vyūha* or similar terms should be substituted in place of the word *para*. Alternatively, for universal application, any one of the names Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, or Viṣṇu may be used. Accordingly, the Lakṣmītantra states: "Saying, 'Oṃ Oṃ, may the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva be pleased. In this case, only the basic mantra for propitiation (*prīti-mantra*) has been stated.

The mantra for the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and the mantra for the offering of enjoyment (*bhoga-dāna*) must also be obtained from elsewhere, as they are required for the presentation of each enjoyment; for this reason, all three mantras are indispensable. Thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"The resolve, the offering, and the gratification—these are the three [sets of] three."
"One should perform [the offering] in all enjoyments, taking into account the place, time, and other factors.

For this very reason, the mantra for the granting of enjoyment (*bhogadāna*) spoken by the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* has been included here in the section on the worship of Sudarśana within the *Īśvarasaṃhitā*, which is an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the *Sāttvata-tantra*. However, the mantra of formal resolve (*saṃkalpamantra*) is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Then, with a concentrated mind and having formed the *añjali* gesture, one says: 'Oṃ Bhagavan...'"
Having said, "I shall honor [you] with a seat," one should then offer the seat.
Thus [ends verses 75–76].

Thus, when the mental worship has been accomplished, the Lord Himself—withdrawing His own manifested form out of a desire to bestow grace upon His devotees—reabsorbs that form which was made manifest according to the method to be described later: "The primordial form exists non-differently, like the seed of a banyan tree," characterized by the mere qualities (guṇamātra) of the unmanifest. He says "Now" (atha) [to introduce this]. He will state the same further on as well: "But the dismissal (visarjana) is to be understood as occurring when the sequence of rites is completed. || 76 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the second chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya—the ornament of the Mauñjyāyana lineage and worshiper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The Third Chapter.
Nārada said:
O lords of sages, the Lord of the World spoke again in the course of conversation.
The supreme propitiation of the other, the fourfold Self, is as previously described. || 1 ||
Now the third [chapter] will be explained.
The fourfold nature (cāturātmya) is threefold within the triad of states beginning with deep sleep;
it is clearly manifest in that state [of waking], while in the fourth state it stands as the supreme, characterized by its qualities.

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa instructs [Saṃkarṣaṇa] on the worship of the Vyūha residing in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), following up on that context. This is because the Turya-vyūha—which is non-manifest (*avyakta*), characterized solely by its qualities (*guṇamātra-lakṣya*), non-different from the Supreme as will be stated in the passage "established as non-different from the form of the Self like a banyan seed"—was already mentioned previously along with the Supreme Lord, who resides in the Turya-state, in the verse "accompanied by His own forms, Acyuta and the others, which are themselves formless.
Therefore, he says "again" (*punar*). || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:

One should worship that Unborn [Lord] in the lotus-stamen of the letter *Ha*, at the level below known as deep sleep (*suṣupti*), according to the fourfold sequence called "origination" (*prabhava*). || 2 ||
Understand how that occurs through the fourfold knowledge and science:
the Blessed One, whose form is permeated by Brahman, exists as the knower. (3)
Standing in the center of the pericarp like a pillar, it becomes an object of knowledge for the sake of its own assistance to those performers of ritual action who sacrifice to Brahman.

"Listen to the sequence of worship for the *suṣupti-vyūha*," he says with the verse beginning "The letter *ha*. Since the heart-lotus consists of the letters beginning with *a*, it should be understood that its pericarp (*karṇikā*) is of the nature of the letter *ha*. Thus, he will state in the fifth chapter: "O Great-minded One, that lotus which is the eternal support of all, whose root is the letter *a*, rests upon the letter *kṣa* in the lake of Ananta."

"Having the letters as its stalk and all remaining phonemes as its leaves"—thus [it is described]. This refers to that which consists of such a pericarp (*karṇikā*). The meaning is that it is situated below the previously mentioned fourth state, which is of the nature of space (*gagana*). In the state called deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is a fourfold manifestation through the divisions beginning with Vāsudeva; this means by the sequence known as "origination," that is, the order of emanation. That is to say, from Vāsudeva down to Aniruddha. "Learn the procedure for how one should worship that unborn, supreme Blessed One (*bhagavant*) previously mentioned, by means of the fourfold knowledge-vidyās, namely the four mantras to be described."

In this context, because the multiplicity of the one Supreme Lord is established through the distinctions of Vāsudeva and others in the various abodes such as the Fourth State (turya) and so forth, the statement "one should worship Him who is unborn" expresses non-duality. For it will be said: "O Mahāmati, just as the sun, though being only one, appears to possess multiplicity by depending upon various receptacles of water while remaining in the sky."
Thus, although the Blessed One is one, he attains plurality by resting upon various mantras and within the states beginning with the fourth (turya). || 2-3 ||
I am that supreme Brahman, free from the known and the knower, imperishable,
whose nature is light that never sets, and which is non-different from all.

Having been told this, [the Lord] says in the verse beginning with "vedakatvena" (along with the following half-verse) that, because [this reality] is unfathomable to those who perform ritual actions (karmins), for their benefit the Blessed One himself, remaining within the center of the previously mentioned pericarp of the heart-lotus, assumes the state of being the knower in the form of the Śabdabrahman and the state of being the object of knowledge in his supreme form. || 3-4 ||
From the eastern part up to the northern,
O wielder of the plow, the supreme Lord Vāsudeva divides himself by means of his own self through the differentiation of qualities.

Furthermore, he states "from the eastern part" (prāgbhāgāt) [verse 5], explaining that the same [deity] there becomes fourfold in the four directions, beginning with the east, according to the distinction of qualities.

But with his own nature unobscured, he abides in the eastern quarter through knowledge consisting of the six qualities; then, in the southern quarter, he abides through knowledge indeed augmented by power.
By means of His sovereignty and valor, the Supreme Lord abides in the western quarter;
by means of His splendor and power, He is established in the northern quarter.
He states the detailed explanation of their distinction of qualities with two verses beginning with "anujjhita": || 6-7 ||
Although the Blessed One is formless, consisting of manifestations and characterized by qualities,
even so, his form has been figuratively attributed to him here as was previously stated.
But on the two auspicious palms of the second form,
there was a clearly manifest conch made of lines, and a large plow was likewise very distinct.
The right hand of the third is marked with a beautiful arrow;
that of the fourth is likewise marked with an excellent sword, and both hands of the fifth are marked with conch shells.

Since this *suṣupti-vyūha* has the nature of the previously mentioned *turya-vyūha*, it is characterized solely by its qualities (*guṇa*); nevertheless, because there exist differences in the wheels (*cakra*) and other marks (*lāñchana*), just as there are differences in the qualities, he says "even though" (*yadyapi*) in three verses [8–10] that the form described by others is also figuratively attributed (*upacaryate*) here.
With his face turned downwards by the power of his hands and upwards by his own nature,
he attained manifestation through these very characteristics.

However, he states the distinction of all four as being merely having downward-facing hands and upward-facing faces, without possessing the *varada* and *abhaya* mudrās like those of the other forms, by saying "downward-facing" (*avāṅmukha*). || 11 ||
Indeed, it establishes the persistence of the practitioner’s state within this array (vyūha), due to its similarity, its possession of six qualities, and especially its equality. || 12 ||
Because it is peaceful and partless, no distinction exists;
although I previously spoke of it by means of pairs of qualities, [it remains one]. (13)
Although each individual form of the Blessed One is primary in its own right,
there nevertheless remains a quartet of qualities that is established as a collective whole.
One should always cultivate the continuity of each of these;
having thus understood the state of Brahman, which consists of one's own bliss and is characterized by vibration. (15)

Thus, even though [the object] is made manifest by means of marks and so forth, because there is no difference [from the original] due to reasons such as similarity, it becomes an object of experience for the perceiver; this is what he states with the words "etāvatā" (by this much). || 11-15 ||
He who, with a concentrated mind and pure intellect, worships with enjoyments consisting of the nectar of Brahman, enters the stainless state at the end of the body.

In this regard, it has been stated that all four [means] possess six qualities. With the verse beginning with "evam" (15–16), he describes the fruit of worship performed preceded by knowledge, which is itself conjoined with power.
Now, listen to the fourfold mantra which expresses the sixfold attributes of Brahman; it eternally bestows liberation upon those engaged in ritual action, as previously indicated. (17)
"Listen to the fourfold array of deep sleep," he said, beginning with the word "now. || 17 ||
Having first taken the seed-syllable situated at the eye,
one should thereafter place it below that [previous syllable], prior to the eleventh spoke, starting from the navel.
The third phoneme of the rim (nemi) is this third syllable;
the second [syllable] is from the eighth phoneme of the hub (nābhi), conjoined with the fourth vowel and so forth.
Then, know that the ninth [syllable] belongs to Nemi and is the fifth [vowel] alone;
the syllable following the eighth is joined with the second vowel. (20)
One should know this as the sixth; the seventh is beyond the tenth.
Then, having taken from the second tenth, one should place it above. (21)
From the eighth [mantra], this group of eight belongs to the second [mantra].
Then, the first letter from the second [mantra] and the one following the eighth from that same [second mantra]; ||| 22 ||
The second [circle] is endowed with eleven [spokes] starting from the rim;
the third rim is likewise pure, starting from the eleventh [spoke] of the first.
First from the rim, and then from the nave, one marked with eleven;
then taking the sixth from the rim, it stands above that fifth.
Then, O Mahāmati, having taken the second [part] alone from the rim— which was joined as the second to the hub and as the third to the rim— [he should proceed].
After that, one should join the four-syllabled word "namo bhagavate" for the agent;
this mantra is declared to consist of twenty-one syllables. || 26 ||
It remains undivided by the distinction of words, yet it indeed becomes one syllable more;
the first word consists of the preceding letter, while the second consists of five syllables. (27)
The third consists of six syllables, and the fourth is likewise;
know, O Great-minded One, that the fifth has two syllables, and the sixth is the same. (28)
Now, furthermore, learn this second great mantra, by knowing which there shall be no further rebirth for the worshiper. (29)
Having taken the syllable situated in the middle, which is preceded by the navel (nābhi), and then that which follows it;
first, the rim (nemi) of that very [syllable] should be joined with the thirteenth navel.
The second syllable from the other [second], the word for the Self of all powers;
the second syllable from the twelfth, and then the first from the second.
Know that the fifth [set] consists of these three alone from among those situated outside;
and the second [set] is derived from the eighth, conjoined with the eleventh from the center.
The eighteen-syllable mantra consists of the word "namo namaḥ" joined with [the deity's name].
Of this, the first part is a single syllable, and immediately following that is a three-syllable word. (33)
The third [part] consists of six syllables, while the fourth consists of four syllables;
the second is proclaimed to have two syllables, and the other belongs to the two feet. (34)
Now, O best among those who know mantras, I shall declare the third mantra, by knowing which one attains the supreme mental purity regarding ritual actions. (35)
Taking the seed-syllable situated in the center, then the first from the eleventh [letter],
then the third from the rim (nemi), below that, and above that, indeed the one following the hub (nābhi).
Then, one should take the first letter from the eighth [group], joined with the second vowel;
likewise, one should gather another, the first letter from the eleventh [group]. (37)
The tenth syllable and the eighth syllable from the end of the *nemi* [mantra], joined with the second syllable of the *nābhi*, constitute the first syllable of the *nemi*. || 38 ||
Taking the syllable following the tenth, which is endowed with the three *nābhis*, and joining it with the ninth letter from the second, which is likewise followed by a *nābhi*. (39)
The tenth [digit] is purified by that number; then, from the exterior, the fifth;
the second from the rim (nemi); and below that, it is joined with what is beyond the nave (nābhi).
One should extract the second syllable from the tenth letter as a three-syllabled word for *prāṇa*;
then, one should likewise take the first syllable from the eleventh, taken alone. (41)
Then, the second [part] is joined with the hub (nābhi), and the third belongs to the rim (nemi);
thereafter, another part is provided with thirteen hubs in the outermost [sections].
Above the third *nemi*, one should place another [mark] beyond the ninth;
then, from the circle of the first *nemi* up to the navel, it should be joined with the second [mark].
Now, the second [mantra] is indeed external, consisting solely of a salutation;
this king of mantras is endowed with twenty-three syllables.
Now their classification according to the previously mentioned number of feet is also stated:
know that the first has one syllable, while the second has nine syllables. (45)
The third is indeed two syllables, and the fourth is remembered as three syllables;
then the one situated above has six syllables, and immediately after that is one of two syllables.
Now learn from me as I speak the fourth mantra, by the mere knowledge of which supreme consciousness arises. (47)

He explains the method of extracting all four mantras and their respective word-divisions, beginning with "Having taken the seed-syllable situated in the [letter] 'a'... and ending with "...the two-syllabled [mantra] is remembered as being within. Since the path for explaining this has already been demonstrated, it is easy to understand. Having first drawn the wheel of letters (*varṇacakra*) and performed the extraction of the letters according to the stated sequence, [the mantras are]: *Oṃ apratihatānantagataye parameśvarāya kartre namaḥ* and *Oṃ amoghasarvaśaktyātmane bhagavate namo namaḥ*.

Oṃ, obeisance to Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, Vyāna, and Parā Udgama; Oṃ, obeisance to Acyuta, Avikṛta, Ananta, and Adhyakṣa. Thus, there are four mantras consisting respectively of twenty-one syllables, eighteen syllables, twenty-three syllables, and twenty syllables. (18–47)
Know that the fifth is likewise situated within; it is traditionally remembered as consisting of two syllables.
In whatever instances an excess of syllables among the words is cited, [it is this].
Therein, first, one should place the word beginning with the Vyāhṛtis at the navel.
Regarding the manner in which the number of syllables in the words is completed, he says "where": in the previously mentioned fourth chapter,
Nārada said:
Then the Blessed Lord, whose eyes are like red lotuses, being gracious with a most serene countenance, spoke of another procedure, O twice-born ones. (1)
The Blessed Lord said: Out of compassion for those engaged in ritual action, he by whom the Self was brought, even while in the state of sleep,
gradually to manifestation upon the lotus of the syllables of speech.

Now the fourth [chapter] will be explained. He says "atha" (now) by means of two verses, stating that he describes the procedure for the manifestation of the dream. By which ritual action the Self—the Supreme Self—is brought to manifestation, i.e., made manifest like the individual soul (jīva) as the Self within the dream, upon the lotus of the heart; "he describes that procedure"—this is the connection with the preceding verse. || 1-2 ||
It is augmented by the undivided and complete majesty of the sixfold qualities,
and it shines with uninterrupted rays of light, such as white and others, which are themselves indivisible.
Beholding the pure god, who was radiant with his own splendor,
[he] again took recourse in the center of the pericarp, assuming a divine body composed of mantra.
Then, by his own power and with time whose form is unperceivable,
he himself indeed withdraws that manifest form which possesses the characteristics previously described.
Having thus withdrawn the deity consisting of mantra, O wielder of the plow,
he remains filling [the space] from the root to the tip of the pericarp with his own splendor.
O Great-minded One, having ascended by means of the form of the Brahma-pillar,
[he established] the four gentle forms which extend in all directions.

First, he describes the characteristics of the Blessed One known as Viśākhayūpa, who is the source of all four [Vyuhas] beginning with Vāsudeva, in four and a half verses beginning with "abhinnaiḥ. The meaning is that He is augmented by the power of the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) in their undivided and complete state; unlike Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, there is no division into pairs of qualities, and like Vāsudeva, He is full of the sixfold qualities, neither deficient nor excessive.

The meaning is that it is radiant with undivided rays of light, such as white and so forth—shining like Vāsudeva and the others, without a distinction of separate colors like white, red, yellow, and black, yet brilliant with all four splendors. It has arisen by its own radiance; the meaning is that it is of the nature of pure light alone. Having first beheld the deity known as Viśākhayūpa, having seen him previously in the form of light; one should then, resorting to the tip of the pericarp, behold the mantra-body, meaning one should behold him as having become an embodied form.

The grammatical connection is: "one should again behold Him withdrawing that form. Thus, having withdrawn the body consisting of mantra, and having filled the space from the base to the tip of the pericarp with His own splendor, He remains in the form of the sacrificial post (yūpa) of Brahman; being devoid of a physical form, by resorting to the nature of pure light, He attains the status of the central sacrificial post within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, which serves as the locus for Vāsudeva and the others who constitute the branches. This very point is elaborated in the Lakṣmītantra: "In the manifestation of the emanations (vyūha) from the emanation, [the Lord] fills every intervening space with His splendor, from one station (pada) to another station."
Worshipped as a mass of splendor, unmanifest and devoid of physical form,
he is called Viśākhayūpa, being augmented by various forms of knowledge and other virtues.
"In each respective state, from that [Supreme Being], the fourfold branch of forms beginning with Vāsudeva indeed manifests in succession, O Śakra.

Furthermore, the etymological explanation of the term *viśākhayūpa* is stated in that very same place: "The branches are proclaimed to be Vāsudeva and the others of the all-pervading Lord; the Blessed One is the *viśākhayūpa*, for he spreads out and performs that [manifestation]. (3–7)
In the east, with a white body that surpasses the brilliance of the sun,
the Blessed One himself becomes manifest in the form of Vāsudeva.
Immediately thereafter, with a splendor equal to a ruby,
that Lord indeed rises in the southern quarter in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
And in the western direction, he is manifest under the name Pradyumna, with a form exceeding that of the hundred-rayed sun scorched by its own heat.
Then the Supreme Lord sat in the northern direction with the nature of Aniruddha, his complexion resembling the autumnal sky.
The original form of all of them is traditionally held to be identical in configuration;
they all possess the splendor of ten million suns and have lotus-like eyes.
With the canopies of moonlight from their teeth, they illuminated the quarters of the sky;
adorned with pearl necklaces and other ornaments, they possessed the appearance of ten thousand full moons. (13)
Adorned with their own garments resembling shimmering nectar and wearing excellent garlands,
they held superior weapons raised in their hands and were not bereft of their respective emblems.
Their lotus-feet were marked with white water-lilies emerging from lines [of light], and their faces were occupied with pacifying the suffering of humble people. (15)
With hearts full of compassion, they are intent on uplifting the world;
they stand in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of their own bodies. || 16 ||

Now, beginning with the word "gentle" (*saumya*) and ending with "situated in the midst of a circle of flames" (*jvālāmaṇḍalamadhyagāḥ*), he describes the characteristics of Vāsudeva and the others (verses 7–16).
In this very way, this Blessed One is to be fully honored through preliminary practice,
by means of each individual part in succession, according to his sovereign power.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, having worshipped the Supreme Lord with continuous offerings in succession, starting from Aniruddha and ending with Mūrti; || 18 ||
By means of two *praṇavas* and with a perfectly purified intellect, according to the procedure known as *apya-ya*, the wise who are devoted to the heart-sacrifice [should perform it].

With three verses beginning with “evam eva,” he describes the mental worship of these [deities], Vāsudeva and the others, according to the sequence of their origin and dissolution; that is to say, in the order of creation. This extends from Vāsudeva down to Aniruddha. It is performed with two *praṇavas* (the syllable Om), meaning with the mantra of devotion mentioned in the second chapter. However, while it was said there, “May the Supreme Lord be pleased with me,” here, in place of the word “Supreme” (*para*), one should employ the name of whichever deity is appropriate—Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, or another—in accordance with the context. (17–19)
Now I shall declare the mantra of this great-souled deity known as Viśākhayūpa, which bestows discernment through knowledge, even for one whose body is divided. (20)
Having taken the first [syllable] from the end of *varṇaṃbhakṣastha*, then the second from the eleventh [position],
the third as distinct from the second [of] the *nābhi*, and [the fourth] from the *nemimaṇḍala*.
The second [syllable] is indeed the word for the form of external fire;
then, one should withdraw only that which precedes the eleventh. 22.
The third syllable is joined from the outside with that which follows the navel;
then the letter following the tenth, and after that, the one preceding the eleventh.
Immediately after that, one should extract the syllable presided over by the eleventh vowel;
then, there is indeed a supreme syllable joined with the second [vowel] of the navel.
The second [syllable] alone is from the external; likewise, the first is from the eleventh [circle].
Then the third is from the rim (nemi), followed by the second conjoined with its own vowel (svarasaṃyuta).
O Amalalocana, that which follows the tenth is pure, and it precedes the eleventh; it is joined with the eleventh at the navel at its end.

One should take the letter following the third [consonant] joined with *nābhi* (the letter *u*), which is white in color; then that which is joined with the second [consonant] of *nābhi*, following the eighth [vowel].
Following that, with "Nemi" as the second [syllable], it is accompanied by "Namaḥ";
this great mantra consists of twenty-four syllables. (28)
The first part of this [mantra] is traditionally known as the single syllable preceded by the Praṇava;
the second is said to consist of three syllables, and immediately after that is the one of five syllables.
O Great-minded One, the fourth word of this mantra consists of six syllables, the fifth consists of seven syllables, and the sixth word consists of two syllables.

First, he states the Viśākhayūpa mantra, beginning with "atha" and ending with "mahāmate. "Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, whose form is splendor, who is independent of others, and who is not dependent on others"—this mantra of twenty-four syllables is thus extracted. (20–30)
For the Supreme Lord, the primordial God and all-pervading one, exists at all times as the very nature of various mantras, abiding in the beginning, middle, and end of everything.
Now, he clarifies the intention that Viśākhayūpa, mentioned previously, is indeed Paravāsudeva himself, by saying "by various names. (31)
Within its own fourfold group of the four manifestations (vyūhas), characterized by the distinct qualities of tranquility and so forth,
it abides primarily as the three deities.

Thus, he states "caturvyūha" (the fourfold manifestation) to show that even within the fourfold array of the peaceful (*śānta*), the arisen (*udita*), and so forth, Paravāsudeva alone exists in the form of Vāsudeva contained within each respective array. Here, because the Vāsudeva contained within the peaceful and arisen arrays is non-different from Parātpara-Vāsudeva, both are fulfilled by a single mantra; furthermore, since no individual mantras are stated for the three [deities] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa as they are subordinate to him, it should be understood that the primacy of the peaceful-arisen Vāsudeva consists in his status as the principal (*aṅgin*).

However, since each of the four mantras beginning with Vāsudeva has been mentioned in relation to each of the three groupings—such as deep sleep (suṣupti) and the rest—it should be understood that therein Vāsudeva possesses primacy, characterized by his status as the foremost. || 32 ||
Just as the sun, O Great-minded One, though being only one while stationed in the sky, appears to be manifold by taking recourse to various bodies of water; || 33 ||
In this way, although the Blessed One is one, he assumes multiplicity by resting upon various mantras and within the states beginning with the fourth (turya).
For the sake of favoring those subject to rebirth, according to the power of their various inclinations, learn from me as I speak the fourfold group of mantras. (35)
Thus, with two and a half verses beginning with "yathā" (33–35), he confirms through the method of illustration that even a single other entity possesses manifold forms.

Indeed, by virtue of being the denoters of the manifestations of colors such as white and so forth, [the letters] reside in the sense organs in sequence; and that letter which follows the tenth, preceded by the navel, [is the one in question]. (36)
Below the navel, preceded by the rim (nemipūrva), there is that which is endowed with thirteen;
then the second syllable from the twelfth, and after that, the one following the second.
And know that the fifth [set] consists of these three alone from among those situated outside;
then, from the eighth, the second is indeed pierced by the eleven at the navel.
The five-syllable mantra for Vāsudeva follows immediately after that;
this thirteen-syllable mantra is indeed proclaimed as the first. (39)
I shall now describe in due order the extraction of the others as they exist:
the syllable situated in the axle, and immediately after that, the second from the navel.
Then, following the previous mantra, one should give three steps;
thereafter, at this point, the fifteenth [syllable] preceded by the syllable Oṃ is assigned to the navel.
Know that the mantra consists of those very three words joined together;
then there is that which consists of sixteen syllables, preceded by the *praṇava*, beginning from the navel.
Of the words possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, two are to be placed before this triad of mantras; know them by the number of the preceding mantras. (43)
Now listen to the division of the words, which is devoid of single vowels;
for all [mantras], the first two words are traditionally held to consist of a single syllable each.
The third consists of two syllables, while the fourth has four syllables;
the fifth indeed has five syllables—thus it is declared for the three [sections]. (45)
O wielder of the plow, thus has the four-fold nature of that one called Pradyumna,
who abides in the state of dream, been briefly proclaimed.
And he performed meditation and worship accompanied by mantras, out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees.

Now, he explains the extraction of the four mantras of the *svapnavyūha*, beginning with "Next, the quartet of mantras" and continuing until the end of the section. Thus, the quartet of mantras is extracted as follows: *oṃ aṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*; *oṃ āṃ namo bhagavate saṅkarṣaṇāya*; *oṃ aṃ namo bhagavate pradyumnāya*; *oṃ aḥ namo bhagavate aniruddhāya*. || 35-46 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrīsāttvata-saṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Sātvatabhāṣya, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Mauñjyāyana family and a worshipper of the lotus feet of the Lord of Yadugiri.
The Fifth Chapter.
Nārada said: Then Hari, the Lord of All, spoke again to the best of brahmins.
This is clearly for the sake of removing the delusion of living beings who possess the plow [of virtue]. || 1 ||

Now the fifth [chapter] will be explained. Here, moreover, he states the definition of the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*) with the word "atha" (now). The syntactical connection is: [He] spoke to Sīrin, that is, Saṃkarṣaṇa, for the purpose of removing the delusion of *bhavins*, that is, of those subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*). || 1 ||
The Blessed One said:
O high-minded one, that which rests upon the shoreless expanse of the lake, which is the root syllable *A*, eternal, and the lotus that is the support of all—[that is the source]. (2)
The stalk of letters consists of the vowels (ākāra), while all the remaining phonemes are its leaves;
resting upon the eight directions, it stands like a wheel.
Within the center of that lotus, on the plane known as Jāgrat (the waking state), the Lord is to be worshipped and meditated upon;
how this is to be done is now being explained.

Having first described the nature of the heart-lotus as being composed of phonemes (*varṇa*), he states that the worship of the *jāgrat-vyūha* (the waking manifestation) should be performed upon its petals, which are designated by the state of waking, in the "Ananta-lake" (*anantasaras*). This means a great lake (*mahāsarovara*). Here, the status of the letter *kṣa* as a lake should be understood because it is the primary [phoneme] of the five powers of Brahmā (*brahma-śakti-pañcaka*), which are the cause of the world's origin. As it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"O Lord of the Gods, [the series] beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *śa* is characterized by the unfolding of power (*śakty-unmeṣa*)."
The syllable *kṣa* itself arose as the Great Turbulence (*mahākṣobha*), known by the name of Truth;
from that came the one called Vāsudeva, and with him arose Sāṅkhya and Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Pradyumna is to be known by the name Śākha, and Aniruddha indeed by the name Śākhi;
these five supreme powers (śaktis) consist of the nature of the five Brahmās.
"Those manifestations, non-different from me, are the causes of the world's origination;
they are my powers, like the flames of a great fire. Thus it is said.
In this very way:

"The supreme, self-cognizable, and eternal form of consciousness is my [nature]; that essence of speech is the letter *A*, the source of all verbal expression. Thus, one should understand with supporting reasoning that the letter *A* possesses the status of being the root of the majesty proclaimed by Lakṣmī. Furthermore, it is appropriate that this *A* serves as the stalk (*nāla*), as it has been stated: "That very [consciousness] is intended as the second vowel in the form of bliss. It is described as having all other letters as its sprouts (*pallava*); that is to say, all the remaining letters previously mentioned, beginning with the letter *I*, are themselves the sprouts or leaves of which it consists.

In this context, accepting that the word "all" (*sarva*) is used in a figurative sense, one should state that only the letters beginning with *i* and ending with *sa* constitute the petals; for in the third chapter it is stated, "But below the pericarp (*karṇikā*) consisting of the letter *ha*, in the station called deep sleep," thus assigning the status of pericarp to the letter *ha*. That lotus, which rests upon the eight directions and stands in a circular form like a wheel by resting its own petals upon all the directions—in the midst of its leaves, the Blessed One is to be worshipped and meditated upon.

The two words "jāgrat" (waking) and "saṃjñapade" (in the state of consciousness), along with the word "adhaḥ" (below), are qualifiers of the petals. It is clearly evident that the space within the heart-lotus corresponds to the fourth state (turyāpada); the location of its pericarp to the state of deep sleep (suṣuptipada); the location of its filaments to the state of dreaming (svapnapada); and the location of the petals situated below those to the waking state (jāgratpada). || 2–4 ||
Having observed it as complete with its own splendor through the seed-syllable *praṇava*, situated above its own pericarp and extending to the end of the filaments.
Then, from the four seed-syllables of Brahmā preceded by the *praṇava*,
[there arose forms] resembling *kadamba* flowers, crowded with hundreds of rays of light.
One should meditate upon the fourfold form of the All-pervading Lord as it has been described according to the sequence of the directions—
the mantra-form with its characteristics clearly manifest, surrounded on the outside by the [elemental] manifestations.
Indeed, it has arisen from the Supreme as something resembling a spark,
entered within the expressive word, and has attained manifestation.

First, having visualized with the seed-syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), which denotes it, the Supreme Lord—the cause of the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*)—who stands filling the light from the center of its pericarp up to the filaments; then, one should perceive the fourfold form of Vāsudeva and the others arisen around him in the directions starting from the east. This he states in four verses beginning with "the Supreme. [The meaning is: from the four syllables consisting of the four Brahma-seeds, namely *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*.
Indeed, the pure fivefold Brahman is to be known as that which begins with *śa* and ends with *kṣa*.

"O Lord of the Thirty-three, Śa, Ṣa, Sa, and Ha are to be known as the [seeds] beginning with Aniruddha," according to the statement in the *Lakṣmītantra*. Alternatively, the meaning is that they are derived from the four seed-syllables beginning with Vāsudeva, which will be mentioned later. By the phrase "having clearly manifest characteristics" (*suvyaktalakṣaṇam*), it is stated that, in comparison to the waking state (*jāgrat-vyūha*)—which is like a waking perception and is thus very clearly manifest (*suvyakta*)—the dream state (*svapna-vyūha*) is only slightly manifest (*īṣad-vyakta*), since its objects are not within the range of perception as they are merely characterized by qualities (*guṇa-mātra*). This is said with respect to the deep sleep state (*suṣupti-vyūha*), which is beyond the range of perception because it consists of mere qualities alone. || 5–8 ||
Therein, the first form of the Blessed One possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon;
it has four arms, a serene countenance, and eyes resembling white lotuses.
Clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with a golden banner,
he grants fearlessness to the terrified with his principal right hand.
In his left hand he holds the treasury of knowledge, and the king of conchs;
on the other [left] side behind him, however, there is a raised sword in his right hand.
In such a manner, she sat upon the surface of the earth with her mace resting on her left side;
she had one face, four arms, and the form of a peak of vermilion.
Wearing garments resembling the color of flax flowers and marked with the palm tree, he is equal to the first Lord by means of his two principal hands. 13.
In one hand he held a plough and a discus, while in his other hand was a pestle and a mace;
he possessed the radiance of a multitude of fireflies appearing at night during the rainy season.
Clad in garments of precious silk, adorned with the dolphin-bannered emblem, he has one face and four arms; this is the third Supreme Lord.
O Great-minded One, his two principal hands should be visualized as before:
in the left rear hand a bow, and in the right five arrows. (16)
Resembling the Añjana mountain, clothed in very white garments,
four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with the mark of the moon.
The first pair of hands of this [deity] is also proclaimed to be like that of the first [deity];
then, in order from the right, the next two hands hold a sword and a shield.
He states the specific characteristics of Vāsudeva and the others with the words beginning "Therein, the first," and so forth. (9.18)
All of them wear forest garlands and are marked with the Śrīvatsa;
they are adorned upon their chests with the Kaustubha, the king of jewels.
Adorned with beautiful crowns and diadems, necklaces, armlets, and anklets; with variegated tilakas upon their foreheads and shimmering makara-shaped earrings. || 20 ||
Indeed, they should always be meditated upon as adorned with various beautiful garlands, flower wreaths, and fragrant ointments such as camphor.
He states their common characteristics with three verses [beginning] "wearing forest garlands" (vanamālādharāḥ). 19–21.
Furthermore, by means of the yoga of coming, one should meditate upon the Lord Aniruddha on the eastern, northern, and middle petals, with a body that is white and black.
One should meditate upon Pradyumna within the western petal situated in the middle;
indeed, at the time of dissolution, he is of a dark-yellow complexion.
In the rite of the counter-current (pratisrota), one should meditate upon the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, who stands between the west and the south and bears a body that is yellowish-red in hue.
O high-minded one, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, should be meditated upon in the center and in the eastern and southern directions with white and red splendor.
Due to the extreme purity of his intention, the All-pervading Lord is like a crystal stone; having reached different locations, he indeed appears as two distinct splendors.
He grasps the variegated form characterized by withdrawal;
now I shall describe the group of four mantras in sequence—listen! (27)
With the words beginning with "again" (punar), he describes the variegated form of those [deities] situated from Īśāna to Āgneya, arranged in a downward sequence. || 22–27 ||
Having taken [the measurement] within the axle, from the navel forward and beyond that;
[it is] divided by the second navel, from the rim forward and beyond that. (28)
Then, having taken from the tenth [mark] the first,
the third, the second, and the fifth starting from the navel, one should mark them along the rim.
Then, from the ninth [letter], the second seed-syllable following it should be applied;
below that, the second [syllable] which comes after the twelfth should be employed.
Then, immediately after that, one should fashion the fifth [part] joined with the navel;
following the eighth, there is another pure [part], likewise preceded by the rim (*nemi*).
It is proper that the second [foot] should not be placed on the second circle of the rim;
rather, one should place that entire foot upon the Lord of Yoga alone. || 32 ||

At the end of that, one should place the word "cakriṇe" (to the wheel-bearer), and then the eight syllables of the rim (nemi) joined with the western [syllable] of the nave (nābhi); having placed them at the end of that.
One should first place the pure [mark] from the eleventh [unit] forward, and then from the eighth;
the foot of the banner should be placed at the third unit beyond the rim (nemi).
First, it is divided from the navel by one-eleventh part;
thereafter, the pure fifth section is divided from the rim of the wheel by one-eighth.
The second [syllable] is joined with its vowel, followed by "sa se"; then there is a two-syllable word, and after that, the word "vāsudevāya" should follow, accompanied by "namaḥ. (36)
The mantra consists of thirty-six syllables; its division is now described.
The first word is proclaimed to have eleven syllables. (37)
The second consists of five syllables, while the third is remembered as having three syllables;
the fourth has six syllables, and the fifth indeed has five letters.
O best among those who know the words, know that the sixth word consists of seven syllables;
having taken it from the navel-center at the end of the *praṇava*. (39)
Then he declares the mantras for the four [deities] in sequence with the words beginning "atha caturṇām" and so forth.

Starting from "akṣāntargatam ādāya" and ending with "padavidāṃvara," the thirty-six-syllable mantra—*oṃ amādhurāyādbhutamayāya yogeśvarāya cakriṇe suparṇadhvajāya pītavāsase vāsudevāya namaḥ*—is thus extracted. || 27-39 ||
Then, from the fourteenth [mark], the eight spokes are joined to the nave;
the second [set] is purified from the tenth, and then one should again collect [the remaining parts].

Below that, from the ninth letter up to the end [of the row], starting from the navel, it is endowed with the fourth [vowel] and so on, and is pervaded by the eleven vowels; then, from there, the second [row] begins from the tenth.
Then, from the outside, the eighth [digit] from the navel is joined with the fifteenth;
likewise, the fifth alone from the rim and the second from the eighth.

One should extract this syllable, which is preceded by the third of the letter *na* and joined with the third of the letter *nābhi*; it is indeed the first [syllable] from the beginning of the *ārā*. 43.

One should give the second syllable from the tenth letter, marked with the eleventh [vowel] from the navel; this five-syllabled word should be placed at the end for the one whose banner is the palm tree (Tālaketu).

Furthermore, at the conclusion of that, for the five-syllable mantra of the blue-clad one (Nīlavāsas), [one should take] the first from the first [syllable], and then the second conjoined with a vowel. 45.
One should place the first [syllable] before the rim (nemi), then the eleventh from that;
the fourth from those on the outside, and two beyond the hub (nābhi).
The second [syllable] is the single word *saṅkarṣaṇāya* derived from the outside;
the third [syllable] is the first [syllable] of the rim (*nemi*), joined with the vowel *ā*. (47)
O high-minded one, this mantra, consisting of thirty-six syllables, is indeed pure externally and is followed by the word "namaḥ. (48)
The first word of this [mantra] consists of six syllables; immediately after that is one of five syllables;
the third, however, has ten syllables; and from there follow three words of five syllables each. (49)

Beginning with "Oṃ" at the end of the *praṇava* and starting from "atha ādāya," ending with "trīṇi pañcākṣarāṇyataḥ," the thirty-six-syllable mantra is thus extracted: *oṃ āṃ saunandakine saṃvartakine tālaketave nīlavāsase kāmapālāya saṃkarṣaṇāya rāmāya namaḥ*. (39–49)

Then, having taken the seed-syllable located at the axle from the fifteenth [syllable] of the navel, one should place the word "held by Śārṅga" (śārṅgadhṛte) thereafter; after that, the four syllables.
Then, having first taken the syllable preceding the *nemi*, and then the first from the beginning,
and the third from the outermost, he gave those three syllables indeed for the Banner.
Then, from the third [group], one should take the first; then, from the first [group], the first again; that should be applied below it, and the second syllable from the eighth [group].
Then, the fifth from the outside conjoined with the second vowel;
and by reference to that, the eighth, which is indeed that same [vowel] alone. (53)
After "nābheḥ" comes the eleven-syllable "ākrāntam," followed by the six-syllable "padaṃ sanatkumārāya," and immediately thereafter the five-syllable [mantra].
Then, "padaṃ jagatpriyāya pradyumnāya namaḥ"—this mantra consists of thirty-four syllables; listen now to its constituent words as well. (55)
The first should be known as having six syllables, and the second is indeed likewise;
the third has five syllables, while the fourth has six syllables.
Know the fifth [mantra] to have five syllables and the sixth indeed to have six syllables;
the sixteenth is situated on the axle, and the second is from the navel, while the tenth is indeed from the [following] one.

Then, beginning with "athādāyākṣagaṃ bījam" and ending with "ṣaḍvarṇaṃ ṣaṣṭhameva hi," the thirty-four-syllable mantra is extracted as follows: *oṃ aṃ śārṅgadhṛte makaradhvajāya raktavāsase sanatkumārāya jagatpriyāya pradyumnāya namaḥ*. (50–57)
For indeed, it is then occupied by that very [seed] alone from the ninth onwards;
then, having taken [the seed] at its end, one places the first of the first [group] after the last.
O Mahāmati, it is not proper for a single syllable to be joined with a second syllable;
rather, there are two syllables at the beginning of the word, and those very same ones again at its end. (59)
Then, from the ninth [syllable], the second; from the first, the first;
then the third; and then indeed from the rim (nemi), that which is joined with the second vowel. (60)
The second [syllable] is solely from the exterior, and the seventh is from the navel-circle;
then, with the sixth, one should place the second [syllable] as it is occupied by the rim (nemi).
Then, one should take the first letter from the tenth *nemi*, the fifth letter from above that, the fourth letter from the other [side], and the second letter from the circle of the *nemi*. (62)
Immediately after that, one should join the second [syllable] with the two [preceding ones];
then the letter following the tenth, conjoined with the third vowel. (63)
Then, the third [syllable] from the rim (nemi), joined with the fifth from the hub (nābhi), combined with the second vowel, and the second [syllable] from the ninth [position], with care. (64)
Indeed, that which is the first from the tenth [syllable] should be applied below this very [line];
but for the one clad in black (Śiva), the second foot is pure and has a rim (nemi).
Following that, accompanied by a salutation to Viṣvaksena,
this thirty-two-syllable mantra is indeed further divided according to its constituent words.
Now understand from me the words, which consist of one syllable more:
the first word has two syllables, while the second has nine syllables. (67)

Three [names] consist of five syllables each, while another, the sixth, is known to have seven syllables; these are for the purpose of recollecting the Lord when the moment of dissolution has arrived. (68)

Beginning with "The sixteenth [syllable] is situated on the axle from the navel" and ending with "the sixth is remembered as having seven syllables," the thirty-two-syllable mantra is thus extracted: *Oṃ aḥ nandakānandakarāya ṛśyadhvajāyāniruddhāyāsitavāsase viṣvaksenāya namaḥ*. (57–68)
Listen now again to another set of four mantras in brief:
the first [mantra] consists of the eleventh letter [ṇa] joined with the fifth vowel [ū]. (69)
The third [syllable] is joined with that same vowel from the rim of the wheel;
then the seventh is from the exterior, conjoined with the second vowel.
The second [syllable] is the *praṇava* alone at the beginning and end of the *nemi*;
the eighth is pure; and from the outside, the second and then the eighth.
Furthermore, it is joined with the rim as the second part, but beyond the nave;
thereafter, one should perform only the second external salutation.
Then, starting from the navel, there is a second [line] consisting of three [units] out of respect;
below that, a second pair [of units], joined with the fifth [unit] from the outside of the navel.
Now, that which is joined with the second from the navel and the eighth from the supreme;
The second is exclusively external salutation; beyond that [is the third]. (74)
Then, from the axle-position, the second [syllable] with devotion;
from the twelfth, the first; and then the fifth from the circle of the rim. (75)
Indeed, this triad alone, as well as the second [syllable] from the eighth [vowel], is pervaded by the eleventh vowel; [this is] "Vāsudevāya vai namaḥ. (76)
The first mantra consists of seven syllables, while the second has six syllables;
the third is equal to the first, and the fourth consists of twelve syllables.
This set of four mantras, free from the division of words,
must be guarded with great effort by those who know the ritual rules and desire spiritual accomplishment.
Having understood this, one should satisfy [the deity] as before with nectar-like enjoyments;
thus Adhokṣaja, possessing four forms, is surrounded by the gods of his own manifestation.

Furthermore, regarding the worship of the *vyūhas* according to the order of dissolution (*apyaya*), he states the fourfold mantra with the words beginning "at the time of dissolution" (*apyayāvasare*). Thus, the fourfold mantra beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Vāsudeva is declared: *oṃ puruṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ satyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ acyutāya namaḥ*, and *oṃ bhagavate vāsudevāya namaḥ*. (Verses 68–79)
"From the wheel [arise] Caturaṅga and the others; this is indeed the group of mantras belonging to the all-pervading Lord Cāturātmya, proclaimed together with its secrets in brief. (80)

He concludes the point stated thus far with the words "from the four-limbed" (caturaṅgāt). This means: from that which is distinguished by the four limbs known as the hub, the spokes, the rim, and the felly. || 80 ||
Indeed, it exists as non-different from the primordial form, like the seed of a banyan tree;
it is liberated from all activity and is supreme from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
That primordial nature of consciousness is indeed the Great One, consisting of pure awareness;
it possesses the luster of a thousand fires, suns, and moons, and is characterized as the abode of bliss.
He states the definition of the fourth array (turyavyūha) with the verse beginning "by non-differentiation" (abhedena), [consisting of] one and a half verses. || 81–82 ||
Know that the fourfold nature (cāturātmya), which is the seed of all ritual actions and the locus of all conceptual constructions, is the second [form], O one of stainless vision. (83)
He describes the characteristics of the *suṣupti-vyūha* with the verse beginning "vahnyarka... (82–83).
It is eternal, bearing an eternal form, radiant with the splendor of the sun,
and divided by the distinctions of white and other colors, as well as by its upward and downward positions.

The third [form] is the Cāturātmya, which bestows the fruit of the enjoyment of isolation (kaivalya), brings about the destruction of the seed of worldly existence, and is beautiful with a mass of nectar. 85.
He states the characteristics of the array of dreams in two verses beginning with "nityam" (84–85).
Presiding over its own material nature (prakṛti), which brings about persistence, origination, and dissolution, and is endowed with all instruments, it emerges and sets. (86)
Know that to be the fourth [state], by whose command the universe stands;
it assumes fourfold forms, such as white and so forth, during the Kṛta Yuga.
O Great-minded One, in the Tretā age, [the sequence] begins with red and ends with white;
when the Dvāpara age arrives, it is yellow, black, white, and red.
In the Kali age, the Supreme Lord assumes black, white, red, and yellow colors respectively during the four periods of transition between the ages (yuga-sandhyā).
Understand from me that form which is the commonality of diverse manifestations:
it is white and red at the end (of time), and thereafter red and yellow.
Following that, there is yellow and black, and immediately after, black and white;
the distinction between these is to be known by the weapons, garments, and emblems previously described. (91)
Otherwise, due to their equality, by what means could the division here be determined?
It is, however, according to the sequence of the yugas, days, nights, half-periods, and praharas.

He describes the characteristics of the waking manifestation (jāgrad-vyūha) and its variation in color according to the different ages (yuga-bheda) with the verses beginning with "sthityutpatti" and ending with "vibhāgo'trāvadhāryate. In the Lakṣmītantra as well, the characteristics of the manifestations are elaborated in this very same way: "The characteristic of the abode of bliss is that which possesses the luster of a thousand fires, suns, and moons."
O Vāsava, know that to be the seed of all actions, the locus of all conceptual constructions, the state of deep sleep, and the first of the fourfold nature.
Then, indeed, within the state of sleep, the Lord divided himself by himself through his own power,
according to the distinctions of the directions such as east and so forth, in the forms of Vāsudeva and the others.
Through the distinction of concise and detailed descriptions of the qualities, the Supreme Person [is described] with most wonderful [forms] resembling white, red, and golden clouds.
Indeed, through forms equal to the primordial form, he abides in four ways;
[this state] bestows the fruit of liberation and enjoyment, and brings about the destruction of the seed of worldly existence.
The second is the fourfold self (cāturātmya), which is beautiful with an abundance of nectar;
then, in the state of waking, the Lord [is perceived] through the distinctions of white, red, and so forth.
With four arms and noble limbs, marked with the conch, discus, and other symbols,
their bodies variegated by various banners, they are known as Vāsudeva and the others.
The All-pervading Lord, by means of His own divine play, remains divided into various manifestations;
He is the unsurpassed God of fourfold nature abiding in the state of waking.

One should contemplate that everything—comprising the causes of persistence, origination, and dissolution, and endowed with all instruments—is contained within his teaching; the entire universe abides in his command.
"The fourfold nature is threefold in the triad of states beginning with deep sleep;
it is clearly manifest in that fourth state, where the supreme, characterized by the qualities, abides. (Verses 86–92)
Having performed the visualization of the divisions and constantly beholding the Lord,
[one should place Him] in this body at the head, the heart, the navel, and again below that.

Therefore, for the sake of prosperity—or otherwise, for liberation—one should meditate from the top of the head down to the feet; specifically, one should contemplate the neck, shoulders, knees, and ankles according to the characteristics described in the Sandhyā-vidhi.
"By means of the yoga of creation and dissolution, he attains the supreme goal"—thus [it is said] regarding the single form, the manifestations (vyūhas), and the entire expansion (vibhava). 95.

With the three verses beginning with "yugābda," he describes the differences in time and the differences in locations within the body of the practitioner for the recollection of Vāsudeva and the others. "Ālakṣya" means having meditated upon; "bhūtaye" means for the sake of sovereignty (aiśvarya); "muktaye" means for the sake of liberation (mokṣa).

The meaning is as follows: for those who sequentially meditate upon the four abodes (dhāman), beginning with Vāsudeva and the others, in the four locations starting from the head, the worldly, mundane fruit is attained; furthermore, for those who meditate in reverse order—starting from below the navel up to the head—in the four locations, the fruit in the form of the [divine] forms (mūrti), beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Vāsudeva, is accomplished. This refers to the fourfold group beginning with Vāsudeva, which possesses the characteristics described in the *Sandhya* [section], having a variegated form consisting of white, red, and other colors, assumed according to the distinctions of the junctions of the ages (*yuga-sandhi*).
The descent, as well as meditation and worship preceded by mantra, have been taught through a single samādhi according to the distinctions of one's own station and place. (96)

He concludes the stated meaning with the verse beginning "iti" (95–96). The sense is: of the single-formed Supreme Self, Vāsudeva; of his manifestations (*vyūha*), such as Vāsudeva and the others; and of the differentiation of states, such as the fourth (*turya*) and so forth.
Now, the distinction known as differentiation (bheda), preceded by its descent (avatāra), and pertaining to the establishment of the state of being for all [beings], is being described here. (97)
He says "the distinction" [in verse 97] to state that the distinction among these is now being explained.
The sixfold attributes beginning with the Primordial God, the fourfold nature marked by purity—this triad is indeed the power of the Supreme Lord for the sake of creation. (98)

One should first remember [the Self] as having become liquefied through non-duality, by means of the fourth state (turyātman), eternally arisen, established in the supreme state, and characterized by immobility. || 99 ||

He states the distinction with two verses beginning with "the sixfold policy" (ṣāḍguṇyam). One should meditate upon the supreme power of the Lord—which is the nature of the power of capacity—as this triad [of powers] in its threefold manifestation of deep sleep and so forth, becoming restless for the sake of creation. One should meditate upon the Lord himself, who is characterized by motionlessness, who has become non-restless, who is eternally manifest, and who is higher than the highest, as being non-different from the fourth state (turya) through the form of the fourth manifestation (turyavyūha). This is the meaning. || 98-99 ||
Then, if one should wish to worship that which is characterized by a specific manifestation,
one should conceive of it according to one's own intellect immediately at that time.
That power of capability is constant, which itself attains vibration;
where the practitioner has established his seat, it gives birth to the mantra like a spark of fire. (101)
One should meditate upon that [seed-syllable] like a star appearing from the sky within the pericarp;
then, from the center of that, one should remember the worshipful deity arisen.
Either in the form of the primordial image, or consisting of the fourfold manifestation,
or as each individual form of the fourfold manifestation separately.
Alternatively, indeed by means of the Vaibhava [form], which consists of various manifestations,
one should place his assembly of limbs (aṅga-saṃgha) resting upon the petals of the lotus.
Outside the lotus is the retinue; for each mantra together with its śakti, whatever [mantras] such as the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) exist, they are placed according to the sequence of the directions.

With five and a half verses beginning with "atha," he describes the sequence of the Lord’s incarnations for the purpose of worship: "If a practitioner (sādhaka) desires to worship the Lord—who is characterized by specific manifestations and distinguished by His various forms known as the Paravyūha, Vibhava, and so forth—the Lord, having perceived that practitioner through His own intellect and knowing him to be facing toward Him, moves of His own accord immediately at that time, following that very desire, by means of His power of sovereign capability."

The practitioner (sādhaka) is the minister (mantrī); wherever he has established his seat, whatever mantra he desires, he brings that mantra forth like a spark of fire. The sense is that by the mere vibration of that [power], the mantra arises like a spark from a fire. One should contemplate that mantra as having come from space, like a star, into the center of the pericarp—the middle of the heart-lotus. From the midst of that, from the middle of the mantra, one should contemplate the Lord of Mantras (mantranātha), the object of worship, in the form of the primordial manifestation, the nature of Paravāsudeva.

Alternatively, one should remember [the Lord] as having arisen—whether as the fourfold manifestation (*vyūha*) in its distinctness, or as each single form in the nature of a solitary individual image, or else in His majestic form (*vaibhavīya-rūpa*) consisting of various shapes through the distinctions of Padmanābha and others. (100–105)
One should place [the deities] within the web of filaments; however, the powers (śaktis) are in the middle of the petals.
That Lord of Mantras who is solitary is devoid of power and devoid of limbs.
One should again worship that [deity] within the network of petals by means of sound alone;
such is the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) of the God, the Supreme Self. 107.

Regarding the phrase "of the mantra together with its powers" (*saśaktikasya*), he speaks of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) on the petals starting from the east, as well as the placement of their respective retinues outside the lotus. Thus, it should be understood that the rule for the placement of powers such as Lakṣmī and others on the petals is generally applicable (*prāyikatva*). For, in this very thirteenth chapter, it is stated: "The group of six resides in the web of filaments; there, two are in the east and west, two by two in the north and south, and those [others] in the left hands."
Thus, it has been stated that the Śaktis are situated even in the place of the filaments (kesara). Furthermore, in the seventeenth chapter [it says]:
"One should place the goddess Śrī in the portion of the rim (nemi), Puṣṭi to the north, Nidrā situated in the rear region, and Sarasvatī in the front portion."

Thus, the placement of the Śaktis (śaktinyāsa) has been described even outside the lotus. Furthermore, in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and the *Pārameśvara*, it is stated: "In the pericarp of the Lord, [one should worship] Śrī and Puṣṭi, and then on the other two sides"; thus, the worship of the Śaktis on both sides of the Lord within the pericarp itself is prescribed. (105–106)

Regarding the Lord who is characterized by both being devoid of power (*niḥśaktikatva*) and being bodiless (*niraṅgakatva*), he states that worship may be performed even at the site of a single part by means of the mantra alone, in the verse beginning with *niḥśaktika*. (106–107)

Having thus correctly described [the procedure] in brief, one should now perform the external worship of the image on the altar with the offerings previously brought, or upon the lotus of the wheel within the icon.
He concludes the stated meaning with the word "iti" (thus). || 107-108 ||
On a wheel produced from substances such as gold, or on a solitary lotus,
in the center of the ground of the auspicious pedestal, or indeed on a perfectly smooth surface alone.
Having meditated again and again with one's own mantra for the sake of attaining the fruit of liberation,
[the deity] should be worshipped according to the rules, preceded by pure devotion.
He describes the external sacrifice and its constituent parts with the verses beginning with "vedyām" (108–110).
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the venerable Sātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya* composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshiper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The Sixth Chapter.
Nārada said: O best of Brahmins, I shall duly relate that which was spoken by the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi).
In this context, the material sacrifice (dravyayāga) of Baladeva will also be described immediately hereafter. || 1 ||

Now the sixth [chapter] will be explained. He says "I shall speak" because he intends to speak of the external sacrifice (*bahir-yāga*). A material sacrifice (*dravya-yāga*) is a sacrifice performed with materials such as the *arghya* offering; the meaning is that it is an external propitiation. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said: Whatever leaf, flower, or other offering may be seen upon the pedestal,
having gathered it with one's hand and placed it in a pure spot, indeed—
Having swept the auspicious seat with cow-hair brushes, yak-tail whisks, peacock feathers, or kusha grass, or else with a very white cloth; || 3 ||
Immediately thereafter, having washed it with much water filtered through a cloth, [he should do so] while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra preceded and followed by the *praṇava*.

First, he describes the method for purifying the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) with three verses beginning with "whatever" (*yatkiñcit*). "Leaves, flowers, and so forth" means leaves of *tulasī* and other items previously offered to the Lord. "With that which has the *praṇava* at its beginning and end" means encapsulated by the *praṇava*. "With the twelve-syllable [mantra]" means with the twelve-syllable mantra of Vāsudeva. Thus, it is stated in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] that the purification of the auspicious seat and so forth may be performed at another time;
or else, O twice-born ones, immediately after entering the sacrificial hall.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] from the beginning to the end of the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), one should perform the other [rituals] one after another;
or else, at that very time, having performed the placement of the auspicious seat, thereafter—
"Having first performed the three paths according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform everything as stated for the image at the commencement of the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha. (2–4)
There, one should meditate upon the King of Wheels as consisting of the entire world, as the refuge of all gods, as the essence of all supports, and as being inwardly absorbed.
Then one should worship Him with the syllable Om, his own name, and the word "namas" at the end,
using offerings of water (arghya), touch, incense, and garlands made from various flowers.

He describes the worship of the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) hidden within the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) with two verses beginning with "sarvalokamaya. "Cakrarāṭ" means "the King of Wheels"; the shift in case-ending is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. "Ālabhana" refers to fragrance, so called because it is that by which a limb is touched or smeared (ālabhyate ālipyate 'nenāṅgam). "Nānāsragudbhavaiḥ" means those from which various kinds of garland-arrangements arise; that is to say, they are distinguished by various forms and sounds through the divisions of double-stranded, triple-stranded, and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning is "produced by various kinds of flowers.
