It should be understood that the word *srak* (garland) refers solely to the flowers themselves; for this very reason, even later in the section on fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), in the passage "the garland, incense, and honey-mixture," the word *srak* is accepted as referring exclusively to the flowers.

If it is asked, "Even in that case, what fault is there if the word *srak* refers to a garland (*mālikā*)?"—we reply: What is the use of our dispute? For in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the word *srak* is explained by Mahālakṣmī herself as referring to flowers, in the passage: "Then one should offer [an offering] consisting of flowers, and likewise one consisting of incense materials"; for she does not say, "Then one should offer one consisting of a garland (*mālya*). Furthermore, in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra], in the section explaining the materials for the fire-oblation (*homadravya*), it says: "With fragrant [flowers] such as land-lotuses (*sthalapadma*) and white flowers and the like."
He was gratified with land-lotuses and other flowers, such as white ones and so forth.

"O Brahmins, it bestows incomparable good fortune very soon," as stated regarding the offering of mere flowers alone. Furthermore, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the section defining the measure of oblations (*āhuti*), there is the statement, "with fruits and unbroken flowers," which specifies that flowers must merely be unbroken; and because there is a tradition of performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) with mere flowers alone, the word *sraj* (garland) should be understood as referring to flowers in general.

Furthermore, the statement to be cited later in the section on ornaments and seats—“bound by garlands, strings, and threads from ear to foot”—should also be understood as supportive here, since these very verses have been expounded by the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) as well. In his commentary, however, it is written: “By ‘garlands arising from various wreaths’ [is meant] flowers that serve as the cause for the manifestation of various kinds of wreaths; for the *Vaijayantī* states: ‘*Mālya* refers to both a flower and a garland. This is unsatisfactory, because the qualification would be redundant.

Furthermore, because there is no transgression in the worship of the *pīṭha* by means of garlands and so forth; at this juncture, the worship of the deities of the *pīṭhas*, such as Ananta and others, should also be performed according to the method to be described in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. (5–6)
Then, one should prepare four jars made of gold or other precious materials,
filled with filtered water and adorned with garlands and other ornaments.
One should place perfumes, all medicinal herbs, gems, fruits, seeds, kuśa grass, and water upon the base in the four outer corners.
Having said, "Oṃ, I prepare the arghya," one should place it on the northwest (vāyu) point;
likewise, one should place a water-pot in the northeast (aiśānī) for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana).
For the purpose of bathing, [the vessel] should be placed in the southeast corner, and likewise for the water for washing the feet in the southwest;
then, there should be the auspicious jars accompanied by their corresponding sub-jars (upakumbha).

Now, he describes the arrangement of the vessels with three and a half verses beginning with "tataḥ. Here, substances such as perfumes, all medicinal herbs, gems, fruits, seeds, and *kuśa* grass are mentioned without distinction for all four offerings, beginning with the *arghya*. Their specific distribution, however, should be understood from what will be stated in the eighteenth chapter. Thus it is said in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*:

"Having placed the vessels upon the support according to their own prior rule in the directions starting from the northwest (Vāyavya), one should perform the respective arrangement with the appropriate mantras."

Furthermore, although only the four [offerings] beginning with *arghya* are mentioned here, the second *arghya* which will be described in the eighteenth chapter must also be included, as it is required for the worship of the *pīṭha* and other rites. Although the worship of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*) dissolved within the *pīṭha* is mentioned prior to the preparation of the vessels here, that [second *arghya*] must be understood immediately after it, because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*). Thus he will state in the seventeenth chapter:
"Then, having worshipped the *arghya* vessel with flowers using the partless (*niṣkala*) mantras..."
Therefore, having drawn up a small amount of water from that other vessel into the bowl, |||
One should perform the worship of the yoga-pīṭha preceded by meditative realization (anusaṃdhāna). Thus [ends verses 7–10].
One should place a group of four [deities] outside, well-worshipped according to the sequence of the directions;
this limb of the sacrifice, preceded by the image of the Blessed One, was previously described.

Now, he describes the placement of the eight jars all around with the word "atha. "Accompanied by the subsidiary jars" (upakumbha) means together with the four jars to be placed in the intermediate directions. Alternatively, it means accompanied by the four subsidiary jars to be placed according to the method that will be described in the sections on pacification (śāntika) and so forth in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. "The quartet of auspicious jars" refers to the four jars to be placed in the four cardinal directions as previously mentioned. || 10-11 ||
Having brought one auspicious mark from among them into the center,
and having removed the arghya and other offerings that were consumed, he should then pay homage.

Regarding the placement of any one of the images of the Lord and so forth within those eight jars, he says "of the Lord" (*bhagavad*). This means it was previously stated (*prāgudīritam*) at the end of the fifth chapter (or sixth, depending on the numbering). This refers to the section concerning the worship of the solitary mobile image and so forth upon the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*). In this manner, the placement of the eight jars all around should be performed. However, in the context of the worship of a fixed image (*sthirabimba*), that is not the primary subject; for this very reason, it was not mentioned in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]. (11–12)
Then one should wash it with water using a brush made of uśīra grass or bamboo;
it should be marked with the discus and other symbols from before, or otherwise auspiciously bound as prescribed.

He speaks of the purification of the *bimba* (the image), beginning with the words "that which was consumed" (*bhuktam*). This refers to the *arghya* and other offerings made on the previous day, or alternatively, to the *arghya*, flowers, and so forth offered to the Lord at the time of approaching and worshiping Him. [This is done] with *uśīra*, a bamboo brush (*vaṃśakūrca*), or a *lājaka-piñcula*. (12–13)
Having filled the arghya vessel with water and placed it before him,
one should indeed cast sesame seeds, flowers, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds into it.
One should recite the mantra four times while holding it in the palm of the hand;
then the omnipresent deity assumes the form of the mantra. || 15 ||
Having summoned him with his own mantra, using the words "come hither," just as the all-pervading wind is directed by a fan, O Great-minded One. (16)
For in that very same way, the Blessed One, having been invoked,
indeed manifests his form after having projected it from the lotus of his heart onto the mirror of the devotee's being.
Having completely restrained [the breath] on the outer altar, at the conclusion of the mantra's utterance,
one should visualize the mantra returning from its own place as it has emerged.

Now, he describes the sequence of invocation with five verses beginning with "purāṅkitam" (marked by the [discus] and so forth). By the phrase "marked by the discus and so forth," a vessel made of material substances such as gold is meant. By the phrase "or as it is bound," a vessel made of leaves such as those of the *palāśa* tree is meant. And thus, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"Having taken up the *arghya* vessel, produced from gold, silver, or other materials..."
"Whether made of stone, clay, or wood, or else fashioned from the leaves of the *palāśa* or lotus.
Here, "with water" means with the primary *arghya* water; for it is said:
"In the invocation, in the presence [of the deity], in the confinement [of the vessel], and likewise in the worship..."
Regarding the dismissal, one should always perform the offering of the *arghya* from the vessel first;

thus [the author] will state later. The meaning is that the *arghya* vessel is a separate vessel prepared for the purpose of invocation (*āvahana*). And so it is said in the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "Then the vessel containing the invoked [deity] is washed with waters."
One should fill it with the root mantra and lift it up with both hands.

"In this [space] level with the forehead, one should invoke Keśava within. Here, *siddhārthakān* means white mustard seeds. "The mantra joined with the word *āgaccha*" means the specific mantra for each particular form (*mūrti*), because it has been stated: "Having summoned [the deity] with its own mantra, using the word *āgaccha* at the end. Likewise, in the *Pādma* as well: "One should recite the mantra four times, joined with the word *āgaccha*. Thus, the fourfold recitation of the mantra at the time of invocation is also stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Having recited the *Tāraka* (Om) four times, one should recite the *Tārikā* (Hrīm) three times."

The following is a restatement of the meaning expressed by the verse beginning with "Then [I invoke] the all-pervading God. This illustration—stating that the wind is omnipresent—is given to generate confidence in those of dull intellect regarding the invocation of the Blessed Lord. He will likewise state in the chapter on installation (Pratiṣṭhādhyāya):
"O Blessed One, although You are indeed all-pervading, I nevertheless invoke You, just as one draws forth the wind with a fan;
just as fire, though hidden, emerges through friction."
"For even though you have been invoked, you likewise approach the worship.
By the phrase "having caused [the deity] reflected in the mirror of one's own being to enter," one should visualize that Tāraka as if it had arrived from space within the pericarp;
then, from the center of that, one should remember the Adorable One who has arisen.

Thus, the meaning previously stated is recalled. The word "on the altar" (*vedyām*) is indicative of the *bimba* (the image) and so forth. The meaning is: having performed the withdrawal [of the deity] and prayed for the state that concludes the worship. Here, one should also understand that bringing about proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and facing toward the deity (*sāmmukhya*)—as in the case of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and others—is required. "At the conclusion of the recitation of the mantra" means at the conclusion of the respective root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Furthermore: "I invoke Lakṣmīśa, the imperishable Supreme Self."
"May the Supreme Person, the Lord of the World, the divine Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, assume this form out of a desire to show me favor."

Thus, the mantra mentioned in the *Lakṣmītantra* is the one intended here. Now, if it is asked: "Since these five verses also concern invocation (*āvāhana*), why are the two verses beginning with *purāṅkita* not mentioned in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and the *Īśvarapārameśvara*?"—the answer is true; for there [it says]: "Having filled [the vessel] with fragrance, water for honor (*arghya*), and flowers, while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the seat before Hari’s head."

It should be understood that the meaning of those two verses is already subsumed by this very [instruction], because the *arghya* water contained in the vessel for invocation is to be sprinkled over the image specifically through the hands joined in the *añjali* gesture. Furthermore, the pouring of the four substances—sesame seeds, flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and white mustard seeds—as prescribed by the statement "one should throw sesame seeds, flowers, *dūrvā*, and *siddhārthaka* therein," is fulfilled by the filling of the primary *arghya* water itself.
If it is asked: "If the purpose of throwing those four substances is thus already served by that [primary water], why are they mentioned again in the *Sātvata*?"—the answer is true.

In the absence of other substances for the water for the feet (pādya), dūrvā grass is used; for the arghya, mustard seeds; for the water for sipping (ācamanīya), kakkola is recommended; and for the water for sprinkling (mārjana), [the same applies].

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Padma-purāṇa*, although one might add only a single substance when other materials for the *arghya* and so forth are unavailable, it should be understood that the substances are mentioned again here in order to ensure the inclusion of all four—sesame seeds (*tila*) and the rest—in the *arghya* used for the invocation (*āvāhana*). Furthermore, such an invocation pertains to the worship of mobile images, ritual jars, mandalas, and the like, but not to fixed images;
as it is said: "Or else, [one worships] the embodied Supreme Lord situated in the temple, Viṣṇu, who bears the conch and discus, and has been brought down by gods and *siddhas*."
[The deity] installed by sages or men endowed with devotion should be worshipped in its image with one's own mantra, without the ritual of invocation (āvāhana).

This is because it is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "When [the deity] is present, the state of being face-to-face—that indeed is the invocation of Hari"; and because it is likewise established in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* and the *Pārameśvarasaṃhitā*. (13–18)
One should always visualize [the deity] as having arisen at the end of the offering of water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya);
then, one should worship him with enjoyments appropriate to the time.
During the bathing, anointing, offering of garments and garlands, as well as adorning [the deity],
and likewise during other forms of enjoyment and worship, one should meditate [on the deity] in the lotus posture and so forth.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, that very same [form] appears seated and compassionate before one’s face, even without a physical image, upon any other support. || 21 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with "mantram," he explains the visualization of the different modes of abiding for the deity invoked upon the pedestal, the water-jar, the mandala, and so forth, in accordance with their respective ritual applications. (18–21)
Having entered the reflection by means of its own form as the reflected image, it remains there;
it then assimilates for itself the entire incorporeal power of enjoyment.

In the case of the *bimba* (the divine image), there is no such exertion of contemplation (*bhāvanā-śrama*), for it directly accepts enjoyments in the very form of Brahman; thus he says, "in the form of the *bimba*. And so it is further elaborated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"When the body has been fashioned, [the deity] first remains in that very form;
while enjoyments are being offered, she is the supreme power consisting of the Self (*manmayī*)."
"In that regard, one should remember that [devotion] as being directly present, just as Hari accepts it.
Although this is stated even in the section on the worship of the image (*bimbārcana*) in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"With water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), garments, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and unguents..."
One should meditate upon him as standing there, having been honored again with water for the feet and water for sipping.
(At that time, meditation is described in the Padma Purāṇa:
At the time of bathing, one should sit in the lotus posture or a comfortable posture; for the offering of food, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should sit in the svastika posture.
In other ritual services as well,
the worshipper should meditate on the deity as either standing or seated, according to the specific requirements of each rite.

Thus it has been stated; nevertheless, that [instruction] refers primarily to the worship of the *kumbha* (the ritual jar) and so forth. Alternatively, it should be understood as referring primarily to the meditation on the *bimba* (the image) itself in that manner, and not—as in the case of the *kumbha* and other vessels—as being primarily the meditation on the Lord alone residing within them. Regarding this, many specific details required for the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), worship (*arcana*), and so on, which will be described in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*, are to be adopted. || 22 ||
Having offered an excellent seat to the Lord who had been invited,
he likewise provided an ordinary footstool adorned with a soft carpet.
Having offered water for the feet, the arghya, the honey-mixture, and water for sipping,
he [worshipped] himself along with his sons and wife by prostrating with eight limbs.

Now, he describes the offering of the services beginning with the seat in two and a half verses, starting with the word *vinivedya*. Here, setting aside the order of recitation, first the *arghya* (water for honor) is to be offered, then the *pādya* (water for the feet), immediately after that the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping), and then the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture). Among these, the *arghya* is to be placed upon the head of the Blessed One by means of flowers, according to the statement in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The *arghya*, consisting of water from which flowers have been removed, is to be offered on the head with the third [case-ending]."

At that time, the ringing of a bell should also be performed, because it has been stated regarding Īśvara and others: "In the invocation, the *arghya*, the incense, the lamp, and the enjoyment of the food offering," and "Having offered the *arghya* accompanied by the sound of the bell at the head of the mantra. However, the water for the feet (*pādya*) should be given twice, according to the statement in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā: "O best of Brahmins, in the giving of the *pādya*, one should offer it twice at the lotus-feet. Now, the acceptance of the *pādya*, the wiping of the feet, the cloth, and the foot-ointment should also be offered.

The *ācamana* (sipping of water) should be offered three times. Thus it is stated in the *Aniruddhasaṃhitā*: "One should offer the *ācamana* three times and touch [the mouth] once after reflecting. At that time, meditation is also prescribed in the *Pādma*: "At the time of giving the *ācamanīya*, one should meditate upon the Teacher of the World as if he were actually receiving the water for sipping."

In this context, the offering of perfumes, flowers, garlands, lamps, and incense immediately after the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), as well as the presentation of betel-leaf (tāmbūla) immediately after the honey-mixture (madhuparka), should be understood as prescribed in the Īśvara-pārameśvara and other scriptures. Accordingly, the mantras for the ritual services beginning with the seat (mantrāsana) are stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Invocation, prostration, rising to greet [the deity] immediately thereafter, the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), the greeting 'Welcome' (svāgata), and the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭhikā)."
The offering of water for honor (arghya), the reception of water for the feet (pādya), the washing of the feet, the touching [of the body],
and the anointing of the feet with water mixed with powdered sandalwood.
The water for sipping (ācamanīya) is for the purpose of receiving and seeing;
the water for rinsing (upasparśana) is for the application of anointing substances such as sandalwood and the like by means of a liquid coating.
A garland of flowers, the offering of incense, the presentation of honey-mixture (madhuparka), camphor, betel leaf... [and so forth]. || 23–24 ||
Immediately after offering [the gift] with a mind full of devotion,
one should then inform the Blessed One, placing both hands upon his feet.

He states the offering of oneself and one's own by saying "with my son," etc. [This is done] by prostrating with eight limbs, which refers to the eight-limbed salutation (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) to be described later. Now, the announcement of the offering of oneself is also stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"I am your slave, O Lord of the World, together with my son, family, and possessions.
I am your servant; command me, and always employ me in what is beneficial. (24–25)
O Lord, I have made manifest for you this excellent bath;
it is a supreme, highly auspicious, and great bathing-seat complete with a footstool.
"Quickly prepare [the place] for bathing out of a desire to show me favor;
then, indeed, provide two bathing seats for the Lord. (27)

Then, with two verses, the Blessed One speaks a request for the purpose of bathing: "Having placed the two hands upon His feet," and so forth; here, the meaning is that the hands are placed separately [on each foot]. Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Having worshipped the Foot of the Primordial God, one should grasp the right foot with the right hand, and then the left foot with the left hand, according to the mantra."
Thus [ends the section] 25–27.
With his head bowed in devotion, he should offer the arghya upon the [deity's] head;
then, having presented a golden vessel adorned with jewels as a recipient for the offering.
One should indeed offer water for the feet from the foot-basin to the two lotus-feet;
then, after that, one should offer a pair of beautiful sandals and a bathing garment.
An excellent vessel filled with fragrant śāli rice for the sake of the Mother,
a mirror with the luster of the full moon, and immediately thereafter, scented water.
Then, for the purpose of washing his hands, he should provide an auspicious footstool;
and thereafter, a tooth-stick for the sake of receiving purification of the mouth.
One should provide a tongue-scraper and indeed a rinsing of the mouth;
thereafter, the water for sipping (ācamana) should be given again, followed immediately by that for the purpose of anointing the body.
Abundant fragrant oil and flour made from wheat and śāli rice,
mixed with the powder of *rajanī* and slightly infused with *padmaka*.
Next, camphor should be given for the purpose of anointing;
immediately thereafter, warm water mixed with salt should be provided for the purpose of bathing.
Sandalwood ground for the purpose of anointing the face and infused with camphor;
and abundant cow-derived products—milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey—for the purpose of bathing. (35)

The author states the services beginning with the bath and the seat through the verses starting with "snānāsanam" and so forth. Here, although the footstool is mentioned after the offering of scented water for the purpose of washing the hands, the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) takes precedence over the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*); therefore, the footstool should be offered immediately after the offering of the bath and the seat. This is because it is stated in the very verse of supplication: "The supreme, most auspicious, and great bath-seat, together with a footstool.
For this very reason, in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, the offering of the footstool is prescribed immediately after the bath and the seat.

Now, one might ask: since the mention of the footstool is observed in both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] following the washing of the hands—in the passage, "But for the purpose of washing the hands, there is then an auspicious footstool"—what is the status of that? It is true. In both those cases, because they present the *Sātvata* verses exactly as they stand, a redundancy is observed. However, in the *Lakṣmītantra*, it says: "Having obtained permission, thereafter [one prepares] the unsurpassed seat for bathing, then the footstool, the *arghya*, and then the reception of the *pādya*."
Water for the feet, sandals, a bathing cloth, a small measure of rice,
a mirror, scented water, and water for washing the hands.
A tooth-stick, water for rinsing the mouth and sipping,
scented oil, and powder made from rice and wheat.
Next, for the purpose of anointing the body, [use] a mixture of turmeric powder slightly infused with lotus;
thereafter, for the purpose of bathing, [use] a paste combined with *khalī*.
"Hot water mixed with sandalwood and moon [scent] is for the purpose of anointment.

Because this is an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the verses of the *Sātvata*, there is no tautology regarding the footstool. Therefore, that repetition does not serve to establish the ritual procedure; rather, it should be understood as being for the sake of completing the verse.

Just as in the *Mānasa* section on the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*) in the *Pārameśvara*, although the statement in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*—“The King of Mantras is in the center of the pericarp; Lakṣmī and the others are in the filaments, etc.”—is established, one accepts the non-contradictory meaning and, setting aside the contradictory status of Lakṣmī and the others, accepts only the status of the Heart-mantra and so forth; in the same way, you, long-lived one, should be satisfied here as well. For this very reason, our venerable grandfather did not mention a footstool after the offering of water for washing the hands in the *Sātvatāmṛta*.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Regarding the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), the *Pārameśvara* states: "And thereafter, for the ritual, one should use a tooth-stick produced from a tree other than the *akṣīra*. In the *Kapiñjala* as well, it says: "One should perform the cleansing of the Lord's teeth with a mango stick. Furthermore, that [tooth-stick] may even be made of gold; this is stated in the second chapter of the *Pārameśvara* itself:
"With [sticks] sixteen finger-breadths long, free from bends and knots..."
"Or likewise with items made of gold and so forth, or with *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and the like.

This refers to the acceptance of the cleansing of the mouth (*mukhaśuddhi-pratigraha*), which means the acceptance of the rinsing of the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa-pratigraha*). The rinsing of the mouth (*mukhaprakṣālana*) means the gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*). Furthermore, after the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) should also be offered, according to the statement in the *Pārameśvara*: "The water for the gargle and the water for sipping, along with betel-leaf perfumed with fragrance. Regarding the oil, which should be abundant and highly fragrant, the method for offering the oil is to be understood as it is explained in detail in the *Samārādhanādhyāya* and the *Mahotsavādhyāya* of the *Pārameśvara*. "Powder of *rajanī*" means turmeric powder.

*Padmaka* is likewise well-known in medical treatises (*vaidyakagrantha*) as a specific fragrant substance used for removing oil and grime. This meaning will be stated very clearly in the chapter on consecration (*pratiṣṭhādhyāya*): "Then, having anointed it as before, one should wash it according to the rule with water from a *camasa* vessel. And *khali* is a substance used as a means for removing dirt. (27–35)
The juice of sugarcane is pleasing to the heart; in its absence, sugar-water, water with *dhātrī* fruit, and immediately thereafter water with *lodhra*, [are recommended]. (36)
Water with red sandalwood, excellent water from the *rajanī* plant, water from the *granthi* leaf, and then water from the *tagara* plant; || 37 ||
Next, water of priyaṅgu, then water of māṃsī, after that water of siddhārthaka, and then water of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhi). || 38 ||
Then there is water with leaves and flowers, as well as water with fruits and seeds;
after that, scented water, and then water with gold and jewels. (39)
Immediately thereafter, the water of the sacred fords and rivers was mixed solely with the water prepared for the purpose of bathing. (40)
O Mahāmati, this should indeed be performed in sequence, accompanied by water for honor (arghya) and flowers, through the method of alternating intervals between the various ablutions.
One should perform the washing and the offering of arghya from the arghya-pitcher.
[One should fill] a jar completely with water, along with turmeric and rice grains.

Now, he describes the method for the ritual bathing with the twenty-five jars of milk and other substances, beginning with the words "gavyam" (cow-derived products) and so forth. *Dhātrīphala* is the *āmalaka* fruit; *lodhra* is white *lodhra*, as Amara states: "The *lālava* is the variegated *lodhra*. *Granthipallava* is *sthauṇeya*; as Amara states: "*Granthiparṇa*, *śuka*, *barha*, *sthauṇeya*, and *kukkuṭa* [are synonyms]. *Tagara* is likewise well known. *Priyaṅgu* is *phalinī*; as Amara states: "*Priyaṅgu*, *phalinī*, and *phalī* [are synonyms]."

Now, one might object: "Is there not also the statement in the Amarakośa, 'The two feminine terms *kaṅgu* and *priyaṅgu* denote [two types of grain],' and since there is no decisive criterion for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*), should not *kaṅgu* alone be understood here? If this is argued, we say no. Because *kaṅgu* is already present in this bathing water used for sowing seeds (*bījavāri*), the word *priyaṅgu* occurring here must be accepted as referring to the *phalinī* plant. This is further supported by the association of the two terms with fragrant substances mentioned both before and after them. *Māṃsī* is *jaṭāmāṃsī*. *Siddhārthaka* is white mustard (*śvetasarṣapa*).

The detailed description of the substances for the waters of all herbs, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, perfumes, and gems is clearly stated in the chapter on bathing (*snapanādhyāya*) in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras], and should be adopted here. Furthermore, the required rites such as the consecration of the jars (*kalaśādhivāsa*) and so forth should also be taken from that very source. In this context, however, the rites of the daily bath (*nityasnāna*), the preliminary offerings (*nityaṅka*), the germinating of seeds (*aṅkura*), and so on, are not to be performed. As it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"In the daily bath, there is neither the tying of the protective thread (*kautuka*) nor the offering of germinating seeds;
the bathing with powders at night is not desired, nor is the construction of a pavilion site."

Because it is stated, "Indeed, [the water] is mixed with the very water prepared for the purpose of bathing," one should add a small amount of bathing water even to the twenty substances such as *dhātrī* fruit and water; for, according to the statement in the *Lakṣmītantra*, "But these waters, combined with bathing water, are to be offered," it is understood that the addition of bathing water applies only to the liquids beginning with *āmalaka*, excluding the pentad of milk and so forth.

The phrase *arghyapuṣpasamanvitam* (accompanied by the offering water and flowers) should be understood as an adjective for the word *kṣālanam* (washing), since these very verses are also set forth in the *Pārameśvara*. In certain ritual applications, with the intention that the phrase *arghyapuṣpasamanvitam* qualifies the substances for bathing, it is stated that one should pour a little water from the bathing jar (*snānīyakalaśa*) and a flower from the *arghya* vessel into the substance jars (*dravyakalaśa*). That [interpretation] contradicts the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa-lakṣmītantra*, because therein, beginning with "Milk, curd, and cow's ghee... [the procedure is described differently].
Gold, jewels, rivers, sacred fords, and pure water, respectively.
These waters, together with the water for bathing, should be offered;
likewise, the *arghya* water from the *arghya* vessel should be offered at intervals between the baths.
"One should offer a cleansing with water containing flowers from time to time.

Thus, the presence of flowers is made a qualification of the cleansing water. "Accompanied by the *arghya* flower" means together with the flowers that have been cast into the *arghya* vessel for the purpose of worship. Here, it is stated that among the various ablutions with jars of milk and so forth, there should be an intermediate bathing with *arghya* water and the simple offering of *arghya*. If one has the means, offerings such as garments should also be given. As it is said in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara*:
"For each substance, however, [one should perform] the touching of the *arghya* with a cloth, [and likewise] with perfumes and garlands."
Having worshipped with incense, one should then perform the consecration with that [water];
likewise, the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), as well as perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps.
"One should offer everything in due order, or only the *arghya* alone.
Now, one might ask: "If, during the bathing of a large image, the *arghya* water is insufficient for the secondary bath (*upasnāna*), what is the solution? True;
at that time, by means of jars filled with pure water joined together without intervals.
One should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) and the offering of the *arghya* water for the substances;

indeed, the procedure for these has already been stated in the chapter on bathing (*snapanādhyāya*) of the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*. As for the consecration mantras for these twenty-five jars, they are found in the section on the *Damanaka* festival of the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*, beginning with "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇa," while the preceding jar [is treated] as before.
Of him who is established within meditation, by means of the second jar, however—
Then again, with the third jar, [one recites] "Nārāyaṇa";
then again, with the fourth, [one recites] "Nārāyaṇa."
With the mantra "The thousand-headed Puruṣa," [he should worship] from the fifth pitcher;
with "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self," indeed from the sixth pitcher.
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman" is indeed from the seventh [verse],
while "Whatever exists in this world" is from the eighth pitcher.
With the ninth [verse], "anantam avyayaṃ kaviṃ," one should perform the consecration;
with the tenth, "adho niṣṭyā vitastyām tu," it should indeed be so.
The continuous [channel] is indeed by means of the vessels; with the eleventh, however, is "laṃ";
and in its center, with the twelfth, is indeed "mahānagniḥ."
"He torments his own body" is indeed by the thirteenth [verse],
and "standing in the midst of dark clouds" is indeed by the fourteenth.
"In the middle of that crest" is indeed with the fifteenth [verse],
and "the god who is the controller of all" is indeed with the sixteenth.
One should perform the consecration with the vases situated in the outer enclosure;
however, if there are none in the outer enclosure, one should do so with those previously stationed [in the inner enclosure].
That which arose from the navel-lotus is [the fire];
by applying the vertical *puṇḍra* with the mantra residing in the fire, one attains the supreme state when situated in the southern direction.
On his right arm, O Brahmin, Viṣṇu, having gone there,
said "iti" (thus), while Varuṇa, stationed on the left, said "aśnantīti" (they eat).
"Viṣṇu is the Lord whose primary nature is masculine," [he said] by means of that which pertains to Vāyu;
"this is the Great Upaniṣad," [he said] by means of that which pertains to Soma.
"Oṃ" is the first name, associated with Īśāna;
"I am the Puruṣa Vāsudeva" is the one associated with the center.
Or else, having consecrated [the deity] with the sixteen mantras of the Puruṣasūkta in their proper order by means of the jars situated in the outer enclosure;
Having performed the ritual ablution in sequence with the previously mentioned mantras residing in the Brahma-sūtra, using pairs of jars situated within the inner enclosure.

And at the end, one should sprinkle with the remaining three [verses] using the central pitcher. Thus it is said. Here, the meaning is that [one sprinkles] with the sixteen mantras previously mentioned from the Brahma-sūkta, beginning with "The thousand-headed one" (*sahasraśīrṣam*) and ending with "O Brahmin, on the right arm. By the count of two each, this means with two mantras at a time. With the remaining three, [the verses] beginning with "Viṣṇu eats what has been eaten" (*viṣṇunāttamaśnantīti*). Furthermore, there are twenty-three mantras belonging to the Mahopaniṣad, beginning with "Verily, Nārāyaṇa was alone" (*eko ha vai nārāyaṇaḥ*) and ending with "He who [knows] this Great Upaniṣad" (*ya imāṃ mahopaniṣadam*).

In this regard, it should be understood that the *Brahmasūkta*, consisting of nineteen verses beginning with "The Puruṣa of a thousand heads" and ending with "He who [knows] this Great Upaniṣad," is what is intended. Now, one might ask: since these verses beginning with "The controller of all" are not seen in the manuscripts of the *Mahopaniṣad*, how can they be considered part of the *Mahopaniṣad*? This is true; however, this doubt has been refuted in the *Siddhāntacandrikā*, which defends the practice of wearing the *taptamudrā*. For instance, in the *Pādmapurāṇa*, it is stated: "Especially for Brāhmaṇas residing in any of the stages of life (āśramas)..."
Indeed, the Vaiṣṇava discus must be worn according to the prescribed rite, as enjoined by the sacred injunctions.
A Brahmin should indeed bear the Sudarśana on his right arm, and he should bear the conch on his left; thus do those who know the Veda understand.

Thus, the meaning is that the wearing of the *cakras* and so forth is proclaimed in the *Mahopaniṣad*. If it is asked, "How can this be considered *śruti* (Vedic revelation), given that this mantra is not seen in modern editions of the *Mahopaniṣad*?"—the answer is no, because it is found in ancient manuscripts. Its absence in modern manuscripts is to be attributed to scribal errors and the like. It is not only this particular mantra that is not seen in modern manuscripts; rather, the entire eight-verse *Brahmasūkta*, beginning with "The controller of all" (*nāyameva mantra*), is not seen there. And yet, this mantra is indeed heard within the *Brahmasūkta*.
Nor does the status of being a *śruti* (Vedic scripture) suffer by that much, because the *Brahmasūkta* is cited in many passages throughout the scriptures of the Blessed One (*bhagavacchāstra*).

If it is objected: "Since it was stated here that only the eight-verse *Brahmasūkta* is seen [in those texts], it is understood that only the eight mantras beginning with 'sarvasya vaśinam' constitute the *Brahmasūkta*. How then can you claim that the nineteen mantras beginning with 'sahasraśīrṣam' also constitute the *Brahmasūkta*?"—we reply: We have stated this in accordance with the *Saccaritrarakṣā*.

For in that context, it is stated: "Here too, the *Brahmasūkta* consisting of nineteen mantras, as recited in the *Mahopaniṣad*, is precisely what is adopted from both the *Brahmasūkta* and the *Paramātmasūkta*. In the first mantra of the *Mahopaniṣad*, one should know that there are two readings: "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇaḥ" and "Eka eva nārāyaṇaḥ. (34–42)
Then, having placed in one hand that [vessel] which has been smeared with perfumes and the like and adorned with garlands and so forth, and in the other hand a small bowl (mallaka), || 43 ||
Having whirled it while it emits smoke from white mustard seeds, one should cast it outside over the head;
then, having offered a well-washed, new cloth.

Next, he describes the procedure for the rite of royal ablution (*rājanavidhi*) following the bath with two verses beginning with *saṃpūrṇam*. In the phrase *saṃpūrṇam*, the word *snānīyaśeṣeṇa* (with the remainder of the bathing water) is to be supplied. Thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Filled with the water remaining from the bath. It is also stated in the *Īśvaratantra* and the *Pārameśvaratantra*: "Then, with the remainder of the bathing water, [one should wash] that which is fashioned from gold and other materials. *Mallaka* means a shallow bowl. "In one hand" means in the left hand; "in the other" means in the right hand.

From the statement that it is smoking due to the *siddhārtha* seeds, its being enveloped by fire is understood. In this context, the fire from the incense vessel (*dhūpapātra*) alone is to be supplied. Regarding the phrase "waving over the head," it means waving [the vessel] all around the head of the Blessed One; and that is done only once. "Outside" means outside of the great door (*mahādvāra*). Thus, it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Having placed that [incense vessel] in the left hand, and another [flower vessel] filled with a profusion of flowers and joined with the fire of the incense vessel."
Having once whirled [the offering] over the head of the God of gods, together with white mustard seeds or incense materials that are emitting smoke.
"One should dismiss [the deity] at the outer door by means of a person who has been initiated and is intent on service, or even by a pure woman. Thus it is said.
It has already been stated that the offering of the lustration (*nīrājana*), the water for honor (*arghya*), and so forth is not the primary subject here; one should perform those at that very time.
However, at the conclusion of the ritual bath, one should engage in the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures.
One should always avoid performing worship with offerings such as the *arghya* during that [bath] occasion. Thus it is said.

Thus, the performance of the *nīrājana* rite is also to be carried out during occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) worship; this is its purpose. Now, it is stated that its performance may take place either at the conclusion of the offerings of ornaments and the seat, or in both cases: "O Brahmin, it is likewise performed in the daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) worship."
Finally, for the sake of pacifying all defects and for the sake of all protection, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord with bathing materials and offerings.
"One should provide the enjoyments mentioned for the ornaments and the throne, or at least some of them;

or one may do so in both cases according to one's wealth and desire. Furthermore, it should be understood that the vessel used for the *nīrājana* at the end of the bath is to be filled with the *arghya* water or with pure water alone, because it is said: "Either with the water drawn from the *arghya* vessel, or again with pure filtered water. (42–44)
Two other garments, perfumed with scents and incense, are used for wiping the body and removing the water from it— one to be worn below and the other above.

Now, with the verse beginning "sudhautaṃ" (44–45), he describes the offering of two garments for the purpose of touching the limbs, followed by the offering of the lower garment (*antarīya*) and the upper garment (*uttarīya*).

Having purified another location beyond the part of the water-channel, starting from the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), with many jars of water, and having caused [the image] to descend there— || 46 ||
If the image of the Blessed One, together with its pedestal, or even without it, has been worshipped,
one should visualize the deity as merged into space and wash [the vessel] completely clean once again.

He describes the purification of the *bhadrāsana* with two verses beginning with "from the part of the spout" (*praṇālabhāgāt*). "From the part of the spout" means from that portion of the spout—which is characterized by its specific dimensions according to the method stated in the second chapter as "the makara-mouthed spout is marked by its measure"—and which serves the purpose of discharging the water for the consecration and other rites. "From the *bhadrāsana*" means from the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*). "The other place" means the entire area of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), excluding the auspicious throne.

Having purified [the area] with many jars of abundant water and having washed it, one should—meaning one should place—the image of the Blessed One, which was situated on the bathing throne, onto a seat upon that purified spot. It follows from the context that one should also wash the *bhadrāsana*. Since the image of the Blessed One is situated upon the *bhadrāsana*, the sense is that one should first wash the entire area, then place the image elsewhere upon a seat, and finally wash the *bhadrāsana* as well.

If it is worshipped without that [statue] and without an image—that is, if it is worshipped upon the pedestal alone, according to the manner previously stated as "in the middle of the site of the *bhadrapīṭha*, or on a perfectly smooth [surface] alone"—then one should contemplate the deity as "floating in the sky," meaning one should meditate on him as situated in space. Because he is situated above [the shrine], one should wash everything completely; the meaning is that one should wash the location of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) and the *bhadrapīṭha* all at once.

The sense is that, since the Blessed One is seated upon the *bhadrāsana* itself during meditation, its cleansing is impossible. This has been stated likewise in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Then one should purify the *bhadrāsana* with full jars, and one should meditate on Hari as submerged in space. In explaining the meaning in this way, the qualification "from the part of the *praṇāla*" would serve no purpose; therefore, another meaning is described. To wit: "from the *bhadrāsana*" means "belonging to the *bhadrāsana*."

"From the part of the water-channel" (praṇālabhāgāt) means from the part immediately adjacent to the water-channel. Regarding "another location" (aparasthānam), having washed and purified the entire other area—that is, the area where the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) is located—and having brought down the image onto that cleansed spot, one should also wash the part of the water-channel. Everything else is exactly as previously stated. If the reading is "the location of the auspicious seat" (sthānaṃ bhadrāsanasya tu), this meaning should be understood as the most natural one. These same two verses were also spoken by Īśvara and Pārameśvara.

Therefore, it has been written in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*: "If [the deity] is worshipped without the *bimba* (the original image) in items such as a broom (*kūrca*) or a mirror, even for those who possess only the vessels, this very [method] is the logical one, [resulting in] 'merging into the void' (*khapluta*). That is inconsistent, because even the broom, the mirror, and so forth are worthy of being established elsewhere. || 46-47 ||
Furthermore, four jars should be filled with fragrant water;
except for the bathing jar, the ritual arrangement for the others should be performed as previously described.

He speaks again of the preparation of the *arghya* and so forth with the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*). Since here only the preparation of the *arghya* and so forth is mentioned once more, it is understood that even for the bath and the seat, one should offer the *arghya* and so forth using exactly those *arghya* substances already prepared for the mantra-seat and other stages. In this way, it should be understood that the *arghya* and so forth prepared for the ornament-seat and others are also utilized for the enjoyment-seat and so forth, because it is appropriate to prepare the *arghya* and so forth again in those cases.

Here, by the statement that "apart from the bathing jar (*snānakumbha*), the other four jars for the *arghya* and so forth are to be filled with scented water," the installation of the five jars—beginning with the *arghya* jar—on the mantra-seat and elsewhere is established.

If it is objected: "But in that [text] only four jars are mentioned," we reply: True; we too acknowledge this. Nevertheless, the installation of the second *arghya* jar, which is to be described in the eighteenth chapter, is also intended there; otherwise, the four jars would not be established here apart from the bathing jar.

But surely you are ignorant of the meaning of the *saṃhitā* passage! His intention is as follows: the four jars should indeed be filled as before; however, it should be understood that the mental construction (*kalpanā*) for the other three—excluding the bathing jar—should take the form "I mentally prepare the *arghya*" and so forth. If this is argued, we say no, because filling the primary bathing jar [only] would be improper.

Furthermore, although both Īśvara and Pārameśvara explicitly state in their own words that five jars (kumbha-pañcaka) are to be established, they say only: "The four jars should be filled again with fragrant water. In the context of your intended meaning, it should have been stated that "the five jars are to be filled," yet it was not stated thus.

But one might object: why is there such strict necessity regarding the intention of Īśvara and Pārameśvara? For in the section on mental enjoyment and sacrifice in the *Pārameśvara*, although it would have been appropriate to state, "Lakṣmī and the others [should be placed] upon the filaments and so forth," the statement from the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* alone—"Lakṣmī and the others [should be placed] upon the filaments and so forth"—was actually set forth. If you ask, "Why should it not be the same here as well?", the answer is: true.

In that context, although it is stated in the section on the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) that "Lakṣmī and the others [are worshipped] on the filaments and so forth," even in the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*), only the worship of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and the others is prescribed; likewise, nowhere else is it stated that the five jars (*kumbhapañcaka*) are to be filled. || 48 ||
Then, having brought the Blessed One into the center and offered him a seat,
[he beheld] the Supreme Lord seated there upon the third throne, inlaid with jewels.
Having meditated upon [the deity] adorned with devotion, and having worshipped him thoroughly with offerings such as garlands and sandalwood paste,
one should immediately worship the two sandals with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for washing the feet (pādya).

Now, he describes the offering of ornaments and the seat with the verse beginning "having brought down into the center" (49–50). Having visualized the Supreme Lord seated there, adorned with enjoyments such as garlands and sandalwood paste, one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose—this is the implied meaning. Alternatively, in the phrase "adorned," it should be understood that the future sense is intended, meaning "about to be adorned. (49–50)
Water for sipping (ācamana) should be offered again, as well as a footstool;
and having anointed [the deity] with fragrant substances such as sandalwood paste out of devotion, [one should proceed].
He fanned himself with a spread peacock-feather fan,
arranged his hair, groomed his beard, and prepared his flowers and betel with a pair of scissors.
Having offered two white silk garments to the God of gods,
he should immediately thereafter offer a sacred thread along with an upper garment, a crown, and so forth.
There was excellent and variegated ornamentation extending as far as the anklets on her feet, and a diverse head-garland adorned with loose flowers. (54)
Then one should give a beautiful bracelet, bound with garlands and cords from the ears down to the feet, and thereafter a protective amulet-thread (pratisara).
It is variegated with mineral pigments such as saffron and the like, made from white thread,
filled with soft cotton, and knotted at intervals.
Collyrium with its applicator stick, betel leaf perfumed with fragrances, a golden tilaka-mark for the forehead, and mouth-perfume that brightens the countenance. (57)
There was an earring-flower, a great circular mirror,
and a rampart radiant with variegated flowers and blazing with the luster of jewels.
One should burn auspicious guggulu incense, combined with refined incense,
accompanied by the pleasant sounds of bells and by [the image] being moved with the arm.
Sandals, a white umbrella, a palanquin, and whatever else such as a chariot,
along with vehicles up to an elephant, accompanied by banners and the Garuda emblem on the flagstaff.
Furthermore, the white and black chowries, as well as the knowledge of the measures, are for the purpose of fulfilling these secondary enjoyments. (61)
Accompanied by the sounds of victory from kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and other instruments, along with various songs, dances, and the playing of stringed instruments. || 62 ||
He should worship with hymns, mantras, prostrations, and circumambulations;
indeed, he should offer a footstool and a seat for the meal to the Lord.

He states the secondary offerings (anupacāra) to be presented on the ornament-seat (*alaṅkārāsana*) in the passage beginning with "having worshipped well with water for honor and water for the feet" and ending with "worshipped with prostrations and circumambulations. In the phrase "with sandalwood and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes saffron and other such substances; thus, the *Pārameśvara* states: "Anointing with rubbed saffron, musk, and animal oils. Furthermore, the fanning should be understood as being for the purpose of drying the moist fragrance; likewise, the *Lakṣmītantra* says: "Sandalwood and other fragrant substances, and fanning for the purpose of drying."

*Keśaprasādaka* refers to a *kūrca*, meaning a comb; as it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The *vivecana* of the hair is its cleansing with a comb. *Puṣpatāmbūlakartarī* means a pair of scissors for flowers and betel. *Muktapuṣpasamanvitam* means accompanied by loose, unstrung flowers—meaning, together with the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Thus, the *Pārameśvara* states: "Then one should offer loose flowers according to the season. And in the *Lakṣmītantra* as well: "Ornaments such as crowns and so forth should be offered to the Supreme Self."
Garlands of various forms were fashioned from flowers of a pure, sattvic nature.

"A handful of flowers [should be offered] at the pair of feet with heaps of blossoms from the enclosure wall. Thus, *pratisara* means a purifying thread (*pavitra*). "With minerals" (*dhātubhiḥ*) means with red ochre and the like; "with saffron and the like" (*kuṅkumādibhiḥ*) means with saffron, turmeric, gorocana, and so forth. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*:
"Or else, with turmeric and gorocana, or with the minerals for the purifying threads (*pavitra*)."

O Brahmins, someone should duly wrap the knots with soft cotton; this is an indication for gold, gems, and so forth, since the filling of the interior with gold, gems, and the like is also prescribed in the case of the *īśvara* (the presiding deity) and others. "Mukhavāsa" means that by which the mouth is perfumed; it refers to camphor. "Rocana" means together with *gorocana*. "Prākāra" [should be adorned] with variegated flowers; "resplendent with the luster of jewels" means shining with its own radiance resembling that of jewels. Here, other qualifying attributes mentioned in the case of the *īśvara* and others should also be understood as applicable.
With many large-flamed lamps filled with sesame oil and clarified butter,
"Immediately thereafter, one should worship with [incense] made of unbleached, fresh, pure white [resin], wrapped in wicks, and knotted with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients.

This means it should be combined with refined incense, or mixed with incense such as *agaru* (sandalwood) and so forth. The addition of camphor is also prescribed for the Lord and others: "Abundant, fragrant, sweet, and mixed with camphor powder. In this context, mixing with clarified butter (*ājya*) should also be performed, because it will be stated in the *Samayapariccheda*: "For the purpose of incense, *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter should be offered, or another substance if that is unavailable. The phrase "prepared by the moving arm" implies that they are fashioned [into sticks] by the hand.

In this context, it should be understood that both the lamp and the incense must be accompanied by the ringing of a bell; for it is stated regarding the Lord and others: "At the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the incense, the lamp, and the enjoyment of the food offering. The term *vāhana* means a vehicle made of gold or other materials. Thus, it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The lamp, the incense, the vehicle, and the sentient [deity], as well as the insentient. *Mātrāvitta* refers to wealth (*draviṇa*) intended for the purpose of *mātrā*, where *mātrā* is that which is measured, delimited, or fulfilled.

This means [the enjoyment] of lamps and the like, which produce joy for the eyes, and of praises, instrumental music, and songs, which produce joy for the ears. These very enjoyments are explained in the *Lakṣmītantra* as being "visible" (*sāṃdṛṣṭika*) and "based on conceit" (*ābhimānika*). For it is said:
"Those by which pleasure is produced through sight alone are considered 'visible' (*sāṃdṛṣṭika*)."
Those auspicious and magnificent objects, such as lamps,
vehicles, and the like, as well as enjoyments that produce merit and satisfy one with flavors, are likewise beneficial.
Those [offerings] such as water for sipping and water for rinsing the mouth are called *ābhyavahārika*;
they consist of pleasant, delightful, and soft-to-the-touch objects which satisfy the Unborn One with enjoyments.
Those enjoyments consisting of touch— preceded by water for the feet, the guest-offering, and a seat—
as well as perfumes, may be either tactile or edible.
The winds and other elements are established [therein], while the last ones possess the scent born of transformation;
for those enjoyments consisting of sound, such as hymns, instrumental music, and song, are indeed composed of sound.
"And those [practitioners] characterized by wretchedness, joined palms, and so forth, are known as those who are conceited (*ābhimānika*).
Thus, through these four kinds of enjoyments (*bhoga*) by way of the path seen in the scriptures.

In this context, however, within the section on the festival of purification (*pavitrôtsava*), since only a threefold division of enjoyment will be stated—namely, as *aupacārika* (symbolic), *sāṃsparśika* (tactile), and *ābhyavahārika* (ingestible)—the term *aupacārika* itself includes the enjoyments described in the *Lakṣmītantra* as *sāṃdṛṣṭika* (visual) and *ābhimānika* (conceited). Furthermore, in this passage, the phrase "of the *aupacārika* enjoyments" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that stands for the *sāṃsparśika* enjoyments as well.

For in this very context, it will be stated that "the knowledge of the measures (mātrāvitta) indeed fulfills the objects of sensory contact (sāṃsparśika-bhoga)," thus establishing that the knowledge of the measures fulfills the objects of sensory contact. For this same reason, in the *Pārameśvara*, it is further elaborated that "for the sake of fulfilling all enjoyments, O best of the twice-born," thereby confirming that the knowledge of the measures fulfills all enjoyments.

Moreover, in the section on the Purifiers (*pavitra-prakaraṇa*), it will also state that there is another measure which fills the gaps in the metaphorical enjoyments (*aupacārika-bhoga*): "The seeds of the metaphorical enjoyments have indeed been prescribed."

The time for taking this mere seed-measure (*bījamātra*) has been stated in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] as being immediately after the offering of the cow-measure (*gomātrā*) which is a constituent part of the *madhuparka*, while seated upon the seat of the *bhojya*. Furthermore, the seeds to be taken should be cultivated (*grāmya*), because it is stated in that very same *Mahāhavis* section: "The *madhuparka*, the cow-measure, and the seeds to be cultivated are in the west. The term "seeds to be cultivated" refers to seeds whose production is accomplished through human effort, such as plowing and so forth; the meaning is that wild (*āraṇyaka*) seeds do not require such accomplishment through effort. The procedure to be followed in the event that seeds are unavailable is also stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"But even when seeds are not available, a single fruit is recommended;
or else, one of the seeds may be used according to the requirements of that particular time."

The details regarding their measurements and so forth should be consulted in that very [text] where they are explained at length. A *taṇḍulamātrā* (a measure of rice) is to be given at the very time of offering the *dravyamātrā* (a measure of wealth), because it is not mentioned elsewhere. The author will state the difference in timing for the *gomātrā* (a measure of cow) and *tilamātrā* (a measure of sesame) right here. However, in the *Lakṣmītantra*, by the use of the plural number in the statement, "And the measures (*mātrās*) filled with jewels, which fill the gaps in one's enjoyments," it is understood that all four—the *dravyamātrā*, *taṇḍulamātrā*, *bījamātrā*, and *tilamātrā*—are to be given simultaneously.
In the *Pārameśvara*, it is established that the *śālimātrā* is restricted solely to the act of bathing:
"The *śālimātrā* should not be performed in a sacrifice that is devoid of the bathing rite."

"Other measures (mātrā) should be prescribed for every rite of worship. For this very reason, even in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the measure of rice (*śāli-mātrā*) is prescribed specifically for the bath and the seat, whereas the measure of cow-products (*go-mātrā*) is mentioned after the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). However, in the *Pādmapurāṇa*, all of them are prescribed at once:
"sesame seeds, cloth, gold, betel-leaf, and also rice."
Fruits, the clarified butter from cow's milk, cows, grain, and wealth as it may be.
"One should offer this morsel of cow's food to the preceptor in the presence of the deity.
This means [one should do so] with hymns and mantras such as "jitaṃ te" and others. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"O Great-minded one, one should perform the recitation of hymns and mantras beginning with 'jitaṃ te'."
It should be presented both individually and collectively, especially when joined with appropriate statements.
Thus [ends the section] from verses 50 to 63.
It was covered with an excellent *asūraka* cloth made of fine linen and cotton;
then, pure and fragrant water for worship was prepared in a vessel.
Immediately thereafter, [he should offer] madhuparka consisting of curd, honey, and ghee;
then cool water for satiation, and the powder mentioned previously.
To effect the removal of the male organ, the Lord should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
having offered a cow that is well-adorned, beautiful in form, and decorated with garlands.
Then there was abundant food offering, consisting of many kinds of eatables and edibles;
all the flavors beginning with the sweet, as well as vegetables along with fruits and roots.
One should offer pure and sweet beverages like the *madhuparka*,
and one should provide all the water required for sipping (*ācamana*) as well as the water for respectful reception (*arhaṇa*).
Then sesame seeds, excellent jewels, and betel leaf;

furthermore, he describes the services for food and seating with the words beginning "with a footstool" (*sapādapīṭham*), etc. [The phrase] "with a choice cushion made of fine silk or cotton" means with a soft covering made of silk or similar material spread over it. "Water for honor" (*arhaṇajalam*) means the water for the *āpośana* rite which is a constituent part of the *madhuparka*, or the primary water for the *arghya* offering prepared in a vessel and set aside in a separate bowl.

And so he will state in the section on the application of the primary *arghya* within the chapter on the preliminary consecration (*dīkṣādhivāsa*): "With that water, one should perform the honoring (*ārhaṇa*) as well as the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). Regarding the phrase "joined with curds, honey, and ghee," milk should also be added, because it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "For the purpose of the *madhuparka*, auspicious items such as curds and milk are not [excluded]. The water for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is the drinking water intended for satisfaction after the offering of the *madhuparka*.

That too is indeed the water for the primary *arghya* offering, because the application of the primary *arghya* will be stated later in the words, "one should perform the taking after pouring forth. "Pouring forth" (*praṇayana*) means sprinkling into another vessel; "taking" (*ādāna*) means grasping it after that act. This has been clearly elaborated in the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*: "Having established the satisfaction [of the deity] and having perfumed it with the *arghya* water. The "powder" mentioned previously refers to the powder for rubbing the body (*udvartana-cūrṇa*), which was mentioned in the context of the bathing seat.

For the purpose of castration and for the purpose of rubbing the hands; having offered a cow—this offering of a cow should be understood as being for the purpose of filling the deficiencies in the *madhuparka*. And thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Afterwards, water for sipping (ācamana) should be given, along with the measure of a cow belonging to the *madhuparka*. Following this measure of the cow, the measure of the seed (*bīja*) should be offered. This is because it is established in the case of Īśvara and others that: "One should first offer the herbs beginning with *śāli*, the tree rich in garlands and fruits, and the [divine] form."

"Abundant" means copious. "Naivedya" refers to the eightfold oblation consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other offerings. "Edibles" (*bhakṣyāṇi*) are cakes (*apūpa*), and "foodstuffs" (*bhojyāni*) are fruits. Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Edibles are those beginning with cakes; foodstuffs are fruits; lickables are those beginning with honey; suckables are mangoes and the like; drinkables are those beginning with milk, accompanied by after-drinks. By the phrase "all flavors, sweet and so forth," it is indicated that all six flavors are fit for offering to the Blessed One.
Even though [the rice] is prepared solely from the grains of unhusked *vrīhi* rice.
Food sprinkled with milk and clarified butter, combined with molasses, sugar-candy, and fruit,
and prepared without alkaline salt, is called the sacrificial oblation for the gods.

Thus, it has been stated that only sweet-tasting food is fit for the deity; nevertheless, this should be understood as applying only to the context of vows (vrata) and sacrifices (yajña), since elsewhere it is taught that all tastes whatsoever are to be offered. Accordingly, it is said in the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*: "For the sake of peace, during vows and sacrifices, one should prepare the supreme oblation (havis)—cooked without pungent salt, and provided with jaggery, milk, and fruit."

The discrimination between what is acceptable and what is unacceptable among vegetables, fruits, and roots; the rules for preparing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); the preparation of beverages and the like; and the various methods of offering these to Īśvara and other deities—all this should be understood as explained in detail [in the scriptures]. An offering consisting of even a mere sesame seed and a jewel should be presented in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials. Thus it is said: "In the case of Īśvara, [the offering may consist of] sesame seeds, or else fine jewels, or else [sesame] in a golden or silver [vessel]."
"Having placed it in a vessel for the sake of the measure, one should then offer it to the God. Thus [it is said].
Betel-leaf, perfumed with cloves, nutmeg, cardamom, cinnamon, and camphor.
It was abundant, provided with nutmegs and betel nuts, and possessed many fragrant leaves.
Mixed with camphor powder and blended with pearl powder,
it is accompanied by citron fruit and provided with coconut fruit.
And at the end, bowing down, one should offer betel leaf to the Lord of the World.

The object of knowledge (jñeya) should be understood as having the characteristics thus described. The word "again" (punaḥ) is used because betel had already been offered previously upon the seat of the ornament. (63–69)
Having smeared his hands with fragrant substances, he should then perform the binding of the mudrās.
Having clearly joined the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers from both hands in pairs, with their tips turned away from each other, they should be brought together.
From the roots to the tips of the nails, with continuous effort, one should likewise place the remaining fingers and thumbs upon the upturned palms.
By means of the lower-and-upper union, likewise on the left and right;
having extended the index finger upwards and the thumb facing it, [one should join them]. || 72 ||
Having established [the deity] in the region of the heart, one should then perform the recitation (*japa*).

Regarding the characteristics of the binding of the *mudrās*, [the text] begins with "smeared with fragrance" (*gandhadigdhau*) and ends with "should be performed" (*kāryā*). Here, prior to the application of the paste to the hands, one should wash the hands with the water of the second *arghya* offering; after the application of the fragrance, one should perform the mutual worship of the two hands with that same *arghya*. For it is stated in both the *Īśvarapārameśvara* and the *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]: "In the binding of the *mudrās*, there is the sprinkling of the hands, as well as their washing and their worship," thus specifying the use of the second *arghya*. The same applies to the section on the binding of the *mudrās*.
Having indeed washed both hands with fragrant water drawn from the *arghya* vessel, they shall become clear and utterly stainless.
Having purified them with offerings of food, incense-bowls, and other vessels,
and having smeared them with excellent fragrances, they should honor one another with the *arghya* offering.

"Having displayed the mudrās for the root and other mantras in their proper sequence"—thus it has been clearly stated. As for the method of binding the mudrā: having joined the pair of middle and ring fingers very clearly back-to-back from the base to the tips of the nails so that they are continuous with one another; then, having placed the two index fingers and the two little fingers in successive order on the left and right of the upturned palms; and finally, having extended the two thumbs forward toward the [index fingers], one should place this mudrā upon the heart.
This should be known as the root mudrā of the arrays (vyūha). || 69-73 ||
With a crystal rosary, or with the joints of one's own fingers. || 73 ||

At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed worship with perfumes and incense according to one's desired number along with the best of garlands, one should then [worship] those who consist of the Blessed One.
Having worshipped them in due order and presented the food offering (naivedya), one should then satisfy them in the fire with oblations ending with the *mātrā* syllables.

Regarding the recitation (*japa*), he says "atha" (now). In the phrase "with a crystal rosary," one should understand that the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites for the rosary beads have been explained in accordance with the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* in relation to Īśvara and the other [deities]. Regarding the phrase "or with one's own fingers," a specific rule is stated in the *Pāñcarātrarakṣā*:
"O Lord of Devas, beginning from the base of the little finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the ring finger, one should perform a million-fold recitation."

The difference in the fruits of recitation (japa) according to its divisions—vocal and so forth—is stated in the Lakṣmītantra: "Vocal recitation is for the sake of minor rites; whispered recitation is for the rite of accomplishment;
mental recitation bestows liberation and fortune; and that which consists of meditation brings about all perfections."

At the conclusion of the *japa*, he again describes the services to the Blessed One with the words "with garlands," and then states the rule for the presentation of gifts with the word "then. "Consisting of the Blessed One" means belonging to the *bhāgavatas*, that is to say, the *pāñcarātrikas*. Here, by the use of the plural number, four are intended. Thus he will state in the fourteenth chapter: "Having spoken thus and having duly honored the four *pāñcarātrikas*."

Regarding the phrase "having worshipped thoroughly," it should be understood that this is done with *arghya*, perfumes, flowers, and incense. Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Then, indeed, having worshipped with *arghya*, [perfume], flowers, and incense. Regarding the offering of the food (*naivedya*), the meaning is that one should give one portion out of the four parts into which it has been divided. Accordingly, the *Pārameśvara* states: "At the time of the initial offering, however, having divided that into four parts—the *prāpaṇa*, the *madhuparka*, and other types of food—"

"One should give to them one portion, preceded by the offering water (*arghyodaka*). The phrase "ending with the *mātrā*" means ending with the giving of the *mātrā*. Accordingly, it is said in that very same [text]: "One should cause the fourfold *mātrā* to be given to the Ācārya. "Fourfold" means distinguished by the different types of rice grains, seeds, and sesame. It should be understood that whereas previously the *mātrā* substances were those already offered to the Blessed One, now their distribution to the devotees (*bhāgavatas*) is performed separately. It was stated by the Lord that if the giving of the *mātrā* to the Ācārya had been performed at the very time of the offering to the Blessed One, there should be no further [separate] giving now.

"Or rather, having given them [the offerings] up to the *tanmātras* at the conclusion of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), one should present [to them] everything from the guest-offering (*arhaṇa*) up to the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) at this time.
For those who act in this manner, even their worship must be performed with the mantras of the Lord, just like the worship of the Lord himself. And so it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Then, having invited gurus— whether they are identical with me (Manmaya) or Vaiṣṇavas—
one should offer [the gift] for their satisfaction while reciting my mantra.
Thus, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the offering made by one who acts in this way is stated to be the fifth ancillary limb (*aṅga*).
From the internal sacrifice of the mental organ up to the offering of one's own self.

O Sage, that which is called *abhigamana* is the first limb of the sacrifice; it consists of the great worship with offerings such as water for the hands (*arghya*) and flowers, along with all other articles of enjoyment.
Know that, O Nārada, worship performed with external offerings,
such as that which is done with curds mixed with honey and clarified butter, or with an animal sacrifice, is designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga).
O Sage, the third limb of the sacrifice is indeed the fourth: the worship with food, which consists of the giving away of what has been offered according to the previously mentioned rule.
The fifth is known as the *saṃpradāna*, which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice;
the sixth is the propitiation of the fire (*vahnisaṃtarpaṇa*), and the seventh is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyāga*).
"The offering into the fire of the vital breaths by name is the eighth, namely the concluding sacrifice (anuyāga).
Thus [ends verses 73–75].
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) purified by valid means of knowledge, auspicious, conforming to one's wealth, provided with four enclosures, and adorned with a thumb-mark; || 76 ||
The width of the excavation is prescribed as either one-third or one-half [of its depth];
it may be circular, shaped like a discus, a conch, or a lotus, or it may be square.
Or else, it may be marked with the emblems beginning with the mace and ending with the discus.
Now, describing the sixth limb, the satiation of the fire, he first states the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in two and a half verses, beginning with "pramāṇapariśuddham" (76–78).
O Mahāmati, those which are useful for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) are these. 78.
The ritual vessels, such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, should also be marked with them;
having smeared and adorned them with pure pigments such as lime and the like, [they should be consecrated].

With fragrant substances such as sandalwood and preceded by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should apply the marks of the Lord—such as the discus and conch—to the vessels like the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, just as one does for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Thus he says, "in the fire-rite" (*agnikārye*). Regarding the marking of the pit and so forth, he says, "with lime and other materials" (*sudhādyaiḥ*). Here, the eightfold consecrations of the pit, beginning with striking it with flowers, which are required, should be understood as those taught in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and summarized from the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* and *Pārameśvarasaṃhitā*. (78–80)
And in the middle of that, leaning against the eastern part with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass. || 80 ||
Starting from the southern direction, one should draw a line extending toward the north;
above that, one should clearly draw three lines.

"One should draw a single bolt-line (argalarekhā) in the center of the pit (kuṇḍa), starting from the south-eastern part with the tips pointing eastward and ending in the north, using the tip of a blade of kuśa grass," so it is said; "in its middle" [refers to this]. Upon that, one should draw three lines with spaces between them, starting from the south and ending in the north, with their tips pointing eastward; thus it is said, "upon that. That these three lines have the deities Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā as their presiding deities is to be understood from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* and the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvṛtti*. (80–82)
Then, one should sprinkle [the vessel] four times with the water of the arghya offering while reciting the syllable Om.
Having worshipped that [liṅga] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth, one should meditate upon it as being like the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha).
One should perform its installation with the Praṇavas, as previously described.

He describes the fourfold sprinkling with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) using the *praṇava*, the worship with flowers using the *praṇava*, and the meditation on the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as being like a *bhadrapīṭha*, by means of the verse beginning with "fourfold" (82–83).
On a square ground in the Kauṇḍa [mandala], having placed eight full vessels as jars in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions on the outside, || 84 ||
Regarding the placement of eight full jars in the eight directions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he says: "In the four corners," etc. (verse 84).
Above and below the four girdles, in the four cardinal directions,
one should worship Vāsudeva and the others, who are seated upon silken mats.
