Indeed, by means of the yoga of absorption even in the intermediate directions— from the bottom up to the top—
one should worship them in sequence with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and flowers.

He describes the worship of Vāsudeva and the others in the four directions starting from the east outside the pit (*kuṇḍa*) upon the *kuśa*-grass bundles placed on the girdles (*mekhalā*), proceeding from top to bottom in the order of emanation (*prabhava-krama*); and likewise, the worship of Aniruddha and the others in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, proceeding from bottom to top in the order of dissolution (*laya-krama*). This is stated in the two verses beginning with "ūrdhvādhaḥ. Thus, this worship upon thirty-two *kuśa*-grass bundles pertains specifically to a pit having only four girdles, as there is no room for it otherwise.

In this context, regarding the worship of Aniruddha and the others in the intermediate directions according to the order of dissolution (*apyaya*), one should know that the previously mentioned fourfold mantra is as follows: *oṃ puruṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ satyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ acyutāya namaḥ*, and *oṃ bhagavate vāsudevāya namaḥ*.
Now hear briefly another fourfold mantra for the recollection and worship of the All-pervading Lord when the occasion for dissolution arrives.
Because of this statement, when worship is performed according to the sequence of manifestation (*prabhava-krama*), the four mantras of the waking array (*jāgrad-vyūha*) remain truly awake. (85–86)
A bundle of soft *darbha* grass, a sapless stone-slab, combined with dried cow-dung powder and fragrant stone (*gandhāśman*). (87)
Having placed a portion measuring one *droṇa* into the fire-pit and having spread it out,
or else having taken the sacrificial fire into a copper vessel or another [vessel], || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with *mṛdudarbha* and consisting of one and a half verses, he describes the casting of powdered darbha grass and other materials into the vessel as the means for quickly igniting the fire; [he mentions] *gandhāśmanā*, meaning by means of sulphur (*gandhaka*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "In the case of *gandhāśman*, however, it is *gandhaka*. (87–88)
Whether it be made of forest-wood, or worldly material, or born of jewels, or produced from a mirror,
[it belongs] to the Lord, the Master of the Heart, who is known as Kālavaiśvānara.
Regarding the bringing of the fire, he says: "In a copper vessel," etc. "Araṇya" means produced from the forest. The method for churning the fire-drills (*araṇi*) is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"One should meditate on Śakti, who is the soul of all, as the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*);
and one should meditate on Hari, who consists of all splendor, as the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*)."
"One should churn [the fire] properly with the *tārā* [mantra], and likewise with the *anutārā*.

Thus, this very [rite] should be known as the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) for the fire produced from the fire-sticks (*araṇi*). Hereafter, the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) of the fire, beginning with the naming, should be performed; however, the fire produced from gems and the like is to be consecrated by the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). And so it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"When fire arising from metal, stone, or gem is employed according to necessity..."

"Or even in the worldly [rite], one should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) beginning with the impregnation (niṣeka). Thus, the prescription for the purificatory rites of the fire beginning with the impregnation is set forth in the *Īśvarapārameśvara* according to the *Śrījayākhyatantra*. For that purpose, the invocation of Lakṣmī and so forth within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is also mentioned; furthermore, many other specific details required here and there have been collected from those very two [texts] and should be adopted. || 89 ||
The luster accompanied by the Maruts should be joined with the external fire;
having whirled it four times, one should then cast it into the interior of the sacrificial pit.

He describes the unification of the splendor of the Blessed One residing in one’s own heart with the fire situated in the vessel in the verse beginning with *kāla*. For it is well known that the Blessed One is designated as Kālavaiśvānara (the Fire of Time). Thus, in the Pauṣkara, in the section on the worship of Viṣvaksena:
"The form of the all-pervading Lord, whose nature is the Fourth State (*turyātman*), which is called Kālavaiśvānara—that very deity, O twice-born, is proclaimed as Viṣvaksena."

"Abiding through the distinctions of the Āhavanīya and other fires for those who sacrifice in the Makhayajña, taking up the oblation purified by the Ṛgveda, he satisfies the entire world. The meaning of "followed by the Māruta" is that the Māruta is of the nature of the *recaka* (exhalation). Alternatively, the meaning is that the *mantra* itself is the Māruta; for both [interpretations] have been stated regarding the Lord and others: "Having drawn [the breath] by means of the wind-form of the mantra, [the offering] emerged from that," and "Having repeatedly exhaled, one should deposit [it] into that previously worshipped vessel of fire. The meaning of "by light (*bhāsā*)" is that it refers to the sixth quality of the Blessed One known as *tejas* (splendor). As he will state later in the section on the Nṛsiṃhakalpa:
That which is called the quality of *tejas* (brilliance) is indeed the sixth quality, distinct from the group of [other] qualities.
"Having thus meditated upon him as the common essence of all splendors belonging to the Supreme Brahman, one should cast [the oblation] into the middle of the fire-pit with the Netra-mantra. (90)
Having indeed whirled it four times, one should then cast it into the interior of the sacrificial pit.
Having offered the fourfold fuel-sticks, purified and consecrated with the *praṇava*, one should thereafter perform the sweeping around [the fire]. || 91 ||
Indeed, moving in a clockwise direction with the palm of his hand moistened,
he [stroked] sideways and downwards, not showing the surface of his nails.

Regarding the phrase "having whirled," he describes the installation of the fire in the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the throwing of four fuel-sticks (*samidh*) above it for the purpose of kindling. Here, "four fuel-sticks" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for sacrificial wood. Thus he will state in the seventeenth chapter: "Having made it smokeless with pure, dry fuels. He describes the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) with the words "thereafter" (*tadanu*). Sweeping consists of gathering together the scattered fires within the center of the pit. (90–92)
Then, one should provide a layer of *kuśa* grass that is even, with its roots and tips unbroken;
it should extend from each direction up to the northern quarter, leaving a gap at the beginning of the southern quarter.
With four qualities and in four ways, they are mutually covered by their foremost parts;
from the eastern ends, starting from the eastern portion, extending as far as the northern range.

He describes the *paristaraṇa* (strewing) with the two verses beginning with "tataḥ. It is stated generally that one should perform the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) by laying down an equal number of *kuśa* grass blades, with unbroken roots and tips, in every direction. However, the specific detail is stated: starting from the southern quarter and ending in the northern quarter, one should lay down four blades each in the three directions in sequence, with intervals (*sāntaram*) between them.

In this context, it should be understood that the description of the fourfold strewing with intervening spaces for the triad beginning with the south is intended for the purpose of arranging the vessels (pātrāsādana) which will be performed in connection with the duals. This is because the arrangement in pairs will be taught specifically for the triad beginning with the south, whereas since there is no such arrangement in the eastern direction, the strewing with sixteen *darbha* blades is to be understood as being without intervening spaces.

Here, by the phrase "starting from the east," the fact that the grass tips of the eastern and western coverings should also point northward is indicated. Since it was previously stated in general terms that "one should lay down the covering in every direction," this specific detail—that [the covering] extends from the eastern part as far as the northern region—is now demonstrated. These very same verses have been set forth many times in the *Pārameśvara* and other such texts.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*: "But in the southern direction and so forth, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding 'or' (*vā*). This is merely a conceptual option (*buddhi-vikalpa*), because when explaining the reading [of the text], the intermediate term (*antarapada*) would otherwise be left without recourse; furthermore, it would result in the unnecessary consequence of performing the fourfold strewing (*paristaraṇa*) even in the eastern part, and it would lead to the fault of redundancy with the phrase "from the eastern part as far as the northern region. (93–94)
Having brought down all the implements for the fire-oblation, preceded by the sacrificial vessels,
one should place them above that, to the south of oneself.
O Mahāmati, one should perform the establishment of the substances by employing two pairs of duals; indeed, it should be joined with the number sixteen (twice eight).

With the second [mantra] consisting of eight syllables, having placed together in one place the raft made of discarded darbha grass, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— this being the group of four— [he should perform the rite].
Then, one should place together a garland, incense, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the seeds;
as well as silk, a seat with hair removed, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Immediately after that, having placed four vessels for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), as well as a pair of praṇītā vessels, a water-pot (karaka), and a vessel for the arghya offering; || 99 ||

Now, he describes the placing of the sacrificial implements upon the surrounding grass (paristaraṇa) with the words beginning with *homa*. "Preceded by the sacrificial vessels" (*homabhāṇḍapurassaram*) means preceded by the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, since it was stated previously that "the vessels are the *sruk*, *sruva*, and so forth. He first describes the sequence of placement on the southern surrounding grass with the words beginning with *dakṣiṇasyām*. "With loose darbhas" (*muktadarbhaiḥ*) means with kuśa grasses that are not tied together in the form of a bundle (*kūrca*) or the like; that is, with simple kuśa grasses. A small mat (*paraṇḍikā*) is characterized by those [grass blades].

The *kūrca* is a tuft of grass used for the purification and wiping of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as for other such purposes; it may be made of silk or of hair from a tail. The *kuśa-kūrca* is a tuft of *kuśa* grass used for the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The *viṣṭara* is a bundle of grass used for the worship of the jars starting from the east, for the consecration of the *praṇītā* vessel, and for other related rites. (95–99)
A pair of vessels for the *praṇītā* water, a water-pot (*karaka*), and a vessel for the *arghya* offering. || 99 ||
Having first placed this other set of four before [the fire],
one should prepare fuel-sticks of the length of a span and an abundant amount of dry fuel.
Having placed the eyelash-cloth and the heart-cloth on the left side,
one should first bring everything to a state of purification with the water from the arghya vessel.

He states the materials to be placed upon the western covering with the words "praṇītā" etc. He states the seats for the northern covering with the words "prādeśamātrāḥ" etc. Regarding "pakṣmakam," it means a fan (*vyajana*), so called because it is grasped (*parigṛhya*) for the purpose of fanning the kindled fire; this is from the root *pakṣ* in the sense of "grasping. In the commentary of Pārameśvara, "pakṣmakam" is interpreted as "fine" (*sūkṣma*) and used as an adjective qualifying the sweat-wiping cloth (*svedahṛdvastra*); however, that is inconsistent, because it is impossible to place [the items] according to the sequence of a *dvandva* compound.

In some instances, due to a confusion regarding the entire passage in the *Pārameśvara-prayoga*, it was written that "the two cloths for the heart [are used] with tears and sweat," based on the intention that "tears" refers to the moisture located on the eyelashes; however, that too is contradictory, as it was previously stated in the *Dīkṣā-pariccheda* that [the materials include] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and whatever other implements are required for the fire-oblation (*homa*).

Because it will be stated later: "Everything up to the edge of the eyelashes, provided with two large vessels. Furthermore, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyā*, regarding the matter of placement (*āsādana*), having begun with the words "In this regard, the distinction is as follows," the spontaneous placement (*svacchanda-āsādana*) was described.

This [procedure] is prompted by a lack of discrimination; for in that case, there is the placing of four items—such as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), garlands (*sraj*), and so forth, including the shaken-out hair—upon the southern spreading of grass (*dakṣiṇaparistaraṇa*). Therefore, it is clearly understood that one must place the four items beginning with the *praṇītā* water upon the western spreading of grass (*paścimaparistaraṇa*) in front of oneself, and place the fuel sticks (*samidh*) and so forth upon the northern spreading of grass (*uttaraparistaraṇa*). He states the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of those items already placed: "with the *arghya*," etc.

At this juncture, the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be performed on the four sides of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), because the enclosing sticks will be described in the eighteenth chapter with the words, "The enclosing sticks are indeed fuel-sticks of *Palāśa* wood, complete with their tips. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement of Īśvara and others: "One should worship the four enclosing sticks with the *Śikhā-mantra*. Thus, after the placement of the enclosing sticks, one should perform the worship of Indra and the other deities in the pitchers starting from the east, preceded by the placement of the *kūrca* grass-bunches;
then, one should offer seats (*viṣṭara*) into the mouths of the pitchers with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
In those [circles], one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), each situated in their own respective direction, in due order.

Thus it is stated in the *Īśvara*. In the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and the *Pārameśvara*, the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) is prescribed only upon the *kūrca* grasses surrounding the jars. (99–101)
Then, having taken the vessel for the water and the vessel called *praṇītā*,
one should place within it a *pavitraka* made of four blades of *darbha* grass.
Lifting water again and again with his hand, the practitioner should pour it back into that very place while muttering the fourfold mantra. (103)
Furthermore, one should sprinkle everything with that water using the sacrificial grass mat;
then, one should perform the sprinkling of the remainder over the mat in all directions.
Having again filled it with water, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord within it, worship Him, and then install Him immediately before oneself.

He describes the procedure for the consecration of the *praṇītā* waters with four verses beginning with "ādāya. The meaning is that one should recite the fourfold mantra pertaining to the Self—the previously mentioned quartet of mantras beginning with Vāsudeva. (102–105)
Having sprinkled the fuel sticks with the water of the *arghya* offering and having divided them into four parts,
one should worship them with *arghya* and flowers using the twelve-syllable mantra.
Regarding the throwing of the fuel sticks, he says "having sprinkled"; this means with the twelve-syllable vidyā, that is, with the all-pervading twelve-syllable mantra. || 106 ||
When another excellent vessel has been placed in front,
one should offer the *arghya* water along with the *pavitra* there and then install the *cakra*.
Having meditated upon the fourfold form above that and worshipped it in due order,
one should place that vessel in the north and worship it once again.
He describes the sublime nature of that which is not produced by others through two verses [107–108]: "Sublime."
Then, having taken the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī) and having poured into it the clarified butter that was previously liquefied,
[he should do so] with his hand raised above the butter-vessel.
Taking it up again, one should carefully place four stalks of darbha grass, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length, at the top upon the support.

Having grasped [the instrument] with the palms turned sideways and upwards at intervals, one should press it with the pair of the ring fingers and thumbs so that the middle [of the instrument] becomes bent. || 111 ||
One should bring the clarified butter four times with those [ladles] and pour it out four times;
indeed, by means of alternating intervals, one should do so facing one's own fire.
Then, one should cast [the materials] into the center of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with the Praṇava repeated the prescribed number of times.

Regarding the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya), he says "the vessel for the clarified butter" and so forth in four and a half verses. Here, by the statement "having poured the melted clarified butter into the vessel for the clarified butter," two of the ten types of consecrations of clarified butter mentioned in the *Jayākhyatantra* are indicated: namely, "placing on the hearth" (*upādhiśrayaṇa*), which is called "liquefying" (*ādrāvaṇa*), and "transferring to another vessel" (*parivartana*) for the removal of defects; these are what is meant by the term "making it pure" (*prasādīkaraṇa*). By the phrase "one should bring the clarified butter four times" (*caturunnayet*), [this process is completed].
O Brahmin, one should lead it forth and lead it back; one should cast kuśa grass into the fire of heat.
These two purificatory rites are proclaimed as "submerging" and "emerging."

Thus, the two aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have been stated. Furthermore, the other six types of purificatory rites mentioned in the *Jayākhyatantra* should be understood as being summarized in the *Īśvaratantra*. "With the aforementioned *saṃkhyāna-praṇava* eight times" means with eight recitations; for it has been stated that one should bring [the breath] four times and raise it four times. (109–113)
Then, having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles together with a bunch of *darbha* grass, || 113 ||
One should perform the removal of dust by washing with warm water;
having rendered it stainless with a brush and having heated it thoroughly with flames.

Having sprinkled [the implements] with arghya water, having worshipped them, and having set them down, he describes the consecration (saṃskāra) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with two verses beginning with "The *sruk* and *sruva*... Regarding the phrase "having worshipped," the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* and their respective mantras are those mentioned in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, which are subsumed within the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]. (113–115)
With *kuśa* grass that has many branches, unbroken tips, roots, and is perfectly even. || 115 ||
Then, having taken the purifier with the left hand, one should place it upon the ring finger of the right hand; it is fashioned from four segments.
Immediately after that, having indeed formed the gesture of the finger-ring (aṅgulīyakarūpa),
one should touch the fuel and other materials with drops of consecrated clarified butter (ājya).

Alternatively, he describes the wearing of the ring-pavitra on the left hand and the wearing of the pavitra on the right ring finger with the two verses beginning with "bahuśākhaiḥ. Regarding the characteristics of the pavitra, it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"The pavitra for Viṣṇu as the presiding deity (adhidaivata) should always be four finger-breadths [in length];
the knot for Mahāviṣṇu as the presiding deity should be one finger-breadth [in width]."

"Viṣṇu is the presiding deity (adhidaiva) of the two bracelets, which are said to be two finger-breadths [in width]. Thus [it is stated]. Regarding the sprinkling of consecrated clarified butter (ājya) upon the fuel-sticks (samidh) and other materials, he says "consecrated," etc. "With *vipruḍ* drops" means with droplets. (115–117)
Then, for the sake of pacifying all defects without exception, one should offer one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations of the fire that has been brought forth, according to one's own capacity.
Listen now to how, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual act, oblations of sesame seeds soaked in ghee together with pure clarified butter (havis) are to be offered. 119.
And when the oblation has been offered, at the conclusion of the root mantra, one should utter the word ending with the *praṇava*: "Purify the fire, purify! (120).
Then, with that very [substance] in its established form,
the wise one should subsequently offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) consisting of four *palas*.

Now, he describes the oblation (*homa*) for the purpose of purifying the fire with four verses beginning with "niḥśeṣa. "Catuṣpalīm" means measuring four *palas*. Regarding the measure of a *pala*, it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Four grains of rice make a *kuñja*; eight of those are called a *māñjiṣṭha*. [A *pala* consists of eight *māñjiṣṭhas*.]
"One hundred and sixty [māṣakas] make one niṣka; eight niṣkas make one pala.

At this point, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the fire, beginning with *niṣeka* and ending with *vivāha*, as well as the designations of its tongues (*jihvākalpanā*), should be understood as they are summarized in the *Īśvara*, *Pārameśvara*, and other scriptures. (118–121)
Once his defects have been completely purified,
he should again perform the fire-oblation (homa) that produces perfect awakening and grants the pacification of the state of insentience.
Having recited the root mantra accompanied by two *praṇavas*,
one should offer either a thousand or a hundred oblations.
In the same manner, having gratified [the deity] with clarified butter (ājya), one should likewise offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Now, with two and a half verses beginning with "tasya," he describes the oblation that awakens the fire. 122–124.
Then, having attained his true being, he beholds the all-pervading Lord within.
Then one should take refuge in Viṣṇu, the unborn, who is the very life-force, and become absorbed in Him;
for this performer of ritual action, established in the sacrifice and destined for liberation, [this is the path]. 125.
By its own will, it spontaneously becomes a constituent part of the sacrifice;
it divides itself into four parts from within the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having resorted to the sequence of the directions according to their nature as the presiding deities of the elements,
[he is established] first in the east in the form known as Āhavanīya, and then in the south.
Immediately after that, he remains in the western [quarter] in the form of the *sabhyā* fire;
then, by means of the division known as the *gārhapatya*, he stands in the north.
The Self, which is the cooker of the rice, abides in the middle as the self of all; yet, by virtue of the relationship between the container and the contained, it exists with a blended form.

By means of this oblation (*homa*), Agni, having attained existence and beheld the Lord within, becomes one with Him. Having himself assumed the status of being a constituent part of the sacrifice performed by the officiating priest, he remains for the sake of propitiating the Fourfold Self (*cāturātmya*) in four ways—namely, through the divisions of the Āhavanīya, Sabhya, Gārhapatya, and Audanapacana fires. He stands as his own self in the east and other directions, and in the center, he exists as the form conjoined with the relationship of container and contained. This is stated in five and a half verses beginning with "Then" (*tadā*). (124–129)
The embers and the flames, as well as the power whose nature is burning—this triad of characteristics constitutes the substratum; that which is supported is the all-pervading consumer of oblations.
The eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of All, is indeed the source of the self;
having thus correctly understood in the past that supreme Vaiśvānara existence, [one attains liberation]. 131.
Then, having made a firm resolve, the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) should engage in the ritual action;
he should first offer water and then perform the invocation as before.

He explains the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum with the verse beginning "embers" (along with the following half-verse). Thus, by this [verse], he states that immediately after the thorough knowledge of existence, one should engage in ritual action; he says "thus" (*evam*). At this juncture, the worship of the Fire-god, augmented by the Lord and others, should be undertaken. (130–132)
One should first offer water, and then perform the invocation as before.
"By means of the reality that has dissolved from manifestation, yet which is of an imperishable nature...

Now, he describes the invocation of the Lord into the midst of the fire with the words "one should perform. By the phrase "dissolved from manifestation," it is understood that the very [deity] who was worshipped in the icon (bimba) and so forth is here invoked. "By means of the reality" means by means of the form consisting of mantra. || 132-133 ||
For indeed, whatever great mantra-body belongs to the Lord of All, [that is he]. (133)
O you of stainless vision, that [reality] should be understood as consisting of the signified and the signifier;
furthermore, it abides as pure universality within the framework of metaphorical designation. (134)

He states, in two verses beginning with "sarveśvarasya," that the mantra-body of the Lord (Īśvara) is primary even when devoid of the mantras for the offering of enjoyments (bhoga-dāna), and that it possesses a twofold nature in the form of the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka). Here, by the term "invocation" (āvāhana), the entire procedure—from the preparation of the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) up to the worship of dissolution (laya-bhoga)—is also implied. It has been explained in the same way regarding Īśvara and the other [deities]. (133–135)
Having taken that collection of fuel-wood which was previously divided into four parts. || 135 ||

Sprinkled on both sides with clarified butter, [the offering] produced from *brahma* and milk-trees is placed in the middle of the four parts between the two *brahma*-walls of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should place [the marks] starting from the eastern part up to the northern limit in successive order;
the first four [squares] fall between the northeast and southeast corners.
One should place another [line] resting between the directions of Agni and Nairṛta,
and having established the third [line] touching Nairṛta and Anila.
The fourth group of four is indeed constricted by the station of Vāyu and Īśa;
thus, in brief, it is divided into four parts by means of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Having divided a single sacrificial pit into four parts for the four fires, which possess a single body in accordance with the requirement of the fourfold nature (cāturātmya). || 140 ||
Whenever a person may be suitable for whatever object, or for a rite such as installation and so forth, for the purpose of satisfying his own form; || 141 ||
At each respective time, he should carefully take [the fuel] from its own place.

Previously, at the time of the *praṇītā* consecration, the sixteen-fold fuel was divided into four parts; now, for the purpose of distributing it among the *āhavanīya* and other fires within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he describes the throwing of the fuel into the various directions—starting from the east—between the location of Brahmā and the southern boundary, by confining it within two respective corners, with the verses beginning "In the east, fourfold... and ending with "...carefully from its own place. (135–142)
Taking a second fuel-stick made of *tvaṣṭaka* wood, he said: || 142 ||
Having divided it into two parts with clarified butter as before, one should sprinkle it;
then, having placed it in the south, it should be situated in the middle, facing the south-eastern direction.

He speaks of the division of the fuel and so forth with the words "the second. Having first divided the eight pieces of fuel into two, one should subsequently sprinkle them on both sides with clarified butter as before. Even though, in the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*, it is said: "The fuel produced from the milk-tree (*brahmakṣīradruma*), sprinkled with clarified butter on both sides..."

Since it is stated, "having taken them up and divided them into two," one understands that the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are to be divided into two parts immediately after the sprinkling with clarified butter (*ājya*). Nevertheless, because the meaning must be explained in a way that does not contradict the root text—and since the root text states, "having divided them into two, he should sprinkle them as before with clarified butter"—and because even in the section on the sixteen fuel-sticks, the sprinkling with clarified butter is mentioned only after the fourfold division, the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*); therefore, this applies to those two cases as well.

The meaning should be described as follows: the pouring of clarified butter (ājya) occurs immediately after the act of dividing [the fire] into two. For this very reason, our venerable grandfather has also explained the meaning in the *Sātvatāmṛta*, even while following the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, in a way that does not contradict the root text. In a certain ritual procedure of the *Pārameśvara* tradition, it is stated: "having sprinkled [it] all over with clarified butter, having divided it into two"—this [other view] is contradictory to that. (142–143)
Having placed [the vessel] in the south and the one situated in the southeast in the middle. || 143 ||
Having taken clarified butter, one should then place one portion at the station of Nairṛta and another in the north, while confining [the third] within the stations of Vāyu and Īśa.

He describes the sequence for placing the fuel with the verse beginning "having placed" (*nidhāya*) and including a quarter-verse. The meaning is as follows: having placed four pieces of fuel in the fire—occupying the southern middle and confined by the *nairṛta* and *āgneya* corners—one should likewise place another set of four in the northern middle, confined by the *vāyavya* and *aiśāna* corners.

Thus, by the mention of being confined by the *nairṛta* and *āgneya* corners, and by the mention of being confined by the *vāyavya* and *aiśāna* corners, it is established that the placement of fuel should be performed in the eastern and western positions within the southern and northern sectors of the fire.

If it is argued that the casting of the fuel-sticks (idhma) from east to west is self-evident, we say no; for in the previous section on the casting of sixteen fuel-sticks, it is stated: "The first four fall toward the east by means of the feet of Īśāna and Agni," and "having placed the third so as to touch Nairṛta and Anala. Thus, it is taught that the casting of the fuel-sticks may also extend from south to north. Without understanding this point, someone has displayed his learning in vain regarding a certain ritual application of the Pārameśvara [Tantra].

For instance, according to the *Idhmāṣṭaka* (eight-fuel) method: having joined a single fuel-stick with its tip pointing upward to the root against the southern wall inside the pit, and likewise having placed a triad of fuel-sticks from the center of the pit toward the southeast and southwest corners, one should then place another tetrad in the north wall, the center of the pit, and the northwest and northeast corners. || 143-144 ||
With a mantra consisting of four counts and adorned with the *praṇava*,
one should offer four oblations with the *sruk* ladle on the south, and likewise on the north.
Know that the two eyes of the fire consist of the Sun and the Moon.

Therefore, regarding the fire in the south and the north at the place where fuel is cast, he describes the oblation of clarified butter (ājya-homa) in accordance with that number, as well as the fact that those two places are the eyes of the fire consisting of the Sun and the Moon, by means of the verse beginning with "catuḥsaṃkhyena" (number four), which consists of one and a half verses. In the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, however, it is stated that there is a joining of the Sun and the Moon within the fire in the south and north by means of their respective mantras through the offering of oblations; this too is summarized in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*. Furthermore, in that very same place, the preliminary Āghāra-homa is also included along with the two Ājyabhāgas.
... ... ... Then one should pour the *āghāra* clarified butter; it is poured from the base of the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and rests upon the fuel-sticks.

Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, one should contemplate the thousand-rayed sun within it by means of its seed-syllable, and place it to the south of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having meditated upon the other ladle as the full orb of the moon by means of the syllable named Soma, one should then offer it to the north. (145–146)
That which is indeed the interval between these two is remembered as the mouth of Agni.

In that regard, one should first offer seven pieces of fuel (samidh) in sequence. By the words "of these two," he explains that the space between them constitutes the mouth [of the fire] and that the seven pieces of fuel are to be offered therein. "Seven pieces of fuel" means: fuel-stick, flower, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), seed, sacrificial porridge (caru), and clarified butter (ghṛta). This is because all seven—starting with the fuel-stick and flower—are conventionally designated as "fuel" (samit) based on the etymological derivation: "that by which the fire is kindled (samidhyate) or made to blaze. (146–147)
Indeed, one should offer four such offerings, each well-provided and sprinkled with clarified butter.
First, one should offer into the fire a number of wooden sticks smeared with saffron and other substances,
followed by garlands, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), seeds, grains, and clarified butter, in their proper sequence.
In that regard, this specific rule is prescribed for the offering of food as fuel:
having first prepared the caru-oblation on the consecrated fire, one should place it before [the deity].
Having first opened [the vessel] and looked into it, and then having sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering,
one should subsequently touch it with four blades of *darbha* grass together with fire.
In the midst of that, one should pour four oblations of clarified butter with mantras;
then, taking the *sruk* ladle there, one should likewise offer four [oblations] in the same manner.
Then, one should take a morsel of food measuring four finger-breadths;
having placed that upon the *darbha* grass with the *sruva* ladle, one should likewise pour clarified butter over it as before.
One should offer four oblations into the fire and then cast the food-oblation;
again, one should carefully take up four ladles of clarified butter in the fire.
Then, having prepared food sprinkled with clarified butter as before, one should again offer an oblation;
in this very manner, one should likewise offer four [oblations] according to the previous procedure.
Having offered the oblations of food (*annāhuti*), one should then offer those known as *ājya* (clarified butter).

Regarding the sequence for their homa, he says: "having sprinkled with ghee, four in number," beginning from there and ending with "one should then offer those known as *ājya*. "Sprinkled with ghee" means sprinkled with ghee on both sides, because of what was stated previously: "sprinkled with ghee on both sides. He specifies "each one" (*ekaikām*) in order to dispel the doubt that they might be offered simultaneously here as well, since in the previous section on the offering of fuel-sticks (*idhma-homa*), the simultaneous casting of four sticks at once had been mentioned.

By the phrase *supuṣkalām*, freedom from defects such as being eaten by insects is expressed. "Previously" means prior to the time of placement (*āsādana*). By *kuṅkumādina* ("with saffron, etc."), the word "etc. includes camphor and musk. *Srag-dhūpa-madhuparkam*: *srak* means a garland of flowers; this is because the *Lakṣmītantra* states, "Then one should offer that which consists of flowers. *Dhūpa* refers to incense such as *guggulu*. *Madhuparka* is a mixture of milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter. *Bījāni* (seeds) refers to mung beans and the like. *Annāni* (foods) refers to milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and so forth. *Ājyam* is cow's ghee.

In total, seven oblations are to be known. "In due order" means without transgressing the stated sequence. That is to say, one should offer the oblations in sequence: first a wooden fuel-stick (*samidh*), then a flower, then incense, then the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), then the seeds, then the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and finally the clarified butter (*ājya*). In some copies of the *Sātvata* and in the *Īśvara-pārameśvara* texts, the corrupt reading "bījānyājyaṃ yathākramam" (seeds and clarified butter in due order) has been written.

Accordingly, in certain Pārameśvara rituals, it is written that after the seed-syllable oblation (*bījāhuti*), there is an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*), and after that, an oblation of sacrificial pap (*carvāhuti*). This is inconsistent, because it is impossible for such an introduction to occur—given that previously there was a general mention of the offering of food and fuel-sticks (*annasamit*) without specifying them, whereas here this particular rule for the offering of food and fuel-sticks is being enjoined—and furthermore, because it is stated that "one should offer the oblation called *ājya* thereafter," which indicates that the offering of the fuel-sticks called *ājya* occurs after the oblation of sacrificial pap.

Regarding the phrase "prepared in the previously consecrated fire," the method for preparing the *caru* (oblation) should be understood as that which will be described in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). "In its midst" means in the middle of the *caru*. "One should pour four ladles of clarified butter" means one should sprinkle the *caru* with clarified butter from the *sruk* spoon four times. "A mouthful of food" means a morsel of food the size of a hen's egg; this is according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "A mouthful is said to be the size of a hen's egg."

In the passages "then, taking the *sruk* there, one should likewise offer four [times]," "above that, as before, ghee," and "one should offer the tetrad into the fire," it should be understood that this is done with the *sruva* spoon. Then, having sprinkled the food with clarified butter (*ājya*) as previously described, the meaning is that one should sprinkle the *caru* oblation with ghee from the *sruk* ladle four times.

By the phrase "by means of the preliminary practice," it is understood that there is a fourfold pouring of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle into the *sruc* offering-spoon; therein the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) is placed; over that, again, a fourfold pouring of clarified butter with the *sruva* and four offerings of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*); and after the oblation of the *caru*, again, four offerings of clarified butter with the *sruc*. Thus, by the statement "having offered four oblations of food," it should be understood that the oblations of food likewise number exactly four.

Thus, by stating that there are four kinds of fuel-sticks (*samidh*)—namely, wooden sticks and food-sticks—it is understood that the oblation (*homa*) of the five [types of] fuel-sticks, including flowers and so forth, is also performed in a number of four. In the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna* and its ritual application (*prayoga*), sixteen oblations of food and sixteen oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) are prescribed; however, that is based on a misconception, for it says: "One should offer exactly this quartet according to the previous ritual procedure."

This is because the four food-oblations (*annāhuti*) are explicitly mentioned by name in the passage beginning with "hutvāpy annāhutīnām," and because the clarified butter oblations (*ājyāhuti*), which are performed four times before and after each food-oblation, amount to a total of thirty-two.

In reality, however, it should be understood that both the commentators and the authors of ritual manuals have been led astray by the fact that, in many Śiva-scriptures (*pārameśvara-pustaka*) and in this very section, the text runs from "one should cast the fourfold [oblation] with mantras into the clarified butter" up to "one should give into the fire. For this very reason, it is written in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*: "In that regard, he states the specific details of the fuel-sticks at the end: 'There, regarding the offering of food-fuel-sticks, [it is done] with five [verses]'";
thus, the two verses fallen in the middle did not enter their scope of expectation at all. (147–155)
At its conclusion, [one should worship] with flowers freed from water and mixed with arghya. || 155 ||

One should worship the Lord four times with the mantras or with the *praṇavas*. Then, it says "at the end," referring to the fourfold worship of the deities situated in the fire with flowers. This means [the worship] is performed with clarified butter mixed with the *arghya*—that is, combined with the *arghya*—for otherwise there would be a contradiction with the statement "devoid of water. For this very reason, the offering of *arghya* and so forth with clarified butter alone is stated in the *Pādma*: "Having offered [the oblation] preceded by the *arghya* and ending with the presentation, one should sacrifice once with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*). By "mantras" is meant the mantras of Vāsudeva and others; or else, by "with the *praṇavas*," the plural number implies that they are recited four times.

The meaning is that while the *mūrti-mantras* (form-mantras) differ for each individual [deity], the *praṇava*, due to its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), is one and the same for all. Here, by the term "with the *praṇavas*," the four mantras beginning with the eight-syllabled one are also implied; for they too are pervasive insofar as they take the form of an exposition of the meaning of the *praṇava*, and because the word "praṇava" is used to designate them as mantras. Thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "In the Pāñcarātrika ritual procedure, he shall have three *pada-mantras*."
"Salutation to Viṣṇu," "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," and first,
"Salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva."
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Person, O Primordial One!
O Purandara, this fourth is the *padamantra* of the *praṇava*;
those who know the ancient tradition recognize these mantras as being accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*.
"The Kevala, the Tāraka, and the four beginning with that [the Śrīvidyā]—
these five pervasive mantras are proclaimed in the Pañcarātra.
For this very reason:
Having sprinkled the fuel sticks with the arghya water and divided them into four parts,
one should worship them with arghya and flowers using the twelve-syllable vidyā.

Thus, although the fuel-sticks (*idhma*), divided into four parts with reference to Vāsudeva and the others, are to be worshipped with their respective mantras, it is stated "by means of the twelve-syllable vidyā" because of the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of the twelve-syllable mantra. Similarly, in the section on the purification of the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*), it is said: "having washed [it] with the twelve-syllable [mantra], preceded and followed by the *praṇava*. Now, one might ask: what is the rule here that in both cases the pervasive [mantra] is the twelve-syllable Vāsudeva-mantra, since that has not been mentioned previously? That which is the twelve-syllable [mantra] among those already mentioned is indeed to be taken.

If it is argued that this should be the fourth mantra mentioned in the section on worship during dissolution (*pralaya*), we say no; for that [mantra] is already utilized within the section on worship itself according to the sequence of dissolution, and because it is restricted to a single individual manifestation, it is not applicable in the section on the worship of the Fourfold Self (*cāturātmya*). Furthermore, since the worship is stated here to be performed with the *praṇava* alone, there is no restrictive rule that one must choose any one of those [four mantras] specifically. Thus, it is established that the all-pervading twelve-syllable mantra alone should be taken. In this way, the daily sacrifice (*nityayāga*) is to be understood as ending with the worship with flowers.
And so it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Then, having taken handfuls of flowers, one should worship her residing in the fire."
This much constitutes the daily sacrifice; hereafter, one may cast oblations for the fulfillment of desires.
"If he should have a desire, [he should perform] that which is appropriate for each specific injunction.
Then, for the sake of attaining liberation, one should perform a fire sacrifice according to one's ability. || 156 ||
Then one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with a hundred [recitations] at the beginning and a thousand at the end;
or else, one may offer it with four [oblations], each accompanied by a set of four mantras.

Then, for the sake of liberation, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a number of [offerings] such as a hundred or more, according to one's capacity; at its conclusion, one should offer a single *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) using the four mantras of Vāsudeva, or else one should offer four *pūrṇāhutis* for each mantra—so he says with the verse beginning "then" (verse 157). Regarding this, many specific details required here—such as the various types of optional oblations (*kāmyāhuti*), the quantity of the sacrificial materials, and the procedures for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), and *pūrṇāhuti*—should be understood as they have been explained in the sections concerning Īśvara and the others. (156–157)
One should perform the worship again as before, having wiped the *sruc* with *darbha* grass so that it becomes free of oil,
using the [ghee] previously set aside.
Having first filled it with water, he should sprinkle it with that vessel or with the [same] vessel,
starting from the east outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and proceeding clockwise.
Then, having cast [the water] upwards with the purifier or with the hand, one should offer the remainder upon one's own head; then, [one offers it] in its own place, facing downwards.
Immediately thereafter, one should place those two [the *sruc* and *sruva*] in the vessel for oblations along with the ashes.

With three verses and a quarter, he describes the purification (*saṃmārjana*) of the *sruc* and *sruva*, the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), and so forth, preceded by the secondary worship (*uttarapūjā*). Regarding the phrase "as before" (*prāgvat*): at the time of placement (*āsādana*), it means with the water previously set down in front of oneself—that is, with the *arghya* water—since the *Īśvarapārameśvara* states: "Having filled [the *sruc*] from the *arghya* vessel, [one should perform the circumambulation] outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in a clockwise direction. The word "that" (*tām*) refers to the *sruc*. By the use of the particle "and" (*ca*), the purification of that [the *sruc*] with *darbha* grass and its filling with *arghya* water are also expressed.

"With that vessel" means with either the *sruc* or the *sruva*. "In the upper [part]" means in the upper part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). "In its own place" means where they were previously placed. "In the sacrificial implements" means in the *sruc* and *sruva*. (158–161)
Indeed, one should apply four vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) using earth purified by water alone. || 161 ||
"One should apply [the ash] in the shape of a lamp-flame on the heart, the shoulders, and the forehead.

Regarding the application of the *tilaka* as an ancillary part of the fire sacrifice (*homāṅga*), he says "with ashes. The mantras for this are stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "On the forehead and the two shoulders, with the mantras of the head-armor (*śirastanutra*); and on the heart."

Thus, one should not suspect that the wearing of the *tilaka* with ashes is contrary to the practice of Vaiṣṇavas, because it is an integral part of the fire ritual (*agnikārya*). Accordingly, in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*, in the section on the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), it is stated: "In that regard, since this [application of ashes] is prescribed for one who has already applied the vertical mark and worshipped Vāsudeva immediately after the fire ritual, it must be understood by your long-lived self as being included within that very fire ritual. (161–162)
Thus, when the fire-ritual has been completed and offered, || 162 ||

The manner in which the distribution to the ancestors (pitṛ-saṃvibhāga) should be performed is now described. Having thus offered the oblation (homa) to the Blessed Lord, one should then perform the distribution to the ancestors; this is what he states with the word "evam" (thus). The method for offering the oblation to the Blessed Lord should be understood as that demonstrated in relation to Īśvara and others. (162–163)
Near the yoni of the sacrificial pit, one should spread kuśa grass with its tips pointing toward the south.

He describes the location for the distribution [of the offerings] of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as being either near the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), on the surface of the ground, or above it. || 163–164 ||
Then, having scattered sesame seeds along with silver water upon the star.

One should meditate there sequentially upon the fathers and then the grandfathers. Regarding the meditation on the ancestors, beginning with the father, it is said "upon the layer" (*staropari*), preceded by the scattering of sesame-water upon a bed of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south. Here, by the terms "father" (*pitṛ*) and "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*), the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) and the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) are also implied; however, above the layer, they should be placed in order according to their respective names, ending with the foremost [ancestor].
One should meditate upon [the deities] as having attained a form identical to that of Puruṣa and the others.
They praised their fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers,
as well as their ancestors, according to their respective lineages.
Thus, according to the statement of the Pārameśvara [Tantra]. (164–165)
And then, for the satisfaction of all, one should offer it to the deity. || 165 ||
Having placed four food vessels that have been sprinkled with water, or four morsels of food,
upon the covering cloth, one should then worship them with the arghya offering and other rites.
Then, in due order, through the dissolution (*apaya*) by means of the fourfold mantras belonging to himself,
he should offer water with sesame seeds preceded by the mantra, together with the [deceased's] name and lineage.
One should offer [the oblation] from the *arghya* pitcher to all of them in due order.

Now, with three verses beginning with "for their satisfaction" (*tṛptaye*), he describes the offering of the *piṇḍas*, the worship beginning with the *arghya*, and the presentation of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*). Here, regarding the phrase "having offered to the deity," it should be understood as the food and so forth remaining in the cooking vessel, because what has already been offered cannot be offered again. And thus it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Those who worship the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the gurus..."
That portion previously set aside for the purpose of the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga),
from that he should take a small amount and perform a distribution among the ancestors,
his kinsmen, and likewise those who depend upon him.
One should perform one's own secondary sacrifice (anuyāga) with what remains after the distribution;
or else, taking whatever remains in the cooking pot and placing it in a vessel,
one should offer it to the deity as before and then perform the ancestral rite (pitrya) with that.
Those Brahmins and others who are devoted to the Vaiśvadeva and are Vaiṣṇavas,
having taken a portion of what is obtained from that which has been eaten by the Lord,
and having performed the Vaiśvadeva with that, [should do so] with the remaining portion.
"But they should maintain their livelihood through the breath and so forth according to the prescribed rule, O best of the twice-born. Thus [it is said].

These verses are cited in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*: "Regarding the vessels for food and drink, in the *Pārameśvara*, it is said that when the leaves of the *tamāla* and *kadalī* have been first washed..."

"Having divided the food into four parts and placed [them] with the *praṇava* (Oṃ)," this is what should be understood as stated [in the text]. Regarding the instruction "having placed [the portions] upon the *stara*," the mantra is also stated in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra] as before: "With the mantras beginning with *svadhā* and ending with *avasāna*, preceded by the syllable Oṃ."
O Brahmin, [these should be] adorned with the heart-mantras and likewise endowed with their respective designations.
"Thinking, 'I shall fashion the piṇḍa,' one should then proceed as before. Thus it is said.

Covering with *darbha* grass over the *piṇḍas* was previously established; furthermore, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and so forth—who were meditated upon above the layer of grass, was prescribed in that very same place.
There, with the *praṇavas*, the tips of the *darbhas* were directed toward the south and sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds.
One should place blades of darbha grass in the form of channels above the funeral cakes;
one should contemplate them as having entered [the body] through the paths of the channels in due order.
"Then, saying 'I invoke the ancestors,' he [invokes them] standing facing east upon the seat (*staras*).

Regarding the phrase 'with the *arghya* and so forth,' the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) includes fragrances and other such items. Furthermore, having gone to the top of the seat while saying 'I invoke the ancestors through the application of yoga,' [he performs the rite] with the four mantras belonging to the fourfold self—namely, with the four previously mentioned mantras beginning with *oṃ puruṣāya namaḥ*."

"One should offer water with sesame seeds preceded by the name and the lineage"—the practical application (*prayoga*) here is as follows: *oṃ puruṣāya namaḥ; to Nṛsiṃhaśarman of the Mauñjyāyana lineage, who is my father in the form of Puruṣa, I give this water with sesame seeds*. In the same way, the formula should be adapted for the grandfather and the others. The mantras for the offering of the *arghya* and other items should also be understood in this very manner. (165–168)
Then, having seated the four [disciples] on their seats for that purpose, || 168 ||
Having obtained those Brāhmaṇas who have attained the goal in the supreme reality and are followers of the Pāñcarātra,
[he should place] two facing east and two facing north.
Even in the absence of [all] the attainments, one may install a single [deity] facing north;
then, one should perform their worship in sequence, as in the Cāturātmya rite.

With offerings such as water for honor (*arghya*) and unguents, including all enjoyments ending with the final oblation (*mātrā*), appropriate for each respective occasion, and free from anything that should not be accepted. || 171 ||

Now, it is said that one should feed four Brahmins or a single Brahmin with intent for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), by means of identification (*tādātmyena*). "Having fixed their gaze" means those who possess knowledge of Brahman. "With enjoyments" means with edible foods. "Ending with the *mātrā*" means ending with the giving of even a sesame seed immediately after the meal. Here too, the same mantras as previously mentioned are used for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Everything else is to be understood as being like the *śrāddha* rite. Many specific details required here should be adopted from what was taught by the Supreme Lord (the *Pārameśvara*).
Furthermore, they must remain established in silence and well-restrained;
with their speech controlled and their focus purified, they should direct it toward Janārdana in the form of food.
Through that [food], the ancestors who eat attain eternal satisfaction; therefore, silence accompanied by mental distraction must be avoided by those intent on ritual action. 173.
He states with the verse beginning "by them" (and continuing for one and a half verses) that silence on the part of those who eat at a *śrāddha* ceremony brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
That which is auspicious and infallible is the effect in all things;
it is [expressed] by means of the unmanifest nasal syllables consisting of the conventions of the limbs. 174.
Regarding that, he states "therefore" [verse 174] to show that faulty silence is to be abandoned, while faultless silence is to be adopted.
When [the practice is performed] with the unmanifest nasal syllables consisting of the secret signs of the limbs... || 174 ||
Silence maintained by merely closing the lips causes the loss of that accomplishment;
rather, it is that which proceeds through one's own excellent intelligence regarding all things. (175)
That silence which is not taught by words bestows all accomplishments.
He describes the faults and virtues of silence in two verses beginning with "yat" (174–176).
Therefore, indeed, for those who partake in a śrāddha or in a divine rite for the ancestors, || 176 ||

One should offer everything like an oblation (naivedya) within the prescribed boundary in front [of the deity], so that they remain silent until the time for the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana). || 177 ||

Then, for the sake of establishing the absence of defects such as the violation of the conventions regarding the limbs (*aṅga-saṃketa*) up to the final sipping of water (*uttarācamana*), he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), indicating that all objects required for that [rite] should also be placed before him within the boundary (*maryādā*). The method for determining this boundary has been stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Then, with ash consecrated by the Weapon-mantra (*astra-parijapta*), or with a wooden peg (*śaṅku*), or with smooth stone powder, or with a boundary-line (*parighā*) drawn by one's own power (*svadhā*); one should draw it outside his seat, longer than a cubit (*śama*) in length, and equal to a cubit in width;
as before, one should bring it to a state of purification. (176–177)
By this very rule, during a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice or ritual performed regularly,
men must always provide a distribution of excellent wealth for the ancestors.
He states that such a distribution among paternal kinsmen pertains to those who possess wealth, using the word "according to rule" (vidhinā). || 178 ||
Or, having performed the rites ending with the offering of water and sesame seeds, he should give fruits and roots according to his capacity;
for that purpose, he should give at least a mouthful to cows or to beggars.

But others, having prepared water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) for the sake of the ancestors, should give according to their ability either a mouthful of fruit and roots or [something] to a cow or a mendicant; thus he says, "having performed" (kṛtvā). || 179 ||
Because that which is offered when Acyuta is worshipped with divine great mantras—whether it be small or abundant for the sake of the ancestors—becomes inexhaustible for them. (180)

He says "because" (yasmāt) to show that even if something is given for the sake of the ancestors in this manner, it becomes infinite through the power of the mantra. In the same way, it should be understood that although the distribution to the ancestors (pitṛsaṃvibhāga) is performed at the three times of day, it need only be done once—either after the morning worship or after the midday worship—according to the statement: "The sixth [rite] is the satiation of the fire, and the seventh is the sacrifice to the ancestors."

The doubt that—because the distribution of offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛsaṃvibhāga*) is stated to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the worship of the Blessed One—one must perform it at every instance of worship in order to accomplish the performance of the rite with all its auxiliaries—is refuted by [the mention of] Īśvara and Pārameśvara.
For it is said:
"Where the twelve-fold sacrifice (*dvādaśakālejyā*) is to be performed due to the expansion of the elements..."
There, one should perform the morning worship endowed with its eight limbs.
The two final ancillaries may be performed either with or without that [offering], and having completed them,
one should perform the distribution to the ancestors and the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga) as prescribed.
"The Guru may perform [the rite] at his own will during the daily midday worship;
or he may perform one of the two—the eight-limbed or the six-limbed—at the three times of day.

By this it is established that even when both the worship for one's own sake and the worship for the sake of others are performed by a single person, the distribution of offerings to the ancestors need not be done separately for each; for that [distribution] is to be performed only once on a single day.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata), the performance of the five-fold daily duties (*pañcakālika-dharma*)—consisting of *abhigamana*, *upādāna*, *ijyā*, *svādhyāya*, and *yoga*—is prescribed? Among these, *ijyā* performed for one's own sake is done by those who lack the qualification for [worship] for the sake of others. Since you, who possess such qualification, have already fulfilled your purpose through the worship of Śrīmannārāyaṇa and other deities manifested in divine places known as "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*), such as Śrī-Yādavādvī and so forth, what further need is there for worship in one's own home known as "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*)? [Reply: True. "Worship for the sake of others is like the sun, whereas worship for one's own sake..."

As stated by the Lord: "Like a lamp in a house," even when one's purpose is already fulfilled by the light of the sun, the lighting of a lamp in one's own home is still required; for the worship for one's own sake is likewise necessary.
"O King, the food of one in whose house an image of Keśava does not reside must never be eaten, for it is equal to forbidden food."

Thus, because it is stated that the worship of the image of the Blessed One is necessary even in one's own home, and because there is qualification for both types of worship—whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others—it should be understood that for us as well, the propitiation of the Blessed One for our own sake is mandatory.

Now, it may well be that you possess the authority for worshiping for your own sake and for the sake of others, as well as the necessity of worshipping the Lord in your own home. Indeed, many among your followers are authorized for both their own benefit and the benefit of others; yet it is not the case that everyone performs worship for the sake of others at all times. Therefore, one who performs worship for the sake of others must also perform worship for their own sake. If it is asked, "What rule is there that the distribution of offerings to the ancestors (pitṛ-saṃvibhāga) need not be performed by each individual?"—who has stated such a thing? It has been stated thus.

If, during a state when no other people are present, one person alone performs both the worship for one’s own sake and for the sake of others, then the performance of the distribution of offerings to the gods and ancestors may take place either in a temple or in one’s own home for the sake of others; however, it should be understood that our view is that if there is a difference in performers, each must perform the rite individually.

If it is argued that, this being the case, even in a temple dedicated to another deity, since there may be a difference in the performers during the morning worship and other rites, a distribution to the ancestors (pitṛ-saṃvibhāga) would have to be performed for each individual worship—this is not so; because a difference in performers is not mentioned therein, because the division of the twelve periods of time for the morning worship and other rites is taught with reference to a single performer, and because it is nowhere stated that a distribution to the ancestors must be performed at every instance of worship.

Nor can it be argued that the *homa* for one's own sake and the distribution to the ancestors (*pitṛsaṃvibhāga*) have not been mentioned at all; for here, following the offering to the fire, the distribution to the ancestors is prescribed as something to be performed near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the instruction, "one should spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south near the womb of the pit. This distribution to the ancestors must be understood as pertaining to worship for the sake of others (*parārtha*), because worship for one's own sake (*svārtha*) must be performed in a uniform manner.

If it is objected: "In that case, many inconsistencies are observed in the *Saṃpradāyapradīpikā* regarding worship for one's own sake (*svārthārcana*) as described by you; for instance, the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the distribution to the ancestors (*pitṛsaṃvibhāga*) are not mentioned," [the reply is: True. In that work, the sequence of worship was presented according to the method taught by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra for the easy understanding of those who are qualified solely for worship for their own sake.

However, we—who are qualified for both worship for our own sake and for the sake of others—must understand that in both cases, the performance of worship, installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), and so forth, must be carried out precisely according to the sequence stated in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and our own *Saṃhitā*.

If it is asked, "Why is the satiation of the fire not performed for one's own sake even by those who perform the practice according to the methods taught in the *Śrīsātvata* and other scriptures?", it is replied:
"In the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*), however, [the rite] consisting of obligatory and occasional duties ends with the oblation (*homānta*)."

One should indeed perform the worship in sequence, concluding each with the respective fire-oblation (*homa*). However, in the case of the secondary ritual procedure (*anukalpa*), it concludes with the recitation (*japa*); thus, one should understand, O long-lived one, that we perform it ending with the recitation because even the practice ending with *japa* is supported by the *Pārameśvara-tantra* and other scriptures. For this very reason, the worship ending with *japa* is stated for the obligatory (*nitya*) rite. Furthermore, in the *Kriyādīpa*, which follows the obligatory rule, the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*) is shown as ending with the *homa*.

Now, in your own commentary on the *Īśvarasaṃhitā*, it was stated that this distribution of offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛsaṃvibhāga*) should be performed after the fire-oblation (*homa*) during the performance of the mere morning worship (*prābhātikārcana*). That is inconsistent, for [the text states]:
"Morning, midday, and evening—these are the three times in their proper order;
the remaining ghaṭikās at those times are for one's own ritual duties."
In the case of a secondary option (*anukalpa*), however, there may be only one time, namely midday;
or, O twice-born one, according to one's capacity, there may be two times: midday and night.

If it is argued that this is because the *Mādhyandina* midday worship alone is prescribed in the *Pārameśvara* and other texts, whereas the morning worship alone is not mentioned anywhere, we reply: Your Honor should be satisfied with the fact that the performance of the morning worship alone is also possible on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions. 180.

Afterward, having petitioned the Supreme Lord for the sake of maintaining his bodily existence, and having received permission, he should indeed perform the sacrifice to the Self according to the prescribed rule. (181)
Having first presented the food offering (naivedya), one should take all the eatables into a vessel,
offer them to the deity, and purify them with water.
For she is the embodiment of truth, unperceivable, and the destroyer of the defects of food;
she is the fourfold self within the mind, and she is to be meditated upon as the very meditation itself. (183)

The Lord Pradyumna, whose essence is taste and who is known as the presiding witness, is established in the state of sweetness within food; while the wielder of the plow (Balabhadra) resides in its form and its potency.
The enjoyer is the Great-Souled Lord Vāsudeva himself, for he is unborn;
then one should drink a handful of water consecrated by reciting the four *praṇavas*.
Then, having offered four oblations of food into the mouth-vessel with that same [mantra],
he should thereafter eat as he pleases, using the desired morsels.

Now, with six verses beginning with "paścāt" (afterwards), he describes the procedure for the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*). "Ātmayāga" means the subsequent sacrifice. The reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) is to be known; it is ordained that, for the sake of the self's own realization, one should always perform a sacrifice with food and with that [self] itself.

"Along with the remnants of the sacrifice, water, fruits, and so forth"—thus it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*. Regarding the phrase "having purified it with water," the *Saccaritrarakṣā* explains: "The mention of purification is for the purpose of removing the possibility of defects such as being gazed upon by unworthy persons or having become stale. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and having offered it to the God," one should understand this to mean offering it to the Inner Self (*antarātman*). Thus, the *Saccaritrarakṣā* states:
"Meditating on Hari in his heart, being composed, he offers the food to Him."
Then, taking a measured portion of food with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
Then, one should offer oblations in sequence, saying: "Svāhā to Prāṇa," "and to Apāna," "and to Vyāna," "to Udāna," and "to Samāna, Svāhā."

Thus has the statement from the *Karmakāṇḍa* been cited. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, it is written: "having offered [the food] to the God who has become the image in one's own home. That is irrelevant, because this sentence is intended to refer to the offering to the Inner Self (*antarātman*). Accordingly, in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*: "Having cooked pure food on the cooking hearth, he brings it to the Blessed One upon the altar. Having worshipped the Blessed One upon the altar, he gives it to those who prepare it."

In the section concerning the investigation of the meaning of the secret Vedic scriptures (*rahasyāmnāya*), after stating that the phrase "they offer it to the Creator" (*dhātra upanayanti*) refers to the Inner Self (*antarātman*)—explaining that even those who perform ritual acts, having obtained food, worship the Blessed Lord on the sacrificial altar and offer it to Him; and that the Creator, having received what was offered, partakes of it himself and sustains his dependents with the remainder—the text cites the *Sātvata* statement beginning with "and having presented it to the God, and having purified it with water," as proof of that point.

If it is argued: "In the very secret scriptural passages (rahasyāmnāya) cited by you, it is indeed stated that food offered to the Lord should be given to the *kāris*, and that those *kāris* should perform worship to the Lord for their own sake using that very food; how then is this irrelevant to the present topic?"—you are ignorant of the intended meaning. Who could possibly dispute that point? Worship of the Lord with food obtained from the *kāris* is universally accepted. However, such a meaning cannot be attributed to the phrase "and having offered it to the Deity" (*vinivedya ca devāya*).

It should be understood that this statement does not describe the performance of ritual acts by those who perform them; rather, it describes the manner in which one who has worshipped the Lord, having offered the *kāri* (sacrificial fee), performs the concluding sacrifice (*anuyāga*).

If it is asked, "Why should the Lord be abandoned for one's own sake by one who has worshipped Him for the sake of others? we reply: He is indeed to be accepted, worshiped with leaves and other offerings, and served with prostrations and the like performed by oneself. However, it should be known that there is no opportunity for oneself to perform even this eight-limbed (*sāṣṭāṅga*) worship [for oneself].

For this very reason, in the *Pārameśvara* and other scriptures, it is stated that for one performing the twelve-fold worship (*dvādaśakālārcana*), there is only space for the daily rite (*āhnika*) even during the three periods of the day; however, no specific time for the worship for one’s own sake (*svārthārādhana*) is indicated for each occasion. Nor should it be argued: "Granted that there may be no room for the worship for one’s own sake for one performing the twelve-fold worship, what contradiction is there in the worship for one’s own sake for one who performs the three-fold worship (*trikālārcana*) and so forth? For even then, the very fact that the time for the worship for one’s own sake has not been mentioned constitutes the contradiction. [Objection: "But the three times—morning, midday, and evening—are well-known."
At that time, however, the remaining ghatis belong to one's own karma.
Thus, for the wise one who has attained the single path and is dedicated to the welfare of others without contradicting his own interest, the [appropriate] times have been declared in due order.

If you ask, "Is it not heard in the *Pārameśvara* that 'the same applies even for one who is initiated, whose mind is devoted to the Siddhānta'?"—we reply: In that context, by the phrase "of his own ritual" (*svasya karmaṇaḥ*) and by the word "own interest" (*svārtha*) in the expression "without contradicting his own interest," only the obligatory daily rites such as bathing are meant, and not the worship performed for one's own sake (*svārthārādhana*). This is because the latter, like the sacrifice for others (*parārthayajana*), must be accomplished over many hours by another agent. Furthermore, you yourself previously stated that the worship for both one's own sake and for the sake of others must be performed by the very same person.
In this regard, what is the determining factor? It is precisely the impossibility [of otherwise] that serves as the determinant.
If it is asked, "How can one's own worship, which usually takes many *ghaṭikās* to accomplish, be performed quickly at that time?"—it is replied:
"The most excellent form of propitiation is said to have the festival as its limit."
That which ends with the oblation (homa) is declared to be middling, while that which ends with the offering of food (prāpaṇa) is the lowest.
"However, this worship of Hari, ending with incense and lamps, is considered 'minor' (kṣudra)," according to the statement in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Thus, one should perform it either briefly or in detail, in accordance with the place and time.
"One should never omit [an offering]; one should worship me even with a mere handful (añjali).

From this statement in the *Lakṣmītantra*, it should be understood that the abbreviated option (*laghupakṣa*) is to be adopted. Accordingly, it is stated in the third section of the *Pāñcarātrarakṣā*: "When one's capacity is slight, there is contracted worship; beginning with a single offering (*upacāra*), the procedure extends up to a thousand offerings according to one's respective capacity and other factors. Furthermore: "In the case of the omission of an offering, it is said that there is sin and so forth: 'If [the offering] lacks fragrance, there is fear; if it lacks flowers, there is confusion.'"
In the absence of food offerings, there is famine; in the absence of mantras, death.
If worship is performed without mantras, without the prescribed ritual, or at an improper time,
it will constantly cause fear for the kingdom, and that particular village shall perish.

And so forth; all of this refers to the defect incurred when one who is capable of performing the complete ritual and possesses the full materials for worship—whether for the sake of prosperity such as kingship and kingdom, or for other optional (*kāmya*) rites—fails to provide those specific items due to greed and the like, or proceeds by means of a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) despite being capable of the primary method (*mukhyakalpa*). However, it is clearly stated that this does not apply to the performance according to one's capacity in obligatory (*nitya*) rites by one who is free from desire (*niṣkāma*).

Regarding the statement "food is the essence of rasa, known as the Adhyakṣa," one should contemplate that within the *vīrya*, *rūpa*, and *rasa* of food, Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others reside respectively in the form of mere strength (*bala*), potency (*vīrya*), and splendor (*tejas*), because strength and the other qualities are attributes of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Vāsudeva, however, the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), should be contemplated in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and power (*śakti*), because knowledge and the other qualities are attributes of the enjoyer. Thus, in the section on the Great Oblation (*mahāhavis*) in the *Pārameśvara-tantra*, it says:
"One should offer strength, potency, and splendor as the *arghya* flower;
one should contemplate them with the *netra-mantra* alone, according to the scripture."
Then, in one's own right hand, the powers of cognition, sovereignty, and action— the enjoyers whose nature is that of the instruments— should be remembered with their respective mantras.
