Having touched it again and again according to one's enjoyment, with the bound *grāsamudrā*.
"Indeed, those [offerings] which exist within the food-form of Viṣṇu are to be presented;
they arise from the distinctions of taste, potency, and so forth, and consist of the nature of splendor, vigor, and strength.
Thus it is said in the Lakṣmītantra as well.
Uttering the *tārikā*, one should perform [the rite] and visualize me standing before him.
The divine [energy], consisting of the bliss of Soma, which has sequentially attained the state of being food and so forth,
whose form is that of potency, essence, and flavor, and whose nature is splendor, potency, and strength.
"One should meditate upon the Self as the imperishable enjoyer, whose form consists of sovereignty, power, and knowledge—the lotus-eyed Supreme Person.
Regarding the instruction "one should drink a mouthful of water," the ritual sprinkling (pariṣecana) should also be performed. And so it is stated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"Having sprinkled [the food] with water using the Astra-mantra, and having rinsed it around with water using the Tāra-mantra,
one should then spread [an underlayer of ghee] and offer the water, and thereafter the Prāṇāhuti offerings."

Furthermore, it has been established that the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) are offered into the mouth-cavity (*vaktrakuṇḍa*) by means of that very [seed-syllable], namely the *praṇava* (Oṃ). Therefore, one should not be disturbed by the abandonment of the mantras for the well-known [Vedic] oblations to the vital breaths; for it was declared in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*: "In those cases where the fire-oblation (*homa*) into the mouth-cavity is prescribed with the Lord’s own uncommon mantras, no contradiction with Vedic norms should be suspected, since this is justifiable as being like other specific duties fixed by the *Kalpasūtras*.
Thus, there is also no rule that the oblation to the vital breaths must be performed with the *praṇava* alone; for it is stated in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*:

By whichever mantra, however, the bringing forth of the deity residing on the altar and so forth is performed according to the sequence of external propitiation, that is designated as "offering" (vinivedita).
O best of the twice-born, they should offer oblations into the mouth-shaped fire-pit with those respective mantras, using the syllables preceded by *prāṇa*, either four, five, or three times.

But the twice-born who are purified by exclusive devotion and devoted to the dharma of the three Vedas should offer oblations five times in succession with the mantras beginning with *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

"To the God residing in the heart, to Viṣṇu, the all-conquering"—thus [it is said]. Now, in this case, if one follows the method of offering oblations directly with the mantras specific to the Lord who is the inner self, rather than using the mantras for Prāṇa, Apāna, and so forth, then an independent *anuyāga* (subsequent sacrifice) is prescribed here without the remnants of what was previously offered. Otherwise, the fault known as *niveditanivedana* (offering what has already been offered) would occur. For this very reason, the word *naivedya* is used here in the phrase "having first taken the food intended as an offering (*naivedya*) and placed it in the vessel," and not the word *nivedita*. The natural meaning is that *naivedya* refers to that which has been set aside for offering to the inner self.

If you argue that this being the case, even the statement "having purified it with water" becomes meaningful, then you have never heard of the *Saccaritrarakṣā* and other such works; for in those texts, the fault known as *nivedita-nivedana* (offering what has already been offered) is avoided by the logic of the *savandana-abhiṣeka* (consecration with a ceremonial bath). Furthermore, words such as *naivedya* meaning "that which has been offered" are frequently cited in various places therein. (181–186)
Having sipped water for purification, one should go again to the house of the Blessed One,
being self-restrained and having placed [the senses] upon the ground along with the mind, intellect, and ego.
Like a tortoise, one should always keep the four feet and the head as the fifth in that very place, accompanied by circumambulation in this manner.
Having paid homage with the eight-limbed prostration and sat before the Lord, one should study the scriptures and investigate the meaning of their words. (189)

Now, following this sequence of worship, he describes—through three verses beginning with "Having sipped water"—the entry into the Lord’s abode preceded by ritual rinsing, the manner of performing the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) there, and the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) consisting of the study of the Āgamas. By the use of the singular form "with the eight-limbed [prostration]" (*aṣṭāṅgena*), it is indicated that these two verses together constitute a single instruction for a single prostration.

For this very reason, even in the *Nityagrantha*, the venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) employed the singular form in the passage: "having prostrated before the Lord with the eight-limbed prostration," and cited these same two verses as the illustration of the eight-limbed prostration.
Now, in this determination of the rules of conduct,
[one should honor] the temple, the God and Goddess, and the Pāñcarātrika teacher.

One should perform circumambulation from a distance for the Aśvattha tree, the Vaṭa tree, a cow, a multitude of the virtuous, and the house of the guru; however, one should do so from close by for the image of the Lord.
"One should pay homage to the four directions with prostrations like a staff.

He will also state this in the plural later on. If one asks, "What is the status of that [plural form]?"—it is true; however, it should be understood that in that case, there is also a distinction of location in the phrase "to the four directions."

If it is asked: "Have you not heard the statement from the *Pauṣkara* which prohibits an odd number of prostrations, stating, 'That which consists of one, three, five, seven, and so forth, is indeed uneven'? and likewise the statement from the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* following that, "In that regard, one should perform the circumambulations and prostrations in pairs"? To this it is replied: The performance according to those [odd numbers] applies specifically to those devoted to the *Pauṣkara*; however, for those devoted to the *Sātvata*, it should be understood that the performance of prostration occurs only once, as indicated by such [formulas] as "Salutation to you once; salutation to you twice," and so forth.

Since both positions are declared by the Śruti and likewise established by the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), one should study the Āgamas and investigate the meaning of their statements. Regarding this, in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* it is said: "In this context, listening to, reflecting upon, expounding, and reciting the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, hymns, the Upaniṣads, and the mantras that pervade both [systems]—which serve to please the Lord and delight one's own mind—as well as engaging in debates and discussions, act like oil for the lamp of discriminative knowledge.
Harshness, falsehood, slander, and idle chatter—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech."

It should be understood that this summarizes the point: "All activities which, as demonstrated by such examples, obstruct the arising of verbal evil, become *svādhyāya* (recitation/study) either collectively or individually, according to their respective possibilities. (187–189)
But when the time of twilight has arrived, having bathed up to the hips or having washed them,
he should then perform the changing of his garments.
Having worshipped the deity with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other articles, one should then sacrifice to the fire;
thereafter, having approached the bed, one should perform recitation (japa) according to one's ability. || 191 ||
Having concentrated upon the external deity established in the state of non-reliance,
one should [proceed] by means of that very effortless and unobstructed splendor.
At that very moment, sleep indeed came upon him;
then, having overcome both sleep and fatigue, he arose at midnight. (193)

Now, with three and a half verses beginning with "When [the time] has arrived," he briefly describes the sequence of duties to be performed, from the evening bath up to sleep. Here, by the phrase "having bathed" and so forth, the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites is indicated. Regarding the phrase "having worshipped the Deity," the method of worship, and regarding the phrase "one should sacrifice to the fire," the method of the oblation (*homa*) is to be understood exactly as previously stated. By this, it follows that for both one's own sake and for the sake of others, worship at both times is primary, since it was stated without distinction.

If one possesses wealth, the twelve-fold worship and other rites prescribed by the Pārameśvara and other scriptures should be performed for the sake of others, since they were taught specifically with that purpose in mind. Furthermore, it should be understood that the evening sipping of water (ācamana) continues until the end of the Anuyāga.
For the twice-born, eating in the evening and morning is enjoined by the Śruti:
"One should not eat in between; this rule is equal to the Agnihotra."
Thus, since even eating at night is scripturally sanctioned;
[one might object: "But here, the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga) has not been mentioned explicitly," as it is also stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Having performed the twilight worship according to rule and having approached me with devotion..."
One should practice yoga according to the prescribed method with a mind purified by the scriptures.

In this [text], the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) is not mentioned; yet for both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] as well, it is stated: "One should perform the evening worship, consisting of six limbs and concluding with the *bali* offering," and "At the three times [of day], one should practice one [form of worship] with eight limbs and the other with six limbs. Thus, in these statements which are clearly present, how can the subsequent sacrifice at night be considered scriptural? True. It should be understood that this was stated in that manner because, in all these cases, there is no absolute rule (*naiyatya*) regarding eating at night. For it is said in the *Pādma*: "Then, when the western twilight has arrived, [the rite] is enjoined there."
Having performed all [rites] such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa), [one worships] the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa).
Having performed worship according to the rules, in full detail as before,
he should eat, lie down upon his bed, and then rise during the deep of night.

"Having sipped water, having become pure, and having meditated upon the Supreme Person"—thus, even eating at night has been mentioned. Now, one might object: "Since eating at night lacks necessity (naiyatya), it was not established; yet, on days such as the Ekādaśī fast, since eating during the day also lacks necessity, how is that [eating] established? We reply: because daytime fasting occurs only occasionally, whereas nighttime fasting is common on the five festival days (pañcaparvan) and so forth, the establishment or non-establishment of the offerings for day and night should be understood accordingly.

In the *Pañcarātrarakṣā*, the Vedāntācāryas have likewise justified the fact that the daily sacrifice (*anuyāga*) is not mentioned in the eternal scriptures (*nityagrantha*): "For thus, on days of fasting such as the Ekādaśī and others, the daily sacrifice is omitted; at that time, the sacrifice consists of only seven limbs. For this very reason, the commentators did not mention it in order to indicate its non-obligatory nature. And the purpose and time for it should be fulfilled on that day by means of one or another [practice], such as Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), yoga, and so forth, as appropriate."

By the phrase "consisting of seven limbs" (*saptāṅga*) here, it is stated that the distribution to the ancestors (*pitṛ-saṃvibhāga*) must be performed even on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions. It should be understood that this consists of water mixed with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), not the feeding of Brahmins, because on those very occasions—such as the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and others—the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) sometimes occurs at dawn. Therefore, even though the sacrifice has already been performed previously, the midday sacrifice which arrives at its own time is said to consist of seven limbs; thus, the distribution to the ancestors mentioned after the meal is not in the form of a food-śrāddha (*anna-śrāddha*), but rather consists solely of water mixed with sesame seeds.

If it is asked, "But how is it that you have stated that the distribution to the ancestors (pitṛ-saṃvibhāga) occurs even after the morning worship on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and other such occasions?"—this is true. That [statement] refers to the context of worship for the sake of others, because the morning worship is also prescribed therein, as explicitly stated in the text: "There, one should perform the morning worship endowed with the eight limbs. Since, in the context of worship for one's own sake, only the midday worship is mentioned, it should be understood that the performance of the distribution to the ancestors immediately following that is not contradictory even for us.

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that at the time of one's own ritual worship, only the midday worship is appropriate? How then have you accepted the evening worship as well?"—this is true. However, its status as an ancillary limb (*aṅga*) of that [practice] should be seen as explicitly stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the *Pādma*, and other texts. Regarding the instruction "one should perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity," what is intended here is the recitation of mantras consisting of the study of the scriptures (*svādhyāya*); for the well-known sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) must be performed only after the offering of the oblation (*havirnivedana*).

And likewise, there is a summary in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā*: "Now, when the sun is turning red, one performs the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃ-sandhyopāsana*) and the evening fire-oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*) according to the sūtras; then, according to one's capacity, preceded by approaching the Lord and offering oblations, one takes food. If the meal is omitted due to some cause, there is the recitation of the *prāṇāgnihotra* mantras; thereafter follows the sequence of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and yoga appropriate for the night."

Regarding the phrase "having concentrated the deity outside," the meaning is "together with the Blessed One who is situated outside. The meaning of "until sleep comes" is that one should concentrate upon—that is, meditate upon—the deity stationed outside in the supportless state (*nirālambapada*). Here, once meditation has been performed by first effecting the cessation of the mind through effort, sleep does not occur. With the intention that in the absence of such [sleep], the composure of the mind required to perform yoga does not arise, it is said: "by the mind which is effortless and unceasing."

The connection of both these words [“abahiḥ” and “hṛtkamale”] is with the word “samādhāya. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, it is explained as “not outside, in the heart-lotus. That is weak, because in the *Sātvateśvara*, the *Pārameśvara*, and other such texts, as well as in the *Pañcarātra-rakṣā* and others, the reading is seen to be uniform: “having placed the deity outside” (*samādhāya bahirdevam*). Furthermore, by accepting that reading, no inconsistency in the meaning arises. (190–193)
Then, having risen at midnight, he was one who had conquered sleep and overcome fatigue.
Having sipped water from the very water contained in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
and having paid homage to the Guru and the Deity, he should sit down upon a seat of antelope skin.

Now, demonstrating yoga, he describes the preliminary duties for it with the verse beginning "samutthāya" (having arisen), which consists of one and a half verses. This verse has been explained specifically in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* as follows: "This is the rule regarding the time for yoga for those devoted to this *Saṃhitā*. Its practice is prescribed during a time of silence and at the time when all are asleep, because of the possibility of an excellence of one-pointedness [of mind]. And it has been stated that there is no contradiction in the rules for these various times, as they follow the respective capacities and other factors of the individual. In that context:
"One should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) containing water, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a Vedic text, and two auspicious golden earrings."

By stating "by that which remains in the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu)," it is indicated that even for a yogin of the Blessed One, the carrying of a water-pot along with the ritual of holding water as prescribed by Manu and others is enjoined. The word "tu" (but/however) suggests the specific rule mentioned in one's own scripture, as well as the touching of the right ear in the event of a lack of water; for they record: "In the case of inability to perform the ācamana and when water is unavailable, or during the aforementioned occasions, one should touch the right ear. Regarding the sipping of water (ācamana), it is performed once for both purposes: as the cause for ending sleep and as a constituent part of the subsequent rite. This is done by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application).
Regarding the expression "seated on a deer-skin," it is a reference to the principal element [of the compound] "clothes, deer-skin, and kusha grass" as mentioned in the Gītā. || 193-194 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) characterized by withdrawal using the four mantras;
one should place Aniruddha from the feet up to the knees. 195.
One should place the mantra named Pradyumna from the kneecaps up to the navel;
one should then place the Sāṅkarṣaṇa mantra from the navel up to the region of the ears.
Having offered the fourth [oblation] from the ear up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
he then remains seated in his preferred posture, such as the lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should maintain the conceit of one's own self as being fourfold, holding the body, head, and neck level together with the chest. (198)

Now, with three and a half verses beginning with "nyāsam," he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the four mantras beginning with Vāsudeva upon one's own body in the order of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*), sitting in any one of the postures such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), and the assumption of the identification (*abhimāna*) with the fourfold self within oneself.

Regarding the instruction that one should "resort to the conceit of the fourfold self," it should be understood that this refers to maintaining an identification with each respective form during the time of reciting and meditating on those specific mantras; otherwise, it would be impossible to simultaneously resort to identification with all forms at once, and because such identification will be taught individually for each. Furthermore, within this very section on the worship of the fourfold self, the practice of yoga and so forth by means of the four mantras has been explained.

It should be understood that there is no rule stating that yoga must be practiced using these very mantras even in the context of the worship of a single form (ekamūrti) or the worship of the vibhava forms; rather, it should be performed with the mantras appropriate to each respective context.

[Objection: But has it not been stated in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* that, with the exception of the fourfold mantra (*mantracatuṣka*) and so forth, everything else is common even to those established in other *saṃhitās*? By this, it is understood that for those established in this *saṃhitā*, yoga in all ritual sections (*prakaraṇa*) occurs through the fourfold mantra alone; for in that [text], it was not said "even for those established in other ritual sections. [Reply: We say: because the worship of the Fourfold Self (*cāturātmya*) is treated here in detail, whereas the other ritual section is abbreviated, [the rule applies] even in the other ritual section.

It is not stated [in the text] that it is "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). It should be understood that by this very term "common," the purpose for those established in other *saṃhitās* is also accomplished; what need is there for further reasoning? Otherwise, if the practice of yoga were restricted for everyone solely to the fourfold emanation (*vyūha*), then: "The first indeed bestows the fruit of liberation (*kaivalya*); the second bestows both enjoyment and liberation; the third is for the sake of enjoyment alone; and the fourth is always for those who are awakened. [This restriction would be untenable. Thus, it is known that the commonality applies even to those belonging to other *saṃhitās*. [This would contradict the fact that other forms are also used. Therefore, it must be understood that the status of being "common" establishes the same goal for followers of other traditions as well. Thus, according to the distinctions in the fruits for those initiated by the *parā* and other mantras to be described hereafter, the practice of yoga would not be possible for those who have attained only the supreme mantra (*parātpara-mantra*) out of a desire for liberation (*kaivalya*), nor for those who have taken authority over merely the *vibhava* mantras out of a desire for worldly results (*kāmya*). Therefore, it is established that for whichever mantra one has devotion, the practice of yoga should be performed with that very mantra. (195–198)
The gaze should be fixed on the tip of the nose with the eyes slightly closed;
the tongue should rest against the palate, and the rows of teeth should be kept apart.
The two elbows should be held slightly touching the lips;
then one should place both hands below the navel in the region between the thighs.
By means of the lower-and-upper union, having sequentially secured the body from left to right with the yoga-band, one should thus maintain the form steady.
Having contracted that very [breath] from the place of its descent upwards, one should expand it by means of the letter *ha*,
which is devoid of phonetic form and whose shape is unperceivable.
Now, with four and a half verses beginning with "evenly" (samam), he describes the sequence for maintaining the body, head, and other limbs at the time of practicing yoga. (198–202)

One should gradually withdraw the mind that has entered into sense objects; one should indeed cause it to dissolve into the intellect, and that [intellect] one should cause to abide within its own sphere.

Then, having withdrawn the mind from the sense objects and joined it with the intellect (*buddhi*), one should place the intellect upon the Lord, who is its own proper domain; thus he says, "from the objects. Accordingly, in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* and the *Śāṇḍilyasmṛti*, it is said: "This is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this is the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—the contemplation of their relationship is proclaimed as Yoga."
"Yoga is the steady abiding of the intellect in Brahman through the senses,
whether they are engaged or disengaged from the various activities of the Lord.
Thus [says] Parāśara in the third section of that same work.
"That specific movement of the mind which depends upon one's own effort, its union with Brahman is designated as yoga. (203)
Having composed yourself by means of the self together with the mantras, listen as I describe how [the process] proceeds step by step up to the stage of the waking state. 204.

Having stated the meditation on the union of the inner self (pratyagātman) with the Supreme Self (paramātman) abiding in each respective state—from the waking state up to the fourth state (turya), accompanied by the recitation of the corresponding mantras—he says, "Listen, I shall explain that in detail," [concluding] with the words "having composed oneself" (samādhāya). Thus, it is said in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā*:
"One should place the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), entirely free from all states, into Brahman;
this is both meditation (dhyāna) and yoga; everything else is merely an elaboration of the text."

And Yājñavalkya says: "Having made the mind free from activity, one should place the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in Brahman. "Free from activity" means devoid of external mental functions. || 204 ||
One should visualize the previously mentioned lotus, presided over by the fourfold Self (Cāturātmya), with all its forms completely tranquil and resembling the midday sun.
Then the king of mantras, having turned back through the intellect with a self non-different from it, [repeated] one hundred times both Aniruddha and the state of waking.
Through the power of reciting that mantra and by being bound to the state of identity with it,
his greatness arises along with its corresponding knowledge.
Through practice, at the end of the year, that [mantra] becomes endowed with non-duality;
then, having reversed the mantra of Pradyumna two hundred times, (208)
"Whoever this is, that am I; indeed, by means of this very non-duality, through such constant practice, the wise man becomes one whose doubts are severed. (209)
And by its power, through that very time, it is born;
indeed, by this sequential application accompanied by the increase of recitation.
And he should also place the entire previously mentioned collection of mantras [there],
as long as the Blessed One shines in the location characterized by the previously described marks.
With his form dissolved, he is stainless, infinite, and a treasury of splendors;
he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, peaceful, incomparable, and undisturbed.

Having composed oneself by means of the self and having abandoned the act of recitation therein, one should proceed until one attains identity with that [reality] through the non-differentiation of the meditator and the object of meditation. || 213 ||
When, through practice, the yogi attains stability in that samādhi which is free from all objects of perception, he then becomes one with Brahman, O Blessed One.

He explains the method of yoga in detail, beginning with the words "having the form of the midday sun" and ending with "then one attains Brahman. The meaning of this is as follows: having meditated upon the lotus of one's own heart as presided over by the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*) through its various respective stages, and contemplating oneself as unified with Aniruddha who resides in the waking state, one should recite his mantra a hundred times every day. In this way, through the power of reciting that mantra, both his knowledge and his majesty become possible for oneself as well.

In this way, when one year has been spent practicing yoga, one becomes endowed with identity with Aniruddha. Immediately thereafter, having dissolved Aniruddha along with his mantra into Pradyumna while cultivating the meditation on identity—thinking "I am Pradyumna"—and reciting that mantra two hundred times every day, one should spend another year. By this, the power of Pradyumna is attained.

In this manner, practicing the Saṃkarṣaṇa mantra, the Vāsudeva mantra, and the fourfold group of mantras beginning with Svapna-Vyūha-Aniruddha and ending with Vāsudeva, as well as the fourfold group of Suṣupti-Vyūhas—each for one year, increasing the number of recitations while meditating on identity with each respective deity—one should gradually dissolve each mantra into the subsequent mantra; finally, dissolving even the Vāsudeva of the Suṣupti-Vyūha into the Supreme Vāsudeva who abides in the previously described state of Turya (the Fourth).

Through the contemplation of identity with That, one should recite that mantra until, by means of the non-differentiation between the meditator and the object of meditation, one attains absorption in It; having reached that point, one should then abandon the act of recitation. When, through such practice, one attains stability in samādhi—which is devoid of the relationship between the Lord as the object of knowledge and the yogi as the knower—then one becomes Brahman. The meaning is that one becomes Brahman itself; in other words, one attains supreme equality.

It has also been stated that in every instance where one thinks "this is I," one resorts to an identity with each respective manifestation (*vyūha*); by this, the establishment of his own non-duality (*advaita*) with them is demonstrated. Here, the oneness of the nature of the pronoun "who" (*yaḥ*) should be reflected upon; for: "What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self—he who perceives the Self as other than what it truly is?"

Thus, it has been stated that through erroneous cognition there is a reversal of the result. However, in that case, identity in every respect must be understood; for when there is identity of mode, the conventional usage of "reality" (tattva) occurs, as in the expression, "This is that cow. If it is objected:

"Is it not the case that the error belongs to you yourselves, who deny the identity of essential nature established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as, 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second,' and 'That thou art'? We reply: Are we now making a determination of reality? What is the use of a dispute between us two regarding a matter already determined by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra and others?

Indeed, here it is taught repeatedly and very clearly that pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*) is established: "Then, having composed oneself by means of the self together with the mantras, in due order"; "by the self which is non-different from that"; "endowed with that non-duality"; "he who is this, I am he, by this very non-duality, always indeed"; "until, through the absence of distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation, one attains identity with That"; and "then one becomes Brahman. Thus, pure non-duality is taught more than once.

If it is argued: "All these collections of statements are contradictory to you who do not accept non-duality (*advaita*), and they have not been examined in your own commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and other works; therefore, we disagree on this matter," [the response is: True. That collection of statements has not been examined in the commentaries and so forth as if it were a part of one's own school's scripture; nevertheless, since scriptural passages, histories (*itihāsa*), and Purāṇas of a similar nature have been examined, it should be understood that these [statements] also achieve their purpose. And all of this has been examined by the Vedāntācāryas in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā*; it should be seen there. (205–214)
Then, having abandoned the meditation seat, he should gradually master his fatigue;
and when that is completed, remaining on his bed, he should pass the time until the end of the night.
Thus, after the practice of yoga, he speaks of rest until the *brāhmamuhūrta* with the word "tataḥ" (thereupon). || 215 ||
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, having risen from bed and bathed, one should worship the Lord of the World and perform the offering of fuel into the fire.
And one should offer oblations of sesame, ghee, and so forth, according to one's ability, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess and for the completion of all rites. (217)
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the sprinkling and other rites as before;
then [one should worship] the deity seated upon the pedestal and the fire situated within the sacrificial pit.
Having withdrawn the two types of nyāsa by means of the mind from one's own body,
one should perform the complete reabsorption of the arghya and other offerings.
Following the dedication of the sacrifice, as well as from the sacrificial pit and all the ritual grasses and so forth,
along with the very act of smearing, one should cast everything into the water.

He briefly states the sequence of duties beginning from the *brāhmamuhūrta* (the hour of Brahmā) in five verses, starting with the word "Brāhma. The phrase "two types of *nyāsa*" means the pair consisting of *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) and *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment). Thus, immediately after the conclusion of the *nyāsa*, one should perform the *anuyāga* (subsequent sacrifice) and so forth. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"Having applied the *tilaka* from the place of sacrifice and having withdrawn the *nyāsa* performed upon oneself, the wise man should indeed perform his meal and other such activities."
In the Lakṣmītantra as well, it is stated:
"Having withdrawn the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the rest, and having received [the offerings] with the armor (varma) and weapon (astra) mantras,
and having withdrawn the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga)."

Thus, since the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) was withdrawn prior to the meal, it is understood that the *nyāsa* must be performed again at the commencement of the evening worship. Even though the *Pārameśvara* states: "The morning time is indeed the best; however, at all three times, one should duly perform the ritual placement of mantras upon oneself, the hands, and the body."
One should perform the heart-sacrifice, the purification of the locus, and the ritual of the body—both the elemental and the daily—at dawn; at other times, one may act according to one's desire.

Thus it has been stated; nevertheless, that [rule] refers to those who have not yet withdrawn their ritual placements (*nyāsa*) during the midday worship and other such rites. However, at the commencement of the evening worship, the withdrawal of the *nyāsa* must necessarily be performed, because the *nyāsa* was already withdrawn prior to the midday subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*), and because worship without the [withdrawal of] *nyāsa* is improper. (216–220)
Whoever, endowed with devotion and faith, should sacrifice according to this rite for one day, three days, seven days, a fortnight, or even a month; || 221 ||
Even he would go to the supreme abode, how much more so one who remains here for as long as life lasts, with his girdle firmly fastened, being of great intelligence.
He states the fruitfulness of such propitiation even when performed according to one's capacity by means of two verses beginning with "sakṛt" (221–222).
Thus, O pure-eyed one, I have correctly explained to you in brief the auspicious sacrifice pertaining to the fourfold self, including both its external and internal aspects. (223)
By knowing which, the inexhaustible seed of ignorance comes to an end for living beings who are devoted and whose minds are purified, even before long. (224)
He concludes the stated meaning with two verses beginning with "iti": || 223-224 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Fourfold Self," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Sātvatatantra-bhāṣya, composed by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrī Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The Seventh Chapter.
Nārada said:
O twice-born ones, listen now to that action which brings about the highest bliss, as it was spoken again by the gracious Lord to Lāṅgalin.

Now the seventh [chapter] will be explained. Nārada said to the sages: "Listen to the ritual known as a vow (vrata), which was instructed by Vāsudeva to Saṃkarṣaṇa," beginning with the words "With a gracious mind" (prasannena). || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen to this merit-bestowing discourse consisting of Brahman, which burns away the accumulation of demerit and grants perfection without delay to those who have understood it in its true essence.

The Blessed One said to Saṃkarṣaṇa, "Listen. It is meritorious, bringing about merit; it is the burner of the accumulation of non-merit and the destroyer of sin—"action" is to be supplied as the subject. || 2 ||
The Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, consisting of four aspects and imperishable,
is that which itself manifests as the four-armed form in the state known as waking.
Surely, for the sake of pacifying the suffering of existence for those whose nature is bound by karma,
he has assumed that form which bestows liberation by pervading all states of being.
Then, by means of the yoga of dissolution, having brought each of their own fourfold forms to transformation through that union, they abide within the Self as before.
Furthermore, for the sake of favoring living beings, [the Lord] indeed manifests in various forms,
while not abandoning the splendor of his body, together with the sequence of the directions.
But by means of the individual male forms, each consisting of three types [of weapons],
they are joined with the manifest discus and so forth, beginning with Vāsudeva.
For the castes who are rich in superior qualities such as [the performance of] sacrifices from the beginning of creation and do not worship another deity,
he attains eternal manifestation by virtue of being their progenitor.

The previously mentioned fourfold group beginning with Vāsudeva—which is higher than the highest and known as the eternally manifest *vyūha*—has manifested in the form of the aforementioned waking *vyūha*. For the sake of removing the suffering of transmigration for those individual souls (*jīvātman*), it has appeared in that very form and descended into the waking state through the process of dissolution into the quarters of space. Having withdrawn the fourfold forms beginning with Puruṣa back into its own self, it then manifests again for the sake of favoring transmigrating beings, each [deity] being threefold in three ways as the triad of Vāsudeva, Keśava, and so forth.

Saṃkarṣaṇa appears in the form of a triad beginning with Govinda; Pradyumna in the form of a triad beginning with Trivikrama; and Aniruddha in the form of a triad beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa. Accompanied by manifest emblems such as the discus and others, He attains eternal manifestation as the nourisher of those who are solely devoted to the Blessed Lord. This is stated in the six verses beginning with "the Supreme Brahman" (3–8). By the phrase "without abandoning the beauty of His body," it is indicated that the specific colors previously described for the fourfold Vyūha of Vāsudeva and the others in the waking state apply equally to the triads and tetrads beginning with Keśava.
Relying upon which, those who are well-awakened proceed by means of the practice of giving, virtue, vows, and so forth, to the supreme abode from cyclic existence in no long time. (9)
Thus, he states the purpose of the manifestation in the form of Keśava and others with the verse beginning "yām" (verse 9).

For one who would perform ritual action with the thought "this must be done," or who would exercise lordship under the guise of devotion or the pretext of a vow— for him, this sequence has been prescribed.

Therefore, he says "it should be performed" (kartavyam iti) to indicate that the sequence for performing the vows for the propitiation of Vāsudeva and others, as well as Keśava and others, will now be described. "Sovereignty" (aiśvarya) means that which pertains to the Lord; the meaning is "his propitiation. Alternatively, it means "that which brings about such things as sovereignty in this world. In both cases, this is an adjective qualifying the ritual action (karman). || 10 ||
On the tenth day of the month of Kārttika, at the arrival of night,
[one should perform the bath] with ghee, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or with the water from the feet of the image.
Having purified his own mouth-cavity and expelled the impurity residing in the stomach,
he should remember the Lord, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and place kuśa-grass water in his hand.
Preceded by its casting off, one should perform the mental resolve regarding the vow:
"Oṃ, to the Lord of Vows, O God, whose form is eternally pure... (13)

On the evening of the tenth day, by consuming one of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, he effects purification of his own body; then, preceded by the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and after sprinkling water from *kuśa* grass, he makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding Kārtika with two and a half verses. Regarding the phrase "with ghee, with the five products of the cow, or with the water from the feet of the Image," it should be understood that each subsequent option is superior. Thus, in the third section of the *Saccaritrarakṣā*, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states: "Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) on earth, one obtains all of that by placing the water from Viṣṇu’s feet upon one's head."
Whatever merit a person may gain by performing ablutions and drinking the water of the Gaṅgā, such merit is obtained simply from holding her stream upon one’s feet.
Whatever holy place exists within the three worlds— such as Prayāga, Puṣkara, and others—
it dwells eternally there at the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Indeed, Śaṅkara himself knows the greatness of the water from the feet [of the Lord] in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam,
for he bears upon his head the Gaṅgā, which originates from Viṣṇu’s feet.

"Having incurred a transgression, one attains purification at that very moment by drinking the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, even after undergoing a penance such as the Kṛcchra or the Aghamarṣaṇa. And so forth. The sense is that in the absence of this [water], the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be taken, and in the absence of that as well, ghee should be taken. Thus it is stated in the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the chapter on ablution (*snapanādhyāya*).
In the absence of the five products of the cow, clarified butter alone is prescribed;
for one who cannot obtain the five products of the cow, clarified butter is used in their stead. Thus it is said.

By the phrase "remembering the Lord, the impurity residing in the belly departs," *prāṇāyāma* (breath control) is indicated; as he will state in the section on the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*: "Having meditated on the Lord situated in the region of the navel and having seized the impurity, one should cast it out through the path of the breath up to the limit of the *dvādaśānta*."
Having drawn in the sinless [air] together with the wheel of wind through the tip of the nose,
O Lord of Mantras, for the purpose of filling the body;
One should meditate upon that [Self] residing in the heart by means of the breath whose movement has been restrained. Thus (ends verses 11–13).
"Oṃ! To the Lord of Vows, O God, whose form is eternally pure;
for a year I shall propitiate you, the Unborn, with intense devotion.
With self-restraint, lying upon a bed of *darbha* grass on the surface of the earth, one should pass the night. || 13-14 ||
He states the mantra for the resolve: "Oṃ, to the Lord of Vows. By "paripīḍaiḥ" is meant by fasts. || 13-14 ||
Being self-restrained, he should spend the night on the ground upon a bed of *darbha* grass.
Then, on the morning of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), having bathed and meditated upon the Lord Adhokṣaja,
he should worship Him as before with various auspicious names.

Thus, immediately following this resolve, he describes lying down upon *kuśa* grass on the bare ground during that night with the half-verse beginning "prayataḥ. He describes the duties for the dawn of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) with the verse beginning "ekādaśyām. The phrase "by various other names" means by the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names) and so forth; the word "having praised" (*stutvā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. || 14–15 ||
Listen now to how they stand, positioned from right to left with their two hanging hands, richly adorned with a lotus and a conch shell. (16)
With the index and middle fingers bent inward and positioned in the center, the auspicious conch is held with its opening facing upward, resting upon the edge of the palms. (17)
It was like a white lotus with its stalk, fully blossomed,
with only a small portion of its creeper-like stem remaining beyond the wrist.
One should meditate upon the Lord’s [hand] hanging down with the face turned downward and the thumb [extended].

With three and a half verses beginning with "With the two hands," he describes the method of meditating on the insignia of Vāsudeva. In the hanging right hand, a white lotus—resembling a conch, fully blossomed, and extending beyond the wrist with only a small portion of its stalk remaining—is held by the index finger and thumb at the palm region, facing downward; likewise, in the left hand, a conch is held between the bent index and middle fingers at the palm region, facing upward.

The meaning is that one should meditate [upon Him]. Now, if it is argued: "Previously, the waking-form Vāsudeva was described as having four arms; now, by mentioning only two emblems, He is understood to have only two arms—does this not constitute a contradiction for you? [We reply: What does that matter to you? The defining characteristic would apply in both ways. (16–19)
Having performed everything up to the end of the oblation, he should then meditate with unblinking eyes.
One should perform worship during the middle of the day, omitting the bath at the end of the day,
accompanied by various hymns of great significance along with songs and instrumental music.
Having passed the night, at dawn he should then worship Aja (the Unborn), who is fourfold and unmanifest, preceded by ritual bathing and concluding with the rites of the Anuyāga.
Then, when the lord of the night has risen and the sun has set,
one should perform worship for the sake of atonement and prostrate oneself upon the ground like a staff.
Then, one should perform circumambulation four times in the four directions;
having uttered each [mantra] at the beginning of each [direction], one should step forward four steps at a time.
Then, having composed hymns and mantras expressive of that [deity] which arise from one's own nature, together with a collection of sentences that manifest its specific manifestation; 24.

Then, having performed everything up to the end of the *homa*, and meditating upon Him once more, when midday arrives, he should perform worship according to the rules; then, having performed the evening worship excluding the ritual bathing, and having passed that night in vigil accompanied by various songs, instrumental music, and hymns imbued with profound meaning, on the morning of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), after bathing and duly worshipping the Lord who is fourfold in nature, he should complete the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) and perform the evening worship, seeking forgiveness for his transgressions.

He describes the ritual procedure with the words beginning "until the end of the fire-oblation" (homāntam) and so forth: while performing four prostrations like a staff toward the four directions and circumambulating four times, one should stand before each [deity] and recite the hymns, mantras, and verses that express their respective qualities. || 19–24 ||
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed Vāsudeva of immeasurable luster!
You are liberated from passion, hatred, and other defects, and you are the embodiment of all virtues. (25)
O Lord, preeminent in the power of wisdom, homage to you, the creator of the universe!
O Saṅkarṣaṇa, large-eyed one, omniscient Supreme Lord! 26.
O God, whose self is sovereignty and valor, O Pradyumna, Lord of the worlds!
Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Lord of all, who pervades the universe. (27)
Victory to you, O Blessed One, Aniruddha, Great Puruṣa, Primordial Being, whose power and splendor are the cause for the preservation, origination, dissolution, and protection [of the world]. (28)

He himself uttered the fourfold hymn-mantras beginning with *jitaṃ te* for Vāsudeva and the others, using the four verses starting with *jitaṃ te*. Here, by taking the first quarter-verse from the first verse, the second from the second, the third from the third, and the fourth from the fourth, it is presented in the form of a single verse in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the *Pādma*, and other texts. Furthermore, its pervasiveness over the eight-syllable mantra and others is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"In the Pāñcarātrika ritual, there shall be three mantras for this [deity]: the *pada*, the *mantra*, and the *astra*."
"Salutation to Viṣṇu," "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," and first,
"Salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva."
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One!
O Purandara, this fourth is the *pada-mantra* of the *praṇava*.
Those who know the ancient lore know these mantras to be accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*.
They are: the solitary *tāraka*, and the four beginning with that [the *pada-mantra*].
"These five pervasive mantras are proclaimed in the Pañcarātra. Thus [it is said].

It should be understood that even more than this, the collection of hymn-verses set forth in the *Padma* and other [Purāṇas] constitutes an exposition of the meaning of the mantra known as *jitantā*. The commentary on the *jitantā* mantra is to be found as stated in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. (25–28)
By this very procedure, worship of Viṣṇu must be performed by a twice-born man free from desire throughout both fortnights until the end of the year. (29)

Thus, performing every month on both fortnights the fast and the vigil on the tenth day preceded by the rule of consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and on the twelfth day performing the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) preceded by the worship for the fulfillment of the vow, as well as worship and so forth in the evening for the sake of seeking forgiveness for transgressions, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the vow without desire in whatever manner possible until the end of the year; thus he says, "according to the rule" (vidhinā). || 29 ||
In this manner, worship beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa and ending with Vāsudeva is ordained as that which must always be performed by the Kṣatriya caste.
For a Vaiśya, the lineage beginning with Pradyumna and ending with Musalin is prescribed;
for a true Śūdra, it is always that beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Pradyumna. (31)

He states the specific rule for the Kṣatriya with the words "In this manner. He states the specific rule for the Vaiśya with the half-verse beginning "Pradyumna and the rest," meaning up to Musali (i.e., Saṃkarṣaṇa). He states the specific rule for the Śūdra with the half-verse beginning "The virtuous Śūdra. || 30-31 ||
Now, pay close attention to the specific details regarding the meditation on the forms:
in the case of Saṅkarṣaṇa, there is a beautiful lotus in his [left] hand, while in the right hand he holds a mace.
One should contemplate it as being grasped from the middle by the hand with its face turned downwards,
effortlessly using only two fingers, beginning with the thumb.
As before, understand that Pradyumna holds a lotus in his left hand;
likewise, the king of weapons [a spear] is held in the right hand above two fingers.
As before, there is a lotus in the left; now the fourth [hand] is described.
As at the beginning, there is a lotus in the right, and a mace in the left as previously stated. (35)
Thus has been described the meditation upon the primary forms, together with their worship,
for the sake of the daily and occasional rites, and for the attainment of the state of supreme liberation.

Since previously only the meditation on the insignia of Vāsudeva was mentioned, he now describes the meditation on the specific insignia of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, beginning with the words "mūrtinām" and ending with "niḥśreyasapadāptaye. By the phrase "like a lotus," it is understood that just as the arrangement and manner of holding the lotus in the right hand of Vāsudeva were previously described, so too is the mace in the right hand of Saṃkarṣaṇa; the meaning is that it hangs down with its face turned downwards.
"By the thumb and the other two fingers" means by the index finger and the thumb. By the phrase "as before," the downward-facing nature of Vāsudeva’s lotus and so forth is indicated. (32–36)
But for those of the castes, beginning with the Brahmins, who strive with effort to seek [liberation] through absolute isolation preceded by devotion, the practice of vows is prescribed. (37)
On the tenth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform everything previously described;
having performed an anointing with water and kuśa grass while remembering the Lord, one should recite this: || 38 ||
O primordial one, who consists of all beings, grant me your supreme state;
sever my worldly bonds and dispel the darkness of ignorance.
Then, having meditated, he should worship the four-formed God as before, using secondary and primary names, great epithets, and words such as "Victory! (jita) and so forth.

Then, by means of the individual [words] separately and also collectively, and again each one individually through the application of different expressions of the meanings, and finally by the collective [meaning] in another form. (41)
O high-minded one, one should perform this worship for each and every image in due order; everything beginning with prostration should be repeated as prescribed.
Listen now to the placement of the marks up to the fourth [finger], accompanied by their grasping, as taught by the descendants of Maudgala who are solely intent upon the fruit of liberation. (43)
In this vow, there is an indication of the four deities by means of horizontal lines from one's own side toward the region [of the deity], outside the circle known as the breast. (44)
In his right hand, there is clearly a mace with its fist grasped;
and from the hollow of his left side, the king of conchs emerges.
One should always remember the thumb resting on the outside of the circumference;
likewise, the excellent conch should be meditated upon in the second [finger] of the principal hand. (46)
The wheel and the big toe are situated above; in the left hand, which is in the fist, is the mace of Pradyumna; on the left is the mace, while the right is filled with sound.
One should visualize Aniruddha’s lotus on the right, radiant as the sun; and on the left, a wheel held by the index finger, with its three spokes touching the thumb. 48.
In this way, the practitioner attains the fruit from meditation as it truly exists.

Now, regarding the specific divisions of time for the vow to be observed solely by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and the distinctions in the placement of marks (*lāñchana-nyāsa*) and meditation, [the author] speaks, beginning with "preceded by devotion" and ending with "the practitioner attains the fruit. "Up to the Fourth" means up to Aniruddha. "With those ending in Maudgala" means with those ending in Śūdra. In the phrase "on the right, however, of the first, the mace-bearer," "of the first" means of Vāsudeva.

"Diagonally" means from the region of one's own side; "outside the circle called the breast" means on both sides, that is, outside the chest area. "Equal to that" means as far as the primary hand, that is, the right hand. "Of the second," namely Saṃkarṣaṇa. "In the same way" means like the hand of Vāsudeva. "Filled with sound" refers to the conch. "In the three" means in the index finger and the others. (37–49)
Furthermore, a vessel of food with milk is prescribed for him month after month.

At the conclusion of the vow, for the sake of making a gift, one should offer gold, jewels, and sesame seeds; and for those who have observed the vow without desire, there is always the ritual gift of a cow at the end.

With the verse beginning "sakṣīram" (along with milk), he states in one and a half verses the materials to be offered monthly by those observing the vow without desire, as well as the materials to be given at the end of the year.
Every month, for those who possess desire, there shall be a vessel of curd with boiled rice,
fruits accompanied by gold, and at the end, the gift of land itself.
Sesame seeds, a water-pot, and worship with leaves, flowers, and so forth—these are prescribed according to one's ability; for the poor, gold is considered equal to a cow.

Likewise, with one and a half verses beginning with "month by month," he states the substances to be given by those who possess the requisite means. With the half-verse beginning with "of the poor," he states the giving of gold according to one's capacity as a substitute for the gift of a cow or the gift of land for those who are unable [to give the primary gifts]. In the phrase "equal to a cow" (*gosamam*), the word "cow" (*go*) also denotes "land. (51–52)
In the case of Śūdras, however, for the acts of giving, worship, and the performance of vows at all times, food that is not yet cooked is prescribed;
or, if it is already cooked, it may be offered according to the wish of a Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the Śūdras, it is said in the *Dāna* [section] that at the conclusion of the vow, uncooked food should be given; or, if permission from a Brāhmaṇa is available, cooked food may be given. Since it is established by the injunction, "Śūdras who have resided with Āryas may perform cooking," that Śūdras also have the authority to cook upon the permission of a Brāhmaṇa, the statement "or according to the wish of the Brāhmaṇa" should be understood as being non-contradictory. Thus, the meaning is that worship should be performed in a manner that is not in conflict with the specific duties (*dharma*) of one's own caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*). || 53 ||
One does not attain excellence through worship in the same way that one attains it through one's own karma;
therefore, one should always perform worship according to one's own specific qualification.
He states that it is caused by one's own karma. || 54 ||
A Brahmin is authorized for the worship of Vāsudeva and other deities everywhere, whereas Kṣatriyas and others are not; therefore, one should perform what is prescribed by the scriptures.

In the worship of the Blessed One, there is eligibility for all—including Kṣatriyas and others—just as there is for Brāhmaṇas; therefore, it must be performed according to one’s specific eligibility. Thus he says, "in all respects. || 55 ||
Maudgala should pass these days with devotion, eating only at night;
for indeed, the consumption of *paripīḍa* is prescribed for him at the beginning and end of the vow.

"For a Śūdra, there is the eating at night on the eleventh day as an alternative; he should observe fasting only on the eleventh days at the beginning and end of a vow," so it says: "he should lead [him]. (56)
Starting from whichever month is preferred,
however, those elder brothers who desire liberation and are intent upon their duties should proceed gradually.
On the tenth day, the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the twelve-year vow should be made; then, having completed the year as before with monthly offerings, [the vow is fulfilled]. 58.
When the year has passed, one should propitiate Vrateśvara, the Lord of the World, from the first day of the month in which the rite is to begin until that same day of the following month. (59)
Having begun for one year as before, he should worship and please the Lord;
having thus accomplished this great vow for twelve years in this sequence, [he attains success]. (60)
At its conclusion, however, the qualified performer should worship twelve Brahmins with gifts, garments, and ointments according to his capacity.

Now, regarding the Brāhmaṇa’s other twelve-year vow, he says [the passage] beginning with "yathābhimatamāsa" (according to the chosen month) and ending with "yaṣṭavyam adhikāriṇā" (it should be performed by the qualified person). The meaning is "by those previously mentioned. That gift which was prescribed previously for every month should here be performed every year; however, the gift prescribed at the end of the year should here be performed at the end of the twelve years—this is the meaning. (57–61)
Indeed, by whatever rite one worships his own form, this very task must be performed;
for this vow, beginning with the month of Jyeṣṭha, is to be observed with devotion by a Kṣatriya.
In brief, the Vaiśya should begin with the month of Āśvayuja, while the Maudgala should maintain the sequence beginning with the month of Māgha. 63.
This divine vow is the highest, bestowing the fruit of liberation;
it is ordained for all castes and is never contradictory at any time.

With three verses beginning with "svamūrti," he describes the performance of this vow by Kṣatriyas and others as well, according to the difference in time; the meaning is: "by means of the worship of one's own form" (svamūrti), that is, through the sequence of Saṃkarṣaṇa and so forth prescribed for each respective caste. (62–64)

I shall describe another excellent vow, which removes impurity from the beginning of creation and is equal to ten thousand cāndrāyaṇa fasts, as something that must be performed by those engaged in ritual action.
For others whose selves are purified and who desire nothing but the single fruit of liberation,
there is the granting of liberation upon the fall of the body for those who sacrifice solely to the Fourfold Self.
On the tenth day of the month as desired, one should offer water,
having bowed to Vrateśvara as before, for the duration of two years.
One should especially make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) in the month of Śrāvaṇa and also in Kārttika;
indeed, from the month of commencement until the very end known as completion.
One should increase the twelve fasts by one at a time;
having performed the worship up to the fire-oblation as before, one should worship those who are absorbed in that [deity].
Then, for those who are suffering, one should perform a reduction for one year;
however, in the month of Āśvina, the preliminary [rite] should be performed for twelve nights.
One should omit [one meal] each day until the year is completed;
then one should perform the conclusion of the vow as before, with worship and other rites. (71)
I have described this vow to you according to the sequence of its increase and decrease, by which the eternal state is indeed attained without effort. (72)

Now, beginning with the verse "Equal to ten thousand *cāndrāyaṇas*" and ending with "the eternal state is attained," he describes another vow to be performed for two years, characterized by an increase and decrease in fasting. (Verses 65–72)
Therefore, listen now to the vow called Dvādaśa, which is the most excellent and auspicious of all vows;
for it yields equal fruit at its conclusion for both those who perform it without desire and those with desire. (73)
However, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the ritual arrangement should be performed;
from midnight until dawn, it remains unerring.
O wielder of the plow (Balarāma), one should indeed perform the practice of eating only at night after honoring [the deity], even without fasting,
and thus do so repeatedly until the end of the eleventh lunar day.
Indeed, the worship of the fourfold self (Cāturātmya) should be performed through the logic of dissolution;
one should not eat on the eleventh day, for a vigil is prescribed there.
Having worshipped the Primordial God on the twelfth lunar day according to the prescribed rite,
when midday has arrived, one should worship those who are identical with Him according to the rule.

With devotion and according to one's ability, one should offer even a single morsel of fodder to each of the four cows every day; however, the feeding of the cows must never be omitted at all times by neglecting one's own capacity.
Together with the aforementioned gifts,
O wielder of the plow, when that day of the dark fortnight arrives, one should be further intent upon the performance of the vow.
One should perform the worship of Keśava and the other deities at the three junctions of the day as previously described;
on the twelfth lunar day, however, one who observes a fast should worship the Lord Dāmodara.
One should perform the rites beginning with giving and worship as prescribed for the bright fortnight;
and in this manner, according to the sequence of the Prābhava [kalpa], one should worship the other form.

Through the forms [of the deities] and by means of that which is called "dissolution," he who is unwearied throughout the year—whether he be an authority or a devotee—Adhokṣaja is pleased with him. (82)

Now he describes the vow known as the Dvādaśākhya-vrata, beginning with the words "the most excellent and auspicious of vows" and ending with "Adhokṣaja is pleased with that. On the first day, which is the *pratipad* (the first lunar day), the *kalpanā* means the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). On the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), [one should worship] Ādideva, meaning Vāsudeva.

Thus, beginning from the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of Caitra until its twelfth day, one should perform the worship of Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Vāsudeva alone, each in turn day by day; and likewise, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight until its twelfth day, one should perform the worship of the forms starting with Keśava. During both fortnights, there shall be fasting and a vigil on the eleventh day. On the remaining days, one should eat only at night. At midday, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, or in their absence, provide a mouthful of food for a cow; furthermore, the aforementioned gift should be made every fortnight. (Verses 73–82)
Therefore, I shall now describe the vow known as the Ṣoḍaśa, which is indeed most auspicious;
it is performed at night as before on the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha.
Having taken up the vow, one should perform worship from dawn until the following morning,
or according to the rules for Vāmana and the others, at the three junctions of the day for twelve days.
Then, having worshipped on the thirteenth day the Lord who bestows the fourfold aims of life,
one should worship Aniruddha and the others at the beginning and end on the following day.
The third [form], however, on the fifteenth day, has the characteristic of being completely tranquil and manifest;
thus, the fourfold nature (cāturātmya), joined with other forms, exists in three ways.
Having propitiated [the Lord] with supreme devotion while fasting on the eleventh day,
and having completed that worship on the fifteenth day according to the prescribed rule, || 87 ||
These four, who are absorbed in that [Brahman], should be worshipped with a mind purified by faith;
thereafter, at the end of the day, one should perform the sacrifice of the self (ātmayāga), preceded by ritual worship.
Thus, in the month of Āśvayuja, one should again commence the ritual at the beginning of the lunar festival;
the worship of the forms beginning with Padmanābha is prescribed in their proper sequence.
Having fasted on the eleventh day and completed everything as before,
when the month of Pauṣa arrives, he should then worship Nārāyaṇa and the others.
On the twelfth day, one should likewise perform that group of twelve and the three arrays;
from that day in the month of Caitra, the worship of Viṣṇu and the other deities begins.
When the year has been completed, one should perform a special worship for those who possess knowledge of the true vows, together with the three arrays (vyūhas). || 92 ||
"Before the Lord, [he should worship] the sixteen foremost of the twice-born according to his own capacity.

Now, he describes another vow, beginning with "known as the Ṣoḍaśa" and ending with "of the sixteen according to his own capacity. Here, there are twelve [forms] beginning with Keśava and four beginning with Vāsudeva; thus, there are sixteen forms in total. The worship and other rites of these sixteen in the aforementioned sequence is called the Ṣoḍaśa-vrata. Alternatively, it should be understood that it is called the Ṣoḍaśa because of the worship of the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva, performed month by month during the four months starting with Āṣāḍha.

It should be understood that the worship of Vāmana and others in Āṣāḍha, Padmanābha and others in Āśvayuja, Nārāyaṇa and others in Puṣya, and Viṣṇu and others in Caitra is prescribed because they are to be worshipped starting from the presiding deity of each respective month. Indeed, it is well known that Keśava and the others preside over the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa. The meaning of "beginning and ending with Aniruddha and the rest" is that it starts with Puruṣa and ends with Vāsudeva. On the following day, the fourteenth, the intention is that the first of these is the Svapnavyūha, beginning with Vāsudeva.

On the fifteenth day, the full moon, its manifest characteristics are completely stilled; this means it is both manifest and unmanifest. This is the third array, namely deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The fourfold nature exists in three ways; that is to say, it is threefold through the distinction of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (Verses 83–93)
It was satisfied by what had been offered as remnants, yet remained insatiable, being permeated by divine food.
For those observing vows, a meal combined with the remnants of the oblation is beneficial;
thus it is on both the bright and the dark fortnights.

Now, regarding the food to be consumed by those established in such vows, he says: "that which remains after being given. This verse has been explained in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*. For instance: "‘Dattaśiṣṭa’ means that which remains after the portion has been offered. By means of what remains in the cooking vessel from the food intended for the deities—namely, the remnants of the *havis* offering and the remnants of the *caru*—it is beneficial for all those observing the vow who are established in the nature of the Blessed Lord; because it wards off the undesirable and brings about the desired, it must certainly be eaten.
Here, the word ‘bhojana’ is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). (93–94)

Beginning from whichever month is desired, one should perform the sacrifice in sequence; furthermore, at the beginning of each festival (parvan) and so forth, one should worship the eleven lords of the months once each.

On the twelfth day, having observed a fast, one should worship the Lord of that month together with the fourfold nature (Cāturātmya), arising from the distinctions of their respective causes and so forth.
Know this meritorious vow to be the means for the spiritual perfection of the elderly, women, and children;
it should be performed daily by true Vaiṣṇavas, as it is non-contradictory [to other duties] and free from weariness.
By householders who have previously provided great enjoyments accompanied by gifts according to their ability, and by those established in celibacy, forest-dwellers, and mendicants; 98.
Having previously accumulated wealth by whatever means possible— always and at all times through begging and other methods that are never contrary to dharma— (99)

He speaks of another vow, beginning with "Thus, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight" and ending with "always preceded by begging for alms. Its meaning is as follows: in whichever month one desires, starting from the first day (*pratipad*) of either the bright or the dark fortnight—or both—up to the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), one should worship the lords of those months, starting from the lord of the first month, in a sequence of one per day. Having observed a fast on the eleventh day, on the twelfth day one should worship the lord of that month, who is Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, or Aniruddha, according to his causal nature.

One who, having first worshipped the fourfold self (cāturātmya), performs acts such as giving charity, should understand this very clearly: if a vow is observed in the month of Caitra, Viṣṇu is the lord of that month; thereafter, Madhusūdana and the others—the lords of the eleven months beginning with Vaiśākha—are to be worshipped on the first lunar days (pratipad) and so forth. Viṣṇu is the lord of that month, and the four [forms] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Vāsudeva, who constitute his causal basis, are to be worshipped on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).

Viṣṇu is the lord of that month, and the four [forms] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Vāsudeva, who constitute its cause, are to be worshipped on the twelfth day (dvādaśī). This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. Later, it will be clearly stated that each one of the group beginning with Vāsudeva is the cause of each respective triad beginning with Keśava. (94–99)
But where there is supreme contempt for gain such as alms obtained for the sake of maintaining one's family and so forth—it is there that a wise person should dwell. (100)

Now, explaining the ongoing discussion regarding the nature of alms and other materials, he says "kuṭumba... [verse 100], stating that a wise recipient should reside precisely where, upon receiving such things, much humiliation arises for the giver. *Bhaikṣam* means what is begged; as Amara states: "Bhikṣā, yācñā, vārthanā, and ardanā. *Avajñā* means disrespect; as Amara states: "Rīḍhā, avamānanā, and avajñā. || 100 ||
Whatever a donor gives, preceded by worship and with devotion, all that donor’s inauspiciousness remains resting upon the supplicant. (101)
For this reason, he says "the giver" [in verse 101], because honor is an obstacle specifically for the recipient.
But for one who feels contentment when gain is disregarded, the fault arising from receiving gifts shall depart to a very great distance. (102)
Having understood this regarding worthy recipients who are devoted and of purified soul,
one should never cause a division of mind among others.

Therefore, he says "paribhūtaḥ" (disregarded) to show that even when a gift is given with disrespect, if the recipient remains contented, that acceptance is not tainted by fault. Regarding "lābhe" (in the acquisition): it means in the acquisition of objects such as alms; "paribhūte" (when disregarded) means when treated with contempt, that is to say, when the gift is offered with a lack of respect. Amara states: "anādaraḥ paribhāvaḥ" (disrespect is disregard).

Thus, knowing that giving with reverence brings about the welfare of the donor, one should generate the intention for acceptance through respectful requests and the like toward worthy recipients who are unwilling, even if they do not desire it; however, one should not generate such an intention toward unworthy recipients—this is what he states with the words "thus" (evam). || 102-103 ||
Where both the giver and the receiver are of defiled nature, that gift is destroyed for both of them, serving only to ruin their visible and invisible merit. (104)
Regarding the point where both the giver and the recipient are of a defiled nature, he states that the gift is fruitless. || 104 ||
Having first thus resolved with effort upon the purification of the mind, which is endowed with the purity of inner disposition, one should proceed to a divine abode.
Either a perfected hermitage (siddhāyatana) for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the vow, or else a delightful hermitage situated near a city or similar place. (106)
For by this, the vow of practitioners here shall be accomplished without obstacle;
one who is pure in action, speech, and mind, devoted to austerity, and intent on ritual performance.
O Blessed One, he who does not worship another deity, being in truth absorbed in you—whether in some manifestation of majesty, in a form, or in an emanation—is one of excellent intelligence. (108)
"One should remain fixed in focus through devotion, by observing the arrival of a trustworthy person.

Having first ascertained that purity of mind brought about by the purification of one's disposition (*bhāva*), one should go to any one of the abodes of perfected beings (*siddhas*) or humans for the purpose of performing the vow (*vrata*). There, one should fix one's mind upon the Blessed One—whether in his form of manifestation (*vibhava-ākṛti*) or his form of emanation (*vyūha-ākṛti*)—until the conclusion of the vow. Thus he says "prāgevam" and so forth in four and a half verses. "Divine" means self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*). (105–109)
Out of compassion for him and for such beings as well. || 109 ||
The Lord himself became manifest in the form of the earth;
know that place indeed to be a divine sanctuary that bestows liberation. (110)
In connection with this, he states the definition of the divine sense bases (*divyāyatana*) in the verse beginning with "tasyāpi" (109–110).
By the gods perfected in mantra, by the foremost sages, and by those who are stainless, [this was done] for the peace of the people of the land and also for their own renown. (111)
Having meditated upon a stone on the surface of the earth as being composed of the form of mantra,
or having recognized a purifying tree, or one that is pervasive, as a refuge for the deity.
Having restrained that [power] and then emitted what was dependent upon it,
know that such is the characteristic of the abode as it exists for the Lord of All.

Having established the presence of one's own mantra there, together with its embodied form and worshipped with leaves, flowers, and other offerings, that is known as a perfected sanctuary (siddhāyatana).

He describes the characteristics of the *siddhāyatana* (the abode of the perfected ones), beginning with the words "by those who have attained mantra-perfection" and ending with "that is remembered as the *siddhāyatana*. Regarding the phrase "and having dismissed that which is dependent upon it," the manner of dismissal is stated in the twenty-fourth chapter:
"Salutation to you, the Self residing here, and to the Lord of All.
Pardon [us]; descend elsewhere; remain here as the conscious Self (*cidātman*)."
This is to be understood as that which will be described hereafter:
"In this regard, [the linga] is either self-manifested (svayamvyakta), established by siddhas, or installed by the wise."
It was established as the embodiment of mantra by the foremost sages, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, rākṣasas, and chief asuras;
and it was indeed established by the lords of men who were experts in the Vedas and related sciences.

Thus, it should be understood that even the eightfold divisions mentioned by the Supreme Lord, such as the Siddhas and others, are included within the category of the Siddhas alone; for even the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and so forth are included among the *vibudhas* (gods), and because in the phrase "by the foremost sages and the Amalas," the word *amala* indicates others as well. (111–114)

However, that which has been established by Brahmins and others for the attainment of fruits and for the upliftment of their own lineage should be known as an *āyatana* (a temple or shrine). || 115 ||
He says that the human sphere is for the attainment of the fruits. || 115 ||
