Know that for the all-pervading and omnipresent Lord, the Master of All, who has entered into the constituent parts of ritual action, His established nature is characterized by fixed attributes.
He concludes the stated meaning with the word "kriyā" (action). || 116 ||
And from the location of the palace gate up to where the sound of the conch shell ceases—in all directions starting from the east—that area indeed becomes the Vaiṣṇava field. || 117 ||

Regarding the extent of the Vaiṣṇava field surrounding the temple of the Lord, he says "prāsāda" and so forth. The meaning is that the Vaiṣṇava field extends all around as far as the sound of the wooden peg (śaṅku) struck near the door of the vimāna is heard. || 117 ||

This [attainment] is said to be twofold when received from a deity brought down by a Siddha, and threefold when received from a self-manifested [deity], for those whose selves have been cultivated until the end of the body. (118)

The fruit, beginning with *sālokya*, is to be understood sequentially; for it is double in the place of the Siddhas and triple in the place of the Self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*). With three quarters [of a verse], he states the measurement of the Vaiṣṇava field starting from "brought down by the Siddhas" (*siddhāvatārita*); and with three quarters, he states that the Vaiṣṇava field bestows fruits such as *sālokya* according to its distinctions as self-manifested and so forth, starting from "at the end of the body. The meaning is "from the Vaiṣṇava field. In the phrase "beginning with *sālokya*," the word "beginning" (*pūrva*) includes *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*. "Sequentially" means in the order of human beings and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the attainment of various distinctions such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) occurs upon reaching other deities, whereas upon reaching the Blessed Lord, the *śruti*, *smṛti*, and *sūtra* passages—namely, 'He attains supreme equality,' 'They have attained My own nature,' and 'And because there is a mark of equality in respect of enjoyment alone'—demonstrate that all four states, including *sālokya* and the rest, are possible for each [devotee] individually? How then is the statement here, which speaks of the attainment of only one specific fruit such as *sālokya*, not in contradiction with that? To this we reply: True.

This doubt has also been resolved by the teachers of the Vedānta in their *Saccaritrarakṣā*. For it is said: "Even upon attaining the Blessed One, there exists such a distinction—as among the gatekeepers and others in the worlds of Viṣṇu and so forth—and thus, for the sake of indicating the difference in what is attained by those who desire such [distinctions], they are mentioned separately.

As they have said: 'Some dwell in the worlds of Viṣṇu; others desire his proximity; still others assume a form similar [to his]; and others attain union (*sāyujya*), which is declared to be liberation.'"

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "in sequence," if it is explained as meaning "in the sequence of sālokya, sāmīpya, and so forth," there is no room for this very doubt, because every sacred field (kṣetra) is capable of bestowing all four fruits, beginning with sālokya. || 118–119 ||
The mind of men, which is covered by impurities due to the power of the wicked senses, [is purified]. (119)
At the end of that time, he attains complete purification in the abode of Nārāyaṇa—
he who performs these vows with a focused mind.
He attains his desired goal without delay by crossing over [the ocean] with the boat of devotion;

thus, with three quarters of a verse beginning with "duṣṭa," he states that the Vaiṣṇava sacred field brings about the purification of the mind. The word "yataḥ" (since) should also be supplied here. He states that the performance of vows in the temple of the Lord yields immediate fruit in the verse beginning with "nārāyaṇālaye. (119–121)
Therefore, those who possess faith [should act] for the sake of attaining both seen and unseen fruits. (121)
"These vows must be performed with a focused mind.
Therefore, he states that these vows must necessarily be carried out by those who possess faith: "by the faithful," etc. (vv. 121–122).
One should never give way to despondency on account of the breaking of a vow.
By his mere will, the Lord truly sprinkles those of purified soul with nectar throughout the entire duration until the end of their vow.

Even if a vow that has been commenced is interrupted for some reason in its midst, one must not abandon it from that point. For it is said in the verse beginning with "nāvasādaḥ" (one should not despair) and its half-verse: the attainment of the fruit occurs simply by performing the practice from the moment of the mere resolve, "I shall perform the vow," until its completion; it is for this very reason that no despondency should be felt, meaning one should not succumb to lack of fortitude.
This same point was established by the lords of the Vaṅgivaṃśa in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*, where it is cited:
"In this manner, whether for one day, or two days, or even three days..."
Whether for a month, a year, or even as long as life lasts,
a Vaiṣṇava who conducts himself with supreme devotion shall remain happy for a very long time.
Even if this commenced action is interrupted midway by an obstacle,
there is neither misfortune nor fruitlessness, nor is there any loss of the portion already performed.
When commenced rites remain incomplete and other actions are interrupted,
all this indeed occurs— both in the case of Vedic rites and others as well.
"Even a very small portion of this, once performed, remains inexhaustible for a very long time;
and by its own power, it protects its performer from the fear of worldly existence. Thus [it is said].

If it be argued that this concerns the propitiation of the Lord and not the performance of a vow, we say no; for even this vow is of the nature of the Lord’s propitiation, and the Lord’s propitiation is itself of the nature of a vow lasting a hundred years. For this very reason, in the *Vaṅgivaṃśeśvara* [text], within the section on daily worship, it is said:
"O Lord, this person, desiring to propitiate You, wishes to perform a vow. To ensure the fulfillment of his resolve, please fulfill his heart's desire."
Thus, because this very verse that is to be recited in the *Vratavidhāna* has been summarized here, it should be understood that there is no distinction between the two. || 122-123 ||
Having understood this, one who fears the terrors of saṃsāra and desires to attain all goals must always remain fixed in resolve. (124)
Having understood this point, one should possess a firm mind toward the Blessed One for the sake of attaining all human goals; thus he says, "having known. (124)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for Vows," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, the son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrīmauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The eighth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
This vow is without mantra, common, and universal to all the world. Listen now to the two mantras declared according to the division of white and black. || 1 ||

Now the eighth [chapter] will be explained. Previously, the vow (*vrata*) without mantras was described; now he says, "Listen to the vow with mantras," meaning that while the general vow common to all people—that is, shared by the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—is universal, the vow accompanied by mantras is to be performed by Brāhmaṇas alone. Indeed, it was stated in the [second] chapter regarding those Brāhmaṇas who follow the Veda and are engaged in mixed sacrifices: [The text continues: "For the Brāhmaṇas who speak the Veda and are joined in mixed sacrifices..."
The authority for the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) lies solely within the mantra, and not otherwise;
it belongs truly to the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, as well as to those who have taken refuge [in the path].
"But the authority [of this] is over that which is without mantra, in the sequence of the activity of the fourfold manifestation. Thus [ends the first verse].
Having first requested the Guru— who indeed bestows both the seen and the unseen— he,
having ascertained that the disciple’s mind is firm, should construct the maṇḍala for that purpose.

First, the disciple should request the guru; then, having ascertained that the disciple’s intellect is firm, the guru should draw the mandala for the sake of his vow—this is what is meant by "previously" (prāk). The sense is that, having made the request, the disciple becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. || 2 ||
In the center of that, upon the pericarp, the fourfold Self (Caturātmā) should be worshipped,
looking toward the four directions in sequence, beginning with Vāsudeva.

He states that "in the middle of that" (tanmadhye) [the worship] should be performed as the adoration of the fourfold self, beginning with Vāsudeva, upon the pericarp in the center of that maṇḍala. || 3 ||
Then, one who knows the ritual observances should worship the six limbs, from the heart to the eyes, in sequence with offerings such as the *arghya* and other enjoyments previously procured.

Immediately following that, he describes the worship of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) and the adoration of Vāsudeva and the others with arghya and other offerings in the verse beginning with "hṛdādi. As for the location for the worship of the limb-mantras, it was stated previously: "The four [limbs] beginning with the heart arise from the body of the Lord, starting from the heart."
One should place [the petals] of the lotus starting from the east and ending in the north;
and on the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, one should place the weapon-mantra in due order.
"The eye is situated within the mass of filaments, and the wheel is above the three navels"—this is to be understood as it will be explained in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. (4)

Then, one should place the wheel, accompanied by the collection of mantras, into the consecrated fire within another sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and offer oblations with fuel-sticks (samidh) in due order.

Thereafter, with the verse beginning with "tataḥ" (5–6), he describes the meditation and the satiation of the Blessed One, together with his maṇḍala, in the midst of the fire using abundant sesame seeds mixed with rice and ghee.
Having now purified his head with the water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka).
Having made the disciple bow his head and knees, the master should cause him to hear:
"Desiring to propitiate you, he wishes to observe this vow."
"O Blessed One, for the sake of the fulfillment of my resolve, please grant the desires of this [devotee].
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should then cause flowers to be offered.

Then, having sprinkled the disciple with the *śiromantra* and having caused him to place his knees and head [upon the ground], and having made known the verse of worship (*ārādhanaśloka*), one should cause the flowers held in the joined palms of the disciple to be offered upon the mandala; thus he says with two and a half verses beginning with "arghyodakena."

Although this verse—beginning with "If he desires to worship you" (*yadyapyasmin tvadārādhanakāmaḥ*)—contains the word *vrata* (vow), and since the two words "this" (*ayam*) and "of him" (*asya*) refer to the disciple standing before [the teacher], this verse should indeed be explained by the Teacher within the context of the *Vrata-prakaraṇa*; nevertheless, because daily worship (*nityārādhana*) also takes the form of a vow lasting for a hundred years, and because the two words "this" and "of him" are also applicable to one's own self, this verse appears even in the *Nityārcanā-kārikā* and other works composed by Vaṅgivaṃśeśvara.
This has been established; therefore, it should be understood that this was also stated by our venerable grandfather in the *Sātvatāmṛta*. || 6–8 ||
Then one should perform prostrations with the eight limbs along with circumambulations,
again and again, without interruption, preceded by devotion and faith.

Regarding circumambulation and prostration, he says "eight-limbed" (aṣṭāṅga). Since prostration must be performed four times even for each of the four forms [of the Lord], the word "repeatedly" (bhūyo bhūyaḥ) is used; however, this does not establish that the prostration must be performed more than once [in total]. || 9 ||
Then, the ritual procedure preceded by mantras should be taught to him:
[the syllable] ending with the letter 'sa', mounted on the sixth vowel, and adorned with the anusvāra.
The seed-syllable (bīja) of the first all-pervading Lord Vāsudeva has been proclaimed;
that very same syllable, when situated within the seed of the individual soul (jīva) and deprived of the sixth vowel, [is the seed of Saṅkarṣaṇa]. || 11 ||
The seed-syllable of Saṅkarṣaṇa, joined with the second vowel,
has the letter *ra* placed between both [vowels] of the first seed-syllable.
The seed-syllable of the Lord Pradyumna is the third [consonant], which grants all desires;
one should place the letter *ha*, mounted upon the *jīva* (the vowel *i*), above the final letter [of the alphabet]. (13)
The seed-syllable accompanied by the *visarga* is the designator of Aniruddha.

Then, with the half-verse beginning with "tataḥ," he states the instruction on the mantra for the sake of the disciple’s observance (*vrata*). With four verses beginning with "sāntam," he states the fourfold seed-syllables of Vāsudeva and the others. "Sāntam" means the phoneme called *ha*, situated at the end of the letter *sa* (i.e., after *sa*), mounted upon the sixth vowel (*ū*), adorned with the *anusvāra*, and joined with the *bindu*. Thus, *hūṃ* becomes the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva. That very same thing is the phoneme called *ha*.

The seed-syllable of Pradyumna is *hrūṃ*. It consists of the letter *sa*, which is situated within the "life-seed" (*jīvabīja*), is devoid of the sixth vowel, and is devoid of the letter *ū*; it is joined with the second vowel and endowed with the letter *ā*. Furthermore, one should place the letter *ha*—which is mounted on the "life-seed" (*jīva*) and situated within the letter *sa*—above the letter *va*, which is the final of the labials (*lānta*). This should be made accompanied by the *visarga* and joined with the final vowel. And thus, *hsvaṃ* becomes the seed-syllable of Aniruddha. Now, if it is asked: "While it is logical and well-known that the letter *ma* is the 'life-seed,' how can the letter *sa* be the 'life-seed'?"—the answer is as follows:
Having first placed the syllable *ha* in three ways, one should likewise place the seed-syllable of the individual soul (*jīvabīja*).
One should likewise write the letter *ka* and the letter *kṣa* three times each.
Thus, regarding the term "life-seed" (*jīvabīja*) found in the verse to be cited, [it is defined] in the *Pārameśvara* as:
"The ninth and the eighth, the one preceded by *nema*, and the last of the *mātṛkā*s."

Having divided each one into three parts in sequence, the twelve seed-syllables (*bīja*) are formed; thus, the fact that the letter *sa* follows [the others] has been very clearly explained—please observe this. Furthermore, through the name Vāsudeva, the syllable *ha* arose, which is the source of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Pradyumna is to be known by the syllable *ṣā*, and Aniruddha indeed by the syllable *śā*.

According to the method stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*, because the letter *sa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Saṅkarṣaṇa, it is conventionally designated as the "seed-syllable of the individual soul" (*jīva*). Because Saṅkarṣaṇa presides over the individual soul (*jīva*), he is conventionally referred to as the "individual soul," as is well known from the statement: "From Vāsudeva, the individual soul named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born. Accordingly, the *Śrīmad-Bhāṣya* states:

"In this context, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the presiding deities of the principles of the individual soul (*jīva*), mind (*manas*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*); therefore, their designation by the terms 'individual soul' and so forth is not contradictory. (10–14)
All of these have two arms and resemble hundreds of suns and moons.
However, there is a distinction here by means of the *tejas* (vital energy) and by its own form, such as white and so forth;
[this is performed] between the index finger and the middle finger of the right and left hands. (15)
The two [attributes], the discus and the conch, of the first [deity] are to be meditated upon above the two shoulders;
with the right hand, however, it is held level with the line of the shoulder. (16)
Holding it with a clenched fist and resting it upon the back of the pedestal,
the mace should be meditated upon in the second hand, which is likewise positioned.
One should remember the blazing Hetirāja, with his hand raised in a playful gesture;
in this way, those two [hands] of Lord Pradyumna are reversed.
With his right and left hands, one should visualize him drawing forth the conch and the lotus, which face the circles of his ears, as in the fourth [mudrā].
However, its stalk is indeed a lotus resting upon the back of the hand.
[The author] describes the method of meditating on the forms beginning with Vāsudeva, starting from the words "two-armed" and ending with "resting upon the back of the hand. (14–20)
And having placed the letter *ha* within the letter *sa*, one should arrange it in six ways.
Know that one should apply the vowels in sequence—second, fourth, sixth, eighth, two, six, and ten—to the [mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Eye (Netra). (21)

These are always to be used as the means for accomplishing the mantras belonging to the fourfold self. Now, he states the seed-syllables of the heart and other limb-mantras common to all four, beginning with Vāsudeva, in two verses starting with "the letter *ha*. Having placed the letter *ha* within the letter *sa*, one should write it out six times and join it sequentially with the vowels of the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, and tenth positions—namely, with the vowel *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ai*, and *lṛ*. Thus, the six seed-syllables become: *hsāṃ*, *hsīṃ*, *hsūṃ*, *hsṝṃ*, *hsaiṃ*, and *hslṛṃ*.

One should apply these [vowels] in sequence to the six mantras of the Heart and so forth, beginning with the Eye. Thus, the conjunction of the eighth, twelfth, and tenth vowels with the three seed-syllables of the Armor-mantra and others is occasional, not universal; for in this very *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*, it is stated:
"And with the second, fourth, and sixth, with the twelfth and the final [vowel], and with the fourteenth, one should apply them in sequence from the *Ar* group."
Thus, he will also explain the conjunction of the three seed-syllables of the armor and so forth with the final vowel. (20–22)
Having first placed the syllable *ha* in three ways, one should likewise place the seed-syllable of the living soul (*jīvabīja*) in the same manner.
One should likewise write the letter *ka* and the letter *kṣa* three times each;
having first placed the twelve seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence at the beginning.
Then, one should repeatedly apply the three syllables known as Vāyu, Dhara, and Āri at the lower part of all [the others]. (24)
All these seed-syllables (bījas) of Keśava and the others are to be understood individually as being mounted upon the sixth vowel and adorned with the anusvāra. || 25 ||

Now, he describes the twelve seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Keśava and the others in three parts across three and a half verses. First, having written the letter *ha* three times (*tridhā*), and likewise having written the letter *sa*, the "seed of life" (*jīvabīja*), one should write the letters *ka* and *kṣa* in the same way three times. Having thus placed the twelve seed-syllables at the beginning, one should repeatedly join to the bottom of all those previously written twelve syllables the triad of letters known as "wind," "earth," and "water"—namely, the three letters *ya*, *la*, and *va*.

All [the seed-syllables] are mounted on the sixth vowel (Ū), endowed with the letter Ū, adorned with the Anusvāra, and joined with the Bindu; these are to be known as the seed-syllables of Keśava and the others. Thus, the practical application is as follows: hyūṃ, hlūṃ, hvūṃ, syūṃ, slūṃ, svūṃ, kyūṃ, klūṃ, kvūṃ, kṣyūṃ, kṣlūṃ, kṣvūṃ.
This very meaning is also clearly elaborated in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Pārameśvara [Tantra]:
"Listen to the characteristics of the mantras of Keśava and the others in their proper order."
The ninth and the eighth, the one preceding Nemi, and the last of the Mātṛkās.
Having divided each one into three parts in sequence, as in the case of the twelve seed-syllables,
one who possesses strength should repeatedly join them all below.
One should not mark with a *bindu* above the position of the seat, which has the navel as its sixth;
rather, one should mark the [mantras] beginning with *Tāra* and ending with the *Hṛdaya*, together with the fourth [mantra], by their respective names.
Keśava is to be named first, then the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
likewise Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama, he who is called Vāmana, Śrīdhara, the lotus-eyed Padmanābha,
Hṛṣīkeśa, and the one renowned as Dāmodara.

"One should fashion the limbs as before with the seed-syllables endowed with long vowels. Here, "the ninth on the rim" means the syllable *ha*; "the eighth" means the syllable *sa*; "the first spoke" means the syllable *ka*; and "the last of the Mātṛkā" means the syllable *kṣa*. "Located above the six seats of the nave" means they are joined with the vowel *ū*. "Ending with the heart" means ending with the word *namaḥ*. In this way, there is a single voice between what was stated by Sātvata and what was stated in the Pārameśvara. However, in the commentary on the Pārameśvara, the seed-syllables of Keśava and the others are written as: *saṃ haṃ kaṃ kṣaṃ*, *saṃ haṃ kaṃ kṣaṃ*, *saṃ haṃ kaṃ kṣaṃ*.

These [teachings] are to be rejected; for, apart from writing the letter *sa* before the letter *ha*, and apart from writing each of the letters beginning with *ha* three times each, as well as writing them in mutual interrelation or even writing merely a portion of a seed-syllable (*bīja*), such acts are the work of a madman. || 22–25 ||
One should indeed draw these three syllables *kṣa-sa-ha* in four parts in sequence;
then, having placed the twelve seed-syllables beneath them, one should arrange them accordingly.
In sequence, from the seventh group, take the second and the fourth;
again, the third, the fourth, the second, and the third. (27)
The second and the fourth, and the fourth immediately after that;
then the third from the eighth, and again the third from the seventh. (28)
One should perform this specific procedure with the ninth and twelfth [vowels];
then, one should join the letter *repha* (r) to the head of those three.
One should place the vowel *ī* above those known as the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consonants], along with the anusvāra for all of them; such is the case for the host of goddesses.
The twelve seed-syllables have been declared according to their proper sequence:
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śakti, and Vibhūti. (31)

"Icchā, Prīti, Rati, Māyā, Dhī, and Mahimā"—with these words, beginning with "the triad of kṣa-sa-ha," he states the twelve seed-syllables (bīja) of the goddesses Keśavī and the others. One should write the triad of kṣa-sa-ha—that is, the three letters kṣa, sa, and ha—in four ways each, sequentially. When this is done, there are twelve seed-syllables.

Beneath those seed-syllables, in sequence, from the seventh class consisting of *ya-ra-la-va*, take the second, which is *ra*; the fourth, which is *va*; the third, which is *la*; the fourth, which is *va*; the second, which is *ra*; the third, which is *la*; the second, which is *ra*; the fourth, which is *va*; and again the fourth, which is *va*. From the eighth class consisting of the letters beginning with *śa*, take the third, which is *sa*.

From the seventh previously mentioned group, one should again apply the third letter, *la*, by the word "again" (*punaḥ*). One should apply the letter *ra* below the ninth and twelfth seed-syllables (*bīja*). Furthermore, one should apply the letter *ra* above the seed-syllables designated as the sixth, seventh, and eighth. This is the specific distinction. Above all twelve seed-syllables, one should place the vowel *ī* accompanied by the *anusvāra*. Thus, the twelve seed-syllables have been described. The deities to be invoked for these seed-syllables in sequence are Śrīvāgīśvarī and the others. This very meaning has also been clearly elaborated in the *Pārameśvara*:
Listen to the mantras of those [deities], beginning with Śrī, in their proper sequence.
First, one should spread out the last three letters of the Mātṛkā and the first letter after *kṣa* in four ways;
then, the remaining letters should be joined in due order beneath the twelve [positions].
Fire, water, earth, water, fire, earth, and fire in sequence; then two waters, Soma, and two earths.
One should join the fire-group (the letter Ra) to the sixth, seventh, eighth, and the head (the letter Ha);
then again, above all of them, to the ninth and twelfth (the letters Na and Pha).
"One should adorn [the seed-syllables] with the vowels beginning with 'a' up to 'n', joined with their respective powers;
the seeds joined with the vowel-types and so forth are the friends and others.
Thus, the application here is as follows: *kṣīṃ svīṃ h līṃ kṣvīṃ strīṃ h rlīṃ rkṣrīṃ rsvīṃ h vrīṃ kṣsīṃ slīṃ h lrīṃ*. (26–32)
To the one whose form is the ocean, svāhā; this mantra for the lotus begins with the syllable Om.

Having performed [this] for the one who moves within all, and then for the one whose form is the sky, the mantra for the conch is proclaimed as beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā. || 33 ||
"Oṃ" is for the Veda alone, and "vidye svāhā" is indeed the word for the Knowledge;
this is declared to be the mantra of the mace, and now that of the discus is being told. (34)
At the end of the syllable *oṃ*, one should place the five-syllabled word for the "All-Powerful One" (*prabhaviṣṇave*).
At the end of that, however, the word "Time" (*kāla*), then "to the Form" (*mūrtaye*), followed by *huṃ* and then *phaṭ*. (35)
These are the four mantras for the four [emblems] beginning with the lotus.

Now, he states the four mantras for the lotus, conch, mace, and discus with the words beginning with "to the one whose form is the ocean" (*samudramūrtaye*). Thus, the ritual application here is as follows: *oṃ samudramūrtaye svāhā*, *oṃ sarvāntaścāriṇe gaganamūrtaye svāhā*, *oṃ vedamātre vidyāyai svāhā*, *oṃ prabhaviṣṇave kālamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ*.

In this context, it should be understood that because the ocean presides over the lotus, the sky over the conch, Sarasvatī over the mace, and Time over the discus, the words "ocean-form" and so forth refer to the lotus and the other [emblems].

The presiding authority of Padmā and others over the ocean and other elements is to be understood as it will be explained in the thirteenth chapter. This tetrad of mantras for Padmā and the others is to be employed in the worship of the Vāsudeva and other primary manifestations (vyūha), as well as in the worship of the secondary manifestations (antara-vyūha) such as Keśava and others. However, in the worship of the Vibhavas, the mantras of the weapons, which will be described by another method, are to be taken. For this very reason, this same tetrad of mantras for Padmā and the others was propounded by my venerable grandfather in the *Sātvatāmṛta* within the section on the ritual of worshipping the Nārāyaṇa form. (32–36)
The single añjali-gesture is common to all mantras. || 36 ||
One should employ [the mudrās] conjoined with their respective mantras.

Now, he describes the *añjali-mudrā* common to all mantras with the words "sāmānya" (general). Although it might follow from the statement that this *añjali-mudrā* alone is common to all that this very one should be employed everywhere, nevertheless, because certain specific mudrās will be described here in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa* and other texts, and because certain specific mudrās have been demonstrated in the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* and the *Aiśvara-tantra*, it follows that for those [mudrās] distinct from them, only the *añjali-mudrā* should be displayed.
The object of awakening. || 36-37 ||
The two hands, joined at the wrists, should be interlaced and opened wide. || 37 ||
Then, having pressed both elbows against the navel like a staff, one should sway slightly; thereafter, one should look upward while keeping those two hands raised.
Having established secrecy, this mudrā is to be employed in the rite of propitiation.

Regarding the mudrā to be employed at the time of propitiation, he says in two verses beginning with "śliṣṭau": having made one's own hands joined together and opened wide, and having brought the two elbows of those arms together continuously up to the wrists, one should fix the hands like a staff at one's navel and move them slightly upward and downward. This mudrā is to be employed after establishing secrecy; that is to say, it is to be kept secret. (37–39)
Having approached the previously established image, or having positioned oneself directly behind it. || 39 ||

"One should obtain," he says, "an image endowed with all the [auspicious] marks (lakṣaṇa), in which the mind finds serenity; whether it be a self-manifested image or another image possessing the [proper] marks and well-consecrated, for the purpose of fulfilling one's vows, it may be obtained according to one's own preference. (vv. 39–40)
One should have a pedestal made of gold and other precious materials, or one endowed with the prescribed characteristics.
The height should be three-quarters [of the width], or twelve finger-breadths in extent;
it should be square, have four legs, and be raised by half its width.
Taking one-third from each of their respective widths,
one should construct with that [measurement] a lotus in the center, endowed with all the proper characteristics.
Outside of that, however, is a wheel marked with all its constituent parts, consisting of twelve spokes;
there resides the imperishable and infallible [power] within the hearts of the Siddhas, immortals, humans, and others.
Then, the seal of the lotus feet, characterized by the form released from the pressure of soft and elevated treading, should indeed be fashioned within the pericarp.
Having thus prepared the base (ādhāra) or the pedestal (pīṭha), one should meditate upon it as being endowed with worship.

Or, for the purpose of worship without an image, one may prepare a mere pedestal; its characteristics are stated in the passage beginning with "made of gold and so forth. "Śama" means four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) in width. As the *Vaijayantī* states: "A śama shall be four finger-breadths. In the reading "sama," the meaning is that it is level, devoid of depressions or elevations. Alternatively, it means equal in length and width; or, it means three parts less [than a certain measure], or eight finger-breadths.

When one part is subtracted from three parts of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas), it becomes eight finger-breadths. This is also stated in the second chapter: "Made of clay, wood, stone, or metal, or having one, two, or three [parts]. The term *dviṣaṭkāram* means "having twelve spokes. It resides in the hearts of the Siddhas, gods, humans, and others; that is to say, it is the object of their meditation.

"Imperishable" means having disappeared; "belonging to the Blessed One" refers to the state of being free from falling away (*acyuti*). It is characterized by a form that is liberated from the act of treading upon feet—that is, the act of treading (*ākramaṇa*), which is to say, the placing of the foot (*padanyāsa*). Such is the meaning. Although the lotus-feet of the Blessed One are exceedingly tender, it should be understood that because the lotus-throne upon which they rest is even softer than they are, the imprint of the feet becomes clearly visible upon it. This is the "seal of the lotus-feet"; the meaning is the mark of the pair of glorious feet resembling lotuses. (40–45)
Thereafter, one should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) devoid of the lotus-foot mudrā.
Having a form like a full-blown lotus and endowed with the source of the lips,
whether moving or situated in a single direction, one should then perform the observance.

Regarding the characteristics of the *kuṇḍa* for the purpose of worshipping the Lord who possesses twelve forms throughout the year, the author states "with a foot-lotus" (*pādābja*) along with a quarter-verse. By stating that the *kuṇḍa* is devoid of the *pādābja-mudrā*, it is implied that the *kuṇḍa* itself should be marked in its center solely with the wheel (*cakra*) and the lotus (*padma*). If the phrase "devoid of the *pādābja-mudrā*" were construed only with what precedes it, then an alternative view regarding the characteristics of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) would be expressed. In the phrase "endowed with the lip and the womb" (*oṣṭhayonisamanvitam*), the definition of those two should be understood as that which will be explained later in the section on the characteristics of the *kuṇḍa*. "Moving" (*calam*) means having a mobile form.

“Situated in one direction” means it is stationary (*sthāvaram*). Thus, it is said in the *Pārameśvara*: “Therefore, a *kuṇḍa* should always be made, whether it be according to the thread-measure (*sautra*), mobile, or stationary. He describes the performance of the vow with the verse beginning with “thereafter” (46), including a quarter-verse. “Of the twelve-fold self” means of the forms such as Keśava and the others. (45–47)
Beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it lasts indeed until the end of the month of Kaumuda. || 47 ||

Having consecrated the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the mantra of the Lord of the Month and mixing it with water containing gold and kuśa grass, one should drink it on the tenth lunar day after having worshipped Keśava.
Having first eaten the food offered there along with ghee and other items—
which does not produce excessive satiety— one should then use a tooth-stick.
Then, one should sprinkle the bed with mantra-water along with kuśa grass;
staying upon the bed, one should indeed recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.

He describes the sequence of rites to be performed on the night of the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa with three and a half verses beginning with "māse". "Consecrated by the mantra of the month-lord" means it has been empowered by the mantra of Keśava, who is the presiding deity (māseśa) of that particular month. (47–50)
Then, on the eleventh day, at dawn, at midday, or at the end of the day,
one should offer salutations many times to Keśava, preceded by the syllable Om.
One should indeed perform his worship with devotion at the three times of day.

Regarding the worship of Keśava on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) at the three times, he says "on the eleventh" in a verse and a half. From "one should bow to Keśava" up to "many times preceded by the *praṇava*," it is stated that one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava" repeatedly. (51–52)
For that which is all-pervading, the supreme light, formless and indeed stainless; || 52 ||
Thinking that he alone is Vāsudeva, one should then worship the Lord properly with all offerings, such as flowers, which are like nectar to the mind. (53)
Thereafter, one should meditate upon that stainless, liberated, and immutable abode—
compassionate, incomparable, and with its hand resting upon the slope of the hips.
With his right hand, he bestows fearlessness upon his devotees;
he is richly adorned with flowers, ornaments, and garments, and is endowed with both the conch and the discus.
Then, one should meditate upon that light as issuing forth simultaneously from that abode—great, resembling a spark, and ever-shining. (56)
And by that, one should visualize the host of wheels being completely traversed;
then, one should visualize [the deities] arising sequentially from each respective portion of light. (57)
"Three by three, beginning with white and so forth, and beginning with Keśava, [they are] four-armed.

Now, preceded by the mental worship of Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest, he describes the meditation on the forms (*mūrti-dhyāna*), the narration of the emergence of the manifestations (*vyūha*) such as Vāsudeva from Him, and the contemplation of the emergence of Keśava and the others from them, by means of the verses beginning with "The all-pervading supreme light. Here, by the phrase "three by three, beginning with white and so forth," it is stated that the triad beginning with Keśava is white in color like Vāsudeva, and the triad beginning with Govinda is red in color like Saṃkarṣaṇa. And thus, in the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Pauṣkara*:
With the right and left hands behind [the shoulders] in the case of Keśava and the others. || 58 ||
These pairs should be understood in succession as ascending;
[the first pair] is born from the conch and the discus, which is the Vidyā, and then the conch, and then the sovereign weapon (hetirāṭ). 59.
That conch with the lotus, the discus with the conch, the mace quickly;
the mace with the discus, the lotus with the discus, the discus with the conch, and then the mace. (60)

With the two and a half verses beginning with "dakṣiṇottara," he describes the sequence of the emblems located on the two hands of Keśava and the others. "Ka-ja" means a lotus (*padma*). "Vidyā" means a mace (*gadā*). "Tad ambujaṃ sa-śaṅkham" means that lotus together with a conch (*śaṅkha*). In the phrase "vidyāśaṅkham," the word division is "vidyā aśaṅkham"; "aśaṅkham" means a discus (*cakra*). This is because otherwise, for Trivikrama, there would be a commonality of two conchs.

If it is asked, "What fault is there in that?"—it is not so, because of the rule that one must carry each of the four weapons individually. If the reading is *vidyā-cakra*, then there is no need for such a laborious interpretation; the meaning is simply *ari-cakra* (the circle of enemies). || 58–60 ||
In the same way, one should know that for each of the twelve [names] ending with Dāmodara, two [letters] situated below correspond to each pair situated above; listen to this. (61)
The lotus, the mace, the sound, and the discus—of these, that lotus is the supreme weapon, the sound is the Vidyā, and the discus is also the Vidyā;
she is the lotus, the conch, and the water-born one.

"The lotus, the sound [conch], the mace, and the conch, along with the discus and the lotus—[these are] yours. Now, with two and a half verses beginning with "tadvat" (in that same way), he describes the sequence of weapons held in the two principal hands. "Dhvani" means the conch; "tat" means the discus; again "tat" means the discus; "sa" means the conch; and again "sa" means the conch. Thus, the bearing of the four weapons known as the lotus, mace, conch, and discus is common to all twelve forms, Keśava and the rest; however, the distinction between each specific form lies solely in the particular manner in which they are held in the hands.

And that [iconography] is not of a single form due to the differences between the tantras; however, in reality, it generally remains of one voice with what is stated in the *Padma-purāṇa*. For instance: "The lotus, the conch, the discus, and likewise the staff are declared to be the weapons of Keśava on his arms in clockwise order."
Nārāyaṇa is remembered as bearing the conch, lotus, mace, and discus;
Mādhava likewise possesses the mace along with the conch, discus, and lotus weapons.
Govinda should bear the discus, mace, lotus, and conch as his weapons;
Viṣṇu should be the bearer of the mace, lotus, conch, and sword; and so too should Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama should be depicted holding the discus, conch, lotus, and staff;
Vāmana should hold the lotus, conch, discus, and staff; or [alternatively], he may hold the conch and discus.
Likewise, Gadābjapāṇi and Śrīdhara holding a lotus;
then hear of Hṛṣīkeśa together with the discus, mace, and conch.
"Dāmodara is remembered as the bearer of the mace, discus, lotus, and conch weapons;
the twelve forms likewise bear the lotus, conch, mace, and discus. Thus it is said.
In this regard, it should be understood that, apart from the characteristics mentioned by Trivikrama and Padmanābha, everything else is of one form.

If it is objected: "But these stated characteristics of the Nārāyaṇa-mūrti are not observed in the Nārāyaṇa-mūrti situated on Yādavācala," [the reply is: True. However, there is no fault in that, because that which is self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) is beyond all constraints. If it is further asked: "What is the definitive proof that this is indeed a Nārāyaṇa-mūrti? [the answer is: There is well-known traditional authority (prasiddhi) from the Purāṇas. Nor should it be argued that, because the Purāṇic term 'Nārāyaṇa' is all-pervasive (vyāpaka), it cannot serve to determine a specific form.
O best of sages, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, resides in Kurukṣetra and other such places,
while Nārāyaṇa resides on Mount Nārāyaṇācala.

Thus, because the specific forms of Pauṣkara and Īśvara are expressed by their very names; furthermore, the definition of the Nārāyaṇa form stated in the Pauṣkara is indeed observed in the Nārāyaṇa situated on Yādavācala. For it is said:
"In his left and right hands, and from his two mouths, [he holds] the mace and the lotus."
"In the left [hand] and so forth, he holds the conch and the discus, while in the two rear [hands] he holds [the mace];

thus is the Lord named Nārāyaṇa. Now, if it is objected that even a lotus is not perceived in the primary right hand there, one should be satisfied, O long-lived one, by the fact that the lotus exists there in the form of a subtle line; for he will state this in the twelfth chapter.
For it is said: "Because of their functional necessity, even the embodied forms possess hands;
they consist of four lotuses and so forth, being both manifest and unmanifest, as well as quiescent and emergent.
Thus, their manifestation is clearly revealed throughout the three worlds by means of weapons, garments, and banners.
They too bear a multitude of marks upon the soles of their feet,
on their foreheads, on the shoulder-cloths, and on both the backs and palms of their hands.
"On the two body-hairs at the crown for the sake of the realization of those who perform ritual acts.
For this very reason, even the placement of the lotus (*padmanyāsa*) and so forth is mentioned in the section concerning the worship of Īśvara-Nārāyaṇa. Enough with this digression. (61–63)
Furthermore, one should remember the great light that has issued forth from that multitude of abodes.
The triad beginning with Śrī and the triad beginning with Keśava are distinguished [according to their respective groups].

Now, he speaks again of the origin of the group of wives of Keśava and the others with the words "bhūyaḥ" (again). "From that collection of abodes" means from the fourfold forms beginning with Vāsudeva. Thus it is also stated in the *Pādma*:
"The weapons such as Sudarśana, and the ornaments such as the crown."
At the time of the manifestation of the form, these were born together with it.
"The goddesses, Śrī and the others, are each supported by specific manifestations of His form;
from the divine mark of the Śrīvatsa alone, they all were born. (63–64)
It is marked by the mutual relationship of the triad beginning with Kamala. || 64 ||
And standing in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), facing him in the sky and in all directions,
one should fan him with humility using a white chowrie.
He distinguishes the twelve goddesses with the verse beginning "Kamalādī" and the following half-verse (64–65).
Thus is the group of twelve goddesses; now their forms are described:
all of them have faces like the full moon and are adorned with flowers from every season.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
the first triad has the luster of coral, while the other has the radiance of the campaka flower.
One should meditate on the third triad of deities as dark as the cluster of a priyaṅgu flower, and the fourth triad as having a luster equal to the jasmine flower. 68.

One should meditate on a lotus in the hand of the first [form], a supreme weapon in the hand of the second, and a conch in the third; thus one should meditate upon these three in each of the three [groups].
Regarding the phrase "of those ending with the four and three deities," this refers to the sequence beginning with the first [deity] in order.

He explains their forms, insignia, and so forth with the words beginning with "tāsām" (of them). This means that for the first [deity], Śrī; for the other, Vāgīśvarī; and for the third, Kānti—one should meditate repeatedly on these same three, beginning with Kamalā, within each triad of the three starting with Kriyā, the three starting with Icchā, and the three starting with Māyā. Thus, "of those ending with the four and three deities" means up to Mahimā. The meaning is that one should meditate again and again on this very triad beginning with Kamalā. (Verses 66–70)
Having remembered [the deity], one should perform worship accompanied by a night vigil.
One should pass the night with hymns, narratives, musical instruments, and songs.
Thus, having performed the worship at the three periods of the day preceded by meditation on the eleventh day, one should keep a vigil; so it is said in the verse beginning with "smṛtvā" (70–71).
Then, at the end of the night, one should bathe, pure and wearing white garments.
Having equipped himself with the mantra of the Lord of the Month (Māseśa), he should likewise meditate upon the deity;
then, having performed the removal of the offerings, he should carry out the ritual of bathing.

On the twelfth day, having first performed one's daily obligatory rites (nityakarman) in the morning, one should meditate upon the Lord of that month, who has the form of Keśava; then, at night, having removed the materials used for worship and so forth, one should perform the ritual bathing (snapana) to be described at the time of worship—this is stated in the verse beginning with "rātrikṣaye" (at the end of the night), consisting of one and a half verses. || 71-72 ||
First, in the center, is that of the Great Soul Keśava alone;
immediately thereafter is that of the one in the form of Vāsudeva, situated upon the discus.

One should then offer the ritual bath and other services in due order to all those who are established in Prāgarā, as well as to the entire immutable [deity] and to the twelve [deities] beginning with that one.

He describes the places of worship for Keśava and the others with two verses beginning with "in the middle" (*madhyataḥ*). "In the middle" means in the center of the pericarp situated in the middle of the pedestal. By the word "of the solitary one" (*kevalasya*), it is understood that there is worship together with the Goddess in the position of the spokes; however, here it is known to be [the worship] of Keśava. By the phrase "of the nature of Vāsudeva," it is understood that Kāla, who presides over the discus, is also worshipped in the eastern spoke together with Keśava. "Of those twelve beginning with him" means of the twelve forms beginning with Keśava. (73–74)
Then, with water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, curd, ghee, honey, and water containing all medicinal herbs; || 75 ||

Then, with water from seeds, fruits, and flowers, and subsequently with water scented with perfumes and flowers, and then with water containing gold and jewels— each kept separately in a jar— (he should perform the rite).

He states the substances for the ablution with two verses beginning with "ambunā" (with water). Here, it is understood that the ablution of Keśava situated in the center is performed with water; that of Keśava situated in the spokes with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); and that of the deities beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with Dāmodara with the eleven jars of milk and so forth.
Now, [one might ask]: "Is it not the case that for Īśvara and Pārameśvara, [the sequence is] with water, with the five products of the cow, and with milk immediately thereafter?"
With curd, ghee, honey, and water containing all medicinal herbs;
Then, it should be filled in due order with the water of seeds, fruits, and flowers, as well as with scented water, flowers, and water containing gold and jewels.

If it is asked: "Since this very consecration (*snapana*) has been established here as consisting of twelve jars—as stated in the passage 'this supreme [number] of jars is declared to be twelve'—how is it not contradictory that you have explained it here as consisting of thirteen jars? True. We state that there is no contradiction. Is there a contradiction merely because it was said in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] "with water" (*ambunā*)? In that context, although it was taught by the words "with water" and so forth, that [water alone] was not intended to be expressed, because it was stated that "the number of jars is twelve"; rather, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth were what was intended.

Just as in the *Pārameśvara*, in the section on the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), although the statement from the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*—"Lakṣmī and the others [are placed] upon the filaments and so forth"—is set forth, Lakṣmī is not intended there; rather, it is the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) alone that is intended. In the same way, here too, one should understand that the intention is what determines the meaning. For this very reason, my venerable grandfather has taught only the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth in the *Sātvatāmṛta*.

Now, one might ask: what is the point of such effort? For indeed, you yourself accept the use of thirteen jars for the sake of accomplishing the consecration of Keśava who stands in the center; likewise, the use of thirteen jars is desired by me as well. However, it should be understood that because Keśava situated in the center and Keśava situated in the spokes are one and the same deity, their consecration is performed with water alone in separate jars, whereas for Nārāyaṇa and the others, it is performed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth.

And thus, in this case, the ritual bathing consists of exactly thirteen jars. However, since filling two jars with water is not the primary subject here, and because it has been established as consisting of twelve jars, one should fill only a single jar with water. If it is argued that this preserves the meaningfulness of the word "with water" (*ambunā*), we say no; for if both jars were filled with water alone, there would be no room for any of the other twelve substances, such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Furthermore, in the phrase "with fragrance, flowers, and water," because of the singular number used, the meaning is simply water together with fragrance and flowers, rather than two separate substances. Therefore, it must be stated that there are exactly eleven [substances], beginning with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Moreover, in the case of the phrase "with water of gold and jewels," since there is no definitive evidence from the singular number, and because in the section on the ritual bathing (*snāna*) with twenty-five jars, fragrant flower-water and gold-jewel-water are mentioned separately.

If it is argued that it is improper to omit one of the substances mentioned in the passage beginning with "with water, with the five products of the cow" (*nanv ambunā pañcagavyena*) and instead take up only the *pañcagavya* and so forth, we say no; for just as in the *pañcaviṃśatikalaśasnāna* (bath with twenty-five jars) described in the sixth chapter of the *Śrīsātvata*, the bath with twelve jars for the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [tantras] is established by omitting the *śrīrā* and other substances and using only the water of *dhātrī* fruits and so on—which is considered appropriate—so too should this case be understood.

Now, it may be objected: "In that [other] context, twelve substances were established without dispute, whereas here thirteen substances have been mentioned; therefore, among them, which should be discarded and which should be accepted? What is the determining factor in this regard? To this it is replied: that which was stated for the purpose of consecrating Keśava situated in the center should be discarded; however, those which were stated according to the sequence beginning with Arasthakeśava and so forth—those twelve substances are indeed to be accepted.

Among the substances mentioned in the sequence beginning with Keśava, the very impropriety of abandoning any one of them is the decisive factor therein; this should be observed by Your Honor with a subtle vision. (75–76)
White unguents, flowers, incense, honey, ghee, and curd;
various pure offerings for the food-oblation, along with rice mixed with barley. || 77 ||
Having offered [the gift] in a silver vessel fashioned according to one's means, one should not omit even a small amount of silver if a vessel is unavailable. 78.

Now, because the triad beginning with Keśava is white in color, their worship is performed with white-colored sandalwood, flowers, and so forth; the offering consists of barley and rice grains in a silver vessel, and in the absence of a vessel, some silver should be given along with the measure [of the grain]—thus he says in two verses beginning with "white" (sitam). || 77–78 ||
Thereafter, with a serene inner self and through devotion to the guru, he indeed presented that honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other offerings which had been purified by the Blessed One. (79)
Immediately following, he speaks of the worship of the Guru with the words "afterwards" (paścāt). || 79 ||
One should first eat as much rice produced from paddy as one can, accompanied by ghee;
and from that time forward, one should do so every day for the sake of Keśava.
He states the food fit for one observing a vow with the half-verse beginning "yavānnam" (barley-food). || 80 ||
And from that time forward, every single day, for Keśava...
One should perform the worship of Keśava, who is stationed in two places and accompanied by the Goddess, as before: in the center and on the outside.
Then, one should diligently perform the worship of all [the deities], beginning with Nārāyaṇa and the others, together with their goddesses, in due order and proceeding clockwise. || 82 ||
With devotion, according to what is available, one should offer flowers, incense, and so forth,
until the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa arrives.

Thus, until the tenth day of the Puṣya-purity, one should perform the worship of Keśava every day in two locations: in the center of the pericarp and in the region of the spokes. There, in the center, he is worshipped alone; in the place of the spokes, he is worshipped together with the Goddess. Likewise, the worship of Nārāyaṇa and the others situated in the spokes must also be performed together with their respective goddesses in a clockwise direction. This is stated in three and a half verses beginning with "tataḥ" (verses 80–83).
From that time forward, one should complete the entire ritual of the vow according to the previously mentioned procedure, using the mantra known as Nārāyaṇa. || 84 ||
One should first worship that Lord in the center as the embodiment of the Cause (Kāraṇamūrti),
and outside [the central area], together with the Goddess, according to the previous procedure beginning with the ritual bath.
According to the prescribed ritual, this continues until the twelfth day, accompanied by Keśava;
however, in this case, the worship of Keśava is to be performed subsequently.
At the end of the day on the twelfth lunar day, having offered incense,
one should ask forgiveness from Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, who is accompanied by his beloved.

Then, beginning from the tenth day, follows the performance of the vow (*vrata*) with the *Nārāyaṇamantra*. For that purpose, he describes the worship of Nārāyaṇa alone—in his form as Vāsudeva, who is his own material cause—within the previously mentioned pericarp; the worship of Nārāyaṇa together with his consort on the outer petals; the worship of both Nārāyaṇa and Keśava in two locations for the three days from the tenth to the twelfth; and the concluding worship (*uttarapūjā*) of Keśava on the night of the twelfth. He explains this in four verses beginning with "thenceforth" (*tataḥ prabhṛti*). (84–87)
Then, on the following day, one should worship with devotion the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by the forms ending with Dāmodara.
In the center, one should worship Keśava; thereafter, on the spoke situated at the wheel, one should worship Keśava together with his beloved upon that spoke.
In this manner, one should continue every day until that specific lunar day of the month;
thereafter, the worship of the Mādhava image shall take place as previously described.

Starting from the following day until the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa alone in both locations as Keśava; thereafter, the worship of Keśava, Mādhava, and the others should be performed in sequence on the second and subsequent spokes (aras). This is stated in two and a half verses beginning with "atha. "In the spoke of Keśava" means in whichever spoke Keśava was worshipped in the previous kalpa; "in his spoke" means in the spoke where Nārāyaṇa was previously worshipped.

He states with the half-verse beginning "tataḥ" that the performance of the vow in the month of Māgha by means of the Mādhava-mantra should be carried out exactly as before. Here, by the phrase "as previously," it is meant that during the three days from the tenth to the twelfth of the bright fortnight of Māgha, after the worship of Mādhava in his two locations, one should also perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa in his two locations; on the night of the twelfth, the northern worship of Nārāyaṇa is performed; and starting from the following day until the twelfth of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the worship belongs to Mādhava alone.

It is stated that there is worship at two locations; on the second and subsequent spokes, there is the worship of Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, and so forth; and on the twelfth day of that [period], at night, the secondary worship (uttarapūjana) of Mādhava is performed.

During the three days beginning with the tenth and ending with the twelfth, prior to the worship of Mādhava, one should meditate upon Saṃkarṣaṇa—the causal source of the triad beginning with Govinda—as being supreme, like Vāsudeva, in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Therein, one should perform the worship of Govinda in his [characteristic] form; he too, along with the Goddess, should be worshipped in the place of the spokes (*ara*). Since the triad beginning with Govinda, who arose from Saṃkarṣaṇa, is red in color, the sandalwood paste, flowers, garments, ornaments, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth should also be red in color, according to some.
Even though flowers and other such items lack a red color, they are rendered red by some red mineral; likewise, there is the offering of mere parched grain in a copper vessel. || 88-90 ||
When that worship is completed on the twelfth day of the month of Phālguna,
one should meditate upon Saṅkarṣaṇa as being supreme, just like Vāsudeva.
Then one should invoke Govinda, who resides within that [liṅga] and is manifested in form in the center;
he is indeed situated upon the disc together with the Goddess. Having worshipped him there as before, [one should proceed].
Likewise, with red sandalwood and saffron,
as well as with flower garlands, garments, and cooked red śāli rice.
With fragrant red fruits, or with smeared red minerals, or with well-prepared reddish gems and abundant coral ornaments; || 94 ||

Having placed the parched grain (saktu) in a copper vessel and then offered it, he states the specific details regarding that worship with the words beginning "when it is completed" (samāpte). Here, by the phrase "on the twelfth day" (dvādaśyām), the three-day period starting from the tenth day up to the twelfth day is also indicated. (91–95)
And when that worship, including the conclusion of the fire-oblation, has been completed, the observer of the vow indeed— || 95 ||
When three months have passed and Acyuta has become gracious and remains within, the Lord, having assumed the form of the Guru, is to be worshipped with devotion. (96)

Then, at the conclusion of the fast, one should perform the breaking of the fast according to one's ability with garments, ointments, garlands, bracelets, and rings, provided it is done without deceit. (97)
One should gratify Vāsudeva, who is endowed with the three forms;
may his powers grant me the religious merit, pleasure, and wealth pertaining to this world. (98)
May the forms [of the Lord] eternally effect the pacification of obstacles to liberation—He who is the Supreme Self, the transcendent Lord, eternally pure at all times. (99)
"May Vāsudeva be my refuge, for I have fallen into the ocean of existence.
Having thus properly performed this propitiation of Vāsudeva with devotion, [one attains the goal]. 100.

[The author] explains, in six verses beginning with "tad-arcane," that at the conclusion of the *homa*, immediately after commencing the worship of Govinda, there is a special worship of the Guru for the sake of the qualities of the grace bestowed during the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa; and following the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*), the propitiation of Vāsudeva is performed with the water of the *arghya*—accompanied by flowers—held in the right hand, using the mantra consisting of two verses preceded by the *praṇava* and the word *namaḥ*. "The three powers" (*śaktayaḥ*) means Śrī and the other two; "the forms" (*mūrtayaḥ*) means Keśava and the other two. (95–101)
Then, for the second great-souled one, who was endowed with the triad... || 101 ||
From that time forward, one should diligently perform the worship of the one named Saṅkarṣaṇa every day, according to the distinctions of the months, as previously described.

Then, beginning from that time, he describes the performance of the vow (*vrata*) during the three months ending on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, using respectively the mantras of Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana, as well as the worship of Saṃkarṣaṇa—the causal source of those—as supreme within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) throughout those three months, in verses 101–102, starting with "atha."
After three months had passed, when that specific day of the month of Jyeṣṭha arrived,
everything else was performed as previously described with the mantra known as Trivikrama.
One should meditate upon Pradyumna, who is omnipresent and situated within the interior of a lotus in the center;
then, having contemplated Trivikrama as having that same form, one should worship him.
Immediately thereafter, having brought [the deity] from the *saṃsthāna* to another house, he should be worshipped with special care, without abandoning his physical form, in due order. 105.

After those three months, on the tenth day [of the lunar fortnight], he describes the commencement of the vow (*vrataprārambha*) with the *Trivikrama-mantra*; the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon Pradyumna—who is the cause of the triad beginning with Trivikrama—as the Supreme Being in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*); the worship (*arcana*) of that Trivikrama meditated upon in that form; and the worship of him together with the Goddess even in the place of the spokes (*ara*). He states this in three verses beginning with "paścāt" (103–105).
Sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and slightly perfumed with saffron, as well as yellow ointment, flowers, fruits, and so forth, should be offered here. (106)
In the absence of yellow fruits and flowers,
one should dye [the offering] with smooth yellow mineral powder or with saffron.
And having offered a golden vessel filled with ghee at the conclusion of the worship;
or, in the absence of a vessel, gold [coins] according to one's means placed upon the ghee. (108)

Since the triad beginning with Trivikrama, who was born from Pradyumna, is yellow in color, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth of that same color; even if such yellow items are unavailable for some, one should make them yellow using turmeric, saffron, and the like. One should offer a golden vessel filled with ghee, or, if that is impossible, offer ghee accompanied by gold according to one's means—thus he says in three verses beginning with "śrīkhaṇḍam. (106–108)
Then one should perform the worship of the instructor of the vow as before, with gifts of cows, gold, and clothing, so that he may attain satisfaction. (109)
Now he speaks of the worship of the guru with the word "tataḥ" (then). The meaning is: toward the guru who is the instructor of the vow. || 109 ||
At the conclusion of that worship, having taken water in his hand, he should satisfy the second Lord of the World, Saṅkarṣaṇa, by breaking his fast.
With that very same mantra beginning with the *praṇava* as previously uttered, but including the word of salutation, let the transition here be: "May Saṅkarṣaṇa be my [refuge]. (111)

Then, after the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*), he describes the propitiation of Saṃkarṣaṇa according to the previously mentioned method, as well as the modification of the previously stated mantra by omitting the phrase "May Vāsudeva be my refuge" and adding the phrase "May Saṃkarṣaṇa be my refuge," in two verses beginning with *tatpūjānte*. "By the breaking of the fast" means by the feeding of the Brahmins. Regarding the instruction "having taken water in his hand," one should take the primary offering-water (*arghya*) along with flowers. As stated in the section on initiation (*dīkṣāpariccheda*):
"The honoring (*ārhaṇa*) and likewise the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) are performed with that water."
"One should perform the leading forward, the taking up, the pleasing, and the act of gratification.

Since the act of pleasing with the primary *arghya* water will be described later, [the procedure is as follows]: having said "of the Lord and the Supreme Lord," one should afterwards place a flower along with water in the right hand.
"O Nārada, one should place [the vessel] before Viṣṇu with the root mantra"—since this statement from the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* cited above specifies that it should be accompanied by flowers. (110–111)
Then one should worship the Lord Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara for three months, until the tenth day of the bright fortnight arrives.
From that point onward, one should perform everything with the mantra of Hṛṣīkeśa;
and when the opportunity arises, one should remember the supreme nature of Aniruddha.
One should meditate upon Hṛṣīkeśa, who has that same form and is situated within the interior of the lotus,
having worshipped him according to the proper ritual procedure, just as he was previously stationed upon the hub of the discus.
In this regard, one should perform worship with royal offerings and those resembling bees, using flowers, cooked rice, and garments; or, in their absence, with collyrium and other such items.
Having carefully made it golden-yellow and having offered it to the God,
one should apply here an ointment of saffron mixed with black agallochum.
Having offered at the conclusion of the worship a bowl made of purified iron, inlaid with black gems, and filled with black sesame seeds; || 117 ||
Having performed that worship correctly with devotion according to one's means, one should satisfy the third deity as before, [saying]: "May Pradyumna indeed be my refuge. (118)

Then, the performance of the vow (vratānuṣṭhāna) is carried out with the three mantras beginning with Trivikrama until the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada; from that point onward, the commencement of the vow is performed with the Hṛṣīkeśa mantra. Since Aniruddha—the causal source of the triad beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa—is black in color, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, garments, jewels, fruits, and so forth, all of which are black in color. Even if certain black-colored items are unavailable, one should blacken them using collyrium or similar substances. One should take only an incense burner filled with black sesame seeds and perform the worship of the Guru. Then...

In the manner previously described, he speaks of the propitiation of Pradyumna (in the four verses beginning with "atra rājopacāraiḥ" and the seven beginning with "atha trivikramam"). Regarding the phrase "having performed that worship properly," the meaning of "that worship" is the worship of the Guru. || 112–118 ||
Then, month after month, having worshipped Padmanābha immediately after Hṛṣīkeśa, one should indeed worship Dāmodara thereafter.
When three months have passed in this manner, having returned once again on the tenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, then [one should perform] for each respective rite.
Having applied the fourfold nature of the mantras to the four [deities],
and having taken recourse in the designation of the four forms (caturmūrti), one should perform that worship.

Upon the pericarp, on the petals starting from the east, one should place the heart-mantra and the others; in the intermediate directions, the weapon-mantra; and the eye-mantra of the Lord is indeed situated upon the filaments in front.
Then, within each of the spokes, one should worship the ten [deities] beginning with Keśava, using flowers of four colors, as well as garments and ointments. (123)
In the same way, [he should worship] with edible offerings, sacrificial foods, purifying drinks, and fruits;
furthermore, with various other enjoyments such as banners and the like, as well as vehicles and mounts. || 124 ||

Then, with *mātrās* accompanied by gold and with betel-leaf himself, he should perform the observance of the vow for three months ending on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, using the three mantras beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa. Starting from that point until the twelfth day, for three days, the worship of all four—Vāsudeva and the others—is to be performed in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*); the worship of the [five] mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra is on the eastern petals and so forth; and the worship of the twelve forms beginning with Keśava is on the spokes (*arā*). This should be done according to the respective form, using the previously mentioned four types of materials—sandalwood, flowers, and so on—and the four kinds of *mātrās*. Thus he says: "Then month after month..."
And so forth, by means of [the terms] beginning with "ceti" || 119–125 ||
One should satisfy the collection of mantras as prescribed, situated in the midst of the fire.
Then one should perform the worship of the Guru specifically as previously described;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should recite the *prīṇana* hymn first, [saying]: "May Aniruddha be my refuge.
Then one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and subsequently utter this: || 127 ||
By this supreme vow performed today by me with devotion, may the four forms, Vāsudeva and the others, together with their Śaktis, [be pleased]. (128)
"May they attain incomparable joy; may they grant fearlessness to all living beings.

For all of these, there is a libation (saṃtarpaṇa) into the midst of the fire. Then follows the worship of the Guru, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, the propitiation of Aniruddha, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and the simultaneous propitiation of the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva. He states this in four verses beginning with "he should offer libations" (tarpayet). (125–129)
This vow is auspicious and meritorious; it turns one back from the path of saṃsāra.
It involves little hardship, is free from confusion, and bestows infinite fruit upon men.
Therefore, one must certainly not feel despondent while practicing this.
He says, "Blessed," in one and a half verses [129–130], to show that because this vow bestows infinite fruit even when incomplete, one should not fear obstacles in its midst.

Just as service should be performed by lowly or middling people through acts of attendance, so too [should it be done] by forest-dwellers with flowers and the like, according to their ability and without guile. 131.
By means of water, blades of *dūrvā* grass, leaves, the recitation of mantras, keeping vigil, and so forth;
by means of a lamp, sprinkling, sweeping, and smearing with cow-dung [or unguents]. || 132 ||

This vow is to be performed according to one's capacity—either by the middle or the lowest ritual procedure—using merely leaves, flowers, fruits, water, and so forth, or through services such as keeping vigil, lighting lamps, sweeping, and anointing; thus he says in two verses beginning with "yathopasadanaiḥ. (131–132)
One should then bring rice, barley flour, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and other grains for the purpose of worship, for giving as gifts, and for consumption throughout the year. (133)
First, he states the fourfold acquisition of materials for the sake of the vow, beginning with "rice" (vrīhīn). || 133 ||
One should first offer rice for three months;
indeed, it is always beneficial to consume that before eating on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Furthermore, roasted barley flour is the third triad, and ghee;
another triad consists of sesame seeds, and the ritual consumption [of these] is exactly the same.

In the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should first take a measure of rice (vrīhi) before eating, and thereafter consume that rice-food; in the three months beginning with Phālguna, one should give barley-meal (saktu) and consume it; in the three months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, one should give clarified butter (ājya) and consume it; and in the three months beginning with Bhādrapada, one should give sesame seeds (tila) and consume sesame seeds—thus he says in two verses [verses 134–135].
If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) should be complete and the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) occurs alongside it on the following day,
then one should perform the worship and other rites on that Dvādaśī.

He states the determination of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) with the words "it should be" (*syāt*). The meaning is: if the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is complete and remains [into the next day], and if the twelfth day is also complete on that same day; and if the twelfth day is complete along with that [eleventh] and remains even on the thirteenth day—then on the following day, on the twelfth day (specifically on the twelfth day remaining from the thirteenth day), one should perform the worship and so forth, as well as the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) and other rites of the previously mentioned vow. Thus it is said in the *Candrikā* regarding the determination of the tenth day:
"Where the eleventh day is complete and recurs again at dawn..."
And if even a single ghaṭikā of Vaiṣṇavī is seen on the thirteenth day, [it is auspicious].
"Even a householder should perform the later [Ekādaśī]; a householder should not fast on the earlier one.

Thus the meaning of the word "pūrṇā" (full) has been stated. Here, by the very qualification of Ekādaśī as "pūrṇā," its freedom from *daśamī-vedha* (contamination by the tenth lunar day) is also expressed; for it is said in the *Daśanirṇaya*:
"O Brahmin, when [the Ekādaśī] is joined with two *muhūrtas* prior to sunrise..."
When it is called "complete Ekādaśī," the householder should fast on that very day.
Thus, the meaning of the word *pūrṇa* has been explained. 136.
Indeed, for one who wishes to perform even a single [rite] from the midst of the year, he should perform the ritual up to the worship with his own mantra upon that [occasion] as well. || 137 ||

Worship with flowers and other offerings as they are available, together with the previously mentioned limbs; however, the worship of the supreme form (pararūpa) takes place within [the heart], while that of one's own [form] occurs in its respective [location]. || 138 ||
However, the propitiation of that very deity alone by his own name is beneficial;
furthermore, a single breaking of the fast according to the previously mentioned rule bestows abundant fruit. (139)
Therefore, endowed with faith, one should perform two or three [of these rites] according to one's own capacity.

Thus, for one unable to carry out the observance of the Dvādaśī vow throughout the entire year, or on a single Dvādaśī day, he explains—with the verse beginning "saṃvatsarasya" (and the following two and a half verses)—that one should perform the worship of a single form of Vāsudeva or another [deity] within the pericarp using the mantra of that month’s presiding deity (*tanmāseśa*), along with materials such as colored powders, fruits, and flowers appropriate to it; outside, in the position of the petals, one should worship together with that deity’s consort; and one should feed one or three Brāhmaṇas, thereby pleasing the presiding deity of that month.
For a woman who has no other refuge should indeed act in this manner. || 140 ||

"Or, being without a master, she may obtain it with her husband's permission; this vow should be performed even by women who are auspicious or have been auspicious in the past"—thus [the text] says "a woman. The meaning is that such is the fruit of that vow. Since it is improper for an auspicious woman to perform a vow without her husband's permission, it is stated that she must be "permitted by her husband. And so it is said in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "A woman indeed who is not permitted by her father, husband, or son..."
But whatever vow or other religious observance she performs shall be fruitless for her.
But that woman who, without having consulted her husband, observes a fast or undertakes a vow,
takes away the life-span of her husband and shall go to hell.
"Women have no independent ritual action, nor a vow, nor even a fast; service to their husband is ordained for them as the means to attain heaven. (140-141)
Now I shall describe the Cāturmāsya, the supreme vow that bestows liberation.
By performing which, a man obtains his desired objects right here,
having reached a home free from disturbance, or a place that is not crowded with people.
It should be as extensive as one's means allow, either square or rectangular,
provided with a chimney for the exit of smoke and adorned with a series of windows.
One should construct a structure piled with bricks and other materials, and in its center, three pedestals—square, separated, and slightly elevated above the ground. (144)
Then, above the southern altar, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be prepared as before;
in its center, [one should draw the design] with a mixture of sandalwood, yellow pigment (rocanā), and saffron.
