Every month, one should draw an auspicious six-petaled wheel with a central space using cow's milk alone; this bathing pedestal is situated in the northern direction.
Then, on the tenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, when the moon had risen,
he took water in his hand while reciting the mantra known as Vāsudeva.
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, Lord of all vows, infallible one!
By your grace, may my vow be fulfilled for the attainment of you. (148)
Then, on the twelfth day, one should worship Vāsudeva within the interior of the lotus; and on the petals starting from the east, one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others in groups of three.
Having arranged them in a clockwise direction as far as the foot-covering of Rakṣas,
one should place the triad beginning with Aniruddha starting from the petal of the position of Īśāna.
Having worshipped with the rite of dissolution as far as the western petal,
one should again worship the abode of the elements in the center and then in the spokes of the wheel.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship in sequence, beginning from the east: first Vāmana, then his Goddess, followed by the Heart-mantra and then the Head-mantra. (152)
Then Śrīdhara and his consort, Śikhā; Hṛṣīkeśa and his wife, Kavaca; and thereafter Astra and Locana. (153)
One should always perform meditation, bathing, worship, and fire-offerings accompanied by recitation for all [deities] in this very sequence. 154.
Then, on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa in the center;
with two of its petals, one should worship Vāsudeva, and then [the others] on the spokes of the disc as before.
The triad beginning with Padmanābha, as well as the Goddess and those [deities] starting with Hṛt;
then, on the twelfth day of the month of Nabhas, Pradyumna is situated in the pericarp.
The first [deity] is on its petal; then the triad beginning with Nārāyaṇa on the spokes;
likewise the goddesses and the six limbs (aṅgas) within the spokes as before. 157.
Then, on that same twelfth day, one should worship Aniruddha as before,
and subsequently worship the Primordial God (Ādideva) upon his two leaves in due order.
Beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Trivikrama, the Śakti and the limbs [of the mantra] are likewise [assigned] as before;
such is the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika. (159)
There, one should perform the ritual entirely with all the excellent mantras;
on the twelfth day, as before, in the center, one should assume the form of the six limbs.
The forms situated between the spokes and the host of deities stationed on the rim [should be worshipped];
the worship and the fire-oblation (homa), ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), are specifically as previously enjoined.
Thus, this vow with its specific details has been declared in brief;
by performing which one is not born again here in this world of rebirth.

Now, he states the procedure for the Cāturmāsya rites, beginning from "Next, I shall explain that which bestows liberation" until the completion of the section. For the sake of easy understanding, this commentary is written in the form of a practical application (*prayoga*).

Having constructed a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*)—either in one's own home, which is free from obstacles and secluded, or in another location—extending as wide and long as resources permit, provided with upper windows for the exit of smoke and adorned all around with latticed windows; and having fashioned therein three altars (*vedikā*), square and slightly elevated above the ground, constructed of bricks; one should then prepare the previously described sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) upon the northern side of the altar situated in the southern direction.

On the central altar, one should draw a twelve-spoked wheel with its center containing a six-petaled lotus, using saffron mixed with *rocanā* and sandalwood paste ground with cow’s milk; this should be done every month. Above the northern altar, one should install the bathing pedestal (*snānapīṭha*). Then, on the evening of the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, taking water in the right hand while reciting the Vāsudeva mantra, one should say:
"O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, Lord of all vows, O Acyuta!
By Your grace, may my vow be fulfilled for the attainment of You."

Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) preceded by the pouring of water, and having fasted on the eleventh day, one should worship Vāsudeva in the center of the pericarp on the morning of the twelfth day; then, in clockwise order, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha on the petals in the east, southeast, and southwest; and likewise Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa on the petals in the northeast, northwest, and west, following the order of dissolution. Having worshipped Vāsudeva again in the center, one should worship Vāmana, the goddess named Prīti, and the Heart-mantra on the spokes of the wheel starting from the east.

Having worshipped in sequence the *śiromantra* [with the deity] Śrīdhara and his consort named Rati, the *śikhāmantra* and *kavacamantra*, and the *astramantra* and *netramantra* with Hṛṣīkeśa and his consort named Māyā; and having satisfied them all through meditation, worship, bathing, offering, fire-sacrifice (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth; then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Saṃkarṣaṇa in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), Vāsudeva in the petals at the positions of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Padmanābha, Dāmodara, and Keśava in the spokes.

Having worshipped the triad of goddesses—Dhī, Mahimā, and Śrī—as well as the six mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra; then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, having worshipped Pradyumna in the center, Vāsudeva in the two petals situated where Pradyumna resides, and Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, and Govinda in the remaining petals, as well as the triad of goddesses known as Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, and Kriyā, along with the six mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra; then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, having worshipped Aniruddha in the center, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, and Trivikrama in the petals situated where Aniruddha resides, and [the others] in the remaining petals.

Having worshipped in sequence the triad of goddesses known as Śakti, Vibhūti, and Icchā, as well as the hexad beginning with the Heart-mantra (Hṛnmantra), one should, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, perform a special worship according to the rules: in the center of the pericarp, the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva; on the petals, the hexad beginning with the Heart-mantra; on the spokes, the twelve forms beginning with Keśava; and in the position of the rim, the twelve goddesses beginning with Śrī. Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), concluding with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 141-162 ||

Now, he states the procedure for the Cāturmāsya rites, beginning from "Next, I shall describe that which bestows liberation" until the conclusion of the chapter. This commentary is written in the form of a practical manual (*prayoga*) for the sake of easy understanding.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Annual Vow," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the venerable Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Sātvata-tantra-bhāṣya composed by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa, son of the venerable Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of the Lord of Yadugiri.
The Ninth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then the God who wields the discus was urged by the plow-bearer (Balarāma).
O best of Brahmins, listen now as that which is being told by me.
Now the ninth [chapter] will be explained. Nārada says to the sages, "Listen to that which was spoken by Vāsudeva when questioned by Saṃkarṣaṇa," introducing it with the word *atha* (now). || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
Through the division of the subtle and the manifest, I have correctly understood the worship of the Supreme Brahman, including both its external and internal aspects.
Now I wish to hear, O Lord,
the method of propitiating Him whose nature is perfect abundance, which duly grants the desires of all living beings.

He states the manner of the question in two verses beginning with "sūkṣma": "by means of the subtle and the expanded" (sūkṣmavyūhavibhāgena) means by means of the distinction between the supreme expansion (paravyūha); "with the external and internal" (sabāhyābhyantaraṃ) means distinguished by the division between mental sacrifice (mānasayāga) and external sacrifice (bāhyayāga). || 2–3 ||
The Blessed One said:
"O Greatly Wise One, that great assembly of deities belonging to the Vaibhava [class] which was previously described by me— know that each one of them is threefold."
It was indeed prepared for the destruction of the defects of universal dissolution throughout the four junctions of the ages and likewise throughout the ages themselves.
Marked by hands holding blazing weapons in forms such as white, red, and so forth—
this should always be done at the commencement, the middle, and the conclusion of any undertaking.
He alone, assuming many forms for the welfare of all the worlds, manifests his own form as manifold; that [form] is gross, assuming shapes at will.
With a body that was unassuming yet as white as a kunda flower or the moon,
he remained with a joyful mind, seated in the vīrāsana and other postures.
He who effortlessly wielded all divine weapons, whose face was gentle and composed,
and who by his wisdom destroyed the entire multitude of defects for those seeking liberation.
That manifest form, known as "the Tranquil," the most excellent among all forms,
reveals the true path to those whose souls are devoted to meditative absorption.
That form which consists of light is the manifestation known as Śānta;
all [these forms] bestow every fruit upon their worshippers and devotees. || 11 ||
O Mahāmati, for the sake of propitiating each [deity] until liberation is attained, the reciter is indeed prescribed to be of four kinds through non-discursive meditation. (12)

Thus questioned, the Blessed One, beginning with the words "The Vaibhavīya" and ending with "until liberation through non-discursive meditation," explains the threefold nature of the manifestation of his power according to the distinctions of gross, subtle, and supreme. Here, the genitive case in the phrase "of the ages and the junctions of the ages" signifies the locus. The meaning is that he has appeared for the sake of destroying the defects of universal dissolution; that is to say, he has manifested for the pacification of whatever defects arise during the ages and at the times of their junctions. By this, [it is shown] "for the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of the evil-doers."
For the sake of establishing the Dharma, I manifest myself age after age.

This is the meaning that is recalled. "By way of white, red, and other forms" means by way of the distinction of colors corresponding to each respective Yuga. And so it is said in the Śrī Bhāgavata: "Indeed, there were three colors for Him as He assumed bodies according to the Yugas;
[He was] white, red, and yellow, but now He has attained blackness."

"At the commencement, middle, and conclusion of an undertaking" means during the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. "He alone assumes manifold forms" means that at the time of creation he bears a red form, at the time of preservation a white form, and at the time of dissolution a black form. "The gross" means abiding in the state of waking. "Assuming forms at will" means bearing various forms according to his own desire.

In this context, the phrase "that which is manifest" (*vyakta*) and "known as tranquil" (*śāntasaṃjña*) refer to "form" (*rūpa*). Here, by the term "manifest," its dependence upon the states of dream and deep sleep is expressed; by the term "known as tranquil," its dependence upon the fourth state (*turyapada*) is expressed. For it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) is threefold within the triad of states beginning with deep sleep;
it is clearly manifest in that [deep sleep] state, while in the fourth state, it remains as the supreme, characterized by the qualities (*guṇalakṣya*)."

Thus, it has been stated that for one situated in the states of dream and deep sleep there is clarity (*suvyaktatva*), while for one situated in the fourth state (*turyapada*) there is tranquility (*śāntatva*). It should be understood that although the forms are distinct by virtue of being based on the states of dream, deep sleep, and the fourth state, they are described as identical because there is no difference between them in terms of their abiding within the heart and their subtlety. "Form" here means the subtle form. Accordingly, in the fourth chapter of the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, it is said: "O Nārada, through the application of my own yoga, I am indeed the creator, the protector, and likewise the destroyer, in a gross form."
In my subtle form, I dwell within the hearts of all beings;
I also bestow grace upon those devotees whose minds are purified.
"O Brahmin, I pervade the entire universe with my supreme form, which is blissful, all-pervasive, and stainless, just as sap permeates the finest tree.

Now, one might object: "In this [text], it was stated that the *vyūha* itself possesses fourfold nature by virtue of its dependence upon the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*); how then can you speak of it here in the context of its manifestation as an *avatāra*? To this we reply:
The distinction between states such as dreaming and so forth is for the sake of calming the fatigue of meditators,
and also for the purpose of bringing about the cessation [of suffering] for those living beings situated in their respective conditions.

O Lord of the Army, by my will, you alone are the presiding lords over the individual souls in states such as dreaming, and over those whose nature is bound by karma, while remaining established in that [highest] station.
I am to be worshipped, O fortunate one; this is the purpose for the distinction of my stations.

Since the manifestation of the fruit thus described is also required in its *vibhava* (manifest) form, it is logical that the *vibhava*, like the *vyūha*, possesses a fourfold nature through the distinctions of the states of *turya* and so forth. For this very reason, it has been stated by the Mother of the World regarding these four forms of mine in this descent as the *parā* and other archetypal images:
[The verse follows: "In this fourfold form of mine, which is the descent of the *parā* and other [levels]..."

"The states beginning with the fourth (turya) are to be known; this is the pure path. Thus, regarding the phrase "the majesty called 'the peaceful' (śānta)," the meaning of "called the peaceful" is that which is higher than the highest (parātpara). || 4-12 ||
For the purpose of propitiation, the reciter is indeed prescribed to be fourfold:
consisting of names, syllables, the *piṇḍa*, and characterized by the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
From among these, one should then address [the deity] with devotion using even a single one. || 12–13 ||

Now, with the half-verse beginning "O Mahāmati, for each one," he explains the fourfold nature of mantras through the divisions of name (*saṃjñā*), word (*pada*), aggregate (*piṇḍa*), and seed-syllable (*bīja*), as well as the worship of the Blessed One—such as his invocation—by means of one of these. [The meaning is: having addressed the Blessed One who is to be expressed and having invoked him, one should worship him; this is the ellipsis. (12–13)

In this case, by means of a mantra arising from a single compound word, or by one consisting of both [words], the denoted object is treated as if it were a single entity characterized by non-difference. (14)
In that regard, one should indeed perform the visualization of those two according to this procedure;
first, having prepared either the seed-syllable or the *piṇḍākṣara* of the name-mantra.
One should lead [the disciple] toward [the deity], or recite [the mantra] with the beginning and the end; then, having bound the word-mantra by this very rule, one should proceed.
One should [visualize it] as being seated upon the seat of the Praṇava and endowed with the banner of salutation;
for indeed, because of their nature as peace, there is oneness between these two.

Know that the word-mantra (pada-mantra) called *saṃjñā* is the characteristic mark of perfect accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*). Where the worship of the one Lord, whose form is non-different [from the deity], must be performed by either the seed-mantra (*bīja*) or the name-mantra (*nāma-mantra*), or by both the seed-mantra and the name-mantra, he describes there—in four and a half verses—the manner of combining those two mantras and the mantra consisting of the addition of *praṇava* and *namaḥ* at the beginning and end. "By that which has the initial and final" means: that which has the seed-syllable at its beginning and likewise at its end; the meaning is that it is accompanied by the seed-syllable even at the end.
Alternatively, the meaning is "at the end itself together with the seed-syllable. In both cases, it is stated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"In the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end—in all three, or in any one of them."
"Those mantras for which there is either a *piṇḍa* or a seed-syllable (*bīja*) are effective at all times. (14–18)
A single-syllable seed-mantra (bīja) is known to arise either from a vowel or from a consonant. || 18 ||
The king of *piṇḍa* mantras consists of many syllables produced from the conjunction of vowels and consonants.

He describes both the nature of the seed (*bīja*) and the nature of the *piṇḍa* as "arisen from vowels" (*svarottha*). The meaning of "arisen from vowels" is that it has arisen—i.e., been produced—from one or more of the vowels beginning with *a*. Thus it is further elaborated in the *Lokamātrā*: "A single vowel, two vowels, or a pair consisting of a vowel and a consonant."
"Or the seed-syllable may consist of many vowels; it should be understood in these various ways, O Lord. (18–19)
O Mahāmati, [the syllables] are formed from the first and likewise from the last of each group of vowels.
Indeed, the nature of being a mantra belongs to others along with the *bindu*.

Among the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, the two initial vowels and the two final vowels possess the nature of being mantras by their very form; that is to say, by the two [vowels] *a* and *ā*, and by the two final ones, the *anusvāra* and *visarga*. This group of four seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be understood as having been previously established in the fourfold mantra-manifestation of the dream state. (19–20)
Of that which is joined with a single vowel and that which is endowed with a pair of vowels. || 20 ||
O Lāṅgalin, [the Lord] states that even a consonant possesses the nature of a seed-syllable when accompanied by an anusvāra;
indeed, he declares that even a consonant such as the letter *ka* constitutes a mantra only by being joined with a vowel. (20–21)
That which is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the sound called *oṃkāra*, appearing as a mass of radiant light; || 21 ||
Know that the characteristic of the mind is formless, yet its designator is threefold:
in some cases it is a syllable-cluster (piṇḍa), in some cases a seed-syllable (bīja), and in some cases the unstruck sound (anāhata).
And for that [speech] which is being uttered, its transformation is indeed manifest:
it consists of many syllables and many words, characterized by praise and address. (23)

The four—seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), names (*saṃjñā*), and words (*pada*)—are all transformations of the *praṇava*. Among them, the first three are subtle transformations, while the last is a gross transformation; this is stated in two and a half verses beginning with "That which is called the word *oṃ*. The meaning is that it is a variety of forms (*ākārabheda*), possessing the luster of rays, consisting solely of light. It is characterized by consciousness (*cillakṣaṇa*), meaning its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). It is formless (*anākāra*), meaning it is characterized by the [three] qualities (*guṇa*). This very point is also elaborated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"This is an evolution (*vivarta*) of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), crowded with ten thousand rays."
The nature of the mind consists of the essence of true qualities; its division is fourfold:
in some cases it is the seed, in some the mass, in some the name, and in some the word.
The fourth state (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dream (svapna), and waking (jāgrat) correspond respectively to the vyūhas and other manifestations.

And thus, it should be understood that just as the Lord who is the object of the mantra was previously explained as being threefold—by way of the divisions of the supreme (*para*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the gross (*sthūla*)—and among those, the subtle was further explained as being threefold by way of the divisions of the fourth state (*turya*), deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and dream (*svapna*); so too here, the supremacy of the *praṇava*, the subtlety of the mantras known as *bīja*, *piṇḍa*, and *saṃjñā* according to the sequence of the fourth state, deep sleep, and dream, and the grossness of the *pada-mantra* have been stated. (21–23)
That imperishable Oṃkāra bestows great supernatural power upon seeds and other ritual materials;
therefore, one should first offer the great seat with the Praṇava, which is known as Truth.
Therefore, one should indeed place the seed-syllable, inseparable from Truth, upon that;
by means of its own manifestation, one should effect the arising of the form from the seed-syllable. || 25 ||
When the occasion for sacrifice has arrived and the ritual is being performed constantly,
one should contemplate its dissolution just as water on a heated stone.

Thus, because the *praṇava* is eternally manifest, it is placed at the beginning as the support (*ādhāra*) for all mantras; above that, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which evolves from it; during the daily time of worship, the emergence of either the name-word or the mantra from that seed-syllable in the form of its transformation; and finally, upon the completion of the sacrifice, its dissolution back into that very same place—this he describes with the three verses beginning with "the imperishable" (*avināśī*). Since the seed-syllable is of the nature of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and the phonemes situated above it are of the nature of the field (*kṣetra*), the emergence of the form (*mūrti*) is thus described.

By the phrase "one should remember the dissolution," the dissolution of the mantra in its embodied form into the seed-syllable (bīja) is indicated; furthermore, the dissolution of the seed-syllable into its cause, the *praṇava*, should be understood. Thus it is said in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"The mantras residing in the abodes of enjoyment, when worshipped in their proper order..."
One should then clearly visualize them as having entered the body of the principal mantra,
just as tongues of flame enter into other flames, or as rivers flow into the ocean.
O twice-born one, one should contemplate that gross form of the mantra, the locus of all mantras,
as having entered into the subtle sense-organ of the intellect, which possesses both natures.
But others [regard] that subtle [reality], which consists of both aspects in the manner previously described;
they regard that supreme [reality] as having a throbbing form, resting in the supportless state.
One should visualize [it] as having entered the heart-lotus by way of the channel of union (sandhimārga).
Thus [ends verses 24–26].
O Mahāmati, this is like the expansion and contraction of the sun's rays;
however, due to the influence of activity (kriyā), there is here merely the perception of difference.

How can it be established that, at the time of worship, there is an expansion from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of either the name or the mantra—which are distinct from the earth—and a contraction back into it upon its completion? He dispels this doubt by means of the analogy of the sun's rays, [stating]: "By the expansion of the sun... (verse 27).
Where there is neither a seed-syllable nor a cluster (piṇḍa), there indeed follows the Praṇava;
that which is the first syllable of the word-mantra is the designator of light.
Having raised that remaining form from those [remaining] syllables like a tree, [one should worship it]; this is stated in the verse beginning with "na yatra" (and a half).

When a mantra is devoid of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) or a body-syllable (*piṇḍa*), the first letter alone possesses the nature of a seed-syllable; the remaining syllables constitute its form, and their production from that [seed] is what is being described. Regarding the word "utthāpya" (having raised), the word "arcayet" (one should worship) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This very point has been further elaborated by Harivallabhā: "The seed-syllable is the life-force of those possessing seeds; the remainder is proclaimed to be the field."
"For those without seeds, the first is the individual soul (jīva), while the field (kṣetra) is what remains.
Here, "first" means the initial syllable. (28–29)
Only where there is indeed a seed-syllable (bīja) or a body-mantra (piṇḍa), devoid of words (pada).
In that context, the status of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is prescribed for the phoneme named 'A';
the status of being the Field (kṣetra) belongs to the remaining phonemes in their collective form.

In the case of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) or a cluster-syllable (*piṇḍa*) that is devoid of name-words and mantras, he states with the verse beginning "only" (*kevalam*) and its half-line that the letter *a* possesses the nature of a seed, while the remaining letters possess the nature of a body (*vigraha*). It has been stated in this very way by Kamalavāsinī as well: "Let it be said that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is [the essence] of both the seed-syllables and the cluster-syllables."

"But the remaining field is intended... [etc. ... "Thus. The meaning is: of the *bījas* and *piṇḍas*, that is, of the pure *bījas* and *piṇḍas* excluding the *pada*s. Let it be so; the meaning is "the letter 'a' indeed" || 29-30 ||
For the solitary seed-syllable, its own stability is the state of being the Brahman-class;
the falling away from its own nature is the seed, as is the utterance of the seed and its form. (31)

The seed-mantras (*piṇḍamantra*), which are always manifest, are to be understood as being like seeds. With the [verse] beginning with "of the solitary" (*kevalasya*), [the author] speaks for half a verse regarding the domain of the seed and the cluster, even when devoid of the letter *a*. The very state of abiding in itself of the solitary seed is its nature as *brahman* and its nature as a phoneme (*varṇatā*). Its state of abiding in its own gross form and its subtle form is precisely its nature as *brahman* and its nature as a phoneme. Nature as *brahman* means grossness, that is to say, corporeality (*mūrtatva*); nature as a phoneme means the state of being a seed (*bījatva*). The sense is that the state of being the field (*kṣetratva*) and the state of being the knower of the field (*kṣetrajñatva*) are also grounded in a single reality through the differentiation of states.

For instance, the falling away from one's own nature (*svabhāvapracyuti*) is the absence of grossness; that is to say, it is the intermediate state. That itself is the seed (*bīja*), meaning the living soul (*jīva*). The "utterance of the seed" (*bījoccāra*) is the clear utterance of the seed in its gross form; this is the meaning of "form" (*ākṛti*) and "field" (*kṣetra*). In this very way, the arising of the *piṇḍa-mantras* is also to be understood, and the relationship between the field and the knower of the field (*kṣetrakṣetrajña-bhāva*) is to be realized. In the *Lakṣmītantra*, however, this relationship between the field and the knower of the field is established with respect to a seed consisting of a single vowel (*ekamātra-bīja*). But regarding a seed devoid of the letter *a*, it is stated that the vowel itself is the knower of the field. For example: [The text continues with technical details regarding the phonemes. Thus, the relationship between the field and the knower of the field has been explained in the *Lakṣmītantra* with reference to the single-vowel seeds, whereas for seeds lacking the letter *a*, the vowel alone is declared to be the knower of the field. Furthermore, when devoid of the letter *a*, it is designated as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) in the vowel; moreover, it is simply the vowel itself.
The first *mātrā* would be the individual soul (*jīva*), and the second and subsequent ones would be the body;
however, in the single *mātrā*, there would be the individual soul, while the characteristic of the earth is the residual impression (*saṃskāra*).
"When being uttered, it is the *kṣetra*; moreover, in the soundless *piṇḍaka*, the first is designated as the *jīva*, while the remainder they call the *kṣetra*.
Thus, *saṃskāra* means the intermediate state of the word. Indeed, it has been stated in that very same place:
Then follows the third unfolding, which arises from Śakti;
that is the state of Madhyamā, wherein she brings about the refinement of union.

"But the distinction between the signified and the signifier at that time consists of the nature of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Here, "the characteristic of being manifest" means the gross form, which is to say, it has reached the state of *vaikharī* while being uttered. Thus it is said in that very same work: "The state called *vaikharī* is speech consisting of phonemes, arising from refinement (*saṃskṛta*). (31–32)
That mantra which possesses the characteristics of a seed-syllable is indeed the great Vaiṣṇava power.
Through the thorough knowledge, recitation, meditation, and worship of the innumerable, countless, and diverse forms of speech as they truly are— || 33 ||
Through the oblation and by becoming one with that [deity], one attains the seedless state (nirbīja-pada);
indeed, for practitioners, there shall always be the simultaneous attainment of their desired goal.

He states the fruit of the seed-mantra with two and a half verses beginning with "yad" (that which). "Vaiṣṇava capacity" means the capacity that is the very nature of the Lord. "Innumerable" means that because the object to be expressed by the mantra exists in manifold forms, it is beyond counting; therefore, the mantra that expresses it likewise possesses various forms. "From the thorough knowledge of that as it truly is" means from the knowledge of that seed-mantra along with its modes. "The seedless state" means the supreme abode that is without beginning or end.

"He attains" (ṛcchati) means "he reaches," with the word "the practitioner" (sādhaka) understood as the subject. [The phrase] "there would be the attainment of the desired [result] together [with it]" indicates that because the attainment of the desired object is stated to occur together with that fruit which is liberation, it is thereby shown that liberation is primary while the others are incidental. || 32-34 ||

In this very same way, from the thorough knowledge of the mantras such as the *piṇḍa* and the forms of the Lord, there arises [liberation]; however, from the *piṇḍa*, there is the highest stability. (35)
Through the various names and mantras arising from various other worlds, the attainment of all states occurs by means of the thorough knowledge of the designations of those states. (36)

The *piṇḍa*, *saṃjñā*, *pada*, and *mantra* [categories] likewise bestow the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*); however, it is said in two and a half verses beginning with "piṇḍādi" that in those cases there may be stability and so forth regarding fruits other than liberation. "Stability" (*sthairya*) here means the stability of the desired objects other than liberation. "Diversity" (*nānātva*) means their various kinds. (35–36)
Whether with seed (sabīja) or with the ritual ball (sapiṇḍa), these two supreme forms of mantras each produce their own respective fruit; however, one should meditate upon the latter as the superior.

Since Acyuta is the Lord of All, being the nature of both the mantra and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), he exists through his desire to bestow grace in the form of both the pervaded and the pervader. || 38 ||

The conjunction of the name-mantra with both the seed-syllable and the cluster has been stated. In that regard, when there arises an inquiry as to whether the capacity to bestow the fruit belongs to the former, the latter, or both, he states—with one and a quarter verses—that the capacity to bestow its own fruit belongs to the latter alone, while for the former, there is merely the cultivation [of it] in the form of the *kṣetrajña*. (37–38)
He exists in the form of the pervaded and the pervader through the desire to bestow grace. || 38 ||
In its pervasive form, it bestows the supreme fruit, beginning from all enjoyments on the earth and extending up to the greatness of the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya). || 39 ||
For the embodied soul who performs actions and is weary of worldly enjoyments,
his own state is that of the self consisting of the seed-pellet of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), characterized by the absence of veils.

That stainless, pure knowledge which restrains [the mind] and bestows the attainment of the Self—furthermore, reinforcing this very point with its underlying reason, [the Lord] explains, in three verses and a quarter beginning with "yasmāt," that because both the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are of the nature of the Blessed One, the field alone bestows enjoyment and liberation, while the other—the seed-mass which is the knower of the field—bestows the knowledge that accomplishes liberation. [The phrase] "in the form of the pervaded and the pervader" means in the form of the field and the knower of the field; the meaning is that the form of the pervader is characterized by being free from veils (*nirāvaraṇa*). (38–41)
And the waking state of the word-nature consists of both potentiality and manifestation. (41)
In this way, O Great-minded One, there is indeed the oneness of the dream-state of the self-perceived consciousness and the state of deep sleep, which belongs to the mantra known as Piṇḍa.
Indeed, the state of being a manifestation of power belongs to the seed-nature of the fourth state (turya).

With two verses beginning with "śakti," [the author] explains the mutual relationship of power and manifestation among the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth; and among the designations of the words, the clusters, and the seeds, respectively. (41–43)
Although the individual manifestation is traditionally held to be invariably accompanied by the fruit of knowledge, || 43 ||
Nevertheless, [this applies] to the forms of the mantras of the Blessed One, as well as to the Supreme Self, to the primordial Caturātman, or to the Lord alone. (44)
Know that the mantra which is of four kinds bestows liberation and prosperity;
otherwise, that which is prescribed is either unmixed or indeed mixed.

"Know that the fruit is exactly so by virtue of the state [of the practitioner], and not otherwise. Although it has been stated as a rule that the manifestation of the *bhagavan-mantra* beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) bestows knowledge and grants the fruits of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), nevertheless, that refers to the manifestations of mantras such as those of Suṣupti and Vyūha. However, regarding the four types of supreme mantras (*paramantra*), he says "manifestation" and so on in three verses, stating that they grant liberation alone. This refers to the first [category], the Caturātmya, meaning the Turya-vyūha; and to the "mere pervasive one," meaning the one who is higher than the highest (*parātpara*).

The meaning is that "otherwise than this" refers to the collection of mantras taught according to the sequence of the *suṣupti*, *vyūha*, and so forth. "Unmixed fruit" means liberation alone; "mixed fruit" means liberation accompanied by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*). "By the power of disposition" means in accordance with various intentions. The word "gives" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Thus, it should be understood that this arrangement of the subject matter has been made with the following intention: although the supreme mantra mentioned in the second chapter is a *pada-mantra*, it primarily bestows liberation; for this very reason, it was previously stated that yogis should worship that mantra. Therefore, the statement that mantras consisting of general names and words (*saṃjñā-pada-mantra*) bestow enjoyment (*bhoga*) would otherwise appear contradictory. It is with this in mind that the distinction between the objects [of the two types of mantras] has been established. (43–46)
Having understood this, O Great-minded One, one should thereafter worship with various mantras.

"Having known"—he says this to indicate that one should perform the worship of the Lord preceded by knowledge of the multitude of manifestations of the All-pervading One through the secondary, primary, and secret [forms], as well as the distinctions in the fruits of their respective mantras. "The multitude of manifestations" means the collection of incarnations such as Padmanābha and others, which will be described hereafter. (46–47)
Together indeed with the fourfold self, he is of the nature of the great light.
The worship of that [deity] while established in the state of waking was previously described only in brief;
now it is explained in detail, accompanied by the practices of mantra and meditation. 48.

"I shall explain in brief; listen, O long-eyed one. [The author] says this in two verses beginning with "mahājyotiḥ," meaning: previously, the worship of the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*) together with the Supreme Lord was stated in summary; now I shall describe it in detail. "Of the Supreme One whose nature is great light" (*mahājyotis-svarūpasya para-sya*)—this is the meaning. "Together with the fourfold self" (*caturātmanā saha*) means together with the fourfold manifestation beginning with Vāsudeva. For there too, the fourfold manifestation was indeed mentioned in the passage: "Accompanied by his own forms, both formless and those beginning with Acyuta. "Of that which is established in the waking state" (*jāgrat-pada-saṃsthasya*) means of the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*).

"Previously," that is, earlier; "that kind of worship" means that mental worship was briefly described in the second chapter, and external worship was described in the sixth chapter—this is the meaning. || 47-49 ||
The Blessed One himself, desiring to create the universe, became Viśākhayūpa.
Indeed, it arises as one with its own essential nature as the presiding witness;
yet its entire majesty, preceded by pure consciousness, [is fully manifest]. 50.

Regarding the manifestation of the Lord known as Viśākhayūpa—the sovereign of all the *vibhava* deities, who is the pervasive one (*vibhu*) abiding in the first station of the fourfold form (*cāturātmya*)—the author describes the manner of his appearance in two verses beginning with "Viśākhayūpa. "Abiding in the first station of the fourfold form" means: having taken up the majesty preceded by pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvit*), and having gathered the instruments for the means of the *vyūha*, *vibhava*, and *avatāra* incarnations. This very [majesty] was likewise augmented by the Mother of the World (*jagajjananī*) throughout the fourfold forms, beginning with the fourth state (*turya*) and ending with the dreamless sleep (*suṣupti*).
In that [state] endowed with various sovereign powers, the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is well-established;
having taken up all that divine [nature], preceded by pure consciousness.
He divides himself by himself, appearing in forms such as Vāsudeva and others.
Thus [ends verses 49–51].
And likewise, such indeed was the conduct of the gods who were primarily established as supports.

Furthermore, O Mahāmati, the [five] splendors such as white and so forth, the [five] bases such as refuge and so forth, together with the marks, the majestic power, and the weapons—these indeed constitute the seed-syllables. (52)

The six qualities beginning with knowledge, all the powers (śaktis) mentioned therein, the eightfold [powers] beginning with atomization (aṇimā), and the states of maintenance, origination, dissolution, and emergence; || 53 ||
That power, which is fourfold in nature, is called "the Power of the Lord" (aiśvarī).

He provides an exposition of its instruments with the words "and likewise," etc., in three [verses]. The meaning is that the "network of powers" (śaktijāla) consists of Śrī and the other goddesses, such as Śrīdevī. It is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra* that all of these possess the nature of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya): "Of all the divine beings, from Parā down to Vibhavā..."
O Lord of the Thirty-three, your forms consist of the six pure qualities.
Whatever weapons the gods possess, such as the discus and the conch,
as well as their various ornaments and diverse garments—
O Lord of the Gods, there are banners of various forms and splendors such as white and others, as well as diverse vehicles, beginning with the Truth.
The powers (*śakti*) that bestow enjoyment exist in various forms;
they comprise the entire group of internal organs as well as all their respective functions.
"And whatever implements are common to other men, know all that to be produced by the sixfold policy, O slayer of Bala. (51–54)
Just as a great spark of light, having left behind the mass of the sun's rays, [shines forth]. || 54 ||
Just as [the sun] fills its entire range without any other cause, so too is that Supreme Lord, due to His autonomy and His perfection. 55.
Having set aside the four branches of forms beginning with Vāsudeva,
he remains as the lord of the Vaibhavīya host.
Setting in motion this supreme five-spoked wheel by means of his intellect, he impels that which is characterized by origination, maintenance, dissolution, enjoyment, and liberation. (57)

By means of the illustration of a particle of the sun’s brilliance and so forth, [the author] states, through three and a half verses beginning with "yathā," that Viśākha-yūpa alone possesses sovereignty over the deities of manifestation (*vibhava*). Thus, even though the world is augmented in this very way, at the time of manifestation, it exists without the fourfold form.
"Indeed, this Viśākhayūpa, by virtue of his power, brings about manifestation. Now, an objection may be raised:

"In the section explaining the first chapter, you stated that the Vibhava-devas are born from Aniruddha; yet now it is said that Viśākhayūpa is their cause. How can there be no contradiction between these two? To this we reply: True. The lack of contradiction should be understood through the non-difference (*abheda*) of the two. (54–57)
Established in his own station, he should be meditated upon with his own seed-syllable by one of pure nature;
[one should contemplate] his entire bodily form from the crown of the head down to the feet. (58)
The [mandala] should be cultivated as adorned with the seeds belonging to Vaibhava, like jewels;
by those being recited in sequence, it is filled with a flood of nectar as before. (59)
"Through worship, one attains the state of the Supreme Lord very quickly.

With two and a half verses [58–60], he states that Viśākhayūpa’s meditation on his own form by means of its seed-syllable, the meditation on the adornment of his limbs by means of the seed-syllables of Padmanābha and others, and the fruit of that worship are to be remembered.
Listen with an attentive mind to that collection of seed-syllables.
Through His grace, those who have become one with the Blessed One attain supreme perfection.
[This occurs] in a pure, pleasing place, well-smeared and adorned with flowers. (61)
Having drawn the wheel of the Mātṛkās upon a surface smeared with sandalwood powder and perfumed with excellent incense, one should indeed do so again according to this specific method.
By the mere sight of which impurity is shattered into a hundred pieces;
one should write from the beginning with the letter *pra* up to the end of the five groups (*pañcavarga*), placing the middle-end in the center. (63)
The nine letters beginning with *ya* are situated at the navel; those beginning with *a* occupy the sixteen spokes;
and all those beginning with *ka* are on the rim—all as they were in the previous wheel, located upon the axle.

Then, one should worship that wheel, which consists of the Śabdabrahman and is the primordial material cause (pradhāna), according to the prescribed rite with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other offerings in due order.

In order to extract the seed-syllables of the deities of the *vibhava* [manifestation], he describes the arrangement of the wheel of letters (*varṇacakra*) and its worship with five and a half verses beginning with "Listen" (*śṛṇu*). "The ends of the classes" means the letters Ṅa, Ña, Ṇa, Na, and Ma. "As many as nine" refers to the letters from Ya to Kṣa. "In the previous wheel" means in the wheel described in the second chapter. "The letter situated on the axle" means the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ). (60–65)
From the midst of that, one should first extract that which is the cause of all;
it is the syllable situated above, adorned by the letter preceding 'ra' (i.e., 'a') at the beginning of 'akṣa'.
Know this to be the seed-syllable of the Lord of All, which is itself the causeless cause; this very syllable, when accompanied by the Visarga, is remembered as belonging to the Lotus-navelled One.
The second [syllable] is indeed from the group of the rim (nemivarga), and from that, the sixth syllable is from the spoke (arāt);
the eighth is from the region of the hub (nābhideśāt), and the same number [of syllables] is from the circle of the rim (nemimaṇḍalāt).
From the navel, first to the rim, it is the seventh [point] reaching the fifth spoke;
from the spoke, it is the fourteenth, which indeed goes toward the western direction from the axle.
Then the eleventh from the rim, the sixteenth, and the thirteenth;
and the fifth from the region of the navel, and the nineteenth from the rim. (70)
O Mahāmati, the seventh [letter] is at its end, and indeed the ninth;
the third from the navel, and following that, the same number from the rim. (71)
The twelfth is from those situated outside; the tenth is beyond the sixteenth;
then the letter preceding the navel, which is indeed the fifteenth from the rim.
One should take the fourth vowel from the letter *ma*, then the fourth from *na*, the sixth from *me*, and likewise the fourth from the middle consonant. (73)
In that very [mandala], from the fifth [point] outward starting from the eastern direction,
one proceeds to the eighteenth [point] on the rim situated in the southern direction from the axle.
The second [syllable] is from the region of the navel; at its end is the seventh [vowel].
From there, the fourteenth is from the navel; then one should take the sixth from the navel. (75)
In brief, all [the mantras] should be joined with their respective causal deities at the head; they begin with the *praṇava* (OM) and end with *namaḥ*, and are exceedingly replete with splendor.

He describes the sequence for extracting the seed-syllables (*bījoddhārakrama*) starting from the words "tanmadhyāt" up to "tejasā'tīva nirbharāḥ. Having extracted the syllable *na*, which stands above the axle (*akṣa*), one should adorn it with the first anusvāra from the end of the spokes (*arānta*). Thus, the practical application is *nam*. This is the seed-syllable of Sarveśvara Viśākhayūpa. If this very same syllable is accompanied by the visarga, it becomes the seed-syllable of Abjanābha. As for the seed-syllable of Dhruva, it is the second letter of the *nemi* group, the syllable *kha*.

The sixth syllable after *arāt* is the letter *ū*, which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Ananta. Thus, in this sequence, one should extract the sixth [syllable] from the navel; the meaning is to be understood as ending with the seed-syllable of the one reclining on the netherworld (*pātālaśayana*).

All seed-syllables, like the previously mentioned Viśākhayūpa, possess a causal nature and should be joined with the *anusvāra* at the head. They are to be known as beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*. Their application is as follows:

Oṃ no namaḥ, oṃ khaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ūṃ namaḥ, oṃ haṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ, oṃ kaṃ namaḥ, oṃ saṃ namaḥ, oṃ uṃ namaḥ, oṃ auṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ, oṃ yaṃ namaḥ, oṃ taṃ namaḥ, oṃ śaṃ namaḥ, oṃ naṃ namaḥ, oṃ aṃ namaḥ, oṃ jaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ, oṃ laṃ namaḥ, oṃ gaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ paṃ namaḥ, oṃ yaṃ namaḥ, oṃ daṃ namaḥ.

Oṃ raṃ namaḥ, oṃ vaṃ namaḥ, oṃ laṃ namaḥ, oṃ dhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ maṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ, oṃ caṃ namaḥ, oṃ aṃ namaḥ, oṃ phaṃ namaḥ, oṃ raṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṛṃ namaḥ, oṃ thaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ. These are the thirty-eight seed-syllables (bījas). || 66-76 ||
The deities beginning with Padmanābha are to be named in their respective order:
Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātmā, and Madhusūdana. (77)
Kapila, the presiding deity of knowledge; Viśvarūpa, the sky-goer;
he whose self is the boar; Vaḍavāmukha; Dharma; and likewise Vāgīśvara. || 78 ||
O Lord, you are the tortoise reclining upon the single ocean who supports the netherworld (Pātāla),
as well as the boar, the man-lion, and indeed the one who brought back the nectar of immortality.
The Lord of Śrī, possessing a divine body, whose nature is beauty, the bearer of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great one who carried away the Pārijāta tree. 80.
Then the Lord of the World, the peaceful-souled Dattātreya, the great master, the Blessed One who reclines beneath the banyan tree, manifested with a body having a single horn. 81.
The god Vāmanadeha, the all-pervading Trivikrama, as well as Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa. || 82 ||
Rāma, holding a flaming axe, and another Rāma, the wielder of the bow;
the Lord Kalki, the knower of the Vedas, and the Sovereign who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla). 83.
The group of manifestations has been described to you in brief as being primary.

Regarding these, beginning with the words "Padmanābha and others," he states the thirty-eight deities who are to be named in sequence, ending with the words "thus has been told to you in brief. The word *deva* (deity) is an epithet for the one reclining upon the single ocean. *Pātāladhāraka* (supporter of Pātāla) is an epithet for the Tortoise (*Kūrma*). *Divyadeha* (divine-bodied) is an epithet for the Lord of Śrī (*Śrīpati*). *Amṛtadhāraka* (bearer of nectar) is an epithet for the one whose nature is the beloved (*Kāntātman*). *Mahān* (the Great One) is an epithet for the one who seized the Pārijāta tree. *Śāntātman* (peaceful-souled) is an epithet for the Lord of the World (*Lokanātha*).

"Mahāprabhu" (the Great Lord) is an epithet of Dattātreya; "Bhagavān" (the Blessed One) is an epithet of the one reclining on the banyan tree (Nyagrodhaśāyin); "Devah" (the God) is an epithet of Vāmana; and "Sarvavyāpī" (the All-pervading) is an epithet of Trivikrama. "Jvalatparaśudhṛk" (the bearer of the flaming axe) is an epithet of Rāma (Paraśurāma); "Dhanurdhara" (the bow-bearer) is an epithet of the final Rāma (Rāmacandra). "Bhagavān" is an epithet of Kalki, and "Prabhu" (the Lord) is an epithet of the one reclining in the netherworld (Pātālaśayana).

Thus, failing to distinguish between the qualifier and the qualified, it has been written in the Vimānārcanaprakaraṇa of the Pārameśvara commentary that among the twelve forms—such as the Ekaśṛṅga-tanu and others—and among the twelve forms such as Kūrma and others, even though they are all wakeful (jāgarūka), there are eleven forms from Ekaśṛṅga to Pātālaśayana, and eleven forms from Kūrma to Nyagrodhaśāyin. Therefore, this must be understood with great care.

Thus, in this context, the thirty-eight vibhava-devas, beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Pātālaśayana, are to be known. Accordingly, it is stated in the Lakṣmītantra, starting with "Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta," and continuing: "These thirty-eight deities, beginning with Padmanābha, are considered [to be the vibhavas]."

In the fifth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, after describing the Vibhava deities in exactly this same way, it is stated: "These thirty-nine, beginning with Padmanābha, are considered [the deities]. One should understand that on account of this, no mutual contradiction is to be suspected; for there are thirty-eight deities beginning with Padmanābha, and Viśākhayūpa is their single overlord. With the intention of including him as well, making thirty-nine deities in total, it was said: "These thirty-nine."

Since the sovereignty over the Vaibhava deities of Viśākhayūpa was already stated previously—in the passage, "he stands as the lord of the Vaibhava host"—for that very reason, thirty-nine seed-syllables (*bīja*) are mentioned here, with Viśākhayūpa at their head. Furthermore, in the section on meditation (*dhyāna*), the three principal *pūrvas* ending with the *Dhruva-pūrva* were taught earlier;
now, ascertain the entirety of the remaining ones, beginning with the *Śeṣa*.

"Dhyāna is for those whose abode is as far as the Pātāla," thus [the text] will state that Viśākhayūpa also has companionship with the Vibhavadevas. Now, one might object: having begun with "Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta," and then stating, "These thirty-nine, beginning with Padmanābha, are considered [to be the deities]," since the number forty-nine is assigned specifically to Padmanābha and the others, it is improper to include Viśākhayūpa—who was not mentioned there—in order to complete the count. Such an inclusion should only be made when there is no other alternative; yet, in this case, there is another alternative.

For instance, in the passage "the Lord Śrīpati, the God," the word *deva* should be understood as referring to the God who performed the uprooting of Mount Mandara, as described in the *Pauṣkara*, because the same form of the word *deva* is used in both instances and because of the context. Indeed, the *Pauṣkara* states: "The God who performed the uprooting of Mandara, likewise the one who brought the nectar, the bearer of the jar of ambrosia, and he whose body has the form of a woman."
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, the Blessed One likewise severed the head of Rāhu into yet another form; thus, this very Lord is fourfold.

If it is argued that the manifestation [of Viṣṇu] as the uprooter of Mount Mandara is mentioned separately as "endowed with another manifestation, the most excellent of all manifestations," we say no; for in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, beginning with the passage "Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta," the sequence is recited exactly as stated in the *Sātvata[-saṃhitā]*, and since it is stated that "O Great-minded One, everything said therein is found in the Sātvata teaching," the characteristics of Padmanābha and the others must be understood according to the *Sātvata*, and thus the statements in the *Ahirbudhnya* must also be interpreted in accordance with the *Sātvata*.
For in the Sātvata [Purāṇa], the Lord who uprooted Mount Mandara is not mentioned separately;
therefore, that Blessed One, having all his desires fulfilled, acts by virtue of his own inherent activity.

"Having relied upon His own power, He remains again in the form of Padmanābha"—because of this statement, there is no difference between Padmanābha and Viśākhayūpa. For this very reason, in the section on the offering of the sprout (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, it says: "Abjanābha, and indeed Para, as well as Padmanābha and Dhruva. Thus, one should understand through subtle insight that Viśākhayūpa is also included by the very term "Padmanābha. Now, while such an interpretation has been stated for the words of Ahirbudhnya in some way, all [deities] such as Padmanābha and the rest are likewise manifestations of the Lord's glory (*vaibhavīya*).
O Lord of the Gaṇas, they are reckoned as thirty-six in number, according to their primary importance.

If it is asked, "What is the status of the statement in the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā*: 'The thirty-sixfold divisions, beginning with Padmanābha, are deities born from Aniruddha, like one lamp from another, [all] Lords'?", the resolution of that has indeed been provided by the venerable sage Ramyajāmātṛmuni in his *Tattvatrayavyākhyāna*. For he states: "Among the thirty-nine manifestations (*vibhava*) mentioned in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā* declares that thirty-six—the principal manifestations (*mukhya-prādurbhāva*) such as Padmanābha and others—are to be worshipped by those seeking liberation, setting aside the rest."

If it is argued that such a conception of the *gatis* (destinations) is rooted in ignorance—since the venerable Ramyajāmātṛ Muni did not recognize that the word "Vedavit," which occurs in the sequence stated by Ahirbudhnya as "Padmanābho dhruvo'nantaḥ," has the meaning of Vedavyāsa, nor did he study the passage from the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya* that determines its reference to Vedavyāsa—then, O foremost of fools, why do you criticize without understanding the intention of those teachers? [For they cite:
"Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa."
For who else on earth, Maitreya, could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
Thus, regarding the author of the Sūtras, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, whose greatness has been described, their intended view is precisely that he is a direct incarnation (avatāra) of the Lord.

If it is asked: "In that case, how is it that they themselves have stated that Vyāsa is an 'entrance-incarnation' (āveśāvatāra) and is not to be worshipped by those seeking liberation?"—it is true. That [statement] does not concern Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, but rather concerns the twenty-eight other Vyāsas mentioned in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

If it is objected: "But in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya* it is stated—'Among those manifestations, some are direct, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others; others, however, are through the presiding presence of a person distinguished as a seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, such as Paraśurāma, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, and others'—thus the status of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana as an 'incarnation by possession' (*āveśāvatāra*) has been declared. What then is the resolution for that? The answer is: That statement must be understood as referring to a Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana who descended in a different *kalpa*; otherwise, it would contradict the words of the Teacher (Ācārya).

Just as it was explained in the *Tattvatrayavyākhyāna* that the Teacher’s status as a direct incarnation (*sākṣādavatāra*) of the Buddha is established in the *Ācāryahṛdaya*, whereas in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* and other texts his status as an incarnated descent (*āveśāvatāra*) is stated—the contradiction between these two should be resolved by means of different kalpas; you, long-lived one, should be satisfied with this same principle here as well.

If it is objected: "But since it is stated that 'the group of manifestations (prādurbhāva) is primary,' and thus even the thirty-eight deities beginning with Padmanābha are said to be primary manifestations, how can it be maintained that those included therein, such as Kapila and others, are secondary? We reply: Here, the word "primary" (*mukhya*) found in the phrase "the group of manifestations is primary" does not have the same meaning as the word "primary" used in the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā*; for in the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā*, manifestation is declared to be twofold, through the distinction between the secondary and the primary.
For secondary status [is assumed] by my will, just as humanity [is assumed] by will.
The state of a boar, the state of a fish, and likewise the state of a man-lion;
or just as, by my will, the state of a hunchbacked mango tree in the Daṇḍaka forest.
"O General, just as my horse-faced form comes into being through my volition, so too does my state as a subordinate exist by my will alone, and not through [past] karma."

Those primary manifestations, however, are especially distinguished by being portions of my own self; they possess divine splendor that does not abandon their essential nature, yet assume natural physical forms.
Like a lamp lit from another lamp, you have arisen for the protection of the world;
O Lord of the Army, you alone are indeed worthy of worship, for they know all others to be unworthy of worship.
I shall also describe the future manifestations in their proper order;
for the four-faced Lord has been appointed to the task of creation.
The great Rudra named Śaṅkara was appointed for the work of destruction;
likewise, the Buddha named Mohana and the great ṛṣi Vyāsa were appointed.
At that time, during the dispersal of the Vedas,
Arjuna, the best of archers, and the great ṛṣi Jamadagnya were appointed by the Lord.
Pāvaka among the Vasus and likewise Vitteśa—
these and others, O Lord of the Army, were presided over by such manifestations.
All these individual souls are not indeed objects of Vaiṣṇava worship;
O one of immeasurable luster, they have all merely been entered [by you] for the sake of your purpose.
O Mahāmati, all these [elements] are indeed non-sentient because they are insentient by nature;
moreover, they are joined with ego-consciousness, infused with the individual soul (jīva), and presided over by it.

By such statements as these, it has been established that the primary [manifestation] is the direct incarnation (*sākṣād-avatāra*), whereas the secondary is the incarnated possession (*āveśāvatāra*). However, here, by listing both the direct incarnations and the incarnated possessions together and declaring the group of manifestations (*prādurbhāva*) to be primary, it is demonstrated that both possess the status of a primary manifestation; therefore, the meaning of the word "primary" (*mukhya*) should be understood as being commonly established for both, and not merely as being a direct incarnation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "The group of primary manifestations has thus been described by you in brief," one should understand that just as the term *prādurbhāva* (manifestation) includes both primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*) manifestations, so too it includes other types of manifestations as well, since [manifestations such as] Trivikrama and others constitute distinct categories of manifestation. A "distinct manifestation" refers to the internal subdivisions of those various incarnations (*avatāra*). As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "That which arises as a portion of the form, never abandoning its own nature yet appearing as a different configuration of the original form—that indeed is a 'distinct manifestation'."
And they were proclaimed there by Kaṇṭharava himself, as well as by Vāmananātha, who bore a dwarf form,
and by one marked with the signs of a *snātaka* and a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
By means of that very form which bestows happiness upon all pleasures,
known by the name Trivikrama, whose body had traversed the three worlds;
And in the Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā it is likewise stated:
"Know that the Great Lords (Maheśvaras) who have manifested from the previously arisen Vaibhavīya [form] are the principal among those other manifestations, O Lord of Gaṇas."

"From Upendra, who is primary, [comes] Hari in the form of Trivikrama," and so forth. In the *Lakṣmītantra* and the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, it is stated that these are "internal manifestations" (*prādurbhāvāntara*) among the incarnations through possession (*āveśāvatāra*):
"Entering and entering again, he creates gods, humans, and so on."

"The welfare of the world is that which is to be known as another manifestation (vibhavāntara) of the Lord of the World," and, "That which arises from the immersion of power (śaktyāveśa) is designated as another manifestation.

However, in reality, it is Kṛṣṇa himself who is being described by the statement, "The group of manifestations has been told to you in brief as primary. If it is asked, "Why is it said that he is not mentioned?"—it should be understood that the Kṛṣṇa established here is not the son of Vasudeva, but rather the son of Dharma. And so it is stated in the Pauṣkara:

"The Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is Dharma, [manifests] an eternal incarnation; for indeed, from him [proceeds] the first among men, ending with Kṛṣṇa. Now, one might object: "Since only the word 'Kṛṣṇa' is mentioned here, it must refer to the well-known Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva. This is not so, because it would contradict the [contextual] association [of the other two] and because it would contradict the meditation [on all three] that is to be described later. Furthermore, since Ananta is mentioned here, it should be understood that Balabhadra and Lakṣmaṇa are also effectively included.
Ananta will be the first form, Lakṣmaṇa after him, and Balabhadra will be the third; however, in the Kali age, someone else will appear.

This is because it is well-known [in scripture]. Now, one might ask: "Among the incarnations of the Blessed One, for whose sake is the mention of the two incarnations of Śeṣa—namely Balabhadra and Lakṣmaṇa—required? If this is asked, the answer is no, because Śeṣa himself is an incarnation of the Blessed One. For this very reason, Ananta is also mentioned here in the passage: "Padmanābha, Dhruva, and Ananta."

If it is asked: "In that case, why is Balabhadra—who is included within the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish—not mentioned in this group of thirty-eight incarnations beginning with Padmanābha?"—the answer is: True. Just as by the mention of Śrī Rāma, his three brothers Lakṣmaṇa and the others are effectively mentioned, so too by the mention of the one who seized the Pārijāta tree (Kṛṣṇa), his brothers, sons, and grandsons—namely Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—are also effectively mentioned; thus it should be understood.

If it is asked, "Is it not the case that Pradyumna and Aniruddha are also accepted as being included among the incarnations of the Blessed One?"—it is undoubtedly accepted. If it is then objected, "In that case, you are ignorant of the meaning of the Purāṇas," [we reply: In the tenth book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, it is stated:
"Kāma, who was a portion of Vāsudeva, having been previously burnt by the wrath of Rudra, returned to Him once again for the sake of obtaining a body."

In this regard, the commentary known as the *Munibhāvaprakāśikā* explains: "The qualification 'a portion of Vāsudeva' indicates a connection [with him] beginning from his future birth. Now, one might object: 'Is this not said to be the third manifestation (*vyūha*) among the four manifestations (*caturvyūha*), whereas the similarity of name is based on his being a partial manifestation (*vibhūti*)? To this, the distinction is made: he is called a 'portion of Vāsudeva' because his mind is presided over by Vāsudeva, or because he is the cause of that [Vāsudeva's] creation."

If it is argued that, for this reason, it is impossible for Pradyumna and Aniruddha to be incarnations of the Lord (Bhagavān), we say no; for those who have commented upon them have never seen the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya* and other such works, nor have they heard the *Bhagavacchāstra*. Indeed, in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*, it is stated: "Even in His state as Kṛṣṇa, because He does not abandon His fourfold form beginning with Vāsudeva, the 'Fourfold Form' (Caturmūrti) makes known His fundamental *vyūha* even within His *vibhava* [incarnation]."

It has been stated more than once that even Pradyumna and Aniruddha are incarnations of the Lord, as in: "The four forms—Balabhadra, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—belonged to his Yadu lineage; thus, by means of the Vyūha-root, he descended upon Devakī in his unconditioned, supreme form," and "In this case as well, because he exists in the state of the six attributes both collectively and individually, he is the Caturvyūha. Furthermore, in the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Bhagavacchāstra*, it is said:
"Indeed, the incarnation of Viṣṇu will occur in four ways;
likewise, I shall manifest in a fourfold manner in Mathurā."

"Revatī, Rukmiṇī, as well as she named Rati and Uṣā"—thus, the fact that even the four beginning with Balabhadra are incarnations of the Blessed Lord is clearly established. Enough of this digression. (77–84)
That which is the principal among the collection of powers is called the "collection of powers" (śaktisaṃgha). || 84 ||
Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, Dayā, Nidrā, Kṣamā, Kānti, Sarasvatī, Dhṛti, Maitrī, Rati, Tuṣṭi, and Mati is remembered as the twelfth. (85)

Now, with the half-verse beginning with "śakti," he describes the primary group of goddesses. The term "from the assembly of powers" (*śaktisaṃghāt*) is used in the singular to denote the genus. For he will describe in the twelfth chapter sixfold assemblies of the goddesses Śrī and the others, through divisions of one, two, four, six, eight, and twelve. This assembly as well is indeed included within those to be described; however, it is presented here because it is the most preeminent. As for the well-known goddesses of Padmanābha and the others, they are set forth in the *Īśvara* and *Lakṣmī* Tantras. Thus it is said: "Dhī, Tārā, Vāruṇī, Śakti, Padmā, and likewise Vidyā."
Saṃkhyā, Viśvā, Khagā, Bhūḥ, Gauḥ, Lakṣmī, and likewise Vāgīśvarī.
Amṛtā, Dharaṇī, Chāyā, Nārasiṃhī, and likewise Sudhā; Śrī, Kānti, Viśvakāmā, Mā, Satyā, Śānti, and Saroruhā.
Māyā, Padmāsanā, Kharvā, Vikrānti born of a man,
Nārāyaṇī, Hariprīti, Gāndhārī, and likewise Kāśyapī.
"Vaidehī, Vedavidyā, Padminī, and Nāgaśāyinī—these thirty-eight goddesses, beginning with Padmanābha and Śavati," thus [it is said]. (84–85)
Learn from me the bodily ornaments that constitute His primary attributes:
the crown, the Kaustubha gem, the radiant Śrīvatsa mark which is the sign of immortality, and the [conch]. (86)
Vanamālā is Garuḍa; now hear of the principal weapons:
the discus, the conch, the mace, the lotus, the plow, the pestle, and the arrow. (87)
The Śārṅga bow, the sword and shield, the staff, the axe, and the spear;
the noose, the goad, the mallet, the thunderbolt, and the javelin. || 88 ||
Thus, this circle of deities, accompanied by the collection of limb-mantras, remains dissolved within the body of the God of gods. (89)

Then, having described the four primary ornaments beginning with the crown, the vehicle, and the seventeen primary weapons beginning with the discus, he states their absorption into the body of the Blessed One along with their limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in four verses beginning with *pradhānabhūtāḥ*. The term *ītihanta* is an epithet for the axe (*paraśu*). Here, due to a confusion regarding the subject, the commentators on the *Pārameśvara-tantra* have stated in the section concerning the deities of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that there is a ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight weapons beginning with the discus and ending with the power (*śakti*); likewise, in the section on the consecration with a thousand jars, they state:
"One should worship the sixteen missiles (*astra*) beginning with the discus and ending with the thunderbolt (*vajra*)."
"Then, one should place the Śakti in the four squares located at the corners.

In the course of explaining this verse, it was stated that—in order to reinforce the erroneous talk previously mentioned—the compound *cakrādivajraparyantam* is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*. (86–89)
I shall describe the supreme host of gods, the instruments of worldly existence, who abide within the teaching of Him whose forms possess manifold manifestations. (90)
Time, the Ordainer, and the Restrainer; the scripture characterized by various limbs; the lords of knowledge; and Śiva together with Rudra and his attendants. (91)
The assembly of Prajāpatis, Indra with his retinue, the seven ancient sages, and the other planets surrounded by stars and so forth [all came]. (92)
All the clouds, all the nāgas, the most excellent hosts of apsarases, as well as medicinal herbs, animals, and all sacrifices together with their constituent parts. (93)
"O one of pure vision, it has been said that [the universe consists of] sacred knowledge and the supreme knowledge, fire and wind, the moon and the sun, water and the earth. (94)

The great equipment for existence consists of twenty-four items. Now, with the words beginning "I shall speak," he describes the class of deities who constitute the equipment for existence. The terms "together with Rudra" (sarudra) and "together with Gaṇa" (sagaṇa) are qualifiers of Śiva; he is so described because he exists together with the eleven Rudras. (90–95)
Existence (bhava), however, is directly the Pradhāna, all-pervasive and characterized by insentience. || 95 ||
"By the ritual placement (nyāsa) of mantras and the lords of mantras, even he attains the state of being worthy of worship.
Thus, for all living beings, the Supreme Lord [is the cause] in this manner. 96.
Having assumed a formless state by abiding as the inner controller (antaryāmin),
that Blessed Lord, whose desires are fulfilled, nevertheless acts through the power of his own activity.
Relying upon His own power, He remains again in the form of Padmanābha.

Thus, having explained the deities who are the instruments of *bhava* (existence), he states that even *bhava* itself is worthy of worship with the words "He is *bhava*. That from which everything comes into being is *bhava*; the meaning is *prakṛti* (primordial nature). It is *pradhāna*, denoted by the word *pradhāna*. Although He abides as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of all these—the instruments of *bhava* and so forth—endowed with *prakṛti*, and although His desires are already fulfilled, He assumes the manifest form known as Padmanābha for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees; this he explains with the two verses beginning with "Thus... (*ityevam*).
The meaning is that it is partless and formless. || 95-98 ||
In the earth, water, fire, wind, the root, the stalk, and the interior of the petals. (98)
In the lotus composed of the four principles, within the single ocean of the sky,
upon the couch of Ananta in the mental lake, the all-pervasive Lord exists, his body being divine consciousness.
Resembling a thousand suns in radiance, he indeed rested playfully upon his back;
then, within that lotus of his navel, which shone with various jewels—
But he, by his own power, brings forth the Vidyā whose form is sovereign capacity, surrounded by all the embodied forms such as the banners and others who are devoted to that [Vidyā]. (101)

He describes that lotus-navelled form with three and a half verses beginning with "dharā. One should understand, respectively, that the four elements consist of: the earth element as the root, the water element as the stalk, the fire element as the petals, and the air element as the interior of the lotus. "In the belly of the single ocean of space" means in the midst of the ocean whose nature is the space element. "On the mind-born couch of Ananta" means on the serpent-couch whose nature is the mind element.

"Divine body of awakening" (*divyabodhatanuḥ*) means having a divine body whose essence is the principle of consciousness (*buddhitattva*). "Lying on his back" (*uttānasthaḥ*) means lying supine. "In his navel-lotus" (*nābhipuṣkare*) means in the lotus of the navel whose essence is the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*). "Knowledge" (*vidyām*) means the Vedic knowledge in the form of the four-faced manifestation. Indeed, his state of being the body of knowledge has been established in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and other texts:
"Among those [beings], the human Brahmā was created by me as four-faced; from him, the eternal body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), the source of the worlds, [arose]. (98–101)

Thus, for the all-pervading Lord whose nature is that of the Sovereign (Īśvara) and who possesses infinite activity, there exists a sovereign power that is both quiescent and unmanifest, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
As before, one should remember [the deity] abiding in the state of the fourth stage (*turyapada*) within the space of the heart-lotus.

With the verse beginning "Ananta... (along with its half), he describes the locus of meditation for the form of Padmanābha within the heart-lotus. "Peaceful" (*śānta*) means formless (*nirākāra*), that is to say, existing as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). "Manifest" (*vyakta*) means having form (*sākāra*). The sense is that it is to be meditated upon in both ways—both as having form and as being formless. "As before, abiding in the state of the fourth stage" means, according to the method stated in the second chapter, that it is situated in the sky that has neither beginning nor end. || 102-103 ||
Below that, in the center of the pericarp, it shines with the luster of a noble gem.
Illuminating the ten directions, adorned with various body-hairs,
gentle, sixteen years of age, and with eyes like lotus petals.
One should always meditate upon the God who bears the wheel of the universe, whose body is the mace, and who likewise carries the spear known as the Support (Ādhāra). 105.
He who stands as the pillar within this very temple of the universe,
which is characterized by distinct levels consisting of space, wind, and earth.

Regarding the method of meditating on *Dhruva* in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) below that, which is the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says "tadadhaḥ" and so forth in three and a half verses. It should not be understood that this is the well-known, modern Dhruva; rather, it should be known as another one, who is the very form of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavadrūpa*) and the bestower of stability even upon him. Thus, in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "The determination is that the wheel of lights (*jyotiścakra*) is fixed or bound within him with great intensity..."

Because his body is the sky that supports the stars; for this reason, there is the mantra-text: "To the one whose form is the ether. And the visualization (dhyāna) says: "The god who bears the wheel of the stellar sphere. He is the "abode" (saṃsthāna) because everything is established and completed within him. He is the "bestower of the abode" (sthānada) because of the mantra-text: "He is the cause for attaining the supreme state. Indeed, by bestowing the exalted station, he has made even the [celestial] Pole Star (dhruva) fixed; therefore, he is "Dhruva. || 103-106 ||
One should visualize the twelve [deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Saraśāyin, located in the southeast corner upon the pericarp.

In that very place, one should perform the meditation on the twelve forms beginning with Ananta, starting from the east and ending in the northeast; thus he says, "starting from the east. "Agnigam" means situated within the fire-maṇḍala. || 107 ||
