One should likewise place the [deities] corresponding in number to those [petals], situated above the filaments, starting from Kūrma and ending with Nyagrodhaśāyin, within the circle of the support of nectar (amṛtādhāramaṇḍala).

He states that "of that number" means that at the location of the filaments, in the state of dream, one should perform the meditation on the twelve forms beginning with Kūrma; this refers to the lunar mandala within the Amṛtādhāra mandala. || 108 ||

Then, one should [visualize] that which is mounted upon the solar disc, situated on the surface of its petals, extending as far as the reclining Pātāla, including the Single Peak (Ekaśṛṅga) and the rest. 109.

He states "sūrya" etc., that at the place of the palate (dalasthāne), in the state of waking (jāgratpade), meditation on the twelve forms beginning with Ekaśṛṅga should be performed. The methods of meditation for these thirty-six deities, beginning with Ananta, are to be understood as they will be described hereafter. || 109 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner and worshipped with mental offerings arising from the nectar,
one should proceed according to rule through the yoga of meditation, following the sequence of emanation as before.

Furthermore, by means of the yoga of reabsorption, [the deity] should be worshipped for the attainment of results, beginning from his reclining upon the netherworld (pātāla) up until his reclining in the sky (gagana). 111.

He states with two verses beginning with "having placed" that the mental worship of the thirty-eight deities, starting from Padmanābha, should be performed according to both the sequence of creation and the sequence of dissolution; the phrase "ending with Gaganashāyin" means ending with Padmanābha. (110–111)
The host of deities that was mentioned in this collective heart-sacrifice (hṛdyāga),
one should worship them again according to this very procedure, though in a different order.
That triad which has been revealed as residing in three places among the twelve [deities],
one should worship it by placing each one individually in sequence.

One should perform the worship of each individual member of the twelve beginning with Ananta, the twelve beginning with Kūrma, and the twelve beginning with Mīna; thus he says in two verses beginning with "yaḥ" (112–113).

Having first worshipped, according to the previously stated sequence, the first [deity] of each group of twelve within the interior of the pericarp by means of the partless (niṣkala) self, [one should proceed]. (114)
Then, having raised that very [deity] from the center with his entire being,
one should install him as the foundational support everywhere beneath the lotus.
Having worshipped that very [deity] with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings— [one] located at the tip of the lotus-petal,
the second in the middle of the pericarp, and the third above the filaments in front of it— 116.
Having meditated and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then place the third [set] upon the eight petals;
indeed, the twelvefold [set] is everywhere like the lotus-navelled one (Viṣṇu) in the sky.
Surrounded by the deities who provide for his existence, that entire host of deities belonging to the limbs [of the body] was outside the lotus. || 118 ||
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should perform the worship with divine enjoyments as before.

He describes the method for each individual worship in the section beginning with "of each set of twelve" and ending with "with divine enjoyments as before. The first of each set of twelve refers to Ananta, Kūrma, and Mīna; the second refers to Śakti, Varāha, and Vāmana; the third refers to Madhusūdana, Nṛsiṃha, and Trivikrama. The group of eight refers to the eight deities of knowledge (*vidyādevāṣṭaka*), the group of eight beginning with Śrīpati, and the group of eight beginning with Nara.
The meaning is that he is known as the twelvefold one, the one reclining on the single ocean, the one reclining on the banyan tree, and the one reclining in the netherworld (pātāla).

And so is the ritual application (*prayoga*): in the section on the worship of the twelve [deities] beginning with Ananta, one first meditates upon Ananta as formless in the center of the pericarp of one’s own heart-lotus and worships him; then, having raised that very deity from that place, one meditates upon him as having form, supported by the foundation situated below the heart-lotus, and worships him; having worshipped that same deity at the tips of the petals of the heart-lotus, one worships the essence of Power (*śakti-ātmā*) in the center of the pericarp, Madhusūdana in front of it in the position of the filaments, and [the others] upon the eight petals.

Having worshipped the eight deities presiding over the sciences (vidyādhideva) and others, and having meditated upon and worshipped Him who lies upon the single ocean—both with form and without form, like Padmanābha in the sky at the end of the sound (nāda)—one should worship outside the lotus the goddesses such as Lakṣmī, the ornaments such as the crown, the emblems such as the discus, and the deities who are the instruments of time and other cosmic processes.

In the section on the worship of the twelve [forms] beginning with Kūrma, one should worship Kūrma in the place of Ananta; Varāha in the place of Śaktyātman; Nṛsiṃha in the place of Madhusūdana; the group of eight beginning with Śrīpati in the place of the eight presiding deities of the Vidyās; and Nyagrodhaśāyin in the place of Ekārṇavaśāyin.

In the section on the worship of the twelve [forms] beginning with Mīna, however, one should worship Mīna in the place of Kūrma; Vāmana in the place of Varāha; Trivikrama in the place of Nṛsiṃha; the group of eight beginning with Nara in the place of the group of eight beginning with Śrīpati; and Pātālaśāyin in the place of Nyagrodhaśāyin. (114–119)
In an image, in the center of a mandala, outside in the fire, and in a body of water; || 119 ||

One should offer a physical representation of garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, located in the sky, with one's own mantra, upon the head of the deity for whom the mantra has been installed in the center of the pericarp. 120.
"Because that [celestial form] is reflected in the mirror of the door of Brahman.

Having thus described the mental worship (*mānasārcana*), the sequence for the placement of the deity (*devatānyāsakrama*) is exactly the same even in the case of external worship involving the *bimba* and other materials. However, for the sake of worshipping the form situated in the sky (*gaganasthamūrti*), one should offer flowers, sandalwood paste, and so forth, specifically upon the head of the form situated in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). For the reason that the form situated in the sky is reflected in the mirror of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) of the form situated in the center of the pericarp, he says in two verses beginning with "In the form" (*mūtau*).

"In an image" (mūrtau) means in a physical form; "in the center of the mandala" refers to the mandala to be described; "in fire" means in consecrated fire; "in a reservoir of water" means in the middle of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha). The word "embodied" (mūrta) is used as an adjective for garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, in order to exclude purely mental objects. "Embodied" means that which is an object of the external senses. || 119-121 ||
Whenever and in whatever form the mind finds delight in any particular object, [that is what it perceives]. || 121 ||
Whether for the attainment of enjoyments or for the sake of liberation, one should then worship that particular [deity] in the center;
or one should perform the worship with that as the objective, or for one who has fallen from that station.
And because [the Lord] bestows various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) together with the form of withdrawal (*saṃhāramūrti*):

whichever Bhagavān a practitioner has a particular devotion for among the incarnations of the Lord, that very Bhagavān should be worshipped primarily in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) along with one of His forms—such as the one reclining upon the ocean situated in the sky above that [pericarp]. However, in His place, he who was previously mentioned as being worthy of worship in the center of the pericarp should be worshipped; this is what he states in the two [verses] beginning with "yasya" (meaning: of him who has been displaced from that position and raised up from the center of the pericarp).

The meaning is: by one of the forms of withdrawal (saṃhāramūrti), such as the one reclining on the single ocean, the one reclining on the banyan tree, or the one reclining in the netherworld (pātāla). || 121-123 ||
In this very way, through the worship of the limb-mantras, one shall obtain one's desired object. || 123 ||
In this regard, there is indeed a specific distinction in the ritual arrangement; learn that from me.
First, it is taught for the attainment of all perfections (siddhis) pertaining to the world of the earth.

Now, if one should worship only on the earthly realm (bhūloka) itself—using the mantras of the limbs (*aṅga-mantra*) which bear the names of the powers such as Śrī, the ornaments such as the crown, and the marks such as the discus—for the sake of attaining the enjoyments of all the worlds beginning with Pātāla, then the method for the placement of the deities (*devatā-vinyāsa*) is stated [in the verse] beginning with "evam" (thus), consisting of one and a half verses. || 123-124 ||
Then, as before, one should worship Ekaśṛṅga from the last of the twelve;
thereafter, one should place the limb-mantra known as Śrī within the pericarp.
Then one should meditate on another [deity] situated at the tip of the filaments in front of that;
afterwards, in sequence, the sixteen [deities] situated within the petals and at the tips of the petals.
One should meditate upon the supreme abode of all the accomplishments (siddhis) of the netherworld (pātāla), lying in the midst of the mantra as before.

But the Lord of Mantras, supported by that power and situated in the pericarp, becomes known as the "limb" (aṅga) for one who has taken refuge, in the granting of all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis). || 128 ||

First, with four verses beginning with "prāgvat" (as before), he describes the sequence of worship primarily for the sake of attaining success in the subterranean realm (*pātālaloka*) through the *lakṣmī-mantra*. "From the last group of twelve" means from the group of twelve beginning with *ekaśṛṅga*; "one-horned" (*ekaśṛṅga*) means the fish (*mīna*). "Named Śrī" means having the designation *lakṣmī*. "The other" means the *puṣṭi-mantra*.

Subsequently, one should understand that the "twice-eight" (sixteen) located within the petals consists of the ten beginning with Sleep (Nidrā), the four beginning with the Diadem (Kirīṭa), Garuḍa, and the Discus (Cakra). However, the "twice-eight" situated at the tips of the petals should be known as those beginning with the Conch (Śaṅkha) and ending with Power (Śakti). || 125–128 ||
In this very way, for the constant attainment of the perfections of the Bhuvarloka,
one should always remember Ananta, who reclines upon Śeṣa above and below Kamalā.
Now, he states the specific detail regarding the worship for the sake of attaining the Bhūrloka with the word "evam" (thus). "Saraśśāyī" means lying upon the single ocean (the Ekārṇava). || 129 ||
One should worship for the attainment of all the perfections (siddhis) of the sky:
Svastha, Nyagrodhaśayana, Kūrma, and Kamalamūlagata. (130)

He states the specific procedure for worship for the sake of attaining the worlds of Suvarloka and others with the words "one should sacrifice" (yajet). The meaning is that [the deity] is situated upon the Yantra of Lakṣmī located in the center of the pericarp, remaining established within itself. || 130 ||
One should perform the transference of these as well, according to various specific accomplishments, like a primary mantra, at all times and in all places, as previously described. (131)

Thus, he says "of these" (eteṣām) to indicate that one should perform worship primarily with the mantras of the flowers and other ancillaries as well—just like the Lakṣmī-mantra—with the desire to obtain their respective fruits. || 131 ||
Thus, by means of various kinds of enjoyments arising in accordance with the rules,
he who abides within the threefold creation possesses the supreme sovereignty of the Lord.
He concludes the stated point with the word "evam" (thus). || 132 ||
O high-minded one, in each of these—the Pauṣkara, the Vārāha, and the Prājāpatya—it exists entirely in its subtle form. (133)

And relying upon its vastness, it remains as a third part. With one and a half verses beginning with "pauṣkarākhye," he describes therein the exposition of the three creations and their existence through the distinction between the subtle and the gross. "In the Pauṣkara" means in the Pādma-kalpa; "in the Prājāpatya" means in the Brāhma-kalpa. And as it is said in the Śrī Bhāgavata at the beginning of the first Parārdha: "There was a great kalpa named Brāhma."
In that [time] there was a Kalpa wherein Brahmā existed, whom they know as Śabdabrahman.
And at the end of that very [kalpa], there occurred the kalpa which they designate as the Pādma;
for from the navel-lake of Hari, there arose the lotus of the world.
"But this Kalpa which has been described, O Bhārata, is also known as the second, celebrated as the Vārāha, wherein Hari was a boar. (133-134)
Indeed, he is joined to the three emanations by means of the application of the sequence as previously described.
Having taken his retinue along with him, accompanied by the requisites for existence and joined by the hosts of world-protectors, he indeed advanced toward that very place.

He states that in all three creations, beginning with the Pauṣkara, there is an inclusion of the previously mentioned retinue such as Lakṣmī and others, using the words "yathokta" (as stated). || 134-135 ||
The first syllable of the name, adorned by the letter at the end of the spoke,
should be joined with the name according to the path previously specified.
And for the sake of the worship of all, it has been fully revealed in this sequence. || 136 ||

Since the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the retinues have not been explicitly stated, he says in the verse beginning with *abhidhāna* (along with its half-verse): one should join them with the mantras of their respective names by making the very first letter of each name accompanied by an *anusvāra*. "By the *visarga* at the end of the spokes" refers to the previously mentioned wheel of letters; "end of the spokes" means the *visarga*, and "by that" means by the *anusvāra*. (136)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Internal Sacrifice to the Manifest Deities," in the Śrī Sātvata-saṃhitā of the Śrī Pañcarātra.

Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Śrīsātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshiper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The Tenth Chapter.
Nārada said: Then, O Brahmins, the Supreme Lord was urged by the wielder of the plow.
Therefore, let that be heard today with a restrained mind.
Now the tenth [chapter] will be explained. "Listen again to that which Vāsudeva was asked by Saṃkarṣaṇa," thus the sage Nārada spoke to the sages with the word "atha" (now). || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:

O Lord, you have not yet described the worship of the deities of manifestation performed within the maṇḍala, in the fire, outside, or in the midst of water; having made it clear, please instruct us on that.
Saṃkarṣaṇa asks about the external sacrifice, beginning with the word "maṇḍala."
The Blessed One said:
On a ground that possesses auspicious characteristics, level, and endowed with the previously mentioned qualities,
one should draw a mandala there for the worship of all [deities] as one.
It is square, with four doors, and provided with parts such as pedestals;
it is further adorned in the center by a lotus with thirty-six petals.
It was covered with canopies and banners, provided with small bells and mirrors,
and beautifully adorned with arches, fans, umbrellas, chowries, garlands, and precious gems.

Having established the previously mentioned characteristics in their entirety— both those already stated and those yet to be mentioned— Vāsudeva, instructing him, first states in three and a half verses beginning with "sulakṣaṇa" that the drawing of the maṇḍala— which is centered within a thirty-six-petaled lotus and endowed with the aforementioned components such as the *pīṭha*— as well as the decoration of the sacrificial maṇḍala, must be performed.
Then, having placed the seed-syllable of the Lord upon his hands and his body, || 6 ||
Having firmly grasped that identity and established an unwavering self-conception,
and having bound the Vaibhavī mudrā, one should touch all the limbs with it.
Having mentally recited the entire collection of mantras arranged in their proper sequence, and having first recalled one's own body as being composed of all the gods; 8.

Then, with two and a half verses beginning with "tataḥ," he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Viśākhayūpa seed-syllable on the hands and the body, the maintenance of identity with it through the thought "I am Viśākhayūpa," the touching of all limbs with the mudrā whose majesty is about to be described, and the transformation of one's own body into the essence of all mantras preceded by the recitation of the thirty-eight mantras beginning with Padmanābha. The meaning is that the "lordly seed-syllable" refers to the Viśākhayūpa seed-syllable.
This refers to the state of having a body composed of all the deities, such as Padmanābha and others, for one who has taken recourse to identity with Viśākhayūpa.
From the crown of the head down to the feet, his entire body should be visualized as adorned with the seed-syllables of the [deity's] splendor, like jewels;
this is to be understood according to the method previously described. (6–8)
One should visualize the mandala situated within the inner wheel like a blessed throne;
one should worship that mandala, the support of the deities, with the mantra of the wheel.
Regarding the recollection of the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) hidden within, like a throne of fortune (bhadrapīṭha), and its worship within the maṇḍala, he says "within" (antar). || 9 ||
Then, preceded by the offering of flowers, one should perform the mental placement (vinyāsa) of all the mantras there, according to the appropriate method.
Regarding that mandala, he describes the placement of the mantras preceded by the offering of flowers individually with the word "tataḥ" (then). || 10 ||
Then, one should sequentially place the Lord Dhruvātman in the middle of the pericarp,
gazing toward the circle of directions, starting from the eastern petal.
O Mahāmati, one should place the deities beginning with Ananta and ending with Pātālaśāyin outside the lotus, starting from Īśa and extending as far as the position of Agni.
The four [mantras] beginning with the kirīṭa, previously enjoined among the mantras,
are located in the four directions— north, south, west, and east— at the site of Paiṭhīna.
The two pairs beginning with Lakṣmī should be placed in due order right there, starting from the northeast corner (Īśa) and extending as far as the northwest quarter (Vāyu). 14.
Having arranged the pairs, beginning with patience (kṣamā) and ending with intelligence (mati),
outside the pedestal near its front, [one should place] the King of Birds (Garuḍa).
One should arrange four [deities] from the wheel up to the lotus, starting from the foot of Śaṅkara,
extending as far as the wind-corner on the exterior of the pedestal.
And there are two pairs situated in the directions of the north, south, west, and east.
Likewise, there is indeed a group of eight beginning with Lāṅgala and ending with Paraśu.
One should place the four [objects] beginning with the noose and ending with the thunderbolt in the four corners of the Śakti, located in the southern, northern, western, and eastern directions.
From the square near the northeast corner, one should proceed clockwise toward the second square situated adjacent to it. (19)
O one of great intelligence, the arrangement of Time and the others, up to the end of the Sacrifices, must be performed in their proper sequence according to how these sixteen [deities] are situated.
One should sequentially place the pair of Vidyā and Avidyā in the northeast and southwest corners, while Agni and Māruta remain in their own positions.
Having placed the Moon and the Sun at the northern and southern gates respectively,
one should place the Water element at the western gate and the Earth element at the eastern gate.
Then, one should indeed sacrifice to the Unmanifest (Avyakta) at the four corners outside the mandala by means of the name "Bhava," because no other Bhava is known.

Then, a group of ten from among those whose nature was characterized by desire attained perfection, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and possessing power equal to that of the Blessed One. (24)
One who is liberated from ordinary suffering and is appointed by the Lord as a savior from cyclic existence should be placed outside the maṇḍala. || 25 ||
Upendra is in the eastern quarter, Duratikrama in the south,
Mahāhrada in the west, and Vasuretas likewise in the north.
The one called Tejo-dhara is assigned in the middle between the east and the south;
Mahākarmā is in the southwest, while Agṛhya is in the northwest. (27)
One should remember the witness previously mentioned as being in the realm of space, increasing in size, and known by the name Ādhāranilaya, situated below all things. (28)
Outside of them, one should place the Lord of Weapons (hetirāṭ) according to the sequence of the directions with his own mantra,
causing him to illuminate [the area] by means of his own multitude of rays.

Regarding the locations of Dhruva and the others in the maṇḍala, it is stated beginning with "Dhruvātman" and ending with "bhāsayantaṃ niveśya. Thus, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one places Dhruva; in the thirty-six petals starting from the east, the thirty-six deities beginning with Ananta and ending with Pātālaśayana, who gaze toward the circle of the directions (*diṅmaṇḍala*); outside of that, in the four corners starting from the northeast and ending at the northwest, one places the crown (*kirīṭa*), the *śrīvatsa* mark, the Kaustubha gem, and the forest garland (*vanamālā*); then, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one places Lakṣmī in the northern direction and Puṣṭi in the southern direction.

In the western direction, Dayā; in the eastern direction, Nidrā; in the northeast (Īśāna) corner, Kṣamā and Kṣānti; in the southeast (Āgneya) corner, Sarasvatī and Dhṛti; in the southwest (Nairṛta) corner, Maitrī and Rati; and in the northwest (Vāyavya) corner, Tuṣṭi and Mati. Outside of that, near the pedestal (pīṭha), in front is Gaḍaru. Outside the pedestal, in the four corners starting from the northeast and ending with the northwest, there are respectively a discus (cakra), a conch (śaṅkha), a mace (gadā), and a lotus (padma). In the northern direction is a noose (pāśa); in the southern direction, a goad (aṅkuśa); in the western direction, a mallet (mudgara); and in the eastern direction, a thunderbolt (vajra).

In the four inner chambers, one should place the Śakti. Starting from the square adjacent to the northeast corner (Īśānakoṇa) and extending to the second square adjacent to it, within the sixteen squares known as the half-śobhā and full-śobhā containing blue and red lotuses, one should place the sixteen deities who are the instruments of worldly existence (bhavopakaraṇadevatā), beginning with Kāla and ending with Yajña, proceeding clockwise. One should place Vidyā in the northeast corner, Avidyā in the southwest corner (Nairṛtakoṇa), Agni in the southeast corner (Agnikoṇa), Vāyu in the northwest corner (Vāyukoṇa), Candra at the northern gate, Sūrya at the southern gate, and Toya at the western gate.

One should place Vasudhā at the eastern gate; Prakṛti in the outer corners of the maṇḍala; outside of that, in the cardinal and intermediate directions as well as above and below, the ten Siddhas beginning with Upendra; and outside of that, the Cakrarāja in all directions. || 11–29 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should perform the worship with the mantra and mudrās,
using the arghya, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, which have been purified by the rites of inspection and the rest.

Then, one should worship the Primordial God (Ādideva) of those [deities] who have been mentioned in their proper sequence; however, above all of them, one should worship him as before, established in his own place.

Thus, after the placement (nyāsa) of the deities of the mandala, their worship must be performed in due order, and the worship of Padmanābha above in the center should also be carried out; this he states with the two verses beginning with "having placed" (nyasya). In the phrase "purified by inspection and so forth" (nirīkṣaṇādiśuddhena), the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes burning (dahana), nourishing (āpyāyana), and other such rites. || 30-31 ||
Then, having consecrated the fire in a well-prepared sacrificial pit as before,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of all mantras within it, just as in a sacrifice.
Thus, one should first satisfy [the deities] in due order with seven fuel-sticks;
indeed, until the end of the oblation, one should offer everything purified by mantra, each time in its entirety, once for each.
The mantras become manifest before the practitioner, situated in the midst of the fire;
having thus offered libations, he should perform [the rite] one hundred thousand times.
For each one indeed, he should perform a homa with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
afterwards, once the libation for all has been performed, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having returned once more to the interior of the maṇḍala, one should perform worship again for all [the deities] in due order, using only flowers and incense. (36)
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation of all mantras, accompanied by meditation, four or eight times, sequentially. (37)
Then, having filled his cupped hands with a beautiful rosary or with his own finger-joints, as well as with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and fragrances; || 38 ||
Having remembered and recited the mantra consisting of all the gods, one should cast it;
having worshipped everywhere and at all times in due order with devotion through every kind of gift. || 39 ||
Having demonstrated the one sovereign mudrā of all mantras,
which resembles a thousand-rayed sun and bestows all accomplishments, with the syllable *praṇava*.

Now, with the verses beginning "In a well-consecrated pit as before" (32–40), he describes the method for satiating these [deities] within the fire, the procedure for the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) preceded by the worship of the mandala once again, and the display of mudrās preceded by the offering of handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
Having joined the two palms together, one should form a cluster of creepers,
bending them forward while keeping the space between them distinct by means of the two thumbs.
One should form two wrist-bands that are well-joined and extremely steady;
holding the pair of hands hollowed within, one should maintain them with one's own intellect without wavering.
Having seated her between his thighs, he should place his elbows there;
having hidden them with great effort, he should perform the binding of her.

O Stainless One, for the sake of attaining all siddhis at all times, he describes the characteristic of the Vaibhava-mudrā with three and a half verses beginning with *śleṣya*. Having joined the two palms together, having made the collection of fingers bowed, having separated and placed them apart along with the two thumbs, having made the two wrists well-joined and perfectly motionless, and having held the hollowed pair of hands steady by one's own intellect, one should place the elbows on the thighs, resting them firmly in the middle of the thighs.
This is the common mudrā for all the deities of the Vibhava class. || 41-44 ||
In the midst of the sacred site (tīrtha), within the lotus of one's own heart, in the [divine] image, on the altar, or indeed upon the ground.

In this fourfold [mandala], which is eternally free from smoke and contains fire within, one should perform the worship of the mantras for the sake of both spiritual accomplishment and liberation. (45)

He states with one and a half verses beginning with "tīrtha" that the worship of the Lord must be performed daily in four locations, such as sacred fords (tīrtha) and so forth. "On the altar" (vedyām) means on the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) alone, without an image; "on the ground" (sthale) means on a mandala. || 44-45 ||
Then, with handfuls of water filled with lotuses at the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and within the lotus of the heart,
one should worship with external offerings such as arghya, consisting of tangible enjoyments born of the nectar of meditative visualization.

With seven previous offerings of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) accompanied by clarified butter (*ājya*), and with sesame seeds placed in the fire, [the text] describes the various materials for worship appropriate to each respective location in the verse beginning with "sajala" (along with water). Thus, even in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the worship of the Lord within the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) using handfuls of water is clearly established:
"Having meditated upon the support (*ādhāra*) and the seat (*āsana*), [one should perform the worship] of Acyuta in the midst of the water."
Having summoned him who is endowed with the collection of mantras, one should cause him to enter [the mandala].
One should satisfy them with water alone, ending with Viṣvaksena,
using their respective mantras while holding the vessels with both hands in front, in due order.

By these [verses] and others, the procedure for worship within the water has been explained in detail by the eight verses beginning with "pārameśvaro 'pi karaśuddhisamopetaṃ" (The Supreme Lord also [is worshipped], accompanied by the purification of the hands). In reality, however, according to the method stated in the *Pārameśvara*, it is appropriate to perform the practice of hand-purification, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) on the body, and the assumption of identity with the Blessed One (*bhagavat-tādātmya*) even before the worship within the water.

It should be understood that the mention of performing those [practices] prior to the mental worship in the section concerning the worship of the image (*bimba-arcana*) refers to the case of one who, due to an inability to perform ritual bathing in water (*audaka-snāna*) and so forth, has not performed the worship of the Blessed One in the midst of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

If it is argued that, because of the statement, "One should perform the worship of the mantras constantly within this quartet," one must first perform worship in the midst of water before performing mental worship and so forth—this is not so; for it is said:
"As long as one lives, established according to one's capacity in any place whatsoever, one should perform the worship of the collection of mantras in locations such as the heart and others."
With substances such as flowers and water, or in their absence, one should perform the mental worship within the heart as before, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).

This is because, as will be explained, even for those who are incapable [of performing the full ritual], worship at any one of the locations such as the heart and so forth is prescribed. Furthermore, in the *Pārameśvara*, worship at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and mental worship are stated to conclude with the fire-oblation (*homa*). However, by those devoted to the *Sātvata* tradition, the rite should be performed only up to the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), since in the seventeenth chapter it says:
"Then, having meditated, [one should worship] with the most purifying enjoyments born of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*)."
"Having performed worship and even having brought [the deity] down at the end of the recitation (japa), one should sacrifice outside";
thus he will speak specifically of "the end of the recitation. || 46-47 ||
Having worshipped according to the rule, sequentially at each individual step.
Having performed either renunciation or accumulation correctly,
that which has been properly accomplished should indeed be sealed with a mudrā that conforms to the form of the mantra.

Thus, having worshipped the Lord sequentially at the sites such as the center of the sacred ford (tīrtha) and so forth, after each respective worship, if one is free from desire (niṣkāma), one should perform the renunciation of the action performed; if one has desire (sakāma), one should perform its acquisition. In both cases, one should perform the previously mentioned binding of the mudrās; thus he says [in the verse] beginning with "having worshipped" (pūjayitvā) in two and a half verses.

[Objection: It may be argued that it is appropriate for actions that produce other fruits to be abandoned out of desirelessness; however, why has the abandonment even of the action of worshipping the Lord—which primarily produces liberation—been stated? [Reply: This is not so, because for those established in the perfected means (siddhopāya), even the action of worshipping the Lord is to be performed as an end in itself. || 47-48 ||
By which [knowledge] there is no further production of fruit for those who have practiced renunciation, and [by which] the time culminating in the fruit is impelled by the scriptures. (49)
It is not appropriate for us to take away that which has been taught as the binding of seals at the proper times for those seeking results through the perfected ones and others today. (50)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is the binding of mudrās appropriate for those who have accumulated karma? What is the purpose of binding mudrās for those who have renounced all action? In response to this doubt, he states that they are meaningful in both cases with the verse beginning "for the sake of fruit" (phalārtham), which consists of one and a half verses. By means of which binding of mudrās, for those who have renounced action—that is, those who have abandoned ritual acts—the "fruit" does not come forth; the meaning is that even the flower itself is not produced.

However, for those who seek fruits and have accumulated karma, until the time of experiencing the fruit as declared by the scriptures, it is not possible for Siddhas or others to take it away by means of any binding of mudrās. The sense is that just as the wealth in a money-bag sealed with lac cannot be stolen, so too the karma becomes unseizable by others. || 49-50 ||
Other than those mentioned for that purpose, he bestows a seal (mudrā) for the removal of obstacles upon the stainless sacrificers who possess the nature of the principles of action (karmātmatattva).

Thus, while the purpose of the mudrā performed immediately after the worship has been stated, in response to the inquiry as to what the purpose of the rites prescribed for the intervals during the worship is, he states the result—which consists in the removal of obstacles—in the verse beginning with "kāla" (verse 51).
They bestow the mudrā of the essential nature of actions upon those who perform stainless sacrifices.
It causes the melting away of the defects that move both externally and internally;
therefore it is called a *mudrā*, because it also serves to seal what has been performed. (52)

In accordance with both of these purposes, he provides the etymological definition of the word *mudrā* in the verse beginning with "mudam" (joy). The phrase "of those who offer stainless sacrifices" (*amala-yājinām*) means "of those who perform pure sacrifices. The phrase "of those whose nature is action" (*karmātma-tattvānām*) means "of those whose consciousness is intent upon rituals such as sacrifice. The term "of defects" (*doṣāṇām*) uses the genitive case in the sense of the object. Thus, in the word *mudrā*, for the syllable *mud*, the word "gives" (*dadāti*) is to be supplied; for the syllable *dre*, the word "defects" (*doṣān*) is to be supplied. This etymology follows the purpose of the *mudrās* used during the interval of worship.
The etymological derivation "mudrā" from the word "mudraṇa" (sealing) should be understood as referring to the mudrā performed immediately following the worship. || 51-52 ||
Therefore, having first made the mind either naturally composed or bound,
one should always indeed contemplate its pervasiveness by means of each respective mantra.

Having performed either a physical or mental binding of the mudrās, one should contemplate the pervasion of the respective mantras therein; thus he says, "Therefore. The distinction is that in mental worship there is a mental binding of the mudrās, whereas in external worship it is physical. || 53 ||
Even though that collection of branches is permeated by consciousness,
the mantra is the presiding authority therein and bestows its own effect.

He says "by consciousness" (caitanyena) because it is possible for a mere collection of fingers permeated by pure consciousness to possess the capacity to bestow fruits such as the removal of obstacles, owing to being presided over by the mantra. || 54 ||
When this has been done, one should then perform the withdrawal of the mantras from within the mandala as before, into a single [deity] abiding in the sky.
Having recollected that [reality] through the supreme self, one should contemplate the Lord resting in the heart within the sky of one's own consciousness, endowed with his own inherent nature.

He describes the sequence for the withdrawal of the deities residing in the mandala with two verses beginning with "evam" (thus). "In one" means in the lotus-navelled [Brahma] situated in the sky; "by the supreme self" means by the partless form; "in the sky of one's own consciousness" means in the sky within the resonance (nāda). || 55-56 ||
Once the worship of Viṣvaksena has been performed, it is ordained that the remains of what has been offered by the twice-born, as well as flowers, leaves, and so forth, be cast into the water.

Regarding the disposal of the offerings—such as the remnants of the food, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, remaining after the presentation of the *kāri*—he states that they should be cast into the water after the worship of Viṣvaksena, beginning with the words "of the twice-born" (*dvijāteḥ*). || 57 ||
That which was previously offered should not be retained for long; the food offering (naivedya) for the mantra-forms [of the deities] should consist of nothing other than flowers and fruits. 58.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "It should be retained. This means that for whatever reason, the food offering (*naivedya*) presented to the forms of the Mantras—such as the sacrificial oblations (*havir*) offered to the Lord—should not be kept for a long time; with the exception of some flowers and fruits, everything else, excluding the portion intended for one's own consumption, must be cast quickly into water. He will state this very same point quite clearly in the seventeenth chapter:
"Then, having withdrawn everything, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*)."
Having cast whatever leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth into the midst of the water.

"Being free from desire, for the sake of purification, having previously drawn out a small portion, and having first held it purified by mantra, one should eat it while observing silence. Now, regarding the phrase "having previously drawn out a small portion," one might wonder: does this mean drawing out a small portion even before the worship of Viṣvaksena, or rather after that worship but before the pouring of water? In response to this doubt, it should be understood that both alternatives are valid; for it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:

Having set aside one portion for the purpose of consuming it oneself after inspection, and having established one portion for the worship of Gaṇeśa— who is designated as the "consumer of the remainder"—
one should satisfy him with the other portion.
The Brāhmaṇas and others who dwell in the village, who are of virtuous conduct and devoted [to him].

Thus, it has been stated that the extraction of the portion intended for self-consumption occurs prior even to the worship of Viṣvaksena. In that very context, within the section on the *mahāhavis*, however, it is said: "One should cast into the midst of the water what has been offered to Viṣvaksena."
Or else, for the satisfaction of water-born creatures that move within the water,
one should cast a small portion into the water and place the remainder of the food before them.

Regarding those twice-born devotees who are intent upon their own duties, it is stated that they may accept what has been offered to Him. For this very reason, it is said in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*: "The various distinctions regarding what is offered to Viṣvaksena, as well as the ritual procedures established by King Bhoja and others according to their respective *saṃhitās*, are to be observed in works such as the *Prayogapaddhatiratnāvalī*. (58)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Manifest Deities," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Sātvatatantra-bhāṣya composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrī Mauñjyāyana family and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The eleventh chapter.
Nārada said:
O lords of sages, having heard this from the mouth of Acyuta, the wearer of the forest garland [spoke].
He urged him on again so that he might hear what was there today.
Now the eleventh chapter will be explained. Here, [the author] says "having heard" (śrutvā) to indicate that one should listen to that which was asked of the Blessed One by Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to know correctly the characteristics of the meditation on the maṇḍala; for the benefit of those terrified by worldly existence, please describe it."
Saṃkarṣaṇa asks in due order. || 2 ||
The Blessed One said:
Having first established the eastern and western [lines] by means of the staff-yoga from the center thread,
one should then lay down four threads toward the east within the space between those two directions.
Having divided the equilateral [triangle] into two by its center, one should mark that clearly;
then, using a thread of the established half-measure, [one should draw lines] from east to west.
Having produced two crossroads from the southern and northern portions,
one should lay down a thread equal to the east and west over that.

Furthermore, having given equal halves in the cardinal directions, one should lead the four corners by extending the lines through the fourfold crossroads. Thus, one should indeed draw the decorative bands (bhakti).
One should draw four equal lines to achieve a perfect square;
then, dividing that [square] into eighteen equal squares in the four directions.
One should cast the collection of threads there, dyed with *ghaṭikāra* [pigment];
one should fashion the lotus-ground in the center across three successive rows of squares.
Outside of that, one should arrange a pedestal (pīṭha) accompanied by a row of footprints in the eight directions;
having then conceived four directions arising from its four parts.
One should cast four [units] at each intermediate direction in a row of three steps around the pedestal;
then, one should cast four [units] clockwise from each of the four cardinal directions starting from the exterior.
Having purified two by two from among the four sets of four, starting from the outermost,
one purifies the fourth set from the outside for the sake of establishing the gates.
One should diligently purify, step by step in sequence, each of the four directions, including both the exterior and the interior.
Furthermore, by means of all the [remaining] steps, one should sweep away six groups of six from within for the sake of perfect beauty; there, one should place eight red lotuses.
Just as one would prepare the ground for the worship of the gods according to the directions,
one should erase three squares each from the sides of the outer grid.
Know that the syllable situated between those three, which brings about a state of single essence, is the ornament; one should adorn it with a blue lotus. 15.
Having first brought five squares from each corner into the path,
and having completed the corners with the remaining squares, one should then [draw] the outer boundary with intervals.
One should apply three lines and then draw a lotus in the center;
its characteristics, provided with thirty-six petals, are now described. (17)
Near the ground of the *pīṭha*, having first raised [the cord] by one-fourth of a square from the Brahma-position, one should perform a circular rotation with the thread.
Having divided each of the four directional lines into equal parts corresponding to the number of petals, one should divide the space between each pair of lines from the circular boundary.
One should place one hundred and fifty sūtras there, minus six;
that sūtra which is situated at the first step, relying upon that, is the petal of the lotus.
One should perform it with four parts; understand this as follows:
those two threads on the left and right which are internal and adjacent [to the central line]. (21)

One should make the division between those two equal within the space from the tip of the petal to the mark; then, by means of a thread extending from that point and passing through the interior of that mark— || 22 ||
One should draw two half-moons using that same thread with perfect symmetry; then, having fixed it by means of those two threads, one should again draw a thread within.
One should bring the tip of the petal from outside, in proximity to the horn;
thus, by this method, the marked tip of the petal is perfected.

Having rotated [the compass] from the tip of the petal and the Brahma-line by one-quarter of the interval, one should draw the circle for the pericarp; the filaments are drawn with a measurement of two parts.
Then, one should rotate [the compass] from the center toward the tip of a petal by a quarter-measure;
having done so, it should be filled with pure, most brilliant pigments.
Know that the pericarp is yellow, raised, wide-spreading, and provided with seed-syllables;
all the petals, moreover, are white and marked with lines.
One should fashion three filaments on each petal with a reddish glow;
the space between the petals should be black, and the exterior of the circle should have a blazing luster.
The corners of the pedestal are white, while the four directions thereof are red;
the pathway has the luster of sapphire and is adorned with leafy garlands and other ornaments.
Except for the western portion, all the doors are like lotus petals;
they are black, possess all beauties, and are situated at the locations of the doors.
The secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) should be equal to half the size of that [main ornament], like the interior [of the lotus];
the corners (koṇas), resembling filaments (kesaras), should be white and provided with conch-shells.
And [he described] the series of lines outside, in colors such as red and gold, in sequence.

Being questioned by him, the Blessed One first explained the characteristics of the mandala, beginning with "Having prepared it through the application of a measuring-stick" and ending with "the series of lines outside in sequence. The practical application of this is as follows: having made the upper portion of the altar square by means of dropping threads and so forth according to the method stated in "having prepared it through the application of a measuring-stick," and having divided that area into eighteen equal squares, one should cast there a collection of threads colored with a small brush (ghaṭikāra), and [draw] a lotus in the thirty-six squares of the three middle rows.

One should construct it. Outside of that, one should construct a pedestal (*pīṭha*) with a single row [of squares]. Therein, one should form the four cardinal directions starting from the east with four squares each, and the four intermediate directions starting from the southeast with three squares each.

Having performed the rite of circumambulation by means of a single row outside of that, one should—outside of that, in the two rows [of squares] in the directions starting from the east—in order to achieve the four *pūrṇa-śobhās*, combine four squares in the inner row starting from the east with two squares in the outer row; then, outside of that, having fashioned the four doors by means of the four squares situated in the two rows in the directions starting from the east, one should [further] combine two squares in the outer row with one in the inner row for the sake of achieving the *ardha-śobhās* on the sides of the *pūrṇa-śobhās*.

Having unified the central grid (koṣṭha), one should draw eight red lotuses in the four primary directions (prāgādi) which are filled with beauty, and eight blue lotuses in the eight half-beauties (ardhaśobhā). In the intermediate directions (āgneyādi), within the spaces between the secondary beauties (upaśobhā), one should unify the five grids situated in the inner row together with the pathway (vīthī), and then form the corners with the seven grids situated in the outer row. Outside of that, having drawn three lines with intervals in the two rows, one should draw in the center a lotus endowed with thirty-six petals.

The method for this is as follows: leaving a quarter of the measurement from the foot near the ground of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should rotate [the cord] using a thread fixed at the *brahma-sthāna*. Then, having laid a single thread extending east-west in the middle of that circle, and another thread extending north-south above it, one should divide each of the four intervals between the directional threads—measured from the limit of the circle—into nine equal parts each, and then further divide each of those parts into four parts each, and insert the threads.
In total, there are one hundred and forty-four sūtras. Therein, starting from the eastern direction-sūtra, one should form each petal by means of four parts each.

The method for that is as follows: on one side, take the space between the two threads located immediately to the south of the central thread; measure that distance, which is equal to the *prāṇa*, and having made a mark on the central thread from the tip of the petal, draw two crescent-shaped lines starting from the petal-tip toward the left and right using a thread passing through that mark. Then, join the inner thread with those two lines, and from there—

One should bring the tip of the petal outside the proximity of the horn. Then, taking the measurement of the space between the tip of the petal and the Brahma-line (the central axis), one should rotate a circle from the center for the sake of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) using one-fourth of that measure. Rotating another circle with twice that measurement, one should form the filaments (*kesara*). Furthermore, one should rotate a single circle in the middle of the portion of the petal-tip for the sake of the void (*vyoma*). Having done this, one should then proceed to fill in the colors.

Its method is as follows: fill the pericarp with yellow color; the four directions of the pedestal with red; its four corners with white; and following the clockwise procedure, fill [the remaining areas] with black. Having drawn the garlands of petals and so forth on the path with various colors—with the exception of the western sector—all the doors, like the central lotus, are white; the four full ornaments (*pūrṇaśobhā*) are black; the eight half-ornaments (*ardhaśobhā*) are yellow like the interior of a lotus; and the corners are red like filaments.

Having filled [the space] and having drawn conch shells with white lines in the corners, one should fill the three lines with red, yellow, and white colors respectively. Such is the method for drawing the mandala. || 3-32 ||
Having thus performed this investigation, [one should realize] that [the Self] is the self of all, like the body.
Know that the elements are the dust-particles, as well as white, yellow, and so forth;
the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the ornaments, while the organs of action are the decorations.
In this way, all the corners, the gates, and the sense organs [are established];
likewise, there is the outer enclosure, which indeed consists of the triad beginning with Sattva.

The mind is the well-expansed path; pride is declared to be the seat. Intelligence is the lotus, and its presiding deity is the Person consisting of consciousness, whose nature is the seed-syllable. || 35 ||

Since this maṇḍala is the body of the Blessed One, he shows the elements and subtle elements here as well, just like a commonly known body, by means of the verses beginning with "having thus performed" (kṛtvaivaṃ). (32–35)
And here dwells the formless Lord, whose characteristic is bliss;
by the mere sight of whom one's very being becomes eternally serene. (36)
When the falling of the body occurs for those with attachments as well as for those without attachments— mostly for those destined for liberation who have only one birth remaining in this world— (37)
O King, he remains beyond the reach of those engaged in ritual action, having abandoned both external and internal knowability;
otherwise, how indeed could he bring such delight merely by being seen? (38)
Whatever specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) exists as a reality established by internal cognition, that very thing is proven everywhere. (39)
He explains the Blessed One’s presence within the maṇḍala along with its underlying cause by means of the verses beginning with "amūrta" (verse 36–39).
Having thus perceived the previously constructed mandala as a reality, by name it is the "Lotus-navelled Abode," which brings about the destruction of all suffering. (40)
Then, having meditated upon each one in that very sequence,
he should establish the form of the Supreme Lord by means of the seed-syllable previously specified.

Having thus grasped the mandala known as the world of Abjanābha, one should install the respective deities therein with their corresponding seed-syllable mantras and so forth according to the previously stated sequence; this is what he states in two verses beginning with "as the reality" (vastutvena). || 40-41 ||
Now, O Mahāmati, hear how the previously mentioned sacrificial sites (dhiṣṇyas) are to be constructed from this square field thus divided. || 42 ||

Having thus described the characteristics of the mandala, he says "Now" (atha) to indicate, "Listen to the characteristics of the sacrificial pit" (kuṇḍa). The meaning of "from the field thus divided" is: from that which has been divided eighteenfold by the casting of lines according to the method previously stated for the mandala. "Previously specified" means those mentioned earlier in the section on propitiation (ārādhana) and so forth. "Dhiṣṇyas" refers to the fire-houses, that is to say, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). || 42 ||
The fifth [point], beginning with the Brahma-line, is situated in the eastern direction;
one should make a mark there with a long thread positioned at that [spot]. (43)
Having the shape of a half-moon in the space between the two parts, it is likewise equal to those [parts] below, by means of the southern and northern portions. (44)
One should draw two marks situated in a horizontal alignment,
so that there may be a union of twelve parts across the two rows.
The fourth vital point (marman) is that of Brahmā; its measurement and number are as previously stated.
Its two flanks are vital points that are separated by a single intervening vital point.
By means of those two, this is produced by the very thread already established;
furthermore, from the middle, that which is the second vital point proceeds upwards. (47)

Therefore, one should draw a line through the point where the two sides intersect at a distance of three units from the center; using that line as a radius, one should draw a circle for the purpose of the mandala, as previously described.
Then, having drawn a thread from the Brahma-marma of the sixth [point] situated in the western direction, and having extended that thread to the other marman as well; || 49 ||
As far as the base of the wall's purpose extends, up to the vicinity of the tip of the pinnacle—
when two such lines are drawn, the sacrificial site (dhiṣṇya) shall take the form of a conch shell.

First, demonstrating the characteristics of the conch-shaped *kuṇḍa*, he describes the sequence of markings around it for the purpose of establishing the conch-like shape of the central pit (*khāta*) within that *kuṇḍa* field, beginning with the words "the fifth" and ending with "the sacrificial hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) shall have the form of a conch. The meaning of "the first *marman*" is the starting point of the center. A *marman* is the junction point of the line extending east-west and the line extending north-south. (Verses 43–50)
Its outer girdle should be made with equal divisions by means of marks, according to the previously mentioned lines passing through the vital points; understand it thus. (51)
With a cord twice as long [as the side], equal to nine moon-phases (navacandrakalā),
one should make a mark in the eastern direction between the four Īśānas.
One should then make two equal marks, measured by one-fourth of the circumference, starting from the positions of Īśa and Vahni; thereafter, [one mark] should be increased by one part.
Indeed, having marked two other lines equal to that with marks,
one should cast two threads from the wings toward the southern and northern parts.

Having established [the altar] upon the seventh vital point according to the previously described sequence, he explains the method for constructing the girdle (mekhalā) in the shape of a conch shell outside of that excavation, beginning with the words "tasya bhāgasametya" and ending with "pūrvoddiṣṭakrameṇa tu. (Verses 51–55).
It is situated on both sides at the rear part of the life-thread (jīvasūtra). || 55 ||
Having marked two parts each for the purpose of the yoni, like a half-circle,
one should place a thread at the tips of those horns and extend them evenly.
Extending as far as the edge of the excavated portion of the ground, from that point [the base] arises like the leaf of a banyan tree;
such is the auspicious yoni of all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Again, within the womb, one should draw two semicircles using a cord measuring half a part,
likewise provided with two cords.
The fourth part from the corner within the excavation should be avoided;
one should bury half of the remaining space, or as previously stated, an amount equal to that.
The *yoni* should be made one-quarter longer than [the width] and elevated at the back;
it should resemble an elephant's lip, touching the lip at its tip.

Starting from that outer row up to the edge of the pit (khāta), he describes the method for constructing the *yoni* in the east and other directions, as well as the method for constructing the pedestal (*iṣṭha*) with a fourth part of the square cell surrounding the pit, beginning with the words "of the *jīvasūtra*" and ending with "touching the lip of the teeth. The term "*jīvasūtra*" means the central line. "On both sides" means on the right and left portions of the central line. One should dig it to that same [depth].

The meaning is that one should construct a pit whose width and length are equal to the dimensions of the excavated ground area. Alternatively, it means that the width of the pit is prescribed as being one-third or one-half of the [mandala], as stated previously in the section on the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*). This very same point is also stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"For the sake of the pit, one should dig equally inward from the inner enclosure."
"Three-quarters or half a foot" means the lip, which is the covering for the teeth. (55–60)
Having projected a fourth part from the front side of the womb [yoni],
one should then apply two further lines connected to the eastern thread.

He says "in the front part" (purobhāge) [verse 61], meaning that one should lay down three cords: one for the purpose of the excavation according to the previously mentioned marks, one for the purpose of the outer lip (oṣṭha), and one for the purpose of the outer girdle (mekhalā).
One should indeed perform the contraction from the top by means of those two proportions;
likewise, the three girdles on the exterior are formed by three rows of parts.
Having fashioned a square conch upon those three [levels],
the height of the girdles should be equal to their own width.
He describes the gradual contraction of the parts beginning with the lips by means of the term *anupātena*. This has also been stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"One should close the lower parts up to the limit of the girdle.
He describes the construction of the three girdles with the verse and a half beginning with *bhāgapaṅktitrayeṇa*. (62–63)
Regarding the fourfold śrī [designs] in the middle of the conch of the girdles, one should have them marked with the discus; its characteristics are now described.
O Great-minded One, having fixed the Brahma-mark, one should first draw a circle in the center of the field for the purpose of digging, using a cord equal to one-fourth [of the circumference]. 65.
Equal to the outer portion [of the nave], the field of spokes (arākṣetra) extending outward is twice as wide;
and outside of that, it is equal to the portion of the rim (nemibhāga).
Outside of that, by means of one part, there is a square girdle;
then, having rotated from the center, one should again [draw] a circular field with a single circle.
Then, one should first lay down eight threads situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
subsequently, one should drop another set of eight within that [first group].
Therefore, O one of stainless vision, their non-existence must be established by means of the cessation of internal activity for both sides of every proposition. (69)
One should mark with a thread from the navel to the edge of the rim;
and within the circumference of the rim, there should be a measurement of half a part.
One should construct a rim (pradhi) between each pair of spokes;
the hub (nābhi) should be equal in width and height to the spokes, and the rim should resemble the back of a tortoise.
One should fashion the rim like a mirror, with its edge slightly depressed.

Now, regarding the characteristics of the wheel-pit (*cakrakuṇḍa*), it is stated [in the text] beginning from "of the girdles and of the conch" and ending with "the rest is all as previously described. Here, the characteristic of the spokes is stated: one should make a mark with a thread according to the two alternatives for each thread. It should be understood that this is clearly stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "One should make a mark like a fish. (64–72)
All that remains has been previously described; now hear concerning the lotus-shaped [mandala]. || 72 ||
One should rotate half a portion outside the navel for the sake of accomplishing the filaments;
one should rotate the other half portion situated outside the field of the petals.
Having reduced the circumference of the rim by this very same method, one should fashion it so that it rests upon the radius-lines; thereafter, one should create the eight petals of the lotus.
The mark of the half-moon is formed by a thread held by bees at the filaments;
it is positioned at the tips of its horns by means of an outer circumference.

O Great-minded One, one should fashion the tip of the petal with two threads for the whorl of Brahmā and the earth; likewise, the filaments, which are continuous from the base to the top, should be made with two threads each.
One should clearly effect a division equal to the height of the pericarp;
as for the four corners of the conch, one should perform the remaining procedure as previously described. (77)

He describes the characteristics of the lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) with the passage beginning "Now, listen to [the description of] the lotus-shaped [pit]" and ending with "one should perform the remainder as previously prescribed" (verses 72–77).

One part is for the womb (yoni), and four parts are for the series of girdles (mekhalā); the excavation is equal to the preceding [dimensions], but in a circular [plan], the girdles are likewise circular.
"In a square [altar], they have that same shape"; thus is the fivefold set of fire-pits described.
He states the characteristics of the circular and square sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) with the verse beginning "the womb" (yoni), consisting of one and a half verses. || 78 ||
Having understood the time, the number of oblations, and the abundance of the sacrificial materials,
one should perform [the rite] starting from one handful up to eight handfuls.

Regarding the increase in the width of the *kuṇḍa* according to the increase in the number of oblations (*homa*), he says "time" (*kālam*). Here, starting from one cubit (*hasta*) up to eight cubits, with an increase of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) at each step, one hundred and sixty-nine varieties of measurement are to be understood. In the *Pārameśvara*, however, starting from twelve finger-breadths up to eight cubits, one hundred and eighty-one varieties of measurement are stated: "From a measurement of twelve finger-breadths, by increasing it by one finger-breadth at a time, there are one hundred and eighty-one [varieties] up to two and four cubits."
One among these has been described; it is exactly the same for the others as well.
Thus [it is said].
The increase in the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) must necessarily begin from twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula), because in this section on consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
there is a reduction of two finger-breadths down to sixteen finger-breadths;
or, in a six-cubit house, the pit should be made, or the rule regarding the girdles (mekhalā) may apply.

Thus, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) has also been described. In this way, it is clearly stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* that for a fire-offering (homa) of such a number, the pit should be of such a measurement: "And for a fire-offering of fifty [oblations], the pit should be twelve finger-breadths."
In a fire-oblation of one hundred and eight [offerings], the handful should be equal to a cubit;
in a fire-oblation of fifty, it should be a cubit together with the little finger.
"In a *sahasra-homa*, [the pit] is one cubit; in that called *ayuta* (ten thousand), two cubits;
in a *lakṣa-homa*, four cubits; and in a *koṭi-homa*, eight cubits. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the measurement of the girdles (*mekhalā*) for pits starting from twelve finger-breadths is clearly stated in that very same place:
And the measurement of the girdles is twelve barley-corns.
O Great-minded One, for a sacrificial pit measuring twelve finger-breadths, the height of the girdles is proclaimed to be equal to its width.
By thus combining the three girdles together,
their width and height become four and a half finger-breadths.
For a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (ratni), the girdles (mekhalā) are prescribed to be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) [in height];
for a pit measuring one cubit plus a thumb’s breadth, they are two finger-breadths plus half [an aṅgula].
For a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit, the level [of the altar] is traditionally held to be three finger-breadths;
for a pit of two cubits, O best of the twice-born, the girdles are four finger-breadths [in height].
For a fire-pit of four cubits, all [the measurements] should be six finger-breadths;
for one of eight cubits, they are proclaimed to be eight finger-breadths.
Thus [ends the verse]. 79.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sacrificial Pit," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

And thus, the method for constructing the *kuṇḍa* is as follows: first, the site of the *kuṇḍa* is divided eighteen times by means of cord-lines according to the method described for the *maṇḍala*. Then, from the central vital point (*marmasthāna*), one touches the fifth vital point situated in the eastern direction; using a cord as long as two squares with that [point] as a contact-point, one makes a crescent-shaped mark in two squares. Below that, in the two rows, for the purpose of unifying the twelve squares, [one marks] outside those ten [squares] in the two southern squares.

Then, having drawn two crescent-shaped marks horizontally in the two squares following that as before, one should unify the three previously drawn crescent-shaped marks with the thread situated on the pair of *marman* points in the right portion and the thread situated on the pair of *marman* points in the left portion from the center; furthermore, from the second *marman* point situated above the center, one should proceed to the third interval to reach the fourth [point] in the south.

Furthermore, with a thread placed at the vital point (*marman*) situated on the side—that is, on the left side—one should draw two crescent-shaped marks (*lāñchana*) horizontally in the two right compartments and the two left compartments, as before. When this is done, there arises a unification of the twelve parts within both rows below the previously mentioned twelve.

Then, from the center of the western direction, one should extend two threads from the sixth vital point (*marman*) and join them with the tips of the two horns at the previously mentioned half-moon-shaped marks located in the southern and northern portions; when this is done, the form of a conch shell is accomplished.

Having thus marked the perimeter for the sake of the excavation, one should likewise mark a single conch-shaped section outside of that. For the purpose of establishing the *mekhalā* (encircling rim), one should draw a semicircular mark across four squares using a cord as long as two squares in the eastern direction. Likewise, having made two marks across five squares in both the northeast and southeast corners, and having inscribed two marks as before across the four squares on both sides below those, according to the previously mentioned method—

Having extended two threads from the seventh vital point (marman) located on the western side, one should join them with the two tips of the horns at the two previously mentioned marks. When this is done, the form of the girdle (mekhalā) is accomplished.

Then, in the western part, for the sake of forming the *yoni*, one should draw two crescent-shaped marks—one in the pair of squares on the southern side of the central line and one in the pair of squares on the northern side. Having joined one thread from the tip of the southern horn of the southern mark to the tip of the northern horn of the northern mark, one should extend both of them like a banyan leaf as far as the excavated portion. When this is done, the *yoni* is accomplished.
This *yoni* is common to all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) that will be described hereafter.

Again, within that same source, in the southern square from the central line, one should draw two marks in the shape of half-moons using a thread measuring half a square as before; then, as before, one should extend two threads from the tips of their horns.

Then, for the sake of forming the rim (oṣṭha) all around the excavation, one should divide a single cell within the interior of the excavation into four parts; having set aside one part, one should bury the remainder—equal in width to the extent of the excavated portion—either to a depth of one-third or one-half of that. From the previously mentioned length of the yoni, a portion measuring two and a quarter cells should be made at the back, resembling an elephant's trunk, touching the aforementioned rim.

And thus, having left out one-fourth of a square cell from the front of the *yoni* all around the excavated area according to the previously mentioned method, one should first lay a conch-shaped thread for the purpose of the excavation as before; immediately thereafter, one should lay one thread for the lip (*oṣṭha*) and one thread for the girdle (*mekhalā*). One should adjust the placement of those two threads so that the lip is above and the girdle is below, making their intersection contracted. Outside of that, one should construct three square girdles by means of three rows all around.
The height of the girdles ending in conch-shapes should be made equal to the width of the pit;
thus ends the description of the conch-shaped pit (*śaṅkhakuṇḍa*).

Now, the characteristics of the wheel and the pit are described: having divided the square field into eighteen parts according to the previously mentioned method, one should place a thread at the central vital point (marma). Then, drawing a circle with a thread touching the fifth line from the center, one should again produce a circle with a thread touching the sixth line, and then make another circle with a thread touching the ninth line.

Among these, it should be understood that the first circle is for the purpose of the excavation, the second is the location of the nave, the third is the location of the spokes, and the fourth is the location of the rim. Outside of that, in the row [of the outermost circle], only one square-shaped girdle (mekhalā) should be constructed.

Having again rotated the previously mentioned inner circle by one [unit] from the center, one should lay down eight lines there in the cardinal directions such as east and so forth, and in the intermediate directions such as southeast and so forth. For the sake of establishing the spokes (*ara*), one should mark the two sides of each line—extending from the inner circle to the hub-circle and from the inner circle to the rim-circle—with the help of a thread confined within the inner circle, making marks like fish-tails (*matsya*). Then, between each pair of spokes within the rim-circle, one should fashion a single felly (*pradhi*).

In this case, the navel should be made with a height equal to the width of the pit (kuṇḍa) and resembling the back of a tortoise; the rim (nemi) should be made like a mirror, slightly depressed at its edge. One should perform everything else as previously described.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the wheel-pit (cakrakuṇḍa).

Now, the characteristics of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) are described. Therein, as with the wheel-shaped pit (*cakrakuṇḍa*), one should first prepare a mandala for the purpose of the excavation. In the second, the central mandala (*nābhimaṇḍala*), one should divide it into two parts: half a part for the accomplishment of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the other half for the accomplishment of the filaments (*keśara*). Having thus divided the mandala into two, one should likewise divide the rim mandala (*nemimaṇḍala*) outside the field of the spokes (*arākṣetra*) into two parts; the first part should be unified with the field of the spokes. One should set aside the upper part for the accomplishment of the tips of the petals.

In the outer field (*arakṣetra*), for the sake of accomplishing the eight-petaled [lotus], one should form two crescent-shaped marks facing each other in the eight directions starting from the east, using a thread obstructed by the circle of filaments (*kesaramaṇḍala*). Then, using two threads positioned at the tips of those horns and extending outside the circle of petals, one should form the tips of the petals. One should clearly effect the division of the filaments, which extend continuously from the base and are equal in height to the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Outside the circle of petal-tips, one should draw four conch-shells in the four corners. The remainder is as before.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit.

Now, the characteristics of the circular (*vṛtta*) and square (*caturaśra*) [fire-pits] are stated: In a field divided into eighteen parts according to the previously mentioned method, one should leave sixty-four squares in the center for the purpose of the excavation (*khāta*) as before; outside of that, one should arrange the *yoni* with one row and arrange the four girdles (*mekhalā*) with four rows. However, it should be understood that in a circular pit, the excavation and the girdles are circular in shape, while in a square pit, they take that same (square) shape.
One should fashion the rim (*oṣṭha*) and the *yoni* for these two types of pits exactly as before.
Thus end the characteristics of the five types of fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*).

Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Sātvata-tantra-bhāṣya composed by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrī Mauñjyāyana family and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O leaders of sages, having heard this, that wielder of the club (Balarāma) spoke thus.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he questioned the Lord of the worlds.

Now the twelfth [chapter] will be explained. Here, it is said that Saṃkarṣaṇa asked Vāsudeva about the meditation on the Lord as the Manifested Power (*vibhava-deva*), beginning with the word "Thus" (*evam*). || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O delighter of Lakṣmī, I wish to hear from you the characteristics of the meditations for all the mantras arranged in their proper sequence.

He states the manner of the question with the words "of those situated in their respective order. "O Lakṣmīnandana" is an address to Vāsudeva, meaning "O you who gladden—that is, delight—Lakṣmī. || 2 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
You have already heard what was previously declared regarding the three principal ones beginning with Mukhya and ending with Dhruva;
now, attend to the account of the remaining ones, beginning with Śeṣa.
"Meditation on those whose abode is the netherworld (Pātāla) is as it has been established.

Thus questioned, the Blessed One replied with the half-verse beginning with "of the three. This means [meditation] on the primary ones, such as Viśākha, Yūpa, and so forth. It means [meditation] on the three: Viśākha, Yūpa, Padmanābha, and Dhruva. Previously, in the ninth chapter, meditation on Viśākha-Yūpa was set forth in passages such as "the blessed Viśākha-Yūpa himself, out of a desire to create the universe," and meditation on Padmanābha and Dhruva was set forth in passages such as "thus for all of them," and so forth.

"Of the remaining" means of those left over. This refers to the thirty-six *vibhava* deities, beginning with Śeṣa and Ananta and ending with those whose abode is Pātāla—that is, those who recline in Pātāla. || 3-4 ||
