The Lord of the World is indeed one alone, [yet He appears manifold] through His powers such as His essential nature (svarūpa) and others.
Listen now to the conceited form of that Lord of All, who, though infinite even in his manifold manifestations, acts out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
Regarding that, he says "He is one," etc., in one and a half verses, instructing [the listener] to hear first the form of Ananta.
Resembling the snowy mountain (Himalaya), with a face like the full moon,
he was indeed endowed with a multitude of hoods made manifest by his own jewels.
He carries the plow and the discus with his two right hands,
while with his two left hands he holds the conch and the mace.
That which possesses all powers eternally present, which is omniscient and infallible—
may that fulfill the desires of those performers of action whose minds are turned inward.

He describes the manner of his meditation with three verses beginning with "tuhinena. The meaning is that his remaining duty consists of being foremost in service to the Blessed Lord. If it is objected: "By this, one only understands that Ananta is possessed by the Blessed Lord, but not that he is a direct incarnation; how then can he be included among the primary manifestations (mukhya-prādurbhāvas)?"—the answer is no, because only those bound souls who are presided over by the Blessed Lord are excluded from the primary manifestations. The meaning is that he shall fulfill—that is, bestow—whatever is desired in the minds of his own inward-looking devotees. As for the location of Ananta, it is described in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Śeṣa, worshipped by all the gods, remains stationed at the base of Pātāla.
Neither his valor, nor his nature, nor his essential character,
nor even his form can be described or known, even by the gods of the three realms.
Who will describe the prowess of him upon whose hood the entire earth rests, reddened by the tips of the jewels of his hoods like a garland of flowers?
Thus [ends the section] 6–8.
Then Śaktīśa should also be meditated upon, with eyes resembling lotuses, assuming a form at will, gentle, and with a smiling countenance. || 9 ||
Out of compassion for his devotees so that they might perceive the fruits and other signs,
he pressed the earth with his two feet and his two hands.
He possesses a splendor that conforms to the age (yuga), has four faces and four arms;
his embodied form holds the discus and mace in his hands, while his unembodied form is marked by the lotus and the water-lily.
It brings relief from distress like the moonlight through a lotus,
and it reveals the knowledge consisting of various mantras to those of pure soul.
And likewise by Samyag-vākpati, by Kambu who is the embodiment of sound,
by Ājñāpratīkṣaka, and by the pair of mace and discus.
Impelled by him, the one who destroys the fear of worldly existence swiftly slays those who cause distress to the virtuous with his lion-like mouth. 14.
In the form of the Boar, whose nature is nectar, he nourishes all beings;
and by means of the Kāpila form situated in the west, he effects the withdrawal [of the world].
Indeed, for those devoted to and full of faith, he is always remembered within the heart, in the midst of space, upon the earth, in the midst of fire, and within water. || 16 ||
Out of compassion for the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
he himself manifests in a fourfold way through his fourfold nature.
With a body equal to his own self, marked with the conch and lotus,
and joined by the plow and other implements in embodied form, yet devoid of faces.
It should be by means of a color that corresponds to the [subject's] own color, whether it be similar or dissimilar,
which follows one another exactly as previously specified, and not otherwise.

Now, he describes the meditation on Śaktyātmā with eleven verses, beginning with "Śaktīśa. The meaning is that he assumes the form of Will (icchā) and possesses various forms through the distinctions of the vehicles, goddesses, arms, and weapons to be described hereafter. He is "marked by the formless, the lotus, and the water-born," where "formless" means having the nature of a mere line, "lotus" refers to the conch (śaṅkha), and "water-born" refers to the lotus (kamala); he is marked by these two. Thus, it should be understood that the descent of Śaktīśa arises either from the Vyūha or the Vibhava [forms]. For, in this very chapter, he will state: "But the collection of the fourfold selfhood which is situated upon the ground of the lotus petals..."
Likewise, O lotus-eyed one, from among the gods of the realm of form (vibhava-devas), [he emerged].
But the one, whose essence is power, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those of purified souls,
assumes a form arising from many divisions while stationed upon his excellent vehicle.

Thus, his status as an *aṃśāvatāra* (partial incarnation) has been stated in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "Now, the partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatārāḥ*) are those whose splendor conforms to the [specific] *yuga*s. Likewise, he is Viṣṇu because of his pervasion of the universe through powers such as pervasion and control, according to the mantra: "To the one whose self is all powers" (*sarvaśaktyātmane*). And it should be understood that he is one among the three forms (*trimūrti*), as stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "He who is the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa is known by the name Śaktīśa. (9–19)
Madhusūdana, who possesses the luster of the sun at the time of universal dissolution, should be meditated upon;
he has eight arms, broad shoulders, and is marked by the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice on his hand.
Likewise, he holds the conch and the discus, as well as the arrow and the bow,
for the sake of worldly engagement and withdrawal through the two personified qualities of rajas and tamas.
And the pair of hands of the Lord, resting upon his ear-ornaments, is to be meditated upon.

Now, with two and a half verses beginning with "pralayānala," he describes the meditation on Madhusūdana. It is stated in the Pauṣkara that this incarnation belongs to a specific manifestation of the Lord:
"The slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is indeed a manifestation of the Supreme Lord."
"Know this to be another manifestation of the all-pervading Lord Padmanābha.
Thus it is said; and his location is also described in that very same place:
"And he, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, is stationed upon the surface of the earth."
"In the field of earth consisting of milk and water, frequented by gods and demons. (20–22)
The Lord of Knowledge, the Blessed One with four faces and four arms.
He has a long beard and matted locks, and carries a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary;
he possesses the luster of a full-blown red lotus and is marked by white lotuses held in his hands.

Now, he describes the meditation on the presiding deity of knowledge (*vidyādhideva*) with one and a half verses, beginning with "the presiding deity of knowledge. Although it might seem that the phrase "four-faced" and the phrase "emitting the Vedas from his mouths" have the same meaning—since the former is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra-text of the presiding deity of knowledge, namely "to the knower of the Vedas" (*vedavit*), and since there would otherwise be the contingency of redundancy in the subsequent statement "one should remember [him]" or "one should meditate"—and thus the natural interpretation of the sentence "therefore, one should remember him emitting the Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda, from his mouths" is that it connects with what precedes it; nevertheless, [this is not so] according to the omniscient ones.

Since that statement was subsequently interpreted by the venerable Śrīmat Parāśara Bhaṭṭāraka as being directed toward the meditation on Kapila in his *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*, it cannot be moved from its position by those such as ourselves.

Furthermore, although this presiding deity of knowledge (vidyādhideva) is known to be Viriñci because his characteristics—such as having four faces, matted hair, a water-pot, and a rosary—have been described, nevertheless, in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*, these [beings] beginning with Brahmā are not invariably included among the enumerations of the Lord’s incarnations (*avatāra*). Moreover, they are enumerated as objects of creation in the sections on cosmogony, just like gods and humans; on the contrary, they are designated as distinct from His manifestations (*prādurbhāva*), being characterized by features different from those manifestations.

Because of the designation by the term "another manifestation" (*prādurbhāvāntara*), and because of the conventional usage [of terms] such as "arising from a mere fragment of the Lord’s glory" (*bhagavad-vibhūtileśodbhavatva*) and "functioning dependent upon that particular manifestation" (*tat-prādurbhāva-viśeṣādhīna-pravṛttitva*), the nature of Brahman as a manifestation is denied. Furthermore:
Time, the sky, the Controller, the scripture characterized by various limbs, the lords of knowledge, and Śiva together with Rudra and his attendants.
The "assemblage of Prajāpatis" refers to Indra along with his retinue;

thus, it has been stated that the aforementioned class of deities who serve as the instruments of worldly existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*) constitutes the "assemblage of Prajāpatis," and within this, even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is included. Therefore, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "to the Supreme Self" (*paramātmane*), it should be understood that this is not Viriñci as the presiding deity of knowledge (*vidyādhideva*), but rather a direct manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
Now, in the Śrī Pauṣkara...
Know that the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha was the manifestation of the Lord, and that it was followed by another manifestation of that all-pervading Padmanābha.

By such statements, it has been repeatedly declared in so many words that even Madhusūdana and others are distinct manifestations (*prādurbhāva*). If it is asked whether this contradicts their status as manifestations, the answer is no; for while the aforementioned reasons taken together contradict the status of Caturmukha and others as manifestations, there is no room for such a collection of reasons in the case of Madhusūdana and the rest. (22–23)
One should then meditate upon Him as emitting from His mouths the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda;
He has the luster of smokeless embers and holds a conch, a lotus, and a rosary.

One should meditate upon that Kapila, the storehouse of splendors, who possesses the majesty of a full-blown red lotus, whose essential thread is composed of the deities and other [principles], and whose hand is in the gesture of granting fearlessness. 25.

Now, he describes the meditation on Kapila with two verses beginning with *śrutīriti*. It should be understood that the plural number in *vaktrebhyaḥ* is used for honorific purposes; alternatively, one may state that he possesses four faces at his own will. His role as the promulgator of the Vedas (*śrutipravartakatva*) has been established in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya* itself, in the passage: "Satyavṛtti, Trivikrama, Maharṣi, Kapilācārya," where it says: "By such a denotable being of great majesty, who has stepped across the three Vedas, he is called Trivikrama.
The word *tri-* refers to the three Vedas as proclaimed by the best of sages.

"He traversed all of them in succession in that manner, and is thus remembered as Trivikrama," and also, "The great sage [is so called] because of his vision of the Vedas as they were spoken. His residence at the bottom of the netherworld (Pātāla) is well known. However, regarding the location of his form as an image (arcārūpa), it is stated in the Śrī-Pauṣkara: "But on the shore of the eastern ocean, on ground possessing auspicious characteristics..."
"Having assumed the form of Kapila, the Lord Vāsudeva remains [there]";
thus it has been established. (24–25)
The Lord who is the Sovereign of all, abiding within as the witness,
sustains all entities arising from his own power, like a crystal stone.
But for those devotees manifested through ignorance who possess grosser forms, [He reveals] that beginningless Lord of the World externally, so that they may attain the state of existence.
One should meditate upon the one who dwells between heaven and earth, possessing all forms, with many faces, feet, and hands, and marked by many makaras. 28.
Although he possesses many faces and is adorned with many arms,
he is indeed endowed with thirty-three various faces.
With forty great divine arms, four more than the usual number,
he holds Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Dakṣa, the Sun, the Moon, the Siddhas, as well as the Śruti.
But these [faces] situated above the face of Puruṣa consist of Piśāca, Agni, Marut, Śaila, Dvīpa, Gandharva, and Vāri. (31)
One should meditate upon the southern face of the All-pervading Lord with mouths situated above,
emerging from the great clouds of the netherworld, the quarters, and the world of the stars and planets.
One should meditate upon the western face, accompanied by Tārās, along with Yakṣas,
Antakas, Ambu, Nāgas, and others, as well as the Vasus, Nakṣatras, and the hosts of cows.
One should meditate upon the southern [face], with the faces of the Boar situated above,
as well as the great tenfold set of weapons beginning with the lotus, which constitute his fourfold nature.
For that [image] is elevated with the four auspicious marks beginning with gold, as well as the eight weapons of the World-Lords, a book, and a rosary. (35)
A golden ladle and water-pot, along with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, as well as darbha grass, an antelope skin, an umbrella, and a beautiful white chowrie. (36)
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the two jars, and the altar accompanied by the fire;
the full orbs of the moon and sun, and the jeweled mirror of the lord of serpents. (37)
A divine garland of flowers, a fan, and likewise a creeper with universal leaves should be remembered upon the arms of this Lord, arranged in symmetrical positions.
Just as it has been described in sequence, so that no reversal occurs, this world [is filled] with various kinds of rays arising from the body. (39)
One should remember the Lord of the World illuminating the heart-lotus and other centers;
then one should remember oneself in the form of a swan, the enjoyer of the sacrifice of knowledge.

Now, he describes the meditation on the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*), beginning with "The God who is the Lord of all within" and ending with "one should meditate upon [the faces] in the heart-lotus and so forth. Above the eastern human face, there are eight faces beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śruti; above the southern Narasiṃha face, seven faces beginning with Piśāca and ending with Vāri; above the western Kapila face, seven faces beginning with Pātāla and ending with Tārā; and above the northern Vārāha face...

The seven faces beginning with Yakṣa and ending with Gogaṇa should be understood as making thirty-three faces in total. Regarding the phrase "together with the Tārās," here the word *tārā* refers to the principal lunar mansions (nakṣatras) starting with Aśvinī, while the word *nakṣatra* refers to the other lunar mansions; otherwise, there would be redundancy. Similarly, in the phrase "with the waters" (*vāribhiḥ*), the term *vāridhi* (ocean) is intended; by the word *ambu*, only water is intended. Regarding the phrase "by the Nāgas and others," the meaning is that the first among the Nāgas is Ananta.

The term *cāturātmīya* means belonging to the manifestation (*vyūha*) consisting of Vāsudeva and the others. The "tenfold group of weapons beginning with the lotus" refers to the ten weapons known as the lotus, conch, discus, mace, sword, ploughshare, pestle, arrow, bow, and shield; since these weapons were previously described as the emblems of the four forms of Vāsudeva in the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*), their status as *cāturātmīya* is very clear. The "eight weapons of the world-protectors," such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and the spear (*śakti*), are well-known and are established as belonging to Īśvara and the other [world-protectors]. As for the station of the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*), it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"O Lotus-born one, [it is found] in Śvetadvīpa, Kurukṣetra, and on the Himavat mountain."
The Lord Viśvarūpa is also stationed on the edge of the altar.
Thus [ends the section] 26–40.
He who possesses a luster as smooth as jasmine and the moon, with a golden beak and a massive body;
whose feet are rajas and tamas, and whose form is pure sattva—the Supreme Lord.
One should meditate upon the vision of Dharma and Adharma as consisting of Agni and Soma,
adorned by a pair of wings situated to the south and north.
But outside, he saw that very same person standing in the water, resembling the snowy mountain.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Acyuta in the form of the Haṃsa according to the prescribed rule.

Now, he describes the meditation on the Haṃsa with three and a half verses beginning with "Haṃsa. Its location is stated in the Śrī-Pauṣkara: "Know that the King of Haṃsas is worshipped by the Siddhas and immortals in Śvetadvīpa. (40-43)
But one [stūpa] made of external materials, which generally possesses a single characteristic and is properly constructed, first attains heaven for those who desire it. (44)
Within the sacrificial altar, that which is indeed one great sacrifice alone is eternally of the nature of austerity, sacrifice, recitation, and meditation. 45.
But it is through the completion [of the rite] that He ordains the final liberation for those who sacrifice;
He is the Sacrifice-Person, Brahman, Vāsudeva, the unborn Hari. (46)
One should indeed meditate upon the Self in the form of Sūka, possessing a luster like the mountain of collyrium,
with feet marked by the limbs of sacrifice and having the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) as his fangs.
"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ," [he is] the body whose mind is solely fixed on the Śabdabrahman, swiftly washing away the mire of ignorance for those who have sought refuge. 48.
By the physician, with a vessel that is imperishable and stainless, for the sake of pacifying the existence of living beings who are perfumed by latent impressions. (49)

Now, he describes the meditation on the Boar with the verses beginning "consisting of external substances" and so forth. "By the physician" means by the one consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*). "With the tip of the snout" means with the front of the boar’s face. Thus, the state of having the limbs of a sacrifice as his body is also clearly stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The Vedas are in your feet, O you whose tusk is the sacrificial post; the sacrifices are in your teeth and the sacrificial altars in your mouth.
You have fire as your tongue, the *darbha* grasses are your body hairs; O Lord, you alone are the Person of Sacrifice (*yajñapumān*)."
O Great-Souled One, night and day are Your two eyes; the state of Brahman, the giver of all selves, is Your head;
all the hymns are the mass of Your mane; and all the sacrificial oblations, O God, are Your sense of smell.
"O Lord, whose mouth is the *sruk* ladle, whose deep resonance is the sound of the *Sāman*, whose body is the *Prāgvaṃśa* hall, and who is the joint of all sacrificial sessions;
O God, eternal Self, you are the hearing of the merit of public works and sacrifices—be gracious, O Blessed One!
Thus [it is said]. Its location, however, is in the venerable *Pauṣkara*.
"In the form of a sow, indeed in that very field," thus [it is said].
The Blessed One, possessed of great majesty and embodying the six perfections in their fullness,
took his joined palms from his own most tranquil Brahman-reality.
And by means of his own splendor, he performs a sprinkling for those consumed by defects;
in his gross form, that unborn one [acts] in the ritual of external worship. (51)
One should meditate upon that [face] as being inflated by wind like a mountain of smokeless embers, greatly blazing, and marked with the face of a horse. 52.
With his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, his eyes like molten gold,
he was drawing up with the tip of his trunk the water-fuel produced from the three worlds.

Having completely reduced that [obstacle] to ashes while emitting a hissing sound from the mouth, he describes the meditation on the *vaḍavānala* (submarine fire) with the words beginning "Mahāvibhūti," and so forth. Its location, however, is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "The horse-natured one is at the mouth of the mare (*vaḍavāmukha*). (50–54)
The pure generality of phenomena (dharmasāmānya), which is without beginning or end and all-pervading.
That which is difficult for the awakened to obtain without a mind of grace toward him—listen now to its most sublime form for the sake of attaining that supreme state. (55)
Resembling the snowy mountain, with a gentle countenance and four arms,
he bore both desire and wealth under the guise of a conch shell and a lotus.

One should then remember Dharma, who stands upon the path of the virtuous, restraining both [mind and speech] with his intellect, holding a white rosary in his hand, and possessing excellent hands. (57)

Now he speaks of the Dharma-incarnation with three and a half verses beginning with "Dharma. The phrase "those two, desire and wealth" means that He carries both desire and wealth, as stated previously. By this, one should not be deluded into thinking that the well-known Dharma itself is an incarnation of the Lord; for it is merely an instrument (*upakaraṇa*) for Him. Thus, in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "Because the well-known Dharma is an instrument for the Lord who possesses that character (dharma), it bears His name; even though the Dharma is well-known, He is the 'possessor of dharma' (*dharmī*) because He is the common instrument for all. Furthermore,
The Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is dharma, is eternal manifestation;
for it is from him that the first among men appeared, ending with Kṛṣṇa.
He who always protects [this] in such a manner, endowed with the five times, the six duties, sacrifices, and religious observances, and accompanied by recitation and meditation;

"The Brahmin Nara, who consists of four forms, is Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and the Lord known as Kṛṣṇa; he is a manifestation of the All-pervading One. Indeed, the high-souled one, whose form is Dharma, [resides] in Dharmāraṇya, which is honored by the gods."
But he, who is worshipped by the worlds, remains intent on bestowing grace upon the worlds.
And thus it has been very clearly established in the venerable Pauṣkara. (54–57)
The entire collection of speech, as well as all imperishable objects,
exists within the nature of that one whose form is consciousness and whose luster is stainless, as its inherent power (śakti).
Or else, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Vāgīśvara, whose face is like that of a noble horse, who resembles the fire from a sun-crystal, and who is adorned with many arms. (59)
A lotus, a rosary, an altar adorned with the three sacred fires,
the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles filled with clarified butter, and a seat accompanied by the *soma* plant.
One should also remember the darbha grass, the deerskin, and the girdle in his six left hands;
and in his left hands, one should likewise remember the book and the conch shell.
In one hand he holds a staff, a water-pot, and a ladle—this triad;
and in the fifth [hand], a vessel filled with sacrificial offerings consisting of both cultivated and wild grains.
With sacrificial materials consisting of *sruva*-ladles, roots, fruits, and leaves, along with ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
it was equipped with all the utensils required for the stages of life (*āśrama*) and the *camasa* vessels.
In his sixth arm, there is the object of meditation, consisting of the Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda,
which have become circular, along with the Vedāṅgas, the Upavedas, and the Saṃskāras, all equal in measure.

Now, he describes the meditation on Hayagrīva with the verses beginning with "consisting of speech" (*vāṅmaya*). "Joined with Soma" means accompanied by the Soma creeper. The various types of seeds from cultivated and wild lands should be understood as they are explained in the section on the cooking of sacrificial offerings (*haviḥ-pāka*) in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]. And in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and seventhly *priyaṅgu*; these are the seven, while lentils (*kulutthaka*) are the eighth."
Furthermore, O Sage, śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka,
as well as veṇuyava and likewise markaṭaka are prescribed.
"These fourteen medicinal herbs are indeed known as belonging to both the village and the forest.
Thus it is said.

One should meditate upon a vessel full of these seeds in the fourth hand, a vessel full of sacrificial materials in the fifth, and a *camasa* cup equipped with the requisites for the stages of life (*āśrama*) in the sixth hand. Its location is described in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "In the worship of me, O Goddess, [it is] on the black horse and at the Aśvoda in the field of the earth. (58–64)
Indeed, when the flow of the earth of transformations has ceased and one is in the state of the ocean of qualities, having first made the fourfold [mental states] permeated by one's own power; 65.
One should meditate upon the Omniscient One, who, possessing the nature of the Puruṣa, remains seated up to the limit of Prakṛti,
reclining upon the couch of the serpent-king and possessing the luster of refined gold.
He is known as Devamarṇavaśāyin (the one reclining on the ocean of gods), surrounded by his embodied forms such as the Discus and others,
being massaged by Lakṣmī, and overcome by sleep.
Indeed, being fanned with affection and praised with sacred knowledge,
he whose self is the tortoise should then be meditated upon as a tortoise by the intellect, O wielder of the plow.

The meditation on Him reclining upon the single ocean is described in three and a half verses beginning with *vikāra*. "The fourfold [group] preceded by the mind" means the quartet consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). That He is accompanied by the fourfold group of powers (*śakti*) such as Lakṣmī is also established in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "Indeed, that incarnation of Viṣṇu known as 'Reclining on the Ocean'—I abide all around him, having assumed a fourfold form."

"Lakṣmī, Nidrā, Prīti, and Vidyā—thus [the powers] are divided. Now, one might ask: is this an incarnation of the Blessed One in the form of the Four-faced One (Brahmā)? For it is said in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "When the three worlds were a single ocean, Brahmā was of the nature of Nārāyaṇa..."
Reclining upon the serpent-bed, he lies there, nourished by the devouring of the three worlds.

If it is argued that this establishes that Brahman alone lies upon the single ocean, we say no; for this incarnation who lies upon the ocean is the very support even of Brahman. At that time, Brahman’s state is one of reclining upon the lotus from his navel. As for the statement regarding [Viṣṇu] having resorted to a bed of serpents, it is explained in the *Viṣṇucittīya* as being "enduring the intervention of the lotus from the Lord's navel. (Verses 65–68)
Then, O wielder of the plow, one should meditate with the intellect upon the Self in the form of a tortoise, like a tortoise.
The eternal one, possessing the luster of molten gold, who by his own power resides in the waters, has two feet consisting of the pair of kalās beginning with Śakti.
And [the Lord], enriched with the digits (kalās) beginning with Śakti, while emitting [the sound] and taking refuge in the triad [of powers].

Now, he describes the meditation on Kūrma with two verses beginning with "kūrmātma. His location is shown in the *Pauṣkara*: "In Rasātala, however, is the one whose self is Kūrma. This, moreover, is the incarnation of Kūrma who serves as the support for the entire universe, based on the wording of the mantra "for the support of the worlds" and from the visualization "having feet marked by the pair of pairs. There also exists the incarnation of the face of Kūrma alone; and thus it is said in the *Pauṣkara*:
"On the region of the earth bounded by the salt ocean, frequented by the Siddhas..."
And the Blessed One, bearing the conch and the discus, remained there with the face of a tortoise.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 68–70.
Resembling the flax flower, he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
He is the constituent limb of the sacrificial implements, capable of lifting those who have sunk [in the ocean of existence];
he is the support for the manifestation of his own power, possessing the rays of will, knowledge, and action.
Constantly arising with waves of sparks of various specific cognitions,
it stands tearing asunder the intense and undiminished delusion within the heart.

He describes the meditation on that unborn Supreme Lord—who bestows food, who is beyond description, and who is without birth—in three verses beginning with "resembling the flax flower. One should understand that while the previously mentioned Varāha was the actual (sākṣāt) Varāha, this one is the "Man-Varāha" (nṛvarāha); this is known from the meditation [verse] stating "bearing the conch, discus, and mace," and also because the *Pauṣkara* Purāṇa again indicates the location of Varāha by saying, "The Varāha at Kokāmukha, and at Vārāha, the best of mountains. (Verses 70–73)
And one should meditate upon the Lord, the Man-Lion, who has the luster of refined gold.
He was surrounded by blazing sparks of fire arising from his own body;
he was the creator of the discus and the conch, possessed of a massive form and most terrifying.
With both hands illuminated by rows of rays from the jewels on his six beings,
he perfectly bestows with his intellect the boon of fearlessness upon all living beings.

Now, he describes the meditation on Śrī Nṛsiṃha with two and a half verses beginning with *niṣṭapta*. "Embodied Brahman" means the Supreme Brahman with form. In the reading *brahmamūrtim*, it means one whose body is vast. With both hands illuminated by the rays of the qualities of goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*), he bestows both fearlessness and boons; that is to say, his two hands, adorned with rows of nails consisting of pure *sattva*, are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons. As for his location, it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "O twice-born, Nṛhari is at Kṛtaśauca and also in Ujjayinī."
"Thus, he is situated in three ways in the place known as Viśākhamūla.

Furthermore, the location of the exclusive incarnation as Nṛsiṃha is also established in that very same place: "In the Vindhya forest, O Pauṣkara, the Self in the form of the Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendrātmā) is to be known; he is the destroyer of the sins of all embodied beings. (Verses 73–75).
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, who resembles a cloud filled with nectar, who brings forth the nectar of immortality,
who wears yellow garments, and who has one face and four arms.
With his hand placed upon the slope of his hips, adorned with the conch and the discus, and bearing the form of a mountain, he carries [the earth] from the middle by means of his right [hand]. (77)
Pervaded by pure knowledge and dispelling the fear of the arising of karma, he who is affectionate toward his devotees perfectly instructs his devotees with his own wisdom. (78)
It is the nectar revealed by churning the ocean of milk with Mount Mandara; it is the antidote to hunger, thirst, and other ailments, and is free from all disease. (79)

One should meditate upon the pure and imperishable Self, which dwells in the midst of the ocean called Māyā, as nectar beyond comparison, by means of the practice that destroys [the need for] food. 80.

He describes the meditation on the bringing of the nectar (*amṛtāharaṇa-dhyāna*) with the verses beginning "Amṛta... and so forth. Its location is stated in the *Śrīpauṣkara*: "In the region of the Milk Ocean, a field frequented by gods and demons, there dwells the Lord who holds Mount Mandara in his hand, worshipped by the gods."
Right there resides the god Amṛtajit, served by the Siddhas;
he assumes a beautiful form and likewise holds a vessel of nectar.
And there stands Mṛtyujit, the conqueror of death, for the sake of the Siddhas, the Munis, and the gods.
Thus [ends the section] 76–80.
One should meditate upon the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī, who has the luster of the interior of a lotus,
whose two hands are adorned with the abode of Kamalā and the lord of weapons.
Bestowing the pair [of Śiva and Pārvatī] with ease during the wedding of the Goddess,
he manifested his own beginninglessness along with that of Prakṛti.
This primordial nature (prakṛti) is permeated by my hands, while I am permeated by the products of nature (prākṛta);
since I am the substratum of this form, it is essentially identical with me.
Relying upon which, those devoted to meditation clearly cross over this ocean of qualities, so difficult to traverse, with ease and in no long time. (84)

He describes the meditation on the Lord of Śrī with the verses beginning with "dhyāyet" (one should meditate). It has been explained in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya* that "Prakṛti is Lakṣmī, the mother of the world. (Verses 81–84)
With eyes unsteady from intoxication, the god, whose youth had blossomed forth, possessed the luster of a full-blown red lotus and did not abandon his own mindfulness. (85)
One should meditate upon him who causes wonder in the three worlds, who assumes a lovely form,
and whose moon-like face is filled with the nectar of bliss.
He was resplendent with a water-pot held in his hand,
and he was slaying the enemies of the gods with the arrows of his playful side-glances and words.

With three and a half verses beginning with "with eyes unsteady from intoxication," he describes his meditation on the beloved, whose hands grasp mango creepers covered by swarms of bees. Regarding this incarnation, it is said that its nature consists of both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
for that enchanting form which is heard of as the "bearer of nectar" is the very mother of the world.
At that time, existence and non-existence were perceived equally there in that form:
by the gods in the form of men, and by the non-gods (asuras) in the form of women.
"That it has been accomplished together with me—this birth of mine is a great marvel. || 85-88 ||
The one known as Rāhu, who is terrifying and whose nature consists of the ego-identification with the forms of the Kalās, [is the eighth]. || 88 ||
Indeed, with his form consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
he incessantly devours the embodiment composed of Agni and Soma, which is beneficial to those engaged in ritual action.
He who exists internally in the form of the vital breaths and externally as the moon and sun is the presiding witness over their conquest for those whose souls are devoted to true meditation.
One should clearly visualize that [deity] externally as motionless through the state of awakening, with a luster like a dark blue cloud and eyes resembling lotus petals. (91)
Having the appearance of the midday sun, with twelve spokes raised aloft,
[he holds] a lotus playfully with his left hand resting upon the slope of his hips.

Holding a heavy mace and seated upon the surface of the earth, Rāhujit describes his meditative state with the words beginning "kalāmūrti," and so forth. It should be understood that he too dwells in the region of the Milk Ocean; for it is stated in the Pauṣkara: "Mṛtyujit stands among the Siddhas, the sages, and the gods. (88–93)
And that rim of the wheel of time called ignorance is difficult to restrain. || 93 ||
Relying upon this samādhi, one shakes off the body through the power of recitation,
sacrifice, ritual acts, and so forth, by means of the quality of tamas.

One should meditate upon the Lord, who is as radiant as a royal sapphire, who obstructs the expansion of those [impurities], who blazes with rays of pure consciousness, and whose throne is the noble being Garuḍa. 95.
Adorned with the arms of true knowledge whose nature consists of various weapons, [he holds] the discus, the lotus, the mace, the arrow, the goad, and the spear. (96)
In the six right hands, he holds a spear, two nooses, and a bow;
in the left arms, a mace, a hammer, a terrifying shield, and a sword.
He describes the meditation on the slayer of Kālanemi with the verses beginning "called ignorance" (avidyākhyā), etc. (93–97).
O King, the Lord of Gods, whose deeds are effortless and whose prowess is manifold and marvelous, should be remembered as one who resembles a ripe mango and who has surpassed the Pārijāta tree. 98.
Even for embodied beings who are devotees engaged in continuous practice,
he who has taken root in the ground of awakening is indeed impermanent and yet deeply captivating.
The tree of karma is shaped like a banyan branch, characterized by the bonds of ignorance; it is extensively spread out and covered with the fruits of delusion and illusion. (100)
For the sake of accomplishing their uprooting, that Lord of the Universe always dwells within those persons worthy of grace, entering them by means of a mere portion out of compassion. (101)
Having become one whose nature is discernment, supporting the canopy of the arms of knowledge,
possessing the face of sovereignty, virtue, detachment, and tranquility, he bears the power of consciousness.

Having taken up the multitude of weapons that are self-restraint and likewise the collection of weapons that are the observances, and having conquered the group beginning with the senses, he is indeed the one who bestows the fruits of action upon those who perform them. (103)
One should meditate upon that form of his which is victorious over the gods, possessing twelve arms, wearing divine garlands and garments, and adorned with celestial ornaments. (104)
That face with beautiful eyes, with the beloved placed upon his left lap, [holds] a sword, a discus, a mace, an arrow, a club, and the best of trees. 105.
In the six right hands of the Lord are the conch, the goad, and the bow; and in his left arms are the parasol, the serpent, and the noose.
The Goddess was embraced by his sixth arm, which held a lotus, while she, her mind fixed on him incessantly, had her hand joined with his chest.

Being fanned with a white chowrie out of humility, the Lord spoke of his meditation on the seizer of the *pārijāta* tree with the words beginning with "having the luster of a mango fruit. [The term] "doṣada" means the destroyer of defects (*doṣacchedaka*), according to the root *do* in the sense of "cutting apart" (*avakhaṇḍane*). His abode, however, is described in the *Śrīpauṣkara*:
"Having reached the field of the Boar (*sūkarakṣetra*), the Lord whose vehicle is Garuḍa..."
He stands mounted upon Garuḍa, marked by the Pārijāta tree held in his hand.
"Along with the Siddhas and the hosts of gods, O Pauṣkara, [he dwells] even in the sky. (98–108)
The Lord of the World, the large-eyed one, who is saluted by all the gods. || 108 ||
One should meditate upon him seated on the lion-throne with eyes closed, sitting in the lotus posture (padmāsana), possessing a splendor like the interior of a lotus. 109.
His intellect is permeated with compassion, his hands are marked by the conch and the lotus, and he points out the three paths of knowledge, dispassion, and the true Dharma. || 110 ||
He describes the meditation on the Lord of the World with two and a half verses beginning with "the Lord of the World. It should be understood that his other form is an incarnation of the Buddha:
"Lokeśvara is the peaceful body, whose other form is the Buddhist [deity];
he is the restrainer of the qualities of the intellect and the refuter of the fault of violence."
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"O Brahmin, the station of this [deity] is situated within the Magadha region, resting upon the earth of Mahābodhi;
there dwells Janārdana, the God of gods, whose very self is the Lord of the World."
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara [Tantra]. (108–110)
Then one should remember the one named Datta, the embodiment of knowledge, free from taint,
who dwells in the meditative absorption of men, sages, and gods whose souls are devoted to *samādhi*.
And [he saw those] who had only slightly attained the essence [of truth], following the path of Brahman,
illuminating that very path with the mass of their own radiance.
Together with the mind, he is the one who effects the negation of the forms of the winds,
as well as of the Vedic scriptures, mental states, and likewise of traditional customs.
For he is indeed the protector of the social classes and the stages of life,
while the tree of his intellect remains unshaken within the single ocean of his mind.
And one should also meditate upon him situated above, rich with the creeper of self-conceit—dark like a mountain in the rainy season and blazing with splendor like fire. (115)
He who destroys the web of obstacles and the accumulation of sleep and laziness,
appearing in the form of an eminent twice-born man, whose nature is like a blooming lotus.
He himself should be meditated upon as having two arms, holding a staff, *darbha* grass, and a rosary.

Now, he describes the meditation on Dattātreya with the verses beginning "Then one should remember the one named Datta," and so forth. The word "should remember" (*saṃsmaret*) is to be construed with what precedes it. (111–117)
The Lord reclining on the nyagrodha tree, who has conquered ignorance with the moonlight of his teeth.
Seated slightly supine, with two arms, in the form of an infant;
likewise, he remains with weapons cast aside, abiding in the essence of peaceful sleep.
His intrinsic nature was unshaken by the power of yogic illusion,
as he simultaneously exhaled and inhaled with his two breaths.
"Indeed, everything up to the realm of Brahmā consists of that which is dominated by *prakṛti* (the material cause).

With three verses beginning with 'The moonlight of His teeth' (*dantajyotsnā*), [the Lord] describes the meditation on His reclining upon the *nyagrodha* tree. The meaning of 'dominated by *prakṛti*' is 'consisting of *prakṛti*. It should be understood that the one previously mentioned—who lies upon the single ocean—is the agent of the occasional dissolution (*naimittika-pralaya*), whereas this one is the agent of the primordial dissolution (*prākṛtika-pralaya*). The definitions of the occasional and primordial dissolutions are found in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
'Among these, the occasional dissolution is that in which the Lord of the universe sleeps.'"
And when it returns to its primordial nature, that is the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-laya) of the universe.
Thus [ends the section] 117–120.
By means of a non-human form, whose nature consists of concealed limbs.
Then, one should meditate upon the presiding Lord situated in the midst of the water of his own *māyā*, adorned by the multitude of qualities such as knowledge, which serve as his wings. (121)
One should meditate upon the Brahman arising from oneself, which has issued forth, shines with a single horn,
and carries it even at the time of the end of the kalpa.
He beheld the earth, formless and vast, filled with hosts of Prajāpatis,
as if with a body of pure and stainless pearls.
Then that Lord, whose soul was a fish, remained with eyes closed.

Now, he describes the meditation on the Fish Incarnation (Matsyāvatāra) in four verses beginning with "apauruṣeṇa. The meaning is "in the form of a boat," that is, in the form of a vessel; for Amara states: "The word *naus* is feminine, as are *taraṇi* and *tari*. It should be understood that at that time, Mahālakṣmī herself assumed this form of a boat. And so it is said in the Lakṣmītantra: "That auspicious incarnation of Viṣṇu known by the name Mīnadhara..."
“By way of [her] successive acts of grace, I am there, assuming the form of a boat.

As for its location, it is stated in the Pauṣkara: “The Lord, whose self is the fish, is in the waters. The location of Mīnavaktra is also mentioned in that very same place: “The Lord Mīnavaktra resides on the mountain Naubandhana. (120–124)
He who, out of compassion for the wise who are constantly afraid of worldly existence, [acted] himself... (124)
Seated within the heart, resembling ten thousand suns,
he conquers by means of the rod of discipline the terrible power of ignorance along with the host of enemies that are the senses.

O Brahman, for the sake of attaining happiness, one should quickly restrain [the mind] and meditate upon that very [deity], who has short limbs, is dark-complexioned, and has eyes like lotus petals. 126.
With the worlds situated within it, adorned with matted hair and bark garments,
that umbrella is in his left hand, while the Vaiṣṇava staff is elsewhere.

He describes the meditation on Vāmana with the verses beginning with "yo nityam" and so forth. "Having conquered ignorance" means having dispelled *avidyā*. "Brahmanandana" means that which causes bliss to Brahman; the meaning is "knowledge. Its location, however, is described in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "In the *kanda* and *mālā*, within the hollow of the lineage (*kula*), on the Himālaya mountain."
"The dwarf, of dwarfish form, established in his universal manifestation.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 124–127.
Having transcended the light of the sun, moon, and fire,
the infinite Lord known as the Fourth (turya), who sustains the manifestation of consciousness, remains established.
Impelling from his own station the nectar-like radiance— the power that generates bliss— for those performers of action whose souls are purified, even though she was unwilling to leave.
One should meditate upon him alone as being above the three worlds, possessing a green luster,
and adorned with a multitude of arms equipped with various mudrās and weapons.
He carried the enemy-destroyer with his staff-like leg as a palanquin,
bearing the Vaijayantī banner for the sake of the victory of the gods who desired triumph.
A sword, a discus, a mace, a staff, an arrow, a goad, a hammer, a spear, an axe, and the lord of mountains—these ten are held in his right arms. (132)
A conch, a javelin, a bow, a noose, a trident, and trees;
a thunderbolt, a razor-edged sword, a plow, and a great mace. 133.

In their left hands, these other ten [deities] are to be meditated upon as being endowed with mudrās, characterized by [the gestures of] holding the hair-tuft and the neck, while their hearts are filled with fear and wonder. (134)
The five mudrās of the Lord are to be meditated upon in his five right hands: those known as Varada, Bhūti, Yuktā, and Abhayā. (135)
One should visualize Gopanī in as many right hands as there are [of Viṣṇu].
He describes the meditation on Trivikrama with the words beginning with "having stepped," etc.; the meaning is that Śakti, who generates delight, is Gaṅgā. And so it is stated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"The incarnation of Viṣṇu known as Traivikrama is remembered as supreme."
"Ganga, who generates delight, originates from his foot; thus [it is said]. As for her location, she is in the Śrīpauṣkara in the Middle Country, while Pauṣkara is in Kurukṣetra on the Ganges."
"Having reached the bank of the Yamunā, there stands a great further manifestation known as Trivikrama, whose form traversed the three worlds. (128–136)
By him, the Sūtra of the World was taught along with its constituent parts for those of immeasurable self.
He should indeed be remembered in four ways according to the nature of the six qualities, without the previously mentioned forms, and devoid of both the insignia and the weapons. (137)
May the four [stages] beginning with *japa*, ending with *yoga*, *kriyā*, and *tapaḥ*, protect [us]; they bestow true prosperity and liberation. (138)
Nara was devoted to Kṛṣṇa, and by his own will, he appeared both separately and together with him;
there, Nara had the luster of coral and his eyes were half-open.
With his inner being absorbed and his mind fixed solely on the Śabdabrahman,
he uttered the unperceived mantra characterized by the word, speaking it softly.
Adorned with a crystal rosary held in his hand,
he was counting the revolutions of the rosary beads with his left hand.
Then one should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa, white as a water-lily,
with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, peaceful, and with his mind fixed upon the lotus of the heart.
And one should meditate upon Hari, who is golden-hued, holding a water-pot, and uniting his own self with the supreme, imperishable state. 143.
With his hands folded upon a seat, demonstrating the ritual procedures,
he was incessantly reciting the scripture preceded by the Pañcarātra.
He was dark, with the hue of a blue lotus, with arms raised and matted hair;
he stood upon one foot and was striking the wind-god.

One should contemplate him as teaching the Ekāha, Trirātra, Ṣaḍrātra, Dvirātra, Ṣaḍrātra, and other such observances, as well as the Atikṛcchra penance, and fasts lasting for a fortnight or a month. (146)
All of them wore black antelope skins as upper garments and were clad in saffron robes;
all bore the marks of Brahman and were entirely devoted to Brahman.
Surrounded by their principal sons, all of them devoted to every goal, they acted at the appropriate times for the sake of inspiring the virtuous. 148.

Now, he describes the meditative absorption (dhyāna) of the four beginning with Nara by means of the verses starting with "jagatsūtram. It should be understood that the roles of protector of recitation, yoga, ritual action, and austerity belong respectively to Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa. Regarding their locations:
"The Lord of the World known as Nara is eternally present and stationed in delightful regions of the earth that are worshipped by the perfected ones (siddhas)."
On the mountain named Govardhana, the Lord Hari, the sovereign of all, resides;
he is present when that place is worshipped and during the processions of the cows.
By means of his unimpeded power known as the "Excellent Axe," the Blessed One cuts down the deeply rooted trees of karma belonging to those who act.
One should meditate upon that very [deity] as two-armed, with the splendor of the rising sun, clothed in the skin of a black antelope, and marked by a hand holding an excellent axe. (150)
He who brings to rest for yogins that terrible night-stalker of the mind, which has the ten sense-faculties as its mouths, by means of a net of arrows consisting of discernment; (151)
He alone, the soul of the universe, should be meditated upon—he who has the luster of a water-laden cloud, whose eyes are like red lotuses, and whose hands are marked by the bow and arrow. 152.
He describes the meditation on Paraśurāma with two verses beginning with "asaṅgaśaktyā. Regarding his location:
"In the best of mountains called Mahendra, the twice-born Lord known as Rāma stands, holding a battle-axe and being the end-maker of the Kṣatriyas. (149–150)

He describes the meditation on Śrī Rāma with two verses beginning with "daśendriyānanam": "His abode is on the mountain Citrakūṭa; there dwells another great Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals. (149–152)
He who indeed divides the mandala of speech—the Vedas—characterized by its own essential nature and splendor, into three parts, beginning with the Paśyantī state, which arises from himself; || 153 ||
That Blessed One, who has the luster of an *atasī* flower, should also be remembered as he rises sequentially through the locations beginning with the heart, by means of the wind of awakening. 154.
Carrying in his left hand a book containing the meaning of all the scriptures, he teaches the meaning of the scriptures with his right hand exactly as it truly is.
And in order to prevent weariness among those whose understanding conforms to the [successive] ages,
he who knew the three times indeed divided the single Veda into four parts.

Now, he describes the meditation on Vedavyāsa with the verses beginning with "The sphere of the Veda of speech" (*vāgvedamaṇḍalam*). "Characterized by the radiance of its own nature" means that its essential form is the light situated within; for it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "Abiding in the heart, it remains manifesting the very light of its own nature. This amounts to saying it is of a purely tranquil form. "The sphere of the Veda of speech" means the Śabdabrahman (the Brahman as Word). He divides it threefold, preceded by the *paśyantī* [state], meaning he divides it into the three distinctions of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.
These states of the Śabdabrahman have been clearly explained in the *Lakṣmītantra*.
The opening of consciousness is known as sound (śabda), and the opening of sound is said to be the object (artha).
The arising of the emerging sound is the first manifestation of power from the tranquil Self.
That is renowned as *nāda*, which at that time is unmanifest and subtle;
together with *nāda*, that *śakti* is celebrated as "the Subtle" (*sūkṣmā*).
That which is called the "drop" (bindu) is here said to abide as the smooth [state], though it is the expressed object.
That state is named Paśyantī; it is divine and of great exaltation for me. Beyond that is the third unfolding (unmeṣa), which arises from Śakti.
That middle stage there brings about the connection;
at that time, the distinction between the signified and the signifier consists of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
But the fourth unfolding of power, which is beyond the intermediate state,
is that condition called Vaikharī, in which phonemes and sentences arise clearly.
I possess a power whose nature is action, which follows the form of consciousness;
it animates the succession of the unfolding of power, beginning with the primordial sound (nāda).

"Then one sees [the levels] Śāntarūpā, Madhyamā, and likewise Vaikharī"—this should be understood as a qualification of the three states beginning with Paśyantī, which arise sequentially in the locations starting from the heart, preceded by the wind of consciousness (*bodhamāruta*). Vaikharī is the manifestation of sound; Madhyamā is conjoined with the intellect (*buddhi*).
And because it has been said: "The subtle, non-departing speech is that which perceives the illuminated meaning. (Verses 153–156)
And for those who delight in the dharma of giving, who perform sacrifices and rituals, who are devoted to austerity and the study of sacred texts, and who are liberated from rebirth— 157.
And for the sake of their protection and to manifest their fitness [for liberation], the Lord of the World arises within the lotus-grove of their hearts. (158)
Having mounted the steed of the mind and taken up the weapons of self-discipline, he surely and swiftly uproots that [defilement] which has arisen from hundreds of previous births. (159)

For the sake of accomplishing pure consciousness, one should meditate upon that [deity] mounted on a noble horse, whose body is enveloped in armor, in order to sever the web of worldly tendencies. 160.
His forehead was adorned with a white turban, and he wore matted locks that were not excessively long;
he possessed a radiance like molten gold and was situated between two quivers.
With his hands busily occupied with arrows, bows, and swords, and bearing scimitars, spears, and axes, he indeed protects the performance of sacrifices, Vedic study, and the giving of gifts.
[He will] destroy those of dark complexion whose souls are devoted to unrighteousness.
Then, with the words beginning "and those who delight in the dharma of giving," he describes the meditation on Kalki. His abode, however, is described in the Śrī-Pauṣkara:
"The Lord Viṣṇu, in the form of Kalki, stands there being praised by the twice-born."
And having reached the river Vipāśā with a disciplined mind, he remained composed.
Thus [ends the section] 157–163.
The pervasive Lord is the reality that is the substratum of all realities and consists of all powers.
Manifesting the qualities of all the senses yet devoid of all senses, and the support of all worlds—he who stands below that [lotus] is to be meditated upon. 164.
Seated upon the infinite couch, possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of an aeon,
he is endowed with rows of blazing flames and is enveloped in garments of fire.
Surrounded by a multitude of personified weapons, such as the discus and others,
Lakṣmī stands at the region of the Lord’s feet, while Cintā stands to his right.
Sleep is located in the region of the head, while nourishment (puṣṭi) is situated to its left.

He describes the meditation on the one reclining upon the netherworld (pātāla), which is the refuge of all principles, with the words beginning "sarvatattvāśrayam. The locations of Padmanābha, the one reclining on Śeṣa in the netherworld, the one reclining on the single ocean, and the one reclining under the banyan tree are established in the *Śrīpauṣkara*:
"In the Ocean of Milk is Padmanābha; Hari has the serpent Śeṣa as his couch."
And because the Grandfather was born from the navel-lotus, he remained there.
Relying upon form in four ways, she alone exists within this entire universe for the welfare of all the worlds; listen now as to how that is so.
O Brahmin, having reached his bed situated at the bottom of Pātāla and taking up the Vaṭa fire, he is the one who finally withdraws the universe.
Having resorted to the foot of the banyan tree at Prayāga, which is worshipped by the gods,
and having made the entire world a single ocean, he reached that divine tree.
O twice-born one, that Blessed One remains on that bank upon the earth;
one should meditate upon his bed beneath the banyan tree, which bestows a divine state.
That he is thus endowed with these four powers is also stated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"I am the incarnation of Hari known as Anantaśayana."
Established in the four directions of that [being] who has attained the state of the Fourfold Self (Cāturātmya) are Lakṣmī, Cintā, Nidrā, and Puṣṭi, endowed with these names. (Verses 163–167)
This meditation on the principal deity has been described in brief. || 167 ||
Knowing which, they turn back from birth, death, old age, and disease;
their manifestation is clearly evident throughout the three worlds, neither by weapons, nor by garments, nor by banners. (168)
They too bear a multitude of marks upon the soles of their feet,
on the forehead, on the back, and on the two palms of their hands, even though they lack the [royal] seal.

In the section concerning the hair on the head for the sake of identifying the practitioners, he concludes the matter already stated by mentioning the description of the fruits, beginning with the words "pradhāna" (the principal). He states in two verses beginning with "nāstraiḥ" that although these deities of manifestation lack the specific insignia such as weapons that characterize their respective forms in the hands and other limbs according to the sequence described, they do possess insignia on their feet, foreheads, and so forth; these must be examined with great care. These two verses are also expounded in the section on temple worship (*vimānārcana*) in both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Agamas].

However, in some manuscripts of those two [works], the word "na" (not) is not seen in the phrase "astrairvastrairdhvajairyeṣām. This is due to the negligence of the scribes, as it contradicts the original text. Alternatively, even the reading of that [phrase] has already been shown to have a valid interpretation within the commentary on the *Īśvara-saṃhitā*. In the *Pārameśvara-saṃhitā* commentary, it is explained in such a sequence: "by standing, sitting, and so forth in the range of the feet; by the three eyes and so forth on the forehead; by the various types of arms on the shoulder-bands; and by arrows, discuses, and so forth on the back," and so on.

That is inconsistent, because the word *liṅga* is universally established as referring specifically to the discus and other [emblems]; furthermore, it will be stated explicitly in the very next verse with the words, "He does not abandon the *liṅga* of Acyuta. (167–170)
Even for a transmigrating being who is by nature a Vaiṣṇava. || 170 ||
He does not abandon his unfallen mark; how much less so when he possesses a form of manifestation?
As for what was previously stated by me regarding the freedom of action for all, [it applies only to those who have not attained this state].
The characteristics of his feet, arms, complexion, face, large [body], waist, and limbs are visible everywhere and at all times, whether as one or as many. 172.

He reinforces the stated point with the word "api" (even/also) by means of further reasoning. In the words "jantoḥ" (of a living being) and "vibhavākṛteḥ" (of one who has the form of an incarnation), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). The meaning is this: at the time of examining the marks according to the *sāmudrika* [science of physiognomy], the marks such as the discus (*cakra*) are seen on the hands and other limbs of ordinary Vaiṣṇava devotees alone; how then could there be any doubt regarding the presence of such marks on Viṣṇu himself, who is an incarnation of his own power (*vibhava*)? Thus, there is no room for doubt.

Regarding all the aforementioned Vibhava-devas, the verse beginning with "sarveṣām" (of all) and consisting of one and a half verses states that, just as it was said that "the forms of Kṛṣṇa are innumerable," they possess the capacity to assume innumerable forms at will through their arms, colors, weapons, and so forth. || 170–172 ||
But one should not effect a change of form, for the instrument possesses the power to take any form at will;
since its activity exists as something distinct within the temple of the universe. (173)
At the times of the maintenance, dissolution, and creation of the gods, each [deity] has its own [function];
even though this rule is thus established, nevertheless, by the power of the Lord (bhagavat), || 174 ||
But from the assembly of the fourfold self, that which stands upon the ground of lotus petals likewise [arises]; O lotus-eyed one, [it arises] from the midst of the manifested deities.
But the one whose essence is power, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those of purified souls,
assumes a form arising from many divisions while stationed upon his noble vehicle.

Thus, he states with the half-verse beginning "But not... that even the possession of form by all [deities] does not produce a cognition contrary to their true nature, because there exist their respective distinct functions which determine each particular form.

Although thus the rule that all [deities] possess the capacity to assume forms at will (*kāmarūpadharatva*) is established, nevertheless, not all gods simultaneously assume such forms. Among the *jāgrat-vyūha* deities such as Vāsudeva and others, or among the *vibhava* deities such as Padmanābha and others, one assumes many forms through various mouths, arms, weapons, powers, and vehicles for the sake of protecting the world, and thus attains the designation "Śakti" (Power). This he states with the two and a half verses beginning with "satyevam. The meaning is that the fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) situated upon the petals of the lotus is known as the *jāgrat-vyūha*.
Now, within that lotus, on the plane known as the waking state, the Blessed One is to be worshipped and meditated upon;
how this is to be done is now explained.
Thus, it has been stated that the waking manifestation (jāgrad-vyūha) indeed resides upon the surface of a lotus petal. || 173–176 ||
Listen as I describe that [deity], by remembering whom, meditating upon whom, and worshipping whom, a person quickly attains whatever his heart desires. (177)
Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya are the lords of birds;
this fivefold manifestation is indeed a modification of the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa). || 178 ||
He whose entire body is of human form, extending down to the range of his feet,
who has two arms and the luster of snow— that Satya is the presiding deity of the vital breaths.
Suparṇa is the color of a ruby, stainless, and has golden eyes;
Garuḍa has a golden luster and crooked eyebrows and reddish-brown eyes.
Tārkṣya was indeed of squinting eyes, resembling a rain-cloud;
the fifth was Dravatkanakanetra, who had a variegated luster.
Suparṇa and the others have four arms, possess gentle forms, and are unperturbed;
they all have feet like those of birds and are adorned with circles of feathers.

They have pendulous bellies and well-nourished limbs, adorned with earrings and other ornaments; they possess curved eyebrows and large, round eyes, with faces like beaks and smiling countenances. (183)
Established through their sovereignty over the vital winds such as apāna, they possess great strength and massive bodies; among them, the fifth has a red beak. (184)
The left hand of the first [deity] indeed rests below the foot upon which he stands;
the right hand is illuminated by a very white rosary of beads.
In this very manner, the two arms of Suparṇa are to be understood:
the other, the left one, is at the level of the navel, turned upward, and filled with wonder. (186)
The right [hand] is full of clusters of flowers and turned upward;
know that there are two [hands] of Garuḍa in the region of the heart in the form of a joined palms gesture (añjali). 187.
In that very place, the two hands of the fourth [deity] are joined in the *sampuṭa* gesture;
in the right hand is an amṛta-pitcher, while in the left is a venomous serpent.
For the fifth [finger], two [joints] are the remainder; and for the three [fingers], it is equal to two.
If indeed the right hand is pressed upon the foot of the one to be empowered (ādheya), [it is so]. 189.
At that time, the movement of the rosary was indeed prescribed to be on the left;
for him whose two palms were positioned beneath the feet of the one to be invoked. (190)

Know that vehicle, which is identical with the Lord (Bhagavan), to be one whose thread [of the body] has been cast off. Now, he describes the varieties and characteristics of that vehicle as it is engaged, beginning with the words "by the recollection of which" and ending with "identical with the Lord. From the range of the feet—that is, starting from the feet—the entire body of which is "puruṣa," meaning the whole body is in human form. It is the "deity of breath," meaning the lord of the vital breaths. It is "kekarakṣaḥ," meaning one whose two eyes are slanted or squinting; thus it is described. According to Amara, "baliraḥ kekare" (the word *kekara* refers to one with squinting eyes).

Although the state of having crooked eyes is already established by the word *kekara* alone, the separate mention of the word *akṣi* (eye) here indicates that the word *kekara* refers to anything merely crooked.

In the *Pārameśvaravyākhyāna*, however, it is written: "Keṅkarākṣa has his eyes half-open due to the power of meditating upon the Blessed One. This should be investigated. "Śabalābhaḥ" means having a variegated or multicolored appearance. "The left hand of the First [Lord], the True One" refers to the left hand. "Situated beneath the feet of the one to be supported" means situated beneath the lotus-feet of the Blessed One who is mounted upon his own shoulder. The right [hand], however, is resplendent with a rosary (*akṣasūtra*).

Here, by means of the two *ca* particles, it is indicated that it is possible for the left hand to sometimes hold the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and for the right hand to sometimes have its foot placed beneath it; as it is said:
"If indeed the right hand is pressed down by the foot placed upon it, then the movement of the rosary is prescribed in the left."
Thus it is said. Now, [it may be asked]: "All the foremost birds hold a handful of flowers with both hands, their fingers interlaced with their respective thumbs."

Thus, according to the statement of Īśvara and Pārameśvara, there should be the holding of a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) in both hands; however, the meaning is that when the right hand is pressed down by the feet of the Lord, then the movement—meaning the shifting—for the sake of counting, occurs with the rosary situated in the left hand. If one objects, "This is not correct," [we reply]:
"Know that he whose two palms are situated beneath the feet of the One who is to be supported (the Lord), from whom the rosary has been removed—that vehicle is identical with the Lord."

Because of this contradiction with the statement [of the scripture], once the meaning spoken by the Blessed One is established, how could the statement "know that [mantra] as having its movement through the threads removed" apply? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "with both hands, the beads strung on the two thumbs," it should be understood from the context of the *puṣpāñjali* (handful of flowers) section that there is only a single rosary strung on the two thumbs. Alternatively, it should be understood that both thumbs are mentioned for the purpose of indicating that the rosary may be held on either the right or the left thumb.

The two arms of Suparṇa—that is, his two principal hands—are likewise characterized by the description of Truth (satya). The other left hand—the left rear hand—is "with wonder," meaning it is endowed with the gesture of astonishment (vismayamudrā). The right rear hand, however, is "filled with clusters of flowers," meaning it is possessed of clusters of Mandāra blossoms. "With face turned upward" means that it is palm upwards. Thus, in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, it is said:
"Suparṇa, however, with his two rear hands, starting from the right..."

"Holding a cluster of *mandāra* flowers, [he wears] the seal of wonder. This means that for Garuḍa there are two [hands], namely the pair of rear hands. For the fourth [deity], Tārkṣya, there are two [hands], meaning the pair of rear hands. For the fifth, Vihageśvara, on the right there is the rear right hand, and on the left there is the rear left hand—this is the meaning. Of the three—Garuḍa, Tārkṣya, and Vihageśvara—the "remainder" refers to the two remaining principal hands. "Equal for the two" means equal for Satya and Suparṇa; that is to say, similar to those two principal hands.

If it is argued that what was stated previously—namely, "the two of Garuḍa," and so forth—refers to the two primary hands, while the "remainder of the three" refers to the two rear hands, meaning they are similar to the two rear hands of Suparṇa, we say no. For if one explains the matter in that way, the support for the two lotus-feet of the Lord mounted upon those respective shoulders would be unestablished; furthermore, it would contradict the corroboration provided by the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, which states: "The fifth is the Lord of Birds; with his right [hand] he holds a jar of nectar, and with his left, the Lord of Serpents."

Now, is it not the case that a single meaning for both the root text and its commentary is possible everywhere? Even if the contradiction has been resolved here according to your method, [the texts still state]: "Garuda bears them in reverse order;
Tārkṣya, however, always bears them in the two rear positions, on the right and left."
"Kadrū, as well as the jar of nectar"— with these words,
all the foremost of birds held handfuls of flowers with both hands joined by their respective two thumbs.

Furthermore, such a statement would contradict the root text (*mūla*). If it is asked what the resolution to this is, the answer is: true. Even in the case of a contradiction with the statements of the *upabṛṃhaṇas* (supplementary texts), there is no transgression. For instance, in that context, because the section concerns the state in which Truth (*satya*) and the others are attendants of the Lord as the primary subject, and because at that time the status of being the Lord’s vehicle has not yet been attained, it is stated that all of them hold a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with their two principal hands; this is consistent with the root text in the case of Suparṇa and Vihageśvara.

It has been stated that with his two rear hands he holds a cluster of flowers and the *vismaya-mudrā*, as well as the jar of nectar (*sudhā-kumbha*) and the lord of serpents (*phaṇīśvara*). However, since it has already been stated that Garuḍa and Tārkṣya hold handfuls of flowers with their two principal hands, it would be inconsistent for them to again hold the *añjali* gesture with their two rear hands. Therefore, it should be understood that these two [rear] hands hold the emblems previously assigned to Suparṇa and Vihageśvara, but in reversed positions.
As for the visualization of Satya and the others while they serve as the mounts of the Lord, it has been written according to the original source in the section on Īśvara (verses 177–191).
But intent on bestowing grace, he remains within the lotus-like expanse of the bird's wings.

Endowed with the power born of white jasmine and accompanied by asuras and excellent [beings], he is likewise endowed with Śrī, either seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and so forth, or alone. || 192 ||

Know that [seat] to be the Garuḍāsana by virtue of the clearly manifest arrangement of its parts. Regarding the manner in which the Lord is situated upon the vehicle characterized in this way, he speaks in two verses beginning with "anugraha": "[He is] seated upon that which is endowed with the most excellent cushion (masūrakavara), which is the very excellence of His own splendor and inherent power. (191–193)
His sister, Meḍhbhū, was protected by him as he moved with great speed.

Regarding the passage beginning with "vīryapātāt" (due to the emission of semen), he explains the purpose of the protection of the Lord’s genital region by the head of the Lord of Birds as it was moving along: "meḍhrabhūḥ" means the earth of the penis; "sodarā" means together with the abdomen; "vīryapātāt" is a locative case used in the sense of the elision of a verbal suffix (lyap); and "aṇḍajena" means by the bird Garuḍa. (193–194)
For the sake of the welfare of other worlds, and out of affection even for those who meditate. || 194 ||
The one whose vehicle is Garuḍa is remembered for the purpose of manifesting direct perception.
He states the purpose of the Blessed One’s mounting of Garuḍa with the words beginning "loka... (verse 194–195).
Therefore, [this was] indeed from the Blessed One Viṣṇu, who had assumed such a form.
One should contemplate the state of [the Lord] seated for the sake of the success of one who has been summoned.
The author states "therefore" (tasmāt) to show that the practitioner must contemplate the various seats of the Blessed One for the sake of attaining those respective fruits. || 195-196 ||
With his left foot drawn in, he may be seated upon a lotus or stationed in the air. || 196 ||
He who destroys the desired fruits intended by others with his left hand, while remaining undistracted from the right hand up to the knees, is known as Acyuta. 197.
Until liberation, the right [channel] shall be the practitioner for all accomplishments;
it is taught that everything remains established in a straight state for the seeker. (198)

In this way, the svastika and other [mudrās] are indeed formed; however, they are prescribed for one who is seated upon a throne, a kahlāra lotus, or a lion-throne, and are performed without a vehicle.

The Blessed One, with his left foot drawn in, wards off the undesirable; thus he says, "withdrawn" (*upasaṃhṛta*). "Left" (*vāma*) means contrary or adverse. With his right foot contracted, he brings about the desirable; thus he says, "until liberation" (*āmokṣāt*). "Right" (*dakṣiṇa*) means noble or generous. Without those two [postures], standing upright, the Blessed One performs everything—warding off the undesirable and bestowing the desirable; thus he says "all" (*sarvam*) in half a verse. In this way, various types of postures such as the *svastika* and others are possible even for one seated upon a throne without a vehicle; thus he says "by the *svastika* and so forth. (196–199)
And here, by virtue of his mastery over yoga,
the Lord of Birds assumes a multitude of faces and arms, equipped with the supreme weapons of the lords of serpents.
Either by the power of the Lord’s command, or for the sake of the Lord’s own satisfaction, or for the sake of the world’s victory and prosperity, or for the peace of those seeking refuge. (201)
And indeed, in various forms throughout diverse world-systems,
the Hero, whose movement is unimpeded, wanders all alone.

Just as the Lord of Śaktis (Śiva) who has mounted his own power, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) also, by his command, wanders everywhere alone in various forms—through his faces, arms, weapons, and so forth—for the sake of protecting the entire world; thus he says "vihagādhipatiḥ" in three verses (200–202).
Now, understand from me as I speak the form of Śaktīśa mounted upon that [seat], which is indeed divided into many different varieties. (203)
"Listen to the different forms of Śaktīśa," he said, [referring to] "of him who has mounted upon that. || 203 ||
He should always be depicted as bestowing peace with his right hand,
while holding aloft a conch shell with his left, for a moment as previously described.
This form, however, belongs solely to the two-armed Śaktīśa;
moreover, by means of this very form, he manifests in six ways.
Together with the group of consorts, or even individually starting from one, that which is joined with Lakṣmī as before is the single form of the Lord. (206)
Then, the second [form] situated between Śrī and Puṣṭi is proclaimed.
First, his form as Kevala with two arms was described; now, by means of the verses beginning with "saṃyacchantam," he states his sixteen-fold divisions along with Lakṣmī and the others. || 204–207 ||
The Supreme [deity] is surrounded by a group of four ending with Śrī, Ādi, and Māyā.
Know that the fourth [cakra] is pervaded by the six beginning with purification (śuddhi);
and the fifth by the eight beginning with prosperity (śrī) and ending with nourishment (puṣṭi). || 208 ||
Know that the sixth [chapter] is endowed with the group of six beginning with Lakṣmī;
O Halāyudha, they are Śrīdevī, Kīrtidevī, and Jayādevī. (209)
O Bhagavati, Aparājite, you are the fourth [power], Māyā, the binding force of this entire universe; you are pure, stainless, eternal, and the power of knowledge.
Prakṛti, Sundarī, and Ṣaṭka are said to bestow all perfections;
they are Lakṣmī, the treasury of sound, the granter of all desires, and the increaser of joy. (211)
The group of eight consisting of Yaśaskarī, Śāntidā, Tuṣṭidā, and Puṣṭidā, as well as the twelve [mantras] in the Vaibhava-yoga, are indeed those that bestow fame upon the goddesses. 212.
He states the names of the four beginning with Śrī, the six beginning with Śuddhi, and the eight beginning with Lakṣmī [in three or five verses]. "Śabdanidhi" means Sarasvatī. || 207–212 ||
And that [form] beginning with Lakṣmī is to be understood within this division of the Supreme Lord;
furthermore, in this way, the sevenfold division of the Four-Armed One is to be known. (213)

He says "the group of six" (*dviṣaṭkam*) to indicate that the group of six beginning with Lakṣmī should be understood as previously stated in the ninth chapter. By "in the *Vaibhava* [section]," he means in the section concerning the description of the deities of the *Vibhava-yoga*.
