Now, one might object: "But such an interpretation contradicts the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the *Sātvata*, because therein it is said: 'In a single way, in two ways, four ways, in six ways, and likewise in eight ways...'"
Furthermore, listen to my names there, which are twelvefold.
I am Śrī, the woman of excellent complexion, seated on the lap of the two-armed one;
O Vāsava, on both sides of him are the forms of Śrī and Puṣṭi.
In the four directions, Śrī, Kīrti, and Jayā likewise belong to him alone;
having assumed various forms, I am enjoyed by that Viṣṇu as "Mayā."
Listen, O Indra, to my sixfold name as it resides in the six corners of that very [mandala]:
Śuddhi (Purity), Nirañjanā (The Stainless One), Nityā (The Eternal), and Jñānaśakti (the Power of Knowledge).
Likewise, Aparājitā is the sixth, while Prakṛti is the supreme;
and I myself am established in eight forms within the directions of that very [Prakṛti].
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, the bestower of all desires, the increaser of affection,
the bringer of fame, the giver of peace, the giver of contentment, and Puṣṭi as the eighth.
I abide in twelve ways within the twelve corners of that very [mandala]:
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śakti, and Vibhūti.

"Desire, Affection, Delight, as well as Illusion, Intellect, and Greatness"—thus, the group of six beginning with Lakṣmī and Vāgīśvarī, as stated in the eighth chapter of the *Śrīsātvata*, has indeed been established. Therefore, regarding the term "vaibhavayoga," one might argue that since *vaibhava* means "this [power] of the All-pervading One (*vibhu*)," its meaning here should be described simply as "the vow and worship pertaining to the Lord. If this is argued, we reply: True, but this is not your fault; rather, it is the fault of the scribe of the *Lakṣmītantra*.

Yaśas has, through oversight, written the verse beginning with "Śrīśca vāgīśvarī kāntiḥ" in place of the verse beginning with "Lakṣmīḥ puṣṭir dayā nidrā" and so forth. Even though you have justified that very point, it does not establish your intended position, because in the thirteenth chapter, in the section on meditation (*dhyāna*), the group of six consisting of Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, and the others mentioned in the ninth chapter will be explicitly stated by your own voice.

If it is objected that the reading appears identical in every instance across the *Lakṣmītantra* manuscripts, and how therefore it can be considered an error, we reply: no, because following the first manuscript, the same erroneous reading has spread everywhere.

Just as in the *Pārameśvara* manuscripts, in the chapter on the characteristics of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*), the very well-known verse for the meditation on the lotus—beginning with "the lotus white as a jasmine flower"—is seen written erroneously with the intent of meditating on the mace (*musala*), namely "the mace white as a jasmine flower"; so too should this [reading] be understood.

If it is asked, "Where is it well-known that a lotus is white like a jasmine flower (kunda)?"—then let your honor look at the very chapter on the worship of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara-arcana-adhyāya).

If it is further asked, "What does that matter? Should there not be one single meditation verse for both the lotus and the pestle (musala)?"—why do you require a pestle-blade (musalakisalaya)? For he will state here itself the individual meditation verses for the lotus, the pestle, and so forth. It is precisely according to this [tradition] that the meditation verses for all the weapons have been written down in the Pārameśvara.

Is it not the case that what was stated by the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) is not a mere oversight, but rather the intended view of the author of the *Saṃhitā* itself? For instance, in the *Pauṣkara*, it is taught that one should meditate on Soma as having a "cold weapon in hand," thus [depicting] Soma with a *śiśira* [weapon], and Prajāpati as "having a staff in hand," thus [depicting] Prajāpati with a mace (*musala*). However, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, a mallet (*mudgara*) is taught for Soma and a lotus (*kamala*) for Prajāpati. In both cases, however, the meditation on the weapons has been described.

If you argue that this very point has already been established in the *Pārameśvara* regarding the "frost" (*śiśira*) and the "lotus" (*kamala*), then you are indeed one who knows the vital points (*marmajña*). Nevertheless, it is possible that such a description of meditation might occasionally occur due to the notion that "frost" and "hammer" (*mudgara*) are synonyms. Likewise, because it is impossible for the notion of non-difference between the "lotus" and the "pestle" (*musala*) to arise, that [reading] must simply be the result of a scribe’s error. Alternatively, it should be understood that the insertion of the word "frost" into the verse on the meditation on the hammer was intended precisely to indicate another alternative view mentioned in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Thus, negligence is established in both ways. Enough of this digression; let us return to the subject at hand. (212–213)
Furthermore, in this manner, the sevenfold division of the four-armed [form] is to be understood. || 213 ||
But indeed, by means of the two [emblems], the conch and the discus, held in his left hand,
he bestows upon this world eternal peace through the first of them.

With his second [hand], he brandishes a mace while keeping it to the left (aprasavya). Although he has four arms, he may have a single form with only two arms; including forms accompanied by Lakṣmī and others, one should know that there are seven forms in total, comprising six types. He states this with the half-verse beginning with *punar*. With the verse beginning with *kiṃ tu* and its half, he describes the sequence for holding the four emblems of the four-armed form. By the phrase "bestowing peace" (*śāntiṃ yacchantam*), the holding of a lotus is indeed indicated, because it was previously stated in the definition of the nature of Śakti: "He brings relief from distress with a lotus possessing the luster of the moon. (213–215)
Furthermore, by means of the four hands according to the previously stated sequence. || 215 ||
By holding the four [powers] beginning with Abja in mutual relation,
it assumes a twelvefold form, while remaining solely devoid of power (niḥśaktika).

He states with the verse beginning "furthermore" (bhūyaḥ) that the form with four arms arises in twelve ways through the mutual transposition of these [objects], the lotus and so forth. As for the sequence of holding the lotus and other objects in twelve ways, starting from the primary right hand and ending with the primary left hand, they are: lotus, mace, discus, and conch; lotus, conch, discus, and mace; lotus, mace, conch, and discus; lotus, discus, conch, and mace; lotus, discus, mace, and conch; and lotus, conch, mace, and discus.

The conch, mace, discus, and lotus; the conch, lotus, discus, and mace; the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; the conch, lotus, mace, and discus; the conch, mace, lotus, and discus; and the conch, discus, lotus, and mace—these are to be known in their respective order. || 215–216 ||
Furthermore, O lotus-eyed one, that group of twelve, together with the collection of powers, exists as sixfold by means of that very one additional [power]. (217)

Thus, abiding in many ways with a four-armed body alone, he states in the half-verse beginning with "again twelvefold" that each of these individual forms further becomes sixfold through the distinctions of the powers (śaktis) such as Lakṣmī and others. The phrase "by the pair of powers" means by the assembly of goddesses. Here, the singular form "cayena" is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), because it has been stated that there are assemblies of powers distinguished by groups of two, four, six, eight, and twelve. "By one more" means by one more than Lakṣmī; this is because of what was stated previously: "That which is joined with Lakṣmī as before is one divine form."

It should be understood that because the aggregate consists of multiple entities, the two powers (*śakti*) have been described with separate qualifiers by means of "one plus one. Thus, the meaning is that he exists in many ways even with a four-armed body; specifically, he is endowed with eighty-four distinct forms in total: twelve in his simple forms and seventy-two in forms accompanied by Lakṣmī and other powers. || 217–218 ||
Furthermore, there are seven types [of forms] according to the increase of arms, beginning with six. || 218 ||
"Understand how the Lord abides in manifold ways.
He then says, "In sevenfold [forms]," instructing [the disciple] to hear about the seven varieties of forms, beginning with the six-armed and ending with the eighteen-armed. (218–219)
He has six arms, eight arms, and he bears ten or twelve arms.
Measuring two, seven, sixteen, and eighteen cubits, and adorned with eighteen [ornaments], it is the beginning of the Kevala [state] for all; as before, the division is sevenfold.

He states [this] with the verse beginning "six-armed" (219–220), explaining that for all seven [deities] starting with the six-armed one, sevenfold divisions arise—both as solitary [forms] and as accompanied by their Śaktis—just as before.
Listen to me as it truly is, marked by the arrangement of his weapons:
the six-armed one holds a sword, a lotus, and a mace in his right hands. (221)
With his three left hands he holds a bow with an arrow, a conch, and a supreme weapon;
with his eight right hands, however, he holds a mace, a pestle, a discus, and a sword. (222)
In her left hands she holds a conch, a goad, and a noose, along with a bow together with an arrow;
while her right hands are endowed with a sword, an arrow, a mace, a lotus, and a spear. (223)
He has ten arms; in his six right hands are a bow, a conch, a discus, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness, adorned with twelve arms in total.

He holds in his right hands the lotus, the sword, the discus, the arrow, the mace, the goad, the conch, the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and the spear; and in his left hands, the mallet and the bow. 225.
The fourteen-armed [deity] holds in his seven left hands the conch, mace, goad, noose, club, mallet, and plow. || 226 ||
With his sixteen principal hands, he should bear a staff, a lotus, a vajra, a wheel, a sword, a spear, and an axe, together with a mallet.
The [eight] hands hold the gesture of fearlessness, a lotus, a sword, a spear, a staff, an excellent goad, a conch, a discus, a mace, a thunderbolt, a noose, a plough, and a bow. (228)
With his eight left hands, Viśvajit holds a lotus, a sword, a mace, a thunderbolt, a discus, an arrow, a boon-granting gesture, and a goad. (229)
Bearing eighteen arms, he holds a staff in his right hands,
as well as a conch, the gesture of fearlessness, a plow, a spear, a mallet, a pestle, and a bow.
The All-pervading Lord carries these—incomparable axes and nooses—with his left arms for the purpose of subduing the wicked and for the protection of the virtuous. (231)
He describes the various weapons of the six-armed [deities] and others, beginning with "Listen to me as they truly are" and ending with "for the protection of the virtuous," in verses 221–231.
Furthermore, with his own two mouths alone, he of immeasurable prowess especially leads these very beings, who possess distinct forms, into [his own state]. (232)
These forms have already been described; now, [the author] says "furthermore" (bhūyaḥ) to show that they attain a state of distinction by means of two faces alone. || 232 ||

And for the benefit of those who cannot endure the splendor of a lion, whose souls are intent on the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa), and who are terrified of worldly existence beginning with women and the like.
When the lunar portion (āmṛta) is indeed in the fiery (taijasa) division, which always receives the oblation from the right,
the Lord should effect a reversal through the left and right faces.

O Lotus-eyed One, for the sake of increase as well as for the pacification of splendor (*tejas*), [the Lord] describes the distinction of the transposition of the southern and northern faces with two and a half verses beginning with "siṃha" (lion). Since His own southern part is already composed of splendor, if there were also a lion-face—which is even more intensely splendid—therein, the worshippers would be unable to endure that combined splendor. Therefore, for the benefit of those seekers of liberation who are worshippers, the meaning is that the splendorous lion-face moves to His own left side, which consists of nectar, while the boar-face takes its place in the southern part, which is composed of splendor.

|| 233-235 || The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata, which is marvelous and extraordinary, and which has never before been seen by any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he can make his body visible to all beings throughout the entire billionfold world-system, from the world of Brahmā down to the Avīci hell. And yet, even though he makes it visible, no one is able to perceive him, except for those who have previously made aspirations to see him. This, Ānanda, is the second great miracle of the Tathāgata, which is marvelous and extraordinary, and which has never before been seen by any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he can make his body invisible to all beings throughout the entire billionfold world-system, from the world of Brahmā down to the Avīci hell. And yet, even though he makes it invisible, no one is able to perceive that he is not there, except for those who have previously made aspirations to see him. This, Ānanda, is the third great miracle of the Tathāgata, which is marvelous and extraordinary, and which has never before been seen by any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else in the world.”
By this reason, indeed, the Blessed One [is established] as both external and internal. || 235 ||
Having unified Agni and Soma through their common nature, he remains thus.

By this reason—the exchange of the two faces—he becomes worthy of service by all, being one whose body consists of unified splendor and nectar; so he says with the word "by reason" (hetunā). || 235-236 ||
Having thus brought the manifest face of Vāgīśa above his own head, (he should worship it). || 236 ||
With a five-faced body, it proceeds in manifold ways from its very root for the sake of self-realization for those meditators who are devoted to the Śabdabrahman.

He states with the verse beginning "Manifest" (vyaktam) and its half that [the Lord] also bears the face of Hayagrīva in the center of his four upper faces for the sake of favoring those who are devoted to the worship of Śabdabrahman. 236–237.
And for the purpose of filling all the worlds down to the netherworld (pātāla),
he assumes various forms and proceeds again one by one.

By means of the half-verse beginning with “from the netherworld (pātāla) upwards,” he describes the tenfold division of colors, such as white and so forth, based on distinctions [of form]. The meaning is that this Blessed One, having gone himself to all the worlds beginning with Pātāla, desiring to protect them, assumes various forms; by means of each individual distinction—namely, the distinctions of arms, weapons, powers, and faces—he resorts to each respective form and proceeds in a tenfold manner, starting with white. Furthermore, the phrase “and possessing a luster according to the age” means that, in accordance with the sequence previously mentioned, he attains the various color-distinctions of white, red, and so forth, through states corresponding to each particular age (yuga).
Thus, it should be understood that through the previously mentioned variations of arms, faces, and colors, there are one thousand four hundred and eighty distinct forms of Śaktīśa. || 238-239 ||
Without mouths, he who is endowed with the majesty of omniscience is Nṛsiṃha and the others. || 239 ||
Aniruddha, however, bears these forms as Tārkṣya;
thus, having mounted Garuḍa, Pradyumna may bear that body.
Saṅkarṣaṇa, who resides upon Suparṇa, also assumes manifold forms; the Lord, the soul of the universe, abiding in truth, proceeds in many ways.

For the sake of pacifying the suffering of gods, *siddhas*, humans, and other beings, [the author] states the following with three verses beginning with "vinā vaktraiḥ" (without faces), explaining that among Vāsudeva and the others—according to the manner previously described in the passage beginning with "Now, from the assembly of the fourfold self, that which stands upon the lotus-petal ground"—whichever one exists as the essence of power (*śaktyātmatva*), he possesses all the distinctions of arms, weapons, and powers exactly as before, except for two faces such as those of Nṛsiṃha; however, the vehicle is distinct according to the sequence of Satya and the rest. || 239–242 ||
The four castes are born from a womb, and they likewise exist within other forms.
He states with the half-verse beginning "Of the four" that the four colors, white and so forth, mentioned by Vāsudeva and others, are also possible in other forms whose essence is Śakti. || 242 ||
When the color and insignia of the first four-armed form of Viṣṇu and those of another form are identical, it is the pair of banners that serves as the differentiator. (243)

Since a doubt regarding the specific form may arise because the four-armed Vāsudeva and the one whose essential form is Śakti are identical in their color and insignia, [the author] states "of the four-armed one" to show that each respective banner serves as the means for generating knowledge of the distinction between those two forms. || 243 ||
By means of that banner known as Tāla, which stands to the left (apasavya),
one's own form always attains a differentiation of its essential nature along with its own embodiment.
Since this applies everywhere, he states "apasavya" [in verse 244] to indicate that the specific form of that deity is to be understood by means of the banner located on its right side.
Because, by virtue of their functional purpose, even the forms [of the deities] possess hands;
thus, the four lotuses and so forth—which are formless—are here rendered as formal, whether in a state of tranquility or of arousal.

The reason for this is stated as "because" (*yasmāt*). The emblems, such as the lotus held in the hand, belonging to Vāsudeva and the others, sometimes become formless by assuming a peaceful form according to the specific task at hand, and sometimes become embodied by assuming a willful form. Therefore, the distinction between them is not known through their emblems; rather, the distinction between their respective forms must be understood by means of their particular banners (*dhvaja*). This is the meaning. || 245 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Meditation on the Manifest Deities," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya—who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshiper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
In this sacrifice, however, which possesses a single seat characterized by universal commonality,
all [deities] beginning with Kirīṭin are indeed to be meditated upon in their specific forms.
At the time of worship during the specific sacrifices, their form is again [visualized] as having four arms, four faces, and being endowed with garments, garlands, and ornaments. (2)
For all [deities], one face and two arms are always prescribed.

Now, the thirteenth chapter will be explained. Here, first of all, in the section concerning independent worship (*svātantryenārcanaprakaraṇa*), one should meditate upon them as having four faces and four arms, along with all ornaments such as crowns and emblems; however, in the section concerning dependent worship (*pāratantryenārcanaprakaraṇa*), one should meditate upon them as having only two arms and one face—thus he says in two and a half verses beginning with "yāga."

For this very reason, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the *Lakṣmītantra*, and other texts, within the section on the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), the Kaustubha and other ornaments are described as having only two arms. One might object: "But then, in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* and the *Pārameśvarasaṃhitā*, even in their sections on the sacrifice of enjoyment, the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha are said to have four arms, and by the phrase 'vomiting forth with its own mouths,' the conch is said to have four faces. What is the status of that [contradiction]? Indeed, it is true. In those cases, the verses concerning meditation for the worship of the independent Lord as taught in the *Sāttvatasaṃhitā* were transcribed exactly as they stood. Nevertheless, later in that very same work:
They should be meditated upon as possessing their own natural luster, two-armed, and resembling [the form of] Puruṣa.
Since it has been stated that "those beginning with Kirīṭa are [the deities] whose forms are the mace, the garland, and the woman," there is no room for dispute. 1-3.
Wearing a crown, with a gentle countenance, golden-hued, and of great stature. || 3 ||
Surrounded by splendors endowed with various forms and shapes,
he remained suspended in the air in the characteristic posture of a Vidyadhara.
He describes the meditation on the crown with the verse beginning "kirīṭa" (3-4).
One should meditate upon the Kaustubha, the sovereign of gems, which has the form of a mountain of rubies,
illuminating the ten directions, and is fixed upon His joined feet.
He carries one [hand] at the center of his chest with the palms joined together,
and likewise holds another above his head.
He describes the meditation on the Kaustubha gem with two verses beginning with "padmarāga" (5–6).
Then one should meditate upon Śrīvatsa, who resembles a mountain of crystal,
seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) with his hands placed at his sides.
He bears the *kūrmamudrā* with his two principal hands.

Regarding the meditation on the *śrīvatsa*, [the author] says in the verse beginning with *sphaṭika* (using one and a half verses). The *kūrmamudrā* means the seal that destroys ignorance (*avidyādalinī*), because it will be stated in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*: "One should contemplate the Lord’s seal called *kūrma*, which is the destroyer of ignorance. Its definition should also be understood as it will be stated in that very same place. (7–8)
The Blessed Garland, multiform and captivating, is to be meditated upon. || 8 ||
Endowed with all fragrances, gentle, and with a slightly blossoming face—thus he describes her as the object of meditation, adorned with a forest garland. (8–9)
One should meditate upon him who stands within a circle of light rays, leaping forth, and holding a weapon.
Waiting for the command of the All-pervading Lord, he was short-limbed with red eyes,
possessing a lotus as white as a kunda flower, gentle, and with a face slightly smiling.
She was emitting a sweet sound that brought pleasure to the sense of hearing;
she held a mace resembling a mountain of gold, and she was slender with eyes like blue lotuses.
Illuminating the expanse of the sky with a web of rays arising from herself, she beheld the lotus-eyed Śaṅkha, who resembled the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya). 12.
He vomited from his own mouths that [teaching] whose essence consists of scriptural authority and so forth;
he resembled an evening cloud, possessed a plow, and had terrifying eyes. (13)
With emaciated limbs and elevated shoulders, possessing a body as firm as a diamond and preeminent in strength;
with a slender belly and a mace, he was enveloped by a series of blazing rays of light.
Resembling a heap of glowing coals, long and exceedingly harsh,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, he was the very embodiment of arrows and weapons.
And he held a sharp bow of various forms, with a long range and fierce prowess,
golden-hued and adorned with a network of small bells.
One should meditate upon Nandaka, who is dancing, brandishing his own hand which resounds like a great rain-cloud and is encrusted with rays of light. (17)
Resembling the autumn sky, biting his row of teeth, with a shield resembling the solar disc, he possessed a gentle form. || 18 ||
One should meditate upon Daṇḍa, whose body and eyes are red, who constantly and forcibly devours multitudes of weapons with his own mouth, and who holds a clenched fist. 19.
Bearing a wrathful form, biting his own lower lip with his teeth,
possessing the color of Indra’s bow, and wielding an axe of terrifying prowess.
With eyes like molten gold, bearing matted locks of blazing flames,
holding a noose entwined with a multitude of serpents, and possessing a tongue like lightning, he was terrifying.
He had the pale luster of a golden bee, a terrible mouth, and blood-red eyes;
he was lean-limbed with long arms, tawny-eyed, and held a goad.
With a terrifying face, fierce, and possessing the luster of a mountain of split collyrium, he held a mallet that shone with a hundred rays; he had broad shoulders and a massive body. (23)
Wearing a mass of matted locks, he was gentle with eyes like white lotuses,
and bore a thunderbolt as brilliant as a diamond, marked by long, white claws.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, with blazing golden eyes, possessing the power and radiance of lightning, yet with a countenance and gaze as peaceful as a tranquil fire. (25)
Emitting a deep, rumbling roar again and again,

he describes the meditation on each of the seventeen weapons, beginning with the discus and ending with the spear, in the sequence of one verse for each, starting from "situated within the circle of his own rays" and so forth, in seventeen verses (9.26).
All these leaders of the asuras await the command of the All-pervading Lord. || 26 ||
Standing on very level pedestals, they rose up and moved about;
with their hands placed upon their hips, they were intent on waving fly-whisks as fans.
Excluding the four [hands] beginning with the crown and including the lotus,
his right hand threatens the multitude of the wicked.
At the time of meditation, however, one should meditate upon the well-known, formless insignia of each [deity] located at the crown of the head of all.

He states the common characteristics of all [the attendants] with three and a half verses beginning with "ete 'stranāyakāḥ. "These" refers to Kirīṭa and the others; "leaders of weapons" (astranāyakāḥ) refers to Cakra and the others. "With hands placed upon the hips" means having their left hands resting on the surface of the hips. "Engaged in fanning with chowries" means having their right hands holding chowries and fans. A slight distinction between the weapons and the ornaments has been stated in the verse beginning with "sapadmaṃ."

The construction of the sentence is as follows: one should meditate on [the Lord] together with the lotus (*sapadma*), excluding the fourfold set beginning with the crown—namely the crown, the *kaustubha* gem, the *śrīvatsa*, and the forest garland—and [meditating on Him] with His right hand brandishing the discus and other weapons while threatening the multitude of the wicked. It is stated that even at the time of offering the chowries and fans, He threatens the multitude of the wicked out of fear that, if they were merely occupied with the service of offering the chowries and fans, the wicked ones such as the *asuras* would find an opportunity to engage in their evil deeds as they please.

Alternatively, in the phrase "or threatening," the word *ca* (and) has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). The meaning is that one should visualize the right hands of the [deities] such as Cakra as either raised with a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) or endowed with the *tarjanī-mudrā*. However, if the reading is "raised with a fly-whisk" (*cāmaravyajanodyatam*), there is no such sequential distinction; rather, the meaning becomes clear that only the four [deities] beginning with Padma possess right hands raised with fly-whisks, while the others are simply endowed with the *tarjanī-mudrā*.

In a certain ritual procedure of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara-prayoga), it is stated that the weapons, such as the discus and others, possess the state of being raised like chowries and fans, while the fourfold set [of ornaments], including the lotus and crown, is endowed with the *tarjanī* (threatening) mudrā. This is inconsistent, because the words "the threatening one" (*tarjayantam*) and "the fourfold set" (*catuṣṭayam*) do not share the same grammatical gender; furthermore, since the capacity to threaten the host of the wicked belongs only to the weapons, it is impossible for the ornaments to possess it.

For this very reason, although the lotus is included among the millions of weapons, it is understood that because it is a *līlākamala* (a play-lotus) and is inherently gentle, it cannot threaten a multitude of wicked beings; thus, the description "with a lotus" (*sapadma*) is made along with the other ornaments.

If it is objected: "Previously, it was stated that the Kaustubha jewel, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the two staffs were occupied with other functions by the hands; how is it now possible for those same [limbs] to have the hands resting on the surface of the hips, or to possess either the hand-held chowrie or the Tarjanī mudrā? We reply: No, because the characteristic previously mentioned refers to the four-armed form, whereas the one mentioned now refers to the two-armed form. (26–29)
The crown is to be known as Hutabhuj, while the Kaustubha gem is Prabhākara;
Śrīvatsa is himself Śaśāṅka, and the garland is the six Mādhavas and the rest.
O Great-minded One, know that the king of birds is Prāṇa, the wheel of time;
the lord of waters is indeed the lotus, and the goddess Sarasvatī is the mace. (31)
Space is the conch, the plow is the medicinal herbs, the pestle is the lord of serpents;
know that sound and the other sense objects are the arrows, and the bow is the leveller (Samīkaraṇa).
Nandaka is known as all the scriptures, and the shield is remembered as the earth;
indeed, the staff should be understood as destiny, and detachment is remembered as the axe. (33)
The noose is Māyā, the goad is Kāma, and the mallet is indeed Ahaṅkāra;
stainless Vijñāna is the Vajra, and Samādhi is said to be the Śakti.

Now, he speaks of the presiding deities of the crown and the other ornaments with the verses beginning "The Crown" (kirīṭa), etc. The meaning is that Mādhava and the others are the [presiding] lords. Even in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra], it is said: "The Lord of Waters is indeed the lotus; the Goddess Sarasvatī is the mace;
the Discus is indeed the foundation of the worlds; and the King of Conchs is the Śabdabrahman."

Thus, the presiding deities of the mace and the lotus are indicated by the very words mentioned by Sātvata, whereas the presiding deities of the discus and the conch are stated by different words. Therefore, in that context as well, the meaning is "the foundation of the world" (*lokapratiṣṭhā*) and "time" (*kāla*), because it is well known that time is the support of all things. Furthermore, it should be understood that *śabda* refers to the *śabdabrahman*—the ether (*ākāśa*)—in the sense that "it expands (*bṛṃhati*) within it. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, it is stated that the foundation of the world is the earth (*bhūmi*). That [interpretation] must be investigated. (30–34)

Now hear in due order the meditation upon that multitude of beautiful women who have been described as belonging to the pervasive Lord in His divided form— both those who possess a support and those who are without support.
Cintā has the luster of Indra’s bow; Lakṣmī has the radiance of a red lotus;
Puṣṭi is fair as gold; and Kīrti is white as a water-lily. (36)
Jayā is remembered as resembling the luster of the sun; Māyā is like collyrium; Śuddhi is like the Kiṃśuka flower; and Nirañjanā has the hue of the Guñjā berry. (37)
The eternal power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is radiant like the bandhujīva flower, white and red;
and Aparājitā should be known as having the color of a full-blown blue lotus. || 38 ||
The nature [of the goddess] has the luster of a red lotus; Sarasvatī is white and yellow;
and the Siddhi that grants all desires has a radiance like that of a sapphire. (39)
She who has the luster of a mass of vermilion should be known as the increaser of joy;
she with the luster of milk brings fame, and she radiant as coral bestows peace.
Contentment resembles frost; compassion is like lapis lazuli;
sleep is similar to a magnet; and forbearance has a yellowish-red luster. (41)
Radiance is like a mirror; fortitude is as bright as yellow orpiment;
friendliness has the luster of the bandhūka flower; and delight resembles red ochre. (42)
The *mati* goddesses all possess the luster of emeralds and have joyful faces.

Now, with the verses beginning with "bhinna-rūpasya," [the author] explains the sequence of colors and meditations for the previously mentioned goddesses such as *Cintā*. It should be understood that *Cintā* is the aforementioned goddess situated on the right side of the one reclining in the netherworld (*pātāla*). One should discern through subtle observation that her meditation was taught first because she is not included within the groups of two starting with Śrī, the group of four starting with Śrī, the group of six starting with Śuddhi, the group of eight starting with Lakṣmī, or the group of twelve starting with Lakṣmī.

If it is asked: "But since Prītividya, who is included among the four goddesses situated around the one lying upon the single ocean (ekārṇavaśāyin), is not included within this group of two and so forth, why is her meditation not mentioned here as well?"—you are a fool; even an infant knows that the words *vidyā* and *sarasvatī* are synonyms.

In the phrase "tuṣṭidāpuṣṭidāṣṭakam," since that which was previously designated by the word *tuṣṭidā* (giver of contentment) is again referred to here by the word *tuṣṭi* itself—as in "tuṣṭistuhinasaṃkāśā" (contentment, resembling snow)—it is understood that the words *tuṣṭidā* and *tuṣṭi* are synonyms. Likewise, the synonymy of the pairs *prīti* and *prītivardhanī*, *puṣṭidā* and *puṣṭi*, and *śāntidā* and *śānti* is unrestricted.

Therefore, the venerable one should be satisfied with the understanding that because *prīti* and *vidyā* are also included within the groups beginning with the dyad (*dvika*), their separate meditation was not mentioned. Since the meditation on *lakṣmī* has already been stated at the very beginning, her meditation is not repeated for the dyad, the tetrad, the octad, or the duodecad. Likewise, since the meditations on *tuṣṭi* and *sarasvatī* have already been stated within the octad itself, it should be understood that they are not mentioned again in the duodecad. (35–43)
Wearing divine garlands and garments, they were adorned with various ornaments. || 43 ||
Adorned with divine garlands and garments, they rested by their own husband;
he states the common characteristic of all these goddesses as "divine garlands" and so forth. (43–44)
Furthermore, there are four powers belonging to the All-pervading Lord while he is reclining upon his bed.
Those previously mentioned, situated in the eastern direction, cause the Unborn to vibrate;
as for the triad located in the three other directions, it is intent upon his conveyance.

With the verse beginning "four" (and continuing for one and a half verses), he describes the manual activities of the fourfold group of Śaktis, beginning with Lakṣmī, who stand all around him as he reclines upon Pātāla. || 44–45 ||
Wherever there is one Śrī of the Lord, there the aforementioned arrangement is established;
wherever there is one Śrī of the Lord, there [the other] is either on the left or even on the right.

He states that [the form] has Lakṣmī as its sole object in the passage beginning with "where. This was mentioned previously in the verse: "Seated upon a lotus throne and so forth, or indeed alone, accompanied by Śrī.
[It is said: "The Goddess is embraced by the sixth [hand], which holds a lotus."
Then, with her hand resting on his shoulder, the queen, whose mind was constantly fixed upon him, [spoke].

Regarding the phrase "being fanned with a white chowrie out of discipline," the meaning here is that he is so described. And likewise, in the Lakṣmītantra: "I am Śrī, the fair-complexioned one, seated upon the lap of the two-armed [Viṣṇu]. (46)
Wherever the two known as Śrī and Puṣṭi are located, they are to the south and north [of the central deity];
seated in the lotus posture, she stands upon the two wings of a bird.
One has hands adorned with lotus stalks, while another has soft jars in her hands;
she is the primordial body of the all-pervading one, consisting of both fire and moon.
His two powers are likewise unmixed and possess distinct characteristics:
the power of the enjoyer is known as Lakṣmī, while that of the agent is indeed Puṣṭi.
For him who has descended for the sake of worldly enjoyment out of compassion for the worlds,
that pair of imperishable powers arose simultaneously with him.

"For that whose transformation is proclaimed as manifold"—with these four and a half verses beginning with "The pair known as Śrī and Puṣṭi," he states the characteristic of the two named Śrī and Puṣṭi. The meaning is: the transformation of that pair of powers is manifested as manifold; that is to say, it is shown through various distinctions such as the forms of *cintā*, *kīrti*, *jaya*, *māyā*, and so forth. (47–51)
Indeed, that which consists of the four goddesses situated within the four directions as petals—|| 51 ||
The spear, axe, weapon, and goad are in her hands respectively;
thus he describes the characteristics of the four powers, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and the others, in the verse beginning with "dikpatra" (51–52).
A group of six is situated within the network of filaments; among them, two are located in the east and the west.
Two by two, in their left hands, are the conch, the discus, the mace, the plow, the bow and arrow, the sword Nandaka, and the auspicious [mace]. (53)

He describes the characteristics of the goddesses beginning with Śuddhi by means of the verse and a half beginning with “the hexad. “Two in the east and west” means there is one Śakti in the eastern part and one Śakti in the western part. “Two by two in the north and south” means there are two Śaktis in each of the two northern corners and two Śaktis in each of the two southern corners. And so it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*: “Listen to my sixfold names as I reside in the six corners of that very [mandala]. (52–53)
The eight excellent beloveds situated within the petals should be understood as the first eight [syllables] of her left hands.
The bilva fruit, a rosary, a garland, a mirror, a cluster of flowers, a seat, a small bell, and a collection of weapons, O lotus-eyed one. (55)
He describes the characteristics of the eight powers (śakti) with the two verses beginning with "patramadhye" [54–55]. "Śrīphala" means the bilva fruit.
The hand that bestows peace (the *śāntida*) should be known as the one with the twelve [fingers], while the one with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) has ten;
by means of their internal arrangement, all [of these] are marked with the fly-whisk (*cāmara*). || 56 ||

"And those seated in the *svastika* posture, with minds delighted within"—with the half-verse beginning with "to be known," he states the definition of the six groups of signs starting with Lakṣmī; with the phrase "within," he states the definition common to all. "By means of internal connection" means by means of holding [the hand] with the right hand. (46–47)
O wielder of the plow, [this is] for this Saṃgha, which begins with two and ends with twelve. 57.
By means of colors such as white and so forth, by the transposition of marks, by the conjunction of identical marks, and indeed when that [confusion] has been eliminated; || 58 ||
Furthermore, from the two hands—the Varada and Abhaya—whether joined with each other or used individually, a multitude of various divisions is to be understood as before. (59)
O one of great intelligence, the remainder is indeed the equipment for existence, which is the accumulation of the gods; it is well known, but by the lotus-born ones and others, it is as before.

One should understand that, like Śaktīśa, the various divisions of the Śaktis are manifold, distinguished by such differences as the reversal of colors (white, etc. and emblems (the lotus, etc.). To this effect, he says [in verses] 57–59, beginning with "of the group of two, etc. The meaning is: "of the group of two, etc. refers to the pair consisting of Śrī and Puṣṭi. "Of the twelve" means the group of six pairs beginning with Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, and Dayā. "Of the assembly" (*saṃghasya*) is a singular used for the class; the meaning is "of the five assemblies.
Since the deities who are the instruments of worldly existence (*bhava-upakaraṇa-devas*) are well-known, their characteristics should be understood as being established everywhere. || 57–59 ||
The remainder is the equipment for existence, for that is indeed the accumulation of the gods;
it is well known, O one of great intelligence, but by the lotus-born ones and others, as before.
All of them should be meditated upon as marked on the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet;
they are distinguished throughout the three worlds by their weapons, garments, and banners.
They too bear a multitude of marks upon the soles of their feet,
on their foreheads, on the shoulder-patches, on their backs, and on both palms of their hands.

In the manner described above, since even the ornaments of power (*śakti*), the weapons, and the emblems are indistinct, he states in one and a half verses that these should be observed on the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and so forth, saying "the remainder" (*śeṣam*). (60–61)
For he who is always indeed devoted to all beings, being intent upon devotion, faith, and vows; || 61 ||
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship with offerings beginning with tactile sensations;
he shall soon attain the desired fruit that culminates in liberation.
He states the fruit of worshipping these [deities] in two and a half verses beginning with "bhakti": || 61-62 ||
It is surrounded by an entourage ending with the crown and weapons;
indeed, it is the desired form to be worshipped with devotion. Or else, [it may be] that which is to be worshipped. (63)
"Or [the worship] should be performed with the retinue released, characterized by one's own meditation;

likewise, worship should be performed either accompanied by the meditations on the retinue such as the crown and so forth, or even without those, through the mere meditation on the specific form of the Blessed One alone. Thus he says with the verse beginning "kirīṭa" (63–64).
By means of worship, he surely bestows his own state along with its fruits.
Having understood this, the practitioner should perform worship according to his own desire,
with all enjoyments equal to his own power and with a completely pure body.
In the heart, on the altar, in an external image, in a temple, or in one's own home—
provided it is free from many walls and devoid of smoke, burning, and the like.
In a delightful shelter, free from contact with others, one should remain in meditative cultivation. || 66 ||

Knowing that the Blessed One bestows even the fourfold aims of human life (caturvidhapuruṣārtha) regardless of whether the worship is performed in either manner, one should perform worship—according to one's own inclination and according to one's capacity—with enjoyments acquired [for the purpose], whether in the mind, on the external altar, in the image, in the temple, or in one's own home; thus he says with three verses beginning with "He ordains" (vidadhāti). 64–66.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Meditation on the Deities of the Ornaments and Weapons," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, the son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The fourteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
For the sake of the non-interruption of both the constant and the occasional [rites]...
O lords of sages, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) then urged Viṣṇu to action.

Now the fourteenth chapter will be explained. Here, it is said that Saṃkarṣaṇa asks Vāsudeva about the action that brings about the non-interruption of obligatory and occasional rites: "For the sake of non-interruption" (verse 1).
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O lotus-eyed one, those by whom the mind has been set upon constant worship until the end of life, with a heart purified by faith— [2]
Since their sudden disappearance results in the impossibility of even enjoying those pleasures,
I now wish to know the means for their pacification.

He states the manner of the question with two verses beginning with "yair" (by which). The meaning is: regarding those *bhāgavatas*, due to an accidental lapse—that is, a lapse of daily vows and so forth not preceded by intentional thought—and due to the non-availability of enjoyments—that is, the lapse of secondary [or occasional] offerings and the like. "Yaḥ syāt" means whatever fault might arise. The question is: "I desire to know the pacification of that. (2–3)
The Blessed Lord said:
"For one who, without a mind of greed, has no possibility even of enjoyments;
and for one who, without [worldly] capacity, has the renunciation of kṛcchra and other such penances. (4)
He whose daily [observance] is impaired by the affliction of diseases such as fever, and who fails to perform the Cāturmāsya rite without [the necessary] independence; || 5 ||
O one of great intelligence, listen to what is prescribed for his benefit:
namely, the knowledge of the proper measure for the fulfillment of tactile enjoyments. (6)
The ends of those perceptions that are heart-pleasing are drenched with the oblation;
indeed, the seeds of ceremonial enjoyments have been established.

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva himself analyzed those various causes of faults and stated their respective remedies with the words beginning "lobhabuddhim" (the mind of greed). "Without the mind of greed" means without the desire for material objects; the sense is that [such enjoyment] would be impossible or perish without it. "Of whom" means of which person acting as the agent. "The impossibility or loss" refers to the non-occurrence or destruction of enjoyments—whether they be mental, tactile, or consumable.

The meaning is: "Listen to that which is beneficial—namely, the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta) prescribed by the scriptures as a benefit for whichever person the non-attainment or loss of the Cāturmāsya vow might occur due to dependence and lack of independence; and [listen to] the 'filling' of the 'measure of wealth' (*mātrāvitta*) consisting of gold, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth, which is given daily at the time of worship for the sake of the objects of enjoyment related to touch (*sāṃsparśika*), such as garlands and sandalwood."

The meaning is that it serves to fill the gaps created by the loss of enjoyments. For those things designated as "heart-pleasing" which are edible, food soaked in *havir*—that is, anointed with clarified butter (*ājya*)—is the filler. For the secondary enjoyments such as the royal umbrella, chowries, and so forth, various seeds such as mung beans and others, prepared for the sake of the sacrificial measure (*mātrā*), are the fillers. (4–7)
The Cāturmāsya restraint consists of the fulfillment of vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, combined with special modes of worship.
This beautiful and auspicious daily recitation from the Sūtras, like a variegated string of pearls,
always brings peace to those who are devoted.

Having thus explained the expiation for the omission of ritual enjoyments (*bhoga*), he now shows the expiation for the omission of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other observances with the words "of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth. For the vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, the restraint of the *Cāturmāsya*—that is, the rules for the *Cāturmāsya* vow described in the eighth chapter—conjoined with special worship, serves as a supplement (*pūraka*).

Now, he demonstrates the expiation for the omission of daily rites (*āhnikalopa*), which follows in sequence: the *pratisara* known as *pavitra*—variegated, auspicious, resembling a string of pearls, made from thread or linen cloth, and so forth—is an ornament for devotees; it "brings peace" (*śamaṃ nayati*), meaning it leads to the pacification of the fault arising from the omission of daily rites. It should be understood that this expiation applies even to the omission of the *cāturmāsya* vows, because those are included within the daily rites themselves. For this very reason, no separate expiation for them is mentioned.

And thus, when there is the occurrence of omissions regarding mantras, ritual actions, substances, and so forth, vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* are performed. The vow of the *Cāturmāsya* (four-month rite) fulfills those [other vows], and the *Pavitrāropaṇa* (consecration of the sacred thread) fulfills even that. Therefore, it is stated that this [rite] serves as a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). And so he will say explicitly: "Having performed the act of fulfillment for asceticism, charity, vows, the prescribed daily rites (*āhnika*), and all sacrifices and enjoyments... (8–9).
And one should perform that during the four months, on an auspicious day,
from the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha until the end of Kārttika.
That period, from the full-moon day until the end of the lunar month,
lasts from the Cancer transit (saṃkrānti) until the completion of the Libra portion.
That period of eight fortnights, known as the solar *madhyama*, is characterized by the four-month season beginning from the eleventh day [of the lunar month]. || 12 ||
Know that time to be indeed Vaiṣṇava, the most excellent, which bestows all perfections;
for until this time is attained, there may be some obstacle.

Therefore, demonstrating its procedure in detail, he first states the time for its performance with the words beginning with "And that" (*tacceti*). Starting from the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha—that is, from the full moon of Āṣāḍha—until the day of the full moon in the month of Kārttika; know that this entire duration is the lunar measure known as *cāndra*, and that it is the final or lowest [measure].

From the transit of the sun into Cancer until the exhaustion of the [solar] course through Libra; that is, beginning from the sun's entry into Cancer up to the end of its occupation of Libra. Alternatively, it means until the exhaustion of the enjoyments in Libra—that is, the fruits such as rice and grain—up to the point of their reaping and gathering. Or else, it means until the conclusion of the "course" (ābhoga), which signifies the full extent of the month of Libra.

Know that the time consisting of eight fortnights—that is, that which has eight fortnights—is called the solar time (sauramāna) and is considered middling. The time characterized by the four-month period, beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and ending on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika—meaning the duration of four months—is called the Vaiṣṇava time (vaiṣṇavamāna) and know that it is the best.

In the *Pārameśvaravyākhyāna*, regarding the passage "ekādaśyādi cānto yaḥ," it is written: "The beginning (ādi) is the commencement on the eleventh day; therein lies the sacred ford (tīrtha). This requires investigation. (10–13)
However, due to some obstacle, this period has not yet been reached. || 13 ||
Another time may also be carried out by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.
He says "because of non-attainment" (aprāpteḥ) [in verses 13–14], meaning that when the superior time is not obtained, the Veda is to be practiced during inferior times and so forth.
And in the midst of that, one should duly perform the completion of the sacrifice.
During the three days previously mentioned, characterized by the full moon and other such occasions,
those observing a fast should perform the preliminary rite of Prātisarya.

He states that the *pavitrāropaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread) should be performed during any one of the three most excellent times, using the word *saṃpādya*. The meaning is that it is "to be accomplished" or "must be performed. *Tanmadhye* means "among those," specifically among the three periods beginning with the most excellent. *Yāgapūrakaṃ* means that which fills the gaps in the worship of the Lord. *Paurṇimādyupalakṣite* means "characterized by the full moon," i.e., occurring on the full moon day, the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), or at the time of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*). *Prātisarīyakaṃ pāvitrakam* means the sacred thread (*pāvitraka*) intended for each respective occasion. || 14–15 ||
Having performed worship on the tenth day and offered oblations into the fire at the onset of night,
one should invite the Lord of Gods and offer incense preceded by the arghya offering.
O Imperishable One, you are eternally satisfied by enjoyments consisting of your own bliss;
nevertheless, I, being satisfied by devotion, worship you for the sake of my own spiritual perfection.
Having offered mouth-fresheners and other items, and having spoken thus regarding the tooth-stick,
he should then worship [the deity] with fragrant substances and a collection of white threads.
Having colored a single auspicious refuge, or many equal to it,
with saffron and other pigments according to their beauty and one's own ability, || 19 ||
It should be adorned with flowers made of Jāmbūnada gold, embellished with various jewels,
along with their stalks, or else with beautiful ones fashioned from silver.
Having fumigated a new vessel, covered it with a cloth, worshipped it with the *praṇava*, and placed it before the Lord. (21)
Having encircled the temple of the gods— both the exterior and the interior sanctuary known as the *yāga*—
four times with a white thread of that same quality.
Then, having entreated the assembly devoted to the five times and the group of Vaiṣṇava ascetics intent on the six duties, he [spoke].
"In your presence, I shall worship the Lord with devotion tomorrow; therefore, please grant your presence out of a desire to favor me. (24)
On the eleventh day, one should indeed perform the ritual acts such as bathing with special care;
thereafter, remaining intent on recitation and praise, one should carry out the entire sequence of rites ending with the fire-oblation (havana).

Having stood before the one to be propitiated, one should spend the night in vigilance. Now, beginning with the words "on the tenth day" and ending with "one should spend the night in vigilance," the author describes the rite known as the *pavitraka* (purification) to be performed on the tenth and eleventh days. "Having performed worship" means having worshipped according to the prescribed rules within the water-jars (*kumbha*), the mandala, and the images (*bimba*). "And having offered oblations into the fire" means having fully gratified the deity in the sacrificial fire; for thus, the worship of the four locations has been established in the *Īśvara*, *Pārameśvara*, and other scriptures regarding the days of preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and so forth.
Alternatively, in the phrase "having performed worship," only the worship of the image alone may be intended.
But when the consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is performed for the image alone, [the procedure is as follows].
Then, the consecration and the worship as described should be performed for the image itself;
likewise, one should avoid performing them for that which has entered the fire within the mandala of the pitcher.

Thus, according to the teaching of the *Pārameśvara*, for one who is unable to perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) over two days, the consecration should be performed on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) alone; for one who is unable even then, the consecration is to be performed immediately. Prior to the consecration, the placing of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) have been taught. As stated in the *Īśvara*:
"On the tenth or the eleventh day, one should first perform the preliminary consecration rite;
or, as an alternative, one should perform the consecration on the eleventh day."
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the twelfth lunar day, or if one lacks the capacity,
on the day preceding the preliminary consecration, after having performed the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
"On the day of the consecration (adhivāsa), the director of the rite should perform the binding of the protective cord. Thus it is said; and likewise in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Having performed the sowing of seeds as before on the seventh day prior, and having performed the consecration (adhivāsa) as before during the two days preceding [the main rite]," so it is stated.

"O best of the twice-born! If there be an absence of materials or a lack of capacity, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) immediately on the twelfth lunar day according to one's ability. Thus it is said.

On the day of the preliminary consecration, following the worship at the four locations, one should offer a single *pavitra* to each [deity] in the passage beginning with "and having invited the Lord of Gods" (*ānimantrya ca deveśam*). This is likewise stated in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras].

Having prostrated before the Lord of the gods of gods, he then took a single purifying thread (pavitraka) that had been purified by burning and moistening, and sprinkled with the water of the arghya offering.
"Having perfumed [the image] with incense and fragrance while it is situated in the four positions,
and having offered [oblations] in due order, one should present incense preceded by the *arghya* offering.
Thus it is stated in the section on the preparation of the *pavitra*.

"For the sake of addressing the All-pervasive Lord who has descended into the four stations, one should offer a purifying thread (*pavitra*)—either one for each [station] or two for each—which is primordial and peerless.

In this regard, although the number of threads, the arrangement of knots, the preparation of the interior, and so forth regarding these *pavitra*s have not been stated here, they should be understood as taught in the *Īśvarapārameśvara* and other such scriptures. Alternatively:
According to one's desire, with threads fashioned as one pleases, or with knots made at will,
or even with the sacred ash (niśā), yellow pigment (rocanā), or the metal of the purifiers.
O Brahmins, someone should duly tie knots [in the thread],
having filled the interior with flowers, or otherwise simply [without them].

Thus, since even the abbreviated procedure (*laghupakṣa*) for both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [tantras] has been stated, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) even if the rules for stringing together the threads (*tantugranthi*) and so forth are not obtained from another source. If it is objected: "But surely, since even the fashioning of a thread according to one's own desire (*yathecchāgranthikalpana*) is not mentioned in the root text, that too must indeed be taken from elsewhere," we say no; for the fashioning of the thread is established by the very phrase "resembling a necklace of pearls" (*muktāhāropamam*). In the passage, "Having wound it with a white thread fourfold, with its own quality (*tadguṇena*)," the meaning of *tadguṇena* is "fourfold" (*caturguṇena*).
For, having wound it fourfold, one should [construct] the sacrificial temple from within.
Performing four circumambulations while recollecting the armor mantra (varmamantra).
Thus, because of this explicit statement in the Pārameśvara [Tantra]. (16–26)
Having again worshipped the Lord of Gods at dawn according to the prescribed rites, || 26 ||
One should indeed adorn him with ornaments, beginning from the head with the *praṇava*;
and with many appropriate forms, one should speak this with palms joined in reverence: || 27 ||
Neither out of pride nor out of delusion have I abandoned my duties;
you alone know everything, O Lord of All, who dwells within the heart. (28)
O Supreme Lord, even though I acted there without desire and according to my ability,
this action was performed by me for Your sake and for Your pleasure.
Having spoken thus and having honored the four Pāñcarātrikas with devotion toward the Blessed One, according to his ability, with garments and wealth.
Likewise, having gratified with various kinds of pure food the celibate students, ascetics, and elders who have reached the end of the Pratisarā; || 31 ||
Having asked for forgiveness and followed [the deity] out, one should take one's meal preceded by the offering of *naivedya*.

Then, on the morning of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), after performing the daily worship (*nityārcana*) and the worship of the four stations (*catuḥsthānārcana*), there is the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra-samarpaṇa*). Following the presentation of the sacrificial food (*havirnivedana*) and other rites, one should offer prayers with the two verses beginning with "nāvalepāt" (not out of pride). Then, through the ritual service to the Lord, he describes the worship of the four types of performers—beginning with the celibate student (*brahmacārin*)—and of the devotees (*bhāgavatas*), including the offering of the sacred thread, the consumption of the sacrificial food, the seeking of forgiveness for transgressions, and the performance of the personal sacrifice (*svānuyāga*), using the verses beginning with "punarabhyarcya deveśam" (having again worshipped the Lord of Gods).
"By coverings" means by garments; such is the meaning. (26–32)
On another day, he should perform renunciation according to the prescribed rules.
Having removed the garlands and other offerings, one should offer new ones day after day,
until they reach a state of withering, or one may discard them on the fourth day.
Regarding that, he states the dismissal of the *pavitra* on the very next day with the half-verse beginning "on another day.

Alternatively, while performing the daily dismissal of the flowers alone, he says with the verse beginning "having removed" (along with the following half-verse) that one should perform the dismissal of the *pavitra*s specifically on the fourth day, preceded by a special worship. Beyond this, the installation of the *pavitra* for both the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the Supreme Lord (*Pārameśvara*) is also stated:
"for one night, or three nights, or five, or seven nights."
Having established the pavitraka, one should then perform the renunciation ceremony (saṃnyāsa).

"Or rather, O Brahmin, having set aside the ornaments, one should remain [in that state] until the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Kārttika has arrived. Furthermore, many other specific details required here should be observed in the works concerning Īśvara and others. (32–33)
But preceded by the special sacrifice, at the appropriate time for the Kāris;
when this has been done, then eternal accomplishment (siddhi) occurs.
In every way, however, the heart's desire of those who worship is likewise [fulfilled]. || 34 ||
He states the fruit of this with the words "thus" (evam). || 34 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Sacred Thread," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrīmauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Regarding austerities, gifts, vows, and the prescribed daily rites (āhnika),...
Having performed the act of completing the enjoyments of all sacrifices without remainder. || 1 ||
On another day, indeed, one should perform the bathing of the deity to be worshipped with mantras on the fourth or the seventh day, at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or at a confluence of rivers.
In a river flowing to the ocean, or in a natural pool, or in a lake, for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord and for the pacification of one's own suffering. (3)
For the delight of the immortals and for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
for the nourishment of all beings and for the welfare of the worlds.

For the sake of pacifying the defects of the land and for the welfare of cows and Brahmins, the fifteenth chapter will now be explained. Having thus performed the rite called *pavitrāropaṇa*, which fills all deficiencies, he states with the verses beginning with "tapaḥ" that on the day of its removal (*avaropaṇa*), the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the deity must be performed immediately thereafter. (1–5)
It has many branches with unbroken tips, together with its roots, yet it has not flowered.
Facing east and taking up a blade of darbha grass, he should first sprinkle the ground with the syllable *praṇava*;
then, with that same [blade], he should establish its root as before.
One should worship its central stalk, which remains in a subordinate position,
and meditate upon it as pervaded by the Great-Souled Lord of Mantras.
Know that transformation belonging to the Supreme Self to be what is called direct perception—
that stalk which contains many embryos, is lofty, and is the most excellent among all stalks.
The *puṃs-tattva* (the principle of the individual soul) is conceived as being endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest;
its designator (*vācaka*) should be employed as that which is joined with the *haṃsa* and possesses two characteristics.
The fourfold [structure] preceded by the mind (citta) should be strung together externally with its own words, facing downwards and ending in the unmanifest (avyakta). 10.
With [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) characterized by subtlety;
likewise, one should similarly bind the five [senses], such as hearing and the rest, with their own names.
Thereafter, he binds the organs of action, then the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātras),
and then the pentad of gross elements, ending with the earth element.
With the remaining stalks, one should bind it like a raft, up to the limit of the top-knot cluster,
or even without that cluster, reaching as far as the crown of the head.
And from a certain point above that, it indeed does not return again;
thus, a multitude of shafts has been conceived in many ways according to the number of the principles (tattvas).
Furthermore, when sections have become separated or one has been broken, a state of alteration arises; therefore, one should bind it firmly. (15)

To that end, he describes the method for fashioning the *kuśa*-brush with the verses beginning with "bahuśākham" (having many branches). "Bahuśākham" means endowed with many stalks (*kāṇḍa*). With that very *praṇava*, one should make its root—the root of the *darbha*-cluster—presided over; the meaning is that one should contemplate it as being pervaded by the Supreme Self. "The transformation (*vivarta*) belonging to the Supreme Self," meaning ending in the form of the Blessed Lord. "Called the Presider (*adhyakṣa*)" is an epithet of the transformation. The "Presider" is a specific variety of the subtle form of the Blessed Lord. Thus it is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "O twice-born, that great gross body of His is the locus of all mantras."
One should meditate upon that which has entered into the subtle, the perceptible, and indeed that which possesses both natures.
But others [say] that the supreme, which is of the nature previously described, is subtle and possesses both natures;
that supreme one, whose form is radiant, rests upon the supportless state.

"One should contemplate [the mantra] as having entered the heart-lotus by way of the path of accomplishment" (iti). "The reality" (tattva) means the individual soul (jīvātman); "its designator" (vācaka) means the life-mantra (jīvamantretyarthaḥ). "Joined with *haṃsa*" means joined with the syllables *haṃ* and *saḥ*. "Characterized by two" means consisting of two words. And thus, the extraction of that mantra is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"By the immeasurable thread (*aprameya-sūtra*), by the one called space (*vyoma*), and by the nectar (*amṛta*)."

"Or else, by means of the self as declared in the *Tritāra*, conjoined with the Supreme Lord. This very meaning is clearly elaborated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The word that refers to the inner self (the *pratyagātman*) is 'Soma,' and then [the word] 'Sargavat'. And thus, the mantra signifying the individual soul (*jīva*) should be understood as "I am He" (*ahaṃ saḥ*). "Preceded by the mind" (*cittapūrvakam*) means the fourfold group of principles (*tattva*) known as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). "With their own words beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*" means with the respective names in the dative case, encapsulated by the syllable *Oṃ* and the salutation *namaḥ*.

The organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. The pentad of subtle elements consists of the five beginning with the subtle element of sound. The pentad of gross elements consists of the five elements beginning with space and ending with earth; this is the qualification [of the term]. By the remaining stalks—meaning by the *kuśa* stalks in addition to the twenty-five stalks [of the sacrifice]—[the meaning is established]. (5–15)
In this manner, the purificatory grass-bundle (pavitraka) produced from darbha shoots should first be prepared;
therein, the mantra and meditation are to be applied according to their established form.

Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth, and having adorned [the deity], one should recite this. Having thus prepared the sacred thread (*pavitra*) and worshipped the Blessed One there preceded by meditation, one should pray; thus he says in the verse beginning with *darbhamañjarījaṃ* (along with its half-verse). In the absence of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) or an image, however, this preparation of the *darbha*-sacred thread should be performed. When those are present, it should be understood that the bathing in the sacred water itself is to be done. Likewise, in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*, it is said: "One should perform the bathing properly in a sacred image, especially in the case of a *tīrtha*."
Or, in the absence of those [specific images], one should perform it upon an image intended for daily bathing.

"One should perform [the rite] in the image that is intent on perpetual festival; in its absence, in the sacred thread (pavitra); and in the absence of that, in an auspicious cluster of darbha grass. (16–17)
O Blessed One, you alone are the sacred ford; you alone are the supreme sanctuary.
I know in truth that everything is presided over by you alone;
and therein, the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) ordained by you bestows auspiciousness.
"That which I shall now carry out today out of a desire to favor you"—with this intent, he spoke the two verses of prayer beginning with "tvam" (you). (17–19)
Having thus made this request, O Blessed One, [he beheld] the mantra-form, both supreme and inferior.
Having placed him upon a leaf-plate or indeed upon a vehicle of Brahmā, preceded by auspicious sounds such as the chanting of the Vedas, the singing of hymns, and the blowing of conchs; || 20 ||
Having led it to the vicinity of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and having placed it there on the bank,
he then took the vehicle facing eastward and the purificatory grass (pavitraka).
One should form [the gesture] as if upon the earth-maṇḍala on the palm of the left hand,
while holding it with the middle part of the right hand.

Having descended into the midst of the water, he should indeed immerse himself along with it. Having thus informed [the deity], having placed that purifier (pavitra) in a vessel or on a *brahmayāna* (a palanquin for the Veda), and having brought it to the vicinity of the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) accompanied by the sounds of Vedic instruments, he should deposit it there facing the east. Taking the purifier and placing it in the palm of his left hand as if it were resting upon the orb of the earth, and grasping its center with his right hand, he should descend into the middle of the sacred bathing place and bathe together with it—thus he says "evam" (in this manner) in four verses (19–23).
Indeed, they quickly establish their presence there at that very moment.
And all the holy bathing places (tīrthas) situated throughout the three worlds remain for a moment at that reservoir of water, in the form of mantra, for the sake of protection.
In that place, there would be a gathering of all the sacred sites and pilgrimage centers; how much more so where the Blessed One, Adhokṣaja, resides in the form of mantra! 25.
Requested by the practitioner, he should bathe with a mind intent on bestowing grace upon all.
At that time, at that sacred ford (tīrtha), he describes the power of the presence of all holy fords through three verses beginning with "sannidhim. (23–26)
The wise man, a knower of reality, who has reached a sacred ford by this method; || 26 ||
One should bathe kinsmen, friends, and others; by the grace of the Mantra-form, they shall soon obtain the fruit of pilgrimage without effort. (27)

Thus, with the verse beginning "The learned man" (vidvān), [the author] states in one and a half verses that even for people situated in distant lands, bathing at a sacred site (tīrthasnāna) yields fruit by means of a tuft of grass (kūrca). In the phrase "of kinsmen and others" (bāndhavādīnām), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object; the meaning is "those kinsmen and others. (26–27)
But the ritual procedure should be performed without that vehicle and its musical instruments;
know this, O one of great intelligence, to be the specific distinction in this rite. (28)

Regarding this, he states the distinction with the words "but" (kintu). The meaning is that the mounting upon a vehicle and being accompanied by auspicious musical instruments are fit for the Blessed One alone, and not for anyone else. || 28 ||
Having meditated upon that swan-like soul, which is the universal, indestructible, and divine form consisting of consciousness, and which is connected with the designations of particularity; || 29 ||
Having visualized the *pavitraka* in that same form, he should then bathe it with water;
in this manner, he may likewise bathe many others, either with that same [single] thread or with many [threads].

Since this body has become the very body of the Blessed One, one should remember it too as being identical with the Blessed One and cause it to be bathed through the sacred vessel; thus he says in the two and a half verses beginning with "sāmānyam. (29–30)
Indeed, for those situated at a distance, the bath should always be performed using seats;
O high-minded one, when the bath has been thus completed, on the second day— || 31 ||

He says "thus" (evam) to indicate that one should cause the bath to be performed for many relatives and others using either a single purifying thread (pavitra) or with separate purifying threads; the meaning is for those who are far away, such as those who have gone to another village or those who have passed to another world. || 31 ||
When the ceremonial bath has been completed in this manner, O Mahāmati, on the second day—
Having placed him upon the honored chariot and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites,
one should perform the festival known as the Procession (yātrā), preceded by the distribution of food.
Accompanied by dancing, singing, and instrumental music, and joined with a vigil for one night, two nights, or three nights, performed with devotion. (33)

Thus, immediately after the *avabhṛtha* bath, having placed the Lord who resides in the *pavitra* upon the *brahma-ratha*, having worshipped Him, and having performed His ritual propitiation, one should conduct a festival procession by circumambulating the village; so he says in two and a half verses beginning with "sampanna. The intention is that after the festival, a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) should also be observed during that night. The repetition for two or three nights applies only to the festival, not to the bathing. (31–33)
He who performs once a year at the end of the year a festival consisting of ritual bathing and other rites for the Lord of Mantras attains supreme accomplishment.
In the section concerning the Pavitrotsava festival, he states the fruit [of the rite] with the words "once" (sakṛt) and so forth. || 34 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Purificatory Bath," in the venerable *Sātvatasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Sātvatatantra-bhāṣya composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrīmauñjyāyana family and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The sixteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
O lords of sages, the Lord was again addressed by the one wearing a garland of forest flowers.
But hereafter, I shall speak that which is for the benefit of the entire world.
Now the sixteenth chapter will be explained. Here, the Lord says, "I shall speak that which was asked of Vāsudeva by Saṃkarṣaṇa. (1)
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord, those Brāhmaṇas and others who have entered into this sequence—how are they to be initiated? This is what I wish to know.
He states the manner of the question with the word "deva" (O Lord). || 2 ||
The Blessed One said:
"O wielder of the plow, hear from me in due order the threefold means of initiation for the castes as they have been described— briefly stated, it bestows all perfections."
Being thus questioned, Vāsudeva said, "Listen to the means for the threefold initiation in due order. || 3 ||
Having understood the characteristics previously described, a certain exceptionally steadfast man,
terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, desires nirvāṇa.
Possessing a mind steady through dispassion, he remained for a long time in the house of his guru in the state of a servant, free from weariness and agitation.
He states with two verses beginning with "pūrvokta" that, for the sake of initiation (dīkṣā), residence in the teacher's household must first be undertaken.
Having ascertained his need, one should certainly summon him, seat him before oneself,
and inquire regarding what has been done and what remains to be done, from that moment until the time of death.
Having correctly understood the strength of the fault,
one should diligently purify it through the prescribed penances, beginning with the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*.
