The Teacher says that, having understood the strength and weakness of those faults, he should effect their pacification through the prescribed expiations; this he states in two verses beginning with "jñātvā" (having known). 6–7.
O wielder of the plow, however, due to the inability [to endure] many afflictions,
[the period may last] until the mind becomes serene, or for twelve days.
He should be employed in the measurement [of the vessel], in purification, in begging for alms, in eating only at night,
and in the effort of offering praise, sweeping, bathing, and gathering flowers and other such items.
In the hermitage of the Vaiṣṇavas, within the divine temple of the Lord,
one should constantly behold the form of the Blessed One from the pedestal upward.

He says in three verses beginning with "bahūnām" that, for those unable to fast for many days, one should engage them in meritorious acts such as hymns of praise to the Lord for twelve days, or until their minds are purified, or even by eating only at night (*naktabhojana*). Regarding the phrase "beholding the form of the Lord from the pedestal": this means seeing the image of the Lord from the base up to the crown;
for one who beholds Puruṣottama from the pedestal to the top of the head, sins perish instantly—how much more so minor offenses (*upapātaka*)!
Because of this well-known fact. || 8-10 ||
He whose body was previously defiled by evil deeds has now had his mind purified through devotion to the Blessed One.
Having fasted for a day and night, with his nails and hair shorn,
he should then prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with water containing kuśa grass, using the heart-mantra and the others.
Having consecrated it four hundred times with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva,
the wise one should thus bathe Him with that [mixture] for four days.
Every day, four times from dawn until the arrival of night,
he should fill the fourfold Brahma-tīrtha again and again and drink from it.

Having sipped water for purification at intervals with the mantras recited in succession, one should eat until satisfied; at the end, one should consume food consecrated with milk and clarified butter.
Or one may subsist on fruits and roots for four days and nights;
thus, for those who have surrendered with devotion, [the Lord] protects them from evil even as long as life lasts.
Today I have described to you this supreme expiation for those who have desisted from sin, which effects the purification of the body and is accompanied by the Brahmakūrca rite.
He describes the expiation accompanied by the *brahmakūrca* rite with the verses beginning "abhijātatanuḥ" and so forth (11–17).
Having previously understood the magnitude of the three kinds of faults,
one should constantly practice the giving of gold and other gifts whenever the opportunity arises.

He says "having known" (jñātvā) to indicate that even the giving of gold and other such acts should be performed when there is an excess of defects; the meaning is "of the three kinds," namely, those of body, speech, and mind. || 18 ||
From the previously prescribed time, there shall be a reduction by a fourth part for one who has committed a minor offense in due order; thereafter, one should drink the *brahmakūrca*.

He says "from what was stated before" to indicate that during a time of distress (doṣakāla), one should effect a reduction by a fourth part of the previously mentioned period for the Brahmakūrca penance. Thus, the general penance for the Brāhmaṇa caste has been declared. || 19 ||
It is said that there is a commonality with respect to time and the excellence of color;
for expiation indeed destroys all defilements for everyone. (20)
Having understood the progressive severity of the first misdeed,
the lord of the twice-born should extinguish it by means of fasts lasting two, three, or four months respectively.

He states in two verses beginning with "by time" that even when there is an excess of [bodily] humors (doṣa), an increase of two, three, or four months should be made there as well; the meaning is that one should exhaust—that is, destroy—that evil deed. || 20-21 ||
One belonging to the royal (Kṣatriya), Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste should increase [the period] by one [month] respectively, beginning from a period of one month and so forth in due order. 22.
He states that the expiation increases twofold, threefold, and fourfold respectively for kings and others, beginning with the verse "nṛpa" (verse 22).
Even one who was formerly of evil conduct, an eater of all things, ungrateful, and an atheist,
would take refuge with faith in the Primordial God if he were to seek shelter.
Know that person to be faultless by virtue of the power of the Supreme Self;
how much more so one who, afflicted by remorse, is established in this teaching! (24)

One who has desisted from evil deeds and has taken refuge in the shadow of devotion becomes free from fault even if he is intent on transgressing the Lord’s command, solely by virtue of having sought refuge in Him. To show how the faultlessness of one who is devoted to this teaching and has sought refuge is established as a matter of logic, He says "durācāra" (of evil conduct) in two and a half verses. By the phrase "desisting from what was done and not done," the renunciation of all [worldly] duties is indicated. "In the shadow of devotion" means that whose shadow is like the shadow of devotion—that is, having sought refuge. (23–25)
Thus, for those whose faults have been completely purified, as well as for that which has been accumulated over many births, || 25 ||
O high-minded one, for the sake of destroying impurity, having first performed the Narasiṃha rite,
one should now bestow the initiation preceded by the mantra.
For the propitiation of that very Lord of Vaibhava is indeed to be performed properly for four months, both externally and internally. (27)

Having first understood the strength of their disposition for eight months or a year, and having recognized the pure intentions of those worthy of liberation as well as the grace of the Supreme Lord; (28)
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the initiation known as *vibhavavyūhasūkṣmā*.

Since the previously mentioned expiations, such as the *brahmakūrca*, only serve to pacify those defects committed in this present birth, one should also grant the initiation into the Nṛsiṃha mantra for the sake of pacifying the defects accumulated over many previous births, and have him perform the worship of Nṛsiṃha through that mantra. Then, having ascertained his mental purification and so forth, as well as the Lord’s grace upon him, one should grant the initiation into the mantras of the Supreme (*para*), the Manifested (*vyūha*), and the Empowered (*vibhava*) forms. He states this in four verses beginning with "evam" (25–29).
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
By what signs is it to be recognized that the sins of practitioners have been destroyed? (29)

"O Lord of Kamalā, through correct propitiation, grace is obtained from the mantra; how is it to be known that the favor of the Blessed One has arisen therein? Thus Saṃkarṣaṇa asks, [referring to it as] "that which is to be fully understood. (29–30)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Your serenity of mind is indeed incomparable, and your increase of splendor is truly extraordinary."
For those who possess qualities such as fortitude, enthusiasm, contentment, and lack of miserliness, it should be understood that the mantra-soul stands present before them. (31)
If the application of rites such as those for pacification (śāntika) and so forth achieves success even without delay, one should understand that this is due to that very cause.
The King of Mantras, when perfected, burns away evil and is serene; if applied, it bestows virtue, pleasure, and wealth before long. (33)
The eightfold powers beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as various other yogic accomplishments,
together with the perfection of the self, were then remembered as being fully satisfied.
Being thus questioned, he states the causes for that knowledge with the words beginning "serenity of mind" (cittaprasāda) and so forth. (30–34)
In whatever manifestation or form one's mind finds delight,
one should indeed perform initiation with that very [form] for the sake of pacifying one's impurities.
Having propitiated him and having engaged him for the aforementioned period,
[he did so] for the sake of testing his fitness regarding all matters until the final dissolution.

Thus, there is no fixed rule that the initiation (*dīkṣā*), worship (*ārādhana*), and so forth must be performed solely with the *Nārasiṃha* mantra for the purpose of destroying misfortune. Regarding the *vaibhava* mantras, he says in the verse beginning with "yasmin" (and continuing for one and a half verses) that whichever [mantra] one has a preference for, by that alone it should be performed. The previously mentioned time refers to a period of four months, eight months, or a year. (35–36)
For the purpose of examining fitness regarding all things until the attainment of peace. || 36 ||
Or by means of the Nārasiṃha mantra, or any other mantra of one's choice,
through initiation, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, vows, and so forth.

By means of ritual action alone, and through extremely exalted pacification rites, even without the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, one understands that sin has gone to destruction. (38)
At that time, O lotus-eyed one, he should meditate [on this].

Since the initiated person, by virtue of seeking liberation, is devoid of desire for all objects and thus lacks even rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*), the destruction of his sins is to be understood through signs such as the clarity of mind alone, rather than through the signs of specific supernatural powers (*siddhi*). This is stated in the three verses beginning with "of the fitness" (36–39).
For the attainment of the greatness of the sixfold qualities of the majestic supernatural powers (siddhis). || 39 ||

For the sake of attaining supreme bliss and prosperity, one should receive the three excellent initiations from a preceptor who is well-pleased, who has been requested [for instruction], and who has consented.

Immediately following that, he states with the verse beginning "siddhīnām" (and a half) that one should request the Guru and receive from him the three initiations of Paravyūha, Vibhava, and so forth. || 39-40 ||
Out of compassion, or even without being requested by them,
he should act for those whose sins have been purified, who are terrified, and who seek refuge.
For it is indeed appropriate for refined and disciplined people in the task of washing away their sins. || 41 ||

He states in the [verse] ending with "with compassion" (sānukampena) and the following half-verse that even if not requested, the Guru should himself, out of grace, bestow initiation upon worthy disciples. || 41 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Pacification of Sin," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The seventeenth chapter.
Nārada said:
Then, O best of sages, the Lord of Śrī was further impelled.
For the benefit of those who fear worldly existence, this was composed by the Lord Sīrapāṇi.
Now, the section on the Śrīnṛsiṃhakalpa will be explained. Here, Vāsudeva was questioned by Saṃkarṣaṇa; thus [the author] says "atha" (now). 1.
Saṅkarṣaṇa said: By what rite does the Lord, the protector of the universe, the man-lion, attain favor toward men who worship him? (2)
He states the manner of the question with the words, "O Blessed One. || 2 ||
Having heard this, the Blessed One spoke: "Listen as I speak;
[I shall teach] the mantra that bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation, which is majestic, embodied, and the conqueror of delusion."
The color-wheel of the great-souled Nṛsiṃha, which eternally assumes forms at will, has been previously described; it should be kept well-concealed beneath the surface of the earth.
Being thus questioned, Vāsudeva said, "First, listen to the Nārasiṃha mantra," and having heard this, [the king did so] with the half-verse. (3–4)
The previously mentioned wheel of syllables (varṇacakra), however, [should be drawn] on a well-concealed spot of ground.
Having smeared [the surface], then having drawn [the diagram] and worshipped it according to the rule,
one should then extract the mantra of manifold and wondrous power.
Having first taken the Praṇava and joined it at the end,
[one takes] the ninth from the letters of the navel, and above that, the fourteenth from the spokes (arā).
Above that, one should place the syllable situated within it like a sphere;
this syllable, ending with "namaḥ," is indeed the designator of the Supreme Self.
The six qualities, beginning with knowledge, have indeed been previously mentioned as being located in the heart and other centers;
for that very purpose, one should simply write that syllable in its sixfold form.
One should duly apply [the letters] from the second, fourth, sixth, twelfth,
penultimate, and fourteenth positions of the group in their proper sequence.
One should mark all [the limbs] with the seed-syllable on the head, excluding the fifth;
for all of them, the Praṇava (Oṃ) is placed first, and one's own name is applied at the end.
At the end, one's own mantras should likewise conclude with "vauṣaṭ" in their proper order;
however, [the mantra] beginning with "Oṃ namo bhagavate nārasiṃhāya" [is used for the lion-mantra].

Having first remembered [the deity] as possessing a physical form by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, one should worship with the primordial mantra together with its limbs, abiding both externally and internally.

He explains the extraction of the *nṛsiṃha* seed-syllable preceded by the arrangement of the wheel of letters (*varṇacakra*), the methods for its limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), and the twelve-syllable mantra with the words beginning "the wheel of letters" (*varṇacakra*) and so forth. "The previously mentioned" means that which was stated in the ninth chapter. "Above that" means above the letter *kṣa*; "the fourteenth spoke" refers to the vowel *au*, and "above that" means the *anusvāra* situated within it. Thus, it becomes *oṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ*. "That alone" means the mere letter *kṣa*.

By the second, fourth, and sixth [vowels], namely *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*; by the twelfth, *ai*; by the last, the *visarga*; and by the fourteenth, meaning *au*—this is the sense. The phrase "from the group of consonants" (*arādvargāt*) applies everywhere. "With the head" means with the *anusvāra*. "Excluding the fifth" means excluding the seed-syllable accompanied by the *visarga*. "One's own classes" refers to the six classes beginning with *namaḥ* and *svāhā*. Thus, for example: *oṃ kṣāṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ kṣīṃ aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā*.

Oṃ kṣūṃ, to Power (śakti), for the crest (śikhā), vauṣaṭ; Oṃ kṣaiṃ, to Strength (bala), for the armor (kavaca), hūṃ; Oṃ kṣaḥ, to Prowess (vīrya), for the weapon (astra), phaṭ; Oṃ kṣauṃ, to Splendor (tejas), for the three eyes (netratraya), vauṣaṭ—these are the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra). || 4-12 ||
Then, having obtained authority and been initiated with this mantra,
the wise man, devoted to faith and constant in his practice, remains free from doubt.
Always delighted by the commands of the guru, forever free from the web of speculative reasoning and idle talk,
he is constantly devoted to his own duty— whether he be a forest-dweller or a householder.
Listen to the procedure by which one should propitiate the mantra.
He states, "Now," with two and a half verses [13–15], that one who has previously been initiated by this mantra should perform the propitiation of the Blessed One.
Having previously acquired all enjoyments indeed by righteous means. || 15 ||
Having bathed, with his waistband tied, observing silence, wearing clean garments, and holding the arghya water and flowers,
he should perform the worship of the deities stationed at the door and so forth, and then sit upon his seat.

Demonstrating the procedure for that worship, [the author] speaks with the verse beginning "upārjya" (and a half-verse) regarding, first, the procurement of the materials for worship; the rules for the worshipper such as bathing and so forth; and the taking of one's seat after first worshipping the deities of the door. It should be understood that because the actual sequence of performance (*krama*) is more authoritative than the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), the acquisition of offerings (*bhoga*) occurs immediately after bathing and other preliminary rites. Alternatively, the meaning "previously," i.e., on the preceding days, should be explained, since offerings such as rice grains can be collected even on previous days, provided flowers and the like are not required.
In the evening, one should perform this purification of the elements through the two types of concentration (dhāraṇā),
accompanied by the mantra alone as well as by meditative visualization (bhāvanā).

Now, he says "sāyāmām" [in the verse], meaning that one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). This refers to the two types of *dhāraṇā* consisting of burning (*dahana*) and nourishing (*āpyāyana*). Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "The fivefold *dhāraṇā* and the two-fold [process] have been prescribed in brief."
"And through burning and nourishing, when [the practitioner acts] for the sake of his own purification from the body," thus [it is said]. (17)
Having meditated on the deity situated at the region of the navel and having gathered the impurity,
one should cast it out through the path of the breath up to the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
Having drawn in the mantra-lord, which is free from evil and accompanied by the wheel of breath, through the tip of the nose for the purpose of filling the body; || 19 ||
One should meditate upon that [Self] residing in the heart by means of the breath with its movement restrained,
for the purpose of calming the mind and indeed for the mastery of the vital air.
Then, one should gradually expel only the external air;
thus, for the others, each subsequent [breath] is performed without the final exhalation (recaka).
One should always perform this according to one's capacity, with a gradual reduction over time;
then, one should [visualize] the Lord of Mantras at the *dvādaśānta*, resembling molten gold.

He describes the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with four and a half verses beginning with "situated in the region of the navel" (*nābhideśasthitam*). By the path of the wind means by the path of the wind at the end of the first exhalation (*recaka*) of breath control. Accompanied by the wheel of air means accompanied by the wind of the second inhalation (*pūraka*) of breath control. By the wind whose movement is obstructed means by the wind of the third retention (*kumbhaka*) of breath control. This has been explained in exactly this way in the *Nityavyākhyāna*. (18–22)
Then, at the dvādaśānta, one should contemplate the Lord of Mantras, resembling molten gold.

Then, having meditated upon that which resembles a thousand suns situated in the center of a circular mandala, and having released it from the subtle elements (tanmātras), one should burn away one's own body.
Then, having meditated on the syllable of the crest at the tip of the big toe of the right foot as having the form of the fire at the end of an eon, enveloped in flames.
With that, one should meditate upon one's own form blazing forth on all sides;
one should contemplate the flame born of the body as having dissolved into the Lord of Mantras.
Having mentally focused upon that divine and tranquil form,
one should sprinkle one's own body with a stream of nectar from one's own mantra.

Then, having drawn that image along with its mantra, one should place it within the heart. He describes the method for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in five verses beginning with "at the *dvādaśānta*. The meaning of "at the *dvādaśānta*" is at a distance of twelve finger-breadths above the crown of one's own head. And so it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Having caused Hari to exit through the southern door from the *suṣumṇā* [channel] to the outside..."
Resembling a thousand suns, situated in the center of a circular mandala,
he sat in the supreme station, radiant with the hue of molten gold.

"But having meditated upon him as the very essence of the mantra, twelve finger-breadths above," [it is said]. "Released by the subtle elements" means released by the subtle elements beginning with smell (*gandhatanmātra*) according to the sequence of the withdrawal of the principles (*tattvasaṃhārakrama*). "From his own mantra" means from the Lord residing at the *dvādaśānta*, who is the object denoted by that mantra. "That image" refers to the deity situated in the center of the circular maṇḍala twelve finger-breadths above one's own mantra. (22–27)
Then, one should assign the radiant twelve-syllable mantra to both hands.
From the wrist to the tips of the nails, preceded by the root mantra,
[the mantras] from the heart to the weapon are placed upon the fingers beginning with the thumb.
"In all [fingers], by means of the joining of pairs, the eye is placed upon the nails and the tips.

He describes the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with two verses beginning with "atha" (now). The "twelve-syllable [mantra]" means the previously mentioned twelve-syllable Nṛsiṃha mantra. "Preceded by the root mantra" means preceded by the previously mentioned seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha. "By means of the joining of pairs" means simultaneously on both hands. (27–29)
One should place the twelve-syllable mantra upon the body, from the top of the head down to the feet.
One should likewise place the root mantra, which constitutes the living soul and resides within that [body],
as well as the six limbs beginning with the heart and ending with the eyes, each in its own proper location.

He describes the *aṅganyāsa* (placement of limbs) with two verses beginning with "from the head" (*āmūrdhna*), [stating that it is] in the form of radiant energy (*tejorūpa*) without shape (*vinā ākṛteḥ*). "In one's own sphere" means in the locations such as the heart and so forth; "with one's own pair of fingers" means by means of the mudrās of the heart and other limbs to be described; "without shape" means being formless (*nirākāra*). || 29-31 ||
On the left side of his chest was the Śrīvatsa mark, possessing a luster like that of the full moon.

Having placed upon his chest the Kaustubha gem, which possesses the brilliance of the fierce-rayed sun, and having placed around his neck a forest garland produced from various lotus groves and flowers; || 32 ||
One should place a lotus in the right hand and a conch in the left hand;
furthermore, a mace in the lotus-hand and the king of discs in the conch-hand.
Then one should place a sword in the right hand and a bow in the left hand;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should place Śrī on the right side and likewise [the other deity] on the left.
One should place Puṣṭi ending at the ankles, and Sarasvatī in the middle of the face;
then, one should place Nidrā behind with both hands.

He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the ornaments, weapons, and powers with the verses beginning "Śrīvatsam" and so forth. In this manner, the placement of the ornaments and other items should also be performed on the two hands; for it is not prescribed that the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) alone should be done without the hand-placement (*karanyāsa*) for any of the mantras. And thus it is said in the *Pārameśvara*: "That supreme power of the All-pervading Lord which resides within the hollow of the heart-lotus..."
Assuming a wind-like form, she is established in ten ways;
by her own will, she has emerged through the flow [of breath] via the path of the hands.
Relying upon the ten channels, those very [channels] are considered to be the fingers;
for this very reason, O best of the twice-born, in the form of the Lord known as Śakti.

"Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of the collection of mantras, one should then perform the placement upon that which consists of the elements. Thus, although this mental activity known as nyāsa is traditionally taught,
it does not establish a firm state properly without ritual action.

"Furthermore, since that [power] is dependent upon the hands, the prior placement (nyāsa) of those two is prescribed. And for this very reason, in the *Īśvara-pratyabhijñā*, the *Parameśvara-pratyabhijñā*, and other texts, the placement of the crown (*kirīṭa*) and so forth is also mentioned for the hands. Moreover, this is the intention of the author of the root-text as well; otherwise, he would not have mentioned the placement of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and others on the hands here. (31–35)
Having formed the mudrā, one should contemplate the visualization and cultivate the thought, "I am the deity.
Then, with the name preceded by the Praṇava and accompanied by a salutation— (36)

One should first arrange the seat ending with fire (the syllable Ra), preceded by the remainder (the syllable Ha). Then, having ascended that [seat], one should perform its visualization within one's own heart.

He states the contemplation of one’s own divinity, preceded by the display of the *mūla* and other mudrās, with the half-verse beginning "the mudrā. This has been clearly stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* as well:
"I am that Blessed Viṣṇu; I am Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
indeed, I am Vāsudeva, the all-pervading, the abode of beings, the stainless one."
"O Sage, having attained such a very firm ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)... [Thus it is said].

One should not, on this basis alone, suspect an identity of nature between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the Supreme Soul (paramātman); for in the third section of the *Śrī Pañcarātrarakṣā*, the *Samārādhanagrantha* is also established as follows: "After performing the placement of marks (*lāñchana*) and so forth, having formed the ritual gesture (*mudrā*), one should meditate upon the Lord and contemplate, 'I am the Lord'. Other texts from various *Saṃhitās*, such as "Having formed the root-gesture (*mūlamudrā*) and others, one should contemplate, 'I am the Lord'," follow the same reasoning here.

In this context, as in passages such as "one should meditate on the mind as Brahman," the fact that these are injunctions for contemplative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is very clear due to the presence of the particle *iti* and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated that even through such a form of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), one merely attains immediate fitness [for the next stage], as in the case of the deposition (*nyāsa*) of divine mantras through the contemplation of identity with the deity:
"By performing the limbs [of worship] in a non-material way, the practitioner becomes worthy of the rite of adoration (*pūjā*)."
Otherwise,

having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa within his heart, he should worship himself in the form of the deity with offerings of water for honor (arghya) and incense, along with other enjoyments concluding with incense.

Thus, how does the immediate subsequent duty cohere? For in the contemplation of identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-aikya*), there could be no further meditation on Nārāyaṇa in the heart. Nor is the contemplation of identity of essential nature appropriate for one who is engaged in the remaining duties (*śeṣa-vṛtti*). Therefore, the position of a "rule of viewing" (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*) must be accepted here. Or rather, since another alternative is possible, it is not proper to intend a rule of viewing; hence, the designation [of the Self as Brahman] occurs because it persists in all [states] through its being the body of that [Brahman], its dependence upon it, and so forth.
And with that intention, the author of the Bhāṣya will state "svaniyāmya" (governed by oneself) and so forth; thus it has been very clearly established. || 36 ||
Then, with his own name preceded by the syllable Om and accompanied by a salutation, || 36 ||

One should first arrange the seat ending with fire (the letter Ra), preceded by the remainder (the letter Ha). Then, having stepped upon that very [seat], one should perform its visualization within one's own heart.

Now, with the verse beginning with *atha*, [the author] states that for the purpose of worshipping Mānasa, one should perform the ritual arrangement (*parikalpana*) of the *pīṭhas* starting from Ananta and ending with Agni within one's own heart, using their respective names in the dative case followed by the word *namaḥ* preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ). In the *Pārameśvara-tantra*, however, following the method described in the *Jayākhyatantra*, the arrangement of the waking seat (*jāgradāsana*) in the heart is taught through such passages as "one should meditate between the navel and the penis. But since the dream seat (*svapnāsana*) is mentioned here [in this text], the division of locations mentioned there should be understood here as well, according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, the distinction between the dream and waking seats is shown in the *Pārameśvara* itself.
The dream state consists of the seat beginning with Śeṣāhi and ending with Vahni;
the waking state consists of the seat beginning with the Ocean of Milk and ending with Bhāvāsana.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 36–37.
Having brought to rest all conceptual constructions, one's own pure consciousness, which is the stainless nature of Brahman, manifests by its own will from that state of transcendence.
Furthermore, by means of the nature of the sound of another [word], through its essence as light, and again through the state of manifestation—
even when that [manifestation] has thus dissolved— (39)
The dismissal, however, should be understood as occurring when the sequence of ritual actions is completed;
this is the procedure for the invocation of the mantras taught in the Krama system. (40)

Then, following the sequence of worship (*ārādhanā*) which is the process of the manifestation of the Lord upon that seat, he describes the sequence of dismissal (*visarjana*) with two and a half verses beginning with "the nature of Brahman" (*brahmasvarūpam*). "Free from conceptual construction" (*vikalpoparatam*) means devoid of specific attributes (*viśeṣaṇarahita*); that is to say, it is of the nature of pure knowledge (*kevalajñānasvarūpa*).
As for the statement, "The mind expands conceptual construction within the group of the sense organs;
conceptual construction is the manifold arrangement, and that is called a specific attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*)," [it refers to the state prior to such mental activity].
The connection with a property (dharma) is said to belong to the substratum (dharmin).
This conceptual construction (vikalpa) is to be known as fivefold, according to substance, action, quality, and so forth.
Thus it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*. The meaning is that it "manifests" (*vivartate*) again, becoming manifest through its connection with specific attributes. (38–40)
This is the sequence for the descent of the mantras taught in their respective orders.
Indeed, the mental visualization of the branding and other rites, as well as their conceptualization, must always be understood by the worshiper during every single ritual act. (41)

He states that this very sequence of invocation and so forth is to be understood for all propitiations of mantras as well, by means of the verse beginning with "the sequence" (krama), which consists of one and a half [verses]. || 40-41 ||
Then, O Lord, one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for the All-pervading One without the placement on the hands;
having meditated, [one should worship] with the most purifying enjoyments born of contemplative realization (bhāvanā). || 42 ||
Having performed worship and concluded the recitation (*japa*), one should bring [the deity] down and perform the external sacrifice.

Then, having worshipped within one's own heart with mental offerings—preceded by the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) of the Blessed One—until the conclusion of the sacrifice of recitation, one should perform the external sacrifice; thus he says in the verse beginning with "mantranyāsam" (42–43).
And having meditated with the seed-syllable of the heart using both the right and left hands. || 43 ||
Thereafter, one should produce the Sun and Moon, which arise from the burning of the substances.

Demonstrating the procedure for the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*), he first describes the showing of the mudrās for the burning and replenishing of the *arghya* and other offerings, beginning with the words "with the right [hand]," etc. (vv. 43–44).
Then, having taken water in a vessel, one should pour it there while consecrated with the heart-mantra.
One should consecrate very white śāli rice, endowed with the fragrance of flowers,
many times with the Heart-mantra preceded by the syllable Om.
Or, reciting the Astra-mantra, one should sprinkle the place of one's seat with water drawn from that [vessel],
while also reciting [the mantra] over the ritual implements.
He describes the sprinkling of the articles for worship with the two and a half verses beginning with "toyam" (verse 44–46).
Having removed whatever flowers or other offerings have been consumed from the image of the Blessed One situated in the painting,
one should then perform the cleansing of dust with a cloth.
He speaks of the purification of the variegated reflection [in the verse beginning] "from that which stands in the painting" (47).
One should perform the washing with fragrant water for an image made of metal or stone;
then, one should smear the ground with cow dung mixed with water. (48)
He states the purification of that which consists of metal [iron] with the verse beginning "dhātu" (48).
Then, having smeared the ground with cow dung mixed with water.
There, having first drawn the lines for the mandala evenly, one should draw a square with four doors, adorned with paths, pedestals, and lotuses. (49)
Outside the lotus, one should draw a wheel with three naves, a rim, and six spokes,
using pure colors such as white and so forth, or with various auspicious flowers.
Or, having filled it completely with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, along with mustard seeds, sesame, and rice, or indeed with all medicinal herbs.
He describes the method for constructing the mandala with the words beginning "having smeared" (upalipya), etc. (verses 48–51).
Then, having worshipped the arghya vessel with flowers and the partless (niṣkala) mantras,
one should take a small amount of water from that [vessel] into another vessel.
One should perform the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha preceded by meditative reflection (anusandhāna),
using one's own name preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," in the proper sequence.
One should meditate on Ananteśa, the Lord who consists of the support of all, in the center;
then, in the directions starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast, one should meditate on the four [faces] beginning with Dharma.
One should first place the primary [syllable] of adharma and so forth at the beginning of the east, extending to the end of the north;
above that, one should meditate on a lotus by its own name, and likewise above that.
There, one should remember the sun resting upon the moon on the ground of the filaments, and the fire situated within the pericarp; then, one should worship with perfume and other offerings.
He describes the method for the conceptualization of the seats with the verses beginning with "with flowers" (puṣpaiḥ) and so forth. (52–56)
Having first performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the lineage of gurus,
and having obtained permission, he then takes up a water-pot possessing auspicious characteristics.
Having first filled it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
one should then place within its interior gold, gems, seeds, medicinal herbs, and excellent fruits.
Having placed around his neck a cluster of blossoms with leaves from the branches of mango trees and other such trees—
adorned with a garland of silk cloth and anointed with sandalwood paste— 59.
In the center of that, one should worship the mantra together with its limbs and enclosures in due order;
then, having placed a circle of flowers outside the mandala in the eastern direction.
And one should place that [seat] above it, having consecrated it with the *pīṭha-mantra*.

Now, preceded by the worship of the lineage of gurus beginning with Viṣvaksena and their subsequent permission, he describes the procedure for the installation of the great jar (*mahākumbha*) with the verses beginning "the worship of Gaṇeśa and so forth. If it is argued that because of the use of the general term "Gaṇeśa" here, the meaning might be Vināyaka as described in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, *Lakṣmītantra*, *Pārameśvara*, and other texts—that is not so;
for [the text continues]: "Then, with the remaining food offerings (*naivedya*), one should worship the Lord Gaṇapati."
And he who was indeed worshipped at the very beginning under the name Viṣvaksena.
This is because the specific term [for these] will be stated later. For this very reason, it is said in the *Īśvaratantra*:
"Then one should worship Viṣvaksena, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the Gurus; thereafter, one should worship the Gurus known as 'Supreme' (parama), who are the Gurus of all."
[He saw] the assembly of the eternally perfected ones (ādisiddha), who were solely intent on meditation upon the Blessed One,
who possessed perpetual authority, who had attained [their goal], and who knew the true nature of the Blessed One.

The four other *manavas* and the seven ancient *ṛṣis*—thus is the lineage of gurus described. "The eastern direction" (*prāgdik*) means the east; the elision of the case-ending is archaic (*chāndasa*). "Outside the mandala" (*maṇḍalabāhye*) means outside of the previously mentioned mandala. "Charged with the *pīṭha-mantras*" is an epithet of the *cakrikā*; it means she who has been consecrated (*upajaptā*) and worshipped (*arcitā*) with the *pīṭha-mantras*, namely the previously mentioned mantras beginning with Ananta. (57–61)
Then, the mantra of pure radiance should be brought down from the heart.
By means of action, mind, and speech, and through the path of accomplishment,
practitioners [perceive] that which does not abandon its own nature, like the disk of the sun in water.
One should impel [the deity] with ritual action and recite that mantra with speech;
joined with the word "come" (āgaccha), one should mentally visualize the form [of the deity].

Regarding that, he describes the sequence for the invocation of the Blessed One with two and a half verses beginning with "atha. Having stated that the invocation should be performed by means of the three instruments (*karaṇa*), he has also established that at the time of invocation there are three corresponding functions—known as impelling (*preraṇa*), uttering (*uccāraṇa*), and remembering (*smaraṇa*)—pertaining to each of those three instruments. Here, "impelling" should be understood as the offering of the *arghya* water, flowers, and the *añjali*, the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), the bringing about of presence (*saṃnidhi*), the restriction [of the deity], and the displaying of the *sāṃmukhya-mudrā* and so forth. "Uttering" should be understood as being done four times;
the meaning is that it refers to the previously mentioned *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*. (Verses 61–63)
Having thus addressed [the deity], one should indeed offer water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya) with devotion;
this constitutes the complete worship of all mantras, from their very roots, established in their manifest forms.
One should perform [the worship] with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and so forth, each in its own respective place.
Then, the fourfold [mantras] beginning with the heart (hṛdaya) are projected from the body of the Lord.

Having thus described the sequence of services such as the *arghya* and *pādya* for the Blessed One who has been invoked in this manner, he first states the *layayāga* with the verse beginning "evam" (64–65). The phrase "of those situated in manifestation" (*vyaktisthānām*) means those deposited within the divine, auspicious form of the Blessed One. By this, it is stated that immediately after the invocation (*āvāhana*), the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra and so forth should be performed upon the limbs of the Blessed One just as on one's own body. In the expression "with *arghya*, flowers, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes fragrance and incense.
The phrase "by their respective [mantras]" means by each one's own specific mantra. || 64–65 ||
Then, from the body of the Lord, the fourfold [group] beginning with the heart emerged.
One should place [the petals] of the lotus starting from the east and ending at the north;
and on the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, one should place the weapon-mantra (astra) in due order.
The eye situated within the mass of filaments, the discus above the three naves,
as well as the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, and likewise the forest garland.
In the three-spoked wheel located in the northwestern portion,
one should place a lotus and the sharp-edged sword Nandaka in sequence.
Then one should place the triad [of weapons] situated on the front and right sides;
thereafter, the bow, the king of weapons, and the conch shell [should be placed] to the right of the deity.
One should place the goddess Śrī on the portion of the rim, Puṣṭi to the north,
Nidrā situated in the region of the back, and Sarasvatī in the front portion.

Now, he describes the sequence of the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), beginning with the words "Then it has arisen" and ending with "Sarasvatī at the foremost part. The term *cākrīye* is an adjective qualifying the three spokes, meaning "belonging to the wheel. The meaning of *gadām* (the mace) is "that whose tips are sharpened. Regarding these two modes of worship, the distinction between the formless and the formed nature of the mantras, as well as their designation as dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*), has been explained in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"The powers (*śakti*), the six limbs (*aṅga*), the insignia (*lāñchana*), the lotus and so forth..."
The ornaments, beginning with the Kaustubha gem, as well as the three faces,
and the forms beginning with Satya, were conceived within the body of the God.
Since they are all-pervasive in that manner, they should be worshipped in sequence, all of them abiding within his body as manifestations of light, each in its own respective place.
O Brahmin, this Layayāga is indeed proclaimed for Lakṣmī and the others, performed with their respective mantras and flowers and ointments, without a retinue.
Therefore, one should always worship the retinue residing within the body of the root mantra, whether in the support of the heart-lotus, in the [divine] form, or wherever else.
This sacrifice, known as *laya*, is concise and bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The King of Mantras is in the center of the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), while Lakṣmī and the others are in the filaments (*kesara*) and other parts.
All those [deities] are with form and are individual; that which is called "enjoyment," however, O Nārada, exists through the sacrifice alone as something distinct.
"The worship of the lotuses and so forth is designated as 'the domain' (*adhikāra*).

This means they consist of light and have the nature of radiance; that is to say, they are formless. "Without retinue" means without their respective retinues. The implication is that if one were to postulate a retinue for the retinue as well, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). These very same verses are also set forth in the *Īśvara-pratyabhijñā* and *Parameśvara-tantra*, according to the mantra-assignments (*nyāsa*) taught in each respective work. On the left and right sides are two quivers situated along the path.
One should again place the weapon-mantra at the doors and the mudrā at the four corners.

Then, with the half-verse beginning "vāma-dakṣiṇa," he describes the attendants who are to be worshipped on the paths and other areas of the mandala, as well as the world-protectors (dikpālas) with their weapons outside the mandala in their respective places. "Two quivers" means two pairs of quivers. "The weapon at the doors" means the discus (cakra). The word "again" (bhūyaḥ) is used because the discus and mace were already mentioned previously in the context of the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga). || 71-72 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should then meditate upon the array of mantras as they are situated.
The god who consists of all the gods, the treasury of all splendors,
complete with all auspicious marks, and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
He had the luster of refined gold, possessed all limbs in their entirety, and was most magnificent;
his face was like that of a fierce tiger, and his eyes were like the blazing sun.
It was completely covered with hairs resembling a mass of lightning,
possessing the luster of the petals of a red lotus, and its hands and feet were as formidable as diamonds.
With the mane of the lord of serpents quivering, possessing the brilliance of hundreds of millions of moons, and vomiting internal fire through the apertures of his mouth accompanied by winds; 76.
Uttering its own name with a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution,
it stood within a circle of flames from the fire at the end of the age.
The Lord stands pervading the worlds, possessing six weapons and eight arms;
his limbs are anointed with divine perfumes, and he is likewise clad in celestial garments.
He was endowed with divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
and graced by the Kaustubha gem resting upon his chest as well as the Śrīvatsa mark.
The Supreme Lord was adorned with a forest garland composed of jewels, gold, and fine pearls, as well as a sacred thread.
The arms are joined with radiant weapons such as the lotus and others;
then, to the right, there is a lotus white as the ocean of milk.

One should meditate on the excellent conch in the left hand, its interior filled with the resonance of the Praṇava and surpassing a hundred Himalayan mountains in brilliance; and [one should meditate on] the mace and sword, blazing with light.
Then, in his pair of right hands, he holds a discus with the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction, and in his two left hands, a bow;
thus, by means of his two pairs of hands.
One should meditate upon the mudrā called Karma, which shatters ignorance, belonging to the Lord;
in this very same way, one should contemplate the heart-mantra, white as a water lily. 84.
One should visualize the head as being red like a mountain of rubies;
likewise, one should visualize the form of the *śikhā* mantra as resembling a stone of collyrium.
Just as a mountain of gold is heated on all sides by the sun,
so too should one contemplate the armor-mantra at the time of meditation.
Surrounded by thousands of flames and possessing a luster like that of a magnet,
it is proclaimed as the mantra of weapons, fully endowed with the power of all missiles.
The King of Eye-mantras is like a crest of smokeless embers;
these Supreme Persons, endowed with their own respective splendors, are to be meditated upon as having two arms. 88.
The weapons, beginning with the Kaustubha gem, take the forms of a mace, a garland, and an embrace;
and Śrī, possessing the luster of the interior of a full-blown lotus, is joined with a lotus stalk. (89)
Resembling a ray of the moon, she holds a white chowrie;
like the full moon, she carries prosperity in her hand.
Sarasvatī, possessing the luster of crystal, holds a book of supreme knowledge in her hand; she stands before a golden pitcher that is completely filled with nectar. 91.
The goddess Nidrā should be meditated upon as resembling a full-blown blue lotus, her hand marked by a rosary of beads, and all [the goddesses] adorned with fly-whisks. 92.

"Adorned with garments and ornaments in the presence of the God of Gods"—beginning from "having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*), one should then meditate," and ending with "adorned with garments and ornaments," [the author] states the meditations on the root mantras and so forth. The *avidyādalinī* mudrā is to be understood as that which will be described later. (72–93)
Having meditated thus, one should then perform worship with flowers and other offerings. || 93 ||
With baths, ointments, garments, garlands, incenses, and lamps, and with curd mixed with honey and milk combined with clarified butter; 94.
With various auspicious offerings for the deity— heart-pleasing, pure, substantial,
and sanctifying— and with all kinds of fruits and roots produced in their proper seasons, possessing the six flavors.
By means of [deities] that have been worshipped, freed from defects, and characterized by mudrās and mantras;
or likewise by means of embodied meditations, or by means of seeds (bījas) that have been heated, or through fire-offerings (homa) and so forth.
Since this has been explained in detail in the sixth chapter, he states here in brief the sequence of ritual service (*upacāra*) with the words beginning "having meditated thus" (vv. 93–96).
Then, having consecrated his own hands by sprinkling them with water and other rites,
and having formed [the hand-gesture], he should display the three-pronged mudrā (triśikhā-mudrā) facing the Lord.
Having meditated upon the form of the three sacrificial fires (tretāgni) in the three fingers of the right hand—
clearly with upward-pointing flames— that same [middle finger] is the eldest, while the little finger is the youngest.
Furthermore, he is the embodiment of all forms, beyond darkness, and the bearer of the form of fire;
the Lord transcends the three qualities (guṇas) as well as the three paths.
This manifest [Self], freed from grosser elements and worshipped by the intellect, [is attained] by binding the heart-region with both hands in the form of a casket. 100.

He explains the display of the root-mudrā with three and a half verses beginning with *tataḥ*. "With water" means with the *arghya* water; for it will be stated later that the application of the *arghya* is "to sprinkle the hands during the binding of the mudrā. "By anointing and so forth" means by sandalwood paste and the like; by the word "and so forth," camphor, saffron, and other such items are included. The resulting meaning is that one should press the little finger with the thumb of the right hand, straighten the three fingers beginning with the index finger, and display [the hand] facing the Blessed One. (97–100)
Having formed the *sampuṭa* mudrā with both hands at the region of the heart. (100)
This mudrā, formed by the two arms held close together, is known as the *hārdikī* (the heart-related).
Regarding the heart-mantra mudrā, he says it is the *saṃpuṭa*. The term *hārdikī* means "pertaining to the heart. || 100-101 ||
From the thumb to the little finger, each pair of fingers [should be placed] separately.
With an interval from this Sampuṭa, there should likewise be [the mudrās] for Kaniṣṭha and the others;
namely, the mudrās of the head, the crest, the armor, the weapon, and the eye, in their proper order. 102.

He describes the five mudrās beginning with the Śiromantra in the verse ending with "aṅguṣṭhādi" (101–102). As before, having formed a hollow cavity (*saṃpuṭa*) with both hands, one should separate the two thumbs, the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers, and the two little fingers individually, leaving a space between them. These five pairs of fingers, in order from the little fingers to the thumbs, are to be known as the mudrās of the Head, the Topknot (*śikhā*), the Armor (*kavaca*), the Weapon (*astra*), and the Eye (*netra*).
In this mudrā, the pair of thumbs is placed in the middle of the hands; know that from the index fingers down to the little fingers [are used] for Śrī and the others. 103.

He describes the four mudrās of Śrī and the other śaktis with the words "In this [mudrā]": In this mudrā, which is characterized by five pairs of fingers separated individually according to the previously mentioned method, one should place the pair of thumbs in the center of the hand in the form of a pericarp (karṇikā); then, on the four pairs beginning with the index fingers, the four mudrās of Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, Sarasvatī, and Nidrā are to be understood respectively. || 103 ||
Combined with one's own mantra, it should be applied again and again in due order to the others who have been worshipped; this [mantra] should be employed with the heart and the head. 104.

He states "joined with one's own mantra" to indicate that for others, the heart-mudrā itself, together with the head-mudrā and their respective mantras, should be employed. By the phrase "for others," it should be understood that the ornaments such as the Śrīvatsa, the emblems such as the discus (cakra), the deities of the seats such as Ananta, the gurus such as Viṣvaksena, and the retinues stationed at the doors and enclosures are included.

One might object: "But surely the mudrās for these [deities] have also been taught in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. Even there, it is more appropriate to demonstrate the mudrās for those whose mudrās were not explicitly mentioned by means of their heart-mantras (*hṛnmantra*). This is not so, because one must practice according to the specific method prescribed in each respective *Saṃhitā*.

One might further object: "In that case, the *Sātvatopabṛṃhaṇa* has indeed included the Śrīvatsa and other mudrās taught in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. True; however, in that context, a single general mudrā for all mantras is traditionally taught, namely the *añjali*.
"One should employ that [mudrā] conjoined with its own respective mantra.
Since this position stated by Sātvata has also been established, you, long-lived one, need not be afraid. 104.
Facing each other, they are joined with their branches entwined;
however, the right hand is raised upward, while the other is held below. 105.
For this mudrā, which destroys ignorance (*avidyā*), has been previously described.

Now, he states the characteristics of the mudrā of Avidyādalinī held in the hand of the Blessed One with the verse beginning "paraspara... (105–106). Having joined the two hands facing each other, making them adhere to one another and interlaced by their respective fingers, the meaning is that one should place the right hand above and the other below.
Having thus formed the collection of mudrās and performed worship once more for the Lord, || 106 ||
"One should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, specifically one hundred and eight times.

Having shown the previously mentioned *triśikhā-mudrā* and this *avidyādalini-mudrā* to the Blessed One, and having worshipped again with *arghya* and other offerings, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred and eight times, or according to one's capacity. Thus he says "in this manner" (*evam*). The recitation of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and the others should be performed once each; because they are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the worship of the root mantra, there is no fault even if they are recited only once. (106–107)
In this way, the same [procedure] is prescribed for all [the organs], beginning with the heart. || 107 ||

"There is no fault because [the recitation] is an ancillary part of the ritual action; otherwise, there would be a transgression even for failing to perform the recitation once. Thus he says, "Each one," etc. (vv. 107–108).
Having worshipped him and bowed down with the eight-limbed prostration to the Supreme Lord, || 108 ||
Having recollected [the Lord] and received permission, one should then perform the sacrifice directed toward the fire.

Thus, after the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), preceded by prostrations with eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅgapraṇāma*) and the chanting of hymns such as the *Jitantādi*, one should perform the satiation of the fire with the permission of the Blessed One; this is what he expresses by the word "him" (*tam*). (108–109)
Having first fashioned a sacrificial pit with auspicious characteristics, it was consecrated through the traditional rites.
Having worshipped [the deity] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other offerings, and having brought down the fire there—
well-kindled, smokeless, and purified by striking and other means.
Having worshipped with water-offerings (argha) and nimbu-rak flowers, one should meditate upon the sixth quality-group, which is the quality known as radiance (tejas). || 111 ||
Having thus meditated upon this [fire] as the common essence of all splendors belonging to the Supreme Brahman, one should cast it into the center of the sacrificial pit with the Netra-mantra.
Having made that fire smokeless by means of dry, purifying fuel,
and having worshipped it with sacrificial wood, he should then [place] the mantra-maṇḍala in its midst.
Having meditated upon and worshipped him as before, and having gratified the Lord together with his retinue one hundred thousand times with oblations of ghee and sesame seeds; 114.
One should properly offer the *pūrṇāhuti* after announcing the total number of oblations (*homasaṃkhyā*).

The sequence for the satiation of the fire is stated starting from the word "kuṇḍa" and ending with "after announcing the number of oblations. "Possessing good characteristics" means endowed with the characteristics described in the eleventh chapter. "With purificatory rites" means with those described in the sixth chapter, such as smearing and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having worshipped with *arghya*, flowers, and so on," the method previously mentioned—namely, "having worshipped that [fire] with *arghya*, flowers, and so on, one should meditate upon it as if it were the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*)"—is to be understood here as well. Regarding the phrase "thoroughly purified by striking and so forth":
Having struck him with the weapon-mantra, one should sprinkle him with water from the crest-mantra.
One should worship with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and likewise envelop [the deity] with the armor-mantra;
then, O Nārada, one should drench [the deity] with nectar using the eye-mantra (netra-mantra).
"Then, having offered it by means of *pūraka* [breathing], one should lead it to rest within one's own self.

Thus, the consecrations such as *tāḍana* (striking) and so forth mentioned in the *Jayākhyatantra* are to be adopted. They are also summarized thus in the *Īśvaratantra*: "With *samits*," meaning with the seven types of *samits* previously mentioned; "the circle of mantras," meaning the collection of mantras beginning with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Having announced the number of oblations (*homasaṃkhyā*), the words "to the Blessed One residing in the mandala" are to be supplied. (109–115)
Then [he took] those who were pure, fasting, purified, and had their eyes bound. || 115 ||
One should cause the devotees, who have indeed taken flowers in their hands, to enter there;
and having released the blindfold from their eyes, one should cause them to cast [the flowers] within the maṇḍala.
Then, with prostrations made on all eight limbs accompanied by circumambulations,
the deity, the fire, the preceptor, and the water-pot should be worshipped again and again.
When their capacity—whether intense, mild, or otherwise—is recognized at that time through a state of devotion, then one should perform the initiation for them. || 118 ||

For the sake of the purification of the manifest, the wise one should indeed offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and likewise of clarified butter with the twelve-syllable mantra. (119)

Thereafter, having worshipped with the mantra using the arghya and other offerings, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) along with the collection of limb-mantras according to the previously stated number.
One should perform [the rite] for the sake of purifying the unmanifest, and then offer the *pūrṇāhuti*;
likewise, one should do so with the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*) for the purpose of restoring the original nature.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) unweariedly, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namas," while meditating upon Him who is free from bonds, pure, peaceful, and all-pervading.
Then, out of compassion for his devotees, the knower of mantras should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), filled with all consciousness, using the root mantra.

At this juncture, he describes the procedure for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the disciples into the *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*, beginning with the words "Then, being pure" (*tataḥ śucīn*) and ending with "out of compassion for the devotees" (*bhaktānāmanukampayā*). "Purified" (*śodhitān*) means those who have been thoroughly cleansed by the previously mentioned rites of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), such as the *brahmakūrca* bath. "He should cast [them]"—the ellipsis implies "the flowers held in their joined palms. "The God" (*devaḥ*) means the deity residing within the mandala. "At that time" (*tatkālam*) means with a state of devotion characterized by the signs of devotion to be described later, such as horripilation, tears of joy, and so forth.

"For the purification of the manifest" means for the sake of purifying Prakṛti when it has assumed its gross state in the form of the Mahat-tattva and the rest. "With the twelve-syllabled [mantra]" means with the twelve-syllabled Nṛsiṃha mantra. "With the collection of limbs" means with the group of six mantras beginning with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). "For the purification of the unmanifest" means for the sake of purifying Prakṛti when it has assumed its subtle state. "For the purpose of restoring the essential nature" means for the sake of purifying the conscious principle (cetana). "With the root-mantra" means with the seed-syllable (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha. || 115–123 ||
Thereafter, one should cause him to hear the pledges (samaya) regarding the water-pot, the fire, and the mandala.
"By whatever devotion you have attained that which pertains to this world and the next," [so it is said].
One should not abandon her through action, thought, or speech.
One should certainly not omit the ritual bathing and other such duties unless there is a specific purpose for doing so.
For as long as one lives, according to one's ability, wherever one may be situated—
in places such as the heart and so forth— one should perform the worship of the assembly of mantras.
One should perform worship with substances beginning with flowers and water; however, in their absence, one should offer mental worship as before, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should regard the Lord of Mantras, the Guru, and the Mantra with equality;
one should maintain the supreme secrecy regarding the mantras, mandalas, and mudrās. 128.
Even from afar, one should pay homage to the king of beasts or to a tiger;
however, another animal of similar form or its skin should never be mounted anywhere.
One should not step over it with one's foot, nor should one touch a bed or similar furniture;
likewise, the vessel for eating should be made of lotus leaves or leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
Likewise, one should avoid a seat marked with a conch, a lotus, or similar symbols;
nor should one perform a nocturnal fast or a fast involving total abstinence on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
One should perform special worship on all the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs),
as well as during the solstices and other such occasions, and at the sun's transits (saṃkrāntis).
One should never perform an exorcism for those afflicted by spirits, planets, or diseases using a mantra that has not been mastered.
Whatever sign of accomplishment born of mantra has been experienced, whether in a dream or even directly, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru. (134)
Wherever the manifest seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is seen, one should pay homage after worshipping it with the flowers of speech and by performing circumambulations. (135)
Having shed tears or experienced grief caused by separation,
one should certainly not perform the libations to the gods, the fire, and the ancestors without first bathing.
Except during the period until the umbilical cord is cut, when there is an overlap [of impurities], one must diligently avoid the aforementioned rites known as *sūtaka*. || 137 ||
Since one's own practice has indeed been derived from a particular scripture, one should diligently perform its worship and maintain its secrecy. (138)

One should protect Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as the poor and the helpless, according to one's ability. In this manner, one should grant the rules of conduct (*samaya*) to devoted disciples whose minds are purified. 139.
Indeed, by the preservation of these [mantras], one shall obtain the fruit born of mantra;
having thus performed the sacrifice, one should then perform the sprinkling with the water-pot.

Now, he explains the manner of instructing the disciples in the *samaya* (vows/pledges), beginning with "afterwards he should cause them to hear the *samayas*" and ending with "he shall obtain the fruit born of mantra. The meaning of the first rule is that one should not abandon, even by means of the three organs [of body, speech, and mind], that devotion directed toward the Blessed One residing in the *kumbha*, the maṇḍala, and so forth, through which the attainment of fruits pertaining to this world and the next occurs. "Without the goal" (*sādhyaṃ vinā*) means without [the practice of] consuming medicinal herbs and so forth. "Bed and so forth" (*talpādikaṃ*) means a bed made of tiger-skin and so forth.

In the phrase "he should not touch," the word "with his foot" is to be supplied by ellipsis. "Paripīḍam" means a fast consisting of pure food. "Until the time of the increase of the navel" means after the cutting of the umbilical cord; the sense is that prior to that, there is no state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Thus Jaimini says: "As long as the umbilical cord is not cut, so long one does not incur *sūtaka*;
once the cord is cut, thereafter *sūtaka* is prescribed."
And in this manner,
one should give here gold, or land, a cow, a horse, a chariot,
an umbrella, a goat, clothing, garlands, a bed, a seat, or a house.
When a son is born, the ancestors and the gods come to the house; whatever wealth there is in the home—grain, molasses, sesame, clarified butter, or anything else—is theirs.
"Therefore, it is declared in the *Tādi-parvan* of the *Bhārata* that this is a day of merit.

Even according to the manner stated thus, the established meaning is clearly that Śrī Nṛsiṃha alone is to be worshipped. It was previously stated that the concealment of the mantra, maṇḍala, and mudrās [is required]; by the phrase "one's own practice," it should be understood that the concealment of the scripture is also intended. (Verses 124–140)
Having thus performed the sacrifice, one should then perform the sprinkling with a water-pot.
Then, having first partaken of it himself and requested it for his devotees,
he should take up that which has been offered and give it to a Brāhmaṇa, while reciting the king of mantras.

He describes the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the disciple with the water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*) in the half-verse beginning with *iṣṭvā*. This sequence is to be understood in detail as it will be explained further on.
He states in the half-verse beginning with *ātmanaḥ* that one should request oblations (*havis*) for each deity for the sake of one's own sacrifice and for the payment of the ritual fee (*kāri*).

He describes the payment of the ritual fee in the half-verse beginning with *brāhmaṇāya*. Here, the singular form *brāhmaṇāya* is used because this is the section concerning the worship of the single-form Nṛsiṃha, whereas previously it was the section concerning the worship of the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*).
Having worshipped them with perfumes and incense, he then [honored] those [deities] who consist of the Blessed One.
"Having worshipped them in due order and presented the food offering," thus it is said;
having spoken thus and worshipped the four Pāñcarātrikas.

Thus it should be understood that four types of performers have been described. Even there, in the case of incapacity, only one is mentioned in the seventh chapter; at that time, it should be understood that this single [performer] possesses the nature of the four forms (caturmūrti). "Having extracted the king of mantras deposited [in the fire]" means having withdrawn the three mantras deposited in the sacrificial oblation (havir). This very point has also been stated in the *Pārameśvara* and other texts:
"and having placed them upon the cooked rice (odana) offered to the deity, which has itself been deposited [there]."
"The mantrin should extract the excellent mantras endowed with power, vigor, and so forth, yet devoid of [excessive] taste and potency,
preceded by 'Oṃ,' and then [perform the withdrawal] with the *saṃhṛti-mudrā*. Thus,
[he should invite those] who are perfected in the knowledge of the Vedānta and established in the prescribed conduct.
Having summoned them and worshipped them in due order with offerings of water for the hands, fragrant scents, and so forth.
Having taken what remains of the Blessed One's [offering], and having retrieved the mantra that was deposited,
one should divide it into four parts at the time of the preliminary offering.
"One should give them a single portion of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and other foodstuffs for consumption, preceded by the water of honor (*arghyodaka*).

Thus, since the giving of the *kāri* (wages/fee) was previously stated to be before the fire-oblation (*homa*), and it is now stated that the giving of the *kāri* may also occur after the oblation, it follows that its performance is required at either of these two times. (140-141)
Then one should ask forgiveness from the deity wherever [the image] was brought down;
thereafter, with the remaining offerings, one should worship the Lord Gaṇapati.

He who is indeed worshipped with arghya and other offerings under the name Viṣvaksena, [the text] says "one should ask for forgiveness" (kṣamāpayet) by means of the half-verse concerning the expiation of offenses. The meaning is: "in whichever [place]—in the pitcher (kumbha), the mandala, or the fire. He describes the worship of Viṣvaksena with the word "atha" (now). The term "remnants" (śiṣṭaiḥ) means those remaining after the payment of the laborers' wages.
With food offerings, madhuparka, and other such items, presented to the principal image.

"By means of what remains after the twice-born have consumed it, but excluding one's own consumption," because this is explicitly stated in the section on the worship of Viṣvaksena in the *Pauṣkara*. (142-143)
Then, with food of pleasing form and water, [one should offer] with the heart-mantra.
Then, the mantra-practitioner should cast the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) by moving clockwise from the outer place of worship, starting from the east and ending at the northeast.
Then, with one and a half verses beginning with "in the form of caru," he describes the offering of bali to the elements, Kumuda and the others.
Then, having withdrawn everything, one should perform the dismissal,
casting the leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth into the midst of the water.
Previously, having extracted a small portion for the sake of purification, he should first eat it silently after consecrating it with mantras, being free from desire.

The dismissal (*visarjana*) is stated by the half-verse beginning with "tataḥ. It should be understood that the dismissal here refers to Viṣvaksena; however, the dismissal of the Lord (the deity) must be performed prior to the worship of Viṣvaksena, and this is indicated by the very statement: "Then one should ask forgiveness from the deity wherever He was brought down."

Since the detailed procedure for this has been taught in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, stating that Viṣvaksena is to be worshipped in that very same place—in both the mandala and the fire—immediately after the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the Blessed One, and since it is required here; the meaning is: "having withdrawn the entire assembly of attendant deities and having dismissed them."

With the verse beginning with "vinikṣipya" (and the following half-verse), he describes the throwing of leaves, flowers, fruits, food, and so forth into the water after the worship of Viṣvaksena; the setting aside of a small portion for one's own consumption before that [offering]; and the consumption [of that portion] after that worship. Here, by the word "niṣkāmaḥ" (desireless), it is understood that for one who has desires (*sakāma*), even if a portion has been set aside individually after the worship of Viṣvaksena, its consumption must be avoided. Thus, the statement on the authority of the Āgamas in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā* says:
"Because garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, have been offered for the sake of the Lord..."
Thereafter, it becomes unfit for enjoyment due to being taken possession of by Viṣvaksena.
"For this very reason, the Sātvatas partake of the food offerings and so forth even before that [offering to the deity];
therefore, that is the cause of their excellence alone. (145–146)
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, when the onset of night has arrived,
one should perform the recitation of mantras and meditation, preceded by the libation of water.
In the same manner, the worshiper must constantly perform meditation along with recitation throughout the remainder of the night until sunrise. 148.

Now, following the meal, [the author] describes the evening meditation (*saddhyāna*), the recitation of mantras (*mantrajapa*), the worship (*arcana*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) with one's own mantra in the midst of water at the time of evening, and the meditation and recitation from that point until sunrise, by means of two verses beginning with "at the end of the meal" (verses 147–148).
Having worshipped in this manner day after day, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times; thereafter, the king of mantras becomes perfected.
"It grants all the desired perfections (siddhis) appropriate to everyone.

Thus, when the disciples have performed the recitation (japa) numbering one hundred and eight thousand times daily preceded by the worship of the Lord, the perfection of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) occurs, and from that, the perfection of one's own desired goal also occurs; so he says with the half-verse beginning "evam eva" (149–150).
This has been declared by me for Rudra, the Ādityas, Indra, the sages, and my devotees.

In accordance with the minds of the world and according to the distinctions of the ages, there are indeed the scriptures, the sacrifice, the sacrificial implements, and the pure images and so forth. (151)
That must be understood by you correctly and without contradiction at all times, from the scriptures and from those who know them, for the sake of self-realization. (152)

He states that "what is not mentioned [here] should be taken from elsewhere" by means of the verses beginning with "Rudra, Āditya," etc.; the meaning is "without contradiction," that is, without contradicting the meaning stated by himself. || 150-152 ||
Now, what has been stated here in brief should be spoken elsewhere in detail.
Now, the mantra is fully accomplished through restraints such as celibacy and the like. (153)
Listen to how a practitioner of mantras should employ milk, barley-gruel, vegetables, water, ghee, roots, and fruits in rites for pacification and other purposes. 154.

"Listen to the sequence for the application of the mantra—accomplished through such observances as consuming milk and barley-meal, and the practice of celibacy—in rites for pacification and so forth," he says with the two verses beginning with "atha. (153–154)
Having first understood [the state] through even worldly characteristics arising from one's own body, and having attained the application of dreams, [one perceives] the stability of life. (155)
Then, having reached a beautiful place free from thorns, covered with a net of arrows or else a house in the sky, [he remained there]. 156.
There, having drawn the mandala provided with all necessary implements,
[one should do so] with sandalwood and kṣoda, joined with the moon.
It was filled with fragrant śāli rice powder— possessing the characteristics previously described—
and was free from blemishes, endowed with auspicious marks, and saturated with filtered water.
Its interior filled with gold, gems, medicinal herbs, branches of trees, dūrvā grass, and fruits, it was wrapped in a cloth that had been fumigated, beaten, and dried. || 159 ||
And one should place the eight jars for the directions and intermediate directions outside the mandala, situated on a well-prepared base, using a straight thread as a guide.

Its body was smeared with lime and sandalwood paste, it was filled with parched grain and rice, it was provided with a white cloth neck-tie, and it was adorned with a garland of white flowers. || 161 ||
One should likewise place eight small jars (upakumbhas) upon the [main] jars, each filled with pearls and adorned with seed-vessels (bījamallakas).
Having tied eight jars together with white thread, they should be provided with white whisks and a white canopy above.
Having wrapped it firmly with the severed skin up to the region of the neck, and having done so, one should then bathe; thereafter, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) and other rites.
With night-water, sandalwood paste, and white dūrvā sprouts, one should write the name, with the [mantra] contained within it, upon a very smooth birch-bark leaf. || 165 ||
One should fashion [the seed-syllable] joined with the seed-syllable situated at the edge of the spokes; outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp should be drawn. (166)
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with its face turned downward, having the letters as its petals;
within that, one should write the supreme Lord of Mantras, ending with the fourth vowel.
Then, having drawn the ninth [syllable] outside the lotus, not too far from the *praṇava*,
one should indeed write it twice, facing upwards and downwards along the rim.
Having wound it with a white thread, one should place it in the *arghya* jar;
having set it upon a base of rice flour at the front of the mandala. (169)
Having invoked the mantra from the cavity of the heart into the mandala as before,
one should then worship the Lord of Mantras there with white offerings.
Having meditated upon [the deity] together with his retinue, resembling a hundred moons, emitting the essence of nectar situated within a full moon disc, [one should proceed]. 171.
One should recite "Grant, grant great peace" at the conclusion of the worship;
