then, in the northeastern direction, there is a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) characterized by a full moon.
One should perform the fire-oblation for seven nights with milk, rice, honey, clarified butter, guggulu resin, sesame seeds, and sandalwood.
Consuming only milk, one should worship the Supreme Lord for eight watches;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, [one should bathe the deity] with cool milk from the water-pot.
One should perform the sprinkling with water every day for eight watches;
at the conclusion of the bath, one should meditate upon the Lord of Mantras above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Thus, as the nectar flows forth, there arises eternal peace;
or else, having taken a vessel made of clay, or one of split bamboo, or one of wood. (176)
There, one should perform the arrangement as with lotuses by means of fragrance;
and having ignited [the fire] with ghee, [one should offer] vessels made of flour. || 177 ||
Then one should perform worship with the eight lamps and offerings such as bali; having scattered the seven seeds that have been steamed above that [altar]. (178)
Then, once the water-pot has been worshipped, one should place an incense burner [nearby];
with the flow of incense smoke uninterrupted, one should offer the bali-oblation at the three times of day.
For the sake of the peace of the protectors of the land and likewise for all beings,
one should indeed pour a continuous stream of water seven steps behind [the image].
For the sake of pacification, one should cause the offerings for the bali-mantras to fall by means of the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Thus has the procedure for pacification been explained; now learn the procedure for nourishment (pauṣṭika). || 181 ||

First, he describes the ritual for pacification (*śānti*), beginning with the words "having known" and ending with "and this is the procedure for pacification. "With *śaśin*" means with camphor. "Name" means the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The method regarding the name of the person to be accomplished has been set forth in the *Pārameśvara*, while the nature of the pervasive name will be explained again later.
If the seed-syllable and its power (śakti) are at the end of the *tārā* [syllable Om], and that is its presiding deity,
then [one attains] peace, nourishment, subjugation, victory, and so forth.
Having first uttered the word ending in the accusative case, followed by the repetition of "kuru" (do),
then either the word "yaccha yaccha" (grant, grant) at the end, or [the mantra] preceded by the syllables ending in *praṇava* (oṃ).
"And at the end, one should mark it with the characteristic of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

This means "containing the *sa*" (i.e., containing the letter *sa*). "By the seed-syllable situated at the end of the spokes" means by the *anusvāra*. "The fourth from the navel" refers to the letter *va*; "ending in the fourth from the navel" means ending in *va*. "Lord of Mantras" refers to the seed-syllable of Śrī Nṛsiṃha. "The ninth from the rim" means the letter *ṭa*.

And so is the ritual procedure: first, having ascertained the stability of one's life through worldly signs arising from one's own body and through the attainment of dream-yoga, and having reached an auspicious place free from all thorns, one should prepare a sacrificial hall covered with a canopy of cloth or a net of arrows; therein, upon a central altar, one should fashion a square mandala with four doors, adorned with lotuses for the paths and seats, using fragrant rice-powder mixed with sandalwood powder and camphor.

Having drawn the mandala according to the described characteristics—namely, a wheel with three naves, a rim, and six spokes outside the lotus—one should place a great jar (mahākumbha) on a supporting base in the eastern part outside the mandala. This jar should be flawless, endowed with auspicious marks, filled with strained water and camphor, and replenished with gold, jewels, all medicinal herbs, sprouts, dūrvā grass, and fruits; it should be wrapped in well-perfumed, unwashed white cloth. Having arranged eight similar jars in the eight directions surrounding it, one should fill them with rice and smear their bodies with lime and sandalwood paste.

Having placed eight secondary jars (upakumbha) upon the directional jars—each with its neck wrapped in white silk, adorned with garlands of white flowers, their bellies filled with pearls, and covered with bowls filled with seeds—one should decorate the sacrificial hall with white whisks and canopies of white silk cloth. Then, one should wrap the eight jars seven times all around, up to the level of their necks, with a continuous, firm, white thread.

Having thus prepared all the necessary materials, bathed according to the prescribed rite, and performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other preliminaries, one should write the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*)—enclosed within the letter *sa*—in the center of a very smooth birch-bark leaf using sandalwood paste mixed with yellow ochre water and a pen made of *dūrvā* sprouts. Outside that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp. On each of the eight petals, one should write the letter *va* facing downwards. Inside that [pericarp], one should write the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, accompanied by the letter *va* and enclosed between the syllables *praṇava* (oṃ) and *namaḥ*.

Having drawn outside the lotus, both upward-facing and downward-facing, a numberless series of *ṭaṅkāra* sounds in the form of wave-ornaments (*ūrmikā*) all around, and having encircled that yantra with a white thread, one should place it in the *arghya* pitcher. Then, placing that pitcher upon an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared with rice powder at the front of the mandala, one should invoke the Lord of Mantras from one's own heart into the mandala. Having worshipped him there with white offerings, [one should meditate on him] as resembling a hundred moons, emitting the essence of nectar while situated within a full moon disc.

Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras together with his retinue, at the conclusion of the worship, one should pray: "Grant, grant great peace! Then, in the northern quarter, in a circular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) resembling the full moon, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for seven nights using seven substances—milk, rice, honey, clarified butter, *guggulu*, sesame seeds, and sandalwood—while subsisting solely on milk. Worshipping the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Mantras, every day during all eight watches, at the end of the oblation, [one should bathe] the Blessed One residing in the water-pot with milk and cool water.

And while performing the sprinkling during all eight watches of the day, the practitioner should daily, at the conclusion of his bath, visualize the Lord of Mantras pouring down nectar upon the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). By this, peace is attained.

Alternatively, taking a vessel made of clay, split bamboo, or wood, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus there using only cooked rice. Upon its eight petals, one should place eight lamps made of flour and filled with ghee, set them alight, and worship them with flowers and other offerings. Having scattered seven kinds of parched seeds over that, and having worshipped a water-jar, one should place an incense burner upon it so as to maintain an unbroken flow of smoke; in this manner, at the three times of day, one should offer the *bali* to the guardians of the directions and the spirits (*bhūta*).

One should carry [the vessel] on the backs of those who bear the offerings for as far as seven steps; then, for the sake of pacification, one should sprinkle an unbroken stream of water from the ritual pitcher upon them with the *astra-mantra*. || 155–181 ||
Thus, learn now the ritual for pacification and that for prosperity. || 181 ||
One should indeed prepare the maṇḍala as before, adorned with red sandalwood and using safflower powder mixed with powdered saffron.
Having filled eight small jars with wild rice grains, auspicious copper-colored sesame seeds, and jujube fruits, one should indeed prepare them.
Having wrapped the jars, together with their lids, with red thread,
one should make everything else prescribed here likewise red.
Then, having bathed and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should write the name with yellow pigment (rocanā) using a thick blade of darbha grass moistened with liquid lac.
As before, one should place [the deity] within the interior of a lotus; then, one should apply the seed-syllable facing downwards upon the petals. Listen attentively as I describe it to you. (186)
One should place below the syllable known as the nineteenth (kṣa) the seed-syllable that is the third from the navel (ga), and beneath that, the fifth from the enemy (ra). (187)

One should place the seed-syllable situated within that [triangle], joined with the head [letter] preceded by the end of the spoke and the external ten-day [cycle], resting upon the fourfold seat of the navel.
Then, one should place that lotus upon the seventh embryo from the navel; it should be endowed with the seed-syllable for nourishment and accompanied by the repetition of the word "kurū. (189)
One should indeed write [the mantra] preceded by the syllable Om in the eight directions on the outside;
having encircled it with a red thread, one should place it in a jar filled with honey and water.
Having placed [the offerings] as before, one should perform the binding of the directions with the [mantras] beginning with the Heart;
the binding of the intermediate directions with the Astra-mantra, and likewise the binding above and below with the Netra-mantra.
Then, having invoked the mantra that resembles coral, one should perform the sacrifice;
furthermore, [one should worship] the entire collection of mantras associated with the various scriptures in the world.
Worship with red, thornless, and pleasing flowers is beneficial;
here, an offering of rice mixed with molasses along with royal mung beans is appropriate. (193)
One should indeed prepare various kinds of food colored with *gulara*; if it is available, everything should be made red, but if not, [it may be otherwise]. (194)
One should color it with saffron or some other red mineral;
having completed everything up to the end of the recitation, one should then perform the fire oblation (homa).
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with ghee, sesame seeds as previously mentioned, along with sugar and jujube fruits, one should perform the sprinkling with water mixed with sugar.
As before, [one should visualize] the Lord of Mantras with the object of accomplishment contained within him;
then, one should perform the rite of the bali offering according to the previously stated procedure. (197)
Through the power of this king of mantras, when practiced according to this rite at all times, great prosperity arises within seven nights or three nights. (198)
Thus concludes the procedure for pacification.

Now he describes the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), beginning with "Learn also the nourishing rite" and ending with "by this rule at all times. *Nāma* refers to the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). One should write it as before, situated within the interior of the lotus; the meaning is that one should write it in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Regarding the nineteenth letter of the rim, which is the syllable *ba*, its third seed-syllable from the nave is the letter *la*; it is joined with the fifth vowel, *u*, and preceded by the anusvāra at the end of the spoke, [which is] by means of the tenth [consonant] from the outside, namely the letter *ṭa*. This is the meaning.

One should place the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, situated above the letter *va* as before, within the "navel-seventh womb"—that is, within the womb of the letter *sa*. This means one should write it in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). The "seed" is the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha. It is "endowed with the word for nourishment" (*puṣṭipada*) and "accompanied by the repetition of 'do'"; that is, it is joined with the phrase "nourish, nourish" (*puṣṭiṃ kuru kuru*).

And so is the ritual application: having drawn the maṇḍala as before with saffron powder mixed with the dust of *kusumbha* flowers, and having adorned it with a red moon-disc, one should perform all the preliminary rites such as the placement of the central jar (*kumbha*) as previously described. Then, having filled eight secondary jars (*upakumbha*) with wild rice (*nīvāra*), reddish grains of rice, sesame seeds, and jujube fruits (*badarī-phala*), and having placed them upon the directional jars, one should encircle those [jars] seven times with a red thread. Furthermore, one should prepare whatever else may be required.

Then, having bathed and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other preliminaries, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center of the interior of a lotus on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), using a stylus made of firm *dūrvā* grass and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) mixed with lac-water. Having written the seed-syllable *blūṃ* facing downwards on the eight petals, and having written the sound *ṭaṅkāra* around it as before, one should write the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha accompanied by the letter *va* within the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Having placed that lotus within the interior of the letter *sa*, one should write "Oṃ, grant prosperity, grant prosperity" in the eight directions of that [lotus].

Having wrapped that yantra with a red thread and placed it in a jar of honey-water, one should deposit it in the previously mentioned location. Then, having bound the four cardinal directions starting from the east with the four mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya), the four intermediate directions with the Astra-mantra, and below and above with the Astra-mantra, one should thereafter invoke the deity. Visualizing him as having the luster of coral, one should worship him with red-colored flowers and other offerings, together with the group of attendant mantras previously mentioned for the mandala.

One should worship the Lord with seeds known as *rājamudga*, with rice mixed with molasses (*gulodana*), and with foods colored red with molasses, according to the prescribed ritual. Furthermore, one should make the entire collection of ritual offerings (*upacāra*) red in color; if that is unavailable, one should dye them red with saffron or other such substances, or with minerals such as red ochre (*gairika*).

Having thus performed the worship up to the end of the recitation-sacrifice (*japayajña*), and having offered oblations according to the rules—including ghee mixed with sugar and jujube fruits, and copper-colored sesame seeds—up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sprinkle the deity residing in the water-pot with sugared water as before, and perform the rite of offerings (*balikarma*) in the manner previously described. When this is done for seven nights or three nights, great nourishment arises through the majesty of the mantra. (181–198)
Now, listen to how the mantra-practitioner should indeed perform the nourishment of another as well as of oneself by means of this very mantra. (199)
The mandala is provided with ornaments, adorned with four colors,
equipped with cloth, garlands, and mirrors, and furnished with small bells and fans.
Having carefully filled two jars each with ghee, honey, curd, milk, and well-strained [liquor], separately.
Then, having filled the vessels with madhūka fruits, camphor, grapes, and myrobalan fruits, and having placed them at the mouths of the jars; || 202 ||
The shallow bowls, containing sprouts and sprinkled with cool water, were smeared with lime and sandalwood paste and adorned with white flowers. || 203 ||
Having smeared [the area] with white arghya water, one should place it within the interior of the jar;
for all flowers and other offerings should indeed be white, red, or golden-hued.

Having performed all that which is prescribed for the preliminary rite (upacāra), and having completed his daily observances (āhnika) while wearing clean garments, he should maintain the recitation of the Lion-mantra (siṃhamantra).
With saffron, milk, and a small amount of sugarcane juice,
as well as with honey, [one should write] upon birch bark or cloth that which is situated in the midst of the vowels.
Having given the designation, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus outside;
beyond that, with twice as many petals, provided with a pericarp and filaments. (207)
Next, one should draw a circle outside that [mandala] with twelve petals, then a sixteen-petaled lotus, and then a twenty-four-petaled lotus. || 208 ||
Now listen: for all the petals, the five seed-syllables are to be applied in sequence, starting from the eastern lotus, with their faces turned downwards. 209.

Taking that which is the seventh letter from the navel (the letter *ma*) and that which stands above the fourth from the navel (the letter *u*), again employing the union of the upper and lower [vowels]. (210)
Then one should place [the letter] third from the navel, two below that;
the seventh from the navel is placed below, and the fourth is at the head.
Then, taking the seventh [letter] and placing the third below it,
one should join the nineteenth letter below that, following the color of the rim (nemi).
Again, taking [the thread] from the *nemi*, one should place it at the seventh position from the *nābhi*;
then, one should place the third [position] below that, starting from the region of the *nābhi*.
One should first place the seat for all [deities], beginning with the navel and joined with the five arrows; thereafter, one should mark it with the head in due order.
But by the ninth [vowel], which has reached the penultimate position of the rim,
the king of mantras is here in the center as before, ending with the fourth letter from the beginning of the nave.
Then, one should indeed place the seed-syllable alone, situated between two *vauṣaṭ* words, upon the ground within the intervals between the petals of the four-petalled [lotus]. || 216 ||
Having divided [the space] up to the seventh petal from the center,
one should apply that [measurement] accordingly at the joints of the eight-petaled [lotus].
Having pierced that very [channel] at the navel, one should cause it to reach the end.
Having fashioned the excellent seed-syllable, one should place it within the space between the twelve petals.
Then, one should place the seed-syllable, which is endowed with the word *vaṣaṭ* and resembles cool water, located at the junctions of the sixteen petals.
The seventh seed-syllable from the navel is situated upon the fourth seat;
it is adorned at its end by a fourteenth spoke.
Situated in the middle of this enclosure, one should place the great, flowing nectar,
as before, by circling the outer lotus in a clockwise direction.
Then, having taken the nābhiturya situated above the seventh [circle],
one should mark from the end of a spoke up to the ninth seed-syllable using the first [measure].
This seed-syllable, devoid of numerical count and continuous, should be applied as a wave to the outer enclosure of the lotus.
Having thus written it with white and red [pigments], one should encircle it with a yellow thread;
and having placed it in a jar filled with honey, sugarcane juice, and mango water, [one should proceed].
Having smeared it with sandalwood paste and adorned it with garlands of flowers,
one should place it in the designated spot and then worship the Lord of Mantras.
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus, accompanied by his retinue,
he has the luster of pure crystal and is cooler than snow.
One should meditate upon that white, downward-facing lotus above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
one should remember the sphere of the sky dissolved within the interior of its pericarp.
It was illuminated by the rays of the lord of the night together with all the stars,
and strewn with scattered clouds like the outpourings of the celestial river.
Then, during the worship of the Lord with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and flowers,
one should perform the meditative contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the previously mentioned items in their exact sequence.
Whatever enjoyment he may conceive of, that very thing, having been meditated upon as consisting of nectar,
falls with speed from the sky, overflowing with ambrosia.
One should meditate upon the King of Mantras as being directly the form of nectar itself— nourished, gladdened, immersed, and overflowing with all those various manifestations arising from nectar.
Then, having brought [the deity] down from the heart by means of the sādhana, one should worship externally;
having worshipped and meditated upon [the deity] residing within the womb of the fire, one should then satisfy [him].
With *vilva* fruits sprinkled with *sāmalaira* oil, with fresh *dūrvā* sprouts, and with sesame seeds mixed with cow’s milk and combined with parched grain and rice; || 233 ||
Then, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) combined with sugar, clarified butter, and flowers;
thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling with honey, milk, and water while reciting two mantras.
One should perform the offering of the bali oblation as before with ghee, milk-rice, and auspicious fruits; this shall bring about nourishment. (235)
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for prosperity.

Now he explains the procedure for nourishment (*āpyāyana*), beginning with "Then, by this mantra... and ending with "...one should perform the nourishment. The phrase "situated in the middle of the vowels" means being contained within the letter *sa*. "The word of designation" means the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*). "The seventh letter from the navel" refers to the letter *sa*; "situated above the fourth from the navel" means situated above the letter *va*. This is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). "Taking that very same [syllable] again through the union of upper and lower" means joining the letter *va* below the letter *sa*.

This is the second seed-syllable. Regarding "the third from the navel, the letter *la*, below by two": this means [below] the *sa* and *va* that are to be mentioned. Therein, the seventh letter from the navel is the one called *sa*; it is situated below. That fourth letter, called *va*, is at the top of the head. This is the third seed-syllable. [The fourth is: the seventh *sa*, the third *la*, and the nineteenth from the *ba*-group (the *nemivarga*), which is *ba*. This is the fourth seed-syllable. "Again, taking the last from the *nemi*" means taking the letter *sa*.

The meaning is that it is situated above the letter *sa* on the seventh back from the navel; that is, the letter *la*, which is the third from the region of the navel. This [letter] is situated above the letter *sa* on the fifth back; that is, the letter *la*, which is the third from the region of the navel. This is the fifth seed-syllable (*bīja*). The meaning is "of all the five seed-syllables. Joined with the fifth arrow, meaning endowed with the letter *u*; one should place the seat, the letter *ya* preceding the navel, below—meaning one should join it underneath.

One should mark the letter *ṭa* with a head [the vowel *i*] by means of the ninth letter of the rim (*nemim*) which follows the last of the vowels (*ārope*), accompanied by an *anusvāra*; the meaning is that one should place the letter *ṭa* on top. "Ending with the fourth letter of the navel" refers to the King of Mantras (*mantrarāj*) being in the middle as before; "as before" means as described in the rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). "In the middle" means in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*); "ending with the fourth letter of the navel" means ending with the letter *va*. "King of Mantras" means the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Nṛsiṃha.

The phrase "situated between the two *vauṣaṭ* syllables" is also a qualification of this very "King of Mantras. "The seed alone," meaning the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha devoid of the letter *va*, refers to the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha. "Pierced by the end of *ara*" means ending with the *visarga*. "Joined with the seventh from the navel" means joined with the letter *sa*; thus, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is joined with it. The seventh seed-syllable from the navel is the letter *sa*, which is situated in the fourth seat, positioned above the letter *va*. [It is joined] with the fourteenth from *ara*, namely the vowel *au*, and with the *anusvāra* at its end.

The phrase "situated in the middle of this enclosure" refers to the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, which is enclosed by the two syllables *svā* and *m*. "The fourth from the navel" means the letter *va*; "situated above the seventh" means situated above the letter *sa*. "By the ninth seed-syllable of the rim" means by the letter *ṭa*; "by the first [syllable] at the end of the spokes" means by the *anusvāra*.

Now, as for the ritual application (*prayoga*): here, having visualized the previously described mandala adorned with the four colors, one should decorate that sacrificial site with canopies, flower garlands, mirrors, small bells, chowries, fans, and so forth. Then, having filled two small jars each with ghee, honey, curd, and well-sweetened milk, and having filled shallow bowls with *madhūka* fruits, camphor, grapes, and *āmalaka* fruits, one should place these [bowls] at the mouths of the small jars and sprinkle them with water while reciting the *śiro-mantra*.

One should place shallow bowls (śarāva) smeared with lime and sandalwood paste, filled with white flowers, honored with a white *arghya* offering, and containing sprouts, within the spaces between the directional jars (*dik-kumbha*). Then, one should gather all the flowers and other materials used here that are white, red, or golden-hued.

Then, having performed his daily rites, wearing clean garments, and having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, the practitioner, maintaining the identification "I am Nṛsiṃha," should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—enclosed within the letter *Sa*—upon a birch leaf using milk mixed with a little saffron, sugarcane juice, and honey. Outside of that, he should draw a four-petalled lotus; outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus provided with a pericarp (*karṇikā*) and filaments (*kesara*); outside of that, a twelve-petalled lotus; and outside of that, a sixteen-petalled lotus.

Outside of that, having drawn a twenty-four-petaled lotus and one circle outside of that, one should write the seed-syllable *smryuṃ* on the four petals, the seed-syllable *psyuṃ* on the eight petals, the seed-syllable *sphyuṭ* on the twelve petals, the seed-syllable *spyuṭ* on the sixteen petals, and the seed-syllable *sphyuṭ* on the twenty-four petals, all facing downwards. Having written *vauṣaṭ*, *kṣvauṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ* in the center of the pericarp, one should write the solitary Nṛsiṃha seed-syllable *kṣauṃ* in the fourteen intervening spaces.

Having drawn [the diagram], one should write the seed-syllable *kṣaḥ* in the intervals between the eight petals; having written *kṣvaḥ* in the intervals between the twelve petals; having written *vaṣaṭ kṣauṃ vaṣaṭ* in the intervals between the sixteen petals; and having written *svauṃ kṣauṃ svauṃ* in the intervals between the twenty-four petals; then, outside the circle, one should write the seed-syllable *psaṃṭ* continuously in a clockwise direction, forming a wave-like pattern without numbering the repetitions; and having thus prepared the yantra, one should wrap it with white, red, and yellow thread.

Having placed that jar—which is filled with honey and sugarcane juice—within another full jar, having smeared it with sandalwood paste, adorned it with flower garlands, and set it in the previously mentioned place; then, having meditated upon the glorious Nṛsiṃha, who resembles clear crystal, who is accompanied by his entire retinue, and who is cooler than snow, within the lotus of one's own heart; and having meditated upon the downward-facing lotus situated above the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*);
and having recollected the circle of the sky in its pericarp, which is strewn with the orb of the full moon, the clusters of stars, and the flowing currents of the Mandākinī;
Then, from the center of the lotus in the sky, one should visualize Gaṅgā falling from the top of the Lord's head; by means of that nectar-water, [one should bathe Him].

Having worshipped [the deity] with offerings such as *arghya* and so forth, one should then bring the deity down from one's own heart into the water-pot (*kumbha*) and the mandala according to the prescribed rite. Having worshipped them thoroughly, one should invoke the deity into the fire and satisfy him with offerings of bilva fruits, dūrvā sprouts, and rice grains mixed with cow’s milk, along with white sugar, clarified butter, flowers, and sesame seeds, all sprinkled with ghee. Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should perform the sprinkling of the Lord of Mantras situated within the yantra with honey, milk, and water, as before, using ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should perform the offering of the bali with fruits as before; by this, nourishment occurs. (199–235)
(Thus concludes the procedure for nourishment.
Now, I shall correctly describe the method of protection as it truly exists, by the mere knowledge of which one shall always be free from disease. (236)
Understand correctly that this general [remedy] serves to ward off all known faults, and especially those that are unknown. (237)
Indeed, through the affliction of the stars and planets, the bodily constituents (dhātus) fall into a state of imbalance;
and due to that imbalance, diseases such as fever and others become aggravated.
Indeed, at that very moment of his anger, the seizing spirits headed by the Brahmarakshasas, as well as the Shakinis, Bhutas, and Vetalas, enter into embodied beings. (239)
Know that the cause of all [results] is the action performed in the past;
indeed, [this is overcome] by means of power, mantra, knowledge, and austerity. (240)
Through recitation, study, burnt offerings, and various kinds of gifts, as well as by the application of mantras and medicinal herbs, that [evil] is suddenly destroyed. || 241 ||
However, among all [the mantras], this mantra preeminently accomplishes its purpose;
by the mere recollection of it, malevolent spirits and the like do not enter.
Having prepared the foundation as prescribed for the purpose of worshipping the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin),
and having filled the secondary jars with seeds combined with white mustard, || 243 ||
And having placed vessels filled with sesame and mustard seeds, along with fruits, upon the mouths of the jars and spread them out.
One should place eight iron arrows at equal intervals around its exterior in the cardinal directions;
one should fasten these arrows at their necks with a strong thread. (245)

[One should offer] a great medicinal herb (*mahauṣadhī*) joined with *barhiṣ* grass wings, adorned with a snake’s slough, possessing the matted locks of a spirit (*bhūtajaṭā*), and accompanied by a branch of the *śamī* tree. || 246 ||
With a five-colored thread, starting from the north-eastern quarter,
one should wrap that eight-arrow [diagram] three times in a clockwise direction.
Between each pair of the eight full water-pots,
one should place eight lamps in succession upon a high seat.
Indeed, wicks dyed with great royal lac should be placed in a copper vessel with oil known as rājikā and offered for the lamps.
Then, having tied his topknot and wearing the girdle of muñja grass, he should perform the binding of the directions as before,
mentally intending the flight of all defects.
One should worship the Lord of Mantras with various auspicious offerings for specific desires:
flowers, incense, food offerings, and edible fruits and roots. (251)
Then, having offered all types of seeds together with white mustard, along with black mustard mixed with ghee, and sesame seeds together with fruits. (252)

Then, at the time of midday, having meditated and performed the protection rite by first making it perfectly pure through anointing and other such acts, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having sprinkled [the image] with baths of gold, mercury, and medicinal herbs, and having caused it to enter;
having struck it with the weapon-flower and having gazed upon it from the feet upwards. || 254 ||
Having placed his head upon his bent knees, he should present it to the deity;
having positioned him facing north on a seat provided with a railing.
And when [the site] is marked by stars and likewise provided with the arghya offering and other requisites,
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon it using the six-limbed mantra.
Then, having [placed] the mind upon the fingers, in their respective places, and upon the body,
one should draw a six-cornered mandala with a wheel in front of it.
Surrounded by a mass of flames, one should then place there [the vessel] which is richly arranged as previously described and completely filled with fragrant water.
A set of seven jars should be placed in the middle of those [spokes],
while the six lamps situated in the intervals between the spokes are to be arranged as before.
Having performed [the ritual] in the central jar, one should worship Mantreśvara together with his limbs (aṅgas).
One should worship him with the mantra beginning with the Praṇava: "Obeisance to the beings who are Nṛsiṃha. (260)
Having worshipped, according to the prescribed rule, the assembly of the Lord’s devotees who destroy all faults in the corners with flowers, incense, and other offerings, indeed.
Then one should perform the binding of the directions with weapons and white mustard seeds in sequence;
afterwards, one should strike the patient from the feet up to the head.
Then, having drawn it forth with the fan of one's own hand,
one should cast that web of defects either into the sky or onto the surface of the earth.
Then, taking a fire-vessel that is smokeless and intensely blazing,
one should perform a *homa* offering with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds in that fire which is devoid of fuel.
With the root mantra or the armor mantra, recited one hundred and eight times, accompanied by the word "svāhā" and the phrase "protect so-and-so, protect! (amukaṃ rakṣa rakṣa). || 265 ||
At the end of the mantra, one should place the word and whirl the oblation above the head; then, taking mahiṣākṣa resin together with white mustard seeds, [one should proceed]. (266)
Having recited the mantra, one should indeed fumigate it after covering it with a cloth;
then, having placed a vessel containing water near the fire-vessel, [one should proceed].

Having removed all the remnants of the food offering (naivedya) along with the water into another vessel, as well as the substitute for the sacrificial animal (paśupratinidhi) colored with saffron and other pigments; || 268 ||
If the afflictions based on the elements are mentally constructed by him, then there is indeed no affliction for his sense faculties within those elements. (269)
And having constantly taken up the offering, let him release it by means of the lion-truth,
with the left and right hands in alternating succession.
One should perform an incalculable number of fire offerings accompanied by ritual oblations and circumambulations;
then, having washed the hands that held the oblation with water consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra.
Having taken earth from the sacrificial pit, or indeed from burnt cow-dung,
and having consecrated it many times with the Astra-mantra, [he should apply it] from the forehead down to the range of the feet.
And one should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the back or on both sides;
may there be well-being for you, using water for the arghya offering accompanied by the mantra "yuta."
One should subsequently refresh [the disciple] with drops of water collected from the mantra-vessel;
having meditated upon the mantra situated within the full moon, resembling ten thousand full moons. (274)
One should then sprinkle the great nectar flowing from the *brahmarandhra* of the person to be accomplished (the *sādhya*) throughout the tree of his body, reaching down to the tips of the nails.
Having done this, one should further worship the mantra residing within the mandala and the water-pot (kumbha).
Having indeed placed that pot in the upper part of the bedchamber, [one should proceed].
Having covered that which is situated upon a cloth-covered seat with a garment,
one should also place eight full jars there, positioned in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should offer incense with an uninterrupted flow, a lamp-vessel filled with ghee and other substances,
fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, lamps, parched grain, white mustard seeds, and curd.
Having placed the assembly of vessels before him, he should then offer the bali-oblation when nightfall has arrived, for the sake of pacifying all defects. (279)
Having carefully taken up the long-life incense and lamp that were prepared for the Lord in a single vessel, one should hold them with diligence. (280)
That which was given by one who has become that [deity] should be offered to another, or it may be offered separately to each of the six;
having adorned it with its own lamp, one should place it upon its own vessel. || 281 ||
One should recollect the mantra endowed with the words "rakṣa rakṣa" (protect, protect) and joined with the weapon-mantra (astra),
while circling it over the head of the one to be protected, in the same sequence as it was bestowed.
Furthermore, he should give white mustard seeds consecrated with mantras from his weapons into the hands of those pure-souled devotees of mine who carry the offerings.
Having recited the mantra, one should indeed apply a tilaka on the forehead with ashes;
the practitioner of mantra should first cause the bali offering to flow away into deep water.
Then, at a crossroads, at the foot of a tree, or outside a village or city,
the offering of oblations to the gods and spirits (balikṣepa) is prescribed in this rite.
And one should offer the previously mentioned vessel for fire, which is emitting smoke, along with white mustard seeds;
likewise, using that very same vessel for the bali offering, it should be provided with water.
Having cast the offering near a well, or in a pond, or close to a tree, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with his hands and feet washed. || 287 ||
On a well-smeared protected ground that has been cleared all around,
one should perform the scattering of white mustard seeds upon its center and into a lamp-vessel placed thereon.
Having recited the Astra mantra many times, encased within the root mantra,
one should bind it to his garment for seven nights, performing this every day.
Indeed, by performing this rite, the protection of the vital fluids and the bodily constituents of those who are always afflicted is perpetually established. (290)
Then, on a smeared portion of ground covered with kuśa grass and a deerskin,
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he himself should remain in the protection-chamber together with his assistants.
Either subsisting on milk or remaining without food, devoted to meditation and silent recitation,
he should perform [the rites] pertaining to the beginning, middle, and end during the portions of the night.
The worship, the fire-oblation, and the offering of the bali, performed correctly with groats, water, honey, and clarified butter; 293.
When the first part of the night has passed,
the bali offering is prescribed to be made with a powder made from barley, wheat, and śāli rice, mixed with water and jaggery.
Having rolled three kinds of sweetmeats with the hand,
they should be equal in shape to the flame of a round lamp and to the fruit of the *āmra* tree.
At midnight, one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of those [grains] mixed with milk while still uncooked,
along with well-ground black sesame seeds that have not yet been roasted.
When the night has passed, one should offer an oblation outside the protection chamber with rice, powdered turmeric, curd, dūrvā sprouts, and fruits.
Having placed them on a portion of the path or in a cleared courtyard,
one should then consecrate seven kinds of seeds in a bowl.
One should give it to the daughter of a chief of the twice-born and receive it back from her;
three handfuls in one vessel and seven in another. (299)
Then, in another jar, the knower of mantras should place eleven vessels and three more,
using the seed-syllable of the lion encased within the *astra* mantra.
One hundred and eight, and likewise doubled and tripled in sequence;
with that [number], one should repeatedly draw out water from jars and pour it [into the vessel]. || 301 ||
One [should perform this] on land, others in water; at dawn, midday, and at the end of the day—one should perform this common libation to the beings until its conclusion.
Then, on the following day, having performed the ritual in the mandala with the mantra and having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule, he indeed offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should draw an eight-cornered mandala with white rice flour.
In its center, having drawn a six-petaled lotus situated within a conch shell. (304)
One should place eight jars outside as before, accompanied by lamps;
and having brought down the protection-jar situated at the head into the center of that [mandala]. || 305 ||

Having first removed from that [vessel] the water for respectful offering (arghya), the garlands, the ointments, and the stream of cool water, one should pour in another [liquid] for the purpose of filling it. || 306 ||
Just as the water situated therein indeed undergoes depletion, so too shall there be an increase in all the constituent elements (dhātus) of that which is to be protected. || 307 ||
Having first honored him with fresh garlands, garments, water for the guest-offering (arghya), unguents, and so forth,
one should then worship the Lord of Mantras in the center of that [mandala] as before.
By means of that which causes a great accumulation of the blood-element in men, one should then satisfy [the deity] with fragrant offerings presented with mantras. (309)
Having gathered together the water-offering (arghya), flowers, incense, perfume, and the lamp— all of which have been joined with mantras— one should always cast them into water.
One should perform all the remaining applications as previously described;
then, on the third day, one should construct a square mandala.
Having drawn a hexagon in the center of that [mandala], together with a city and a lotus,
one should place a collection of jars there, surrounded by lamps.
Having performed the sacrifice with that which is offered according to the mantra, one should indeed gratify the Brāhmaṇas;
then, on the fourth day, one should draw [the design] within a circular enclosure.
There is a radiant eight-spoked wheel, and within it is the abode of fire;
having worshipped there the mantra-form and performed the protection as before, [one should proceed]. (314)
Having worshipped the daughter of the king of birds, Kumārī, and likewise the Brahmin girl according to the prescribed rule, one should offer to them what has been presented.
Then, on the fifth day, one should construct an eight-cornered mandala;
within that, one should fashion a conch and draw [the design] situated within the belly of the conch.

The Lord of Weapons, having first performed the ritual application of the five-spoked wheel with its hub and altar, which is the abode of the elements, along with the lamps together with their vessels; || 317 ||
One should worship the God with various offerings such as food, flowers, and so forth;
then, having cast away the food consumed by the God, one should perform the previously mentioned rites.
Then, on the sixth day, one should construct a triangle within the world;
it is indeed the great seven-spoked wheel which consists of the seven worlds.
In the interval between those, one should draw two pairs of maces in the four directions;
in the center of that, within the interior of the jar, one should worship the mantra according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered the sacrifice and taken the *naivedya*, one should place it in a high location;
when it comes to be consumed by crows and other such creatures among the sky-dwellers, [that is auspicious].
On the seventh day, one should construct a square mandala with four gates;
in its four corners, one should draw four conch shells.
Therein, in the center, one should draw a lotus adorned with an infinite number of petals;
and having drawn a twelve-spoked wheel resting upon its pericarp.
One should place eight water-pots, each accompanied by a lamp, in the eight directions;
there, one should perform the ritual application after six days have passed.
The knower of mantras should offer the food oblation (naivedya) accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
in this way, there shall be a gradual accumulation of the elements, beginning with flesh.
The buffalo, the goat, molasses, the deer, the hare,
the peacock, and the ruddy goose— these seven indeed [grant merit] for seven days each.

However, for flesh-eating beings who depend upon the elements of the body, [the offering] should be prepared with juices and other desired things; for a living, moving creature must not be used. || 327 ||
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one who is intent on the highest good must certainly not commit violence against living beings, especially those who desire life. (328)
The lifespan of men surely comes to an end through the killing of living beings;
by granting fearlessness to all creatures, one shall attain an increase in longevity. (329)

Through this mantra, there shall be long life, health, sovereignty, great victory over untimely death, strength, vigor, fortitude, and steadfastness; there is no [attainment] beyond these that comes from the mantra. (330)
Mantra-worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and the giving of gold, cows, and so forth,
bring about prosperity in this world and the next for those established in goodness.
Then, having waited for seven days after the mandala has been established,
one should take up the colored powders, offerings, or other materials as before and discard them.

Thus has the method of protection for those who are afflicted by disease been set forth. Now, beginning with the words "atha rakṣāvidhānaṃ tu" and ending with "sarujānām udāhṛtam," he explains the procedure for the protection of those suffering from illness.

The ritual procedure: For the purpose of worshipping Śrī Nṛsiṃha, one should establish the maṇḍala and the primary pitcher (*kumbha*) as before; then, having filled the secondary pitchers (*upakumbha*) with seeds mixed with white mustard, and having filled their lids (*pidhāna-śarāva*) with mustard, sesame, and fruit; then, having placed eight iron arrows very evenly in the eight directions outside of that; and having tied them by their necks with a strong thread, [one should prepare] a [staff] equipped with peacock feathers and adorned with a sloughed snake-skin and the great medicinal herb *bhūtajaṭā*.

Having wound that set of eight arrows, together with a branch of the *śamī* tree, three times clockwise starting from the northern direction with a five-colored thread; and having placed eight lamps—each situated on an elevated seat in the intervals between the eight full jars, filled with oil known as *rājikā*, contained in copper vessels, and equipped with wicks dyed with vermilion (*mahārājata*)—the practitioner, having bathed, tied his topknot, observed silence, and performed the binding of the directions as before, should resolve upon the flight of all defects.

Having duly worshipped the Lord of Mantras, the glorious Nṛsiṃha, with various auspicious flowers, incenses, fruits, roots, food offerings, and edibles according to the ritual, and having gratified the deity in the midst of the fire with all seeds mixed with white mustard, along with black mustard, ghee, fruits, and sesame seeds; and having struck the afflicted person from the feet to the head with iron flowers while reciting the Netra-mantra and gazing at him; and having made the patient bow his knees and head, one should present [the offering] to the Blessed One.

Having seated him upon a seat that is secured with iron bars, consecrated with mantras, and honored with offerings such as *arghya*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his hands and body according to the rules, using the six-limbed *Śrīmannṛsiṃha* mantra, while mentally reciting it. Then, having drawn a hexagonal mandala containing a discus in front of him, one should place seven jars—filled with fragrant water and adorned with the previously mentioned arrangement—in the center and within the six corners; and having placed eight lamps in the intermediate spaces between the corners according to the method described before.

Having worshipped the Lord of Mantras together with His limbs (Aṅgas) in the central jar, and having worshipped the host of Nṛsiṃha-Bhūtas—which destroys all defects—in the jars situated at the corners with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Nṛsiṃha-Bhūtas," one should perform the binding of the quarters (Digbandha) using white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra. Then, having struck the afflicted person with flowers and mentally drawn out the entire mass of defects from his body by fanning it with one's own hand, one should cast them either into the sky or onto the ground. Thereafter, taking a smokeless, intensely blazing vessel of fire—

When that fire has become fuel-less, one should offer oblations with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds, numbering one hundred and eight, using either the root mantra or the weapon mantra (astramantra), ending with the words: "Protect [Name], protect, svāhā. With each oblation, one should cause the offering substance to circle around the head of the person being protected.

Taking white mustard seeds along with Mahiṣākṣa and Guggulu resin, fumigating them with the root mantra, covering the patient with a cloth, and placing a vessel of water near the fire-vessel; then, having placed all the remnants of the food offering (naivedya) into another vessel, coloring it red with saffron and other pigments, and lifting up that food together with the water, one should mentally resolve: "This is the sacrificial offering (bali) acting as a substitute for the animal, intended for the humors (doṣas) residing within the elements (dhātus) of the patient. [One should then recite: "Whatever affliction this [offering] may have for his sense organs and elements..."
Having taken the offering, one should release it while constantly reciting, "By the truth of the lion!

Thus speaking, one should present the offering. In the midst of the offering, or from time to time, while performing an incalculable number of fire-oblations with the left and right hands, one should circumambulate clockwise for the sake of presenting the offering.

Then, having washed his hands with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, he should take either earth from the sacrificial pit or ashes made from burnt cow-dung, and after consecrating it many times with the Astra-mantra, he should apply vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the patient, starting from the forehead down to the feet. Then, having sprinkled [the patient] with drops of arghya-water combined with water from the ritual jar while reciting: "Oṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ; Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Narasiṃha, may there be well-being for you," he should [visualize] [the deity] situated in the center of a full moon disc within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras, who resembles ten thousand full moons and is flowing with great nectar, and having meditated upon his body being sprinkled by that nectar, one should again worship the deity residing in the jar and the one within the mandala. Then, placing that great jar—along with its directional jars and subsidiary vases—upon a cloth seat at the head of the patient’s bed in the bedroom, and covering it with a cloth, one should arrange the incense burners and lamp vessels as before, maintaining an uninterrupted flow.

Having placed fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, lamps, parched grain, white mustard seeds, and vessels of curd before him, one should perform the offering of oblations when the onset of night has arrived.

The procedure for this is as follows: having collected all the flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings that were previously prepared for the worship of the Lord residing in the central jar among the jars placed upon the hexagonal mandala, and having likewise placed in six separate vessels the flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth offered to the Nṛsiṃha-beings residing in the six surrounding jars, one should adorn each of those respective vessels with its own lamp and arrange them above their corresponding jars.

Reciting the mantra "Oṃ kṣaḥ vīryāyāstrāya phaṭ, protect [Name], protect," he should rotate those jars individually and in sequence around the head of the person to be protected. Then, having summoned virtuous devotees of the Lord to serve as bearers of the *bali* offering, he places consecrated white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) in their hands, applies a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with ashes using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), and has them carry the *bali* to deep water, a crossroads, the foot of a tree, or outside the village or city.

One should perform the offering of the *bali* to the gods and spirits. One should discard the previously mentioned fire-vessel and water-vessel while they are smoking with white mustard seeds, together with that *bali*-vessel.

Having thus offered the bali-oblation near a well, near a pond, or near a tree, and having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should scatter white mustard seeds with the Astra-mantra around the person to be protected who is lying on well-smeared ground, and a single lamp above his head. Then, for seven nights, he should daily tie to the garment of the person to be protected white mustard seeds that have been consecrated many times with the Astra-mantra encased within the Mūla-mantra.

When this has been done, the protection of those afflicted by disease is accomplished. Then, having smeared a portion of the ground in the house of the one to be protected, and having sat down himself upon a seat of *kuśa* grass and deerskin, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), accompanied by assistants, and subsisting on milk or fasting entirely, he should remain intent on recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). At the beginning, middle, and end of the night, he should perform worship, fire-oblations (*havana*), and the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) according to the previously described method.

Regarding the specific procedure for the offering of the *bali*: during the first part of the night, one should present the *bali* with water, barley meal (*saktu*), honey, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). At midnight, having fashioned three kinds of sweetmeats (*modaka*) by hand from the flour of barley, wheat, and rice mixed with molasses—shaped like the flame of a lamp or like mango fruits—one should offer the *bali* with those uncooked sweetmeats accompanied by milk.

At the end of the night, one should offer a *bali* sacrifice on a purified spot outside the protective house—either on a path or at a crossroads—using unhusked black sesame seeds, grains, rice, turmeric powder, curd, and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.

Then, having taken seven kinds of grain and consecrated them with the root mantra, one should place them in a shallow bowl and give it to the daughter of a preeminent Brahmin. From her presence, one should collect three *prasṛti* measures of the seeds in one vessel, seven *prasṛti* measures in another vessel, and eleven *prasṛti* measures in yet another vessel.

Then, having filled those three vessels with water in sequence, one should consecrate the first vessel one hundred and eight times, the second twice that number, and the third thrice that number, using the seed-syllable of Śrī Nṛsiṃha encased within the Astra-mantra. Having lifted one vessel from among them, one should deposit it on dry land at dawn; having lifted another vessel, one should deposit it in water at midday; and again, having lifted the other vessel, one should deposit it in water at evening as well. Until the day of completion, one should perform the general libation to the spirits (bhūtatarpaṇa) in this manner every single day.

Then, on the following day, having worshipped the deity situated within the mandala according to the prescribed rites and having gratified the deity in the fire with offerings up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should smear a spot with cow dung and draw a mandala with white powder. Having inscribed a conch in its center and a six-petalled lotus within that, one should place the eight directional jars—which were previously stationed in the head-region of the bed-chamber—within this mandala upon the eight corners along with lamps; then, having placed the central jar in the middle of the mandala, from that [one proceeds].

Having removed the arghya, flowers, garlands, and other offerings presented on the previous day, once that spot where the pitcher stood has been dried, one should fill it again with a stream of cool water as before; as the water within the pitcher dries up day by day, so too does the increase of the constituent elements (dhātu) of the object to be protected occur.

Then, having adorned [the deity] with fresh garlands, garments, water-offerings (arghya), perfumes, and so forth, and having worshipped the Lord of Mantras there as before, one should satisfy the God with fragrant food offerings purified by mantras that increase the red elements. Following the worship, one should collect all the water-offerings, flowers, pollen, incense, lamps, and so on, and daily cast them into deep water. One should also perform the disposal of the remnants according to the method previously described.

Then, on the third day, having drawn a square mandala and inscribed a hexagon within it, and having further drawn a lotus in its center, one should arrange a collection of water-pots there as before; placing lamps in the intermediate spaces between them and worshipping as previously described, one should satisfy the Brahmins with the sacrificial offerings and other foods presented to the Blessed One.

On the fourth day, having drawn a circle and therein inscribed a five-spoked wheel complete with a hub and rim, one should place a great jar (mahākumbha) in the center, the directional jars (dikkumbha) around it, and lamps between each of them; then, having worshipped the deity there with various food offerings, flowers, and so forth, one should cast all the oblations and other items consumed by the deity into the fire and perform everything else as before.

Then, on the sixth day, having drawn a triangular mandala and inscribed a great seven-spoked wheel in its center, and having drawn four maces in the four directions within that, one should worship the deity situated in the great jar in the middle according to the prescribed rite; and the food and other offerings presented to him should be placed in an elevated spot for the enjoyment of birds such as crows.

Then, on the seventh day, having drawn a square mandala with four doors, having depicted four conch shells in its four corners, having drawn a lotus with countless petals in its center, and having drawn a twelve-spoked wheel resting upon its pericarp; and having placed eight jars separated by lamps in the eight directions and a great jar in the middle; and having worshipped the Deity therein according to the prescribed rite; one should perform the distribution of the offered food and other items as described for the sixth day.

Thus, through worship and other rites for seven days, there occurs a gradual increase of the seven constituents (dhātus) mentioned as "chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. For the sake of strengthening those beings who subsist on meat and depend upon the bodily constituents, one should also provide, in sequence over the seven days, buffalo, goat, jaggery, deer, hare, peacock, and ruddy goose; however, these buffaloes and others, as well as the animal substitutes, should be colored with saffron and similar substances.

One should fashion the forms of the sacrificial animals (*paśu*) as ground flour, according to the previously mentioned method, for those defects which are based on the elements and imagined by the mind. One who desires the life-span of the animals should not kill them directly. Then, when the seventh day has passed, having asked forgiveness from the deity situated in the mandala and so forth, one should take the powders of the mandala, the offerings (*bali*), and other items, and discard them as before. (236–333)
Especially for those who enjoy pleasures, protection from disease is essential. (333)
Indeed, for those devotees who delight in ritual action, who are faithful, and who desire their own welfare,
the task must always be performed by one who is devoted to ritual action and knowledgeable in the mantras.
Where the body is protected by this method, there the spirits bestow all worldly well-being. (335)
Now I shall describe the protective rite of Sandhāraṇī, which is an ornament for the body;
it protects merely by being maintained once the ritual action has been completed. (336)
One should write the name-word enclosed by the Praṇava at the beginning and end, as before;
for that seed-syllable is the support of the name, and one should place it within the interior of the Praṇava.
One should divide that *āvarta* into three parts; all of that resides within the belly of the lion.
The King of Seeds is surrounded by the tenth seed-syllable of the rim.
The seed-syllable, devoid of the vowel *au*, is situated at the seventh [letter] from the navel;
having split it with those residing in all the vowels, one should fill it with that.
Outside of that, one should fashion a six-petalled lotus adorned with the sky [the letter *ha*];
one should then place the mantras beginning with the Heart and ending with the Eye upon the six petals. (340)
One should write the name enclosed by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) in the four directions;
then, in the six junctions of the petals, one should include the words for protection and repetition (*rakṣa* and *vīpsā*).
One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel on the outside, complete with a hub and a rim;
one should place the eighth seed-syllable from the hub within the intervals between the spokes.
Excluding the syllable *ra* from the seventh up to the tenth,
one should pierce the remaining spokes in sequence with those *r*-syllables accompanied by the bindu.
One should place the word "go" (jahī) as a distributive term for each fault, followed by the word "of such-and-such" (amukasya);
and in all the intervening spaces, one should place the Astra-mantra as before.
Having placed the twelve-syllable mantra "Amukaṃ pāhi pāhi" in the center of the wheel, one should likewise place it in the region of the rim.
Then, having carefully drawn outside the mantra-wheel in due order, [the shapes] of a circle,
a triangle, a half-moon, and square cities.
And [the petals] are marked with a drop, a svastika, a kahlāra lotus, and a vajra; by means of the second starting from the navel, and then by the fourth starting from that same point.
One should cause those [names] to be joined with the four syllables in sequence,
together with the seed-syllable and its six limbs, followed by the words for protection.
Having encircled it, one should complete the circle known as the "round" (vṛtta);
having filled the third [layer] situated on the outside with twelve syllables, as before.

Alternatively, one should assign the second and fourth [syllables] in sequence to the eight outer directions, accompanied by the words for protection and repetition, while omitting the name. || 350 ||
One should indeed mix camphor and saffron with *rocanā* (yellow pigment),
along with milk from a tawny cow and the juice of its dung.
Having stirred it with night-water or river water,
one should write [the mantra] on a birch-bark leaf or on a peacock feather during the day.
When an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion is present, at a good moment when the planets have risen,
one should worship it and encircle it with thread and indeed with the sacred relics (dhātu).
By constantly wearing it on the head, the neck, or the right arm, one becomes freed from the defects of fate and increases in prosperity, devoid of sorrow. || 354 ||
For as long as one lives, one remains free from fears caused by external elements;
or, whether for the sake of others or for one's own sake, one becomes one who has accomplished what was to be done. (355)
Then the minister, being at fault, should with great effort seek forgiveness through this virtuous act of bestowing peace by means of the excellent mantra. || 356 ||
For the sake of accomplishing other siddhis through sacrifice, fire-oblation, recitation, and so forth—
thus has the method of protection for those who are afflicted been described.

Now he describes the method of protection even for those who are not ill, beginning with the words "especially for those free from disease" and ending with "by means of sacrifice, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth. "Freed from divine defects" means freed from the suffering pertaining to the divine (ādhibhautika). The so-called divine suffering (*ādhibhautika*) is that which arises from cold, heat, wind, rain, water, lightning, and the like. "Devoid of grief" means freed from the suffering pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*). The term "grief" (*śoka*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other internal sufferings as well. The so-called internal suffering (*ādhyātmika*) is that born of desire, anger, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and despondency;
likewise, it consists of grief, envy, humiliation, jealousy, malice, and so on.
By means of various ailments such as diseases of the head, catarrh, fever, colic, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, swelling, asthma, vomiting, and so forth;

Thus, by those known as eye-disease, dysentery, leprosy, and bodily ailments—this is what is called "affliction" (tāpa). "Released from that which consists of elemental beings" (adhibhūtamaya) means being free from the afflictions pertaining to elemental beings (ādhibhautika). Those pertaining to elemental beings are [caused] by animals, birds, humans, and so forth, as well as by Piśācas, serpents, and Rākṣasas.
And by means of reptiles and other such creatures, the *ādhibhautika* (physical) sufferings of human beings are produced.

Thus has the heating been described. Furthermore, the ritual application is as follows: on an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), when a benefic planet has risen, and at a propitious moment (*sulagna*), the practitioner—having bathed and performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*)—should mix together yellow pigment (*rocanā*), camphor, and saffron with the milk of a tawny cow, the liquid from its dung, turmeric water, and river water. Having taken that paste of saffron and the other ingredients with a pen made of a peacock feather, he should write upon birch bark or similar material in the manner to be described hereafter.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) enclosed by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and containing within it the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śrī Nṛsiṃha; having written that seed-syllable such that it is itself enclosed by the *praṇava*; then having placed that *praṇava* within the seed-syllable and again placed that seed-syllable in the middle of the *praṇava*—after performing this threefold rotation in this manner, and having placed all of that within the interior of the seed-syllable, one should encircle that seed-syllable with the letter *la*, the tenth consonant of the rim (*nemi*), and place the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, devoid of the vowel *au*, situated in the seventh position from the center (*nābhi*).

Having placed the letter *sa* above [the central syllable], and having differentiated it with all the vowels from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*) situated within the *āras*, and having filled it with that, one should draw outside of it a six-petalled lotus adorned with the void (*vyoma*). Having written the six mantras beginning with the Heart and ending with the Eye on its petals, and having also written the name of the person to be protected—enclosed by the *praṇava* and accompanied by the words "protect, protect" (*rakṣa rakṣa*)—in the six junctions between the petals in the four directions, one should draw outside of that a twelve-spoked [wheel] provided with a hub and a rim.

Having drawn the wheel, one should write the eighth seed-syllable, the letter *ha*, at the hub (*nābhi*); then, having excluded the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth vowels, one should place the remaining twelve vowels from *a* to *visarga* (ḥ), each modified by them, sequentially upon the twelve spokes (*ara*). In the spaces between the spokes, one should write: *oṃ kṣaḥ vīryāya astrāya phaṭ amukasya doṣān jahi jahi*. At the region of the hub and on the rim (*nemi*) of the wheel, one should write: "Protect, protect [the name] Amuka," enclosed within the twelve syllables of the Nṛsiṃha mantra.

Then, having drawn outside that wheel of mantras a circular mandala adorned with a *bindu*, outside of that a triangular mandala adorned with a *svastika*, outside of that a semi-circular mandala adorned with a *kahlāra* lotus, and outside of that a square mandala marked with a vajra; one should place the syllable *ya*, the seed-syllable of wind, at the center of the previously mentioned circular mandala; the second syllable *ra*, the seed-syllable of fire, in the triangular mandala; and the fourth syllable, the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛta*), in the semi-circular mandala.

Having written that third earth-seed (laṃ) within a square mandala, one should write the two words "Protect [the person] named so-and-so," enclosed by the seed-syllable with its six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) within a circular mandala. Likewise, within a mandala in the shape of a half-moon, one should write the two words "Protect [the person] named so-and-so," enclosed by the twelve-syllable mantra.

Furthermore, having drawn a triangular maṇḍala, a circular maṇḍala, and a square maṇḍala within a half-moon-shaped maṇḍala, one should write in the eight directions starting from the east, "Protect! Protect! (rakṣa rakṣa), omitting the name alone. Then, having worshipped this yantra according to the rules, encircled it with thread, and fashioned it from gold or other metals, one should constantly wear it on the head, the neck, or the right arm.

By this, one becomes liberated from the fear of the threefold afflictions—the internal, the celestial, and the elemental—for as long as life lasts. Thus, having performed the extraction of the *yantra* and so forth, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, and having propitiated the deity with attributes through sacrifices, fire-oblations, and meditative absorption, one should ask for forgiveness. || 333–357 ||
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the protection of Saṃdhāriṇī.
Now, whoever desires the accomplishment of the Dharma through the supreme mantra, || 357 ||
And understand briefly the procedure for attaining that, as well as for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the ancestors whose offerings have been interrupted. || 358 ||
Having observed a fast on the new moon day for the pleasure of the Creator of the World and for his own protection, he [beheld] the All-pervading Lord situated within the mandala.
Having invoked [the deity] according to the previously mentioned rite, one should unite [it with the image] preceded by devotion,
using water for the feet, the arghya offering, flowers, incense, and gifts such as gold and cows.
With food offerings mixed with sesame seeds and accompanied by kuśa grass,
along with vessels of pure water, one should personally offer handfuls of water.
By the grace of the mantra-form, he shall soon attain the eternal state;
he shall even lead his ancestors, though they be dwelling in hell, to heaven. (362)
With leaves, flowers, fruits, food, and grain; with curd, cooked rice, and the like; with juices, foods, excellent fragrances, garments, and superior minerals.
If he possesses the means, that best of ministers should worship with devotion, using coral, pearls, and rubies, [the Lord] residing in the Bimba or in the Maṇḍala. 364.
When the full moon (pūrṇā) arises at the mouth of the sixty-fourth [lunar day], one who observes a fast and desires the fruit of the dharma of sacrifice will surely attain it. || 365 ||
For he who desires to approach the great ford of the True Dharma should first duly worship the King of Mantras within the mandala, following the proper sequence.
Then, having gathered the necessary materials, one should perform worship preceded by ritual bathing;
[one may worship] an image already consecrated by a Siddha, or one established by a Siddha, or even one made by oneself. || 367 ||
With jars containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice, and filled with all medicinal herbs, perfumes, gems, fruits, and flowers; || 368 ||

Having addressed [the deity] with the mantra along with its ancillaries (sāṅga), one should offer [the oblation] together with water for respectful reception (arghya) contained in jars filled with one hundred and eight fruits, which have been purified by being submerged in water.
If this is accomplished with a mind purified by faith, one will soon obtain the grace of the Lord of Mantras as previously described. (370)
On the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), he who, while fasting, invokes the Lord of Mantras within the maṇḍala and worships him with fruits and flowers appropriate to the season; || 371 ||
For seven days, subsisting on fruits and roots, he was intent on bathing three times a day;
he performed many prostrations with eight limbs touching the ground, accompanied by circumambulations.
He who desires dharma through the giving of desired objects surely attains that which arises from those vows forever. (373)
Having reached the day of the equinox, being self-restrained and fasting,
he should mentally resolve upon the merit desired through the act of giving.
Having prepared a beautiful mandala provided with a fire-sanctuary, [he should worship] with offerings consisting of products from cows, as well as various foods and fruits together with roots. (375)

Having properly worshipped with garlands, incense, lamps, sesame seeds, oblations, and water-vessels, and having then satisfied [the deity], he [should then satisfy] the one who has entered into the fire.
Through sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds mixed with ghee, and rice, dharma increases thereafter; it grows more than a hundredfold through the gift of embodied beings.
Then, having prepared an auspicious mandala either to the south or to the north,
one should invoke the Lord of Mantras and worship him according to the ritual procedure.
With garlands, ointments, incenses, and great lamps fed with ghee and other substances;
with foods piled high with jaggery and sugar-candy; and with milk and rice-and-sesame porridge (kṛsara). || 379 ||
Having gratified the fire-god in the midst of the flames with coconut water, parched grain flour, and ghee, one should then [offer] the mantra with clarified butter and other substances.
By this very rite, merit consisting of *iṣṭāpūrta* is indeed attained;
likewise, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one who is pure and has fasted for a day and night [achieves the same]. (381)
Having first prepared the mandala equipped with all necessary implements,
and having deposited the supreme mantra therein, one should then perform worship according to one's means.
Then, having gratified the fire within with sacrificial fuel sticks or clarified butter and other offerings,
one should subsequently recite the supreme mantra mentally while joined with meditative visualization.
The mantra-practitioner who holds a rosary [in this manner] until the moon and sun are seen shall obtain infinite fruit from worship, fire-offerings, and recitation. || 384 ||
This is prescribed for devotees who are destitute of wealth, whose minds are solely fixed on the mantra, who lack the auxiliary components of the ritual practice, yet desire its fruit. || 385 ||
Through bathing, meditation, as well as yoga, the consumption of clarified butter, burnt offerings, and the observance of virtuous vows;
through excellent food and drink, giving, and the renunciation of everything according to the rule. || 386 ||
The accomplishment of Dharma has been taught specifically for those who possess wisdom;
however, one who desires the accomplishment of worldly aims from a mantra shall attain it without delay.
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic,
having performed the sacrifice there for seven days according to the proper rule, [he becomes] the king of mantras.
He should perform sacrifice according to his means, bathing three times a day and eating only at night;
he should satisfy the fire-god with clarified butter produced at the proper time during the three periods of the day.
With bilva, āmalaka, and lotus fruits— or in their absence, with kuśa sprouts—
he who desires the fruit of the mantra from the Lord of Mantras [should perform worship] at that time.
Indeed, on the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, when conjoined with the lunar mansion Śravaṇa and the day of Saumya,
the great worship of Mantreśa should be performed by one who has observed a fast.
Then, on a dry spot, or within a mandala, or upon an image, or in a water-filled jar,
one should worship the Lord of Mantras with the right and left feet.
Having filled a jar with water from the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, mixed with the water from his feet and accompanied by the prostrating *praṇava* [syllable Om], [he should proceed]. 393.

Having adorned it as beautifully as possible with flowers, garments, and ointments, and having placed it within its mouth along with the fruit resulting from the sesame oblation (tilahoma), [he should proceed]. 394.
Then, [one should offer] honey, clarified butter, sugar, and so forth, as well as curd-rice;
likewise, a large full jar or a vessel made of split bamboo. || 395 ||
Having first offered [the vessel] together with a pair of good sandals to the mantra-form,
he should then summon the recipient there along with a parasol.
Having adorned him with garlands, sandalwood paste, water for honor (arghya), incense, and a garment,
one should then place the water for honor in his hand with the mantra and [offer] that jar.
O high-minded one, having thus propitiated the Source of the World, the minister should be addressed with supreme affection by him who is intent upon securing his own satisfaction as well. (398)
