In this very way, those belonging to the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who have taken refuge in the flawless Nārāyaṇa, do so for the sake of pacifying their own misdeeds.

Having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods at the confluence of the Sannā and Nadī rivers, he then descended into the water up to his navel and offered pure handfuls of water with joined palms.
Having completed the sacrifice to the Blessed One, he should give [the offerings] to the most excellent of Brahmins for the sake of satisfying the deities who dwell in all the worlds. (401)
For the sake of his ancestors born of his own lineage who constantly long for the śrāddha rite, and for the attainment of Śvetadvīpa as well as for the prosperity of his own progeny. (402)
O stainless-eyed one, let alone the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) whether white or black; for those purified by devotion to the Blessed One, any other lunar day whatsoever [is auspicious]. (403)
And that very [nakṣatra] when joined with Śravaṇa and indeed conjoined with Abhijit attains the status of a limb for them, for the attainment of all fruits. || 404 ||
Therefore, having observed a fast, one should worship the King of Mantras on that [day] according to one's wealth or capacity, for the sake of attaining the presence of the mantra. (405)
Whatever gifts there are here, such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, which have been given appropriately to people who have performed their duties. (406)
When properly given by those of purified mind to devoted recipients, these very gifts yield fruits and bring about firmness in existence. (407)
For those who desire to touch the feet of the Blessed One, even this much discourse serves for the pacification of worldly existence: that Hari is indeed present everywhere as Acyuta. (408)
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Swan (Haṃsa), the Lord consisting of all powers, should be known as divided by way of his material form within the sphere of knowledge and action. || 409 ||
Just as bubbles and other [forms] arise from water through a threefold division, so too is the gift, oneself, and the recipient—all of which have Nārāyaṇa as their essence. (410)
Having first understood it through a general cognition, one must then thoroughly understand those three types individually with their specific distinctions when the time for giving has arrived. (411)
Having first inferred with one's own mind the substance characterized by skillful means, this is a certain imperishable capacity belonging to the One of Infinite Power. 412.
But the inner self, whose body is the pride of giving, is I myself, the Lord;
having attained the state of being a worthy recipient out of a desire for my grace. (413)

Having thus understood that this [universe] is indeed the god himself, manifest as the fivefold body through the nature of the five elements, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of his own form by means of the twelve-syllable mantra.

Then, relying on the mantra as the causal condition, one should meditate upon the [deity's] own form— without abandoning its true nature— as a mass of great rays of light, following the ritual of material oblations and so forth.
Thereafter, one should worship with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and unguents,
either with the "Lion-Sixfold" mantra or with one's own [mantra] devoid of its limbs (aṅga).
One should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the Supreme Self, who has become a worthy recipient;
having worshipped Him according to the rules with garments, garlands, and ointments. (417)
One should give a gift preceded by devotion to the Blessed One, accompanied by water; with a mind permeated by the Blessed One, one should thereby perform an act of pleasing him. (418)
By means of which gift, for those who know the Imperishable, it attains the nature of knowledge;
Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, has attained the state of being the referent of every word. || 419 ||
For the sake of pacifying the delusion of devotees scorched by the fire of saṃsāra, one should therefore perform the gift of his image with his own mantra. (420)
Either by means of the twelve-syllable mantra or by some other [mantra], having thus embraced that which is infinite and stainless as one's own self, [one should worship]. 421.
Just as that which is formed by mantras should always be worshipped according to the rules, so too should one worship the Supreme through the self of mantra by means of the bestowing of gifts. 422.
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing the virtuous vow, he who observes the vow of the Blessed One attains the state of Brahman through the nature of the Great Mantra.

And one should always worship with the spirit of Brahman according to the rules the various forms of austerity and sacrifice offered by those seeking that state, which are divided into many different kinds.

So that for those who sacrifice to Viṣṇu, there may be the fruit of liberation before long—[that fruit which is attained] through a sacrifice characterized by many features, whose body consists of various materials and auxiliary parts. (425)
Having thus brought [the deity] into embodied form by means of the sacrificial mantra, one should first perform worship;
one should offer oblations until the conclusion, and at the end of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one attains gold.
Whatever substance was previously offered or given in acts of charity, vows, austerities, and sacrificial rites—[that must now be restored]. 427.
For the sake of the subsequent sacrifice, one should first perform that very [rite] alone;
therefore, having been permeated by it, one should eat that which is purifying and accompanied by the *prāpaṇa* offering. (428)
It shall yield fruit for three nights for those devotees who perform auspicious deeds; how much more so, then, for those who are capable and rely upon this exhortation? (429)
And for those who delight in the dharma of giving, those observing vows, those performing sacrifices,
those fearing existence in the next world, those with few desires, and those seeking merit— (430)
One should perform the ritual libation with mantras using fuel-sticks from the śamī, palāśa, and śrīvṛkṣa trees, as well as from pure trees, and with water in the midst of water.
When the seven days have passed, having raised the mantra from the mandala,
one should, being composed and joined in meditation, perform the recitation one hundred thousand times.

Established in the holy life (brahmacarya), wearing the skin of a black antelope, avoiding unwholesome food, he should indeed renounce alkaline substances, fermented gruel, and oils, remaining free from greed. || 433 ||
Always sleeping on kuśa grass and skins, free from pride and envy, his body was like molten gold as he wandered about. (434)
One should first visualize the bird (the garuḍa) with its face covered by many streams [of nectar],
and the mantra situated within its navel, motionless and facing forward.
[He was] emitting from his own body the lovely luster of various jewels,
like a mass of metals such as gold and fine gems such as moonstones.
In this manner, one should meditate and recite the mantra, while performing worship from time to time;
until its completion according to the rule, the master of wealth himself should perform the recitation at its conclusion.
He should be obedient to commands and compliant, both with his person and his wealth;
he grants the desires of supplicants and enjoys them himself without ceasing. (438)
Endowed with long life and health through the power of the Lord of Mantras, there quickly arises for those who possess wealth and enjoy pleasures the fulfillment of their desires. (439)
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall describe its means of accomplishment:
having prepared a mandala as before in a pure and delightful place. (440)
Having summoned the Lord of Mantras there in a secluded place, one should perform the sacrifice;
thereafter, one should offer oblations for either three nights or seven nights.
One should perform recitation and meditation according to the procedure previously described;
one should meditate upon Hari, the great support of all, possessing the luster of a ruby.

In the center of that, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the supreme mantra, which has the luster of coral and is as radiant as the bandhujīva flower; he should then recite it the previously mentioned number of times.
Having directed his mind toward the enjoyment of women, the practitioner then, at the conclusion of the recitation, [finds them] there, terrified, tormented, and overwhelmed by intoxication. (444)
The wives of gods and kinnaras, the daughters of yakṣas and gandharvas, the siddhas, other celestial damsels, and all women of men and nāgas [were there]. || 445 ||
Indeed, until the end of their lives, they serve that sovereign of practitioners with right action, mind, and speech, through the power of this mantra. (446)
Whatever desire one strives for, beginning with the emergence from Pātāla,
the King of Mantras bestows that very thing through a hundred thousand recitations as well as through fire offerings.
Now, for the practitioner who has desisted from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, I shall explain the tradition that bestows liberation according to its true meaning. || 448 ||
Having again performed the excellent sacrifice with a serene inner self,
one should worship the previously mentioned time and the supreme mantra there in due order.

Having performed the libation according to the prescribed rule with water in either a sacrificial pit or in a body of water, for the sake of removing all defects and specifically for the purpose of expiation. (450)
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times, or as previously stated, according to one's own capacity;
then, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the mantra within the lotus of the heart.
Having made his own consciousness consist of that [light] through the multitude of hair-pores, which is enveloped by hundreds of jewel-flames, he [should do so] with those rays of fire. 452.
He has now completely burned away the entire body composed of the elements, and being liberated from that,
the Lord of Birds remains like the sun, assuming the very form of the mantra.
Then, one should gradually meditate upon one's own self as having the form of the mantra,
transformed into something resembling a sphere of light, devoid of all limbs and members.
That sphere of fire which is subsequently of vast extent, all-pervading, having the form of sound, yet consisting of pure consciousness in the form of existence. || 455 ||
Therefore, having gradually warded off even that conceit known as *asmitā*, one should act so that one spontaneously attains Brahman forever. (456)
Thus, the worship of the high-souled Nṛsiṃha of Vaibhava form has been described in brief, together with the means for attaining perfection.
This should be spoken to my pure devotees who are devoted to their daily rites, whose minds are weary of saṃsāra, and whose selves are restrained. (458)

Now, by means of this Nṛsiṃha-mantra, he explains the procedure for accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, beginning from "atha mantravarāddharma" up to the conclusion of the section. Its meaning is easy to understand. (357–458)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled the Vaibhavīya Nṛsiṃha-kalpa, in the Śrī Sātvata-saṃhitā of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Sātvatatantrabhāṣya, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, the son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Maunjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.

Now, by means of this Nṛsiṃha mantra, he explains the procedure for accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; beginning with "atha mantravarāddharma" up until the conclusion of the section. Its meaning is easy to understand. (357–458)
The eighteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
O lords of sages, when this had been spoken, Kāmapāla [spoke] again.
Out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds, he spoke these words to Hari.
Now the eighteenth chapter will be explained. He says "Thus" [to indicate] that Saṃkarṣaṇa asks. || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
Now, for the twice-born who have attained realization,
whose sins are completely exhausted, and who have ascended here in due order— || 2 ||

O Blessed One, I desire to know the definitive conclusion regarding the three types of initiation, by attaining which a devotee of the Blessed One may quickly become one who has fulfilled his purpose. (3)
He states the manner of the question with two verses beginning with "samprāpta": || 2-3 ||
The Blessed One said: On an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion, lunar day, and ascendant, as observed by the planets,
one should perform the ritual acquisition of the ground for the purpose of consecrating the devotees.
In a meritorious region that is favorable, delightful, frequented by the virtuous, abundant in soft water, fruits, and flowers, and provided with sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass; (5)
In a place blessed with cattle, horses, and rice, and free from small creatures,
he should go to ground of the appropriate color for his caste, possessing the characteristics previously described.
It was entirely free from defects, frequented by noble birds and deer,
and adorned with auspicious sites, monasteries, cow-pens, marketplaces, and houses.
Separated from [the enemy] by reservoirs, hermitages, sacred fields, and people of virtuous conduct,
it was forcibly enjoyed by the good people once they were freed from the fear of floods.
It is surrounded by forests, groves, villages, and urban districts;
whether there is lack of gain or the attainment of gain regarding one's own land among the Brahmins and others.
One should establish ownership by worshipping with one's own mantra,
having first ascertained that the site is free from defects, whether it be excavated or naturally elevated, in accordance with the specific caste requirements.
Having filled it with auspicious clay and interspersed it with small stones,
one should then knead it and subsequently sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having leveled and smeared [the ground] with excellent jewels such as gold,
one should perform the worship of the Lord there, including the portion ending with meditation, just as before.

Then he should conclude the rite there with the offering of oblations to the spirits (bhūtas), the satiation of fragrant waters (surabhīs), and the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born. || 13 ||
To the east of the directions, preceded by the attainment of success, there should be a pavilion adorned with decorations,
beautified by two excellent pillars situated at its corners.
It is adorned with a central royal throne,
and its width is prescribed by tradition to be equal for all, from the twice-born classes down to the Śūdras.
The base may be octagonal or square, provided with a pedestal;
it is characterized by a height of eight finger-breadths, decreasing by one at each stage.
For the sake of its own elevation, one should fashion a pedestal (upapīṭha) for all [the deities];
the width of the pedestals should be double the height of the main pedestal.
The pedestal for the seat (āsana-piṇḍikā) should be joined to the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), elevated by the same measurement as it,
extending one cubit toward the north, and should be duly constructed.
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) upon the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) and having set it down,
one should perform the rite of internal entry on its southern side.
One should construct a sacrificial pavilion (havamaṇṭapa) provided with separate windows, adorned with altars and sacrificial pits, and equipped with well-fitting doors and bolts.
Having smeared [the ground] with water consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra and with cow dung, one should duly make both pavilions beautiful; thus [it is said].
If, due to a lack of wealth, he has been ordained to dwell in the house of a twice-born man,
or in the abode of a teacher with his disciples, he should take up residence there.
As before, preceded by worship and followed by the libation to the spirits (bhūta-tarpaṇa),
[he should offer] boiled rice mixed with curd, parched grain, and ghee, and drenched with honey and water.
It is said that this is the propitiation of the spirits; without it, they remain there perpetually outside, enraged and desiring one's utter destruction. (24)
Therefore, once the site has been prepared with effort and the sacred field (kṣetra) established,
one should always and everywhere offer the bali-oblation for the sake of unimpeded success.

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva first described the method for constructing the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣā-maṇḍapa*), beginning with the words "under an auspicious and favorable asterism" and ending with "an offering everywhere at all times. (4–25)
Having thus performed this auspicious rite with the long, beautiful sound of the bell,
he should raise [the deity] from his own place as before, uttering the great *praṇava*.
Then, one should cause auspicious parched grains,
white mustard seeds, fruits such as the bilva, sandalwood and the like, and yellow pigment (rocanā) to be placed therein.
White flowers, the blossoms of that great tree, tips of green darbha grass, all kinds of gems, and gold—(these he offered). 28.
All medicinal herbs, cinnamon, cardamom, and other auspicious collections of fragrant substances;
as well as padmaka, śaṅkhapuṣpa, viṣṇukrāntā, and kundara. (29)
Seven and seven kinds of grains and seeds were prepared equally—six in total:
śāli rice, śyāmāka millet, nīvāra wild rice, and rice that had been extensively refined.
Indeed, those five [vessels] made of leather and those made of udumbara wood, provided they are free from leaks—even if they are very many—are acceptable. || 31 ||
For the purpose of daily use, even in new vessels,
and for the sake of the rites of water for the feet and sipping, as well as for the offering of curd and cooked rice.
Vessels made of gold and the like, or cups made of soft leaves,
white silk garments, and two pairs of new cloths.
The sacred thread with its upper garment, two well-washed white cloths,
pure silken garments, a bracelet, and a ring.
A rosary made of crystal, one made of leaves consisting of three counts, a wheel made of five metals with twelve spokes and accompanied by a conch shell. || 35 ||
A kutapa blanket, a yoga-band, an eye-cloth, a deer-skin, a garment of *brusīkāśa* fibers, a silk cloth, sandals, and leather shoes. || 36 ||
A staff, a water-pot, an umbrella, and a full vessel of wheat;
garlands of four colors, beautiful, purifying, and light. (37)
A mass of green leaves mixed with dark-green grass, guggulu as a fragrant incense, oil for lamps, and wicks; (38)
A mirror, an incense burner, a bell, and vessels for the arghya and other offerings;
colored powders, a pair of instruments, a *pālikā*, and a white *ghaṭikā*.
A very firm five-fingered ring made of gold or other precious materials, five blades of kuśa grass, a thread dyed with lac, a white thread, a pair of scissors, and a razor.
There should be eight shafts, including the tips, provided with the feathers of a peacock's tail; they must be raised up, firm at the tip, and made either of iron, clay, or wood. (41)
Those bases which have been colored with lime and other substances,
as well as the water-vessels, the water-pitchers, the *bhṛṅgāra* vessel, and the auspicious *karavī*— 42.
Likewise, the water-pot with its base, the vessel without a base, the common vessel, the cooking pot, the water-pot, the ladle, its cover, and the hearth. || 43 ||
A new, auspicious seat with four legs, square and long,
provided with a measured amount of wealth, along with betel and a collection of tooth-sticks.
The fire-drill (araṇi) joined with dry cow-dung, a fire-born gem,
sacrificial fuel-sticks of palāśa and dūrvā grass with their tips intact, and indeed the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Abundant dry fuel smeared with clarified butter, sesame seeds and rice,
and the previously mentioned sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as whatever other equipment is required for the fire oblation (*homa*).
Everything up to the eyelashes, provided with two large vessels,
and from among the aforementioned enjoyments, that which is used for the worship of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having understood that [the deity] enters into the state of being its limbs, one should cause everything to enter [it].

He describes the gathering of the necessary materials (*sambhāra*) with the words beginning with "having done thus" (*kṛtvaivaṃ*). The seven kinds of grains for both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* offerings—distinguished by the categories of cultivated (*grāmya*) and wild (*āraṇya*)—should be understood as those mentioned in the section on the cooking of oblations (*havir-pāka-prakaraṇa*). At this juncture, the *aṅkura* (germinating seeds) and the *pratisara* (protective cord) mentioned in the *Īśvara* [chapter] are to be taken, since the phrase "the *pālikā* and the *ghaṭikā*" is also stated here in the category of materials (*sambhāra-varge*). (26–48)
Out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devoted followers who are subject to worldly existence, the Teacher [spoke] of the All-pervading Lord.
For those who desire divine enjoyments and those who seek the state of ultimate liberation, one should indeed increase each individual [offering] at the Ganges by means of a material substance. 49.
Together with the eternal, unmanifest principle (tattva) and the true mantra-Brahman,
one should offer the sacrificial fee (sārtha) along with the ṛṣis and other components, according to the arrangement of mantras (mantravyūha) as prescribed in the scriptures.
It shall yield fruit for those with desires, and indeed grant liberation to those without desires.
With three verses beginning with "anugrahadhiyā," he states that when there are many disciples, there must be an increase in the sacrificial materials for each one.
Then, accompanied by his companions, he bathed there as before and performed his daily religious rites.
Having entered, even if situated in an unfavorable direction, one should then enter facing the east;
on the path, one should sit in the lotus posture or another such posture upon a hide, preceded by the ritual purification of the mouth.

Now, he describes sitting upon one's own seat preceded by the daily bath and other rites with the words "sasahāya" (accompanied). "Sasahāya" means together with attendants. "Mārge carmaṇi" means on a deer-skin. || 51-52 ||

Whatever grace one should perform for a disciple by means of a mantra according to its specific authority, one should carry out all ritual actions with that very mantra together with its auxiliary limbs (aṅga). || 53 ||

He states that one should perform all ritual actions with that very same mantra, accompanied by its ancillary parts, by which the initiation (dīkṣā) is performed; thus he says, "one should do. || 53 ||
If grace is to be bestowed by means of all the majestic mantras,
or for the purpose of granting all forms of propitiation and gifts, or for the attainment of the twelve [fold] powers, then [this should be done].
One should perform those two types of dhāraṇā with the Viśākhayūpa mantra;
having pervaded the body with its seed-syllable as before, one should [proceed] with those [substances] consecrated by it.
One should perform the mandala with materials gathered previously according to one's capacity.

For the sake of attaining fitness for all forms of worship and other rites, [the author] states in two and a half verses beginning with "samasta" that—using all the *vaibhava* mantras simultaneously during the section on initiation—one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) consisting of the two meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) called burning and nourishing by means of the mantra of Viśākhayūpa, who is the cause of even all the gods of the *vaibhava* [deities]; furthermore, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) upon one’s own body using the previously mentioned seed-syllable of Viśākhayūpa alone, and the filling of the mandala with white and other colors consecrated by that same mantra.
First, with garments, bracelets, and so forth, as well as rings, before the ritual anointings. || 56 ||
Together with a great white turban and white garlands,
along with mouth-fresheners such as betel-leaf and a tilaka mark upon the forehead.
Having made the body stable with a beautiful yogic band, he first describes for himself the adorning with perfumes and so forth in the two verses beginning with "prāk. (56–58)
One should place the seed-syllable of Īśvara in the center of the lotus of the heart.
Then, having touched the two hands with the *padmanābhīya* [mudrā] and the body with the one called *dhruva*,
he should touch the rest from the feet up to the head as before.
One should place the seed-syllable of the Lord, together with its limbs, upon the two hands;
having thus performed it correctly up to the mudrās, one should then withdraw it.
Having consecrated the conch and the discus with his own mantra using both hands, and having subsequently become one with them, he then placed them upon the surface of the earth.

Having observed all that resides therein, one should then proceed with the ritual action. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Viśākha-yūpa seed-syllable in the heart, the Padmanābha seed-syllable on the hands, and the Dhruva seed-syllable on the body. With the remaining thirty-six seed-syllables beginning with Ananta, one should perform a tactile consecration (*abhimarśana*) from the head down to the feet. Again, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands and the body using the Viśākha-yūpa seed-syllable, display the Vibhava mudrā, take up the conch and discus with both hands, consecrate those two with their respective mantras, and maintain the identity of oneself with them, as well as with all the ritual requisites.

He describes the commencement of the ritual action preceded by a visualization of [the deity] as being situated within the wheel and the conch with the four verses beginning with "hṛtpuṇḍarīke" (58–62).
Having consecrated it with the weapon-mantra, one should perform the rite while remaining amidst the bees.
Therefore, having smeared, swept, and scrubbed the sacrificial ground,
he did so for the sake of further increasing his splendor until the limit known as Brahman.
Having placed seeds together with gold and jewels,
he then filled the four vessels with filtered water.
He describes the purification and decoration of the sacrificial hall with two verses beginning with "consecrated by the Astra-mantra" (verses 62–64).
Then, having filled four vessels with filtered water.
In one [vessel], he should first place sandalwood and other substances, along with white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, tips of kusha grass, rice, and sesame seeds. (65)
One should place the unsurpassed relics together with jewels and fruits;
in the second [vessel], one should place four drops of curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk.
With the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one should offer bāhlīka along with flowers, sesame seeds and rice,
dūrvā grass together with viṣṇukrāntā, śyāmāka grain, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā.
And in the third [layer], there should be Padmaka wood combined with Kundareṇu,
along with the entire collection beginning with cinnamon and cardamom, together with camphor and sandalwood.
Having deposited all these auspicious substances into the fourth [vessel], one should indeed perform the joining of the substances for the four [deities] with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra). || 69 ||
Having consecrated all of that with the Astra-mantra and the Root-mantra,
one should perform the worship with flowers and other offerings using that very mantra accompanied by the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
In due order, everything to be meditated upon by all [practitioners] is like nectar.

He describes the sequence for preparing the *arghya* and other offerings with the words beginning with "having strained" (*gāliteneti*) and so forth. "The four vessels" means the set of four consisting of the *arghya*, the second *arghya*, the *pādya*, and the *ācamana*. "In one" refers to the primary *arghya*. Regarding the phrase "sandalwood and so forth" (*candanādīni*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes camphor and saffron, as this is explained in the *Pārameśvara*: "Sandalwood, camphor, and *bāhlīka*. "White mustard seeds" (*siddhārthaka*) means white mustard. "With *akṣata*" means accompanied by auspicious unbroken grains.

In the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, however, the term "unbroken" (*akṣatāni*) is used as a qualification for the *kuśa* grass. "Excellent metals" (*uttamān dhātūn*) refers to gold, silver, and copper; this is explained accordingly in the *Pārameśvara*: "gold, silver, and copper. "Fruitful" (*saphalān*) means endowed with fruits such as those of the plantain tree (*kadalī*); likewise, the *Pārameśvara* states: "One should place the principal offerings (*arghya*), beginning with plantain fruits. "With *bāhlīka*" means together with saffron (*kuṅkuma*). *Viṣṇukrāntā* is well known. *Śyāmāka* is the grain dear to the sages (*munipriya*).

Regarding *śyāmāriśi*: the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, “*Śāmāka* has blue flowers; it is also called *smayāka* and is dear to the sages. *Śaṅkhapuṣpa* is known in the Karṇāṭaka language as *viṣapraharī*. *Padmaka* is well-known in medical treatises (*vaidyagrantha*). *Kundareṇu* means dust (*reṇu*) associated with the *kunda*; *kunda* is a specific type of grass called *vālukya*. The lexicographers (*naighaṇṭuka*) state: “*Vāluka*, *vālukya*, *mukunda*, *kunda*, and *kundaru* [are synonyms]. In the Karṇāṭaka language, it is called *karṇikeya hallu*.

*Reṇu* is *reṇukā*, a well-known specific fragrant substance. Amara states: "hareṇū, reṇukā, kauntī. Alternatively, in the reading "samanvitaḥ kundareṇa," *kundara* is simply the previously mentioned *kunda*. In fact, that reading is more elegant. Previously, in the section on the gathering of materials, [it was stated]: "viṣṇukrāntā and *kundara*" (Amara). Alternatively, in the reading "samanvitaḥ kundareṇa," *kundara* is indeed the previously mentioned *kunda*.

In fact, the reading is indeed more flavorful as it stands. This is because, in the previous section on the gathering of materials (*sambhārārjana*), only the *kunda* was mentioned in the phrase "and the *viṣṇukrāntā* and the *kundara*," while *reṇukā* was not mentioned at all. Regarding the phrase "the collection of *tvak*, *elā*, and so forth": *tvak* is cloves (*lavaṅga*), according to Amarasimha’s definition, "the leaf of *tvak* is *utkaṭa* and *bhṛṅga*. *Elā* is well known. "The collection" refers to the group of substances beginning with those; here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *takola* and *jātīphala* are to be understood.

Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "along with cardamom, cloves, and *takola*, as well as nutmeg. The rules regarding the placement and other details for these items, such as the *arghya* offering and so forth, have been demonstrated in the sixth chapter. Furthermore, the procedures for burning, saturating, and so on, have been demonstrated in the chapter of the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. All of that should be observed as clearly explained in the *Saṃgraheshvara* and other works. (64–71)
In the invocation, in the presence, in the confinement, and likewise in the worship; || 71 ||
At the time of dismissal, one should always perform the offering of the *arghya* from the vessel first;
with that water, one should likewise perform the honoring (*ārhaṇa*) and the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).

One should perform the bringing forward (*praṇayana*), the taking up (*ādāna*), the pleasing (*prīṇana*), and the act of gratification (*prītikarma*). Regarding the application of the primary *arghya* water, he says: "In the invocation (*āvāhana*)," and so forth. "Bringing forward" (*praṇayana*) is the pouring [of water] into another vessel; "taking up" (*ādāna*) is the grasping [of it] preceded by that [pouring]. And this should be understood as having been employed in the ritual sections taught in the *Pārameśvara-tantra* and other texts, such as: "Having established the offering-water (*arghyavāri*) and perfumed it... (71–73).
The sprinkling of all objects, however, is performed with water other than that [already used]. || 73 ||
Indeed, at the commencement of all undertakings and likewise at their completion,
[this rite is performed] for the pacification of deficiencies and excesses, and for the pacification of errors in knowledge.
O Lord, that offering of arghya for the pervasive one should always be performed with the mantra-nature;
likewise, the worship of the main pitcher, the secondary pitcher, and the sacrificial pit is performed with the weapon-mantra.
O Great-minded one, regarding the worship of spirits, elders, and the poor, as well as for the sake of the teacher, the disciple, and oneself, there is both prescribed and unprescribed worship. (76)

He states the application of the second *arghya* (offering) beginning with "anyasmāt" and ending with "ukta-anukta-arcanaṃ prati. The phrase "of deficient or redundant rites" (*nyūnādhikānāṃ kāryāṇām*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. Thus, even for one who is composed, a fault certainly arises in all rites due to error in action or knowledge. The sense is that to pacify that, at the commencement and conclusion of all rites, it should be offered once each to the Blessed Lord.

The meaning is: of the *kumbha*, the *upakumbha*, and the *kuṇḍa*; that is, of the *upakumbhas* belonging to the *kumbha* and the *mahākumbha*, and of the *kuṇḍa*. Alternatively, the meaning is: the *kumbhas* are the jars placed in the east and other directions of the *mahākumbha*, while the *upakumbhas* are the jars placed upon them according to the method described for rites such as *śāntika*.

The meaning of "in the worship of the mantra-weapons and the jar" (mantrāstrakalaśārcane) is as follows: it refers to the worship of the mantras of Vāsudeva and others situated in the secondary jars (upakumbha), in the sacrificial grass-bunches (kūrca) and other items located within the girdles of the fire-pit (kuṇḍamekhalā), and in the weapon-jar (astrakalaśa). It should be understood, however, that the offering of the *arghya* to the one residing in the great jar (mahākumbha) is performed with the water of the primary *arghya* alone. Regarding "in the worship of the elements" (bhūtānāṃ saṃpūjane), the meaning is the worship of Kumuda and the others. An alternative reading, "and in the worship of enjoyments" (saṃpūjane ca bhogānām), is mentioned in the *Pārameśvara*, and it has been explained accordingly by its commentators as well.

It should be understood that in the passages "of the Guru and others" and "for the purpose of the self-worship of Dakṣa’s disciple," the subject matter concerns the worship of the mantras deposited upon their respective forms. This refers to the worship of both those rites already mentioned and those not yet mentioned; thus it has been stated in brief. It has been elucidated in detail by the *Īśvara* and *Parameśvara* [Tantras] regarding the worship of the door-keepers for the purpose of the self-worship of Dakṣa’s disciple.
Likewise, for the palaces, thrones, deities, gurus, and their lineages.
Likewise, in the worship of the deities who reside within the enclosures and coverings of the mandala, and who possess the forms of emblems, limbs, retinues, powers, and ornaments.

At the time of binding the mudrās, one should sprinkle the hands; likewise, one should perform the washing of that [image] during worship. At the time of recitation, one should likewise perform the washing of the rosary. Thus [ends verses 73–76].
One should always offer water for the feet from the third vessel;
then, one should offer water for sipping at the appropriate time from the fourth vessel.
He states the application of the *pādya* (water for the feet) with the half-verse beginning "the offering of *pādya*";
he states the application of the *ācamana* (water for sipping) with the half-verse beginning "the fourth [libation]" (77).
Having first sprinkled with the primary *arghya* water that which was previously placed in separate vessels,
one should then prepare the *pañcagavya* as before, using the [mantras] beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*).

Having offered that water with kusa grass, consecrated it with the first [mantra], and then with the principal *arghya* water, he describes the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and their combination in the verse beginning with "mukhya" (78–79). "With the first" means with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*). || 78–79 ||
Then, with both hands, which consist of the nature of Agni and Soma; || 79 ||
Having brought it to the state of fitness, one should sprinkle with water that which has been brought from elsewhere;
indeed, everything [should be sprinkled] with that water using *kuśa* grass placed at the tips of the seats.

With the half-verse beginning with "atha," he describes the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) preceded by the display of the mudrās for burning and nourishing all ritual implements; "by that" means by that pañcagavya. || 79–80 ||

Then, having taken all kinds of seeds and grains together with white mustard seeds, one should empower them by reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*) over them and meditate upon them as being identical to that weapon.
For the pacification of obstacles, one should swiftly cast [the water] in the ten directions;
then, having withdrawn it with a bunch of peacock feathers, one should indeed deposit it in the eastern direction.

Having internalized that [mantra] and having drawn [the diagram] with sandalwood paste and other substances, the King of Weapons (Hetirāj) describes the scattering of all seeds, grains, and white mustard seeds consecrated with the weapon-mantras in the ten directions for the purpose of pacifying obstacles in two and a half verses beginning with "sarvabījāni. "Hetirāj" means the King of Weapons, i.e., the *cakra*; the specific case-ending is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). (81–83)
Having adorned the water-pot together with the jar as before, || 83 ||
Having meditated upon them as having become embodied with enjoyments ending with garments,
one should perceive that body of the deity as auspicious like the sky.

Then, having invoked Viśākhayūpa into the center of that [mandala], one should worship him, proceeding in order until the conclusion of the mudrās; he is situated in the southern direction of that [mandala].

Having recollected that kurabaka flower as having the form of a weapon-embodiment, and having meditated upon the weapon-mantra within its center and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite; || 86 ||
The wise man, standing with joined palms and holding his weapons, should pray thus to him who destroys all obstacles and is the time that brings karma to its conclusion: || 87 ||
O Lord of the Universe, please accept this sacrificial hall constructed by me; O All-pervading One, remain present until its completion and attend to the requirements of the ritual acts.

Then, one should lead an unbroken stream of water from the weapon-mantra along the wall in a clockwise direction, starting from the eastern part and extending to the end of that square. One should also mentally visualize this.
Having placed that [image] together with the pitcher, one should perform a circumambulation;
having offered the *arghya* to both, [one should place them] in the eastern part, one below and one above.
Having worshipped it and covered it with a cloth, one should place the wheel consecrated by mantras upon a auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) and install it there within the base.
Having worshipped and bowed to the sword and the mantra-vessel,
one should then install the previously mentioned host of guardians of the directions in their respective quarters.
Then, having performed their worship with the Astra-mantra along with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
using the Praṇava and their own names followed by the word of salutation (namas).
One should perform the worship with water for guests (arghya) and other offerings for the archways, banners, and so forth;
then, one should meditate upon the pedestal previously described in the midst of the sacrificial fire-pit.
There, one should perform the worship of the Lord according to the previously mentioned sequence;
then, once the sacrificial pit has been consecrated, one should perform the libation ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before.

Now, he describes the sequence for the worship of the Blessed One in the fires of the *kumbha* and the *maṇḍala*, beginning with the words "the water-pot joined with the jar" and ending with "then the jar is worshipped as before. "Having adorned [it] as previously" means having adorned it according to the method described in the seventeenth chapter, starting with: "Then, having received permission, one should take the jar possessing auspicious characteristics. This is stated in exactly the same way in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, in the chapter on initiation (*dīkṣāpaṭala*):
"Then, having taken [a jar] that is firm, bright, uniform in form, and without blemish..."
A beautiful water-pot, made of clay, gold, or silver,
filled with jewels, gold, excellent perfumes, flowers, and all medicinal herbs.
Abounding with branches of auspicious trees, adorned with silk garlands around its neck,
filled with filtered water, and accompanied by a stream of water— thus it is auspicious.
"And smeared with sandalwood paste and the like, and honored with the offering of *arghya*.

This means [honored] with offerings such as coverings, garments, and other articles. "Having meditated on them as having become embodied" means having visualized the two makers of the jar (*kumbhakaraka*) as being the very bodies of the Lord of Mantras (*mantranātha*) and Sudarśana; for it is stated in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*: "One should behold that body of the deity as possessing stainless luster. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "having meditated and" (*vicintya ca*), it is also indicated that the worship of the Blessed One within the great jar was performed previously.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement: "Standing with palms joined in reverence, one should thus entreat the Lord who holds a weapon. Accordingly, having likewise imagined a seat for the pervasive Lord within the jar for both the Īśvara and the Pārameśvara, as before:
Having invoked the Lotus-Eyed One (Viṣṇu) in the center of that according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation of presence (*saṃnidhi*) and *sannirodha*, up to the conclusion of the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*).

Having performed everything as before, one should meditate upon [the deity] situated in the southern direction in the form of the embodiment of the Weapon-mantra (astra), and worship him according to the prescribed rite.
"And destroying the web of obstacles that ends with karma.

Thus, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the installation of the great jar (*mahākumbha*) in the northeastern direction is prescribed. Therefore, both of these two positions have been demonstrated in the sections on the Great Festival (*mahotsava*) and the Pavitraka Festival (*pavitrôtsava*) of the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* and the *Pārameśvarasaṃhitā*:
"One should visualize [the deity] proceeding clockwise from the eastern part to the end of its foot."
"Or else, O best of the twice-born, [he should go] from the direction of the Īśāna [corner] to the edge of its base.

Here, it is stated that after first sprinkling the wall with a stream of gold while moving clockwise, one should then place [the vessel] there and perform a circumambulation together with the water-pot (*kumbha*). However, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, a simultaneous circumambulation of both the *karaka* and the *kumbha* is also mentioned: "The water-pot should be moved behind [the practitioner], either at the same time or separately."

In this context, although the worship of the arches (*toraṇa*), banners (*dhvaja*), and so forth is mentioned immediately after the worship of the Great Vase (*mahākumbha*), it should nevertheless be performed prior to that worship of the Great Vase. This is in accordance with the previously stated logical consistency and the supplementary explanations regarding Īśvara and others. Furthermore, the worship of the Great Vase should be understood as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the worship of the Maṇḍala as well; for it has been stated that "one should draw the Maṇḍala with materials brought beforehand, according to one's capacity."

Furthermore, later on he will state: "Having applied [the offerings] according to the rule upon the sacrificial mound (khaṇḍila), the jar (kalaśa), and the fire," thus describing the distribution of the oblation among the jar, the maṇḍala, and the fires. (83–95)

Then, having worshipped those who have become one with the Blessed One, together with the lords of the fields, using water for honor, flowers, and other offerings, he should take the bali-oblation contained in the vessel.
Having spoken this, he should thereafter cast [the offering] outside the sacrificial hall:
"Those beings who are devoted to Viṣṇu, and those who follow after them... (97)
"May they, being satisfied, accept the offering and bestow auspiciousness upon me.
Having washed his feet and sipped water for purification, he should enter the sacrificial hall. 98.
Now, he describes the offering of the bali-oblation to the Bhūtas belonging to the Blessed One with three verses beginning with "tataḥ" (96–98).
Then, having consecrated the hearth situated in the eastern direction within the fire-chamber,
he should leave the cooking area and place it in the middle of the sacrificial pit from its own location.
Having cleansed the vessel with the Astra-mantra and smeared its exterior with cow dung,
one should smear its interior with fragrant substances and heat it with blazing Kuśa grass.

Having struck [the disciple] with the flower-weapon and having bound him around the neck with a white thread over which the armor-mantra has been recited four times, one should encircle him and worship him with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites.
Having placed [the vessel] on the hearth and set it upon the fire, one should pour honey, ghee, and milk into it;
then, once the milk has been thoroughly purified and boiled, one should place the rice grains into it with a blade of *aśvattha* wood.
Having consecrated it with the eye-mantra, one should move it with the root mantra;
having brought it down with the heart-mantra and sprinkled it, one should stir it with the crest-mantra.
Having smeared his head and rinsed it with very pure water,
he should adorn himself with sacred ash, sandalwood paste, and the like, using vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*).
One should place it elsewhere upon a seat within another mandala;
then, having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) for its accomplishment, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) of the sacrificial porridge (caru).

One should perform the offering of the oblation with clarified butter, which consists of the essence of light and nectar, using the syllable *haṃsa* together with the bindu, conjoined with the lords of the lotus-navel (the letters *ī*, *a*, and *na*). 106.

In the same way, it is by means of the two syllables *vauṣaṭ* and *vaṣaṭ*, as well as the two *praṇavas*, that [the deity] resides here, for these are inseparable from it; and now, [this occurs] by means of both.
Therefore, having taken that food with both hands joined as a casket, one should remember it as being covered above and below, just as previously described, while holding it in the heart.
Then, when the homa of the collection of substances has been performed and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is completed,
that [substance] contained in the three vessels is extracted by means of the application of an oblation.
Having employed [the offerings] according to the rule upon the sacrificial ground, the water-pot, and the fire,
one should then break apart the remainder— which has been consecrated with that [mantra] and the like— and which is covered with *kuśa* grass.
One should then offer three hundred oblations in sequence with the root mantra, the weapon mantra, and the eye mantra;
and having brought [the rite] to completion, one should indeed perform the final oblation once again.

He describes the procedure for cooking the oblation (havis) as well as the sequence for its division and offering, beginning with the words "Then, having prepared [it] in the fire-chamber" and continuing:
"Then one should draw a mandala with cow dung and other materials toward the north;
there, one should place a seat (viṣṭara) with its edge facing east, and within it, a blade of darbha grass with the heart-mantra. (112)
In the midst of that, one should place the disciple with his feet together and his body held rigid,
facing eastward, with the movements of his speech and mind restrained, and with palms joined in reverence.
One should perform its sprinkling with water using the Astra-mantra as before;
with that same [mantra], one should strike it on the head with blazing white mustard seeds and sesame seeds.
And for the removal of the bonds arising from beginningless latent impressions,
he [should act] with the Astra-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, using a blade of kusha grass from the region of his foot.
Having drawn [the lines] up to the tips of the topknots for the sake of a straight path,
one should remember it as being covered and pervaded by a web of mantras, like a net.
One should bind his eyes with a cloth using the Netra-mantra;
having first made a full añjali-offering of wealth, arghya-water, flowers, and perfumes.
Taking him by the hand or placing him before him, he should cause the boy standing nearby to cast that new handful of water with joined palms into the abode of the deity.
Having seen the mark of devotion in him, whose eyes were opened yet unseen by other people, and who was established on the path of virtue; || 119 ||
Abounding in horripilation, longing, and joy, accompanied by tears of bliss, and joined with prostrations, chanting, prayers, and circumambulations. (120)
Having understood that his inner organ is pure, one should contemplate, "This person is fit.
Then, at that time, contemplating oneself as having the Imperishable as one's self, [one should proceed]. 121.
One should then remember the host of principal deities situated within the discus and lotus on the right hand, each abiding in its own supreme abode.
He was illuminating everything with his own multitude of rays;
one should touch him with that very hand of Acyuta, which holds water.
Having placed that triad upon his back, with his hands joined in a full handful of flowers,
he should indeed conclude the group of mantras for the sake of pacifying obstacles to liberation.
Having led [the deity] back, one should worship the Supreme Lord again with the mantra,
having first understood His internal abiding through the relationship of the substratum and the superstratum.

Then, one should effect a separation from the earth and other elements, from the latent impressions residing in the intellect, and likewise from the self, by means of meditation, worship, and so forth. (126)
Relying upon the reality of the self (ātmatattva), the wheel of karma indeed revolves;
and supported by that wheel, the group of seven rests, having the intellect as its foundation.
And the pervasiveness of ignorance consists in the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, due to the support of the wheel of karma by the omniscient reality of the self. (128)
That wheel of karma, though ever-fickle, indeed continues to grow;
it remains stable only so long as it relies upon the earth and other elements as its support.
As long as the one whose nature is karma has not been awakened by the power of omniscience,
once awakened, he is able to effect its perpetual restraint.

Through action preceded by the propitiation of mantras and established in knowledge, that which is the support—beginning with the earth and so forth—is indeed the essence of being, characterized by human effort. || 131 ||
Having now established it, one should make the tree of karma sapless and turned into a barren creeper, so that, once the fruit of consciousness is released, the tree perishes. (132)

Therefore, for the sake of one's own purification, one should perform the worship of the mantras of the elements and their presiding deities in due order upon the ground in the presence of the Omniscient One.

Having first meditated on the common [reality] permeated by thought, presided over by the Lords of Mantra, and [visualized] the path beginning with earth and ending with intellect as being like a six-petaled lotus. (134)
There, in the center, one should place the lotus-navelled [deity], and on the eastern side, above the filaments,
one should install the group of six beginning with Viśvarūpa and ending with Kṣmādhara.
Having first taken the initial letter of one's own name and made it the seed-syllable (bīja) for those ending with the earth-syllable (kṣa),
one should then meditate upon their sequential placement (nyāsa) in order, situated between the syllables *ba* and *la*, as previously described.
And having first worshipped the seed-syllable *kṣmā* on the six tips of the petals that terminate at the base,
as the support of all the senses, as non-different [from the deity], and then—
It was enveloped by a mass of mental winds situated in the sky;
through yoga, it was perceived as being present higher and higher. || 138 ||
One should worship correctly with the vision of differentiation, and again by way of withdrawal;
[the deity] together with the vajra, marked by the fourth state (turyā), is drunk by means of its own seed-syllable. 139.
Having meditated upon that earth-element (kṣmātattva) as having become a golden lotus in the center thereof,
one should worship the Vārāha mantra together with its limbs and its enclosures in due order.
Having made it rest upon its cause and endowed with a surrounding enclosure, it then stands above the circle of the earth, resembling a half-moon. (141)
Having recollected the city marked with a lotus, which is like the interior of a great white lotus, and having focused his mind on the lake resting within it, he should perform the sacrifice.
First, one should visualize above that a triangle consisting of light, strewn with sparks of jewel-flames and marked with svastikas. (143)
There, in the center, one should worship Nṛsiṃha seated upon a jeweled lotus;
above that is a white circular city marked by clusters of stars.
Having recollected [the deity] seated upon a blue lotus, one should then remember the sky-seated one (Garuḍa) there;
above that, one should remember the formless space characterized solely by sound.
One should meditate upon that [lotus] as having the luster of the sun, with its previously mentioned color and accompanied by a lotus;
then, having worshipped the god Vāgīśvara therein according to the prescribed rite.
Then, within the space of that small cavity, one should recollect that which has the form of a lotus, consisting of the fluctuations of the mind, and possessing the luster of various jewels.
One should worship Viśvarūpa, the Lord of the Mind, situated in the center of that;
and above that, Amṛtagarbha, who is like ten million rays of the cool-rayed moon.
Having visualized the Lotus-Born Lord holding himself by his own self within the lotus, one should worship him who dwells therein as the Lord of the Intellect. 149.

In this manner, having sequentially brought down the assembly of presiding deities from the Supreme [level] for smell, taste, form, touch, sound, and the mental faculty, one should perform the worship. 150.
Having worshipped again and again, he should place that very [mantra] there once more;
those syllables which are the rays of the sources of beings (bhūtayoni) are like lotuses.
One should recollect their established state within this power,
as well as their origin, which consists of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā) and abides non-differently within the Self.
She arose from all the seeds as the sustaining power of Padmanābha;
she emerged from every sphere of sense-objects and was rendered free from them by her Lord. (153)
One should meditate upon her as having a throbbing form, fallen [from her seat], and without support;
when the time for initiation has arrived, one should worship her with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having thus worshipped the seven elements along with the adhibhūta and adhidaiva,
he should afterwards personally worship that disciple with his joined palms.
Then, having gone into the presence of the fire and meditated for three watches (yāmas),
he [should sit] on a seat made of darbha grass to his right, within the temple of the Discus.
Having grasped the right foot of the guru with his own right hand,
he sits down indeed, becoming one in soul through such contact and other means.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord as consisting of light, from the seed-syllable at the feet up to the crest,
suddenly dissolving that which is beginningless, arisen, and formless.
The manifold wheel of formative forces (saṃskāra) impels one along the path of suffering; through the mind of intention, it effects the unification of the channels and the act of intending. (159)
In the same manner, one should offer twelve oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee, along with armor and weapons, into the fire in sequence for the purpose of severing the bonds of karma. (160)
Having investigated this, it must indeed be accomplished by me within the Supreme Self;
therefore, first offer eight oblations of ghee with the root mantra. (161)
Having touched that head with the sacrificial ladle (sruva) filled with clarified butter,
one should offer oblations again with the "Knowledge-mantra" (jñānapada), which is the essence of all qualities.
One should perform the fire oblation according to the previously stated number, by means of the internal and intermediate unions,
correctly up to the state of Īśvara and likewise up to the end of Netra.
Thus, when the rite is completed, the *sampāta-homa* (the oblation of the remnants) arises;
it must be performed through the majesty of the mantra, endowed with all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). || 164 ||

And now, through the propitiation of the All-pervasive Lord and through the correct practice of yoga, one becomes a fit vessel for the qualities beginning with *aṇiman* (minuteness) as described hereafter. (165)
When the rite of the descent has been performed,
one should then perform the satiation of the mantras with clarified butter, offering it once for each, and having performed the worship, one should cause the Lord to hear [the recitation].
The karmic aggregate of this reality whose nature is action, along with its latent impressions and its manifold forms, has been paralyzed by me through your power.
Thereafter, for the purpose of expiation,
one should perform oblations with the seed-syllable internally restrained, using the eight limbs as the sacrificial wood.

To this extent, there occurs the destruction of the birth of a being of great intelligence who has taken recourse [to practice], and whose nature is mixed and characterized by that which is to be abandoned. (169)
Dharma, which yields liberation as its sole fruit, must be adopted immediately; O Acyuta, I shall now describe that manifold dharma which presents itself before us.
By which ignorance, being deeply internalized, indeed goes suddenly to its destruction;
then, having first taken a reddish thread and made it many-stranded.
Having gazed upon it with the eye and purified it with the water of the weapon-mantra,
one should contemplate it from the tip of the big toe up to the end of the crest-lock.
One should then remember that abode of all sufferings and their connections,
having entered the presence of infantile consciousness by means of the path of the gods (devayāna).
Having placed the name, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, upon the head,
and having enclosed it within the heart-mantra, one should proceed by way of the ancestors.
Having brought it together with the thread, one should lead it to equality by means of the Netra-mantra;
having worshipped it with arghya and other offerings, one should encircle it with the Mahātman-kavaca.
Having offered the seven forms with the mantra "oṃ hṛṃ adanyai hṛṃ svāhā," one should then [draw] with white powder consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra. || 176 ||
Having struck the body at the stage of childhood, one should likewise enter up to that limit;
then, one should utter the word "separate [this]" followed by the word for virility (vīrya). 177.
Then, having drawn that out by means of a word denoting knowledge (jñāna) with the particle 'tu' at the beginning and end,
and having made it conform to one's own intellect, one should meditate upon it like the sphere of the stars.
Having joined it within the internal thread by means of the syllable *haṃ* with its bindu,
which contains the river and the *praṇava*, one should place the empowered form within the body.

Having formed a body consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya), known as the subtle transportive body (ātivāhika), which is of the nature of a thread (sūtrātman) and manifested through the power of the Self (ātmaśakti). || 180 ||
Once it has been restrained by the *bala-mantra*, one should then perform oblations for that purpose,
reciting "Oṃ ātmane svāhā" sixteen times.
Having taken up future bonds that are pervasive and bestow pure enjoyments,
knowledge and the other [faculties] always remain here, having resorted to them.
One should join them back to their own mantras in their respective places,
having performed the libation for those who were worshipped according to the proper sequence.
Now, know that the state of the wheel of formative forces (saṃskāra), which rests upon the multitude of principles (tattva) and is indeed all-pervading, has a fixed characteristic. || 184 ||

By means of the pervasion of the principles (tattva-vyāpti) alone, within the body composed of the five elements, [the sequence extends] from the ankles, knees, hips, chest, ears, and eyebrows, up to the hollows of the temples. (185)
From the elements beginning with intellect (buddhi) down to earth, there is a sequence of seven earths;
likewise, there are the various distinctions that arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra). 186.
Those others who are born of the mind and abide together with the intellect, as well as those Buddhists who arise at the same time, and others who preceded them—[all these are likewise]. (187)

But those [entities], divided into many different categories, depend upon the intellect (dhi), which rests upon them—the entire universe consisting of fourteen worlds and endowed with manifold arrangements. (188)
Extending for a hundred crores [of yojanas], frequented by half of the eight wombs, it is stable, rests upon the earth, and must always indeed be understood as such. 189.
O Great-minded One, that group of four beginning with the waking state resides within the waters of the various thousands of millions of mantras. 190.
The state of those endowed with the perfections of yoga, who possess the fourfold nature and have attained liberation, is to be known as residing in the Taijasa plane.
O wielder of the plow, there is a convergence within the state of the vital breath of those whose natures are both quiescent and emergent,
as well as of knowledge and the other powers that have become manifold.
The sky is the support of the times; that form is not perceived.
Yet the phonemes, beginning with 'A', are established in the sixth mental station.
When this [mantra] is recited within the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), those who are attached to the Mother,
whether casting it forth or withdrawing it in this manner, do so indeed for the sake of purification, and even as a mere play.

That Lord, having first entered [the body] and then removed all defects, stands established at the stage of the power of intellect (buddhi-śakti-pada), [presiding over] the principles of action (karma-tattva). 195.
Having withdrawn his own power, he attains eternal peace,
from his reclining upon the netherworld up until the time of Madhusūdana.
One should perceive seven groups of seven and six within the pentad beginning with earth;
for thus [the powers] are established in the mind, as are the triad from Śakti and Īśa.

In the intellect (buddhi) resides the Lord, the Master of All, the Sovereign whose nature is like the lotus-navelled one; he is present once more in the earthly state of all those who are endowed with their own supernatural powers (siddhis).

However, the auspicious state of affairs within the division into fourteen parts (dvisapta) should be understood after discerning the disposition—whether intense, mild, or otherwise—endowed with devotion. (199)
By means of the object of focus, one should establish all beings in their own state;
this is [the procedure] for the rite of consecration during the initiation of Vaibhava.
The sequence has been stated; now, however, learn it with respect to the lower [form]:
from the feet up to the region of the navel, by means of the great elements beginning with earth. (201)
It is pervaded in four ways by the elements ending with air; above that, it is again filled with space as far as the heart, and from that region up to the top of the head.
Having mentally visualized that [the universe] is pervaded by this very sequence,
those beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa are indeed established.
Having traversed the six paths and reached the state beyond the path (adhvātīta) within the intellect (buddhi),
he takes up the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) and, as before, returns to embodied form.
These pervasive forms are surrounded on the surfaces of the earth by innumerable beings of their own likeness who are devoted to separate [deities]. (205)
And all [the powers] always abide within all the preceding numbers;
for, by remembering them through their non-dual nature, they were formerly like water in the six ritual acts (ṣaṭkarma).
One should contemplate that everything is pervaded by those [elements] beginning with earth up to the crest;
[the deity] who is the fourfold self, unmanifest, whose form is sound, and who is formless. (207)
One should meditate upon that very [reality] as being differentiated only by its qualities, like space, and as having an ungraspable body consisting of its own intrinsic nature. (208)
But when [the breath] has indeed transferred into the intellect (buddhi) and is always arisen there,
it takes up the individual soul (jīva) by its own power, even against one's will, and moves upward.
Having dissolved that [world] by his own power according to his own capacity, he remains as one whose self is peaceful;
[he remains so] for those devotees of pure intention who desire nothing but his feet.
And it manifests everywhere within those things permeated by its power; therefore, whatever is perceivable, whether it be fit to be abandoned or limited, [is of that nature]. (211)

"That which [is projected] always comes to be in that very form for those whose selves are constantly cultivated"—in such passages, the eternal substratum known as *vidyā* is the universal commonality of all things. (212)
That [Self] too must be understood as having attained a state of uniqueness; for it is indeed that very Self which, until liberation, constitutes the essential nature of living beings.
O Mahāmati, it exists in a subtle form like a vajra and is fully present;
at the time of initiation for disciples, it should be recognized exactly as it has been described. 214.
In the same way, one should understand this further regarding the analysis of the Sūtra;
first, one should divide the joints sevenfold with saffron and other substances. (215)

Having visualized [the mantra] from the fourteen [vowels], one should then string it together with its own causal [syllables], joined with the word of one's own name, beginning and ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
Thus, when the heart has been filled with enjoyments consisting of attainments,
one should lead them to the one situated in the mandala and offer them as a presentation for the Lord to partake.
Having covered it with armor and placed it before the jar,
the teacher, together with his disciples, should then perform worship once more of the all-pervading Lord, the Soul of the Universe.
With circumambulations, prostrations, and various words of praise,
[he should worship] there on the smeared ground, both within and outside the mandala.
Having placed it in its respective locations and consecrated the eyes, the heart, and the mantra, one should employ it in the five products of the cow, the sacrificial porridge, and the tooth-stick.
One should perform the deliberation on success regarding the tooth-stick discarded after eating if it points toward the east, the north, the west, or the northeast. (221)
Know that this indicates success; otherwise, it is the opposite.
To destroy that [failure], one should indeed offer oblations a hundred times with the Vīryamantra.
Incense, ointments, and the like; powders such as those made from *ghaṭikā* and so forth; sesame seeds with clarified butter, and other suitable substances, O wielder of the plow (*lāṅgalin*). (223)
Having lifted it up and placed it to the north, one should cover it with a very white, unwashed, and new cloth that has been consecrated with the *varma* mantra.

Having worshipped thoroughly with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) using flowers, incense, and unguents, and having asked for forgiveness, one should place the deity— whether situated on the ground, in the fire, or in the water-pot— into the vessel.

Then, on a purified portion of the ground, having placed the disciple upon a bed of kuśa grass consecrated with the heart-mantra with his head facing east, [the teacher] should [draw him in] with a hook over which the *bala* mantra has been recited.
Meditating on the principal mantra while visualizing the body enveloped by the heart-mantra,
one should then cause [the disciple] to sleep with sesame seeds consecrated by the heart-mantra for the sake of obtaining auspicious dreams.
One should place white mustard seeds around the outside of that [mandala];
with the mantra of the outer wings, one should deposit the eight [deities] in the directions as before.
Having wrapped it four times with a white thread as armor while circumambulating it clockwise, one should then exit from the pavilion to the outside.
Having performed the rites such as using the tooth-stick,
he himself should sleep on the ground upon a bed of *darbha* grass, with his head toward the south.
Touching with his two feet the infant lying upon the bed,
he indeed mentally prayed to the Blessed One who bestows liberation.
O Ādiśa, Lord of the World, Omniscient One, who dwellest in the heart!
Therein I unite this performer of ritual action, whose sole refuge is You. (232)
Having received permission, he should indeed perform the application for his disciples;
wherever that is done for them, it shall certainly be eternal.

Then, [the teacher performs] the placing of the disciple upon a seat, the sprinkling [with water], the striking with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds, the tracing of his body with the tips of *kuśa* grass, the pervasion by the mantra, the binding of the eyes, the throwing of a handful of flowers, the touching with the hand of Acyuta, the worship of the mandala, and before that, the worship of the seven elements beginning with earth and the collection of mantras presiding over them; furthermore, he sits together with the disciple near the fire and performs a *homa* for the sake of effecting the separation of the disciple's karmic impressions (*vāsanā*).

The touching at the moment of arrival, the formal announcement, the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*), the conceptualization of the disciple’s body as consisting of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread), the sequence of the pervasion of the elements beginning with earth starting from the ankles, the arrangement of the paths of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) and so forth within the earth and other elements, the location of the various abodes such as those in the netherworlds (*pātāla*), the specific arrangements of the seven elements beginning with earth according to the distinctions of the *vibhava*, *vyūha*, and supreme mantras, followed again by the worship of the water-pot (*kumbha*), the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) by the disciple, the eating of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the cleansing of the teeth.

He describes the examination of the falling of that wooden splinter, its pacification, the dismissal of the deity residing in the mandala from the water-pot and other vessels, the student’s lying down for the sake of obtaining a dream, the performance of protection around him, and the teacher’s own going to sleep after first praying to the Blessed One and performing such acts as cleaning his teeth; then he says one should prepare the northern side of the mandala with cow dung and so forth, starting until the completion of the section.
"The group of six beginning with Viśvarūpa and ending with Kṣmādhara" means the group of six deities known as Viśvarūpa, Vāgīśa, Khagānana, Narasiṃha, Sarasāyin, and Varāha.
Then, from his reclining upon the netherworld up to Madhusūdana;
One should perceive seven, seven, and six within the pentad beginning with earth;
for thus [the principles] reside in the mind, as does the triad from Śakti and Īśa.

The meaning of the statement "In the intellect (buddhi) is the Lord, the Self whose navel is a lotus, the Sovereign of All, the Master" is as follows: beginning from the one reclining on the serpent-bed in Pātāla up to Padmanābha, one should perceive among the thirty-eight manifestations of the Lord (*vibhava-devas*) the seven beginning with the one reclining on the serpent-bed in the principle of earth (*kṣmātattva*); the seven beginning with Nārāyaṇa in the principle of water; the seven beginning with Lokanātha in the principle of fire; the seven beginning with Nārasiṃha in the principle of air; the six beginning with Kroḍātmā in the principle of ether; the three beginning with Śaktyātmā in the principle of mind (*manastattva*); and Padmanābha in the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). This is the intended meaning.
Since the initiation by means of the all-pervading mantra has been described in the *Sātvatāmṛta*, [it is said]:
"By whichever mantra the initiation of anyone is to be performed, that very mantra and its associated [deities] are to be worshipped according to the previously prescribed path."
In this ritual, the application of the constituent parts should be performed according to what has been taught;
one should proceed with the heart and the other limbs ending with the base (mūla) as if they were a single aggregate.
Having thoroughly concealed the entire group of principles within the nature of the inner self at all times,
one should then perform worship as before.

It should be understood that, according to what will be explained hereafter, the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) and others are established within the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth (kṣmātattva). || 112-233 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the ritual for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa-dīkṣā*), in the venerable *Sātvata-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya* composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Maunjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
Nārada said: O Brahmins, this preliminary initiation called *adhivāsa* was indeed taught by Acyuta to Sīra; therefore, he has been urged by him once again.

Now the nineteenth chapter will be explained. Having thus heard about the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa-dīkṣā*), Saṃkarṣaṇa asks again; thus [the author] says: "Regarding the preliminary consecration... (verse 1).
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord, for the benefit of the Vaiṣṇavas, I wish to hear from your lotus-like mouth a concise exposition of the rules for initiation.
He states the manner of the question with the word "deva" (O Lord). || 2 ||
The Blessed Lord said: Listen to the initiation (dīkṣā) of those in the cycle of worldly existence, which indeed possesses both singular and manifold forms;
having attained it, they reach their desired state at the end of the body.
One bestows the fruit of liberation alone; another bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and the third always bestows enjoyment upon those who are awakened.

All [rites] should be performed with the approval of the teacher for the sake of attaining the fruit correctly, for disciples whose minds are purified and who are permeated by a spirit of devotion. (5)
For the elderly, for women, for children, and for those of purified soul,
those [medicines] are beneficial even without a full range of medical practices, which are otherwise difficult to perform.
O high-minded one, having previously deliberated thus with wisdom, and having understood his intention after approaching him together, she accomplished it alone.

Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord, having explained the differences in the fruits of the three initiations (dīkṣā) which are distinguished by the divisions of Paravyūha and Vibhava, and having shown that among those three initiations qualified disciples possess the right [to practice], while for the elderly, children, and women there is qualification even in the absence of difficult conduct, he states with the words beginning "one or many" that one of the three initiations should be performed according to their respective intentions regarding the fruits. In this regard, even a very slight performance is prescribed for those who are incapable, as stated in both the Jayākhyatantra and the Lakṣmītantra:
"Either by means of the sacrifice of the Great Mandala, or from the oblation alone."
Furthermore, this initiation is threefold, being performed either by speech alone or by other means.
"Of one who is rich in wealth, of one with little wealth, and of one devoid of property, respectively. Thus [ends verse 3.7].
Then, having risen from his bed at the passing of midnight,
the teacher should take his water-pot, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) outside, and re-enter.
One should visualize the Astra-mantra before oneself, resembling a mass of fire;
one should enter the deity situated within it, and thus the ritual bath performed with mantras is accomplished.

By means of that excellent weapon, the impurity of sleep and delusion is constantly brought to total destruction; likewise, the pegs, the water-clocks, and the dust-particles there [are destroyed]. 10.
Having taken up [the powder], being mindful, and having ground it with water on the surface of the earth smeared with dry cow-dung, one should prepare the mandala previously described.
For the sake of preserving the auspiciousness, stakes should be placed in the corners,
