and one should also be set in the center for the purpose of achieving the illusion of a lotus.
It does not indeed undergo even slight inequality, just as during the time of night;
for there is a great fault in the teacher and his disciple when there is deficiency or excess.
Therefore, that must always be protected with great effort;
having performed the daily rites at dawn, preceded by a bath. (14)

Having summoned and exhorted the disciple regarding the attainment of auspicious or inauspicious dreams, [the author] now describes, with the words beginning "Then, when midnight has passed," the teacher’s rising from bed, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the mantra-bath, the drawing of the mandala, the performance of the daily rites at dawn, and the examination of the disciple's dreams. (8–15)
Indeed, the assembly of the four forms is situated according to their respective directions.
One should perceive [the assembly] seated in rows, both sitting and standing;
from among them, one should discern either the single reality of the Blessed One or that which possesses distinct characteristics.
The multitude of manifestations, the collection of his marks, and this divine host of women—all these are either one or many. (17)
Or the entire multitude of the instruments of existence, whether existing as a whole or separately, characterized by Rudra, Indra, the Moon, the Sun, water, fire, wind, and space. (18)
The Brahmins, experts in the Pañcarātra and devoted to its practice, as well as the twice-born who proclaimed and recited the Trayī (the three Vedas), [were present]. 19.
The ascetics, pure in being and established in the state of the eternal Brahman, [offered] excellent trees with fragrant scents such as mountain-creepers, garlands, sandalwood, and the like. (20)
Gardens, women, groves, ponds, palaces, and great dwellings;
fruits, seeds, medicinal herbs, or even a water-pot with its contents spilled out after cooking—(these are all inauspicious). 21.
An elephant, a cow, a river, a vehicle, an adorned maiden, an infant, auspicious and sweet songs, a kettle-drum, a flute, and a lute. (22)
A lake filled with lotuses and cranes, a white parasol spread out,
metals such as gold, a net of jewels, and products derived from cows.
A new mass of eyes, a pure collection of unwashed garments, the king, the domestic priest, a feudal lord, and the queen’s mirror. (24)
A fall of snow, a virtuous rain, the rising of great clouds in the sky, blood, raw flesh, leaping through the air, and a tavern; || 25 ||
A flock of good birds and deer, an image of a deity, a white chowrie, and other such things—know these to be bestowers of success. (26)
Listen briefly to those dreams which were inauspicious for me:
the withering of flowers, an earthquake, and a most terrifying eclipse. (27)
Fog, the falling of meteors, a thunderous crash that causes mental distress, entering a pit, curd-rice, and the eating of boiled meat; || 28 ||
The rolling of a chariot, the destruction of a vehicle, the falling out of one's own teeth, laughing excessively like a donkey or a camel, and a forest infested with monkeys and bears. (29)
The place is filled with smoke, burnt, and enveloped in black garments;
there is the drying up of rivers and the like, as well as their very reversal of course. (30)
Even the breaking of a boat, a vehicle, a banner, an umbrella, or a tree brings about failure;
likewise, descending from a mountain or a tree, being naked, or seeing a ghost [is inauspicious]. (31)
An ointment of fat, soot, oil, and clarified butter; staying in excellent mud;
being a buffalo, a snake, or a black man; and coming from the southern direction due to hunger. (32)
The plucking out of nails and hair, the breaking of bones, and so forth—these and other such inauspicious things occur quickly, O Mahāmati. (33)
He describes auspicious and inauspicious dreams with the verses beginning with "But the assembly of the four forms" (4.15.33).
When an auspicious or inauspicious dream has occurred, one should indeed form a resolution in the heart and,
out of eagerness, perform worship and fire-offerings that destroy all inauspiciousness.
Regarding an inauspicious dream, he says that its pacification is attained [by this]. || 34 ||

Having caused the deity to descend according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him in due order; then, having offered libations according to the proper method, one should perform the rites up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 35 ||
Furthermore, he describes the worship of the pitcher and the other vessels in their proper sequence according to the prescribed rule: "by the aforementioned method. (35)
In the northeast or the north corner of the sacrificial hall,
upon the previously described mandala— whether circular or square— [one should perform the rite].
One should cause the disciple—who has bathed, is wearing garlands and garments, and has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa)—to enter;
having gazed upon him, struck him, sprinkled him, and touched him with *darbha* grass as before.
Having consecrated it as if it were an image, one should then touch with the mantra-hand that object situated on the ground which is to be graced, starting from the feet and ending at the head.

He who has conquered the seeds of suffering should bestow the mantra-hand, which has the appearance of a flame, upon the disciple who has bathed, been adorned, and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). He describes the seating of the disciple on a mandala smeared with cow dung and the purificatory rites such as *nirīkṣaṇa* (inspection) and so forth in three and a half verses beginning with "In the northeast corner" (*īśakoṇe*). * Nirīkṣaṇa* is performed with the Eye-mantra (*netramantra*). * Tāḍana* (striking) is performed with sesame and white mustard seeds consecrated by the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). * Prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is performed with water from the Weapon-mantra. * Ālabhana* (touching) is performed with *darbha* grass. * Pīṭha* (the seat) is [consecrated] with that same Weapon-mantra. It should be understood that the rite of *mūrtivat* (as if it were the deity's form) is performed through the ritual placements of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
"With the mantra-hand" means with one's own right hand, which has been visualized as the principal mantra. || 36–39 ||
Taking that from his hand, he should go near the temple of the gods. || 39 ||
Having placed [the vessel] on his left side and again covered his eyes,
he should likewise cast the añjali containing the arghya with his eyes open.
One should perceive the supreme abode, the mantra that bestows the fruit of one's desires;
at that moment, one should give the child a name as is appropriate.
Its names—whether secret, primary, secondary, or as they truly exist, including the general ones beginning with Vāsudeva—are derived from its own limbs in all four [forms]. (42)
For all [of them], whether with distinctions or according to the sequence,
[the names] marked by the twelve forms (dvirdaśaka-mūrti) ending with Svāmin should be assigned among the Brāhmaṇas.
One should again divide the space up to the gods and the Kṣatriyas into twelve parts;
or [one may divide] up to the hands or ending at the edge of the blade, preceded by the insignia and the weapons.

And [the rites] known as the banner-marking (dhvajalāñchana) among kings according to their respective status, as well as those ending with the growth-ceremony (vardhana), preceded by the consecration of the image and its marking. || 45 ||
It has been ordained that for Vaiśyas and those born as Śūdras, [the rites] end with the status of a *dāsa*.

Now, beginning with the words "Taking him," he describes the procedure for giving the disciple a Vaiṣṇava name, ending with the phrase "for those born as Śūdras. At this juncture, prior to the naming of the disciple, the wearing of the *sudarśana* and *pāñcajanya* and the application of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* must be performed; for it is said, "Initiation by heat (*tāpa*), the *puṇḍra*, the name, the mantra, and sacrifice as the fifth," thus establishing that these two [the marks and the name] occur before the naming ceremony.

Furthermore, [the text states]: "The wheel made of five metals, together with the conch, has twelve spokes. Thus, the conch and wheel were previously mentioned in the section on the acquisition of the requisites (*sambhārārjana*), and their heating was established on another occasion.
Now, one might object: "In the section on the acquisition of the requisites, the wheel and conch were not taught for the purpose of heating;
rather, having completed them as hand-symbols (*mudrā*), one should subsequently bring them forth correctly."
Having consecrated the conch and the discus with his own mantra using both hands, and having subsequently become one with them, he then placed them upon the surface of the earth.

If you argue that these two were established solely for the purpose of being employed in ritual action after one has observed everything residing therein, then what contradiction do you perceive in that? Let them indeed be employed even in a well-known instance of heat. Nor should it be said that my contradiction lies simply in being contrary to the Vedas; for hundreds of proofs establishing that [the practice] is indeed Vedic have been set forth in *Saccaritrarakṣā* and in the *Siddhāntacandrikā*, which causes the melting away of the branding of heated seals. May you observe this with careful attention.

Therefore, even in this Tantra which is rooted in the Veda, it is stated in the twelfth chapter: "Those whose manifestation is clearly evident throughout the three worlds by means of weapons, garments, and banners."
They too bear a multitude of marks upon the soles of their feet,
on their foreheads, on their shoulder-cloths, on their backs, and on the palms of both hands.
On the crown of the head, amidst the mass of body hair, for the sake of the realization of those engaged in ritual action—
and even for a transmigrating being who is by nature a devotee of Viṣṇu.

"He does not abandon the mark of the Infallible One; how much less so that which consists of his manifest form"—thus is the wearing of the Vaiṣṇava marks of the Lord clearly established. Furthermore, even the misconception that this statement refers to innate marks has been refuted in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*.

Granted that the wearing of the Sudarśana and Pāñcajanya is indeed established by authoritative means; however, what is this restriction that it must be performed at this very moment during the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*)? If such a restriction were intended, then that too would have been stated by the Lord himself in so many words, just as he did regarding the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Furthermore, if it is argued that even in the Jayākhyasaṃhitā, Lakṣmītantra, Padmatantra, and others, this is not presented as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of initiation, that is true. But who has said that it is a constituent part of initiation?

Previously, it was established in the section on the *sambhāra* (preparatory materials) that those who had not yet received the marks of the conch and discus were to have a wheel made of five metals along with a conch, having twelve spokes. Later, at the time of bestowing the teacher’s insignia upon the disciple immediately after the teacher's consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), he will state: "The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the meditation belt (*yogapaṭṭa*), the conch, the discus, and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).

However, because the branding with the discus and so forth has its primary time prior to initiation, it was not explained during initiation itself as a secondary occasion. In the *Īśvaratantra*, however, it is explained precisely at that secondary occasion.

For there is no rule that because something is prescribed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it must necessarily be performed at that very moment; this is because various times for the wearing of the conch and discus (*śaṅkhacakradhāraṇa*) have been prescribed in different places—such as during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and so forth, prior to the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), after the *upanayana*, or after marriage. However, the time of initiation must by all means not be transgressed, since in the *Pratiṣṭhā* chapter of the *Pārameśvara*, it is stated:
"And those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas [of his lineage]..."
Maudgalya and others, as well as others likewise, must by all means not be devoid of those emblems; therefore, [they should be marked] with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
The [iron] objects, heated by fire and consecrated with their respective mantras,
should be marked in an instant after being worshipped with arghya, perfumes, and other offerings.
When Brahmins and others, as well as Śūdras, are endowed with knowledge of the three Vedas, established in the prescribed conduct, and possess the characteristic marks as described;
"Then they should be known as fit for hearing the sacred precepts (*samaya*) and so forth.
Thus, it is established that only those who possess the aforementioned characteristics are fit for initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now, [one might ask]:
"But in this way, having worn the Sudarśana [disc] heated by fire, O best of the twice-born..."
Having initiated him according to the prescribed rule, one should subsequently employ him in ritual acts.
Thus, it is established that only one who possesses the prescribed marks is fit for rites such as the reception of the *gāyatrī*;
"The discus on the arm belongs to the twice-born, but the discus on the head is divine. For those twice-born ones who lack the discus, worship and giving are fruitless."

If it is argued that by such a statement, one who lacks the prescribed marks is not even fit for the giving away of a daughter in marriage, and therefore the times for initiation (*upanayana*) and marriage—which involve the branding with the discus and other signs—must likewise not be transgressed, then whose view is it that such a transgression is acceptable? The conclusion is that, due to the impossibility [of otherwise fulfilling the requirements], even if the Smārta sacraments are transgressed, the time for the Vaiṣṇava tradition known as *dīkṣā* must by all means not be transgressed. For it is established in the *Pādma Purāṇa*: "Only after being marked with the discus should a learned man take refuge in Vāsudeva."

For this very reason, even out of fear of transgressing the prescribed time for initiation (*dīkṣā*), the marking of the *cakras* and so forth is taught specifically within that section on initiation. However, for those who have already had the *cakras* marked prior to that, such marking is not the primary concern at the time of initiation. Furthermore, if the practice [of wearing them] is already established, there is no sin even at the time of initiation, as it is said in that same context:
"A Brahmin should wear the *cakra* and other marks on his forehead, head, or arm, for the sake of purifying sins and the like, and for the destruction of the afflictions of worldly existence."

This is because [the practice] is established in such works as the *Ādityapurāṇa* as a means of bringing about purification, and because, even for one who previously bore a sectarian mark, its re-manifestation is established when the body becomes defiled through growth and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised:

"In the Viṣṇvāgama and other Tantras, it is prescribed that the branding with the conch, discus, mace, and so on, is for those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*), and not for other embodied beings."

If it is argued that the marking of the *cakras* is understood from such statements even after initiation (*dīkṣā*), we say no; for the phrase "of those initiated" (*dīkṣitānām*) refers to those who are eligible for initiation. In the *Siddhāntacandrikā*, however, it is stated that "of those initiated" refers to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). That is inconsistent, because such an interpretation is accepted out of fear of entering the *tantra*-initiation. This fear is groundless; for in the *Mahābhārata*, in the *Śāntiparvan*, it is said:
"A Vaiṣṇava must certainly enter initiation with every effort. Hari is especially pleased with one who is initiated, and not otherwise."
One should initiate a Brahmin in spring, a Kshatriya in summer,
a Vaishya in the autumn season, and a Shudra in the winter.
"And a woman during the rainy season according to the procedure of the *Pañcarātra*.

Thus, the entry into the *tantra*-initiation (*tantradīkṣā*) is prescribed for all [castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, without distinction. Since these statements have been declared to refer to specific qualified persons, and in the absence of any further determining factor, [the initiation is for] those who possess the defining characteristics—namely, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
He is to be worshipped and served by those who are ever-devoted to their own duties.
At the end of the Dvāpara age and at the beginning of the Kali age,
he was sung of by Saṃkarṣaṇa, having resorted to the Sātvata ritual.

Thus, even the statements from the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata can only be understood as referring to specific qualified individuals. If you argue, "Let them be so; what loss is there for us?", do not speak words that contradict the teaching of the Ācārya. For in the *Pañcarātrarakṣā*, having cited these very passages from the Bhīṣmaparvan, it is stated: "In this way, without distinction, the worship of the Lord and other rites according to the path taught in the illustrious Pañcarātra must be performed by all, including Brāhmaṇas and others."

It has been established that even for those who have reached the culmination of all *sūtras*, the propitiation [of the Lord] and other rites according to the methodology taught in the scriptures of the Blessed One are most highly praised; and thus they are practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). In that very same work, in the second section (*adhikāra*), it is further demonstrated that the venerable authors of the *Bhāṣya* and others, having taken some particular *saṃhitā* belonging to the established doctrine of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* as their primary authority, have compiled the rules for daily worship (*nityārādhana*).

Therefore, by the maxim that "a matter determined in one place applies everywhere," it should be understood that the statements in the *Śāntiparvan* prescribing the entry into initiation (*dīkṣā-praveśa*) apply without distinction to all people. While such a statement from the fifth Veda remains authoritative, what fear do you have regarding that entry into initiation? Without the Tantric initiation (*tantra-dīkṣā*), how can your eligibility for the worship of the Lord and other rites prescribed therein be established? Through initiation, the Brāhmaṇas and other castes (*varṇas*) gain eligibility in due order; so too for those born of natural unions (*anuloma*), but not for anyone else.
"In the ritual procedure for the worship of the Lord, there are secondary (anukalpa) authorities.

Thus, in the *Padma Purāṇa* and other texts, it is heard that the authority to worship the Lord belongs only to those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*). Furthermore, here too, in the second chapter, it is established: "Indeed, there is authority for the four [castes] when the sequence of initiation has been performed. Do not say that this refers to the matter of sacrifice for the sake of others (*parārtha-yajana*), because the authority of the four castes is declared without distinction. Even though you yourselves, in the *Siddhāntacandrikā*, state: "A Vaiṣṇava is indeed one who has obtained initiation as prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa* and other Āgamas,"...
He who bears the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth, without having received initiation into the Tantra,
is to be recognized as a heretic by those who perceive the truth.

And although the initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the *Tantra* system is indeed accepted here, nevertheless, for fear of performing too many requirements, it was stated that the word "initiation" refers merely to the undertaking of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) consisting in the abandonment of other deities. By reflecting upon statements from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources, you should not entertain any fear regarding entry into this initiation. Enough of this digression; let us return to the subject at hand.

The sequence for performing these purificatory rites, such as the marking with the discus (*cakrāṅkana*) and others, at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is correctly set forth in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā*. Even when they are performed at separate times, that same sequence must be followed. At that time, the fire—whether it be the fire of Viṣṇu’s sanctuary, the fire of the Guru, or one's own fire—is used;
and [the disciple is purified] by means of oblations and other rites performed in due order with vessels that have been heated, well-formed, and consecrated.
When one realizes oneself to have become a servant of the Supreme Self,
at that very moment one should mark one's body with the conch, the discus, and other signs.

Thus, what is stated in the Bhāradvāja-saṃhitā should be accepted. In that regard, the fire of the temple of Viṣṇu is indeed Vaiṣṇava. If it is the fire of the preceptor or one's own, it should be consecrated by first performing the installation according to one’s own Gṛhya-sūtra, followed by the procedure for making it Vaiṣṇava as supplemented by the Īśvara-tantra. The wearing of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) should also be performed only after the branding with the discus (cakrāṅkana). As for the triad of sacraments known as the Name, the Mantra, and Sacrifice (nāmamantrayāga), they must be performed at the very time of initiation (dīkṣā), since they are established as being limbs of initiation itself.

If it is argued that, in that case, the simultaneous performance of the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*) is not possible, what harm is there in that? Regarding the naming ceremony on the twelfth day of a newborn boy, the marking with the conch and discus (*śaṅkhacakrāṅkana*) is prescribed in the scriptures; likewise, it is practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭas*).
On the twelfth day, Keśava [is marked] along with the child's kinsmen, by that preceptor Śrīśailapūrṇa of immeasurable splendor.
Having first had him marked with the conch and the discus,
he then playfully gave him the most auspicious name Rāmānuja in the world.

Thus, the practice of the learned masters, such as the author of the Śrībhāṣya, is also proclaimed in works like the *Prapannāmṛta*; therefore, there is no rule requiring the simultaneous performance of the five sacraments (*saṃskāras*).

If it is argued that even though their simultaneous performance is impossible at that time, the simultaneous performance of the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*) is possible after a second initiation (*punarupanayana*) or after marriage, and that such a practice is established by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) as evidenced by the Commentator and others—this is true. For this very reason, we have already previously explained the cause for performing them again at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*). (Verses 39–46)
Then, having risen and paid homage to the mandala, the pitcher, and the guru.
The preceptor, together with the child, should go near the sacrificial pit once the oblation has been offered,
for the sake of ensuring the flawless completion of the performed rite.
Having become the embodiment of the weapon through [the ritual] striking, one should enter its heart as before;
having briefly deprived it of the power of vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) and drawn it out, [one should proceed]. 48.
Having caused him to enter his own place, he should lead him there like a spark of fire,
and having properly separated him, expel him along with the vital air.
On one's own level, [the breath] is restrained from the heart to the end via the left path by this very rite joined with the mantra, which effects the seizing of birth. (50)
Pervaded by meditative absorption on the [divine] form, one should abandon the nature of father and mother;
thereafter, one should offer [the water] consecrated seven times with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra).

Then, having risen from near the mandala and performed prostrations to the Guru and the Deity, the disciple should go with him to the vicinity of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa). After the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa), he should strike the disciple with white mustard seeds and other substances consecrated by the Astra-mantra, and perform the purification of his elemental nature (bhūta-śodhana) through the two meditative concentrations (dhāraṇā) known as burning (dahana) and nourishing (āpyāyana). This is stated in the five verses beginning with "athotthāya" (46–51).
Then, one should give [the armor] consecrated seven times with the kavaca-mantra.

Regarding his other sacred thread (upavīta) that has arisen, and whatever belongs to him—referring to the wearing of a new sacred thread for a disciple of the three castes who is worthy of wearing the sacred thread—the author says "tataḥ" (then). || 51-52 ||
And for one who has, in reality, always fallen into the state of servitude. || 52 ||

Of one born into a lineage that abstains from intoxicants, who has abandoned worldly conventions, who is like a trusted friend, who is established in Brahman, and who delights in the system of ritual action; || 53 ||
The gift of a cow (godāna) is indeed prescribed for the Śūdra caste and not otherwise;
however, he states in two verses [52–54] that the gift of a cow is prescribed for a Śūdra who is worthy [of it], and this applies at all times.
But for those rites concluding with vauṣaṭ, svāhā, and vaṣaṭ, there is a counter-remedy.

When the purpose of the mantras is accomplished through salutation and when grace is bestowed, whatever means for the sacrifice there may be—such as the water-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth—[should be offered]. 55.
Whether well-prepared or unrefined, food attains fitness through devotion.

Since a Śūdra is unfit for the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and other such mantras, the word *namaḥ* (salutation) is to be employed as its substitute within the body of the mantra; thus he says, "Vauṣaṭ. In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, however, it is said that first there is the twelve-syllable [mantra], and afterwards that consisting of eight syllables.
Thereafter, having formally initiated them into the mantras of the deity's forms according to the prescribed rite, [he should proceed].
It is exclusively Vaiṣṇava by name, devoid of the word "namaḥ" and the syllable "oṃ," and free from "huṃ," "phaṭ," "vaṣaṭ," "svāhā," and so forth, beginning with the names of the Keśavas.
Having taught [the Veda] to women, Śūdras, and likewise to those born in the direct order (anuloma), for those who perform the Sāvitrī ceremony, the same rules as for Brahmins shall apply.

Thus, even the utterance of the *praṇava* and the act of salutation are forbidden for Śūdras and others. Elsewhere it is stated: "Neither the tone of the *praṇava*, nor its constituent parts, nor other injunctions are prescribed for women and those of the Śūdra caste; for them, only the recitation of the mantra is permitted."

Thus, the mere utterance of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is prohibited. Therefore, the regulation should be understood according to the distinction between [the mantra] used alone and that used in combination. He says "belonging to him" (*tadīyam*) to show that even flowers and other materials brought by a Śūdra become fit for ritual action if they are offered with devotion to him (the devotee). || 54–56 ||
But for other devotees, [the practice] is prescribed as a means for accomplishing sacrifice.
The proper cessation of attachment to living beings is preceded by the sprinkling [of water] while reciting the *darśana* mantra;

likewise, for the members of the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), the cessation of the conceit of ownership regarding the substances used as sacrificial implements is prescribed. He states this with the three quarters beginning with "therefore, for others" (56–57).
Or, O Great-minded One, one should perform the casting of flowers before an image or at the front of a mandala.

He states with three quarters [of a verse] beginning with "darśana" that the disciples should perform the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) either before the image (bimba) or before the mandala. "Darśana" means looking [at it] with the eye-mantra (netramantra). By this, the worship of either the mandala or the image at the time of initiation (dīkṣā) is indicated. || 57 ||
Either at night or during the period of affliction, one should indeed perform this for the sake of the vow alone;
thus, having first purified the collection of phonemes through such consecration.
One should perform that expiatory libation with the pervasive [mantra] along with its limbs,
a thousand times, including a tenth part, according to the proper sequence.
Having gone and worshipped Kumbheśa, he took the thread situated there;
then, having made the child stand upright, he likewise stretched out the thread.
He states with the half-verse beginning "naktam" that for the purpose of the initiatory vow (dīkṣāvrata), either pure fasting or eating only at night is prescribed.

Thus, with the two and a half verses beginning with "evam," he describes how, following the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) for the Brāhmaṇas and others, one should perform the expiatory fire-offering (*prāyaścittahoma*) according to the order of the castes (*varṇa*) using the root-mantras together with their ancillaries (*sāṅga-mūlamantra*) in a number of one thousand and ten parts (*daśāṃśa-sahasra*). This is preceded by a petition to the Lord residing within the water-pot (*kumbha*), followed by the taking up of the *māyāsūtra* placed near Him, and the stretching of that thread from the feet to the crest-lock (*śikhā*) of the disciple who has become upright. || 58-60 ||

One should contemplate the Lord of Mantras in his manifest form situated in the midst of the fire; one should clearly perceive the path within the pervasive [deity], the child, the thread, and within one's own self.

Having meditated upon the Blessed Lord in His manifest form within the center of the fire, one should contemplate the path (adhvan) within that Blessed Lord, within the child (śiśu), within the thread (sūtra), and within one's own self; thus he says, "the manifest," etc. (verse 61).
Therein, one should recollect the internal nature residing within the body of mantra,
and having brought that divine nature into one's own self, [one should contemplate it].
In the *Śiṣyavigraha* [chapter] of the *Sūtra*, he explains the threefold nature consisting of the objective world (*adhibhūta*) with one and a half verses.
"Threefold" means having a nature distinguished by the divisions of the internal (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the objective (*adhibhūta*). (62–63)
But at the conclusion of the root mantra, one should add "obeisance to the Supreme Self" (parātmane).
Having established the foot, one should offer four oblations;
likewise, having uttered "to the subtle self" (sūkṣmātmane), and then indeed "to the gross self" (sthūlātmane).
Then, for that [deity] who is the self of all, one should meditate upon the entire collection of paths situated within one's own body, from the tips of the toes up to the crest-lock. 65.
In the very order previously indicated, although they are divided into three types,

he [the author] describes their satiation mantras, the number of oblations, and then the recollection of their pervasion within one's own body from the feet to the crest in due order by means of the three root-mantras (verses 63–66).
The structural arrangement of the earth and other elements, as well as their status as objective realities; || 66 ||
That which is to be understood as the presiding divinity (adhidaivata) is the specific power belonging to each;
that which is the internal self-nature (adhyātmatva) of the mantras is prescribed as their presiding principle (adhiṣṭhātṛ). || 67 ||

With the verse beginning "racanā" (and continuing for one and a half verses), he explains the categories of *adhibhūta*, *adhidaiva*, and *adhyātma*; the meaning is that these refer to the mantras presiding over them, namely the previously mentioned mantras such as Varāha and others. (66–67)
Then, having abandoned the two paths, one should take refuge in the dvādaśānta;
having become composed of the root mantra, one should then proceed by means of one's own intellect.
Then, having stepped upon the disciple's portion at the Brahmadvāra-pada by way of the middle path between them,
he should step upon the Pārthiva-pada and bring that power under his own control.
It consists of the seed-syllable, restrained by the heart-mantra, joined with the [syllables of] peace and wrath,
combined with various egg-seeds, and endowed with manifold arrangements.
Thus, having taken up all the powers that are the culminations of the intellect,
one should place them individually and in due order within that heart-mantra-sandwich.
One should meditate upon him as possessing a dual nature, sustaining that body both by his own internal quality and by the supreme, all-pervading Self.

O Mahāmati, having thus performed the withdrawal of the powers of the elements from the form of the Child (Śiśu) at that time, until the end of the destruction of enjoyments, which is the [appointed] time— 73.
Then, having entered the body according to the Sūtra, it proceeds there shining forth by that very same path; indeed, one should manifest it through the intellect as if it were the beginning.

Then, having taken up the internal mantras accompanied by the elements and sub-elements, as well as those established in their own state through the pure, eternal characteristics of knowledge and the mantras; || 75 ||
Then, having emerged from the thread, one should proceed to the locus of fire;
there, through the joining of the parts, one should perform the ritual of mantra-equality.
Having established the collected mantras in their respective positions within the supreme characteristic of omniscience— the all-pervading and universal— || 77 ||

Then, having reached his own body through the door of Brahman, the Guru [describes] the entry of the disciple into the interior of the Preceptor’s body via the aperture of the *brahmarandhra*, the method of dissolving the powers (*śakti*) of the principles (*tattva*) such as Earth and the rest therein, the entry into the internal thread-body (*sūtramaya-deha*), the grasping of the objects of meditation (*dhyātavya*)—both the objective (*adhibhūta*) and the subjective (*adhyātma*)—therein, and finally, having reached the Lord situated within the fire, the establishment of the collected mantras there, and their re-entry into his own body; all this he explains with the words beginning "Now, having abandoned the two paths" (*atha mārgadvayaṃ tyaktvā*).

The "two paths" means the two paths of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the levels (*pada*), because those two are impure. For one who has entered the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*), the state of being composed of the root-mantra (*mūlamantramayatva*) is accomplished. (Verses 68–78)
Having taken up the *sruva* ladle and heated it, [he should recite] the collection of mantras as prescribed.
And together with the multitude of principles (tattvas), preceded by his own name and the syllable Om,
he [should worship] again through the method of conjunction, numbering twelve.

He describes the satiation of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and their presiding mantras by means of the process of dissolution (saṃhārakrama) with the words "the *sruva* [ladle]," etc. The application should be understood in this sequence: "Oṃ kṣmāṃ namaḥ kṣmātattvāya svāhā; for the Earth-principle, this [is offered], not mine. "Oṃ saraśśāyine svāhā; for the one who lies upon the arrows, this [is offered], not mine," and so forth. Here, by the phrase "by the count of twelve" (*dviṣaṭkaparisaṃkhyayā*), it is understood that even previously, in the order of dissolution, the number of oblations (*āhuti*) was twelve. (78–79)
Having drawn [the breath] in by means of inhalation (pūraka) from the disciple’s heart-lotus into one’s own heart,
one should then expel the seed-syllable of Earth (kṣmā-bīja), which is the characteristic of the beyond (paralaksana), through the individual manifestation.
Having restrained [the breath] with the power of consciousness (jña-śakti) by means of knowledge, having drawn it from the fire [element] into the heart,
and having caused it to rest upon the seat of the Praṇava, one should exhale it into the lotus of childhood (śaiśava).

Then, having recollected the consciousness of the disciple as being one alone, he who assumes two forms should meditate upon it in the state of the possessor of power (śaktimat) and power (śakti), and indeed as power itself.
Having again emitted that [element] which is contained within the earth-principle (kṣmātattva) from the sacrificial pit by means of the Śaktimat mantra,
he should [emit it] into his own body through the central path under its own name.
Having directed that purified [earth] toward the single characteristic of recitation and meditation,
one should indeed offer that very earthly seed with the heart-mantra through the rite of oblation.
For the sake of properly assisting him, he should be led to the state of the subtle body;
[the mantra] ending in *svāhā* is for the attainment of enjoyment, while that ending in *namaḥ* is for the attainment of liberation. (85)
For the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation, that very [mantra] which possesses both characteristics should be employed;
however, at the conclusion of ritual actions, one should place it in the state of *sampāda*.

Thus, when the subtle body has been dissolved, one should restore that [consciousness] which resides in the heart-lotus to its natural state by means of the head, according to its respective authority.
Having completed that enjoyment with the Śikhā-mantra one hundred times,
one should meditate upon the attainment of its fruit through the Varma-mantra, as well as its state of dissolution.
Then, one should bring about complete satisfaction with that very [eye] and establish [the deity] by means of it;
the release of that [deity] should be performed with the Astra-mantra, joined with the rite of separation. || 89 ||
Then, having grasped that [offering] with the root mantra, one should again make it one's own;
likewise, one should [take] his Śakti from the pit, characterized by pervasiveness.

Then, O high-minded one, for the sake of pacifying the earth-element (kṣmātattva) which is to be accomplished and is unique, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the weapon-mantra (astra) the previously stated number of times.
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, one should extract the earthen [linga] from the thread of the shoulder;
together with the full [offering], it should be dissolved into the fire at its own place.
Then, by means of the root mantra suddenly impelled from the heart-lotus,
one should project the youthful *śakti* out of one's own body through the exhaling breath (*recaka*).
One should meditate on that which is situated below, pervaded by that [power] as if by something distinct;
and one should likewise contemplate the first path, the *bhauvana*, like a lotus petal by means of the *kabindu*.
And then, above the seed-syllable *Kṣmā*, which has been restrained within the body of the disciple, embraced by manifestation (*vyakti*), and filled with its own power; 95.

Having performed the purgation (*virecana*) for one who possesses power (*śaktimant*) according to the previously mentioned individualized method, one should perform the following: the extraction of the disciple’s consciousness from his own heart; the extraction of the seed-syllable of earth (*kṣmābīja*), which resides in the fire and has been manifested and then cast out; its placement within the lotus-heart of the disciple; the recollection of the disciple’s consciousness in the fire as being the power (*śakti*) internal to the principle of earth (*kṣmātattva*); and then, by means of its possessor (*śaktimat*), the purification of that body and the application of the disciple to the occasion consisting of the recitation and meditation on the seed-syllable of earth. Then, with the mantra *oṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*, one should either say, "Make [this] into a subtle body, svāhā," or "Make [this], namaḥ."

One should perform the rites with oblations using the mantra "Sampādaya namaḥ svāhā" or "Namaḥ svāhā. Likewise, there is the rite for bringing about the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), the oblation pertaining to its authority, and the oblation for the purpose of separating it [from the gross]. Then follows the reintegration of the Power (*śakti*) and the Possessor of Power (*śaktimān*) into the Self, the oblation for the pacification of the Earth-principle (*kṣmātattva*), and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) together with a fragment of the earthly portion of the thread of ritual action. Furthermore, one should establish the connection between the disciple’s body and his power, as well as between the worlds and the paths (*bhuvanādhvan*), just like the relationship between a drop of water and a lotus leaf. This is done in the same manner as with the Power.

He also explains the connection between the earth and the seed-syllable, beginning with "having drawn [the breath] by means of inhalation" and ending with "by means of the individualized attribute as before. (Verses 80–96)
At that moment, however, [he perceives] the path as it truly exists, situated within the seed-syllable. || 96 ||
Out of compassion, those Lords reveal that [path] for the sake of its accomplishment.

At that time, the presiding deities of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and so forth, out of compassion, reveal to the disciple the path situated within their respective seed-syllables exactly as it exists; thus he says, "At that moment" (tatkṣaṇe). || 96–97 ||
One should cultivate detachment in the disciple who reflects upon this with his intellect. (97)
This very essence of the earthly realm is indeed a futile cage of suffering;
and now its vast magnitude has truly entered into the reality of existence.

"How was I here, for whom these [worlds] were not extended?"—by means of these two verses beginning with "viraktaṃ," he describes the manner of reflection of a disciple who has become dispassionate through illumination. (97–99)
Just as a bird, once freed from a cage, dwells in happiness. || 99 ||
"At that time, the child ascends upwards by the power of the mantra.

Beyond this, he describes the similarity between the disciple and a bird released from a cage with the word "vimukta" (released). Although the consciousness of the disciple is liberated from the earth-element (*kṣmātattva*) by the power of the mantra, because it remains mounted upon that [element], it is said that the bird also has ascended above the cage. (99–100)
Then, having informed the assembly, he who remained as their authority... || 100 ||
"May the quality of sovereignty be completely and eternally restrained for him from every side through the power of your grace, just as it ought to be. (101)
For one who has correctly entered into the teaching of the Supreme Lord, the subtle element of smell remains present within him until the end of the body.

With two and a half verses beginning with "the collection" (samūham), he explains the group of mantras starting from the netherworld (pātāla) situated within the earth-element (kṣmātattva), as well as their specific modes. || 100-102 ||
O Lord, Sovereign of the Earth, from this day forward, you must become the destroyer of obstacles to liberation for those who perform their duties. 103.
He describes the manner of the boar’s petition dependent upon that [the Earth], beginning with the words "O Lord of the Earth. || 103 ||
Having thus informed and commanded, and having offered the oblations in sequence, one should draw [the deity] together with Śakti by means of the inhalation (pūraka). || 104 ||

Immediately after this request, [the author] says "iti" (thus), stating that one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the previously mentioned mantras of the principles of earth (*kṣmātattva*) and their presiding deities, and effect the extraction of the conscious principle (*caitanya*), together with its power (*śakti*), from the disciple’s body by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). Regarding the word "ājñāpya" (having commanded), the word "gandha" (fragrance) is to be supplied as an ellipsis, because it will be stated later: "having commanded the taste, like fragrance. || 104 ||
And in that body, one should place the watery seed-syllable (vīja) common to all as before;
and having contemplated the individual soul-power (jīva-śakti) within the center of the sacrificial pit as before.

O high-minded one, having performed purgation, the capable practitioner should thereafter apply himself to that meditative absorption (samādhi) as before, by means of breath-retention (kumbhaka). 106.
Furthermore, having attained this body through fire-offerings, meditation, and so forth, and having indeed completed everything there according to one's qualification; 107.
Having first placed it together with the watery thread-cluster, one should likewise meditate upon the water-element conjoined with its word-mantra as being pervaded by that [thread]. || 108 ||
Having caused that collection of mantras, together with its presiding lord,
to be recited as before, and having commanded the essence (rasa) to be like fragrance, [he should proceed].

Now, he describes the refinement of the water element (*aptattva-saṃskāra*) with five verses beginning with *taddehe*. "In that body" means in the body of the disciple. "The watery seed" means the seed of the water element; this refers to the mantra *oṃ aṃ namaḥ*, as stated previously: "Having brought the first letter of one's own name to the state of being a seed for the elements ending with earth. "With its support" means resting upon the seat of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). "The possessor of power" means the consciousness of the disciple meditated upon as possessing power. "Therein" means within the body of the disciple.

"In that samādhi" means in the samādhi characterized solely by the previously mentioned recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). "Having attained a watery body" means having produced a subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*). "By means of fire-offerings, meditation, and so forth" means by means of the fire-offering of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and other such rites. "Preceded by authority" means exceeding the enjoyment of one's [current] office. "Joined with the *pada*s" means joined with the paths of the *ṇdā* (the *mātṛkā*). "Overwhelmed by that" means overwhelmed by the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) together with his power (*śakti*). "Situated therein" refers to the collection of mantras, meaning the collection of the seven mantras beginning with Nārāyaṇa.

The meaning is: "together with her husband, who was reclining upon the lake. As before, "having caused [him] to hear" means having caused him to hear the verses of prayer previously mentioned. However, there, in place of "the quality of earth as it truly is," one should read "the quality of water as it truly is"; in place of "the subtle element of smell," "the subtle element of taste"; and in place of "O lord of the earth," "O lord of the waters. The same should be understood for what follows. (105–109)

Having thus led that [deity], whose range is the upward path of the letters, to the end of the mind, O Greatly Intelligent One, by means of the final limb, with splendor, and with the weapon-mantra according to one's will; 110.
Then, having extracted [the soul] as before, it should be joined to the sphere of the intellect;
and that disciple, having received the designation, [is united] with the root-mantra released from the six paths.

Having remembered that [consciousness] which is freed from the sheath of the principles (tattva), has attained oneness with the tranquil Self, and has found its mark in the supreme state within the fire of the nature of Śakti; 112.

Then, having joined [the practitioner] in a meditative absorption (samādhi) that is free from all objects of perception, by means of the seed-syllable of Īśvara accompanied by the quality of sattva; || 113 ||
He does not perceive that wherein even mere duality is dissolved in bliss.

Thus, he states with the half-verse beginning "ending with the mind" (*mano'vasānam*) that the purifications (*saṃskārāḥ*) of the four paths—beginning with the path of Mantras and ending with the path of Phonemes, and comprising the principles from the principle of Fire (*tejastattva*) up to the principle of Mind (*manastattva*)—should be performed in sequence.

Now, by means of either the Netra-mantra or the Astra-mantra, he describes the union of the disciple’s conscious self (caitanya), which possesses power, with the path consisting of the intellect (buddhimaya-adhvan), as well as the union of that power with the fire as before, and its application in samādhi—characterized solely by recitation (japa) and meditation (dhyāna)—through the seed-syllable of Īśvara, by means of four verses beginning with "niṣṭhāṅgena. The term "niṣṭhāṅgena" means "by the final limb. This [term] should be understood as qualifying both the light (tejas) and the Astra-mantra, since sovereignty (aiśvarya) is the primary goal therein, while liberation (mokṣa) follows as a secondary consequence.
In that regard, know that for the purpose of pacifying those obstacles, the mantra ends with the weapon-mantra (*astra*);
however, O Great-minded One, in the case of the opposite situation, the mantra ends with the eye-mantra (*netra*).

Thus, it has been established in the second chapter that both [the preliminary and the concluding rites] possess the status of being the final members (caramāṅga) according to the distinction of their respective intentions regarding the fruit. || 110–114 ||
Having offered a hundred oblations in the rite for attaining that [state], || 114 ||
Having brought everything into a state of equality through his own intellect, he [composed] this literary work exactly as it exists, together with the entire web of objects of cognition. (115)
Having become composed and free from mental fluctuations, one should offer the supreme final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
He explains the procedure for the fire sacrifice with two verses beginning with "of the oblations" (āhutīnām). || 114–116 ||
Then, having reached the stage of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), the Guru should again offer oblations.
With the seed-syllable lord, for the sake of the disciple's liberation from transmigration, [the master],
whose mind is established in the words, [should act] with the words constricted by the syllable Oṃ.
Having said, "Become omniscient," one should offer twelve oblations;
likewise, O Blessed One, become faultless and independent.
The Lord of all, possessing all powers, perfectly complete, infallible, and self-controlled; all-pervading, with the six qualities restrained, changeless, and stainless. || 119 ||
Vāsudeva is eternal, with eternally risen knowledge, eternal bliss, and perfectly partless; he is without beginning or end, without destruction, and possessed of all sovereign power.
Having become thus, one should then perform [the rite] once again with the *pūrṇāhuti*.

With the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, he describes the *homa* for the sake of further liberation and cessation through five verses. By "Bījanātha" is meant the seed-syllable of sovereignty; that is to say, by the seed-syllable of Viśākhayūpa. (116–121)
He who desires liberation stands in the state of Īśvara, established in the initiation of Vaibhava.
O high-minded one, wherever he may be situated, by the very power of the Lord's will, he attains the supreme state of the Lord immediately upon the fall of the body.

For one desiring enjoyment, [the worship] is directed toward the two feet of the Lord Padmanābha; for one desiring both, it is through the union of the possessor of power and power on the path consisting of the intellect.

Having extracted him from that state for a duration until the fall of the body, he should be established [in his true nature], just as fire, once separated from wood, remains distinct within it. || 124 ||

Just as [fire] no longer attains equality with the wood once it has been joined [to it], so too a person who has been joined to the intermediate path does not thereafter again attain identity with that [path]. (125)

Now, whether from the plane of the intellect (*buddhipada*), the plane of Vaiśākha-yūpa, or the plane named Padmanābha—or by means of the distinction between the possessor of power and power itself in both cases—having established the consciousness of the disciple there according to his intention for the fruit, one should again extract it from that plane and maintain it within the path consisting of expansion (*vṛddhimaya-adhvā*) until the fall of the body. Furthermore, he states with four and a half verses beginning with "sthitam" that even for the consciousness established in the plane of the intellect, there is a state of identity with that [plane], using the analogy of fire in wood. || 121-125 ||
Having brought about the emergence from meditative absorption and having placed [the disciple] before himself,
he should duly instruct him regarding the white and black paths.

"He who, though of diverse forms, abides without distinction within the Supreme Self"—now, having turned the disciple away from the previously mentioned meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and having seated him before himself, the teacher should perform the instruction on the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvopadeśa*) for him in the manner to be described; thus he says with the verse beginning "samādhau" (126–127).
That which is the supreme Brahman is free from the known and the knower, and is imperishable.
Indeed, by His own power and through the state of being that Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), the Supreme Lord Himself arises for the liberation of all living beings. 128.
He states in the two and a half verses beginning with "vedya" that the Supreme Brahman itself assumes the state of Śabdabrahman for the sake of protecting all conscious beings. 127–128.
Know that unmanifest syllable to be like an indistinct sound on a lute string; it itself proceeds in many ways for its own persistence through the nature of distinct phonemes.

He says "that" to show that this Śabdabrahman, which is indistinct like the sound of a lute string, again assumes manifestness in the form of the phonemes beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. This manifested form is known by everyone. || 129 ||
In this matter of the first syllable, even the Brahmins who know the Vedas do not reach a certainty because of the fourfold nature of its interpretation and the resulting divergent views. 130.

Regarding the unmanifest syllable, which is the first form of the Śabdabrahman, he says "they do not reach it," meaning that without the grace of the Lord, a definitive determination is impossible even for those who know the Vedas. || 130 ||
The Blessed One, whose form is sound, approaches in the form of the *kalās*;
for it is appropriate that those performers of ritual action who are devoted to Him should grasp Him through that [sound]. (131)

He says "sa" (he/it) to show that this very path of the *varṇas* transforms into the form of the path of the *kalās*. The meaning is: by means of the sixfold qualities beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*), which constitute the nature of the *kalās*. The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: for those conscious beings who are established in that—that is, established in the experience of the Lord’s sixfold qualities such as knowledge—and who possess the ritual actions of worshipping Him and so forth, the apprehension of those [qualities], namely the grasping of the attributes such as knowledge, becomes possible through that transformation into the form of the path of the *kalās*. || 131 ||
And as long as there is no form arising from the collection of the six qualities—that which is stainless—tell me, by what other means could that formless [reality] be grasped? (132)

Thus, [the author] says "not so" (na) to address how knowledge of the Lord’s form, which consists of that [sound], can arise in the absence of a transformation of the sound-form into the nature of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya). || 132 ||
All the principles (tattvas) consist of the creative powers (kalās) and are characterized by origination and dissolution;
they are as previously described, beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with the Overlord (adhyakṣa), as has been stated.
From this path of *kalās*, he states the arising of the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with the form of Vāsudeva in the verse starting with "the principles" (*tattvā*). || 133 ||
The mantras have emerged from the principles (tattvas) and are endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā);
they are joined with the six kalās and aṅgalas, and their number is beyond reckoning.
By them, the first state, beginning with the Fourth (turya) and including the Emanation (nirmāṇa), is manifested under the designation of "the states" (pada);
it is for the sake of the self-attainment of those engaged in action, for the sake of delusion, and for the sake of its destruction.
Indeed, that universe consisting of fourteen worlds and composed of the three qualities is eternally impure; it is the object of enjoyment, to be attained, and existing as something distinct. (136)

With three verses beginning with "tattvebhyaḥ," [the author] explains the emergence of the path of mantras from the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the emergence of the path of words (*padādhvan*) from that, and the emergence of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) from that. The phrase "endowed with six parts and six limbs" means they are joined with the six qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty, and accompanied by the heart-mantra and other limb-mantras. In the expression "the fourth and so forth" (*turyādyam*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the triad of states: deep sleep, dreaming, and waking. (134–136)

Thus has the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan), characterized by what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, been described; [it consists of] the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the path of words (padādhvan), excluding the fourth word (turyapada). 137.

For practitioners of action, that which remains is to be abandoned, while that which is required is to be accepted; yet even by virtue of such dependence, that which is to be attained falls into the category of the abandonable.

Concluding the aforementioned subject matter, [the author] states in the verse beginning with "Thus the six paths" (ityadhvaṣaṭkam) that within those six paths, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and the triad of states beginning with deep sleep (suṣupti) are to be abandoned, while the fourth state (turya) and the paths beginning with the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) are to be accepted. This very point is also corroborated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"Excluding the fourth state, deep sleep and the others follow an impure course;
the sequence of worlds (bhuvanapaddhati) has been described as extending from Māyā down to the earth."
That is to be known as the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), which is indeed impure and mired in defilement.
Thus [ends the section on] 137–138.
However, the means for attaining that [state] exists in the supreme, waveless plane,
for one who is established in the state of discernment and has been refined by initiation.
Indeed, when investigated in this manner, that wherein rest clearly arises is the Supreme Brahman, the imperishable one known as Vāsudeva.

He states with the half-verse beginning "vyapekṣayā" that even for one desiring liberation (mumukṣu), those [entities], though pure and existent, fall within the category of what is to be abandoned because of his lack of interest in them.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is to be attained by the seeker of liberation?", he answers with the two verses beginning "kintu. In the word "viśrāma," the phrase "of the six paths" (ṣaḍadhvanām) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 139-140 ||
Just as space is the locus for a multitude of atoms,
so indeed is it the abode of individual souls who have been unawakened since beginningless time.

For that which is to be known as the interval between the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the levels (*pada*), namely both the two paths of worlds and levels, is the abode of innumerable conscious beings; thus he says "the ether" (*ambaram*) with one and a half verses. (141–142)
By the will of the Lord of the Vine, their mantras indeed sport.

"In that twofold path of Māyā, with fruits consisting of pleasure and pain, the mantras sport with living beings who are devoid of will and experience the fruits of pleasure and pain in that sky"—thus he says "vinā" (without). The meaning is "in the path of Māyā," which is to say, in the natural (prākṛta) realm. || 142-143 ||
Of the devotees who are permeated by the will of the Lord, [there is] in the Supreme Lord... [143]
For the gurus who have been initiated and whose souls are devoted to their service,
the mantras situated above the two paths become expectant of their command.

They lead the practitioners of ritual action correctly and by force through the two paths of Māyā, indeed for the sake of attaining their own abode and the enjoyments such as the powers (aṇimā) and so forth. 145.

But for those who are permeated by the will of the Lord, she herself becomes submissive and leads them to her own abode for the sake of enjoyment; thus he says with two and a half verses beginning with "īśvara... (verses 143–145).
And by enjoying that [nectar], those who are most excellent impel [the soul] according to their own power,
even through the force of their own activity, along the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) which is like nectar.

Where one might regard powers such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) as mere blades of grass while remaining established [in that state], there the mantras—by their own power alone—lead the consciousness, which is detached from enjoyment, along the path of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Vāsudeva. This is stated in the half-verse beginning with "of the detached one" (146–147). The meaning is: on whichever path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) the person is established, he should regard the enjoyments experienced on the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, as if they were blades of grass—that is, he should contemplate them as being like grass.
The stainless ones, such as Tattvādhyakṣa and others, were intent on bestowing grace upon him. || 147 ||
They lead [the soul] correctly to the state of non-decay throughout the entire eternal path.

Furthermore, he says "anugraha" (grace), meaning that Aniruddha and the others join the detached person to the path of the *kalās*. Thereafter, Vāsudeva, whose form is the path of the *vikalas*, leads [him] to the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). || 147-148 ||
He is Vāsudeva, the Brahman consisting of the sixfold policy, who bears the form of the path.
Established in his own eternal self, he indeed effects the conjunction of that [word] upon the path designated as Śabdabrahman. (149)
Through the thorough knowledge of that, one attains the perfectly peaceful state of the Blessed One.

Regarding this, he says in two verses beginning with "He" (sa) that the person established therein attains the state of the Blessed One by himself through the thorough knowledge of the path of the castes (varṇādhvan). (148–150)
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord, tell me, what are the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths of the castes?
"O Lord, Saṃkarṣaṇa asks about the knowledge of the caste-banner (varṇadhvaja), by the thorough understanding of which one attains the true state of Vāsudeva throughout the [three] paths. (150–151)
The Blessed Lord said:
[This is for] the Self who has been liberated from the sheaths of the five paths and has attained true being. || 151 ||
Bearing the form of a continuous stream, it attains the state of direct experience.
Sound consists of various colors and is characterized by the previously mentioned marks. || 152 ||
That collection of the fourfold self should indeed be understood as being of that very nature, characterized by sound and light through the process of origination and dissolution. (153)
Indeed, from the letter *sakāra* and from the letter *akāra*, it ends precisely with the letter *hakāra*;
in the source of emanation (*prabhava*), however, the letter *hakāra* belongs to the twelve-fold end for those of fourfold nature.

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva says in three verses beginning with "pañca" that one should meditate upon the previously mentioned path of letters (*varṇādhvan*)—from *a* to *sa* in the order of emanation (*prabhava*), and from *ha* to *a* in the order of reabsorption (*apyaya*)—in the form of the aggregate of the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*). "Of one who has transcended the five paths and sheaths" means of one who has gone beyond the five paths beginning with the worlds (*bhuvana*). "Characterized by the luminous sound" means characterized by the luminous resonance (*bhāsvaradhvani*). And so it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The collection of my fourfold self should indeed be known as being of that very nature."
"By means of the yoga of origin and dissolution, [the breath] is characterized by the sound of the nature of light.
In the power [of manifestation], the letter *ha* at the limit of the twelve belongs to those of fourfold nature.

The letter *a* is also at the point of dissolution (*apyaya*); therefore, the equality of these two is traditionally taught. By the word "origin" (*prabhava*), he states the similarity between the letters *a* and *ha* by virtue of their being located at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). The grammatical connection is that for those consisting of four aspects, [the end is] the end of the twelve. "End of the twelve" means the end of the six groups (*ṣaṭka*) due to meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Here, within the thirty-nine letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, there are twelve emanations (*vyūha*) in the sequence of the four letters starting from *a* and ending with *sa*.

Above that, the letter *ha* which remains has the *dvādaśānta* (the "end of the twelve") as its locus; likewise, in the process of dissolution (*apaya-krama*), starting from *ha* up to the end of *ā*, after the two sets of six emanations (*vyūha*), the letter *a* which remains has the *dvādaśānta* as its locus—this is the intended meaning. || 154-155 ||
In this collection of the array of phonemes, that which is to be known is to be understood through the meditative absorption of knowledge.
Rest, arising, pervasion, and manifestation proceed from Vāsudeva;
indeed, each one of these is to be understood as a distinct form (mūrti). Thus it is exactly so.
Briefly stated, they are joined with the fourfold sequence beginning with rest;
indeed, they are situated in this very manner, arranged like a staff (daṇḍavat). 157.
There are twelve types of concentration (dhāraṇā), characterized by the internal [senses], which serve as a staircase;
having ascended them, one enters the supreme state at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta). || 158 ||

Regarding that path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), [the author] explains—through three and a half verses beginning with *varṇavyūha*—its nature as an object of knowledge by means of the fourfold sequence starting with "rest" (*viśrāma*) according to the order of the letters beginning with *a*; the fact that each individual form, such as Vāsudeva and the others, is likewise endowed with the fourfold sequence of rest and so forth; its structural arrangement like a staff (*daṇḍavat sanniveśena*); and its status as a staircase for ascending to the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) via the twelve types of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) within it. The phrase "starting from Vāsudeva" (*ā vāsudevataḥ*) means beginning with Vāsudeva; this is to be construed with the words "each one of its forms" (*asyaikaikā mūrtiḥ*).

Rest (*viśrāma*) means the subtle state (*sūkṣmāvasthā*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Arising (*udaya*) is the state of *paśyantī*. Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the state of *madhyamā*. Manifestation (*vyakti*) is the state of *vaikharī*. Thus it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "The tranquil form (*śāntarūpā*), then *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and likewise *vaikharī*—these are the four forms. I shall speak of the fourfold object of speech (*vācya*) created by itself."

Vāsudeva and the others are to be understood as subtle, corresponding respectively to the states of *śānta* (peace) and so forth. Thus, each individual form such as Vāsudeva should be known as being endowed with the fourfold set beginning with *viśrāma* (rest). In this context, *viśrāma* is the state of the fourth emanation (*turya-vyūha*), and *udaya* (emergence) is the state of the deep-sleep emanation (*suṣupti-vyūha*). The resultant meaning is that the form of Vāsudeva and the others, characterized by the four states beginning with *viśrāma* denoted by those terms, is established in the arrangement of the letters *a*, *ā*, and so on—which are themselves characterized by the four subtle states denoted by the words *viśrāma* and the rest—standing like a staff (*daṇḍavat*).

Alternatively, the subtle and other states of the phonemes (*varṇas*) are not intended here; rather, by terms such as "rest" (*viśrāma*) and so forth, the states of the fourth emanation (*turya-vyūha*) and others of the forms beginning with Vāsudeva are intended. It should be understood that within each phoneme, there is a sequence of one state per phoneme, such that across each set of four phonemes, there is a complete cycle of the four states.

Thus, within the fourfold set of phonemes (*varṇa*) consisting of the four states, each individual form such as Vāsudeva is to be known. In this way, for the sixteen phonemes beginning with *a*, there are four groups of four; in these, the four forms of the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*), beginning with Vāsudeva, reside. For the four groups of four phonemes beginning with *ka*, there are the forms of the deep sleep manifestation (*suṣupti-vyūha*). Within the letter *ha* at the end of these twelve, the primordial form is situated non-differently, like the seed of a banyan tree.
It is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of all activity and formless.

"The great Cāturātmya, beginning with that [Ha], consists of pure consciousness. By this stated definition, the meaning should be understood as the form of the Turyavyūha. In this way, it should also be understood in reverse order, from the letter *ha* down to the letter *a*. Alternatively, within the sixteen letters beginning with *a*, the waking state is denoted by the term "manifestation" (*vyakti*); within the sixteen letters beginning with *ka*, the dream state is denoted by the term "pervasion" (*vyāpti*); within the sixteen letters beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*, the deep sleep state is denoted by the term "emergence" (*udaya*); and within the letter *ha* at the end of the twelve, the fourth state (*turya*) is denoted by the term "rest" (*viśrāma*).
In each respective case, those various forms of the Vyūhas are to be understood according to the sequence previously stated.

Now, one might object that even the threefold explanation you have provided here is inconsistent, because it contradicts the explanation given by the Mother of the Universe (Jagajjananī). For in the *Lakṣmītantra*, regarding this collection of Vyūhas consisting of phonemes, it is said: "This should be known through the meditative absorption of knowledge (*jñānasamādhi*)."
Rest, arising, pervasion, and manifestation proceed from Vāsudeva.
In this regard, each and every form is indeed to be thoroughly understood in this very manner;
briefly stated, it is joined with the fourfold set preceded by rest.
One should contemplate the god Vāsudeva as the eternal resting place;
the lotus-eyed one, the primordial god, the eternal, whose form is the syllable *A*.
For indeed, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa rest here in dissolution;
therefore, one should meditate upon the form, the emergence, of the god Saṃkarṣaṇa.
For that All-Self has arisen first as the self-existent creator of all; one should contemplate that Lord Pradyumna, the letter *i*, as his pervasive nature.
By means of that which consists of the threefold activity of the triple Veda, the world is attained;
one should meditate upon Aniruddha, whose form is manifest and who ends with the syllable *ī*.
For all powers, such as the creation of the world and so forth, are manifested here;
indeed, they are situated exactly like this, arranged in the form of a staff.
Up to the letter *sa*, my fourfold nature is endowed with four forms;
one should contemplate the letter *ha* at the end of the twelve during the meditation on emanation.
One should contemplate the letter *ha* as Vāsudeva, the state of rest;
one should likewise remember Saṃkarṣaṇa, ending with the letter *sa*, at the time of emergence and dissolution.
In this manner, one should contemplate the divine form of the fourfold self;
there are twelve dhāraṇās of six types each, characterized by the twelve internal [elements].
Having ascended this which serves as a staircase, one enters the supreme state at the *dvādaśānta*;
this is shown to be the first method of the path of phonemes (*varṇamārga*).

If you say that the fact that the words *viśrāma*, *udaya*, *vyāpti*, and *vyakti* refer to the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva has been explained very clearly [by us], then you speak thus only because you do not recognize that our initial explanation conforms to the words of Lakṣmī. For what have we restricted regarding the presence of the four [forms] beginning with Vāsudeva within each set of four letters starting with *a*? Rather, we have stated that the words *viśrāma* and so forth denote subtle states (*sūkṣmāvasthā*) and the like.

In the *Lakṣmītantra*, however, because the meaning of those [terms] is so well-known, their denotation of Vāsudeva and the others has been clearly explained without further elaboration. Nevertheless, there is no fixed rule that those words denote only Vāsudeva and the others, and cannot possibly denote states such as the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and so forth; for later on, in the passage "joined with the tetrad beginning with Viśrāma in brief," it is impossible to deny that words such as *viśrāma* denote specific states. (155–158)
Having thus led the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) of the initiate—which exists as the state known as Śabdabrahman—into the heart-lotus by means of its manifest form; || 159 ||

He says "having led" (*nītvā*) because the method for this path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), being thus constituted, must be taught very clearly to the disciple: "Having taken [the breath] situated within the interior of the heart-lotus, and having fixed upon the sun located there, the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*) stands as the female bee;
she is the power (*śakti*) who gives birth to all mantras, belonging to the pervasive Lord whose nature is peace."
Resounding with the sound born of phonemes— that which is remembered as the Śabdabrahman—
it begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *ha*, assuming the form of a continuous stream of syllables.

The meaning is that [the soul] resides within the heart-lotus in the manner thus described. Here, by the term "of the initiated" (*dīkṣitasya*), it is understood that the word *dīkṣā* denotes the ritual action extending up to the release from the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvamocana*). This has been stated likewise in the *Jayākhyatantra*, the *Lakṣmītantra*, and other texts. By this, the claim made in the *Siddhāntacandrikā* that the word *dīkṣā* signifies the undertaking of observances (*niyamaparigraha*) is refuted, since those observances will be discussed later. || 159 ||
Having sprinkled the ground with water drawn by means of breath, he should,
together with his disciple, sprinkle himself with that same water for the sake of unbroken success.
Having performed the rites as before with the *bhūti* ashes and having bowed to the fire,
he should then rise and, taking that [ashes], proceed to the abode of Acyuta.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World and having communicated the observances of the child—both those that are specific and those that are general—in brief, according to his capacity. (162)

It should be taught exactly as it is; thereafter, its worship is performed within the heart, accompanied by mudrās, preceded by the placement of mantras (nyāsa) and meditative visualization (dhyāna). || 163 ||
The procedure for what must be done, both in brief and in detail, was set forth before him;
then, by him, everything was carried out exactly as it stood.
Then one should perform the worship of the Guru for oneself with wealth and other offerings;
having filled the right hand with water from the arghya vessel.
One should cast [the water] consecrated with the six-limbed mantra upon his head;
then, one should contemplate the maṇḍala with the syllable Om and the solar radiance in his hand.
There, one should place the entire host of deities as before, undivided;
having mentally performed their worship, one should bestow [the initiation] upon his head along with a blessing.
And just as it has been described and as it is desired, O son, may the power-bestowing perfection (vaibhavī siddhi), endowed with the glory of liberation, be yours before long. 168.

Then, having performed the sprinkling of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other vessels with consecrated water, and the application of the sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with ashes, and having first worshipped the Blessed One—whether situated in the mandala or in an image—the teacher, in his presence, instructs the disciple in the observances (*niyama*); he imparts the mantra together with the sequence for mental worship, the ritual placement of mudrās (*mudrā-nyāsa*), and meditative visualization (*dhyāna*); he teaches the procedural method for the performance of worship and other rites; and finally, he ensures that the disciple performs the worship of the Blessed One and the honoring of the guru right before his own eyes. This is the duty of the disciple.

He describes the sprinkling of mantra-water on the head preceded by words of benediction, the placing of the mantra-hand upon that head, and the manner of those benedictory words, beginning with *saṃsecya hutabhugbhūtam* and ending with *mokṣalakṣmīsamanvitaḥ*. Regarding the phrase *tavāstu vaibhavī siddhiḥ*, one should apply it as follows: in the case of the *vyūhadīkṣā*, say *tavāstu vyūhasaṃsiddhiḥ*; in the case of the *brahmadīkṣā*, say *tavāstu brahmasaṃsiddhiḥ*.

For this very reason, it was established by our venerable grandfather in the *Sātvatāmṛta*, within the section on the initiation of the all-pervasive mantra (*vyāpakamantradīkṣā*), as follows: "May you possess the perfection of [his] manifestations and so forth, endowed with the glory of liberation."
