Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that only the three initiations (dīkṣā) regarding the Paravyūha, Vibhava, and [other forms] have been expounded here? What is the basis for the performance of the initiation of the pervasive mantra (vyāpakamantra)? Furthermore, how can the accomplishment of all the deities, beginning with the Vibhava, arise through a single mantra alone? To this, we reply: The basis for that is the *Īśvaratantra*, which is an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the *Sātvata*, as well as the *Pādma* and other scriptures. This is because even a single mantra, by virtue of its pervasiveness, manifests all the deities beginning with the Vibhava. Therefore, it should be understood that the accomplishment pertaining to all the deities is achieved without restriction.

Now, one might argue: "Granted that such a perfection (siddhi) may indeed be achieved, at that time the authority for those initiated belongs only to the pervasive mantra (*vyāpaka-mantra*). For it cannot be said that authority over the various specific mantras is established without the initiation into the *vibhava* and other [levels], because all initiations find their fulfillment through that very [pervasive initiation] alone. To this we reply: In the *Aiśvara-tantra*, it is stated: "O best of sages, one should likewise bestow these three initiations, either upon a single person or sequentially, in order to establish his fitness for the worship of all [deities]."
Or else, O twice-born one, regarding the three pervasive [mantras] beginning with the eight-syllable mantra,
the Guru should instruct [the disciple] on the mantras for the power (śakti), the ornaments, the vehicles, and the weapons;
thus it is stated in the Pādma[-purāṇa].
Having meditated, he should place the mantra, accompanied by the *praṇava*, into the right ear of the disciple,
along with its seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and limbs (*aṅga*).
First, however, having duly meditated upon the twelve-syllable mantra and subsequently the eight-syllable one,
as well as the mantras of the [divine] forms, according to the prescribed rule;

Thus, within this very section on the initiation (dīkṣā) of the pervasive mantra (vyāpakamantra), the instruction for all the mantras of the forms (mūrti-mantras) has been established. And so, it should be understood that just as one gains authority over the mantras of the ornaments, vehicles, and weapons through the initiation of the primary mantra, likewise authority over the mantras of the manifestations (vibhava) and so forth is established by the initiation of the pervasive mantra alone. (160–168)
Thus has been declared the definition of the Vaibhava initiation,
as well as its general application for the entire collection of mantras.

Now he concludes the aforementioned matter with the word "iti" (thus). This refers to the disciple who is engaged in the worship of its majesty—that is, the one intent upon the adoration of its power. "Of the entire collection of mantras" means of the multitude of mantras of the deities whose majesty begins with Padmanābha and ends with Pātālaśāyin. || 169 ||
For by whichever mantra the initiation of anyone is to be performed, that [initiation] belongs to that [mantra] and its [deities], according to the path previously described. || 170 ||
In this matter, the application of the constituent parts should be performed according to what has been stated;
one should proceed with the heart and the other centers ending at the root, as if they were a single aggregate.
Having always thoroughly contemplated the state of being the inner self (adhyātmarūpatā) together with the group of principles (tattvagaṇa),
one should then perform the worship as before.

Regarding these *vibhava* mantras, the author explains the specific details for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of one who desires it by means of any single mantra among them, using three verses beginning with "by which" (*yena*). "Of the parts" (*avayavānām*) means of the *aṅga* mantras. "Like a collection" (*samūhavat*) means like the collection beginning with Pātālaśayana and ending with Padmanābha.

Since this is the section concerning initiation by a single mantra, the resulting meaning is that for the group of seven [elements] starting with Earth, one should perform the application of the seven mantras—beginning with the *hṛdaya* (heart) mantra and ending with the *mūla* (root) mantra—in place of the previously mentioned collection of *vibhava* deities. (17–172)
In the rite of opening the eyes, the seed-syllable of the heart (hṛdbīja) is prescribed for those mantras that possess five limbs;
however, for mantras lacking limbs, the rite is performed using the mantra prescribed for their specific limb.
The Praṇava, together with the word for the ritual action, must be employed;
by this procedure, the initiation into the Vyūhas should always be accomplished for those who desire it. 174.
With the half-verse beginning with "netra," he describes the destination [attained] in the initiation of the five-limbed mantra and the initiation of the limbless mantra. (173–174)
This should always be accomplished by this procedure for those seeking initiation into the *vyūha*.
However, in every single ritual act, one must indeed employ there the fourfold [mantras] beginning with Vāsudeva, which were previously mentioned as the seed-syllables (bījas). 175.

He states the specific detail regarding the *vyūhadīkṣā* with the half-verse beginning with *saṃpādya*. The meaning is that it was previously taught in the eighth chapter by such statements as "ending in the nasal [m], mounted on the sixth vowel," and so forth. (174–175)
In this very way, the primordial mantra, complete in its entirety for the collection of rites,
should be applied in the initiation of Brahmā by dividing it into six parts as before.
In its own form, as it exists in its proper state, and on appropriate occasions;
however, in this context, the prayer to the gods is intended to be expressed in the singular.
The application (*yojanā*), however, should be understood in brief as that which was stated regarding the consecration (*adhivāsa*).

With the two and a half verses beginning with “In this very way” (*evameva*), he states the specific details regarding the *brahmadīkṣā*. The method of dividing the first mantra into six parts has already been demonstrated in the second chapter alone. The use of the singular number for the prayer is to be understood in instances such as “by the power of your grace” (*yuṣmatprasādasāmarthyāt*).

Now, one might ask: since the plural “of the gods” (*devānām*) occurs here, how can there be a prayer to them in the singular? This is true; even there, the plural is used because of the presence of the fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*). Nevertheless...
Indeed, it exists as non-different from the primordial form, like the seed of a banyan tree;
yet, in the ultimate sense, it is devoid of all activity and is formless.

"The primordial Cāturātmya is indeed pure, consisting of consciousness, and great. Thus, because of the preeminence of the Primordial Form alone, only one mantra is taught; it should be understood that the prayer is made using the singular number. The application [of the mantra] is as stated in the *Adhivāsa*: "Oṃ, etc., O Lord of the World, Omniscient One, You who dwell in the heart!"
Therein I shall engage him in that action which has you as its ultimate goal.

The meaning is "of such a form. This application (*yojanā*) is to be understood as being within the scope of this initiation (*dīkṣā*); that is to say, it is to be known by means of this [text], because of the use of the singular number. By this, it is established by implication that in the case of the *vyūha-dīkṣā* and the *vibhava-dīkṣā*, the plural number should be employed in that verse concerning the application. Even there, since the initiation is performed with each individual mantra, the prayer, the application, and so forth must be carried out using the singular number alone.

For this very reason, in the prayer verse beginning with "by the power of your grace" (*yuṣmatprasādasāmarthyāt*) in the *Sātvatāmṛta* composed by my venerable grandfather, the singular form "by the power of your grace" (*tvatprasādasya sāmarthyāt*) was employed.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the *Sātvatāmṛta*, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) by means of the pervasive mantra (*vyāpakamantra*) has been taught; and you yourself have stated that the pervasive mantra has as its object all deities, being designated as the Supreme Manifestation (*paravyūha*) and the Empowered Manifestation (*vibhava*). Since all deities must be invoked in such an initiation, how can the singular number be appropriate? To this we reply: just as a single mantra encompasses all [deities] as its objects, so too should the singular number be understood.

For this very reason, in the *Pādmapurāṇa*, within the *Aṣṭākṣarakalpa* and the *Dvādaśākṣarakalpa*, meditation is described using the singular number alone in such passages as "having four arms and noble limbs," and so forth.

If it is asked, "In that case, why is it that in the section on the worship of the Supreme Manifestation (Paravyūha) and the Emanation (Vibhava) with the eight-syllabled mantra, one must everywhere follow the very meditation described in the *Padma Purāṇa*?"—it is replied: By means of the eight-syllabled mantra, the object of meditation should be contemplated either according to the general method of worship as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* and other texts, or according to the specific form [of the deity]. There is no dispute regarding this. For this very reason, although worship with the all-pervasive mantra (*vyāpaka-mantra*) is prescribed for both the Lord (Īśvara) and the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara), the meditation specifically upon the forms situated in their respective divine locations is what is taught. (176–178)
For this twofold perpetual initiation, there is no fruit other than liberation.
And even there, O lotus-eyed one, initiation pertaining to the fourfold self forcibly bestows upon those of purified soul the attainment of enjoyment of the six qualities. (179)
Whatever fruit arises from garlands, sandalwood, and the like, as well as from the substances used in fire-offerings,
all undergo dissolution along with their material nature through the initiation into Brahman.

What need is there for further elaboration? Although the *vyūha* and *brahma-dīkṣā* bestow liberation alone, he states in two and a half verses beginning with "nitya" (178–180) that worldly fruits also occur as incidental benefits therein.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Nārada said: O best of sages, having thus described the characteristics of initiation to Balarāma, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) spoke this again as it truly is.

Now the twentieth chapter will be explained. Having thus described the characteristics of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the Blessed One further teaches consecration (*abhiṣeka*); thus he says: "Initiation... (verse 1).
Now, for one who has seen the mandala, who knows the scriptures according to their true meaning, who is intent on propitiation, and who has attained the status of a "spiritual son" (putraka), || 2 ||

With the two verses beginning with "atha," he describes the qualified candidate for initiation (*abhiṣeka*), its purpose, and the [proper] time. "One who has seen the mandala" means one who has beheld the mandala; that is to say, one who is established in the *samaya*. He will later state the definition of one established in the *samaya*: "Indeed, merely by having obtained the vision of the mantra-form in the mandala. "One who knows the scripture" means one who thereafter is intent upon the application of the scripture.
Furthermore, it refers to the time from then onwards and from a truly excellent teacher.

For it will be stated [later]: "He who constantly seeks the meaning of the scripture preceded by its recitation. The meaning is: of one who has attained the status of a *putraka* (spiritual son), as characterized by the passage beginning with "He whose [intentions] are known by the Guru" and ending with "That disciple, named *putraka*, is always superior even to one's own son. And the meaning is: of one who is intent on propitiation (*samārādhana*), as characterized by the sequence of passages beginning with "But he who has received initiation as before should be devoted to the propitiation of the mantra."

The resultant meaning is that the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) must be performed at that very time, immediately after initiation (*dīkṣā*), for the disciple who is distinguished by the four qualifications beginning with "one who has seen the mandala. Now, what is the restrictive rule that this consecration applies to one possessing these qualifications? The sense of the text is that the consecration should be performed for the *samayin*, the *putraka*, or the *sādhaka*. For it is stated in the *Śrī-Jayākhyasaṃhitā* that for one who knows the rules (*samayajña*), [the consecration] is always according to the sequence of the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*).
The consecration of the spiritual son according to the procedure for the Great Mantra.
The consecration for the practitioner should be performed according to the rite for a crown prince,
whereas the consecration for the Guru is traditionally prescribed according to the royal protocol.

If it is argued that thus the consecration for all four, beginning with the *sāmayika*, has been set forth, we reply: in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the distinct ritual applications for the consecration of each of those are set forth; here, however, only the procedure for the *ācāryābhiṣeka* (teacher’s consecration) is stated. Therefore, our interpretation alone is the more flavorful [comprehensive] one.

Nor should it be argued that the qualifiers are redundant because the purpose is fulfilled by the mere phrase "one capable of propitiation"; for, by implication, it is stated that only one endowed with all those specific qualities is worthy of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Furthermore, among the characteristics of the *samayin*, *putraka*, and *sādhaka* to be described hereafter, consecration will not be mentioned anywhere as it is in the case of the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*.

It is only in the context of the characteristics of the *ācārya* that consecration will be mentioned, specifically in the statement: "One who is endowed with the previously mentioned marks is especially consecrated. For this very reason, it is said in the *Upabṛṃhaṇeśvaratantra*:
In this manner, indeed, the consecration (abhiṣeka) shall be for those who possess the primary qualification.
"But other eminent sages are to be consecrated by initiation alone"—this has been very clearly established. In the *Pādmapurāṇa* as well:
"A disciple or a son who is all-knowing, free from malice, and has conquered his senses..."
Born into the lineage of teachers, he was capable of both restraint and grace.
One who is capable in rites for pacification and nourishment for those who seek them,
who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, and who aspires to the rank of an Ācārya.
The preeminent teacher, a knower of reality, according to the procedure to be described,
becomes qualified for all the rites beginning with the ploughing [of the site].
One should perform the worship of the maṇḍala and other rites, concluding with the sacrifice of the water-pot (kumbhayāga).
Thus, initiation has been established exclusively for those born of the lineage of the Ācāryas, and only they possess the authority for activities such as plowing and so forth. || 2 ||
For the sake of accomplishing all mantras, or for the attainment of authority,
the guru should at that time perform the consecration of the worthy disciple.

[Objection: But then, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, initiation is prescribed for the four castes (*caturvarṇa*), the four stages of life (*caturāśramin*), and the four types of disciples (*caturvidha-śiṣya*). What is the resolution to this? [Response: This has already been answered: for all those who have reached the culmination of the *Jayā* system, initiation should be granted according to their respective levels of competence. Since only the initiation of the Preceptor (*ācārya*) is mentioned here, and the injunctions for the initiations of the Aspirant (*sādhaka*) and others are not stated, those established in this system should perform only the initiation of the Preceptor.
Alternatively, according to the maxim that "what is not stated here may be taken from elsewhere," there is no fault even if one performs the initiation of the Aspirant and so forth. || 3 ||
In the presence of teachers who know the true nature of the Blessed One, whose souls delight in the Five Times (Pañcakāla), and who have mastered the Saṃhitās.
For ascetics who have fixed their aim, for practitioners, and for great-souled ones,
one should construct a square pavilion in front of the deity.
Equipped with all necessary implements and provided with a *bhadrāsana* in its center, one should perform therein the *sandhāna* (union) beginning with Ananta, as prescribed for the seat (*āsana*).

Having worshipped with offerings such as water for the feet and flowers, he should then place the disciple— who has assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) and joined his palms in reverence— facing the deity.
He was being sung of by beloved women, praised by bards,
sounded with conchs and other instruments, and celebrated with auspicious recitations.
Having worshipped with the eight-limbed rite him who was muttering the supreme mantra and meditating, as it were, upon Acyuta, he took up the Vaiṣṇava water-pot.
Having recited that mantra while remaining there— either one thousand times or even just one hundred times— with a view toward the perfect accomplishment, || 10 ||
For the sake of accomplishment, having visualized him with the luster of molten gold and having consecrated him,
one should utter the mantra ending in "svāhā" from the interior of the heart-lotus in a protracted (pluta) tone.

Having spoken thus, and having meditated upon Him who is as pure as crystal ending with the word "namas," one should carve [the mantra] through the aperture of the palate and remember it as residing in His heart-lotus.

Having correctly superimposed upon the Brahman— which is the embodiment of the power of consciousness and characterized by exhilaration and bliss— all of one's own duties with a focused mind, || 13 ||
He presented a pure and divine collection of scriptures that had been worshipped according to the prescribed rites,
as well as an auspicious rosary— the basis for spiritual practice— and a small bell.

The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the yoga-band, the conch and discus, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the sacrificial cup (*camasa*), the vessel for the *arghya* offering, the *darbha* grass, and the spread black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). || 15 ||
The two sandals, the footstool, the parasol, the seat, the mirror,
the peacock-feather fan, the white chowrie, and the banner of the Blessed One.
Having raised him from his seat and brought all the water used for bathing, he offered him saffron robes and two linen garments along with a fitting punishment.
Having deposited [the materials] in a pure place and worshipped the deity,
he should then satisfy [the fire] for that purpose, ending with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while remaining in the midst of the fire.

Now, he describes the procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*), beginning with the words "of those who know the reality of the Lord" and ending with "situated in the middle of the fire," up until the conclusion. In the phrase "in front of the God," the meaning is "of the God situated either in the mandala or in the [central] image. In the phrase "beginning with Ananta," the word "beginning" (*ādi*) includes *Dharma*, *Jñāna*, and the others. "With eight limbs" means with the eight types of ritual service (*upacāra*). "The Vaiṣṇava jar" means the great jar established for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

One might object: "Is this a fixed rule that the great jar (mahākumbha) must be established for the sake of initiation? For in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and the *Pādmasaṃhitā*, it is stated that a separate jar should be established for the purpose of consecration. If this is argued, we say no; for here [in our text], a separate jar is not mentioned, and because the great jar has already been assigned its function, it will be stated later that the dismissal of the Lord occurs solely by means of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala, according to the words: "Having performed atonement according to the prescribed rite, from within the mandala together with the pit. Thus, it will be taught that the dismissal of the Blessed One is accomplished through the pit and mandala alone.

But surely, the initiation of the preceptor (ācāryābhiṣeka) must be performed for the practitioner (sādhaka). For the characteristics of the practitioner will be stated [in the scripture] as: "One who has previously received initiation and is intent upon the propitiation of the mantra," and so forth. Also in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "When the Guru has indeed recognized that one has attained perfection in mantra, then that disciple is initiated by the Guru through his grace."

Thus it is established. In this way, for a practitioner who has observed vows for a long time following initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of attaining perfection in mantra (*mantrasiddhi*), how could an empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) by means of the great jar (*mahākumbha*) established for that initiation be appropriate? Therefore, even at the time of empowerment, worship must be performed toward the jar, the mandala, and the fire. If you argue that the empowerment is made effective by the very same great jar used on that occasion, you are displaying a gross lack of intelligence.

Is the commencement of initiation performed for the sake of a single disciple alone? When it is performed for many, one should observe with a subtle vision that within the sequence of initiation, he appoints some to the level of *samayin*, appoints the *samayins* to the rank of *putraka*, appoints the *putrakas* to the rank of *sādhaka*, and consecrates the *sādhakas* into the rank of *ācārya*. Thus it is said in the section on the Nṛsiṃha-initiation:
"Then [he initiates] those who are pure, fasting, purified, and whose eyes are bound."
"One should cause the devotees, holding flowers, to enter there.

Have you not heard this description of the procedure for the simultaneous initiation of many? Otherwise, how could the time specified by the statement, "At that very moment, the guru should perform the consecration of the good disciple," be possible? Even in the procedure of initiation performed for only one person, the consecration can indeed take place at that same moment, due to the grace of the Lord and the observation of signs such as the immediate perfection of the mantra. Having released the blindfold, one should cast [the flowers] within the mandala.
Then, with prostrations made with all eight limbs and accompanied by circumambulations,
the deity, the fire, the preceptor, and the water-pot should be worshipped again and again.
When their fitness has been discerned at that time through their state of devotion,
then one should perform the initiation for those disciples, whether their intellects be sharp or dull.

Thus, it has been very clearly established that for those who are *samayins* and *putrakas*, when there is an excess of devotion and an intensity of intellect, initiation (*dīkṣā*) may be performed at that very moment.

Now, if it is asked what proof there is for the statement regarding the performance of initiation for the *putrakas* in that context, [the answer is: removing the doubts of even an ancient wall is impossible even for the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
Having performed the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should indeed cast [the disciple] into the abode of the Deity.
Being satisfied, with his joined palms placed upon arghya and flowers, he [should offer] the mantra correctly.

Thus, according to the characteristics to be described hereafter, the status of a *putraka* (spiritual son) is indeed established immediately after the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and other rites. Therefore, why would the instruction regarding the performance of initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one who has already attained the status of a *putraka* not be effective at that very moment? For it has been stated: "For the sake of accomplishment, [one should meditate on him] shining like molten gold. Furthermore, in the passage "having meditated on him as pure as crystal," it should be understood that this refers to liberation (*mukti*). Indeed, it was previously stated: "Ending with *svāhā* is for the attainment of enjoyment (*bhoga*), while ending with *namaḥ* is for the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*)."

The meaning is that it is accompanied by punishment appropriate [to the offense], namely, the punishment prescribed for each respective caste (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama). By this, the statement "the two garments of linen and saffron" is also explained. || 4-18 ||

Having performed the propitiation according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation from the sacrificial pit, from within the mandala, and from the collection of arghya vessels.
Having prepared a sacrificial circle outside the sacrificial hall with water and cooked rice for all beings while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra), [he should proceed]. || 20 ||
Having first performed the internal offering of oblations while circumambulating clockwise,
and having spoken this [mantra] above, one should then place the remainder outside that maṇḍala.
Salutations indeed be to all the imperishable beings, together with their presiding deities and their weapons;
may there be peace for this child.

Now, with four verses beginning with "kṣāntvā," he describes the withdrawal of the mantras from the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), the mandala, and the collection of vessels for the arghya and other offerings, as well as the sequence for the offering of the bali-oblation. "Of the bhūtas" means of the kumudas and so forth. "Bali-maṇḍalaka" means a place smeared with cow dung intended for the offering of the bali-oblation. || 19-22 ||
Having concluded the worship and other rites,
then, within the circle of conduct (vṛtta-maṇḍala) as before, [one should place] the white lotus in its center.
One should worship the Lord, the master and teacher of all gods, with the remnants of what has been offered;
having gratified him within the fire, one should perform his dismissal.
Then, having deposited that [discus] in a pit in the earth, or within water,
or upon the sacrificial ground, one should meditate upon that twelve-spoked wheel.
Now, with two and a half verses beginning with "pūjādyam," he describes the worship of Viṣvaksena, his satiation, his dismissal, and the relinquishment of what has been offered to him. (23–25)
And having visualized that twelve-spoked wheel upon the sacrificial ground, || 25 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon oneself and worshipped with water for honor (arghya), flowers, and other offerings within that [space],
one should take a vessel filled with water and place it there.
Having performed the sacrifice there with the Vīryamantra, [he should place] in the center the supreme Mantrāstra,
and another vessel of auspicious characteristics filled with honey, water, and milk.
In front of that, one should place the arghya-vessel, and in its center, the Astra-mantra located upon a disc;
having worshipped it according to the rule, one should empower it by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.

Furthermore, with the root mantra conjoined with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, he should again offer [the oblation] within that [fire], using the mantra consisting of the essential syllables (*sārṇa*), which, as before, holds nectar.
One should cause all [the obstacles] to become sleepless by means of the mantra-water, through the pouring of that stream of water accompanied by meditation and recitation. (30)
Then, having distributed among them the nectar-like mantra-drink,
he should subsequently place the excellent Sudhādyasra weapon, accompanied by its mantra, upon the discus.
Taking that water-pot while reciting the weapon-mantra,
one should whirl it as before, and then place it in the center of the stream.

Having filled it completely with water and endowed it with the fruit, [the author] describes the method for bestowing the drinking of nectar (*sudhāpāna*), beginning from "on the sacrificial ground, that wheel... and ending with "having done so, endowed with the fruit. (25–33)
The disciple, with a disciplined mind, should perform [the rite] according to the tradition of the Guru-yāga. || 33 ||
And having offered all the materials required for the sacrifice to him with devotion—through action, mind, and speech—just as in a sacrifice to the Blessed One; 34.
Placing his head and both hands at his feet, one should indeed endure [his offenses] with great effort and a mind purified by faith. (35)
He describes the worship of the Guru with two and a half verses beginning with "guruyāgam. The mantra for the adoration of the Guru should be taken as that stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"Salutation to the Guru, who is the sun, moon, and fire illuminating the dense forest of ignorance, and who brings peace to the scorching heat of the fire of the threefold suffering."
On this occasion, the acceptance of the water from the feet is also mentioned in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having washed the lotus-feet of the Guru with water..."
Having sprinkled himself with that [water], he should then drink from his cupped palms.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 33–35.
Likewise, having duly honored those who know the Pañcarātra, as well as ascetics, Snātakas, and others, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
The *Pañcarātra* states that for all Bhāgavatas, there should be the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. (36)
After a period devoted to massage, having received respectful permission,
he should eat together with his many brothers who were initiated first.
Likewise, with other devotees of the Blessed One, friends, relatives, and kinsmen;
immediately thereafter, he describes the meal together with his brothers by the permission of his guru in verse 37cd–38ab, beginning with the words "saṃvāhana."
Whether at that time or at another, he may indeed go elsewhere together with his disciples.
Indeed, when he wishes to return after following him at his command, he should do so after prostrating himself many times and performing circumambulations. (39)
For devotees of purified soul, until their final liberation, the Guru is the supreme goal of all perfections; therefore, he alone is remembered as the one who must be propitiated.

At that time, or at another time, he describes the wandering with the guru, following him, and then, at the time of returning by his permission, winning the guru's favor through prostrations, circumambulations, and so forth, in the two and a half verses beginning with "vrajantam" (38–40).
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter of the Sātvatatantra-bhāṣya, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrī Mauñjyāyana family and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugiriśa.
The twenty-first chapter.
Nārada said:
Then the Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, was impelled by Tālaketu.
O foremost of the twice-born, listen now to that which concerns me.
Now the twenty-first chapter will be explained. Here, the Blessed One says, "Listen," regarding that which the Blessed Vāsudeva was asked by Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord of the World, what is the nature of the observances (niyamas) that must be imparted by the preceptor to one who has been initiated and accepted into this teaching?
He states the manner of the questions: "The rules," etc. (2).
The Blessed One said:
Indeed, when each observance has been completed according to the teacher’s instruction, the disciple should say "So be it" (bāḍham) in order to extinguish the fire of grief. || 3 ||
Thus questioned by the Teacher regarding each individual rule as it was taught, Vāsudeva should say, "Certainly, certainly," to each one; so he says [in the verse], "to each one. (3)
The shadow of a deity, even when cast upon a vehicle, must not be stepped over; for the group of elders is always to be regarded with the same reverence as one's own preceptor. 4.
One should respectfully attend to his bed, seat, vehicle, and so forth;
one should always perform all the duties in his house with unwearied diligence. (5)
He should not stay on the same seat as his teacher, nor to his right;
he should be well-disciplined, restrained in speech, and await his commands.
In his presence, however, one should not rise to greet others;
nor should one resolve a doubt without his instruction. (7)

He states with the half-verse beginning with *na* that one must not step over the shadow of the Guru, the deity, or their respective vehicles. He states with the half-verse beginning with *guruvat* that one should regard the teacher’s son, wife, and so forth as the teacher himself. He states with the half-verse beginning with *śayana* that one should offer salutations even to the Guru’s bed, seat, and other belongings. He states with the half-verse beginning with *atandrita* that one must remain vigilant regarding the duties of the teacher’s household.

He states with the half-verse beginning with "not" (*na*) that one should not sit upon the same seat as the guru, nor even on a seat to his right. He states with the half-verse beginning with "well-restrained" (*suyantrita*) that one should remain attentive in the presence of the guru, speak sparingly, and await his commands. He states with the half-verse beginning with "that" (*tat*) that in the presence of the guru, one should not perform acts such as rising to greet others. He states with the half-verse beginning with "should do" (*kuryāt*) that one should not resolve the doubts of those who inquire without the guru's permission. (4–7)
The exposition of the scriptures, the practice of yoga, and meditative concentration—
these must necessarily be performed in one's own home, not in the house of the teacher.

He states that activities such as the exposition of the scriptures should be performed only in one's own home, and that they are prohibited in the teacher's home, in the verse beginning with "vyākhyānam" (verse 8).
One must certainly not eat from a vessel marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, or the lotus;
nor from one bearing the marks of stone, wood, a clod of earth, or a wooden plank, and so forth.
It must not be stepped upon with the foot, nor should it be used for the purpose of a seat,
by those who know the teaching of the Blessed One and whose souls are devoted to its fulfillment.

"Indeed, worship should always be performed as is appropriate and according to one's capacity. With the half-verse beginning with "na," he states that one must not eat from a vessel marked with the conch and discus. He further states with the words "tallakṣma" that stone, wood, clay, wooden planks, and so forth, marked with the conch and discus, must not be stepped upon with the foot, nor should they be used for the purpose of a seat. With the words "bhagavacchāsana," he declares that those who are well-versed in the scriptures of the Lord and are devoted to the worship of the Lord as taught therein must perform worship continuously, according to their ability. (9–11)
This god among gods [instructed] the teacher who was a follower of the Pañcarātra regarding the temple.
One should circumambulate from a distance the Aśvattha tree, the Vaṭa tree, a cow, a gathering of the virtuous, and the house of the guru; however, one may do so from nearby the image of the Lord.
One should pay homage to the four directions by prostrating like a staff;
one should not do so while mounted on a vehicle or wearing sandals, nor with shoes upon one's feet.

He describes the manner of circumambulating and saluting the Blessed One’s celestial palaces and other structures with two verses beginning with "prāsādam. It should be understood that the phrase "from afar" was used out of fear of stepping on their shadows. (11–13)
One should not enter the temple of the Blessed One with a distracted mind;
at the time of entering the temple of the Blessed One, one should not touch sandals or shoes with one's feet, nor should one allow the mental faculty to wander elsewhere—thus he says "not. (14)
One should not perform rising from one's seat or salutation at the time of giving an exposition. || 14 ||
It must not be granted entry to those who are not devotees, nor to the foolish, nor especially to atheists, nor to those whose minds delight in mockery. 15.

At the time of explaining the scriptures, he states with one and a half verses the prohibition against rising to greet or prostrating, as well as the prohibition against the entry of those lacking devotion and others. In the phrase "of atheists" (*nāstikānām*), the word "not" (*na*) must also be supplied. (14–15)
The supreme teaching of the Lord must not be disclosed unless it has been honored;
it is not for those devoted to others in their presence, nor for the sake of quelling their doubts. 16.

It should not be disclosed out of greed, nor by unjust means, nor out of fear; nor to an unfit person, nor in the presence of those devoted to other deities. He says "no" [in verse 16–17] to indicate that the scripture of the Lord must not be revealed out of greed, fear, injustice, or to an unsuitable recipient, or in the presence of devotees of other gods.
Whatever is fragrant, such as fruits, flowers, and so forth, that is unprecedented and appropriate; || 17 ||
"Unfit for consumption" refers to that which is devoid of offerings made to the Guru, the Devas, and the Fire.

He states [this] with the words "sugandha" (fragrant) and so forth: fruits, flowers, and other such items that are fresh and suitable must not be consumed without first being offered to the Guru, the Devas, and the Fire. (17–18)
[One should not accept gifts] from a thief, from one who has fallen [from his caste], from a fierce man, or from one possessed by hypocrisy, greed, and pride. || 18 ||
One should not accept even a measure of wealth from one who is devoid of devotion, even as a mere token.
He who wanders here for the sake of a livelihood, carrying the image of the Blessed One, [is a false ascetic]. (19)
He states the prohibition against accepting gifts of wealth from thieves and others with the words "from a thief" (*taskarāt*). Thus, Śāṇḍilya records in his Smṛti:
"One should never accept even a single *kākiṇī* from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or a libertine, even if it is offered, even in times of distress. (18–19)
In the streets and marketplaces of the city, one should never look upon that temple-attendant, nor touch him, nor even converse with him.

He states in the verse beginning with "gṛhītvā" (and the following half-verse) that one should not even look upon a professional temple-priest (*devalaka*) who, having taken an image of the Lord to be worshipped in his own home, wanders through cities and other places for the sake of acquiring wealth. If it be objected: "But might this [prohibition] also apply to an image of the Lord situated within a temple?"—it is not so; because such an image is under the control of the king, it is impossible to bring it out for the purpose of acquiring wealth elsewhere, and thus there is no room for such a doubt in that case. (19–20)
But whoever sings the hymns of the Blessed One in a village or within a city,
the Lord shall always honor him as his own devotee.

He states the perpetual worshipfulness of those who sing the verses of the divine compositions (divyaprabandha) composed by Śrīmat Bakula, Kuṇṭhan, and others, beginning with the words "one should sing. || 12 ||
One who is devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu, who dwells in the temple of Viṣṇu, who is intent on conversations concerning Viṣṇu, and who cleanses the temple of Viṣṇu; 22.
He was indeed a praiser of the Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the dharma of Viṣṇu,
one who sought out the Vaiṣṇavas, and he was always as worthy of honor as Viṣṇu himself.

With two verses beginning with "viṣṇu-", he declares that those devoted to the service of the Blessed Lord are worthy of worship like Viṣṇu himself. "Paryeṣṭikṛt" means one intent on seeking the Vaiṣṇava dharma, or alternatively, one intent on seeking out devotees for the purpose of worship. Amara states: "paryeṣaṇā, parīṣṭi, anveṣaṇā, and gaveṣaṇā [are synonyms]. The instruction to "sing" (gāyet) refers to the worship of Śaṭhakopa and others; likewise, the reference to "Viṣṇu-vrata" and so forth refers to the worship of Śāṇḍilya and others—this is also a delightful interpretation. (22–23)
Having risen early in the morning, one who is always self-restrained should personally gather flowers and other offerings from his own garden for the purpose of worship, using the weapon-mantra.
Or one might go to the forest, for it is free from obstacles in the acquisition [of wealth]; there, both fruits arising from thornless trees and those born of thorny trees are available. || 25 ||

He describes the manner of gathering flowers and other materials for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed Lord in the verse beginning with "prātaḥ" (in the morning), consisting of one and a half verses. Here, in the context of specific forms of worship and the like, the word "morning" may sometimes be taken in its primary sense; otherwise, it would conflict with the time prescribed for the *abhigamana* rite. Furthermore, in all other scriptures, the acquisition of ritual materials is ordained specifically for the second period of the day.

By the word *prātaḥ* (morning), due to the force of proximity, the appropriate time for that [activity] is indicated in order to establish an excess of haste, just as in the statement: "For the twice-born, eating in the evening and morning is ordained by the injunctions. For this very reason, the rising mentioned here does not occur immediately after sleep; rather, it is explained in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Rakṣā* as "the rising from the presence of the Deity following the *abhigamana*," as stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "Then, having risen, one should perform the gathering of flowers, *kuśa*-grass, and so forth."

Such an explanation is appropriate in the context of domestic worship; however, it should be understood that in the case of a temple, since rites such as the morning worship must be performed, the primary meaning of the word "morning" (prātaḥ) is indeed applicable there every day.

If it is argued that the rule stating "having risen in the morning, one should gather [flowers]" and so forth applies only to worship at one's own home, whereas in the case of temple worship, the gathering of flowers and other materials is performed by attendants—this is not so; for it is established that in both cases, what is self-acquired is primary (*mukhya*), while what is acquired by others is secondary (*gauṇa*). If it is further asked, "In that case, how can one who is personally engaged in the act of gathering materials carry out the morning worship and other rites in a temple?"—the answer is: one who is capable carries out everything perfectly. For one who is incapable, there is the secondary mode of performance.

Otherwise, how could the performance of the five-fold daily rites (*pañcakālika*), beginning with *abhigamana*, succeed for one devoted to temple worship? For this very reason, in the *Pārameśvara* and other scriptures, even for one engaged in the twelve-fold worship (*dvādaśakālārcana*), an opportunity is shown for the performance of the five-fold duties. Furthermore, when would the attendants collect flowers and other offerings if not in the morning? How could flowers and such items collected by them at any available time for the sake of domestic worship be utilized in the morning worship?
All [flowers], beginning with white ones, that are pleasant to the heart, fragrant, suitable for ritual action, and acceptable, [are recommended];
whereas those that are foul-smelling, unsuitable for ritual action, and likewise unknown, [are not].
They dwell at crossroads, in the abodes of Śiva, in cremation grounds, and in the midst of forests;
they are mangled by lightning strikes and the like, and are swarming with worms and insects.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth—such as fragrant lotuses and those that are white, red, and other colors—should be avoided with great effort. (28)
Indeed, pure items should always be employed in the ritual worship;
likewise, sprouts and leaves that have fallen upon the ground are also suitable. 29.
Those flowers which are prescribed for worship at all times according to the season are beneficial;
however, worship performed in the home with flowers produced from the Karavīra plant is not conducive to well-being.

Especially for one who possesses desire and is joined with the perfected beings (siddhas), there is no fault otherwise; however, there is a fault [if it occurs] with those such as the insane. || 31 ||
Just as the purchase of fresh flowers that have not yet withered is prescribed, so too must they be offered after being sprinkled with water;
it should not be done otherwise.
Through the observation of the mantra-practitioners, [the mantras] quickly attain faultlessness;
the hearts of those whose souls are devoted to the mantra become purified by devotion. (33)
One should not eat from a bell-metal vessel, nor should one offer the madhuparka and other gifts to the deity therein, even if such items are available. 34.
One should not burn even incense in vessels made of clay or iron;
for the purpose of incense, guggulu mixed with clarified butter should be offered, or, in its absence, another substance.
Accompanied by the ringing of a bell, one should avoid [using] fat, marrow, impure oil, clarified butter, or oil mixed with [such substances] for the purpose of lighting lamps. 36.
For the madhuparka, one should provide auspicious items such as curd and milk for the boatman;
boiled rice made from horse-gram (kaulattha), kodrava, or black śāli rice is beneficial.
He should not eat uncooked food, nor meat, nor anything prepared with the stalks of sugarcane;
furthermore, at the time of performing worship, he must not rise up in haste. 38.

Now, he states the rules regarding what is acceptable and what is unacceptable among flowers, fruits, leaves, sprouts, materials for the *madhuparka* offering, incense, lamps, and substances used for cooking the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), beginning with the words "those arising from thornless trees" and ending with "not produced by the *aravinda* lotus. Thus, the distinction between what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided regarding flowers and the materials for the sacrificial oblation is to be seen discussed in detail in other *saṃhitās* and in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Rakṣā*. (25–38)
And until the completion of the rite, one must not rise with haste due to some obstruction or for any reason during the time of propitiation; thus he says "no. (38–39)
The removal of impurities occurs from the base, the image of the Blessed One, and the auspicious pedestal. || 39 ||

The purification of the image and so forth must not be performed with thorns, iron, or anything other than soft brushes; nor may it be done with peacock feathers and the like, except for soft brushes. He states this [in the verse beginning] with "ādhārāt" (from the base), meaning that it should not be done with thorns and such. (39–40)
He should not bathe, nor sleep naked, nor should he observe silence in the presence of his teacher.
One should not touch any leavings, nor should one eat in the house of the Blessed One;
nor should one do so in the vicinity of fire, nor in a house where intoxicants are kept. 41.

"One should not be naked at the time of bathing or sleeping; one should not speak with arrogance toward gurus; one should not touch what is impure from food; and one should not eat in the temple of the Lord or similar places"—thus he says in the verse and a half beginning with "na. It should be understood that here, for the purpose of merely prohibiting eating, both low and high [persons] are mentioned together, just as Pāṇini mentions them together in the rule "śvayuvamaghonām. (40–41)
For devotees who have received initiation, the meaning of the scriptures is indeed that which is to be manifested;
for others, however, it is the Dharmaśāstra, with a mind free from greed. 42.

"One should always gather disciples who are devotees of Viṣṇu. [The commentary explains: "The scripture of the Lord (Bhagavat-śāstra) should be taught only to those who have received initiation; however, for others, only the general Dharmaśāstra should be taught. Furthermore, one should gather Vaiṣṇava disciples solely for their benefit, without any thought of acquiring material wealth. This is stated in the verse beginning with "of the devotees" (bhaktānām), which consists of one and a half verses (42–43).
Pride, envy, miserliness, greed, delusion, and so forth are non-virtues.

"All [faults], both those rooted in oneself and those residing in disciples, such as pride and other evil qualities, must be gradually reduced until the end of life. Regarding this, he says "māna" (pride) and so forth. "Tānavam" means thinness; that is to say, emaciation. (43–44)
[This was done] for those who had suddenly arrived from dwelling in other lands. || 44 ||
"One should provide beneficial instruction to those whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
He states "unexpectedly" (akasmāt) to mean that beneficial instruction must be given to Vaiṣṇavas who have arrived from another land. || 44-45 ||
He who does not know the reality of the Imperishable (Ācyuta) and the very meaning of the Pañcarātra; || 45 ||

Likewise, one should not establish a connection with him who possesses the true Vaiṣṇava initiation characterized by the various scriptures, but rather with one who follows the different sequence. 46.
He states with one and a half verses beginning with "yaḥ" that no association should be made with one who is not a Vaiṣṇava. || 45-46 ||

One should not intentionally bring about the subversion of the meaning of the scriptures or the scriptures themselves; rather, in this world, such things may occur through ignorance, lacking the traditional lineage of transmission. 47.

He says "no," meaning that one must not cause a confusion between the scripture and the meaning of the scripture. The purport of this statement is thus explained in the *Śrī Pañcarātra-kṣāya*: "In those instances where there is recognition of an unbroken tradition, ritual acts that are seen to be rooted in authoritative sources and are maintained by the succession of practice must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree, nor should anything contrary to them be adopted. (47)

One who is a devotee of the Blessed One, trustworthy, skilled in the characteristics [of things], renowned for his uprightness, and mature, should be questioned regarding the lost characteristics of the meaning of the scriptures. (48)

He says "one should ask" because, in places where the recognition of the traditional lineage has been disrupted by long-term disturbances of the kingdom and the like, that [knowledge] must be learned from the mouths of the elders. || 48 ||
One must always remain free from doubt regarding the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras, and indeed always remain in the presence of the gurus. 49.
He says "mudrā" [in verse 49] to indicate that the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras must be understood without doubt from the presence of a guru.
And one should not seek the favor of the mantras of the Omniscient One without a portion of devotion,
except through the vision of the mandala.
He says "na ca" (and not) to indicate that for the mantras of the Blessed One, one need not seek favor through such means as looking at the accomplished ones (siddhas) or their enemies. || 50 ||
The king of mantras resides in these locations: at the navel-cakra, in the heart-lotus, at the root of the kanda, in the pit of the throat, between the eyebrows, and in the aperture of Brahmā. 51.
He who resembles the sun should be meditated upon during travel, while lying down, and on the road.

With the verse beginning with "nābhi," [the author] states, in one and a half verses, the locations for the recollection of the Lord of Mantras within one's own body and the appropriate times for doing so. (51–52)
One should not eat the meat of deer or boar, nor that derived from fish.

One should not eat the flesh of swans or tortoises, nor the meat of rhinoceroses; because the Blessed One has descended in the forms of lions, boars, and so forth, one should not consume their respective meats. Likewise, he says "and [meat] sold at crossroads," meaning one should not eat such meat. The intended sense is that one should maintain the perception of the Blessed One even toward deer, boars, and other animals. Indeed, it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*, in the section on the instruction of the rules (*samayopadeśaprakaraṇa*):
"The king of beasts or even a tiger should be saluted from afar."
"One should not mount a deer of that shape, nor any other, nor even its skin.
Thus, the prohibition of meat refers specifically to the Kṛta Yuga, because in the Kali age there is a general prohibition [of meat-eating]. (42-43)
Neither do lotus seeds, nor does one climb to the top of a banyan tree in such a manner. || 53 ||
"One should not see that being cut, nor should one touch that petal with the foot.

Thus, because the lotus is supported by the Blessed One, its seeds are unfit for consumption; and because the Blessed One lies upon the banyan leaf, he states "not so" regarding the prohibition against climbing it and the like. (53–54)
It is a field of merit, a great sacred ford, and the unsurpassed hermitage of the Siddhas.
Or else, having approached an assembly of Vaiṣṇavas or a manifest sacred site of Acyuta,
one should prepare a mandala or a twelve-spoked discus.
O Mahāmati, the Cāturmāsya rite should be performed according to the rules,
either within the house preceded by self-restraint, or having fashioned a circle reaching to the wall.

Then, with four verses [54–57], he describes the sacred fields (*puṇyakṣetra*) as the locations for the performance of the Cāturmāsya vows, situated before the image of the Goddess, which is made of four kinds of metal.
And one should always observe these aforementioned rules of conduct as well.

The Guru should constantly bestow these upon the devoted disciples who carry out his commands. He says "endowed with" (saṃyuktān) to mean that he should instruct these disciples in the rules (samayas) previously mentioned in the *Śrīnṛsiṃhakalpa*. (57–58)
Having first recognized the devotee as one capable of carrying out the task, by the teacher (deśika), [the initiation should be performed]. 58.

"May all those [periods] be designated for you, in which [the practice] is indeed carried out. Having first ascertained the disciple's capacity for carrying out [the practice], the periods should be taught to him. Then, having understood that he is capable of carrying it out in whichever [periods] are possible, he should be appointed to those respective periods so that he does not again fall away from the agreement; thus he says with the half-verse beginning "having known" (jñātvā). (58–59)
He should be appointed to various tasks so that he does not fall away again.
For one who violates the observance, the Vināyakas become obstructive; the supernatural powers turn away, calamities indeed arise, and obstacles prevail. (60)
Having understood this, one must indeed speak with caution toward them.

Since a succession of misfortunes arises for one who violates the convention (*samaya*), he says in the verse beginning with "They run" (60–61) that the conventions must be observed with vigilance. "Vināyakas" means specific types of malevolent planetary spirits (*duṣṭagraha*). As stated in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*: "Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and vināyakas... The phrase "they run" means they run toward the violator of the convention. 60–61.
Having churned the ocean of self-restraint with the intellect, one should indeed extract its essence.
Out of compassion, the Guru should bestow the fivefold set of commitments (samayas).

Among these commitments, he states with the verse beginning "the essence" (sāram) that the quintet consisting of fire, devotion, the Guru, existence, and so forth—which constitutes the very core—must be taught specifically. (61–62)
Devotion toward the fire, the guru, the mantra, the scripture, and those authorized therein.
It is certain that [the fruit is attained] through the proper preservation of these five, and by their performance, but not through others independently or according to one's own whim. (63)

"For those who are capable, the accomplishments desired by the mind indeed come forth. He says "certainly" in the [verse] of fifty-three and a half, meaning that by the observance of these five rules (*samaya*), one attains the accomplishment desired by the mind even through the non-performance of other rules. Alternatively, it means that there is an absence of performing other rites according to one's own will and independence without the prompting of the Guru and others. Or else, when construed with the verb "to perform" (*kriyā*), the ablative case in "from the observance" (*paripālanāt*) is used in the sense of eliding the suffix *-tva* (*lyap*). (63–64)
Those who, however, perform [the rite] out of compulsion with an impure mind. || 64 ||
And they who observe their commitments plunge into the dark path;
yet this is protected by one whose mind is perfectly serene.
In this way, one's own self comes to attain serenity for those who desire their own welfare. 65.

He states, in two verses beginning with "yaḥ," that even for those who maintain the observance of the pledge (*samaya*) in this manner, there is fruitlessness if there is turbidity of mind, whereas there is success when that is absent. The word division is *anirmalena*. (64–65)
Surely, for those who are free from impurity and established here on the path of the virtuous—the Samayins, Sādhakas, Ācāryas, and Putrakas—there shall be auspiciousness. (66)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Rule of Conduct," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Therefore, he says "certainly" (nūnam) [in verse 66], meaning that auspiciousness shall accrue only to those disciples of the four types whose minds are free from turbidity.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the Sātvatatantra-bhāṣya, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Śrīmauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The twenty-second chapter.
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
"O Lord, I now desire to know the characteristics of the four [ages]."
By what signs are they to be recognized, and by what is their distinction made? || 1 ||

Now the twenty-second chapter will be explained. Here, Saṃkarṣaṇa asks for the definition of the four types [of yoga], beginning with the occasional (sāmayika), which were previously indicated at the end of the preceding chapter, saying: "The definition. (1)
The Blessed Lord said:
He who is prosperous, full of faith, wise, firm in his vows, truthful in speech, a devotee of the Blessed One, moderate in diet, and free from attachment; || 2 ||
One who is steadfast in the service of the guru, firm in intellect, and free from sloth;
born into a true Vaiṣṇava family and well-purified by the sacred rites (saṃskāras). || 3 ||
Formerly, he was led by his parents to the state of immediate fitness;
free from worldly confusion, self-controlled, and apprehensive of fear in the hereafter. || 4 ||
Longing for the company of the virtuous, greedy for the taste of the meaning of the scriptures, devoted to the accumulation thereof, he stands upon the path of the righteous. (5)
He is always devoted to auspicious deeds, undaunted, courageous, and patient;
he is steadfast, compassionate, and a benefactor to the virtuous.
He indeed always wears stainless garments, his limbs are pure,
he speaks kindly, his face is serene, and he is free from greed for the property of others.
Free from desire for the wives of others, established in the state of right discernment,
and belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, he is unattached to intoxicants and meat.
Devoted to purity and the study of sacred texts, ever-contented and constantly diligent,
he was intent on avoiding remnants of food and always had his body marked by the heat of the chakra-fire.
Great is he who is intent on abandoning pride, envy, and miserliness;
who is ever diligent in rites for the gods and the ancestors; and who is free from deceitful conduct.
He avoided all substances that were unfit for ritual action without exception;
he was affectionate toward his mother, his younger paternal kinsmen, and his true friends.
He is the fulfiller of what has been spoken; he is fearless, always fond of a low seat, and eternally devoted to desiring to stand above all others.

Always adorned by the wise man who takes sole delight in upholding the lineage, [he should dwell] either in another's house through the grace of his guru, or in his own house, or in the house of his guru. 13.
Merely by obtaining a vision of the mantra-form in the mandala, one is indeed consecrated simply by the glance of the guru’s eye, as if by a ritual sprinkling. 14.
He understands that at that very moment he has achieved his purpose;
and from that time forward, through the grace of the perfectly serene teacher, [he attains the goal]. (15)
For he who constantly seeks the meaning of the scripture preceded by its recitation, having heard it, reflects upon those meanings while staying in a solitary and secluded place. (16)
Even when urged, one who is fully satisfied does not fall into a state of pride;
nor does a greedy person teach others for the sake of accomplishing his own self-interest.
He who constantly seeks the meaning of the scriptures does not grasp at them as mere objects of attachment;
indeed, he does not undergo any perturbation even when challenged in an assembly. 18.
At that time, the proponent does not think, "I shall completely conquer," regarding the sacrificial pits,
the mandalas, the mudrās, the mantras, the seats, the images, and the sanctuaries.
And one should always maintain a collection of mantras within one's mind,
because they are possible for him to practice every day during the solstices and other such times.
One should worship the deity, or perform the ritual worship with mantras oneself;
and being instructed by one's guru or others, one should perform the salutation of the feet of the gurus.
One should not subject them to inquiry that might cause them displeasure;
rather, having propitiated them according to the rules, one should ask about what was not understood or what has been forgotten.
Or, having been questioned by the teachers, once he has understood or known [the matter], he should reveal his own established seal after keeping it secret from them. || 23 ||
Then, through the study of the refined scriptures and recitation, he should pray to his own guru for the supreme state known as "Putraka," preceded by the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
In the absence of one's own guru, one should request [the initiation] from one who has been consecrated by him;
or, in his absence, from another who is truly a Vaiṣṇava, following the proper sequence. || 25 ||
For from a non-Vaiṣṇava guru who is established in another doctrine,
the fruit arising from the commonality of substances— along with the ritual system and the mantras— is not obtained.
Surely it comes to fruitionlessness; therefore, one should avoid that [fault].
Through the distinction of substance, mantra, ritual action, and meditative state, the fruit is imperishable. 27.

It arises constantly for those who perform actions because of their non-differentiation from it, and indeed for those who do not perform actions, who possess equanimity toward all things, and whose souls are delighted in the Self. 28.

Indeed, for those who are devoid of worldly conduct and who reject sacrifice, one should know that any association with such a person becomes fruitful only when [the other party] understands this. || 29 ||
He should always be worshipped for the sake of attaining success in this world and the next;
he is to be recognized by these innate and unartificial signs. (30)
By the teachers, the disciple known as the *samayin* is of four types according to birth;
likewise, those preceded by the *putraka* and so forth—these three are to be fully understood. (31)

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva first described the characteristics of the *samayin*, beginning with the words "He who is glorious" and ending with "the disciple is of four kinds according to birth. And thus, one who is distinguished by the aforementioned characteristics, who—according to the procedure for initiation—has had his eyes bound and then released, and has merely beheld the maṇḍala; who is habituated to grasping the meaning of the scriptures and is devoted to the worship of the Lord specifically during the particular times such as the solstices (*ayana*) and so forth—he is to be known as a *samayin*. (2–31)

He describes the specific characteristics of the *putraka* (spiritual son) in the passage beginning with "he who is known by the Guru" and ending with "always superior to [his own] son. Thus, one who has correctly grasped the meaning of the scriptures is recognized by the Guru as worthy of the title "son. Having been granted a handful of flowers to be cast upon the mandala by the Guru, and having been authorized by the Guru with the command, "From this day forward, worship Acyuta here," he is to be known as a *putraka*—one who, whether before the image, the mandala, or in water, is daily devoted to worship through mantra alone (without the rites of meditation, ritual placement, or fire-oblation), and whose habit is the constant reflection on the meaning of the scriptures and so forth. (32–41)
"But now, listen to that which is his specific distinction.

The previously mentioned characteristics of the initiate (samayin) are common to all three, beginning with the son (putraka). However, I shall state his specific distinctions; thus he says, 'In this way' (evam). (32)
He by whom the Guru has been recognized, through whose application [of instruction] the state of having accomplished the goal is attained.
And by means of the scripture learned—whether it be slight, middling, or excellent—and with the intention of favoring him when he is summoned to the abode of Acyuta; 33.
Having performed the preliminary rites such as inspection, one should cast [the image] into the abode of the deity;
being well-pleased, one should properly offer a handful of flowers, unbroken rice, and the *arghya* water, consisting of the mantra itself.
From that time onwards, however, he performed worship by means of mantra alone—without meditation, ritual placement (nyāsa), and so forth, and devoid of the libation to the fire. || 35 ||
For the sake of establishing the state of fitness, [the offering] was given either upon the image or on the ground;
and according to the general rule, the Guru instructed him to worship Acyuta.
Thinking, "So be it," he remained always joyful, considering that which was spoken [by the teacher] as sealed with his own seal, namely the meaning of the scriptures. || 37 ||
He should look after the welfare and security of his guru to the best of his ability;
being devoted to his service, with his mind fixed on him, and intent upon him alone. (38)

Then, having been summoned by his command, he should proclaim the supreme meaning of the scriptures that he has mastered for the sake of his own guru’s renown, even without the two—mantra and mudrā. (39)
Having reflected thoroughly with his own intellect in the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas,
he acted so that he would not fall into a state of envy among the people.
That disciple named Putraka is always superior to [the teacher's] own son.

Regarding the specific characteristics of Putraka, the text begins with "he who was recognized by the Guru" and ends with "always superior to his own son. Thus, having correctly grasped the meaning of the scriptures, he is known by the Guru as one worthy of the title "son."

When he has cast a handful of flowers upon the mandala, and from that time forth is authorized by the Guru with the words, "Worship Acyuta here," he who—whether before the image, the mandala, or in water—is intent on worship through mantra alone, without daily meditation, ritual placement (nyāsa), or fire-oblations, and whose character consists of reflecting on the meaning of the scriptures and so forth, is to be known as a *putraka* (spiritual son). (32–41)
Now learn from me that specific distinction which exists regarding the one called the practitioner (sādhaka). || 41 ||
But one who has previously received initiation and is intent on the propitiation of the mantra, by means of all the rites beginning with bathing and performed while identified as a deity— 42.
For the sake of one's own accomplishment, and not for the sake of pleasing the world,
[one should practice] in a forest, at a sacred site, or in a delightful home.
One should perform the service of the mantra and the offering of arghya; this great vow of the mantra must always be strictly observed, for it is the supreme commitment. 44.
Whatever extraordinary bliss one has intensely attained within oneself by means of one's own power, that wonder must not be spoken of before anyone except the Guru, preceded by an act of worship. 45.
One who is joined with his own mudrā, constantly diligent in his own practice,
and endowed with faith— he, O Blessed One, should be understood as a practitioner who is identical with the Blessed One.

Now, he describes the characteristics of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), beginning with "The specific quality known as the practitioner... and ending with "...the practitioner is identical with the Lord. Thus, one should understand that a *sādhaka* is one who—having been purified by the previously mentioned initiation (*dīkṣā*)—performs the worship of the mantra in a sanctuary, forest, or dwelling according to the rules, accompanied by meditation, ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and so forth, while remaining intent upon its accomplishment through recitation (*japa*) and other means. (Verses 41–46)
Endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned, he is especially diligent and has been appointed by his guru for the sake of favoring his devotees.

He who understands the words of the padamantras as meaningful, according to the relationship between the signified and the signifier, or by virtue of their being with or without auxiliary parts (aṅga). 48.

And for the purpose of the placement (nyāsa) of the hands, the body, the lotuses, and the wheels—whether by means of the even or the uneven, or by the single [method] such as the variegated (citra) and so forth. 49.
Indeed, their application to various objects occurs by virtue of their specific purpose;
furthermore, through the realization of the deity of meditation, there is pervasiveness throughout the path.
Indeed, the state of being the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahmatva) of the deities is itself without marks (nirliṅga);
it correctly manifests through its own phonemes as previously described. 51.

Furthermore, he who understands the consistency of the scriptures through the power of their statements—therein, indeed, there are three kinds of statements: those of divine origin and those spoken by sages. (52)
O lotus-eyed one, consider that speech to be excellent which is rich in meaning, free from doubt, clear, concise, and stable. (53)
That word of the Supreme Lord is established by its own command and bestows liberation;
it is indeed a praiser of the supernatural powers and an instigator of them as well.
Know that the word of the sage is pleasing to all, profound, and capable of providing certainty; indeed, it is capable of providing certainty. 55.
A human statement is traditionally defined as that which is purposeless, disconnected, of little meaning, mere verbal ostentation, and incapable of carrying out its initial assertion. (56)
That which is to be abandoned is a mine of the attainment of misfortune and leads to hell; it merely restates well-known matters, lacks coherent meaning, and is inconsistent. (57)
Moreover, if human speech is to be accepted, it should be like the word of a sage;
such is the scripture (āgama), O Mahāmati, which arises from words that ought to be adopted. 58.
Know that to be the complete revelation of the true path and the doctrine of ritual injunction;
for whatever is correctly inferred from its authority is in accordance with reality. (59)
Thus urged by his devotees, he who is learned in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge always carries out [his duties] without contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Furthermore, he who always bears the wheel and is adorned with his own mudrā should be recognized as a teacher by all those possessing the qualities of the samaya. 61.

Now, he states the characteristics of the teacher (ācārya), beginning with "endowed with the previously mentioned marks" and ending with "possessing all conventional qualities. Furthermore, as an incidental discussion, the threefold nature of the Āgamas—divided into the *divya* and other categories—and the distinction between their intermixture (*saṅkara*) have been shown. In that regard, one should accept that even the teachings spoken by the sages (*munibhāṣita*) possess a threefold division according to the *sāttvika* and other qualities, as elaborated in works such as the *Aiśvara* and *Pārameśvara*. This investigation into their intermixture is to be seen explained extensively in the *Śrī Pañcarātrarakṣā*.

The two terms *anirvāhakamādyokteḥ* ("because the first statement is non-conclusive") and *asaṃbaddham* ("incoherent," meaning contradictory between earlier and later parts), which were mentioned in the section defining human speech (*pauruṣavākyalakṣaṇa*), have also been explained in that very same place. Thus, one should understand that an *ācārya* is he who is endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, whose mantra has been perfected through vows and other practices, who has been consecrated by the initiation of an *ācārya*, and who is fully possessed of the knowledge of the meaning of the *pada-mantras* and so forth.

Now, one might object: "By the words 'one who has previously received initiation' (*pūrvavallabdhadīk�ṣaḥ*), the state of having received initiation is stated for the *sādhaka*; and by 'endowed with the previously mentioned marks' (*liṅgaiḥ pūrvoditairyuktaḥ*), it is stated for the *ācārya*. But since that [initiation] does not exist for the *samayin* and the *putraka*, how can their eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the worship of mantra alone be established? If you ask, 'At what time did they receive the mantra in the absence of initiation?', what is the use of this doubt? Engagement proceeds from the word; cessation proceeds from the word."

Statements establishing that those who are uninitiated lack the qualification for worship should be understood as being intended to prohibit the qualification for worship accompanied by the placement of mudrās (*mudrānyāsa*). As for the mantra, it is received precisely at the time of practicing the scripture immediately after seeing the maṇḍala. (47–61)
He who, having formed an attachment in his heart, perceives the Self as something other than its true state when it is joined to another condition—that lowest of men shall go to hell. 62.
If the sequential order is abandoned, one would not be a vessel for the siddhis.

Even though he stands in a lower station such as that of a *samayin* or a *putra*, by virtue of perceiving himself as having ascended to the rank of a *sādhaka* or an *ācārya* with respect to the *pratiṣṭhā* [consecration], the text states "he perceives" in two and a half verses to describe his even greater fault. (62–63)
One's own conduct, one's own caste, one's own lineage, and the house of one's own guru.

Thus, he states with one and a half verses that falling from one's status (pātitya) can also occur through the concealment of one's own conduct, caste, lineage, and so forth. "In this way" means by means of [practices] such as mantras and mudrās, which were previously prohibited;
"drawn in" means [one who has been drawn in] by the command of those [teachers], yet without the pair of mantras and mudrās.
For the sake of fame, one might speak of the supreme meaning of the scriptures known [only] from one's own guru.
Because their manifestation has been prohibited by such [statements], one should therefore not even speak of their superiority over the *ahaṅkāra*. (63–64)
Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should always avoid pride, lest it lead to the destruction of that [good];
and one should properly observe the relative status of higher and lower in every situation.
He says "therefore" (tasmāt) to show that stating the true meaning is conducive to spiritual welfare. || 65 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
O Lord, what are the characteristics that define the four mudrās, by the thorough knowledge of which the fourfold group ending with the Deśika is understood? (66)
Saṃkarṣaṇa asks about the characteristics of the four mudrās that serve as indicators for the previously mentioned initiates, such as the *samayin* and *putraka*, with the word "mudrā" (verse 66).
The Blessed Lord said: Know that the previously mentioned fivefold [mudrās] of Nṛhari, beginning with the head-mudrā (śiromudrā),
are formed by excluding the thumb and using fingers of progressively fewer digits.
The group of four, however, consists of the four [syllables] ending with the Guru, as they naturally stand. || 67 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Rule for the Distinctions of Empowered Mudrās," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva, with the first half-verse of verse 67, states that the four mudrās—beginning with the *śikhāmudrā*—as previously taught in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*, constitute the four mudrās for the *samayins*, *putrakas*, and others.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The twenty-third chapter.
Nārada said:
Then, O best of Brahmins, Kāmapāla [honored] the Lord of Gods.
Being thus urged, I shall now speak that in brief. || 1 ||
