Now the twenty-third chapter will be explained. Here, Kāmapāla says: "I shall relate that which was asked of Vāsudeva by Saṃkarṣaṇa. (1)
Saṅkarṣaṇa said:
"O Lord, the collection of seeds belonging to the gods of manifestation has been understood by me;
now I wish to know that which is indeed the aggregate of their bodies."
He states the manner of the question: "Known," etc. (verse 2).
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen with an attentive mind to me regarding the collection of piṇḍa-mantras for the deities who have been mentioned in their proper order.

Thus questioned, Vāsudeva said, "Listen to the piṇḍa-mantras," beginning with the word "yathā" (as follows); that is to say, [the mantras] of the deities mentioned in their proper order, namely Padmanābha, Dhruva, and the others. || 3 ||
Below that and to the north, one should decorate [the area] as far as the edge of the axle-holes.
Then, taking the subsequent [syllable] from the region of the eye (akṣa), one should place it below that;
the second seed-syllable of the rim (nemi) is in the middle, and that which is in the center is on the seat.
One should indeed fashion the seven [petals] of the navel, rooted in the sixth support;
know that the eighth above that constitutes the third [lotus].
Then, having taken the eighth [letter] from the left, which is situated in the sixth position,
one should place it in sequence below the second navel.
Taking the third, the seventh, and the fourth from that [starting point],
and then taking the seventh below the navel from the point before the *nemi*, [one should proceed].
Having placed the third [letter] below that as well by way of indication,
one should then place the ninth [letter] from the navel, extending both upwards and downwards.
Know that the second [syllable] in that very place is the seventh piṇḍa;
one should place it above the sixth, starting from the navel. 10.
Indeed, the seventh and the eighth [chakras] follow one above the other in sequence;
then the eighth has ascended from the region of the navel above the seventh.
Below that, situated in the middle, the ninth from the axle is proclaimed;
furthermore, above the fifth from the enemy (the outermost), one should place the third from the navel.
The third from the exterior is at the top of the head; this is known as the tenth piṇḍa.
The second is from the region of the navel, and the third is situated above that.
This eleventh [vowel] is indeed remembered as being above the beginning and end of the *nema*;
then, having placed the seventh [vowel] of the fourth *nābhi*.
Below that, however, is the one preceded by the rim (nemi); this is remembered as the twelfth.
Taking the thirteenth from the rim, one should join it below that in due order. 15.
The seventh and the fourth [vow] are prior to the navel, O Mahāmati;
all these, including the sixth, are the seats, and this collection constitutes the thirteenth.
Taking the fourth from the navel, one should place the seventh above it;
and the ninth upon its head—know this to be the fourteenth.
Having placed the fourth letter from 'na' above and below, that which is the second letter from 'nābhi' is known as the fifteenth. 18.
Having taken the twentieth [syllable] from the external circle called Āra, one should immediately join it with the sixth [syllable], which is Sāntima. || 19 ||
Having placed [the vowel] above and below the seventh consonant, *n*,
know that the second [consonant], which is from the region of the navel, is indeed the seventeenth.
One should place the ninth [syllable] above the seventh from the region of the navel;
then, one should make the eighth [syllable] go upward from the region of the navel to the seventh.
A second [mark] is also below that, from the navel-circle;
it is thirteen units above [the first], and that twenty-ninth mark is indeed above [the second].
The fourth from the navel, the third above that, and the one situated further up;
know that this is indeed the seventh in that very place, as well as the twentieth.
Having joined the eighth letter of the second [varga] above the navel, one should then place the sixth letter from 'ra' below it, followed by the plow-bearer (la). 24.
One should place the ninth [syllable] above the third from the region of the navel; one should place the second below that. Now hear about the twenty-third.
One should join them in sequence: the eighth, the seventh, the second from the navel, and then the first; thus, starting from the sixth, one reaches the top of the head.
Taking the seventh from Nemi, then the seventh below that, which is the third from that;
the one below that is known as the twenty-fourth.
Having placed the third [line] above the navel, the second above that, and the rim (nemi) above that,
the twenty-sixth [syllable] is now described.
One should make the sixth seat from the enemy [direction], and the color should be the third from the navel.
Above that is the seventh; understand it to be different from this. || 29 ||
One should place the twenty-sixth letter minus the final consonant (the visarga), situated above and below the rim;
the seventh from the letters of the nave, and the fifth from the group of vowels.
Taking the first letter after *na* (i.e., *ma*) as the second, one should place it below that;
it is taught as the twenty-eighth from the middle syllable of *mahābuddhi* (i.e., *ha*). (31)
Taking the ninth, the seventh, and the third from the navel, as well as the third again; then, having taken the one situated above the vowel (a), one should place it below that. 32.
The third and the second [syllables] immediately following the region of the navel;
then, taking the second of the navel [syllables], as well as the seventh and the fourth. (33)
Then, from the exterior of the third navel, the first [channel] goes to the head;
thereafter, the ninth [channel] from the navel stands in the middle of the eyes and goes upward.
Then, from the navel of the eighth [digit], one should give the second [digit] above;
immediately following that, the sixth is indeed situated below that very same one.
Sixth, above that, is the one preceding the navel;
having placed the eighth as well, understand the thirty-sixth.
Having joined the seventh, the third, and the fourth [spokes] from the navel-circle,
one should place the thirteenth spoke above them.
Alternatively, one should know that the thirty-seventh [digit] is from the ninth, the third, and the second [counting] from the navel; then one should take it from the region of the navel. 38.
The sixth seat is to the west; the second is above that;
and the ninth is also above that. One should eat the rice-balls (piṇḍas) excluding the first one. 39.
All [the deities] should indeed be adorned with the [seed-syllable] beginning with the letter 'a' at the end of the spokes and so forth;
they should end with "namas," begin with the Praṇava (Om), and be joined with their respective names. 40.

He describes the sequence for their extraction, beginning with "That which is the eighth seed-syllable from the navel" and ending with "joined with their respective names, ending in *namaḥ* and preceded by the *praṇava*. Having placed the letter *ha*—which is the eighth seed-syllable from the navel—above the letter *sa*, and having joined the letter *na* after the syllable below that *sa*, one should adorn it with a *visarga* at the end of the spoke (*arānta*). This is the *piṇḍākṣara* of Padmanābha. It should be understood that the same method applies to the subsequent [deities] as well.

And thus their ritual applications (*prayoga*) are: *hsnaḥ*, *nkhamaṃ*, *hssūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *lsvaṃ*, *kslaṃ*, *kṣraṃ*, *hsyūṃ*, *hssaṃ*, *gluṃ*, *ksraṃ*, *khskaṃ*, *ksvyaṃ*, *kṣsvaṃ*, *kṣvaṃ*, *ghraṃ*, *bhruṃ*, *dbhraṃ*, *kṣsaṃ*, *ssroṃ*, *slvaṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *kṣluṃ*, *hsyūṃ*, *jsvaṃ*, *kyaṃ*, *stryūṃ*, *svūṃ*, *kkhmaṃ*, *hrlaṃ*, *nyraṃ*, *svaṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *kṣmaṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hyūṃ*, *slvoṃ*, *kṣruṃ*, *kṣrūṃ*.

Thus are the thirty-eight *piṇḍa* mantras. Here, with the exception of the first *piṇḍa*, all others should be joined with the *anusvāra*, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, and they should be formed with the names Padmanābha and so forth in the dative case. || 4.40 ||
That [breath] which exists without the tip of the spokes (the palate) and above, or below, or together with the region prior to the navel, or indeed alone—[that is the breath]. (41)
Then, having set those aside, one should perform the worship of all [the deities],
fashioning them like lions, each according to its own *piṇḍa*.
Salutation! Its name is Praṇava; its birth is again according to one's karma.
Until that sacrifice is performed, however, one who is intent on liberation should practice it. 43.
The entire application of those [mantras] arising from seed-syllables, clusters, and words should be performed;
however, their Vaibhava-mudrā must be employed in the rite of worship. 44.
Then the limb-mudrās of the limbs should be applied together with their respective mantras;
all this, along with its support, has been taught by me as proclaimed in the Siṃhamantra. 45.

Indeed, preceded by initiation (*dīkṣā*), the mantras are the means for accomplishing the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*). Now, setting aside those specific seed-syllables (*piṇḍa*), one should perform the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*)—beginning with the heart—for all mantras without distinction using the vowels starting with *ā*, just as in the previously mentioned *Viśvatrātṛ Nṛsiṃha* mantra. One should also display the mudrās according to the majesty described in the tenth chapter. Furthermore, just like the *Nṛsiṃha* mantra, for these [other mantras] as well, preceded by initiation and through worship and so forth, they are the means for accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life; this is stated beginning with the words "for that which, without the *arānta* [syllable], etc. up to the end of the section on the four aims.
This concludes the section ending with "for this is the means of proof," [verses 41–46].
Now, moreover, learn the characteristics of the words and mantras. 46.
Salutations to Him who is beyond the universe, whose stainless state bestows knowledge, and without whom the worship of those things that have attained existence would never come to pass. 47.
Immediately after that, know this twenty-four-syllable mantra for Padmanābha, who is all-pervading; now hear this supreme number. 48.
One should then offer the five-syllabled word to the one whose form is light and whose embodiment is the sky, "to Dhruva," and thereafter the supreme three-syllabled mantra.
For the sake of the fourfold attainment of the stages, one should offer the three-syllable mantra;
then, one should give the stage to Ananta and thereafter to Aparimita.
Next, for the one who is the support of all, and at the end of that, for the one who holds power;
this [mantra] consists of twenty syllables, so now hear the one of twenty-two syllables.
Having first paid homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, who is the self of all powers and possesses infinite forms, one should then [utter] the word "pada" (the goal). 52.
Then [he offered] the great sound to the one whose essence is vigor, then the word "Puruṣa," then the words "Moha" and "Māyā," and then indeed to the Destroyer.

Then, the word "sadoditāya" (to the ever-arisen one), which is the locus of all powers, should be employed; it consists of four syllables and is traditionally known as having twenty-seven syllables [in total]. 54.
Then there should be "pada" for the knower of the Vedas, the delighter of the universe;
then for the Lord of the Universe, and then indeed for the Supreme Self. 55.
This [mantra] consists of twenty syllables; now hear the seventeen-syllable one.
One should form the word for the Self of Knowledge (jñānātmane), and after that, the word "consciousness" (saṃvit). 56.
Then, [one should offer] a foot-offering to the one of luminous intent and peaceful form;
immediately thereafter, to the one of infinite power who pervades all.
Thereafter, this word for the one who consists of the world and possesses a universal form (viśvarūpa) is uttered with twenty-one syllables; listen now to another. 58.
Having taken up the word "existent being" (sat-sattva-pada), then the word "dwelling in the cave" (guhā-śaya-pada);
then [the word] "for the supreme swan" (parama-haṃsāya), and then "wandering in the mind" (mānasa-cāriṇe). || 59 ||
And then there is one of nineteen syllables for Yajñamūrti; following that, one should take the word for Viśvāntarvartin. 60.
Then, "bhuvana-śabdam," followed by the word "varāhāya" and "vibhūti-svāmine"— this [mantra] consists of twenty-four syllables.
One should then offer salutations to the Blessed One, and indeed to the submarine fire (vāḍavāgni), whose fuel is the water of the world and whose state is that of being ablaze. 62.
One should utter "phaṭ" for vigor; this [mantra] is remembered as having that many [syllables] at its end. One should also give the word "prasanna" ending with "sarvāntacāriṇe. (63)
Then, at the end of that, one should indeed offer the word "to the Embodied One" (mūrtaye) and the word "to the Righteous Self" (dharmātmane).
This is the sixteen-syllable mantra; now hear this most secret [mantra] from it. 64.
Then one should offer [the oblation] to Sarvavidyeśvara, and thereafter to Vākpati;
then, taking up the mantra "padaṃ vada vada," one should offer it with "tato vāgvibhavam tu."
This [mantra] indeed consists of nineteen syllables; now I shall tell you another for the sake of bestowing the sovereignty of yoga and for the essence of yogic sleep.
One should grant the station to the one devoted to the Lord who reclines upon the flames;
this [mantra] consists of three times eight syllables plus one. 67.
Having taken up the word "Bhagavat," one who possesses infinite power is able [to master] the two-syllabled word for Him who consists of splendor and sustains the world. 68.
At the end of that, one should employ the word "to the one whose self is the tortoise" (kacchapātmane).
Know this twenty-six syllable mantra, O best among those who know mantras. 69.
Then one should offer [oblations] to Yajñāṅgadeha, Ādya, Mahāpada, and thereafter to Varāha, the Ancient Puruṣa.
Then one should utter the word "prajā," and at its end, the word "pataye.
O best among those who know the systems of mantra, this is the twenty-four-syllable mantra. 71.

Having first paid homage to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha, one should then utter the words "tejonidhe" (O treasury of splendor), followed by "padaṃ dadyāt" (may he grant the step) and "hana hana" (slay, slay).
Then, indeed, there arises a sound born of improper action consisting of five syllables;
for at its end is that which is ill-done, and this [mantra] consists of twenty-seven syllables.

"O Lord, having taken [the mantra] whose form is nectar, which consists of the essence of the power of knowledge, and belongs to the Sovereign of All—this [mantra] consists of nineteen syllables. (74)
O Supreme Lord, having indeed taken up the state of the lotus-eyed one,
there follows the state of the word "sakala" (the whole), which is happiness and auspiciousness.

Then, one should place the word "vāñchita" (desired), followed by "siddhiprada" (bestower of success), then the word "akhiladuḥkha" (all sufferings), and thereafter "śamanāgnaye" (to the fire of pacification). 76.
Then one should place the word "Ānandasundara" and the word "Lakṣmī";
having uttered the word "Pataye," the fifty-syllable mantra is thus reduced by three. (77)

Having first taken up the word "existent-non-existent" (sadasat), then for the Form (mūrti), then for the Supreme of the Universe (viśvottama), and thereafter indeed for the Ocean of Immortality (amṛtanidhi). 78.
This sixteen-syllable mantra of the Lord, whose nature is splendor, is said to be: "To Puruṣottama," and then "the Unobstructed. (79)
Then one should give the word "śaktaye," followed by the word "sarveśvara.
Then, in the phrase "samagrograbhaya," the word "nivāraṇa" follows.
The twenty-seven-syllable mantra has been declared; hear what follows this:
having extracted the word "niyantre" (O Controller), at its end [place] "viśvahetave" (to the cause of the universe). || 81 ||
Following "Oṃ A-nanta-raṃ," there is the mantra consisting of sixteen syllables, beginning with "Parabrahma-sametaṃ ca Setave.
This has been described; hereafter I shall speak further. 82.
In the passage beginning with "padamapratima," there is the absence of the letter *b*; immediately after that, the word "mahāvibhūte," and following that, the word "mahāmāyā. (83)
Then, by adding the word "darśaka" at the end of that for Tālaketu, this twenty-four-syllable mantra has been stated in brief. || 84 ||
One should grant a station to the peaceful self, and at its end, one should place Yama;
one should grant it to the refuge of observances and to the bestower of supreme sovereignty.
The word "Nārāyaṇāya" is recorded as being equal in syllables to the preceding number;
immediately after that, one should utter "Bhavabhaṅgapadāya Kāriṇe. (86)
Then he gave the word "Bhagavat" to Dattātreya;
thereafter, the word "varṇāśramapada," and after that, the word "dharma. (87)

The *praṇava* consisting of twenty-eight syllables is remembered for the purpose of grasping; then follows the word "to the one who consists of all worlds" (*sarvalokamaya*), and after that, "to the omniscient one" (*sarvajñāya*). || 88 ||
Then, for the Lord of All, who reclines upon the banyan tree, there is a foot [of the mantra] consisting of twenty-three syllables; now learn another from me. (89)
Then, taking the word *bhūta*, followed by the word *bhāvanāya*;
then the word *śabda* for the Universal Self (*viśvātman*), and then the word *vimala*. (90)
Then [the syllable] for Niketana, and then the foot for Kandhara;
this king of mantras is said to consist of twenty-two syllables. (91)
Then, having offered a step to Viṣṇu, who had cast aside his weapons;
then a step to the one consisting of Brahman, who wears matted hair and carries a staff.
One should indeed give the word "vidita" at the end for the sake of prosperity;
this mantra consists of twenty-six syllables—learn it from me further. 93.
Then, having taken the word "sarvaśabdam," immediately thereafter one should give the auspicious five-syllabled phrase "vyāpine sahasrārciṣe. (94)
Then one should give the word *trivikramāya*, then the word *aparimita*, and then the word *prabhāvāya*; this is remembered as consisting of twenty-three syllables. || 95 ||
Then he uttered the two-syllable name for the Lord of Men, the foremost of persons, who is devoted to meditation on the Self: "Nārāyaṇa. (96)
The mantra consists of twenty-one syllables; now learn another from me: one should utter the word "Nārāyaṇāya" and then the word "nir-ati. (97)
The word "śayānandamayāya" (to the one consisting of the bliss of lying down) is indeed free from egoism;
following that, for the one attached to the word, this [mantra] consists of twenty-five syllables. 98.
Taking the supreme state from that very Supreme Self, this sixteen-syllable mantra belongs to Hari, the Lord of Yoga. || 99 ||
Having taken the seven-syllabled word beginning with "praṅ" and followed by "namaḥ paramātmane," then the word "kṛṣṇāya," and thereafter the three-syllabled "kamalam. (100)
Immediately after that, the word "dala" is for the wide-eyed one;
then, for the Brahman who is most established in Brahman, there is indeed the mantra of twenty-eight syllables.
Having taken the word "Bhagavan," and likewise [the words] "yugānta" and "dahana," one should then give the word for "flaming" (dīptaye); for indeed, that is the very word for "saṃsāra. 102.
This [mantra] of twenty-two syllables is indeed remembered as the creator who severs bondage;
it is for the Fourfold Form (Caturmūrti) who consists of the four states of existence. 103.
One should offer [the syllable] to the wielder of the arrow and the bow, who has the luster of an autumnal blue lotus;
thereafter, one should offer it to the Blessed One, whose feet are most beautiful. 104.
The thirty-sixth syllable is traditionally taught as "to the body" (śarīrāya) and "the state" (pada);
one should then utter the word "clearly" (viśada), which is the state of the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 105 ||
Thereafter, O Lord, one should indeed give the name to the knower of the Vedas, the learned one, and the all-pervading one; and then the other two-syllabled word.
This has been described with twenty syllables; now hear another [mantra] from this perspective:
one should utter the word "Garuḍa" and at its end, the word "Vāhana. (107)
"Armed with all weapons and missiles," [he says], and pacifies even the inauspicious; then, having shaken off the bonds of karma, he should utter [the following]. 108.
"Protect the Dharma; therefore, one should give; abandon non-Dharma; therefore, one should speak.
This is the thirty-four-syllable mantra; hereafter I shall speak further.
To the form of withdrawal, to the one whose radiance is the fire of time,
to the one who reclines upon the netherworld, and indeed to the one who is the shackle of ignorance.
"Destroy the accumulation"—this is the repetition; immediately after that is the *praṇava*.
This mantra of thirty-five syllables is indeed remembered as the granter of all accomplishments. || 111 ||
All [these names] are adorned with the Praṇava (Om) and embellished with the word of salutation (Namaḥ);
they are especially meritorious when remembered, worshipped, meditated upon, and recited. 112.
There is nothing on earth that those devoted to virtuous deeds do not bestow through their devotion;
now, listen to the characteristics of the sectarian marks, mantras, and scriptures. 113.

Now he states the word-mantras (padamantra), beginning with "The characteristic of the word-mantras" and ending with "by devotion and good deeds on earth. Their application is as follows: Oṃ, salutation to Padmanābha, who transcends the universe, who bestows pure knowledge, and who pervades the universe. Oṃ, salutation to Him whose form is light, whose body is the sky, who is eternal, and who is the cause for attaining the supreme state. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta, the immeasurable, the refuge of all, who sustains power.

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, whose self is all power, to the one of infinite forms; salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the Great Being whose self is valor, who destroys delusion and illusion, who is eternally risen, and who is all-powerful; salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the knower of the Vedas, the delighter of the universe, the Lord of the universe, the Supreme Self; salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the self of knowledge, whose desire is the light of consciousness, to the one of peaceful form; salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the one of infinite power, the all-pervading, who consists of the world, the universal-formed; salutation!

Oṃ, salutation to the one dwelling in the cave of the true being (*sat-sattva-guhā*), the supreme swan (*parahaṃsa*) who moves within the mind. Oṃ, salutation to the embodiment of sacrifice, who dwells within the universe, the world-boar (*bhuvanavarāha*), the lord of all manifestations (*vibhūti*). Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*), whose sacrificial flame blazes with the waters of the world as its fuel; *phaṭ*, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the one who moves within all things, whose form is serene, the very soul of Dharma. Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of all sciences, the Master of Speech; speak, speak, [grant] the power of speech! *Namaḥ*.

Oṃ, salutations to the one who bestows the sovereignty of yoga, to the essence of yogic sleep, to the cloud-like one, to the Blessed One reclining upon the waters. Oṃ, salutations to the one whose self is the tortoise, who possesses the infinite power and strength of the Blessed One, who consists of splendor, and who upholds the worlds. Oṃ, salutations to the Great Boar, whose body is the limbs of sacrifice, to the Ancient Person, to Prajāpati. Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed Narasiṃha, the treasury of splendor; slay, slay the evil deeds born of improper action; salutations!

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Lord of All, whose form is nectar, whose essence is the power of knowledge. Oṃ, salutations to the Lotus-eyed One, the Supreme Lord, the treasury of all happiness and auspiciousness, the fire that pacifies all suffering, and the bestower of the fulfillment of desires; salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is beautiful with bliss. Oṃ, salutations to the one whose form is both being and non-being, the most excellent in the universe, the treasury of nectar. Oṃ, salutations to Puruṣottama, the Lord of All, whose power is unimpeded, and who wards off every foremost fear.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Controller, the Cause of the Universe, the Bridge to the Supreme Brahman; Oṃ, obeisance to Him of incomparable power and great majesty, whose banner is the palm tree that reveals the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā). Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, the peaceful Self, the refuge of restraints and observances, the bestower of supreme sovereignty. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Dattātreya, the destroyer of worldly existence, who upholds the duties of the castes and stages of life. Oṃ, obeisance to the All-Knowing One, the Universal Self, the stainless Lord of All, who reclines upon the banyan tree.

Oṃ, salutations to the creator of beings, the soul of the universe, whose abode is stainless. Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu, whose weapons are cast aside, who consists of Brahman, the soul of the universe, whose abode is stainless, and who is the neck [of the world]. Oṃ, salutations to the all-pervading one, who possesses a thousand rays, who is Trivikrama, and whose power is immeasurable. Oṃ, salutations to the lord of men, the most excellent of persons, who is devoted to meditation upon the Self. Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, who consists of unsurpassed bliss, and who is attached to the state free from egoism.

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Yoga, Hari. Oṃ, salutation! Salutation to the Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa, whose wide eyes are like lotus petals, who is most devoted to Brahman, the Brahman itself. Oṃ, Blessed One, salutation to You who blaze like the fire at the end of an eon, the one who severs the bonds of worldly existence. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, who possesses four forms, who consists of the four states of existence, who bears the arrow and the Śārṅga bow, who has the luster of an autumnal blue lotus, and whose body is more beautiful than the moon.

Oṃ, salutation to the Lord, the all-pervading, the wise one who knows the Vedas of the pure ultimate reality. Oṃ, O Garuḍa-vehicled one, wielder of all weapons and missiles, pacify the inauspicious; shake off, shake off the bonds of karma! Protect the Dharma, abandon Adharma—salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the embodiment of withdrawal, whose radiance is like the fire of Time (Kālavaiśvānara), who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla); destroy, destroy the multitude of fetters of ignorance—Oṃ, salutation! These are the thirty-eight-word mantras. (Verses 46–113)
Then one should give the word *sahasradīdhiti*, followed by *śurita*;
for the body (*vigraha*), there are ten syllables, and for the crown (*makuṭa*), three more.
Then, having taken the desired state for the sake of bestowing accomplishment,
one should immediately give the state of the Great Thought to the jewel.
Know that there is one of fifteen syllables, and hear another of ten syllables;
it contains all the characteristic words and indeed bestows prosperity.
O Mother, having first taken the three-syllabled word "saubhāgya," and then [the word] "sarvaprade," this very [mantra] is ten syllables long. (117)
Now, know that "prāṇātmane atha satyāya" consists of seven syllables;
furthermore, "kālakartre atha cakrāya phaṭ" is proclaimed to have eight syllables. (118)
One should offer a seat to the Soul of the Universe, and then to the Giver of the Universe.
Know this to be the nine-syllabled mantra; now hear the supreme eight-syllabled one. (119)
Having taken up the state of Vidya, one should then perform [the rite] for the one worshipped by the Lords of Vidyā (Vidyeśvara);
first, for the embodiment of Sound (Śabdamūrti), the eight-syllabled mantra of Śaṅkha is prescribed.
One should place the word "rasanidhe" and thereafter the word "bhīmaśabda";
at the end of that, indeed, is the ten-syllabled mantra known as "bhīṣaṇāya. || 121 ||
Know that the thirteen-syllable mantra for the Lord of Beings, who is the pillar of the universe, is "prāg bhuvanādhipataye stambhabhūtāya vai padam"; thereafter, attend to the other.
The ten-syllable [mantra] is for the sheath of the senses and for archery;
it is the state that possesses the roar of the wind at the end of the aeon and the flash of lightning.
One should give the sixteen-syllable mantra for Prabhā; now hear the nine-syllable one from hereon: one should place the word "Mahāmāyā" and then two syllables for the binding. (124)
Having taken the word *dhvaṃsine*, hear this number of words;
then, after that, [the word] *parāya* for the sake of swallowing all weapons. 125.
Know that the eleven-syllable mantra for the one who causes torment and destroys pride is "Santāpakāya Śabdantu Darpavidhvaṃsine"; thereafter, the nine-syllable mantra is stated.
Immediately after that, the word *ajñānakhaṇḍana* for the Supreme One, and then the nine-syllable mantra *trailokyamohana* for the Embodiment. 127.
The phrase "mahāmāyāmaye" is indeed the word that effects universal attraction;
it consists of twelve syllables, and one should then extract the nine-syllable [mantra]. || 128 ||
Having first joined the unbroken word and then applied it at the end,
listen now to the seven-syllable word for valor.
Now learn the five-syllable mantra for the one who pacifies pride:
"tejomālini. These are proclaimed as twenty-two [syllables]. (130)
As before, they are enclosed at the beginning and end, adorned with their own name-words;
one should always place the word of designation at the end of the syllable that concludes the number.

Now, he states the mantras for their emblems (such as the crown) and the mantras for their weapons (such as the discus), beginning with "atha lāñchanamantrāṇām" and continuing until the end of the chapter. Their application is as follows: *Oṃ, salutation to the crown whose form is adorned by a thousand rays; Oṃ, salutation to the Kaustubha, the great wish-fulfilling gem that bestows the attainment of desired objects; Oṃ, salutation to the Śrīvatsa, which bestows the perfection of all auspicious marks.*

Oṃ, salutation to Vanamālā, the mother of good fortune, the bestower of all. Oṃ, salutation to Satya, whose self is the vital breath (prāṇa). Oṃ, phaṭ to the Discus, the maker of time. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Lotus, whose self is the universe and the giver of the universe. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Mace, worshipped by the lords of knowledge. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Conch, whose form is sound. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Plow, which is terrible and fearsome to the tongue. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Club, the lord of the worlds and the pillar of existence. Oṃ, phaṭ to the Bow and Arrows, the sheath of the senses.

Oṃ, to the one whose roar is like the wind at the end of an aeon, whose splendor flashes like lightning, to the Śārṅga bow, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the destroyer of the bonds of Mahāmāyā, to the sword, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one intent on devouring all weapons, to the shield, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one who causes torment, the destroyer of pride, to the staff, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one consisting of the great illusion that performs the summoning of all, to the goad, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one of unbroken valor, to the mallet, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the subduer of pride, to the thunderbolt, Phaṭ! Oṃ, to the garlanded with splendor, to the spear, Phaṭ! These are the twenty-two mantras. (113–132)
One should append the name at the end of the weapons and mantras of the fourteen [deities] in their proper order, ending with the word "phaṭ" for those terminating in Śakti. 132.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Consecration Initiation," in the Śrī Sātvata-saṃhitā of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, the son of the venerable Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, the ornament of the Mauñjyāyana lineage.
The twenty-fourth chapter.
The venerable Nārada said: O foremost of Brahmins, having thus heard the clear definition of the mantras, [the sages asked:]
The Blessed One urged him once more with the palm-tree bannered one (Hanuman).

Now the twenty-fourth chapter will be explained. Here again, he says "Vipra" [to show] that Vāsudeva was impelled by Saṃkarṣaṇa. In this context, because of its divine nature, the active voice (parasmaipada) has been employed instead of the middle voice (ātmanepada). Alternatively, "sattālaketo" is the nominative singular; the person named Sattāketu is Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 1 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa said: Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra,
if one who is composed of the Blessed One desires constant worship, [he may approach] the body consisting of mantra.
"What kind of procedure (vidhi) is prescribed there for one who desires to fashion the image?
The Blessed Lord said:
"It may be made of clay, wood, stone, or even of fine metal."
He describes the manner of the challenge with the verse beginning "brāhmaṇa" (2.3), consisting of one and a half verses.
The image, which is beneficial for the twice-born who seek fruits, appears as differentiated by distinctions;
yet for those free from desire, it is attained as non-differentiated and brings about non-contradiction.
In this regard, know that there is a painting supported by walls, wood, and cloth;
furthermore, according to the sequence of colors, it arises from the void in four ways.
And that [seat] is indeed made of cotton, silk, linen, or hemp;
likewise, it may be made of clay, or of white cloth and the like, or even of various kinds of wood.

[One should prepare a seat] made of *aśvattha* wood arising from the *brahmavṛkṣa*, or born of *śrīparṇī* and *suradāru*, or consisting of *sāla* and *tāla*, or likewise produced from *śāśavanta* and *indusāra*.
Know that for the twice-born and the others, there are thus two [types] each in their respective order;
other than these, the sacrificial trees are indeed firmly rooted and full of essence. || 8 ||
But those common to all four [castes] are for the rites beginning with the consecration of images;
they are remembered as being common for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation, like those made of stone or clay. (9)
Likewise, there are those made of silver, gold, copper, and even brass;
for in this way, the grounds, cloths, stones, minerals, and trees are likewise composed.
All the jewels, such as the diamond and others, characterized by white, red, and other colors, are extraordinary for those desiring results, depending again upon gain or loss. (11)

Thus urged, Vāsudeva first explained the fourfold classification of each of the five types of images—painted, earthen, wooden, stone, and metallic—according to the sequence of the social classes (varṇas) beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. He then stated that the acceptance of images made of those specific materials according to those respective varṇas pertains to those with desires (sakāma), whereas the acceptance of images in general pertains to those free from desire (niṣkāma); this is covered in the section beginning with "painted, earthen, wooden, or stone" and ending with "again, according to gain or loss. (3–11)

One should bring [the disciple] to a state of common illumination through the recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, using the mantras of one's own form; likewise, by worshipping the cause thereof.
In the rite of preparing clay for the feet, one should worship the Earth together with Indra;
likewise, for the sake of cloth and wood, one should worship Varuṇa along with the Lord of Trees (Vanaspatis).
And regarding the connection with precious minerals, [one should worship] the sun, moon, and fire;
indeed, this is done through the medium of the gems, by means of the meaning of the term "mineral," and without the need for a formal ritual installation.

Now, regarding the time of taking the material substances for the purpose of fashioning each respective image, he states in two and a half verses beginning with "samyak" that one should perform, in general, the worship, recitation, and fire-offerings (japa-homa) of the mantras of those specific forms that are to be made, and, in particular, the worship of the respective causal deities such as Indra and the Earth. || 12–14 ||
Likewise, for the sake of the success of meditation by those who meditate, an image made of jewels is not recommended as an object of worship or a seat, such as a wheel, a lotus, and so forth. 15.
She was exclusively of small stature and devoid of the constituent parts of formal measurement;
yet, due to her status as the preceptor of the castes and stages of life, and because she was the sovereign of all, [she possessed true greatness]. 16.

If an image made of anything other than precious materials—specifically those consisting of the excellent elements known as gold and silver—is of small size or lacks the correct proportions of its parts, it is not recommended; the same applies to the *bhadrapīṭha* (the auspicious pedestal). This is stated in the two verses beginning with "ratnāśrayeṇa" (14–16). The phrase "by means of the *arcā*" refers to the place for the worship of the Blessed One—that is, by means of the *bimba* (image). "By means of the *arcanāsana*" means by means of the *bhadrapīṭha* alone.
The practical conclusion is that if an image made of gems, gold, or silver possesses substantial value, it may be accepted even if it is small in size or lacks the standard measurements. (14–16)

Because he possesses the nature of the gods beginning with the Bhūtas, the king, established in his distinguished station, truly deserves constant honor among the highest and most excellent objects. 17.

How much more so, then, for one who desires no fruit, who is always devoted to devotion and faith, and who, merely by the desire for liberation, belongs to an inferior caste—how can such a person be deemed unworthy of objects fit for those of the highest castes? This doubt is resolved through the logic of the following two verses beginning with "varṇāśrama... (16–18). "One who desires no fruit" means one who seeks liberation.
Having understood this, one who desires the various reflected images should practice this with diligence. || 18 ||
First, one should worship the Guhyakas and the household deities with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and with offerings such as arghya;
then, [one should discard] dirt, ashes, chaff, charcoal, hair, insects, nails, and grass.

A stone slab, a brick, or a wall placed upon a common foundation of roots, thorns, hides, or bones will certainly bring misfortune; therefore, one should first [place a layer] four finger-breadths thick.
Having removed the soft clay from the wall and having slightly increased the size of the image,
it should then be purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water, free from the aforementioned defects.
Having further filled that portion of the wall with well-kneaded clay,
he previously fashioned a wooden panel with a weapon, making it as smooth as a deer skin.
Having removed the coating for the sake of purification, one should wash the cloth— freed from the turī—
with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited seven times.

First, with five and a half verses beginning with "Having understood," he describes the methods for cleaning walls, wood, wooden boards, and cloth for the purpose of creating variegated images, preceded by the worship of the Guhyakas, the house-deities, and the gods. (18–23)
With the heart-mantra, the weapon-mantra, and the mantra of the form,
[he should take it] from a sacred ford, a riverbank, a holy field, or a mountain.
Having discarded the earth mixed with impurities and having taken up [fresh] earth from above,
one should then scatter it [over the body], dry it, and [place it] upon a well-smeared surface of the ground.
Having prepared threads of hemp, wool, cotton, and likewise those made from *alasija*,
one should first place them there along with gravel and stone fragments.
One should consecrate it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with a small amount of cow dung and plenty of milk, ghee, and so forth, as well as with the ash of khadira wood.
And together with mustard seeds,
black sesamum, and oil, one should moisten it for twenty-one days, having placed it in an iron vessel or similar container.
Indeed, even without the sight of wind, fire, sun, or moon, that orb—rendered within the auspicious limit—is brought to completion by her alone. 29.

Now, beginning with the words "with the heart-mantra" and ending with "placed within auspicious wood," he describes the methods for collecting the clay and so forth for the purpose of fashioning the earthen image (mṛdbimba). (24–29)
And just as with garments, one should first wash the metals,
and then perform a further cleansing with ashes consecrated by mantras.

Regarding the method for purifying iron for the purpose of fashioning an iron image, he says "like cloth. That [iron] is consecrated by the mantra; that is to say, it is empowered by the *astra* mantra. || 30 ||
But one who proceeds with devotion in the ritual action of preparing the image should everywhere perform the rite of the weapon-mantra for the sake of pacifying all obstacles. (31)
Worship, the fire-oblation, and the offering of bali to the spirits, accompanied by sacrificial fees—
these indeed constitute the common procedure at the time of formal reception.

He states in two verses beginning with "With devotion" (31–32) that, at the time of commencing the construction of the image, one should generally perform the worship of the respective deity's form-mantra and so forth.
Now the specific procedure for the collection of wood along with stones is being stated;
however, at the time of undertaking any [task], one must observe the auspicious omen.
Specifically, during a forest expedition, an auspicious outcome arises from an auspicious omen;
conversely, through an inauspicious sign, the journey will be beset with obstacles. (34)
But by means of silent recitation, rites for peace and prosperity, and the like,
as well as by returning from the forest, he consumes that [sin], because he is a doer of good.

Having worshipped the mantra, having requested permission for the journey, and having offered salutations, he should eat the remains of the food offering (naivedya), moving to the left and with his senses restrained. (36)
Facing the east at the rising of the nectar [of dawn], he should rise and recollect the mantra, having first recognized either his own original form or another form thereof. (37)
He should proceed toward that direction, or, in its absence, toward another direction,
well-guarded by vigilant assistants and skilled artisans.
One should set out with jars containing parched grain, curd, and sugar, preceded by flowers;
a cheerful disposition, great enthusiasm, and the throbbing of the right limbs are auspicious omens. (39)
Auspicious speech, sound, the conch, the lute, musical instruments, fruits and the like, cows, elephants, horses, brahmins, a maiden, new vessels, and clay, curds—[these are auspicious]. 40.
Raw meat, ornaments, wine, fire, ghee, milk, cooked rice, śāli seeds and the like, darbha grass, and mango blossoms; 41.
An umbrella, clothing, a banner, a vehicle, yellow pigment, saffron, honey, a mirror, and a fly-whisk—these are the substances, excluding weapons. (42)
Jewels, the image of the Buddha, wine, a fearless person, living fish, and whatever causes no distress to the mind—these are the signs. 43.
All that is most excellent in the Darśana system is the subduing of weariness and the removal of impurity, from the threshold of one's own house up to seven steps upon the path. 44.
For by this [practice], while walking, one bestows both the sign and the fruit;
having departed from the city or the village, whether for half a krośa or even just a krośa. 45.
One should therefore take an auspicious omen from signs such as mongooses and the like;
furthermore, the sight of a deer within one and a half krośas from a full [auspicious] distance brings benefit.
Success will especially prevail in a direction that is clear;
the sky will be bright and conducive to accomplishment, and the sun and other celestial bodies will be brilliantly radiant.
The wind was pleasant, gentle, moving clockwise, and steady;
free from celestial portents and the like, that time was indicative of success.
The swan, the parrot, the bharadvāja crane, the cuckoo, the wagtail, the peacock, the bee, the ruddy goose, and others such as these are auspicious birds that roam the sky. (49)
Land-dwelling mongooses, gentle creatures, white snakes, house-lizards, muskrats, and jackals—the sight of all these is auspicious. (50)
Among deer, the spotted deer, the lion, the tiger, the hare, and the leopard are all indicators of success; indeed, these are ordained for everyone.
A jackal is especially auspicious when moving clockwise, even if it deviates from its usual path;
likewise, the soft and affectionate calls of birds and other creatures bring about success and bestow happiness.
But when the signs have arisen regarding the activity of the contraction of the elements, it is not proper to wait; rather, one should then practice tranquility.

Having entered the sacred field according to the prescribed rites, together with the previously mentioned special fee for the sake of purifying the mind, he should gaze upon it with his own spiritual luster.
One should look for a stone that possesses good qualities or a tree fit for the task;
one should avoid what is excessively worn and likewise that whose bark is decayed.
It was broken, scorched by forest fires, silent, with a parched surface,
full of sand, riddled with holes, bound together, and bearing hollows.
It was like a rat, a frog, a fish, a snake, a cat, or a hare,
covered with a network of veins arising from its golden and other-colored skin.
Because of the absence of the previously mentioned forms, their perception is beneficial.
They possess the luster of a pigeon, a parrot, or a lotus; they have the hue of honey, madder, or black gram. (58)
Heavy, pleasant to the heart, auspicious, and smooth—therefore it is praised over others;
it is submerged in the earth dear to friends, situated at the bottom of a reservoir of water. 59.
She stood within the forest groves, concealed by a magnificent tree,
just as she was once enveloped by a multitude of creepers and surrounded by medicinal herbs.
Rising from the region of the knees, they are formed into a single mass by Bhṛgu;
she who has a mouth in the sky bestows liberation, while she whose face is directed toward Sutala bestows worldly enjoyment.
Facing the cardinal directions with both hands and having the head turned toward the east brings prosperity and long life;
otherwise, with the head turned away from that, it is considered to bring fame and an increase in glory.
The northern head bestows the increase of one's lineage, health, peace, and whatever else is desired; it grants nourishment, honor, fame, and intelligence.
Having thus previously understood [the proportions], he, with his powerful self and great vigor, together with artisans, forcibly lifted up the back, the thighs, the feet, and the head.

Having brought the Lord of Mantras down onto dry land, facing eastward with his northern side toward the eastern part [of the site], one should worship him with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.

Having meditated upon [the deity] as confined within the stone and having worshipped [him], one should then perform the oblation (homa) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a level spot in one part of the two directions previously mentioned. 66.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should spend the day engaged in meditation and recitation;
at the arrival of night, one should perform worship and the satiation of spirits with offerings (bali).
Having offered his body through the placement of mantras, he should eat the remains of the food offering;
then, muttering prayers, he should sleep on darbha grass to the south of that, with his head toward the east.
As before, having risen at the end of the night for the sake of obtaining a dream,
one should perform one's own duties and offer oblations for the pacification of inauspicious dreams.
Having rejoiced at that auspicious dream, which was clearly heart-stirring,
he beheld himself as a mountain, that very place, and its rocky terrain.
One may see [the deity] resembling pure crystal or like molten gold;
then, appearing like a mass of smokeless embers, one quickly attains auspiciousness. || 21 ||
Then, taking up a weapon along with a mallet consecrated by mantras,
he should strike it four times toward the east, ending at the forehead.
Having first examined the result from the location of the feet or from the center,
one should make it square and elongated, divided by a pedestal and joined with a mechanical device.
Or, having brought separate seats and a beautiful, covered workshop, one should raise up the stone according to the ancient ritual that is appropriate [to it]. 74.

O Mahāmati, for the purpose of a pedestal, one may use stones of various colors or of that same color as desired, provided they possess the quality of the relationship between the primary and secondary parts (aṅga-aṅgibhāva). 75.
In the absence of wood, metal, or gems, even a bamboo staff is auspicious;
however, when these are available, one should certainly not create inequality or a substitution [of materials]. || 76 ||
At that very moment, having brought the auspicious foundation-stone for the jewels,
he prepared three beneficial stones from those arising from males, females, and neuters.
Indeed, because of the absence of all other reflected images, the image of the Lord is established as being made of stone from a gemstone pedestal. (78)
The self-stones (svopalā) in the form of deities such as Lakṣmī grant all perfections; when struck, they indeed emit sparks of fire accompanied by sound. 79.
That stone which is called "man" is indeed devoid of luster, resonant with sound, and weak;
for it possesses neither fire nor sound in its beginning, middle, or end.

She should be known as "neuter" (napuṃsaka) when she stands upon her own feet, bestowing the fruit [of the practice]. The taking of stone has been described; now the taking of wood is being stated. || 81 ||
It was capable of roaming as far as the edge of the mountains, free from wounds, straight, large, and devoid of disease; it had not been scarred by the claws of lions or other predators.
It is not its potency destroyed by wind, lightning, or forest fire, nor does it move outside;
rather, it remains on a raised portion of ground that is well-moistened and possesses the proper characteristics. (83)
Having first performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as before, one should then worship on the following day,
reciting the mantra while focusing on the deity residing therein whose true form is unknown.
Salutations to you here, who have taken refuge in this body, and to you, the Lord of All!
Forgive me; descend elsewhere, and remain here as the conscious self (cidātman). 85.

Then, with a vessel purified by water and smeared with ghee and other substances, while reciting the excellent mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should indeed cut [the thread] with a saw or similar tool. (86)
If it falls facing toward the east, north, or northeast, one should recognize that it portends auspiciousness; if it falls elsewhere, one should perform worship and other rites.
Unfittingly, and without even a portion of divine splendor that cannot be taken away, he indeed desires to fashion an image made of wood that is exceedingly large. (88)
That [form], adorned with many arms, faces, and weapons, is not defiled by the remaining severed limbs that rose from the tree, provided they are proportionate and intact. 89.
And because everything consists of syllables by virtue of devotion and faith, [the same applies] to even a single object when it is preceded by devotion. (90)

He explains the procedure for specifically selecting stone and wood, beginning with the words "In the selection of good stone and wood" and ending with "and everything thereafter consists of clay. This practical application, however, should be observed as it is very clearly set forth in the *Śrīsātvatāmṛta*. (33–90)
Having first performed the ritual collection (saṃgraha), one should fashion the desired form;
now hear about the general, gentle measurement intended for that purpose. 91.
Having engraved the measurement upon a level and smooth portion of the ground with that [line], which is straight, unchanging, pervasive, and of a single form; 92.
Having examined the characteristics of the various parts in detail, that which is one hundred and eightieth part of its own height is one *aṅgula*. (93)
Two aṅgulas make a kalā, an eye, a golaka, and indeed a bhāva;
that which is one-eighth of an aṅgula is proclaimed to be a yava.

And the six-beat rhythm (ṣaṭkala) should be fully understood for the rites of the Bimba and others; the measurements of the face, the navel, the genitals, and the earth are equal to the duration of a tāla, as are those of the thighs. 95.
Likewise, the two shanks, the ankle, the knee, and the neck-joint should each be known to measure three finger-breadths; this is declared to be the measurement. (96)
According to the length or shortness of the faces of those who wear matted hair, one should cast out from the measurement a measure of four kalās or three kalās. 97.
The crown has three, five, or seven peaks and is elevated by eight kalās;
above the forehead of those without matted locks, there is either a crest or a very beautiful diadem. 98.
In this matter, however, the decrease and increase should be performed according to the requirement, by means of one finger-breadth each at the aforementioned divisions. (99)
One should divide the portion of the face intended for the mouth, nose, and forehead into three parts;
then, from the front, the nose should measure one unit (kalā) and be shaped like a sesame flower.
The width of the two nostril-pits is half a kalā, along with their elevation; the measurement from the tip of the nose to the edge of the seat is four yavas.
That [space] is separated from the tip of the nose by a measure of four barley-corns;
the upper lip is half a finger-breadth, while the lower lip is one finger-breadth.
Know that the *golaka* and the chin (*cibuka*) are four finger-breadths wide;
they are situated at the middle portion of the first [section], which consists of the nose and the shoulder-blade. 103.
One should fashion the eye-socket within that [space], with the eyes situated one *kalā* apart;
they should be equal in length to a *kalā* and half a *kalā* in width. || 104 ||
That which has the shape of an utpala petal should be increased by two barley-corns;
one should make it in the shape of a lotus petal, with half a netra for the circular pupil.
The authority for the first [day] or the other [days] is by one-third of the Tārā-dairghya;
that light is five parts, including one and a half barley-corns. 106.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, that eye-socket is prescribed to be three parts [of the face] in width,
measuring twelve barley-corns with an additional barley-corn for the breadth.

The two eyebrows are recorded as being two and a half finger-breadths in length and two kalās in width; in the middle they are two yavas wide, resembling the crescent moon and tapering gradually toward the ends.
In the interval between those two is half a kalā, and their tips lie on the same line;
the two ears are two aṅgulas in width and twice the size of a golaka in length.
The circumference of the neck is two yavas; there are two joints, each four yavas long.
Know that the middle part between them is likewise, and the droṇī here is indeed one and a half aṅgulas.
That hole, which is the measure of the noose, should be half a kalā according to one's preference;
it may range from one finger-breadth up to two kalās, even if there is some irregularity therein.
Free from internal cavities, it should be known as four barley-corns in size;
together with its petals and endowed with its instrument, such is the pair of ears described.
The forehead is four digits wide; the two frontal protuberances (śikhara) are each two globes (golaka) in height, measuring three digits from the base and one digit in width at the front.
Emerging from the region of the hair and situated above the forehead,
one should fashion the face and the mass of locks measuring half a kalā.
One should fashion the circumference of the cheeks extending evenly from the ears to the neck;
in their center, the two round cheeks are defined by the proportions previously mentioned. (115)
Know that the circumference of the head is thirty-six finger-breadths;
it is the distance between the two tips of the ears and the crown of the head. 116.
Know that to be sixteen finger-breadths; likewise, from the back of the two eyebrows, the distance from the forehead to the cavity of the skull should be understood as one and a half tālas.
The neck is like a true conch-shell; indeed, it measures twelve kalās in circumference at its base, middle, and tip, and twenty-one aṅgulas from the base to the tip.
It is eighteen finger-breadths long and one-third of its own width in breadth;
its two shoulders at the base are equal, circular, elongated, and broad.
Its thickness is six aṅgulas; now the measurement of the arm is stated:
from the shoulder to the top of the head is three kalās, and up to the end of the joint it is traditionally held to be six kalās.
The measurement from the joint to the wrist is traditionally held to be nine kalās;
the hand from the jewel (maṇi) to the tip of the middle finger is considered to be seven aṅgulas.
The measurement of the middle finger is to be known as one kalā less; the ring finger is four yavas less than that, and the index finger is likewise [four yavas less]. 122.
The little finger together with the thumb should be known as two kalās;
the thumb is traditionally held to be two joints long, and all the fingers are spread out [in that measure]. 123.
One should file down all [the nails] from the base to the tip, reducing them little by little;
the nails should be made in the shape of a linga, measuring half a joint at the tip.
The measurement at the base of the thumb is four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula);
it should be known that for the three fingers, this is reduced by four barley-corns (yava). 125.
When there is a deficiency of one finger-breadth, the reduction is one and a half *kalās* as before due to the wrapping;
the thumb is one finger-breadth from the tip, and the other three are said to be six barley-corns each.
Know that the middle [measurement] is diminished by half a finger from the tip;
it is the stone of one's own fortune, measuring two finger-breadths and two kalās from the tip. 127.
The palms, including the soles of the feet, are adorned with the lines of Lakṣmī;
from the base of the fingers to the roots of the arms, the girth of the hands is two barley-corns per finger-breadth.
It is recorded that from the wrist downwards, the circumference is four yavas greater;
at the middle, however, its thickness is said to be reduced by half a kalā.
The armlet, extending from the wrist to the base of the forearm, is prescribed to be six kalās;
know that the bracelet at the joint is seven kalās, including one finger-breadth (aṅgula) and less three barley-corns (yava). 130.
The nine globes at the base should indeed be reduced by half a finger's breadth;
likewise, the width above the joint is as previously described here.
Here too, as before, one should personally determine the earth situated within by means of vision;
having abandoned the palm-measure from the limit of the throat, it is made internal by that same measure. (132)
One should make the two breasts symmetrical, with their supporting base being fleshy;
the depression [between them] should be half the size of the heart-sphere, and above it, they should be adorned with the best of jewels.
The two sides of the breasts are three *kala*s less; the breast-circle is three *yava*s [in height];
likewise, the nipple is elevated by one *yava* and its width is equal to that. 134.
The eye-measure is declared to be three and a half yavas; the measurement of the armpit, excluding the shoulder-measurement, is equal from the back to the limit of the shoulder. 135.
Know that Sulocana, who measured five tālas in height, had arms resembling large bowls, broad and fleshy at the midsection, and was capable of encircling his armpits with them. 136.
Know that the circumference of the belly is two tālas doubled (four tālas) plus three barleycorns, minus exactly two finger-breadths. 137.
The navel-maṇḍala should be known as three yavas less than that measure;
its depth is prescribed to be three yavas less than that [same] measure. 138.
The Paridhi (encircling beam) at the center of the navel is three tālas high and possesses three eyes;
its sixfold globular measure is prescribed for half the height of the waist.
The two buttocks are fleshy, resembling the frontal globes of an elephant, and are surrounded by five protuberances;
the line of the loincloth is said to be two finger-breadths wide at its base.
It is one finger-breadth all around; the glans (meḍhra) is known to be three kalās;
its sheath is four barley-corns wide, and its circumference is six fingers.
The two testicles are two finger-breadths in length, with a width equal to that from the base to the tip;
know that the circular opening for the wind is two finger-breadths all around.
The measurement of the thigh should be known as nine finger-breadths for the middle part of the ground;
from the base of the root to the tip, it is remembered as six kalās at the base and three kalās at the end.
The knee-pan is one finger-breadth less [than the thigh] and measures two kalās; in both width and height, it is equal to four yavas. 144.
At the base of the shank, a nine-golaka circumference is to be known;
at the middle it is fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and from there it is five and a half finger-breadths.
In this case as well, know that it is expanded by one-third from the circumference;
however, the expansion should be adjusted according to the middle, the base, and the top.
By means of his two arms, the region of the waist, as well as the collection of fingers, the pair of thighs, and the two shanks, he was endowed with the trunk of an elephant. 147.
The length of the *cāraṇa* is recorded as being one-sixteenth of a *tāla*;
the two heels are the width of two *golaka*s, and in their middle is a space of one *aṅgula*.
It should be performed three times a day, primarily in front [of the deity], and its measure is declared to be equal to one-sixteenth part (kalā),
less three barley-corns from the vicinity of the big toe.
The width [of the foot] from the region of the ankle is one part plus one finger-breadth;
the length from the base of the little toe to the end of the ankle is one finger-breadth for the instep. 150.
From the lower end of the shank, a seven-eyed (seven-fold) wrapping is prescribed;
at that very time, the circumference from the tip is determined to be one digit less.
Having completed the foot according to this rule upon the back of the tortoise,
its length shall be three finger-breadths, and the length of the big toe shall be equal to that.
O wielder of the plow, its circumference should be known to be five finger-breadths;
the forefinger, however, should be made two barley-corns longer than its length.
Then, the middle toe should be made equal in length to the big toe;
the one situated after it (the third toe) should be less than the middle finger by two-eighths (one-fourth). 154.
In the same way, those three-jointed tendons that follow it are as described before;
they are joined by a network of nails resembling the back of a tortoise. 155.
The wrapping of the big toe is said to be two *kalās* less half a *kalā*; for the remaining [toes], it is proclaimed to be four *yavas* less at each step.
Know that the circumference of all [the circles] is three times their diameter;
all these parts are fleshy, gentle, symmetrical, and auspicious. (157)
The two fangs situated outside the row of teeth should be seven barley-corns high;
the measurement for the four middle teeth should be two barley-corns high.
Know that the measurement for all those belonging to that category is four barley-corns;
the width of the two teeth is three barley-corns, and from the tip to the root it is two barley-corns. 159.
All his teeth were even and without gaps; from the middle of his body, his hair grew in auspicious clockwise curls, a sign arising from the birth of a Yuga.

Now, he states the general characteristics of the measurements, such as the height and span, for the image (*bimba*), beginning with "In this way, even for one [of these]" and ending with "the auspicious [image] arising from an odd-numbered birth" (verses 91–160).
This measure is well-ascertained, beneficial, and unerring:
that which possesses captivating charm, uniquely adorned with beauty and loveliness. (161)
Know that these two always exist in a state of mutual dependence;
yet, in some instances, great beauty prevails by overcoming pride. (162)
In some cases, beauty remains while its measure is concealed;
just as even a poor man, if he possesses extraordinary beauty, attains honor in the world. (163)
Even one who is deformed may be exceedingly wealthy, yet he is neither truly handsome nor truly poor;
likewise, a physical form devoid of both [beauty and wealth] becomes unacceptable. 164.
O Mahāmati, because it is always acceptable, endowed with singularity, and possesses perfect measure and beauty, [it is established] out of a desire to bestow grace upon devotees. 165.
The power of the mantra’s presence indeed remains fruitful for one who has correctly practiced it, when that [power] becomes an object of vision within the image situated before the eyes. 166.
Knowing thus that the formless [consciousness] brings immediate delight, one should apply effort for the sake of achieving beauty through measures, weights, and proportions. 167.

Thus, when the image possesses the correct proportions and beauty, the power of the Lord’s presence—which generates unsurpassed bliss—manifests spontaneously within the image and remains there fruitfully, according to the principle stated as “because of the beauty of the image. Therefore, one must exert oneself even more for that purpose; this he states in two and a half verses beginning with *samyaṅmāne ca*. (166–167)
For a straight posture with well-aligned feet, the distance between the feet is three finger-breadths;
for one with uneven feet, it is traditionally held to be equal to a tāla from the tip.
From the middle of those two heels, however, one should know there are two globes for the purpose of supporting the Brahma-nāḍī as well as the two paths. (169)
One should make it perfectly level with a cord, from the body's center, south and north;
for an image with feet even, the distance from the forehead to the top of the genitals [is the measure]. 170.

Having extended the cord and covered it, [one measures] the interval between the navel and the heart, as well as the junction at the tip of the nose and the forehead, which is situated above the *tilaka*. || 171 ||
In this manner, one should lead [the breath] to the tip of the right big toe;
having achieved equilibrium of the limbs, it should be moved from field to field.
By means of the cord, for the sake of eliminating all irregularities of the images, they are completely purified and auspicious because they are surrounded by four, three, or two corners. (173)
The impure and unpurified state arises from the image as the condition of the whole;
the forehead of the horse-faced one is twelve finger-breadths in width. (174)

He describes the examination of the symmetry of the limbs of images with even feet and uneven feet by means of a thread, beginning with "of one who is straight and has well-even feet" and ending with "the standing posture of the image consisting of its limbs. (168–174)
From the measure of eight eyes (twenty-four finger-breadths), four finger-breadths are placed in front;
the nostril-cavity, having a hole of half a digit (kalā), is separated by one part. 175.
The two jaws are eight finger-breadths [in width], and the two corners of the mouth are equal to that;
the two ear-lobes are in the middle, each two finger-breadths wide and elevated by two units.

The bridge of the nose is two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula) wide; above that, it is known to be two kalās. Know that the expansion of the mouth is two yavas in width, proceeding gradually from the front.
One should bring that very [portion] to thinness by striking it with barley-meal;
the two wings of the nasal bridge should be depressed in the middle and joined together. (178)
With two and a half barley-corns [of space] between the eyes and the nose,
there is a petal from the eye-pitcher (dṛgdroṇi) measured by the size of a barley-corn.

Know that the forehead of Nṛsiṃha, together with its decorative mark (sālaka), is as before; the space between the eyes is one kalā plus one finger-breadth, and his face is surrounded by eight eyes. 180.
Now, he describes the characteristics of the face of the Hayagrīva image with the verses beginning "The forehead of the horse-faced one," and so forth (verses 174–180).
Then, from the region of the eight necks, one should draw [the line] omitting the two ears;
then, by the measurement of those two ears, one should lead it again to the edge of the forehead.

Prior to the measurement and before the application of collyrium, the characteristic mark should be one that is marked by the scent of intense passion, possessing blossoming and expanding apertures, and endowed with the bridge of the nose. 182.

In that opening, according to the previous measurement, there should be an additional three barley-corns; it should have a ball at its upper part, and the eye should consist of all the constituent parts. 183.
The lower lip should be known to measure one finger-breadth plus four barley-corns; the face is four and a half kalās, and the remaining length is recorded as that of the jaw.
That swelling should be understood as extending one finger-breadth beyond the measurement of the eye, increasing by one barleycorn;
it diminishes in front, reaching to the corner of the mouth at the end of a finger-breadth. 185.
The entire height is [one unit]; half of that is the pair of eyes, which are full of wonder.
As before, the ears are one unit wide, and their height is half a digit less than that. || 186 ||
The digit of the moon and the union of the pair are equal, as is the three-pearl mark on the eyebrows;
the space between them is the measure of a digit, large and resembling a conch-shell spiral. 187.
The measurement of the portion, which is clearly circular at its top, should be executed;
he describes the characteristics of the face of Śrī Nṛsiṃha with the words beginning "of Śrī Nṛsiṃha," etc. (verses 180–188).
The face of the mountain is said to be one and a half tālas in length. || 188 ||
In its width, it is two finger-breadths less than the measurement from the forehead;
and for the Lord of gentle form who has arisen, it is devoid of any harshness.
The width of the neck-region is one-fourth of that measure;
its thickness above is equal to that, while below it is one finger-breadth.
The measurement of the two jaws is traditionally held to be seven and a half finger-breadths;
the remaining space of the face is that which lies between the two corners of the mouth. 191.
And its expansion from the tip [of the nose] by one and a half kalās and a half-kalā is to be understood as being one finger-breadth (aṅgula) from the two corners of the mouth (sṛkviṇī). 192.
The nostril-aperture and the mouth are as previously described; the two fangs are raised by one and a half kalās, and the bridge of the nose is like the back of a plantain stalk.
The ears, as described by Vajimukha, are at the distance of seven kalās from the tip [of the nose];
the eyes are equal to that, yet their outer corners are sharp and devoid of the yava-measure.
Now, he describes the characteristics of the boar’s face with the verses beginning "In length, one and a half tālas," and so forth (verses 188–194).
The necks of these [deities] are separated by two finger-breadths from each respective part; they are joined together and possess a gentle form as they arise. 195.
Whatever the measurement of Nṛhari’s body may be according to the height of the *vīṇā*, that same measurement, when including the ornaments and expanded, becomes one-half of a *kalā* greater. (196)
His chest, waist, belly, shoulders, buttocks, and calves were well-proportioned; likewise, his nails and palms were perfect, and his body was full-fleshed.
It was complete with extremely curled hairs turning to the right, though it lacked even one face among its three, four, or five, specifically the upward-facing one. 198.
One should effect a contraction with the southern and northern faces, forming two spheres;
therein, the expansion of the upward-facing face is said to be that of the lion's face.
The arrangement of the four [eyes] should be equal for the attainment of liberation;
however, for the attainment of health, enjoyment, and isolation (kaivalya), it should be by half a finger-breadth.
One should direct the gaze downward with both the left and right eyes;
this, together with the aforementioned [posture], constitutes the equality of one facing westward. (201)
Then, with the nostrils, eyes, eyebrows, and ears neither too wide nor too narrow,
one should place the auspicious right face upon the ground with the gaze directed slightly askance.
And likewise, the northern face, which has the eyes of a calf, brings about all accomplishments;
it is deficient because it indicates its own function, and there is the presence of the *nan* mantra. (203)
Therefore, the King of Mantras dwells in peace by relying on this [method] and not otherwise;
and because of his constant presence, the bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas [are likewise pacified]. 204.
They flee at the mere sight [of him], yet they enter [his presence] upon seeing him;
having received the command of the minister with their heads bowed, they depart.
Therefore, one should practice with diligence so that the presence of the image may be maintained;
for indeed, no one undertakes any auspicious work in the absence of its presence. 206.
The fifth face of the omnipresent Lord, who possesses five faces, is indeed to be visualized as having the tusks of a boar, eyes like those of a lion, and a flat nose. 207.
The symmetry between his upper and lower lips should be such that they are separated by half a finger-breadth; clearly, the space situated between them is distinct.
The row of teeth should indeed be made even from root to middle to tip;
then, the two cheeks should be circular and prominent by half a kalā.

The beard should be two *kalās* in length at the front, and the sideburns (*sambandhaveṇī*) should be one *kalā* and half a *kalā* respectively; fashioned according to the previously mentioned measurements, it brings about auspiciousness.
One should bring the faces known as the lion, the boar, and the eagle to a state of gentleness;
this measurement is indeed derived from the lakṣa seen in practical application. 211.
The expansion of the mountain of gentle form was described by Aśvavaktra;
then that which was previously mentioned regarding Nṛhari was also set forth. 212.
Likewise, when the Lord Śaktīśvara is conceived as having faces and limbs,
he is adorned with necklaces, earrings, garments, garlands, bracelets, and armlets.
An image of the mantra-forms, adorned with garlands, sacred threads, armlets, crowns, and so forth, becomes a bestower of success when it is fashioned. || 214 ||

Now, beginning with the words "The neck of these is prescribed... and ending with "...the accomplishment is achieved," he describes the characteristics of the limbs such as the neck of Hayagrīva and others, as well as the characteristics of the faces and other limbs of images having three, four, or five faces. (195–214)
The mandala of the face [of the deity] is formed by the *tāla* arising from the reflection of that vehicle, the life-force deity, which was previously described as fivefold. 215.

The forehead is said to be two finger-breadths [in height], and the hair-tuft (jaṭā) is twice the width of the eyes. The neck is elevated by two finger-breadths, and the chest is recorded as being five kalās.
That belly is eight finger-breadths [in circumference], and the waist is five finger-breadths high;
the thighs are nine finger-breadths high, and the knees are recorded as being two finger-breadths [thick]. 217.
The shanks are eight finger-breadths in height, and the calves of the feet are two finger-breadths;
the circumference of the neck is one kalā less than that.
The expansion of her limbs should always be understood as being equal to that of a *bimba* fruit;
know that the circumference of her abdomen is indeed greater than that measurement. 219.
Know that the circumference of the waist region is indeed four times the measure of the eyes, and that the girth at the base of the thighs is equal to what was stated for the [waist] orb. 220.
That same [measurement] applies to the middle of the shank and the end of the shank;
the foot is five kalās in length and four aṅgulas in width.
The thumb is three finger-breadths from the edge of the hand and is equal to half a kalā;
the fingers, measured from the length of the foot, should be known to decrease successively by one barley-corn (yava).
The navel cavity is very extensive, measuring half an eye-breadth [in width],
extending as far as the middle finger, and nine finger-breadths from the wrist.
Know that his three-fold span of the hand consists of fingers with sharp and elevated nails; his head and arms together in height measure two eyes (two cubits). 224.
The pair of upper and lower arms is recorded as being equal to two tālas;
the circumference of the forearm is greater by half a kalā.
Thus, according to the true rule declared by Bimba, her breasts were prominent, and her eyes,
wide and expansive in their circular fullness, were like lotus petals.
The pair of eyebrows arises from the Narasiṃha [measurement], and the tip of the nose is like the beak of a parrot;
it is half a kalā in measure, long, and its bridge is like the back of an elephant.
That pair of wings, reaching to the region of the belly, should be neither too long nor too short;
they should be spread out by half their length, like the wings of a swan.
Its tail, possessing a hundred branches, is twice the measure of its own wings;
this length, including the wings, is indeed the true measurement endowed with its constituent parts.
Know that this applies universally to all; now the specific [measure] is being stated:
one should likewise reduce the length by three finger-breadths from the two thighs. 230.
