O Mahāmati, one should fashion the elevation of the shank-sections and wrap them with the two shanks; this is called the *bimba*, which is equal from the base of the wrist.
From the region of the knees, measuring half of that plus half a finger, the webbing on the foot is to be known; it is six fingers in width.
Know that for all [beings], everything else is always spoken of as true;
however, the two wings are devoid of feet, and their breadth is equal to their length. (233)
The length of these [birds] as they fly up is their own body-length, while the wing-span of the five [types] when they are standing still should be known as half that measure. (234)
O wielder of the plow, know that taking this measure and excluding the tail, the eyebrows, and the wings, such is the characteristic of the dwarf form. 235.

He describes the characteristics of the array of Garuḍas, such as Satya and Suparṇa, beginning with "that which was previously declared fivefold" and ending with "the half-characteristic of those who stand [in that position]. (215–234)
O wielder of the plow, know that taking this measure while excluding the tail, the eyebrows, and the wings constitutes the characteristic of the dwarf form. 235.
Having taken [the hair] three finger-breadths from the forehead, nose, and mouth,
one should fashion the binding of matted locks (jaṭābandha) above the head.
The measurement from the end of the matted locks (jaṭā) to the base should be five tālas; thus has the characteristic of the image been briefly stated, and now the pedestal (pīṭha) is described.
He describes the characteristics of a dwarf with two and a half verses beginning with "etad" (235–237).
For images that are seated, it should be square; for those that are standing, it should always be rectangular.
For their form is otherwise [than what is perceived] due to its being circular, round, and elongated;
it consists of atoms arising from finger-breadths, or rather, it is composed of *ārādhaka* [atoms]. (239)
The length of the image (arcā) should be equal to the distance from the door to the front of the temple;
the length of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be according to that measurement, and its width half of that.
From above the door, one should first leave three intervals;
then, having left twelve parts from below, the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is indeed three [parts]. || 241 ||
By the remainder of the collection of weapon-parts, the image should be raised;
or else it may be mounted upon a vehicle, whether deficient, middling, or excellent. 242.
The height of its pedestal is established as four-twelfths (one-third) of that [height], and its width everywhere is prescribed as half of the [total] image. || 243 ||
Furthermore, that [icon] of Cāturātmya may have its three parts diminished, or else be devoid of a fourth part, according to the influence of the retinue. 244.
The prescribed length of the pedestal (pīṭha), including its undiminished parts, is the same for all directions—whether it faces the four cardinal points or faces only a single direction. 245.
The thickness of that which is covered with markings is twice its length,
while the thickness of that which is uncovered is one and a half times its length, as previously stated.
The fourfold set of single-seated [liṅgas] is entirely devoid of marks (lakṣman).
Know that each one of them, according to its specific mark, is further of that same number.
The first is Anantāsana, and the second is Pakṣamandira. (247)
The third is marked with a lotus, while the fourth is adorned with a wheel;
thus, indeed, there are sixteen seats common to all. 248.
Furthermore, understand in brief the distinctions according to their divisions;
know the characteristics of the seats (pīṭhas) situated in the directions and those located in the throat. 249.
And because of their mutual arrangement, they again take on the nature of arms;
even when the two wheels and lotuses situated thereon have been dissolved, that [nature] remains.
From the mutual conjunction of those two and from their taking refuge in infinite space within the directions,
understand that there is a multiplicity, whether by way of the nature of pairs or by way of the nature of twos.
With an upward-pointing lotus, there are two [circles], and outside of that, with a downward-pointing one, two by two are to be understood in this manner. (252)
Above, however, there are two lotuses, and below, two wheels;
O Mahāmati, the other [arrangement] should be understood through the reversal of this pair. 253.
Due to the internal and external positions of the two wheels and lotuses, know that there is a reversal of these two; from the upper portion, there is a tetrad.
The lower portion indeed consists of four deities;
this other group of eight seats may be situated either below or above. 255.
It is proper that one should perform [the rite] with either a single discus or a lotus;
for those formed in the shape of discs are indeed based on a single rotation. || 256 ||
"Indeed, there are many petals, and likewise some are provided with a pericarp;
thus has the occurrence of these marks been described by me in various ways. (257)
Now listen to that which constitutes the fundamental seat (pīṭha):
having first divided the seat into twenty parts by means of equal squares according to its original extent. || 258 ||
One part is for the feet and shanks; three parts each are for the two jars (kumbhas);
one part is for the neck-path (kaṇṭhavīthi), and six parts are for the neck above that.
One should fashion the neck-string with one part, the shell-pattern (śuktikā) with three parts,
and above that, the crown (uṣṇīṣa) with two parts.
O one of great intelligence, the extent of the field for the foot has been established by its own parts as four times greater than that of the *kṣetra* in all four directions. 261.
One should fashion a pot from all the remaining clay, provided with sprouts and vārakas;
one should cause the neck-base to enter [the vessel] by means of two parts on all sides. || 262 ||
One should effect entry into the interior by means of a single piercing point at the throat,
ensuring that the emergence of the thread from the entry into the throat is symmetrical.
One should perform the contraction of the oyster-shell [vessel] by withdrawing it from the portion of the neck-thread below the shell down to the opening, by a quarter-measure at a time.
The similarity between the *uṣṇīṣa*, the *ghaṭa*, and the *jaṅghā* should be maintained as it naturally stands;
one should adorn them like a jar with pearls, emeralds, or lotus sprouts. (265)
There, leaving a space above equal to one-fourth of the circumference, one should dig a trough-shaped pit all around, sloping downwards.
Then, at the middle portion of the width, there is an outward projection by one-third of its own measure;
that [projection] is square and extends out from the area of the pedestal.
Having divided that [line] into three parts at the front, one should eliminate two portions of the side;
then, starting from the base, one should properly [draw it] like the tip of a ploughshare using the remaining part.
Having first divided [the ground] threefold from the front and threefold from the base,
one should then dig it from the middle so that the water flows out quickly.
In this way, O Mahāmati, it indeed becomes like the face of a pig;
one might as well make it resemble a conch shell or compare it to the mouth of a sea monster. 270.
This exit of the path, characterized as described for the seats (pīṭhas), one should not perform for the ritual images (karmabimba) whose souls have reached the state beginning with "āśama. || 271 ||
But for those made of variegated clay or wood, and especially for those that are movable;
likewise for the square-shaped [liṅga] and for that which consists of four forms (caturmūrti). || 272 ||
Since the channel at the tip of the form causes both the perfection and the destruction [of the result], there is no harm to it without that [channel] unless for a specific purpose. (273)
Since the general pedestal must be distinguished by its specific support, the seat should be provided with a channel, and the pedestal itself should likewise possess a channel. (274)
Wherever the practitioner offers a bath with abundant water and the like, a clear transgression would occur there every day if it were done without that [ritual]. || 275 ||
In the same way, this is prescribed for those adorned with large images,
whether they are made of metal or stone, for the purpose of the auspicious consecration bath.
When the ritual image has been placed upon the auspicious seat, one should constantly offer it whatever is available, such as curd, milk, ghee, and so forth. (277)
One should diligently lead that water to a portion of ground or a plot of land so that it cannot be stepped upon by feet; that bestows great supernatural power. || 278 ||
Therefore, the water-channel is both prescribed and prohibited;
at the time of its installation, however, you must perform the ritual for the gods. (279)
For those facing east and west, that which is situated in the northern direction is auspicious;
for those facing north and south, it is always prescribed in the eastern part.

Furthermore, from that deity of Bhadrapīṭhī, on the left side, there is the bestower of the accomplishment of goals for those who always worship him; however, by way of reversal, he bestows the opposite upon those who act contrarily. (281)

Having stated the characteristics of the *pīṭhas* preceded by the [description of] the *nirga*, he describes the characteristics of the *bimba* with the passage beginning "Thus the *bimba* has been briefly stated" and ending with "the opposite of the reverse. (237–281)
It should be understood as being like the pedestal (pīṭha) of a palace;
and it is said [to be established] on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and when the planets have been worshipped. || 282 ||

When the ascendant is fixed and occupies a fixed degree, when it is cleared by the aspect of Jupiter, during the northern solstice, when purified of celestial and other portents, and while the sky is stainless in the bright fortnight; || 283 ||
When the excavation has been made down to the water-level and filled back up as before, the ground becomes free from defects and endowed with all auspicious characteristics. || 284 ||

When the filling of the remaining portions has been completed and the ground surface is well-smeared, it becomes divided into sixty-four squares; as before, one should [mark] all directions with a thread.

Having bathed, wearing white garments and garlands, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), with a perfectly tranquil mind, equipped with all the necessary implements, and provided with the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya). || 286 ||
Taking the auspicious water-pot and meditating on Acyuta within his heart,
he was accompanied by Brahmins who followed the single path and were devoted to the true scriptures.
Likewise, having placed that pitcher in the center, one should enter the area of the temple grounds from the base upwards with mantras consisting of the Ṛgveda and permeated by the Lord. 288.
One should perform the inspection of the ground, followed by striking it, sprinkling it,
and then pouring over it the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with water consecrated by mantras.

One should cause the Brahmins, who have been adorned with ornaments, to recite the first four mantras beginning with Oṃ and ending with the word "pavitra," together with the "puṇyāha" (auspicious day) formula. || 290 ||
Then [he assigned] the Bāhvṛcas to the Śākuna hymn, the Bhadra to those consisting of Yajus,
the Sāman-knowledge to the verses beginning with "iḍā māya," and the Atharvaṇas to the verse beginning with "śāntā dyauḥ."
Beginning from the northeast corner and proceeding eastward in each row,
one should [place the syllables] with the twelve-syllable mantra and one's own name at every step.
The deity who is the characteristic of the body, namely Vāstupuruṣa, should be worshipped with curd, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, accompanied by the mantra "natipraṇavagarbha. (293)
Then, one should satisfy the fire with an offering of a sattvic nature; thereafter, one should perform the installation of the pitcher—listen to how that is done. 294.
As before, one should adorn the area of the ground with arches and other ornaments;
outside that earth [of the mandala], in front of the face situated at the pericarp. 295.
One should construct an excellent pavilion (maṇḍapa) equipped with all necessary implements;
within it, there should be a ground area measuring eight cubits, situated between eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), including the sapindikā, should be two cubits in measure and possess the characteristics previously described;
the pathway (vīthī) should be three cubits wide, and thus the total measurement is eighteen cubits.
As before, one should place the ritual implements (sādhana) within each pit;
then, one should construct a pit for oneself on a level ground to the north.
On the south, having caused the deity to descend as before, one should worship in sequence;
on a raised spot above the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), as previously described. || 299 ||
Having gratified [the deities] according to desire and then extracted the group of fires,
he should deposit them into the consecrated fire-pits in the cardinal directions as before.
In the same manner, having extracted and worshipped those situated in the intermediate directions in due order,
one should then establish them in the four cardinal directions according to their respective origins.
Having assigned to each of the four— the Vāsudevas and the others— by name, their respective duties, he established them as the twice-born Ekāyanas in innumerable numbers.
The concluding oblation of the rite should be performed with sesame seeds and rice mixed with clarified butter;
by means of this method of dissolution, [the practitioner] brings the range of the deities beginning with Vāyu under his control.

First, having consecrated the four [Vedas] beginning with the Ṛgveda, one should likewise place them; and by means of those purifying mantras associated with the signs of Acyuta, as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā). || 304 ||
The oblation (havana) should be performed according to the rules with a mind endowed with devotion;
then, having approached the northeast corner (īśakoṇa) together with other Brāhmaṇas. || 305 ||
One should place there the bathing implements previously specified,
beginning with the five products of the cow, each individually in the pitchers.
Having worshipped them with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings, and having consecrated them six times with the Dviṣaṭka mantra,
he should then bring the previously prepared jars together with the stone slabs.
Or else, they should be made from clay produced in an excellent location, or even from fresh stone;
they should be uniform, well-baked, and very solid, or made of clay in the absence of those materials. (308)
Twelve finger-breadths wide and raised to that same measure, or double that if possible, these golden [pedestals] are beneficial for kings. (309)
One should collect a collection of stones that is square, measuring twelve finger-breadths in width, and with a thickness equal to one-third of that. 310.
Having duly established the jars according to the previously mentioned sequence,
[one should prepare] either one [jar] equal in size to a conch-shell, with its neck raised three finger-breadths high.

It should also be expanded according to those same proportions; its excavation is prescribed to be eight finger-breadths deep all around, except for the rim (karṇa), or it may be a large, well-polished conch-shell.
The Lord of Men has been consecrated; he is inwardly pure and accompanied by auspicious grains (akṣata).
Thus, having anointed him from both within and without, and having performed the ritual perfuming (adhivāsa), [he is ready].
Then, with fruits such as gold and other precious gems, with all medicinal herbs, with fragrances, seeds, grains, and with pearls and corals; 314.
One should adorn each [deity] with garments, ornaments, and excellent, auspicious garlands, performing the rite for each one with the twelve-syllable mantra. 315.
For the sake of perfecting the form, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the Praṇavas and the essence of that consciousness;
thereafter, one should worship with various enjoyments beginning with the arghya offering and ending with the bali offering.
When this has been done with the stones, one should subsequently lead [the water] to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should then place the collection of jars together with the stones upon the supporting bases.
Then, having likewise consecrated its foundation stone— either there or outside the pavilion—
one should meditate upon it with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Blazing like the orb of the sun and adorned with a thousand cows,
he then worshipped the mantra and offered oblations a hundred times.
Having placed that jar in the center, together with its limbs and its retinue,
the knower of the Brahman-principle, who is all-pervasive, [should place it] containing within it the entirety of all powers.

From this point upward, [the Lord is worshipped] by means of the powers (śaktis) such as Tiryagā and Vāgā, who are endowed with the forms of their respective vows (vratamūrti), and who are in reality non-different from Him. || 321 ||
There, the king of mantras should cause the Brahmins to recite the "Self-array" (Ātmavyūha),
which indeed begins and ends with the Praṇava, for the sake of realizing the power of the Self.
Having worshipped him according to the rules and immediately thereafter offered libations,
one should install Vāsudeva and the others within the pitchers situated in the various directions.
As before, one should cause the fourfold mantra of self-recognition to be recited for Aniruddha and the others, who are established in the intermediate directions. || 324 ||
Then, by means of the yoga of origin and dissolution, he should devoutly cause him to recite the Puruṣa-sūkta from the Ṛgveda, and the "yuñjate" hymns from the other Yajurveda.
Then [he taught] the Rathantara-sakhya Sāman, the Sāmans consisting of the knowledge of the Sāmas which are composed of the Blessed One, and the Atharvanic mantras beginning with "sahasraśirasam."
Or, all that has been declared may be placed beneficially in a single great jar;
likewise, the oblation itself is prescribed to be performed in the central pit.
But one should cause the mantras to be recited in their proper sequence as they stand;
having thus performed the *sampāta-homa* up to its conclusion with the *pūrṇāhuti*, then—
But the supreme collection of great powers (mahāśakti), characterized by capacity, clearly exists as non-different from the forms of the mantras and so forth. 329.
He is to be joined with the stones by means of his own name and the syllable Om;
likewise, the light of infinite power dwells there as the radiance of knowledge.

All-pervading (sarvagā), speaking Brahman (brahmavadanā), illuminating (dyotakī), possessing the prowess of truth (satyavikramā), and complete (sampūrṇā)—these are said to be the powers that sustain the universe. || 331 ||
Know that stone which is designated as the support for the jar to be all-pervading, the partless power of the Supreme Lord, possessing the commonality of capacity and potency. (332)
Having satisfied [the deity] with the root mantra and the crest-mantra (śikhāmantra),
O wielder of the plow, one should then [offer oblations] into the single opening at the navel of the Unborn (aja) with the single mantra.
However, for that purpose, one should offer oblations with verses consisting of Ṛg-verses; likewise, the Asyavāmīya hymn should be offered with Gāyatrī meters by others.
The oblation should be properly offered by the Brahmins who characterize that pervasion;
having personally performed the full offering (pūrṇāhuti), he should again perform the worship of the deity situated on the pedestal.
Having performed the offering to the spirits (balidāna) and sipped water for purification (ācamana),
he should then proceed to the area of the temple designated for Brahmā, and there he should set down the great stone (mahāśilā).
Recalling the mantra of the wheel together with Ananta by means of the Praṇava,
one should worship while meditating upon the six paths situated within that which has become the seed-syllable.
Immediately thereafter, with the entire collection of mantras and offerings such as arghya,
one should place the mantra-pitcher in the center while looking toward the directions at the door.
One should install the other [deities] in their respective directions according to their positions with their own respective mantras;
then, one should cover each jar individually with stones empowered by one's own śakti.
Then, one should fill the interior of the jars with soft clay and soft sand, using lime for the sake of achieving immovability, while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Then, having wrapped [the image] with eye-cloths, one should cause the Rigvedic verses to be recited;
specifically, the hymn beginning with "ā tvā hārṣa," as well as the Pratiṣṭhā Sāman for those chanting the Sāmaveda.
Those established in Brahman who have well cultivated their minds should repeatedly recite the mantra of power consisting of twelve syllables, ending with the Praṇava.

One should meditate upon that [reality], which has attained a single unified form through the Praṇava, as being established in the powers of the forms and so forth, and consisting of name, form, and action. (343)
Having worshipped his own form there with the twelve-syllable mantra and further with [mantras] that reach the heart, he should perform the ritual dismissal (saṃyaja) of that treasury of splendors.
Then, O Blessed One, one should cause the followers of the Pañcarātra to recite "Oṃ bhagavan bhogaiḥ";
for those who know the Ṛgveda, the verse "arcāmi te"; and for those who know the Sāmaveda, the hymn "arcā". (345)
Then, once the temple site has been taken possession of,
one should place eight [lines] measuring twelve finger-breadths each in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having properly bathed and worshipped the stone possessing auspicious characteristics,
one should gradually restrain within it the intellect and the qualities of the dharmas.
Furthermore, starting from the southeast (Agni) corner up to the northeast (Īśa) position, there is the group beginning with Dharma;
and starting from the east up to the north, there is the group of four beginning with Adharma.
Within the stones, on the ground, a group of six should be placed in sequence, beginning with the first letter and ending with the final letter of the alphabet. 349.
Having thus fashioned the snare of the intellect, permeated by the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman),
one should properly lay it down like a foundational thread, situated upon the floor of the palace.
One should likewise place eight stones for the purpose of the courtyard wall;
upon them, one should properly install the previously mentioned lords of the directions.
One should meditate on that wheel, which is like whirling sparks of fire, pervading the area of the ground within the circle of the earth, extending as far as the courtyard. 352.
Below that is Ābhoga, and above it is the remainder; above that in the sky is Gaganīśvara, along with his weapons and retinue, outside the walls of the courtyard.
One should install the group of eight beginning with Indra, starting from the east and ending at the northeast corner;
likewise, they should be placed upon stones of that same kind situated within the ground.
Having worshipped that [deity] by its own name, one should then cause the Ṛgvedas to be recited;
likewise, those who are "neuter" (klība) and not learned should indeed recite the Yajurmayas which belong to the gods. 355.
Then, having entered the interior of the Devavrata and Sāman halls,
and standing before the embodiment of the mantra, one should contemplate the pervasion of the path.
That which, having sprouted from a seed, previously attained manifestation as far as the pedestal of a palace, indeed [arises] from the stone that serves as the foundation for the pot.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā), as previously described, should be meditated upon according to its actual state;
one should observe the path of the levels (padādhvā) up to the limit of the height of the womb (garbha). 358.
The path of mantra extends from the end of the Śukanāsā up to the altar;
the path of kalā extends to the end of the throat; and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is above that.

Now, demonstrating the procedure for the construction of a temple, he describes the method for installing the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) in its center, preceded by the worship of the Vāstupuruṣa, beginning with the words "it should be understood as being like the pedestal" and ending with "and the path of colors (*varṇādhvā*) above that. Regarding the phrase "when the excavation has been made down to the water-level and filled as before," the term "as before" refers to the ritual of seizing the ground (*kṣmāparigraha*) described in the eighteenth chapter. Thus, the ritual of seizing the ground and so forth, which are explained in detail in the *Pauṣkara*, are required here.

Therefore, that [procedure] should be seen as summarized in the *Īśvaratantra*. Likewise, the ritual for the acquisition of the site (*kṣmāparigraha*) and the ritual for the installation of the water-pot (*kumbhasthāpana*), among others, are very clearly set forth in the *Śrīsātvatāmṛta*. Thus, from the time the deity of the pot is installed within the ground of the temple until the final consecration of the image (*bimbapratiṣṭhā*), these deities are to be worshipped daily. Furthermore, the procedure for their worship every day thereafter is very clearly explained in the sections concerning the worship of the temple (*vimānārcana*) in both the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* Tantras.

However, in the section on the worship of the celestial vehicle (vimānārcana) pertaining to the Supreme Lord, according to the method stated in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, it is said that one should install Lakṣmī with her own mantra upon the four pitchers situated in the intermediate directions (*vidiś*) using the mantras beginning with "teṣāṃ vidiksthitānāṃ ca"; Kaustubha with his own mantra upon the four pitchers situated in the cardinal directions starting from the east; and the Lord—who is the essence of power (*śaktyātmā*), whose form is the imperishable sound (*niṣkala-śabdavigraha*)—upon the central pitcher with the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*).

Regarding this, it has been stated that by means of the verses beginning with "tatra madhyamakumbhasya," the *pariśakti* and *prabhāśakti* are to be deposited on the lid of the central pitcher (*madhyamakumbha*), the *jñānaśakti* on the four lids of the pitchers situated in the cardinal directions, and the *kriyāśakti* on the four lids of the pitchers situated in the intermediate directions. Furthermore, according to the method taught by Sātvata, the alternative of depositing nine powers (*navaśaktinyāsa*) has also been mentioned by means of the verses beginning with "pidhānanavake."

However, the commentators on the *Pārameśvara* have stated: "In the covering of the central jar, in the center is the partless (*niṣkala*) embodiment of sound consisting of six syllables. This is based on ignorance, because the statement "by means of the six-syllabled mantra, [one worships] the partless embodiment of sound" must be construed with the preceding sentence; furthermore, if it were applied later as they suggest, it would result in numerous contradictions.

In the forty-second chapter of the Pauṣkarasaṃhitā, which is the root source of the Pārameśvara, immediately after the statement "by means of the six-syllabled [mantra]," six and a half verses have been skipped before the passage beginning with "Or the supreme goddess Śakti... is stated. Not having understood this, commentators who consider themselves omniscient based merely on their perusal of the Pārameśvarasaṃhitā have spoken in this manner.

Furthermore, it is stated: "In the four cardinal directions of the central lid (pidhāna) of the pitcher is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), capable of sustaining the universe; in its intermediate directions is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), characterized by bliss. Here, both the supreme power (parā-śakti) and the radiance power (prabhā-śakti) did not even come within the range of the commentators' vision, out of fear that, like the powers of knowledge and action, they too might undergo a transposition of the aforementioned positions. In this regard, the worship of the four powers is explicitly mentioned in the *Pauṣkara*: "One should provide a set of nine lids made of copper or stone, as appropriate."
"It is well-rounded or square, very auspicious, twelve finger-breadths [in size], and restrained by four *śaktis*.

The four *śaktis* are also explained in that very same place by the passage beginning with "The *śakti* which is the supreme goddess," and so forth. The meaning—that *jñāna-śakti* resides in the four directions starting from the east, and *kriyā-śakti* resides in the four coverings starting from the southeast—is understood precisely by the word "manifestation" (*vyakti*) in the *Pārameśvara* passage: "But in the collection of manifestations in the intermediate directions. This too is clearly stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "But in the collection of jars in the intermediate directions. Here, the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) for its covering.

Furthermore, the fact that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the powers of the manifestation of knowledge (*jñānabhāsā*) and so forth—spoken of in the passage beginning with "In this group of nine coverings" (*pidhānanavake tv asmin*)—constitutes another alternative (*pakṣāntaratva*), was not even recognized.

Now, one might object: "In that case, no word indicating an alternative, such as 'or' (*yadvā* or *athavā*), is seen there; moreover, if the placement of the powers of knowledge and action were accepted in the eight coverings starting from the front (*prāk*), then the word 'middle' (*madhya*) in the verse 'One should place [the power] in the middle of the covering' (*pidhāne madhyato nyaset*) would be redundant. To this we reply: even in the absence of a word indicating an alternative, its status as an alternative is established simply by reflecting upon the meaning (*arthaparyālocanayā*).

The venerable one should understand that the purpose of the word *madhya* (middle) here is exactly as it is accepted in the passage, "the king of mantras in the middle of the pericarp" (*karṇikāmadhye*). Regarding this, the commentators on the *Pārameśvara-tantra* have stated: "The state of having nine pots pertains to the distinction between circular and rectangular vimānas, because it will be said later: 'in whichever types of palaces'."

That [interpretation] is extremely weak; for the placement of nine jars in the excavated site for the purpose of constructing a temple is common to all types of palaces (*vimāna*), since, beginning with the words "O Mahāmati, among palaces divided into many varieties," the pervasion of the world and other features are stated as being common to all, and because in this *Pauṣkara* [Tantra] as well, the placement of the nine jars is stated to be common to all palaces.

We believe that the commentators on the *Pārameśvara-tantra*, under the delusion that this [text] was the *śikhākumbha*, have provided an explanation in this manner. Enough of this digression; let us return to the subject at hand. (282–359)
Having first leveled everything, one should then begin the construction of the palace,
ensuring that from the base upwards it is neither deficient nor excessive by even a fraction of an angula or a karahasta.
Know that for the sake of auspiciousness and success, the interior of the temple should measure up to twenty-four cubits, neither less nor more by even a single tāla.
Having first calculated the area of the field or its cubic volume in finger-breadths, one should properly divide that by eight; then, having reflected upon what remains, [one should proceed]. 362.
From the letter *e* up to the eighth, there are the banner (*dhvaja*), smoke (*dhūma*), the lord of beasts (*mṛgeśvara*), and the dog (*śva*);
thereafter, the cow (*go*), donkey (*khara*), elephant (*mātaṅga*), and crow (*vāyasa*) are auspicious.
The measures known as one, three, five, and seven cubits are prescribed everywhere;
the thickness of the wall outside that [sanctum] is according to one-sixth of the measurement of the interior chamber (garbha). || 364 ||
Having completely abandoned that measurement, another wall is constructed;
in this manner, it proceeds step by step along with the series of walls.
The area of the temple's sanctum is twice as wide as its depth; however, for a shrine with only a single wall, the measurement of the area is prescribed according to that [single] dimension.
That which was stated regarding the interior should be joined with one-third of it by means of the appropriate method;
even there, one should examine the purity of the income through decrease and increase.

In this manner, understand that the portion which is devoid of the base (pīṭha) and lacks the surrounding wall (nirjagatīka) is commensurate with the measurement of the temple site; understand that the measurement of the temple site is thus constituted. 368.
Then, the *jagatī* womb is fashioned with a sixth part, a quarter, and a third part, consisting of both; that shall be the extent of its construction. (369)
In the four directions, [the projection] is one and a half parts; with three-fifths of that [unit], and indeed with a third part in the middle, the projection (nirgama) is prescribed.
From corner to corner, one should indeed cause each remaining portion to enter [the next];
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be as high as the inner sanctum (garbha), or equal to that pedestal or the petal (dala). || 371 ||
The conception of the marks, locations, and portions for the pīṭha mentioned as the abode of the pīṭha should indeed be performed in the four directions in many ways, beginning with Ananta. (372)
Then, one should indeed make the height of the temple three times the extent of the site,
or two and a half times, or twice, according to one's desire.
One should first divide that [space] equally into twenty-two parts;
subsequently, it should be arranged like a pedestal (pīṭha), and with one part, the masūraka should be made.
Above that, the shank is fashioned, elevated according to the measurement of the womb,
and adorned by deities who serve as its attendants.
The pedestal of the pinnacle (śikharapīṭha) should be made with a pair of shanks in height and slightly more than that above; it is to be characterized by the previously mentioned features.
However, the entrance and the exit there are each measured at half a part;
and here a pinnacle is fashioned, consisting of nine stories.
Having contracted that thread from the city [of the navel] and taken it up to the height of the upliftment, one should extend it upward from the shank from a single, uniform color. 378.
Having quickly restrained him, he should touch the peak of the pedestal;
then, O one of pure vision, he should go outside the temple to that spot on the ground where it first appears.
One should lead the cord from the ear upwards, marking it gradually until reaching the height of the pinnacle; indeed, it should be done in this very manner in all four directions.
O high-minded one, one should pass it along from ear to ear while it is being marked,
as long as that cluster of blossoms on the peak remains with the luster of a white water-lily petal.
Having thus completed the drawing by means of the gaze, it should then be performed tenfold for the purpose of establishing the foundation-section (bhūmikāṇḍa) through the casting of threads. 382.
Above that, however, the āmalasāraka should be made with one part;
then one should apply the various levels according to their respective proportions.

Having abandoned the rules for decrease and increase, as well as the [specific] positions and stages, [the measures] numbering four, three, two, and one are equal in their finger-breadths (aṅgula). || 384 ||
Starting from one's own level, those [levels] should be applied in descending order;
starting from the preceding level, they are placed within the series of levels situated below. (385)
The separation between all of them, however, should be measured by twice that eighth part;
the arrangement of the pedestals within them should be made according to their established positions.

[He is worshipped] with various lotuses complete with their stalks, with all manner of manifestations, or with all the [divine] emblems embodied, established in the aesthetic sentiments of dance and song. || 387 ||
The uṣṇīṣa should be made from the upper portion by one-ninth, emerging with its own quarter-measure;
it should be fashioned from the upper level and free from decorative carving.
Having performed the remaining recitation three times, one should first [purify] the navel with one part as before;
then the throat with the second; and finally, with the third, that which moves upward.
One should fashion the staff (daṇḍa) as perfectly even and endowed with beauty as the fruit of the dhātrī;
having fashioned the nine-fold uṣṇīṣa, one should make the curvature of the pedestal (vedikā) with four [parts]. 390.
The neck-ornament (kaṇṭhamāṇḍa) should be three parts wide and measured by five units;
having previously divided the interior space (garbha) into five, seven, or nine parts.

Having set aside the two parts belonging to the wings, the temple-pipe (prāsādanāḍikā) should be made with the group of parts situated in the middle section, extending out by half the measure of the inner sanctum (garbha). || 392 ||
Whether by a quarter, a third, or even a seventh part, it may be raised;
or it may be elevated by half its peak, resembling the petal of a blue lotus.
Above the pedestal of the pinnacle, it should be fashioned, adorned with divine craftsmanship;
thereafter, one should construct an even more auspicious pavilion provided with pillars.
Adorned with the lord of birds and the circle of Bali,
three pavilions should likewise be constructed at the four gates and in the cardinal directions.
In the pavilion, there should be a pavilion endowed with three entrances;
or one may construct a pavilion as previously described, with an exit according to one's preference.
Now, the extraction (niryāsa) of rathotara, rathaka, and the others is prescribed from their inner core;
that of lāṅgalin is one-tenth part, and [that of] rathaka is one-twelfth part. 397.
Alternatively, they should again be made with a sixteenth part [of the width], like a rim,
smeared on the four sides and adorned with the work of pedestals.
One should complete the cluster of spires and finials on the pedestal in the four directions of the pinnacle, using the same technique as for the chariot-work (rathaka). 399.
One should construct the assembly of doors equally on the four sides of the central area;
then, it is prescribed that [the sanctum] be made from three, four, five, or six parts starting from the womb-chamber (garbha). 400.
It should be twice as high [as the door] and provided with three, five, or nine branches,
joined by two door-keepers or by pot-bellied figures and elephant tusks.
One should perform its installation according to the rules, preceded by mantras;
having bathed it with the root mantra, one should worship it with the *arghya* and other offerings using the *hṛdaya* mantra. || 402 ||
One should establish a station consisting of the elements and jewels at the root of the branch;
for, having completely restrained there, one should recite the mantra which consists of all the supports. 403.
Having meditated upon the eternal [deity] whose nature consists of knowledge and action, one should, by means of the *śikhā* mantra,
arrange a pair of branches on the southern and northern sides.

Having bound the primordial Supreme Lord above that with the Heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), and having brought him into presence and worshipped him within the sky-like expanse of the heart situated in the ether; 405.
The net of elements is twofold: gems, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds;
and those fragrances such as sandalwood, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey. 406.
Having placed all types of rice, all seeds, all medicinal herbs,
and corals within his eyes, he fixed them above the door.
The visible [world] is for the attainment of enjoyment, while the invisible is for the accomplishment of liberation;
there, having restrained the four-footed *sakala* dharma above, [one attains the goal]. 408.
Then, having recited "catvāri śṛṅgā" [RV 4.58.3], one should perform the ritual of the accumulation of oblations with the rays [of light] and pour the full vessel with the root mantra. || 409 ||
One should perform this after the installation of the image, as previously described;
for it depends upon the stability of the abode of the All-pervading Lord.
Know that the temple named Anantabhuvana, which bestows all desires and liberation, is likewise of four types, just like the Pīṭha. 411.
Likewise, it was manifoldly distinguished by the various arrangements of its structures,
and by jars resembling the guardians of treasures (Nidhipālas) and lions, which were like the lords of birds (Garuda).
It is provided with rows of steps marked by conchs and lotuses,
according to the requirements of the door as well as the requirements of the pedestal.
The extent of Aruṇa is prescribed as extending in every direction;
and for Jagatīka, who holds a plow, it is known as the "womb-arisen field. 414.
It should be known that for one who possesses the world, [the measurement] extends in all directions according to that measure;
however, from these [dimensions], one should make [the height] one-quarter greater, while indeed omitting a quarter and so forth from the base.
Having understood the arrangement of the enclosures (āyatanas) situated in the courtyard in ancient times,
know that there are four āyatanas established by palaces located in three directions.

Together with the first [deity] and those situated in the corners, that is known as the five-shrine (pañcāyatana) system; it should be understood as the eight-shrine (aṣṭāyatana) system when including the other three located in the cardinal directions. || 417 ||
Without the one situated in the center, but with two by two located in the directions, that tenfold sphere (daśāyatana) together with him becomes elevenfold. || 418 ||
Know that the twelve āyatanas consist of the two palaces situated on either side of the main street, together with that which stands in the middle. 419.
That very [type] is designated as *adhika*, while another is called *ananta*.
One should construct two temples facing each other at the location of the gateway.
Furthermore, for those situated in the three directions facing the temple,
as well as for those located in the corners, a face-to-face orientation is prescribed with two [deities] each.
One should face the appropriate direction with two [deities] who are mutually desired;
however, two [others] should be situated in the corner regions, facing one another. 422.
O Mahāmati, the doors of the palaces in the infinite abodes should be constructed without hesitation, facing whichever directions one desires.
In that case, there is no fault of mutual obstruction among them, because they have become subordinate members of the primary substratum. 424.
The height of the parapet (paraṇḍaka) is beneficial when it is half, one-third, or one-quarter of the height of the wall (aṅganāt); its width is likewise equal to that height.
And one should make that [mandala] resembling a seat (pīṭha), smooth, or indeed with a turban-like top;
it should be joined with a multitude of ten million [deities] belonging to various classes of gods.
O Mahāmati, that which is a single sphere (ekāyatana) and the female organ (tvagana) is joined with a small ball (laghuparaṇḍa), or it may be merely a ball (paraṇḍaka). 427.

When [the body] has its first part consisting of two sense-bases and so on, up to the end of the twelve sense-bases, and when looking toward a single direction within a square courtyard, [it appears as such]. (428)
Or it may be constructed in a square or an elongated shape within a spacious palace possessing the aforementioned characteristics, especially for temples and courtyards. 429.
O Mahāmati, for seats that are square and so forth, there is always a state of mutual dependence, which is indeed beneficial and contingent. 430.
It is by the power of the ground itself, as well as by the power of the image,
by the power of various fruits, and likewise by the power of beauty.
From a square [altar] comes gain of land; from a long square, wealth;
from a circle, the attainment of all desires; and from a long circle, bliss. 432.
For those who desire both seen and unseen fruits, the worlds beginning with Mahat grant the station of Viṣṇu, health, and the highest earth.
For those Vaiṣṇavas who are free from desire, the supreme state is attained at the end of their descent from that realm.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Image, the Pedestal, and the Temple," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the Śrīpāñcarātra.

Now he describes the characteristics of the temple (*prāsāda*), beginning from the words "having first leveled everything, one should then begin the temple" up until the completion of the section. Here, from the words "the installation of that [temple] should be performed according to the rule" up until "for the abode of the All-pervading Lord depends indeed upon its stability," the procedure for the consecration of the door (*dvārapratiṣṭhā*) is to be understood as having been stated. He will describe the consecration of this temple (*prāsādapratiṣṭhā*) after the consecration of the image (*bimbapratiṣṭhā*). (360–433)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the illustrious Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshiper of the lotus feet of Lord Yadugirīśa.
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Nārada said: O brahmins, that which was spoken by the Sustainer of the Universe to the Preceptor of all the worlds—
I shall now explain the placement of the mantra within the image.
And for the social classes who desire worldly enjoyments, it bestows their present wishes; and for those who follow the four stages of life through tranquility, it grants absolute liberation.
And for those devoted to the dharma of sacrifice, there is assistance and its fruits.

Now, the twenty-fifth chapter will be explained. Here, [the author] says "all," in two and a half verses, stating: "I shall describe the installation of the mantra and the image, as taught by Vāsudeva to Saṃkarṣaṇa, which bestows the fruits beginning with the description of the portions. 1–3.
As before, when there is a pavilion in front of the temple in the [appropriate] direction. || 3 ||
It should be square with four doors, encircled by a garland of darbha grass;
or, in the absence of such materials, it may face whichever direction one prefers.
From fourteen cubits up to thirty cubits, and again from that down to six cubits, [the proportions] depend upon the measurement of the image itself.

He describes the characteristics of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) with two and a half verses beginning with "prāgvat" (as before). "As before" means as described in the section concerning the installation of the ritual jars (*kumbhasthāpana*). In front of the temple, provided there is space in a cardinal direction, one should construct a four-doored sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇṭapa*) there. If that is not possible—that is, if such a location is unavailable—one should construct the sacrificial pavilion elsewhere, in the southern or other directions or intermediate points, facing whichever direction is desired.

From fourteen cubits up to thirty cubits—starting from four cubits and extending to thirty cubits—one should construct the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇṭapa) with its width and length increased in accordance with the largeness of the image, depending on the measurement of the image; or, starting again from fourteen cubits down to six cubits, one should construct it with its width and length decreased in accordance with the smallness of the image. This is the connection with what precedes. (3–5)
In the center of those [mandalas], a platform (sthalā) should be constructed using fourteen parts (two sevenths), and then eight parts;
it should be Samantabhadra (excellent on all sides), very smooth, and paved with baked bricks and other materials.
Starting from the height of a palm tree, in this general rite,
the [measurement] was gradually reduced by an increase of one finger-breadth at each stage.

Regarding that, he describes the characteristics of the altar (*vedi*) with two verses beginning with "kāryā. Among those pavilions (*maṇṭapa*), which vary according to measurements of fourteen *hasta*s and so forth, the ground area for the altar should be made by means of twice seven parts—that is, fourteen divisions. And that [altar] should be "samantabhadrā," meaning it should be provided with a walkway (*vīthī*) on all sides, consisting of eight parts each.

Thus, having divided the width and length of the pavilion (maṇṭapa) into thirty parts, it should be understood that the arrangement of the altar (vedikā) is made with fourteen of those parts; and in the remaining sixteen parts, the arrangement of the walkways (vīthī) is made by eight parts on each side. Regarding its height, the meaning is that the altar should be constructed starting from a height of one cubit (tāla) and increasing by finger-breadths (aṅgula), or decreasing by finger-breadths to be lower. For an altar situated within the sacrificial hall (yāgagṛha) that has a width and length of fourteen cubits, the height is one cubit (tālamāna).

The meaning is that, starting from that [minimum size] up to thirty cubits, as the length and breadth of the sacrificial hall increase, or decrease down to six cubits, the height of the altar (vedikā) must also be increased or decreased by one finger-breadth (aṅguli) respectively, in accordance with that number of cubits. Thus, for a sacrificial hall measuring thirty cubits in both length and breadth, the height of the altar becomes one cubit plus four finger-breadths. (6–7)
The mandala of all [the goddesses] should be in the center, measuring two, three, or eight parts;
it is square, with four doors, and adorned with wheels and lotuses. 8.
To the south is the bedchamber, and to the north is the fire-pit as before;
it should be auspicious, two cubits in size, provided with a girdle, and marked with a wheel and a lotus.

Now, with two verses beginning with "dvistri," he describes the sequence for dividing the site of the mandala and other features upon the altar (vedikā). Among all the various types of altars distinguished by different measurements, one should construct—in due order and as an ornament—a mandala characterized by its squareness and so forth in the center; a bed to its south; and to the north, a fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa) characterized by its equal sides and girdle (mekhala), using portions of two, three, and eight [units] respectively. This is the construction.

Thus, the meaning is that the mandala should be made with two parts, the bed with three parts, and the site for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with eight parts. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, it is written: "By means of two, three, and eight parts respectively, one must not cause a deficiency in the lowering or the rising of the navel. This [interpretation] is a source of ridicule. (8–9)
Below that, one should fashion a square area adorned with a front-facing girdle of cords;
then, on the southern side, one should make it marked with the sign of a wheel.
It is circular in the west and in the north, charmingly marked with a lotus;
it is marked with a conch in all the corners, and their proportions are according to the upper [section].

Now, with two verses beginning with "tadadhaḥ," he describes the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the eight directions starting from the east, located beneath the altar (vedikā). The meaning is that just as the measurement for the upper pit—consisting of two cubits and so forth—is, the same applies to these eastern and other pits. (10–11)
All four pavilions measuring ten cubits [in width] have a single girdle;
however, in this case, everything extending upwards has a girdle.

Regarding the types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) for pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) measuring thirteen cubits and so forth, he says "all" (*sarve*). This means for pavilions measuring ten cubits—that is, for the four pavilions measuring thirteen, twelve, eleven, and ten cubits respectively—all eight pits starting from the east should also have only a single girdle (*mekhalā*); due to the narrowness of the ground, they should be provided with only one girdle, but that which rises upward must remain upon the altar (*vedī*).
The meaning is that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made with all girdles (mekhalā), that is, it should be provided with every kind of girdle. || 12 ||
Below this, all the pavilions (maṇṭapas) are situated with a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
their first [enclosure], including the girdle (mekhalā), shall measure twenty-two finger-breadths.
In a six-cubit house, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made starting from a reduction of two finger-breadths up to sixteen finger-breadths; or else, there may be an additional girdle (mekhalā).

With the half-verse beginning with "ataḥ," he states the absence of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in the east and other directions for pavilions (maṇḍapas) measuring nine cubits and so forth: "Therefore, all pavilions situated below [this size]—those measuring nine cubits, eight cubits, seven cubits, and six cubits—are fourfold pavilions with a single pit; the meaning is that they are provided only with a pit situated above the altar (vedī). Regarding those as well, he states the difference in measurement for the central pit with the verse beginning with "teṣām" (and a half).

Among those four pavilions ending with the six-cubit [pavilion], in the first pavilion measuring nine cubits, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall have a girdle (samekhala) measuring twenty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Thus, in the houses of six cubits and so on, by decreasing the measurement by two finger-breadths in succession, it should reach a pit of sixteen finger-breadths. It is stated that in a house of eight cubits the pit measures twenty finger-breadths, and in a house of seven cubits the pit measures eighteen finger-breadths.

In this manner, the following is also inferred: in a house measuring fourteen cubits (*kara*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measures one cubit plus eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); in a house measuring thirteen cubits, the pit measures one cubit plus six finger-breadths; in a twelve-cubit house, the pit measures one cubit plus four finger-breadths; in a house measuring eleven cubits, the pit measures one cubit plus two finger-breadths; and in a house measuring ten cubits, the pit measures exactly one cubit.

Furthermore, it is stated that there is an increase of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each [increase] from a house of fifteen cubits up to a house of thirty cubits. Therefore, it should be understood that in a house of fifteen cubits, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measures one cubit plus nine fingers; in a house of sixteen cubits, it measures one cubit plus ten fingers; and so on in sequence, until in a house of thirty cubits, the pit measures two cubits. Alternatively, regarding the girdles (mekhalā): for pits of sixteen fingers and so forth, either a single girdle should be made, or more than one—meaning two or more girdles may be made.
The [pedestal] should first be eight cubits high, and from that point on, it should increase by half a cubit;
there shall be no reduction for those [pedestals] ending at six cubits in height, nor for those that are less.
Then, one should subtract four [units] starting from thirteen karas:
namely, eight, seven, five, and four finger-breadths in sequence. (16)

Now, he describes the height of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with two verses beginning with "eight cubits high. First, the initial house, measuring fourteen cubits [in width], is eight cubits high. Beyond that, the pavilions starting from fifteen cubits increase by half a cubit in sequence; the meaning is that a pavilion thirty cubits wide should be sixteen cubits high.

For the four pavilions (maṇṭapa) beginning with thirteen cubits, one should respectively subtract eight, seven, five, and four finger-breadths from the previously mentioned height in cubits; that is to say, one should decrease [the height]. However, for the four [pavilions] beginning with nine cubits and ending with six cubits—that is, for those pavilions with a decreasing number of cubits—the reduction of the height (ucchriti) shall not occur. This means that the height should not be less than ten cubits for a pavilion.

In this context, although the statement beginning with "hrāsa" (decrease) exists prior [to the others] according to the *Mūlasātvata*, it has been explained in this manner because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). In the *Pārameśvara*, however, the recitation itself has been expanded in accordance with the very sequence of meaning. 15–16.
Thus, the width of the bath-houses was equal to their height;
moreover, they were adorned in the middle with sand-pavements.
They are two or four parts wide and, as before, elevated by two or seven parts;
from the bath-house or the front house, they are auspiciously located in three desired directions.

One should construct the hall for the vision and the gift, equal to half the mind [of the temple], provided with a principal [shrine] and a well-proportioned pedestal and bed, together with the auspicious finger-measure jars.
One should fashion the ritual ground for all [deities], adorned with corner pillars, encircled by beautiful windows, and provided with wheels and other symbols as before.

Thus, the term "evam" (in this manner) extends by analogy the characteristics described for the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) to the bathing house (*snānageha*) as well. The phrase "with elevations" (*unnataiḥ saha*) means together with heights; the reference is primarily to the abstract quality of height. He states a specific distinction regarding that with the word "but" (*kintu*). "Adorned in the middle with sand-benches" (*vālukāpīṭhaiḥ*) means beautified in the center of the altar-platforms filled with sand; the words "bathing houses" (*snānagṛhāḥ*) are to be supplied. He states the measurement of the sand-bench with the words "two or four," etc.

The sand-platforms (*vālukāpīṭha*) are to be understood as being fourteen parts wide—specifically two, four, and eight parts—and elevated as previously described. It has been stated that for the construction of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) all around the sacrificial hall (*yāgageha*), a pathway (*vīthī*) should be arranged on both sides with eight parts each. Since there are no sacrificial pits here, it should be understood that the pathway is arranged with four parts each, and the sand-platform is constructed with twenty-two parts. He states the rule regarding the location for constructing the bathing hall (*snānaśālā*) and so forth with the words "the bathing [areas]" (*snānīyā*).

"Snānīyāḥ" refers to the bathing [images]; "houses" is the understood subject. "From the front house" means leaving the sacrificial hall situated in the eastern part; the meaning is that they should be placed in a desired, auspicious, and charming location in the three directions, namely the southern and other directions. He states the characteristics of the house for the opening of the eyes with the word "ardha," etc.

One should construct a hall for the opening of the eyes (*dṛgdāna-bhavana*)—the term *dṛgdāna* meaning "opening" from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting"—measuring half the size of the main sacrificial hall (*yāgageha*) and having a width and length equal to that half. It should be provided with auspicious jars (*māṅgalya-kalaśa*), along with the jars to be described later, and equipped with a fine pedestal and a couch. Regarding the common decoration for the sacrificial pavilion and other structures, he says "of all": [it should be adorned] with beautiful cloths (*sunetra*), meaning canopies (*vitāna*), and with symbols such as the discus and the banner (*cakrādyaiḥ*). (Verses 17–20)
It should be well-established with firm legs, capable of holding bathing water,
and half as long as the sand pedestal according to the initial sequence.
Having increased it by half a cubit and decreased it by four finger-breadths,
and having made its width half of its own length, one should thus construct it together with a spout.
With that [sand], one should adorn the central sand-pavement;
and within it, for the sake of doors, one should likewise decorate the directions of the sacrificial hall.

Now, he describes the characteristics of the bathing pedestal (*snānapīṭha*) with two and a half verses beginning with "well-established" (*susthitam*). It means that it should be capable of holding the bathing water; for the purpose of receiving the bathing water, it should be provided with a surrounding rim (*āvaraṇa*) four finger-breadths high above the pedestal.

The bathing pedestal (*snānapīṭha*) should be made half the length of the sand pedestal (*vālukāpīṭha*), measuring seven cubits in length—being half the dimension of the sand pedestal located in the bathhouse—and its width should be half of its own length. Following the initial sequence, it should be increased by half a cubit up to the thirty-cubit house starting from that point, and decreased by four finger-breadths up to the six-cubit house starting from that point. Having thus constructed the bathing pedestal complete with a drain, one should adorn that sand pedestal with it. (21–23)
By means of the application of the increase of half-measures (*śāśamārdhavṛddhi*), there is a decrease elsewhere, starting from a *kalā*.
One should construct arches (*toraṇa*) outside with sturdy, well-consecrated wood.
They should be five cubits increased by half a cubit;
one should not practice a reduction of them unless there is another [specific] purpose.
One should not insert [the measuring cord] into the ground at a distance less than five *śama*s;
for those increased by half a *śama*, one should increase it by two *kalās* each.
The distance between them shall be one-third of the remainder left after subtracting the entrance from the total length;
all these [pinnacles] should be made with wheels and banners, and adorned with garlands of cloth and clusters of flowers. (27)
[The deities] are smeared with yellow pigments such as *sudhā* and with substances such as sandalwood paste.
Now, he describes the characteristics of the door-arches (*toraṇa*) of the sacrificial hall (*yāgāgāra*) with the verses beginning with "of the sacrificial hall" (23–29).
For this entire [universe], though its parts are distinct, is indeed joined together within a single [consciousness]. || 28 ||
In the sacrificial hall for the Karmayāga, or even without the use of ritual ashes, the site should always be thirty-five cubits long and expanded by one-fourth of that measure in width. || 29 ||
In the middle of that, one should prepare seven platforms measuring four cubits each; the interval between these platforms should indeed be measured at one tāla.
One should indeed construct the ground-pavilion with a reduction of one unit, ending at a distance of two cubits;
this is done by gradually decreasing the measurement from eight finger-breadths by two finger-breadths at each step.
The distance between the land-marks and the narrow passages is two golakas;
in this very manner, the height of all of them is proclaimed.
The measurement for the surrounding path (*vīthi*) has been prescribed according to one's own seat (*pīṭha*).

Regarding the alternative when there is a lack of resources and so forth, he states [the following] with the words beginning "bhinnaṅgam" (having separate parts). "Bhinnaṅgam" means accompanied by separate and distinct parts such as different halls (*śālā*) and so on. This entire ritual—comprising all actions such as the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*), the consecration bath (*snapana*), worship (*arcana*), the fire sacrifice (*havana*), the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), and the rest—should be performed. In the absence of wealth (*vibhūti*) or space (*avani*), or due to a lack of resources or a lack of space, it is joined within a single sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*). Just as it can be performed within the sacrificial hall itself without a separate bathing hall or a hall for the opening of the eyes, so too [is this case].

The remainder of the sentence is: "For the purpose of the layout, one should construct a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) with a field measuring thirty-five cubits and expanded by one-fourth of its own [side]. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, it is written: "The meaning is that one should arrange it so that the various components—the altar (*vedi*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the arches (*toraṇa*), and so forth—which possess distinct characteristics, are appropriately joined together in a single location within the hall. That is weak. The meaning there is that one should conceive of seven sites and seven altars, each having a width and length of four cubits, situated in the middle of that [pavilion].

One should make the separation—the intervening space between the platforms (vedikās)—equal to their base, measuring twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas). When done thus, the intervening spaces between the seven platforms become six tālas each. In the absence of such space for separation, one should provide the separation by reducing it by two finger-breadths at a time, or by decreasing it by one tāla at a time.

One should construct seven platforms (*sthala*) in sequence, each measuring eight *aṅgulas* in size, with a separation of eight *aṅgulas* between each, extending to the limit of two cubits (*dvihasta*), or with an interval measured at two cubits. For those in narrow spaces who require such a separation, one should provide an interval of four *aṅgulas*, which is two *golakas*. As was stated previously: "Two *aṅgulas* are a *kalā*, an *akṣi*, a *golaka*, and indeed a *bhāva*. The height of all these platforms is proclaimed to be exactly the same.

The meaning is that one should make the height of the railings (vedikās) twelve, eight, or four finger-breadths (aṅgulas). The measurement for the surrounding path (vīthi) is prescribed as being four cubits (hastas), arising from its own pedestal; this is the meaning. (27–33)
Or, in such a case of constraint, one should construct two pavilions from the first mentioned pair. || 33 ||
In the center is the pedestal of the pavilion, and its southern direction should be toward the place for the sacrificial apparatus,
which is the site for the installation of the ritual jars (kumbhas).
Thus, in the vicinity of Vāmana, there was the satiation of enjoyments through mantras;
and for the supreme ones, there was the offering of oblations according to the Vedas beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma.
The visualization of the gift should be fixed upon another bed in the place of rest,
according to what has been taught regarding the descent of power (śaktipāta) for the forms in the eight directions of the palace.
Then, one should perform the oblation either on sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila), or in fire-pits (kuṇḍa) intended for that purpose,
or personally in one's own fire-pit, which is excellent and consists of the essence of the four Vedas.
Or, due to the absence of the necessary materials and the lack of suitable officiating priests (mūrtipās), he may perform the entire rite himself. 38.
Whichever [mantra] is to be employed for whatever purpose, one should introduce that very one there;
the instructor of the mantras, moreover, should be highly intelligent and equal to oneself. (39)

One who is skilled in ritual action should be employed on all occasions. Thus, even when there is no space for the construction of seven altars (*vedikās*), he states the alternative of five altars in three verses beginning with "evaṃ vā. When there is a constraint—that is, a contraction of space—one should omit the two previously mentioned pavilions (*maṇṭapas*). The ablative case here is used in the sense of omission (as if from a list). Having excluded the two pavilions for the bathing, leading forth, and opening of the eyes, one should either proceed in this way or construct the five altars according to the method to be described.

As for their application: in the center is the mandala-pīṭha; in its southern direction, immediately adjacent to the south, is the place for wealth (*dhana*), which is the placement of the water-jars (*kumbha*). Immediately thereafter, on the altar (*vedikā*), is the placement of the bathing jars. In the same way, near the left side, on the altar situated near the left part of the mandala-pīṭha, is the "satiating of the offerings with mantras" (*bhogānāṃ mantratarpaṇa*); this means the offering (*havana*) consisting of the satiation of the offerings, such as fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth. This continues up to the location of the primary sacrificial pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*).

In the *Pārameśvaravyākhyāna*, however, it is written: "The 'satisfaction of the mantras' regarding enjoyments means the worship of the jar (*kumbha*), because water constitutes all enjoyments. This is weak, because the primary sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is unavoidable.

If it is argued that, in that case, the worship of the jar would likewise be unavoidable, we say no; for the worship of the jar will be described as taking place specifically on the southern side of the pit.

If it is argued that our stated meaning is also consistent, we say no; for in this context, the word *tapaṇa* is used many times specifically in the sense of "construction" (*bhavana*). It should be understood that the construction of the *Ṛk*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Pūrva* [Atharva] Vedas is described as the fourfold altar (*vedicatuṣṭaya*), while the subsequent construction takes place on the altar immediately following that. Regarding "the gift of sight" (*dṛgdāna*), which means the opening of the eyes, it refers specifically to the previously mentioned altar for the bed (*śayanavedikā*) at the place of rest; the meaning is that it is declared to be beneficial when performed on another bed, that is, on a separate couch.

In the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, however, regarding the passage "of those lying nearby" (*samīpe śayanasthānām*), it was previously accepted that the reading is *samīpe nayanam* (bringing near), and it was written that "leading" (*nayana*) means "opening the eyes. Here too, adopting the same approach, the reading is postulated as "the giving of sight (*dṛgdānam*) is indeed in the place of rest (*śayanasthāne*), for that [is done] on another bed (*anyasmin śayane*)," and it is written that one bed is prepared for the purpose of opening the eyes, while on the other is the well-known bed [for sleep].

Even in the case of seven altars (*vedikā*), the rule regarding the placement of the mandala and other elements is exactly the same. However, it is understood that in that system, the installation of the bathing throne (*snānapīṭha*) takes place on the final southern altar, while the preparation of the bed for the purpose of opening the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*) takes place on the final northern altar. (33–37)
Having personally investigated the matter regarding the acts of offering oblations and worship, [he spoke]. 40.
For he dwells with undistracted mind upon those rites beginning with the generation [of the deity] and ending with the ritual placement (nyāsa).

Regarding his own performance of the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and ending with the ritual placement, the author says "himself" (svayam), describing his state as one who proceeds with a one-pointed mind, preceded by the contemplation of the objects of the rites of fire-oblation (havana) and worship (arcana). (40–41)
Having performed the worship of the water-pot along with the fire-oblation, as prescribed in the ritual for initiation.
Then one should perform the installation of the archways (toraṇas) and the banners (dhvajas).

Having performed the worship of the great jar (mahākumbha), the fire-oblation (homa), and so forth, as well as the installation and worship of the archways and banners according to the method described previously in the section on initiation (dīkṣā-prakaraṇa), he says "having done" (kṛtvā). || 41-42 ||
Furthermore, the eight banners in the east and other directions are distinguished by colors such as white, red, and so forth. 42.
Having established [the deities] upon the middle altar, one should likewise worship the group of four beginning with Satya there in the same manner as before. (43)
Furthermore, one should have the gods recite the Ṛgvedic hymns;
then, with all the colors, one should worship the wheel and the archway on the exterior. || 44 ||
Then, one who knows the Sāman chants should cause the female gatekeeper to recite the Sāman;
thereafter, he should proceed surrounded by those bearing the [divine] forms and holding water for the guest-offering (arghya) and flowers.

The establishment of the eight banners (dhvaja) around the central altar is described by the three verses beginning with "sitā" (white). Therein, one should perform the worship of Satya, Suparṇa, and the others according to the sequence of their emergence and dissolution; recite the mantra beginning with "uta devāḥ"; and perform the worship of the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) upon the multi-colored wheel-banners located at the outer archways. Furthermore, one should recite the mantras of the gatekeepers beginning with "lokadvāram apāvṛṇu. Although the worship of the banners and so forth is mentioned after the worship of the great pitcher (mahākumbha) and other items, it should be understood that this [banner-worship] may be performed even prior to that.
And likewise, in the *Īśvarapārameśvara*: "Or else, first there should be worship together with those who stand at the entrance for these [deities]. (42–45)
Where the Lord of the Universe resides, accompanied by the Brahma-stone of the pedestal, there one should perform the gazing upon them, as well as the striking and other rites. (46)
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with water from ritual jars consecrated with the Cakra-weapon mantra,
as well as with white mustard seeds, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), earth, and sacred ash.

Then, having washed [the image] with ant-hill earth and water, with the water of the *cakrāṅka* herb, and having rubbed it with an unguent, one should worship it and wash it again with the water of the *astra* mantra. 48.
Having honored him with the arghya offering,
he should then bind consecrated white mustard seeds on the right hand and cause him to recite the verse first.
Likewise, he should place all the protective amulets, which destroy demons, upon a *pratisarā* cord;
having wrapped them in fine cloth and mounted them upon an excellent chariot, [he should proceed].
While he recites the commencement of the ritual, one should place [the deities] starting from the south;
however, on the left side, one should place four Brāhmaṇas each for the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda first.
Recalling the weapon-mantra before him, he should proceed himself, destroying obstacles, accompanied by dancers, singers, musicians, panegyrists, and readers of auspicious hymns.
One should recite "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame" together with the verses consisting of the Ṛgveda;
at the end of those, however, one should recite "ekāyanāni" and "oṃ namo brahmaṇe."
In the same manner, having gratified those seeking gold and other riches according to his capacity with the Śākuna Sūkta accompanied by the Śrīsūkta, he should cause them to enter.
The proper location for the sacrificial ground is either inside a temple or elsewhere,
prepared according to the procedure to be described with precious stones and other materials.

Now he describes the approach to the image together with the guardians of the icons (*mūrtipas*), the gazing at it and so forth with the eye-mantra (*netramantra*), the worship including the installation of the six jars containing white mustard seeds, water, and other substances, the binding of the *pratisara* amulet along with white mustard seeds on the right hand of the deity, the recitation of the *rakṣohaṇa* hymns by the followers of the Ṛgveda and the Atharvaveda, the bringing of the image and so forth on a chariot accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, dances, songs, and the like, and finally, the distribution of gold and other gifts and the entry into the sacrificial hall.

From "Then, bearing the *arghya* and flowers" up to "to one's own place from the sacrificial ground," [the procedure is described]. *Cakrāṅkā-oṣadhī* is *kaṭukarohiṇī*; as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "It is *kaṭu*, *kaṭumbharā*, *aśokā*, *rohiṇī*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *matsyapittā*, *kṛṣṇabhedī*, *cakrāṅgī*, and *śakulādinī*. [He should recite] the mantra beginning with "The commencement of the rite by the power of the Lord," or the mantra "Oṃ, the Lord alone [is my refuge], I who am His remnant. (45–55)

Having first performed the preliminary consecration of the materials on the ritual ground as previously described, and having offered a slight worship to the bathing vessels, the stone slab, and the other implements; 56.
Having arranged the gems according to rule and having first established the pedestal,
one should then perform all the rites upon the large image and indeed upon the action-image (karmabimba).
The cessation of mantras is said to occur there at the moment of their emergence;
furthermore, whatever occurs there from the time of the great ablution onwards is all included therein.

O Mahāmati, having understood that the completion [of the rite] must be brought to its full conclusion, one should first perform auspicious actions in such a way that the auspicious moment does not pass away. 59.
