When the image (*bimba*) is large, he describes only the following: its entry into the interior of the temple (*prāsāda*), its installation upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) preceded by the depositing of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*); the performance of all rites such as those in the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) upon the *karmabimba*; the invocation (*āvāhana*) and confinement (*sannirodha*) of the mantra specifically in the original image (*mūlabimba*) at the rising of the auspicious moment (*lagnodaya*); and the immediate performance of the rites ending with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), which are to be performed prior to the great consecration bath (*bṛhatsnapana*), so that no lapse of even a single hour (*muhūrta*) may occur. Thus [he says]: "But within the temple... (*prāsādābhyantaraṃ tu*).

From the words "vetti" up to "muhūrto nāvasīdati," and up to "ā bṛhatsnapanāt," it is stated that [the rite] must be performed within the palace; for it has been said in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]:
"O twice-born ones, when a large image (*bṛhadbimba*) is being installed, a specific procedure is declared:
having first established [the deity] in the ritual hall (*karmaśālā*) as before, for the sake of purifying the form..."
Having bathed it according to the prescribed rite and performed the opening of the eyes,
one should then carry out the extensive consecration bath, or simply a bath with abundant water.

Having performed the bathing ceremony for the stone image and others, along with a brief ritual worship, he should have it raised by many attendants with water for the feet and placed upon the chariot.

"Then, having brought [the image] with effort into the interior of the temple, one should seat it upon a pedestal after first arranging the jewels in the prescribed manner. Thus, it should be understood that while only a bath with abundant water is performed in the workshop, the *bṛhatsnapana* (great bath) must be performed exclusively within the interior of the temple. (55–59)

O lotus-eyed one, in this same manner, one should perform the rite for others who have previously been consecrated with the Citra initiation, provided they are free from the jewel and the Brahma-stone.
The rites beginning with the ritual bath are performed upon the action-image (karmabimba), or else near it upon a mirror;
however, in the absence of the action-image, the rites beginning with the ritual sleep (prasvāpa) are indeed performed upon a seat (viṣṭara).
One should perform everything beginning with the entry and ending with the festival;
having thus caused that image to enter and having now installed it [in its place]. 62.

In the case of a painted image (*citrabimba*), the performance of all rites such as the ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth is exactly the same as for a ritual action-image (*karmabimba*). He states that in the absence of such an image, there is a "shadow-bathing" (*chāyāsnāna*) in a mirror, and that through the use of a tuft of grass (*kūrca*), the rites beginning with the entry into the sacrificial hall and ending with the festival of the consecrated bed (*śayyādhivāsotsava*) must be performed; this he explains in two and a half verses beginning with *evaṃ hi*. (60–62)
Then, having placed offerings of weapons upon an archway constructed from firmly set wooden posts,
he should arrange bathing jars made of gold and other precious metals that are free from blemishes.

Thus, immediately after bringing [the deity] to the sacrificial hall, he describes the placement and the fire-offering (*homa*) there with the *astra-mantra* upon an archway made of solid wood, using the word "thus" (*evam*). It has been stated in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras] that the bringing of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*) must first be performed there, and then the installation of the Brahma-stone upon it. Then, having lowered the image from the chariot or other vehicle onto the sacrificial ground, one should place it within the archway made of solid wood where [the deity] is seated.
Then, on the bathing ground, one should perform oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds with the Astra-mantra;
or else, having previously brought the pedestal together with the Brahma-stone.
Having placed [the deity] upon a pedestal on the ground or upon an altar, one should then bring the image and install it upon the *piṇḍikā*. Thus [ends verses 62–63].
As before, having made them possessed of speech, well-proportioned, free from fear,
and purified by means of inspection and other rites, he should do so with a sympathetic heart.
One should consecrate them one by one with the twelve-syllable mantra;
thereafter, one should worship them with that very mantra using offerings such as water for honor (arghya), garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth.
Then one should perform the oblation of those materials according to one's capacity;
having completed it up to the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti), one should then employ the ritual substances in their proper sequence.

The three [offerings] consisting of water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and water for sipping are to be made with the substances previously mentioned; [the water] originates from a river, clay, or a sacred bathing place, and is offered to the beginning, the end, and the middle of the Nāgas and others.
[The clay] from a lake, from the peak of an anthill, or from that which has been trampled by the feet of an elephant;
[the clay] produced from the furrows of a plough, from the horns of a bull, or arising from fields of rice. 68.
Likewise, [the smoke] arises from a cluster of lotuses in one place, in another from cow dung, similarly from a forest fire, and likewise from a kitchen. (69)
Others, however, should place the ashes of the three sacred fires within one jar,
while in another they should place the five products of the cow together with water infused with kuśa grass.
A jar of oil with ghee, as well as a cup filled with water, along with palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, śamī, and red sandalwood [should be prepared]. (71)
In another vessel, decoction water; in yet another, decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā);
[and] vacā, śatāvarī, kanyā, vyāghrī, siṃhī, and kṛtāñjali. || 72 ||
Golomī, siṃhalomī, kuṣṭha, bhūtajaṭā, and mahāgaruḍavegā were in one pitcher, while lāṅgalin was in another. 73.
Mahānīlā, galūcī, sahadevī, śatāvarī,
viṣṇukrāntā, kārkoṭā, sāhvā, and others such as vahnīśikhā.
In another [section] there is yaṣṭī and vārāhakarṇī, as well as gajapippalī;
in yet another are the śrīphala and other purifying fruits.
One should place jars of curd, milk, and ghee, along with two jars containing honey and sugarcane juice; and one should deposit the roots of lotuses into another pair of jars.
Among purifying trees, especially those that yield milky sap,
one should collect a cluster of blossoms together with flowers, leaves, and fruits.
Now, there is one cluster of jasmine creepers beginning with *jāti*, along with the pair consisting of *rocanā* and the two types of *rajanī*, as well as *balā*, *moṭā*, and *padmaka*. (78)
Thus, one should place five items— darbha grass and dūrvā sprouts, along with a mouthful of rice and a heap of śāli rice sprouts— into one water-pot, and indeed place them in another pot as well.
One should place white mustard seeds and the like, as well as *priyaṅgu* known for its fragrance,
along with *nāgakesara*, into another pitcher.
There are seven cultivated medicinal herbs and seven wild ones in the two jars;
as well as Bāhlīka, sandalwood, and resin combined with camphor. 81.

Others, however, say that this group of four consists of the pure elements in another [realm], such as copper, silver, gold, and so forth; while others maintain that it is a great accumulation of those [elements]. (82)
One should place a cluster of coral on two [vessels] and pearls on the other two;
then, water for the guest-offering (arghya) in one, and water from a river-tirtha in the other two.
A jar of all medicinal herbs, then a jar of very cool water,
and a pitcher of fragrant flowers— these are recorded as the forty.
On the left side of the deity, one should place [the deities] starting from the southeast corner (agnikoṇa) up to the station of Yātudhāna, in sequence, by a count of two each. 85.
By means of the arrangement of ten rows, others are likewise [placed] behind;
starting from the northeast corner (īśakoṇa) up to the domain of Agni (āgneyagocara). 86.
One should place only jars filled with cool water;
furthermore, one should place them seven times upon the bed, starting from the northeast corner.
They were filled with scented water up to the level of the wind-pads;
all were established upon their bases and filled with pure water. 88.
Thereafter, one should worship with the root mantra and the twelvefold self-mantra;
having first encircled it with threads, one should cover it immediately thereafter.

Then, having covered [the deity] with cloth according to the prescribed rites and the connections of the Sūtras, he describes the procedure for placing the jars for the purpose of the ritual bath (snāna), beginning with "having placed the bathing jars" and ending with "having indeed covered them with cloth. This means by means of those previously mentioned [rites] stated in the section on initiation (dīkṣā). Since this bathing is also mentioned in the *Pārameśvara*, it was stated that the substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*) will be clarified later in its commentary.

That is contradictory, because the qualification "by those previously mentioned" would be redundant, and because of the distinct nature (*vaijātya*) of substances such as the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) and others which will be clarified further on. *Camasī* is a specific fragrant substance used for removing dirt. *Triphalā* consists of *nellikkāyi*, *aralekāyi*, and *tārekāyi*. *Vacā* is *baje*; Amara states that *vacā* is *ugragandhā*. *Śatāvarī* is *āṣāḍhī*. *Kanyā* is *lolisarakanyā*; the *Nighaṇṭu* calls it *kumārī*. *Vyāghrī* is *gullī*, *siṃhī*, and *āḍhusoge*. [The term] *āṣāḍhī* [is repeated].

*Kanyā* refers to *lolīsarakaṇyā*; according to the *Nighaṇṭu*, it means *kumārī*. *Vyāghrī* is *gullī*, *siṃhī*, or *āḍhusoge*; *kṛtāñjali* is *saṭṭadakarikai*. According to the *Nighaṇṭu*, *kṛtāñjali* is *nāgabālā*. *Golomī* is *pillagarikai*; Amara states, "golomī and śatavīryā. Although the word *golomī* also has the meaning of *vacā* (as in "golomī and śataparvikā"), since *vacā* was already mentioned previously, here *golomī* refers specifically to white dūrvā grass.

*Siṃhalomī* is *nariyāldahullu*; according to Amara, "the *siṃhapucchī* is the *kroṣṭhuvinnā*. *Kuṣṭha* is *cagalakoṣṭha*; according to Amara, "the disease *kuṣṭha* is called *pāribhāvya*. *Bhūmyañjana*. *Mahāgaruḍavegā* is *garuḍanagarigiḍḍā*. *Mahānīlā* is *kariguruga*. According to the *Nighaṇṭu*, *galūcī* is *amṛtavallī*, and *galūcī* is also *amṛtavallī*. *Sahadevī* is well-known. *Viṣṇukrāntā* is also well-known. *Śatāvarī* has been mentioned previously.

*Kārkoṭā*, *toṭṭigiḍḍā*, *hiṃsrā*, and *kārkoṭakī*—this is the *Nighaṇṭu*. *Siṃhā* is *bilva*; *śailūṣa*, *śrīphala*, and *siṃhā*—this is the *Vaidyanighaṇṭu*. *Vahniśikhā* is *giṇimṛbhinagaḍḍe*; "it shall be *lāṅgalikī* and *agniśikhā*"—thus says Amara. *Yaṣṭi* is very sweet. *Vārāhakarṇī* is *aneladālu*. *Balā* is *beṇṇegaruḍa*; "balā, *vāṭyālakī*, and *ghaṇṭā*"—thus says Amara. *Moṭā* is *agalaśuṇṭhī*. *Padmaka* is well known.

The seven cultivated herbs, such as rice (*śāli*) and mung beans (*mudga*), and the seven wild ones, such as bamboo (*veṇu*) and *śyāmāka* millet, mentioned in the section on cooking in the *Īśvara-pārameśvara*, are to be understood here.

Thus, it has been established by Īśvara and Pārameśvara that the consecration using forty jars placed on the left side is designated as "gross-gross" (sthūla-parā); the consecration using forty jars containing only cold water placed at the rear is designated as "gross-subtle" (sthūla-sūkṣma); and the consecration using forty jars filled with fragrant water placed on the right side is designated as "gross-gross" (sthūla-sthūla).

Thus, the placement of the three bathing pitchers on the left side and other parts of the deity should be performed separately in a dedicated bathing pavilion if one exists; in its absence, it should be understood that the placement of the respective bathing pitchers for each day is to be done from east to west upon the specific pedestal intended for that purpose within the sacrificial hall—this has been explained in that very [text]. Furthermore, the time for each of those baths is stated therein: "On the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should perform the bath known as the 'gross' (sthūla-parā)."

"On the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should perform the bathing (snapana), both gross and subtle. On the fourth day, the bath known as 'gross-gross' (sthūlasthūla) should take place. Thus it is said.
Regarding these baths, their expansion when resources are available and their contraction when they are lacking have been explained in that very same chapter on bathing.
And also by the power of devotion and faith, or according to one's means.
One should perform the threefold gross division twice over;
or in the case of a substitute rite (anukalpa), half of that, or a quarter, or even an eighth part.
O best of Brahmins, there should be either four jars, or two each,
or even one jar for each, consisting of all the ritual substances.
Thus [ends the section] from verses 63 to 90.
Then, at the conclusion of that offering, one should prepare two types of beds.
One should worship that infinite [deity] below, endowed with all requisites;
and above that, one should worship the omnipresent Lord through the yoga of origin and dissolution.
Then one should cause the Sarpasāman to be recited, as well as the Saṃjñā-mantra whose essence is the power of knowledge;
having offered oblations one hundred and eight times, one should subsequently prepare the root-mantra.

Now, with two verses [90–92], [the author] states the preparation of two beds for the purpose of opening the eyes and for the consecration (adhivāsa), as well as the worship of Ananta and so forth therein. "At the conclusion of that offering" means immediately after the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa). Regarding the phrase "furnished with all requisites," the requisites for the bed are to be understood as those mentioned by Īśvara and Pārameśvara. "By way of origin and dissolution" means [placing the deity] in the east and other directions in the form of Vāsudeva, and in the southeast and other directions in the form of Puruṣa and the others. [He recites] the mantra beginning with "The serpent-sāman, the supporter of the people," and so forth, and the mantra beginning with "The Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, whose nature is knowledge and power. || 90–92 ||
Then, having offered oblations into the collection of fire-pits with purifying colors such as white and others that are auspicious,
for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess in that mandala.
One should consecrate [the fire] within the central jar near each individual kuṇḍa;
then, by means of the yoga of origin and dissolution, one should indeed sacrifice to the fourfold self (Cāturātmya). 94.

Alternatively, having offered the heart-mantra and so forth to those situated in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, as well as the weapon-mantra to the eight [directions], and having given the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for that purpose, one should cause [the disciple] to recite from the Full [Vidyā] to the Full. || 95 ||

Having performed the *āśrāvaṇa* immediately after those [offerings] consisting of the *ekāyana-yajus*, one should then draw the mandala preceded by one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, for the sake of pacifying any deficiencies or excesses, there is the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*), the consecration of the eight fire-pits starting from the east, the placement of the water-jars (*kumbha*) near each pit, and the worship of Vāsudeva and the others—or alternatively, the worship with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and so forth—in those [pits] according to the sequence of their origin and dissolution; furthermore, the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the central pit for that purpose, and the worship of Vāsudeva and the others—or alternatively, the worship with the heart-mantra and so forth—in those [pits] according to the sequence of their origin and dissolution.

Regarding the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for that purpose in the central pit, and the recitation from the *Pūrṇa* [section] beginning with the *Ekāyana*, he says "having offered" in four verses. According to the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, the term *āśrāvita* refers to the Atharvaveda. (93–96)
Then, first with the weapon-mantra and then with the water from the auspicious jar, [he sprinkled it]. 96.
Having sprinkled the image, one should then bathe it with clay and water;
immediately thereafter, one should cause the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras and the Bala mantras to be recited there.
Then, with a jar of cow dung, one should cause the cows to drink here while the mantra "Bhūtistvam" is recited by the master of the earth. 98.
Thereafter, one should cause him to recite the four [verses] over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, having worshipped as before according to the rules with water from the camasa vessel, [one should proceed]. 99.
Having washed her, honored her, and settled her upon a bed,
he himself took a metallic probe and consecrated his eyes with mantras.

Now, with four verses beginning with "atha," he describes the placement of the image upon the bed for the purpose of opening its eyes, preceded by the rites of ablution, adornment, and worship using several of the previously established large jars designated as the *snāpanakalaśas*, starting with the water-jars for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. The phrase "with the water of the auspicious jar" (*māṅgalyakalaśāmbhasā*) means with the water from the three jars known as *pādya*, *arghya*, and *ācamana*. Regarding "with the water of the *camasa*": a *camasa* is a specific substance used for removing oil, which was also mentioned previously in the section on propitiation (*ārādhanaprakaraṇa*).
It is described as being mixed with the powder of turmeric (*rajanī*) and slightly infused with *padmaka*.
"Immediately after that, a *camasa* vessel should be given for the purpose of anointing (*udvartana*).
Regarding this, the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna* states: "A *camasī* is a specific type of fragrant substance. (96–100)
Circumambulating while reciting the supreme mantra, he should slightly mark the two eyes;
then, having bathed and been inspected, the artisan should [proceed] with the weapon consecrated by that mantra.
One should reveal it correctly through the ritual prescribed by rule;
one should cause the Sāman known as Vāruṇa to be recited along with the Cāndra Sāman by those who chant the Sāmaveda.
Then, having placed honey and clarified butter into two metallic vessels,
one should fill them with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ" and subsequently offer them as oblations.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] with a stream of nectar flowing from the heart and ending at the top of the head;
one should then meditate on a lunar disc upon his head for the sake of pacifying the striking. 104.
He should give the measuring sticks and other tools along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the artisan;
thereafter, the worshiper of the Guru should perform the gift of a cow (godāna). || 105 ||
Having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the other image-protectors according to one's capacity,
one should thereafter perform the cremation and the rite of restoration (sāpyāyana).

Now, he describes the procedure for opening the eyes, beginning with the words "having consecrated the eyes" and ending with "and the sacrificial fees for the image-protectors. The meaning of "made of radiant material" (*taijasī*) is that it is produced from a luminous substance; that is to say, it is either golden or silver. It should be understood here that both eyes are to be anointed with a single probe (*śalākā*). In other *saṃhitās*, however, it is stated that both eyes are to be anointed with two probes, one of gold and one of silver.

For this very reason, both positions regarding Īśvara and Pārameśvara have been stated: "With that [needle] smeared with clarified butter, or even with silver, one should scratch the left eye. This means [the eye] is consecrated by that mantra; "beheld" means gazed upon with the Netra-mantra. The Vāruṇa Sāman begins with *pramitrāya prāryamṇa* and so forth. The Cāndra Sāman begins with *cāndraṃ cāndraṃ cāndraṃ cāndraṃ cāndram* and so forth. Regarding the word "filling," the phrase "pair of eyes" is to be supplied as the object. Thus it is further elaborated in the Īśvara and Pārameśvara [Tantras]: "One should fill the pair of eyes with honey and ghee in due order."
"Then one should offer oblations with that very root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Thus [it is said].
Other many specific details should be understood as they are set forth in various places. (101-106)

One should install the twelve-syllable mantra up to the crown of the head for the purpose of the Mūrti, as before, in the consecrated [liṅga] which has been joined with the seven pervasions (vyāptis) and purified by sprinkling and other rites. || 107 ||

Having brought [the image] down onto the pedestal and wrapped it with two garments from below, he describes—in the two verses beginning with "having given" (vv. 107–108)—the placement of the image upon the bathing-pedestal, which is endowed with the sevenfold pervasion starting from Ananta and preceded by the rites of burning and nourishing, along with the deposition of the root-mantra and the wrapping with two garments.
Then, with the heart-mantra, the water from the jars, which have been rotated twice in succession, should be poured out in order. || 108 ||

One should cause the Brahmins to bathe and recite the Vedic revelation beginning with "Oṣadhīnām" (Of the herbs), and immediately thereafter, the Ṛgveda hymns beginning with "Yā oṣadhayaḥ" (Those herbs...). 109.
When it has been thus sprinkled with the ten remaining jars,
then [it is sprinkled] with four jars by the four bearers of the forms.

One should cause him to be bathed according to the rules with the Ṛg and Sāman verses first, and then have him recite; from the Ṛgveda, one should have him recite "ud uttamaṃ," and from the Yajurveda, "draviṇam. (111)
Then he taught the Vāruṇa Sāman; from Atharvan, the knower of Sāmans, he received it;
then [he taught] "This is your Varuṇa," and then the purifying Ṛc verse, "pavitraṃ te."
Then he should cause the Sāma-singers to recite the *vasoḥ pavitram* Yajus;
thereafter, having urged them on, he should cause the Ekāyana-singers to recite the *pavitraṃ te* Sāman.
The community of image-worshippers [should recite] the four Pāvamānī verses;
at the end of that, however, they should utter the supreme mantra: "The Blessed One is the Vyūha. (114)
Thereafter, [he should perform] the purificatory mantra "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," and then with all the mantras of manifestation (vibhava-mantras) over which [the materials] have been consecrated.
Having sprinkled with the water-pot, however, by means of the supreme arrangement-mantras (vyūha-mantra).
Having bathed and worshipped [the deity], one should offer more than a hundred oblations.

Now, regarding the remaining jars, he describes the sequence of consecration (*abhiṣecana*), the fire-offering (*homa*) that fills its deficiencies, and so forth, starting from "Then, with the jars mentioned in order" up to "one should offer more than a hundred [oblations]. (Verses 108–116)
Then, having pervaded [the disciple] as it truly is with the syllable Om (praṇava), he should cause him to recite:
"Do not step forth" from the Ṛgveda, and "May life [be granted]" from the Yajurveda. 117.
Since the Sāman is indeed the out-breath and the in-breath, therefore let there be salutation to Prāṇa;
then, O Brahmins, let the supreme mantra "yātavya" be recited by those who have reached the single path. 118.

Then, with the Praṇava, preceded by the recollection of the pervasion of the Blessed One within the image, he describes the recitation of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra in the four Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda and in the Ekāyana, using two verses beginning with "yathāvat" (117–118).
Then the worshipper, endowed with meditation and possessing right intellect, should recite:
"Oṃ! I invoke the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose pair of feet is saluted by the hosts of immortals, the cause of the universe, and the immeasurable one."
The primordial one, whose body is eternal, seated upon the throne of the Praṇava,
possessing the form of a thousand full moons, suns, and fires.
The supreme object of meditation, the one to be known by all knowers of the Vedas,
possessing the gentle forms of Varāha,
Kapila, and Narasiṃha, with limbs adorned by the Śrīvatsa mark and the great jewel Kaustubha—
Holding in his hands the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.

O Blessed One, you are indeed all-pervading; even though I invoke you, you come as surely as wind is drawn by a fan, or as fire, though hidden, emerges from friction; for even when invoked, you likewise come to the place of worship.
O Wearer of the Garland, O Acyuta, O All-pervading Lord, O Embodiment of the Supreme Self,
O Omniscient One, O Protector, O Supreme Sovereign, O Omnipotent One! Come to me, show me compassion, and accept this image.
Accept this worship today out of a desire to show me favor.
Then one should personally recite the four verses of invocation; this he states with the words beginning "Dhyāna... (verses 119–122).

Then, having wiped [the deity] with a cloth, one should worship with the previously mentioned offerings, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); thereafter, one should cause the mantras consisting of the Ṛgveda to be recited.
The mantra "arcāya te" and the Sāman "yac cārcitas tvam," as well as the word "bhagavān"—these are for those who know them; then, when the fire has been gratified, [he should offer]. 124.
Having praised him with the *jita* mantra, he should again cause the chanters to recite that which is known as the *rathantara*, together with the *gāyatra-sāman*. 125.
Having recited the twelve-syllable mantra, bound the mudrā, and prostrated,
one should then petition the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, with the eight-limbed obeisance.
Indeed, by means of this very form now become incarnate, gladden the citizens of the world who do not yet know the truth. 127.
By entering within which, indeed, through the power of even a short time, people attain liberation from the sins arising from thousands of previous births. 128.
For the Blessed One, the Lord who acts for the benefit of the world, being thus worthy of honor,
should then place them upon his hands and feet and cause those consisting of the Ṛgveda to recite them.
Having made the Rigvedic mantra "uttiṣṭha" the consecration for the stable Brahma-chariot, which was well-yoked and provided with milk, ghee, curds, and rice; || 130 ||
For the sake of pacifying the distress caused by famine, one should subsequently have the *Asyavāmīya* hymn recited, accompanied by offerings of fine rice and fruits. (131)
O Mahāmati, one should recite the mantra of power consisting of that [essence] ten times;
one should recite the heart-mantra itself, restrained at the beginning and end, and the armor-mantra with the heart-mantra. 132.
One should cause the sacrificial offering (bali) to be whirled in all directions while it is being presented;
as before, one should perform the scattering of jewels, gold, and garments.

And worship of the divine sense-bases (āyatana) and others should be performed as previously described, as well as for those who know the Pañcarātra, for ascetics (yati), and for celibate students (brahmacārin). 134.
One should also give gifts to those devoted to the six duties and to the wretched;
this applies as long as one proceeds for a hundred steps with the mantra-image mounted upon the chariot. || 135 ||
That chariot, with the sound of musical instruments, brings great fruit of sacrifice;
the worshipper, whose desires are fulfilled and who is firm in his vows, attains this eternally.

Then, having stationed the chariot at the location of the archway (toraṇa), one should worship the Lord with water for the feet, the arghya offering, flowers, and incense; and having offered salutations, one should cause [the hymn] to be recited. || 137 ||
Reciting the entire Puruṣasūkta, which consists of sixteen verses beginning with "uttiṣṭha" and ending with "sajit," he should lead [the deity] into the sacrificial hall. || 138 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon the bed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should complete the journey-offering (yātrā-homa).
Then, at the location of its head, in the jar situated upon the wheel-base (cakrādhāra), [one should perform the rite]. 139.
One should worship the eye, encased within the weapon-mantra, according to the previously stated characteristics;
and having worshipped it again with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth, while it remains upon the bed.
Having covered [the deity] with armor and cloth, one should then stand near the feet of the Lord and place the mantras of the insignia (alañchana) according to their respective positions. || 141 ||
From the feet, one should [place] the twelve limbs; then, from Dāmodara and the others, likewise the mantras of their powers, characterized by radiant pervasiveness.
Then, one should meditate by means of the seed-syllable of Īśvara according to its actual state;
likewise, one should do so with that most excellent mantra, which is identical [to the deity] from the feet upward.
But by the same process of dissolution as before, that very supreme state [is attained] through the pervasive self consisting of inner light, which has speech as its essential form. 144.

Having understood [the Lord] as perfectly tranquil, all-pervading, and like a waveless ocean, one should cause the followers of the Pāñcarātra to recite the Vidyā, the Gada, and other such [scriptures]. 145.

Immediately thereafter, one should cause [the disciple] to recite from the Ṛgveda the mantra known as Dhāraṇā, which pertains to the renunciation of the body, beginning with "jīmūtasya" and "nāsadāsīt". 146.
Having offered oblations in this sequence, O Great-minded One, with sesame seeds and likewise with clarified butter, numbering one hundred and fifty times, using these mantras: 147.
Having properly offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) characterized by the ritual conclusion, one should then meditate upon that supreme Brahman as it has arisen, just as before. 148.

Indeed, by means of its own inherent nature consisting of all powers, which is of the essence of vital energy and strength, just as [the fragrance arises] from the essence of the fragrant substance itself. (149)
Just as a seed exists within the nature of a tree, and the ocean within the form of a bubble,
so too does this indefinable power reside within its own mirror of power.
O high-minded one, having established himself through his own sovereignty, the Lord of the Universe assumes a body in the form of mantra for the sake of perfect propitiation.
The expansion of that which has attained diversity, and the loss of luster of the collection of seeds of consciousness as it proceeds [toward dissolution]. 152.
Even when manifested, it is obscured by a powerful, formless,
and dense thicket of ignorance, which consists of both the eternal and the non-eternal.
Having thus recollected the root mantra, one should visualize [the deity] residing in the heart-lotus of the image,
whose body consists of that very substance and is endowed with the rays of the six powers.
One should remember [the deity] withdrawing [the universe] again by the very path previously described;
thereafter, one should again remember the stainless essential nature (svarūpa) through the form of the image (mūrti). 155.
When that Supreme Lord, having attained autonomy through the nature of mantra, leads [the soul] in this manner according to the previously mentioned rule, then [this occurs]. 156.
One should then urge the Atharvans with "the thousand-headed god," and have the Brahmins recite the king of mantras beginning with "O Dhātṛ, O Adhyakṣa. (157)
"He who has eyes on all sides" is to be meditated upon;
and following that, "Two birds," and then again, "From that god... (158).

Then, having recited the Puruṣasūkta consisting of Ṛg verses, and then the hymn beginning with "tataḥ paratamā tu," one should worship the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśa) as he lies upon his bed according to the procedure for the image.
In order to achieve perpetual presence within the mandala until its completion,
one should effect their confinement and bring them into proximity with great magnificence.
Having duly gratified them along with their limbs and the presiding deities of the forms,
he should draw water from his own form-vessel into a bowl while reciting the mantra.
One should gradually offer [the oblation] upon the head of the image by all [deities], beginning with Ekāyana;
having thus fully gratified the mantra together with its retinue, [one should proceed]. 162.
Then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with abundant clarified butter and other substances,
[he performs this for] the earth and the other elements, which have entered the image as its very self and constitute its limbs.
Because it is complete even in its withdrawal, and for the sake of attaining a state of condensed unity,
there is indeed the pacification of the apertures that have arisen from the very beginning.
For the purpose of nourishing the mantras, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with ritual substances;
specifically, twelve oblations for each of the four "hearts" (caturhṛdaya). 165.

Having first touched the clarified butter (ājya) up to the ankles and reaching as far as the knees, one should offer it into the fire; likewise, one should offer the curd (dadhi) from the navel down to the region of the knees. 166.
One should offer milk from the navel up to the ears, and honey from the ears up to the head;
having combined these, one should offer it throughout the entire body without exception.

Thus, following the invocation (*āvāhana*), there is the cleansing of the image (*bimba-saṃmārjana*), worship with *arghya* and other offerings, the recitation of mantras beginning with "I worship Thee" (*arcāmi te*), the fire-oblation (*havana*) in the central and directional sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and the chanting of the *Gāyatrī* and *Rathantara* Sāmans preceded by the hymn of praise beginning with "Victory! (*jitaṃta*). Then follow the silent recitation (*japa*), ritual gestures (*mudrā*), prostrations (*praṇāma*), and formal petitions (*vijñāpana*). Furthermore, there is the festival of the Lord upon the Brahma-chariot (*brahmaratha*), the consecration of the bed (*śayyādhivāsa*), the application of the insignia (*lāñchananyāsa*), and [the rites concerning] Dāmodara and other [forms], their respective powers (*śakti*), the *Viśākhayūpa* seed-syllable (*bīja*), the seed-syllables of their respective forms, and the *Praṇava*.

Or else, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra from the feet to the head in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*); meditate upon the Blessed One as being perfectly tranquil like a waveless ocean; recite the mantras that effect the withdrawal, such as the *Vidyā* and the *Gadā*; perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with each of the mantras placed upon the image a hundred times; offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); and contemplate the Blessed One as having arisen through his own nature, which consists of all powers, within the heart-lotus of the image.

The recollection of the root mantra endowed with its six powers; the contemplation of the withdrawal of the five-elemental body according to the procedure taught in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*; the contemplation of the arising of the form consisting of the pure mantra; the recitation of the mantras expressive of that [form], such as "The thousand-headed God" (*sahasraśīrṣā devaḥ*); the worship of the Lord seated upon His couch according to the rules with offerings consisting of ritual services, physical contact, and edible food; and the satiation of the Lord in the central fire-pit and the directional pits with seven pieces of fuel wood and other offerings.

He describes the sprinkling of the reflection with water from each respective vessel; then the satiation of the Lord of Mantras together with his retinue using clarified butter and other substances; the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation); and the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) consisting of twelve offerings made with each of the four substances—clarified butter and the rest—preceded by touching the corresponding limbs while reciting the heart-mantra. This is stated in the section beginning with "Then, having wiped [the deity] with a cloth" and ending with "having touched the entire body. (123–167)
Having consecrated the pedestal like an image, the Brahma-stone is likewise divided;
or rather, whichever deity has been prescribed for whom, that [deity] is the one presiding over the vital breath (prāṇa).
Then, having wrapped it with variegated cloths, the Brahma-śilā-homa should be performed one hundred and eight times with the Cakra-mantra.
Then, for that purpose, the Bahvṛcas and others separately [performed the rite] with Gāyatrī verses and with the Ekāyana mantras beginning with "ajasya nābhau. (170)

Having made the path, the objective world, the embodied form, or even the object of enjoyment—which exists separately—the seat (pīṭha) that is the abode of the deities, and having brought this into the understanding; 171.
One should offer oblations oneself with the *praṇava* alone, or with those *vyāhṛtis*,
or with other root-mantras ending in the *praṇava*, O wielder of the plow.

Now, he describes the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) for the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), beginning with "Having consecrated the pedestal like the image" and ending with "O Lāṅgalin," concluding with the *praṇava*. One view is that the pedestal and the Brahma-stone should be meditated upon solely in the form of the Lord’s image; another view is that they should be meditated upon as the presiding deities (*abhimānadevatā*) of their respective pedestals. The presiding deity of the pedestal is either one among Ananta, Kūrma, and Mīna, or all three of them.

The meaning is that for each [deity], whatever is prescribed—such as "a wheel made of eight metals," and so forth, which will be described later. However, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, only Ananta is presented, stating "the deity who presides over the vital breath, Ananta. That is weak, because it contradicts the statement "for whomsoever [it] is prescribed. (168–172)
Then, he should always perform the libation with the vehicle-mantra;
others [should do so] with their own names preceded by the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā. 173.

Then, with the words "then," he speaks of the *homa* [fire sacrifice] using the *garuḍa-mantra* and the *parivāra-mantras*. In certain *Pārameśvara* manuscripts, the ungrammatical reading "tato havanamantreṇa" (then by the offering-mantra) is seen; in its commentary as well, this ungrammatical reading alone is explained as meaning "by the offering-mantra, that is, by a mantra ending in *svāhā*. Others explain it as meaning "by the *parivāra-mantras*. || 173 ||
The retention of those [breaths] that have been satisfied must indeed be performed until the end of the full [cycle], by means of a seat provided with water, with devotion, and with recitation. 174.
[This applies] to the Lord who is the Sovereign of All,
both in his own embodied forms and in his word-natured, formless [forms], as well as to that which consists of the Vedas.

Thus, with these two verses beginning with "saṃnirodha," he describes the final cessation occurring immediately after the installation of all the attendant deities and the Lord, the Sovereign of All, up to the concluding full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). "With water and the seat" means with the arghya-water contained in the kūrca-grass mat.
[The sequence is]: invocation, presence, cessation, and likewise worship.
"At the time of dismissal (visarjana), one should always perform the offering of the arghya vessel before [placing] the vessel [of water].

This is because the offering of the arghya was previously mentioned even in the context of the ritual withdrawal (saṃnirodha). "With devotion" means by means of meditation (dhyāna). The reading "sarvaiḥ svakasya devasya" (by all [the mantras] of one's own deity) is indeed the more elegant one.

The natural meaning is that a "confinement" (saṃnirodha) must be performed by all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and teachers upon their own deities stationed in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍa) in the east and other directions—namely, within their own forms such as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and so forth—and likewise upon the Lord who consists of the Vedas, whose nature is the four Vedas, and who is propitiated in the intermediate fire-pits; this confinement is to be performed within the formless, sound-bodied [deities] existing in four ways as the sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan.

Even when the reading is *sarveśvarasya*, the meaning is exactly the same; however, in that case, the words "by the teachers and the officiating priests" (*ācārya-ṛtvigbhiḥ*) must be supplied as an ellipsis. (174–175)
Having done this and likewise stationed the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in the various directions,
one should satisfy them with milk-rice (pāyasa) in the areas adjacent to the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Having received the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the mantra should then be propitiated by them.
Next, [the author] describes the feeding of the image-guardians (mūrtipa) with milk-rice and so forth in verse 176–177, beginning with the words "having performed" (kṛtvā).
Then, having remembered the God while he was sleeping and having covered him, [he departed].
Having worshipped and paid homage, he should cause all those who are devoted to dance and song, preceded by the reciters of hymns, to enter there. 178.
He describes the assignment of those stationed in the intermediate directions to the recitation of the *praṇava*, and those situated in the cardinal directions to the twelve-syllable mantra;

furthermore, with two verses beginning with "atha," he describes the wrapping of the Lord’s garments, the worship, and the prostrations while He was sleeping; the recitation of the root-mantra until dawn by those devoted to a single goal (*ekāyana*); the recitation of the *praṇava* by the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*); and the employment of various people in hymns, auspicious songs, dances, and so forth. (177–179)
Then, with his hands holding the arghya offering, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), he should proceed to that temple. || 179 ||
Therefore, one should destroy obstacles with white mustard seeds consecrated by the weapon-mantra;
or else, one should first or now dig a pit in the middle according to this procedure.

One should establish the womb [of the mandala] according to one's own measure, dividing it into seven parts; starting from the location of the door, one should mark all directions using equal threads. 181.
In the middle of the door is the end of the quarters; the presiding deities of the quarters are the Piśācas, the Mānavas, the Devas, and he who is the Supreme Puruṣa.

Then, regarding the entry into the interior of the temple: the removal of obstacles therein; the excavation of the pit for the purpose of consecrating the *brahmaśilā* (the foundational stone); the sevenfold division of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) for that purpose; a description of the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of those respective sections; and a discernment of which [deities] such as the Cāturātmya are to be installed or avoided in those various sections, along with the specific fruits resulting from each—this is stated starting from the verse beginning "holding the *arghya*, flowers, and unbroken rice" (*sārghyapuṣpākṣatakaraḥ*) up to the end of the section ending with "this is the rule for those without desire" (*akāmānām ayaṃ vidhiḥ*).
The "eight qualities" (*guṇāṣṭaka*) refer to [attributes] such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which amounts to liberation (*mokṣa*). (Verses 179–192)
O Mahāmati, for others who have been installed except for the four-faced [Brahmā], worship performed in their own proper places brings about accomplishment without delay. 183.
O Lord, if one seeks to propitiate the divine portion by means of forceful aggression, many obstacles will arise; therefore, that path must be avoided by oneself.
Then, O wielder of the plow, by means of the auspicious and divine throne, the middle station known as Śilā is established for the fourfold self. 185.
Above the middle portion of the womb, one should carefully join [the thread];
then, having omitted one part from the back region, it should indeed be joined. (186)
O Mahāmati, at the end of the two stone slabs, a pedestal should be joined above the two parts at the front of the image. (187)
This is beneficial for the installation of this square and elongated pedestal;
such indeed is the rule for the square one, O wielder of the plow. (188)
However, for the sake of constant worship, the altar (vedi) should always be moved forward;
or else, he who constantly worships the Lord should do so upon the pedestal (pīṭha). || 189 ||
That stone must indeed be established by him in the Middle Country;
for such is the power of propitiation and such is the power of the fruit. 190.
The proper installation of the images, together with their pedestals, should be performed;
through the divine and human portions, there shall be results pertaining to both this world and the next. || 191 ||
From the portion belonging to the gods and Brahmā comes the eightfold excellence pertaining to this world; but for those free from desire, there is equality regarding liberation—this is the rule.
If [the vessel] is broken, one should perform the rite again once it has been restored through the power of focused expectation;
when it has been melted with the water of the weapon-mantra and smeared with sandalwood and other substances while reciting the heart-mantra.

Then, by means of the previously mentioned procedure, there is the confinement of the mantras within a pit, obstructed by jars, each being restrained in its own respective place through the power of meditation.
Having performed the worship as prescribed up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should deposit [the offering] there in quantities measuring six, five, or four globules (gola). 195.
One should take a stone that has slightly protruded from its pedestal, which is very stable,
and which was formerly fashioned with nine apertures for the sake of liberation, though it has been swallowed by the pedestal for the sake of worldly prosperity.
Sumantu, however, should teach that even there [the mantra] is established as "pratiṣṭhāsi.
Then, one should place five [syllables] at a time, beginning with the east, according to their respective powers. (197)

Then, in that pit which has been consecrated by washing, anointing with sandalwood paste, and other rites, he describes—in four and a half verses beginning with "bhinna"—the re-confinement of the deities who were previously confined in new jars during the time of the palace's construction, according to their respective locations as determined by [the deity's] intellect and so forth; the worship ending with the satiation of the fire according to the rules; the installation of the stone marked with gems possessing the characteristics mentioned therein; and the recitation of the mantra "pratiṣṭhāsī" (be established).

Generally, however, it means that [the sacrificial pit] should be measured by six, five, or four *golakas* in depth—that is, its thickness (*ghana*) should be twelve, ten, or eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). (193–197)
In the stone pits there, one finds minerals such as diamond and gold, as well as yellow orpiment and uśīra; furthermore, to the south of that, there are grains of rice.
Then there was sapphire, copperas, sandalwood, sesame seeds, pearls, silver, and lead. 199.
Along with uśīra and mung beans, there is a ruby in the north;
then bell-metal with a royal stone and a king-corn (rājendra) along with chickpeas. 200.
One should first place the Viśaṅka in the center, and then outside of that; likewise, one should place it individually in the intermediate directions according to the method of progression. 201.
Iron, beginning with lapis lazuli, then the discus-marked stone and mica;
in the directions of the Lord (East), the Quarter (South), and the Wind (Northwest) are the ṣāṣṭika grain, topaz, and emerald.
Gaurikā, Śārikā, and Maṣūrā are located right here; then follows Yātudik.

Next, he describes the method for depositing jewels and other items into those pits, beginning with "In the east, etc., by means of power... and ending with "...and cause them to recite the six verses. (197–203)
And mahānīla, vaṅga, as well as pāṣāṇamākṣika. || 203 ||
Barley, along with aloeswood, are indeed fiery; likewise are crystal, copper, realgar, wheat, and śaṅkhapuṣpī. || 204 ||
Then, having covered all those things in the center and that entire group of pits with plaster, one should recite the mantra along with its ancillaries at every step.
Having worshipped them, one should cause the recitation of the Yajurveda and the *camasatka* hymns;
thereafter, having placed it within that cavity, one should set down the pedestal.
O Mahāmati, above that is a wheel made of eight metals,
which has as its own support whatever arises from the specific [element] known as the twelvefold.
Above that is a lotus made of gold, or born of that [gold], or even of copper;
for these five, situated in their proper order, reside within the fourfold self (caturātman).
One should place Ananta within the wheel, and Mīna and Kūrma within the Kṛta;
Kūrma and Ananta within the Mīna, and Mīna and Ananta within that [Kṛta].
A lotus is prescribed for everyone; however, one should install an infinite [lotus] for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) in the pavilion during the rite of installation. 210.
Having performed the *nasya* up to the final stage, and having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) here for the ritual action,
the rite with darbha-grass water should be performed as before, together with the bearers of the forms.

Above that, he describes the installation of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the installation of the wheels (*cakra*) and so forth in the corresponding pit, beginning with "one should place the pedestal above that" and ending with "the rite of darbha-water should be performed. The meaning is as follows: whatever is its own natural support arising from the specific [deities] known as the twelve, [it is assigned thus]: for the group of six enemies beginning with Ananta among the gods, the tortoise (*kūrma*) is the support; for the group of six enemies beginning with Mīna, the fish (*mīna*) is the support.

In the *Cāturātmyaprakriyā* belonging to the system of fourfold nature (*caturātman*), this pentad refers to the pentad of the wheel (*cakra*), the serpent (*ananta*), the tortoise (*kūrma*), the fish (*mīna*), and the lotus (*padma*). Thus, the established meaning is that when installing deities of manifestation (*vibhava*) other than Ananta, Kūrma, and Mīna, one should first place the wheel in the pit of the pedestal (*pīṭhagarta*), then on top of that one of those three—the serpent, the tortoise, or the fish—which serves as the support for the respective group of twelve (*dviṣaṭka*), and finally, on top of that, the lotus; these three alone are to be installed.

In the installation of the *cakra*, one should place Ananta in the pit of the pedestal beneath it; beneath that Ananta, the Fish and the Tortoise; beneath the Fish, the Tortoise and Ananta; and beneath that Tortoise, the Fish and Ananta. A lotus is prescribed for all [deities], including the *cakra* and others. However, in the installation of that lotus, one should place Ananta beneath it. Furthermore, it is stated that in the rite of installing Khageśa (Viṣṇu) in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), one should install the *cakra*.

Regarding the phrase "having performed the final libation (pūrṇāntika-tarpaṇa)," it should be understood that this is done with the mantras of the wheels (cakras) and so forth. Furthermore, it is understood that the rite of darbha-water is for the purpose of sprinkling the interior of the womb-chamber (garbhageha) and other areas. (206–211)
Then, having worshipped the deity, one should awaken him and recite this:
"O you whose essence is mantra, withdraw your own fiery form. (212)
O Supreme Lord, may there be gentleness in the common substratum for the sake of stability;
salutations be unto you, Hṛṣīkeśa; arise, O Supreme Lord! (213)
For the sake of showing me favor, take recourse in the ground of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
then, having opened [the door] with the heart, the King of Mantras shall indeed cast off sleep. 214.
Having raised [the image] by force together with the bearers of the image using the Mūrtimantra,
and having exited through the archway, [one performs] four circumambulations.

One should place [the deity] at the front of the door of the pedestal of the temple and, having offered water for the feet, the arghya, and water for sipping, one should cause it to enter with the heart-mantra. || 216 ||
Then, one who knows that [tradition] should teach him the *Śākhādya* without touching it;
after that, the *Catuścakra* and the *Pura ekādaśa*. (217)
Then, with a white silk cloth consecrated by the *varma* mantra,
one should first wrap the stalk of the lotus-feet using the *śikhā* mantra.
Having unified Agni and Soma by means of that which begins and ends with the Praṇava,
and having established them with the root mantra, one should exhale the wind from the left side.
One should recite the two mantras "Pratiṣṭhā" and "Liṅga" in succession,
while firmly maintaining one's own form as peaceful and consisting of Brahman.

Then, when the auspicious moment (lagna) has arrived: the awakening and worship of the Blessed One; the formal petition beginning with "O Mantra-Self" (mantrātman); the lifting up of the Blessed One who has abandoned sleep; the raising him up together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij); his exit through the gateway of the arch (toraṇa); four circumambulations of the temple; the offering of water for the feet (pādya) and other honors at the palace door; his entry within; the recitation of the mantra beginning with "catuścakra"; the wrapping of the lotus-feet with fine silk (dukūla); [and the placement] in the center of the pedestal.

Regarding the installation of the image (*bimbasthāpana*) and the recitation of the consecration mantra (*pratiṣṭhāliṅgamantra*), he says: "Then one should awaken the Deity," beginning from there up to the end of the two mantras, ending with "one should recite them in sequence. The meaning of "having balanced Agni and Soma" is "having performed breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). This has been explained in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna* as well: "One should release the wind from the left" means one should emit the breath through the left nostril.

The two words "pratiṣṭhā" and "liṅga" refer to the two mantras declared in the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda, meaning the mantras beginning with "pratiṣṭhāsi. Alternatively, according to the commentary of Pārameśvara, it is stated that "pratiṣṭhāsi" is a Sāman and "dhruvādyaiḥ" is a Yajus. (212–220)
Since he has emerged for the benefit of all with a nature endowed with the six qualities, he is therefore brought slightly down from the state of Brahman to the portion of the gods.
Indeed, for the sake of attaining the fruits such as liberation, one should—without hesitation—hold that which is already in the hand, while keeping the sense of wonder within the heart. 222.

He states the reasoning for bringing even a small portion of the divine share for the Lord who has been established in the Brahma-pada with two verses beginning with "śāntam. It should be understood that the bringing of the divine share occurs on the left side (*vāmabhāga*). Thus it is said in the *Pārameśvara*: "Even where the installation in the Brahma-pada alone is prescribed, there too one should take a small portion of the substance from the left."

Regarding this, it is written in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*: "By the phrase 'the peaceful form consisting of Brahman,' the previously stated meaning of 'I invoke' is recalled, because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), as in the cases of 'He offers the Agnihotra' and 'He cooks the barley-gruel,' and likewise in the case of 'The twilight bath. However, in this context, there is nothing whatsoever seen that would justify recalling the meaning of "I invoke. Furthermore, the sequence of meaning is to be followed over the sequence of recitation only when there is a contradiction in their respective meanings;
here, no such contradiction is observed.

If it is objected that the invocation (*āvāhana*) at the time of bathing is contradictory because it occurs even before the installation of the image (*bimba*), we say no; for at that time, without the invocation of the Lord, the worship, festival, lying down, consecration (*adhivāsa*), mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*), and the offering of the supreme food (*paramānna*) and so forth would be utterly improper in relation to a mere image.

Furthermore, since you consider invocation (*āvāhana*) prior to the placement of the image (*bimbasthāpana*) to be contradictory, how can you accept invocation prior to the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) as non-contradictory? Moreover, regarding the phrase "the peaceful form consisting of Brahman" (*śāntaṃ brahmamayaṃ rūpam*), [it means] that from the abode of Brahman, the Blessed One has emerged with his own six-fold nature for the benefit of all, having relied upon and taken hold of his own peaceful form—that is, the form existing in the state of both quiescence and emergence (*śāntodita*). Therefore, [one should invite] the deity slightly from that place of Brahman.

How can one perform the recollection of the invocation (*āvāhana*) within the section concerning the instruction on the meaning "one should cause [the deity] to go outside"? What more need be said? (220–222)
Having offered arghya with the entire-body mantra, one should then recollect the root mantra;
then, indeed, with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra recited over it, [one should seal it] as if with adamantine glue.
One should perform the installation of the image, the pedestal, and the stone as a single unity;
then, having meditated upon the root mantra, which possesses the characteristics of the perfectly tranquil Brahman. (224)

Now, with the two verses beginning with "karastham," he describes the application of the eight-fold binding (*bandhana*) preceded by the dismissal of the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) and the formal conclusion of the ritual work. Here, in the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, one might ask: "Since there is no occasion for the binding of the *kautuka* (protective amulet) during each ritual act as there is in the *Padma-tantra* and others, how is it to be released? To this, the doubt is resolved: "In the absence of that [binding] during each ritual act, one should bind the *kautuka* as before at the time of the preliminary water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*).
Thus, this doubt arose only for the commentator of the *Pārameśvara*, and not for anyone else.
Having honored him with the arghya offering,
he should then place consecrated white mustard seeds in his right hand and first cause him to recite this verse:
Likewise, one should place all the jewels that destroy demons within the protective amulet.
Thus, [the term *kautuka*] was used previously in the context of the *kautuka* [rite]. Now, one might object:

"The status of this as a *kautuka* is not possible, because the status of *kautuka* belongs only to that which was mentioned at the time of the water-soaking (*jalādhivāsa*) in the passage: 'having bound the *kautuka* as before'. If you think thus, you should not be deluded. The statement, "Then the *kautuka* held in the hand must be released by means of the heart," was spoken by Sātvata. Since the water-soaking itself was not mentioned there, the sentence "having bound the *kautuka* as before" does not even exist in that context.

Therefore, based on a prior consideration of the sequence beginning with "having honored him with arghya," [it follows that] the dismissal belongs to the *pratisara-bandha* itself; thus, remain composed. (222–224)
"One should remember that everything, from the foundation up to the top of the banner, is pervaded by Him.
Having first performed this general integration (sāmānyasandhāna), it is then specified as follows: || 225 ||
According to their gross, subtle, and supreme nature, the gross [form] is sixfold and extends up to the pedestal stone;
likewise, the subtle is in the pedestal, and the supreme is in the form of the image.

Then, with two and a half verses beginning with "The root mantra," he describes the general integration (*sāmānya-sandhāna*), which consists of recollecting the pervasive presence (*vyāpti*) of the root mantra from its base up to the tip of the banner situated above the temple; furthermore, he describes the specific integration (*viśeṣa-sandhāna*) of that same mantra through its sixfold divisions—starting with the heart-mantra—into the gross form in the *brahma-śilā*, the subtle form on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the supreme form in the image (*bimba*). For he will later state that the banner is positioned at the front of the temple, rising to a height of three parts starting from the spire (*śikhā*) and adorned by the king of birds.
"Having consecrated the flagstaff, one should install it with the *śikhā-mantra*.

For this very reason, it is also established in the *Utsavādhyāya* (Chapter on Festivals) of both the *Īśvara* and *Parameśvara* [Tantras]: "The Garuda-flag is installed at the very tip of the spire (*śikhā*) of the temple. (224–226)
Then one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the deities upon the pedestal (pīṭha);
or else, for those items intended for the service of Śiva, it may be done above the pedestal or even without it.
One should install the deities of the Vibhava class one above the other as before,
beginning from the designated jar and proceeding thereafter according to the supreme worship.
For in this way, by virtue of the arrangement of all the deities, the placement (nyāsa) consisting of wish-fulfilling gems becomes the bestower of success. || 229 ||

Now, he explains the installation of the deities (*devatānyāsa*) with three verses beginning with "vinyāsam. "At the base of the pedestal" (*pīṭhamūle*) means beneath the pedestal, that is, upon the *piṇḍikā*. This refers to the previously mentioned deities who are the instruments of Bhava, beginning with Kāla and ending with Vasudhā. One should install the deities of manifestation (*vibhava-deva*) without them [the aforementioned]. This installation is to be performed among the deities of manifestation, starting from those who lie in the netherworld (*pātālaśayana*) and ending with Padmanābha. The meaning is that one should install all others except for the primary deity (*deva*). Thus it is clearly stated in the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara* [Tantras]:
"O best of sages, this installation is indeed to be performed above the pedestal, but without [the aforementioned deities]."
"One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Vibhava deities one above the other, as before.

In the *Pārameśvara-vyākhyāna*, failing to understand this intention, it was written: "The meaning is that one should perform the placement of this Pratiṣṭhā [form] upon the image suitable for installation, without [the specific] mantra. It should be understood that the placement begins from the location of the jar (*ghaṭa*), starting from the jar previously established in the center of the temple, proceeding upwards until the end of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), following the sequence beginning with the one reclining in the netherworld (*pātālaśayana*) and ending with Padmanābha. (227–229)
Even while remaining in that momentary portion [of time] in the middle of the pavilion facing the God of gods, the King of Birds (Garuḍa) should be installed. 230.
He who was previously consecrated by his own mantra, having bathed and anointed himself, [remains one] with the power of knowledge and the image, even amidst diverse objects. || 231 ||
O wielder of the plow, whether they are situated near the Bimba fruit or elsewhere,
they all invariably attain the state of being limbs at that very moment.
Having completely abandoned everything up to the vehicle, preceded by meditation and worship,
one should personally relinquish the commonality of actions in accordance with what is appropriate.
Therefore, having raised [the deity] from that sacrificial hall and taken him as if he were an image,
one should circumambulate the deity clockwise and place him upon the ground for installation as before.
One should place the pentad beginning with Vajra within a single central cavity;
then, above that, there is the one support which has been described.
And that [element] of the earth (bhauvana) should be placed above its seat as before;
it is to be contemplated within the body, while the remainder is characterized by cognition.
Likewise, one should have the Brāhmaṇas recite the king of mantras, "suparṇo 'si.

Now, he describes the procedure for the installation of the Lord of Birds (Vihageśa) in the center of the front pavilion, beginning with the words "atha maṇṭapamadhye tu" and ending with "suparṇo 'si iti mantrarāṭ. The meaning is that [the deity] has been bathed according to the rules with water containing white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) and so forth, as well as through a great ablution (*mahāsnāpana*). "Anuliptaḥ" means adorned with sandalwood paste and the like; or alternatively, it means anointed with its own specific mantra and refined through the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other rites.

The meaning is that he is consecrated by other purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*s), such as the opening of the eyes, the lying down, and the perfuming. "Together with the image" means together with the primary image of the Blessed Lord. The connection here is that he is consecrated by being of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Indeed, the nature of this [Lord] as consisting of the power of knowledge has been stated in the *Īśvara* and *Parameśvara* [Tantras] regarding Viṣṇu, who is named Saṃkarṣaṇa and possesses the power of discerning knowledge (*vijñāna-bala*).

"The form which is the very nature of knowledge and whose essence is the support of all—O Lord of Birds, this is to be understood as the 'Māhima' (glory) of the Creator of the world. Thus [it is said].

By the words beginning with "yasmāt" (since), it is stated that, together with the primary image (*pradhānabimba*) and so forth, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—such as bathing, worship, and satiation appropriate to each—must generally be performed for the images of all the limbs of the retinue, including Garuḍa and others. The "support" (*ādhāra*) which was mentioned is that which was established in the statement: "In the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), however, for the rite of installing the wheel of the Lord of Birds. "Bhauvana" refers to the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). "The rest" means the remaining five paths, beginning with the path of the levels (*padādhvan*). (230–237)
Having honored that very [deity] with weapons, one should proceed to the abode of the gods. || 237 ||
Then the Lord should be bathed with water-pots placed at his back,
together with all the image-bearers, according to the prescribed sequence.

Then, having performed the worship of the Garuda thus established and having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should consecrate the deity with the forty pitchers previously placed at the rear of the bathing pavilion; thus he says "him" with the half-verse [237-238].
By means of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn itself, and by the repetition of the *gāyatrī*,
first with the Ṛks and then subsequently with four repetitions performed by oneself.
The knower of the Yajurveda should sprinkle [the deity] with the six [mantras] revolving from the heart and so forth;
thereafter, the knower of the Sāmaveda should likewise bathe [the deity] himself with the water-pitchers. || 240 ||
Then, after [the first six], he himself, being a knower of the Atharvaveda, [should perform the rite] with six others,
using pitchers that have been purified by the recitation [of mantras], at various intervals.

And immediately thereafter, together with those belonging to the Ekāyanīya school, he should perform the ceremonial bathing with mantras consisting of the four forms, which have been repeatedly meditated upon.
Then, having taken the remaining water in a jar, one should bathe [the deity] with that jar;
having performed a hundred-fold rotation, [one should worship] today with the form together with its root.
Together with the God of Gods, one should carve [the mantra] upon the head and cause it to be recited.

He describes the method of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) starting from "together with the *aghamarṣaṇa*" up to "it is indeed conquered by all. Regarding the phrase "one who knows the *yajus* should sprinkle with that," the meaning is: with a single water-pot (*kalaśa*) consecrated by both the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn and the *gāyatrī*. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, he himself likewise with the jars," the meaning here is also: with the six jars previously mentioned, such as the *hṛdaya* (heart) jar and others, which have been consecrated. This should be understood in the same way for what follows.

"With four jars consecrated by the *pavitra* [mantras]" means with four jars; for it was stated previously: "The first four of the mantras begin with *Oṃ* and end with *pavitra*. "In between" (*antarāntarā*) means amidst the consecrations with the jars of the *mūrti*-mantras of Vāsudeva and the others. In the phrase "then one should bathe with a jar," it should be understood that the *pavitra* mantra itself is intended. "With the root-mantra" (*samūlena*) means together with the root-mantra; that is, with the supreme mantra of the primordial *mūrti*.
Because that [supreme mantra] pertains to the primordial *mūrti*, it is treated in that very manner. (239–244)
With the mantra "jitanta," one should then conquer all [obstacles] by means of both weapons and water.
Having purified the temple, one should perform the ritual, excluding the bath, beginning with the seat as previously described and ending with the sacrifice and the gift. 245.
Having especially offered a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and to those who bear his form,
one should prostrate before the deity and inform him through action, mind, and speech.
O Lord, since you have entered into the image and were led by me to the bed and other places, please forgive that act of mine, O Acyuta. 247.
Having thus prostrated, made his request, asked for forgiveness, and departed from her presence,
and having sipped water and offered the bali-oblation, he should then proceed to the temple of the deity.

Then follows the purification of the temple (prasādasaṃśodhana): worship according to the rules with offerings beginning from the bath and ending with the presentation of food (havirnivedana), excluding the [final] bath; the distribution of wages (kāripradāna); the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others; prostration; the formal request (vijñāpana); further prostrations and so forth; exiting the temple facing the Lord alone, in accordance with the injunction: "One should not show one's back to the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, or a Brahmin"; the offering of oblations (bali) to the deities of the door and the enclosures according to the rules; and sipping water for purification (ācamana).
Furthermore, O Blessed One, beginning from "the entry into the temple" and "then with water for the weapons," up until "one should go to the house of the deity," [these verses] are stated. (244–248)
There, having worshipped the Lord as before with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the bath,
[he performed the rite] with jars filled with water and clothed in new garments, placed upon a pedestal of grain.

Furthermore, with waters well-filled and consecrated by the heart-mantra, together with the [deities] bearing forms, one should proceed as before through the alternating application [of the ritual]. || 250 ||
Having performed the ritual of bathing according to the procedure prescribed by rule,
he should then worship once more as before in the waterless palace.

Having offered the imperishable [oblation] beginning with the seat and ending with the final gift, having bound the mudrā, recited the mantra, and offered praise and asked for forgiveness, one should go outside. || 252 ||
The master of mantras himself should offer oblations one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred and eight times,
reciting the Saṃhitā according to the proper method, together with its limbs and its retinue.

The image-worshippers [should offer] one hundred oblations each with Gāyatrīs preceded by the Praṇava; those who follow the Ekāyana path should do the same with their own specialized mantras. || 254 ||
Then one should cause the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) to receive the complete Ṛgveda and the others;
at the conclusion of that, one should then have them recite the Ekāyana in due order.

One should personally offer [the oblation] with the mantra "From fullness, fullness" (pūrṇāt pūrṇam), beginning with "You are full" (pūrṇam asi), together with the mantra ending in salutation (namas) and including its constituent parts. || 256 ||
Then, with offerings, he should satisfy all those who have been his ancestors in the past;
having entered and sipped water, he should thereafter ask for forgiveness from the deity residing in the pitcher.
As before, one should first adorn the deity situated in the mandala, and immediately thereafter the deity situated in the sacrificial pit;
then one should adorn those beginning with the Guru with ornaments such as bracelets and the like.
One should offer the sacrificial materials to the Guru or the Guru’s son; [these include] the image up to the Ekāyana, together with all the necessary implements. 259.

[The text describes the temple] provided with female slaves and laborers, and accompanied by pure *devalakas*. Then, on the fourth day, it describes the performance of worship, bathing, decoration, the offering of oblations (*havir-nivedana*), and so forth; the satiation of the fire (*agni-saṃtarpaṇa*); the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the great jar (*mahākumbha*) and other items; and the bestowing of ornaments upon the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others—by means of verses beginning with "having worshipped there with seats and so forth. Although the phrase "on the fourth day" is not explicitly stated here [in the verse], it is understood through an examination of the context, because otherwise it would be impossible to state the worship, bathing, and so forth at that very time after having already described the worship ending with the *bali* offering. Now, regarding this...
Having sipped water and offered the bali-oblation, he should then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, having worshipped the Lord as before with offerings beginning with a seat and ending with a bath, he [proceeded].

If you argue that since [the rite] has been established as being without interval, how can its application to the fourth day be stated, and therefore it must be stated that it pertains to the midday worship (*mādhyāhnikārcana*) and so forth—what is the use of this dispute between us? May you observe that its application to the fourth day has been determined by the two supporting texts themselves, namely the *Īśvara* and *Pārameśvara*.

The meaning is: by means of forty jars (kalaśas) previously placed on the southern side of the bathing pavilion with their cloths removed; "furthermore filled with water" means that when the water previously poured in had dried slightly, they were again filled to the brim; "as before" means as in the case of the gross and subtle ablutions performed on the day of installation; "with their own identifying mantras" means with the Vāsudeva-mantra and others. (249–260)
Having fashioned a pitcher from stone as before, or one made of metal, || 260 ||

Then, together with the mantra-image measuring two *golaka*s, on another auspicious day, in a sacrificial pavilion possessing the previously described characteristics, [one should perform the rite]. || 261 ||

Having accepted [the invitation] according to the rule, and having provided for them both, in accordance with the prescribed method, all the bathing requisites and every other necessary article; || 262 ||
Having placed the image in that pitcher joined with the heart-mantra and other [mantras],
and having made it pure with garments, ornaments, and flowers, one should offer the arghya water and flowers.
He should slowly ascend to the edge of the palace together with the guardians of the images;
there, having first performed the rites beginning with the seating and ending with the ritual washing.
One should perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bīja-vinyāsa), or everything as prescribed for the invocation;
having brought that [deity] and established it in the center, together with the image and the water-pot (kumbha). || 265 ||

O wielder of the plow, having first performed a single contemplation there with the root mantra, which is restrained from the heart to the end and joined with the supreme (Parā), [one should proceed].

Having worshipped the previously mentioned general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), which consists of the [thirty-six] kalās, and having covered it with a cloth, one should bring it to manifestation by means of the sudhā [consecration]. || 267 ||
Then, upon that *piṇḍa* and above it, one should perform the rite together with its ancillaries as prescribed;
afterwards, one should install the temple according to the path previously indicated. (268)
Having anointed and worshipped it with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should then decorate it;
furthermore, for its installation, one should have the Brahmins recite [the mantras] as before.
Having personally restrained the armor-mantra there with a mind fixed in meditation,
he should again perform the entire rite up to its completion according to this procedure.
One should indeed cause the Sāman to be chanted and have those who sing the Sāman recite it;
one should place a disc of *āmalasāra* wood in the center.
