One should meditate on Caṇḍa, who has a form according to one's preference, whose face is directed toward the cardinal directions or the intermediate quarters, who stands upon a staff colored according to his own Śakti, and who is as radiant as the blazing sun.

One should place the wheel-mantra upon that [body], as previously described, along with the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), employing the practice of going and returning, characterized by the water of the objects of knowledge (prameya). || 273 ||
Having previously understood that it has attained the state of a substantial form, one should then perform the reconnection above; not otherwise, O Mahāmati. (274)
He who knows in truth that the Wheel is indeed one in form—pure, bearing the name of Peace, and likewise arising from that which has arisen in peace—is truly wise. || 275 ||

Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, he shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all those dwelling in the various stages of life (āśrama) and over all who are devoted to dharma. || 276 ||

That which is the immortal Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), established as the unconditioned witness, devoid of support, existing both within and without all things, is remembered as the stainless bestower of liberation. || 377 ||
That which is like the ocean of milk, resembling a thousand suns, partless and sharp-edged, is indeed called "Peace" (Śānta), for it bestows yoga. 278.
But that which, by its very independence, without being a subordinate part [of anything else], proceeds by itself, having extended its own activity toward all directions. (279)
Know that wheel which bestows one's desires to be like a slightly curved navel, resounding with internal lines, and characterized by both the quiescent and the emergent. 280.

That which is the sovereign wheel called "the arisen" (uditākhya), having performed everything, abides in the tranquil form of the Perfectly Awakened One; it is indeed not preceded by the navel, yet it has set in motion [the cycle]. 281.
When a mantra is propitiated within that [liṅga], it is indeed considered fully worshipped;
recited and gratified with devotion, it bestows everything upon everyone. || 282 ||
Having thus installed and duly worshipped this desired wheel, which causes the destruction of all obstacles, immediately thereafter— (283)
Having fashioned the flagstaff so that it rises one-third higher than the pinnacle and is adorned with the king of birds (the Garuda), one should install it while reciting the Śikhā-mantra.
Then, [there appeared] a banner of various colors, adorned with clusters of tiny bells,
reaching from the top of the flagpole to half the height of the peak, long and unartificial.
Having made that cloth, previously designated as the "mark," extended by either a twelfth or a ninth part of its length, one should perform the ritual for the presence of the weapons within it.
Having placed [the vessel] at the tip of the flagstaff, one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings.

Now, he describes the procedure for placing the jar atop the temple and the procedure for the consecration of the temple, beginning with "the jar made of stone as before" and ending with "having placed it at the tip of the flagstaff, one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
In that regard, having performed a single contemplation of the first [element], it is joined with the subsequent ones.
"The general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) follows later, while that which consists of the parts (kalātmaka) was indeed mentioned previously"—this refers here to the first stage of contemplation;
having first meditated upon the root mantra, which possesses the tranquil characteristic of Brahman.
One should contemplate that everything from the foundation up to the tip of the banner is pervaded by it.

Thus, what was previously stated should be understood. "Consisting of *kalās*" means consisting of the six *kalās*, namely knowledge (*jñāna*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and so forth; this too was previously stated: "The gross [form] is sixfold, ending with *Śilā*. Here, in this context, beginning from "Indeed, the stainless is called *Śānta*" up to "the king of wheels is indeed named *Udita*," the fourfold division of the wheel according to the distinctions of *Amala*, *Śānta*, *Udita*, and *Uditodita*, along with their respective characteristics, has been set forth. O twice-born ones, hear now a certain distinction regarding the establishment of the wheels by Īśvara and Parameśvara.
One should install there, upon the pinnacle of the temple, a formless wheel having twelve spokes, or eight spokes, or six spokes.
One should place the image, having sixteen or eight arms, in the courtyard;
at the time of its installation, one should mutter the mantra of its name.
One should have those who know [the ritual] recite the *Vidyā* beginning with "The mace...

(*vidyāṃ gadām*) and so forth; by such means, certain specific details such as the recitation of those mantras and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are set forth and should be adopted. Likewise, even in the case of the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Blessed One and other rites, although they are described according to that same sequence, many specific details are to be seen explained interspersed throughout. (260–287)
This has been fully revealed by me regarding images fashioned by oneself. || 287 ||
O lotus-eyed one, the installation in independent systems and in the [astrological] transits, when performed in this manner without any confusion, becomes a bestower of success. (288)
Know that for men who sacrifice to false deities, this [practice] yields no success;

thus has the consecration and so forth been described for those who have themselves fashioned the images. He states in two verses beginning with "svayaṃ kṛtānām" (of those made by oneself) that even in the case of self-manifested [images] and the like, worship and other rites are successful only when there is no confusion regarding the mantras, tantras, and images; otherwise, they bring about defects. || 287–289 ||
Remaining on a single seat or in a single place, [he may manifest] in four, three, two, or more forms. || 289 ||
Just as [the Lord] manifests himself in the world out of a desire to favor the worlds, so too does he establish himself in heaven and other realms by assuming various forms of his own accord. (290)
It is not to be performed by men who know the duties of their castes, nor by those with a single-pointed meditation,
but rather by those established in equanimity of mind, who act out of compassion.

[The sacrifice was performed] by pure priests of various deities who delighted in the distinctions of ritual acts, who were established in the constant recitation of the *praṇava*, whose minds were tranquil, and who were free from envy. (292)

By means of those [teachings] characterized by the arising and dissolution of mantras, mudrās, stages, and meditations, and capable of destroying the defects produced by their improper combination. || 293 ||

Having been duly installed as the embodiment of perfect knowledge, the Teacher of the World—just as the Blessed One himself manifested in a single place and on a single seat in forms of four, three, two, and so forth—it should not be installed by ordinary men; rather, it should be installed by those with special qualifications, such as those possessing equanimity of mind and other virtues. He states this in five verses beginning with "In a single [place]" (189–194).
One should not perform a ritual with a different mantra out of regard for that [other deity]. || 294 ||

The common abode and seat known as Bhava belongs to the gods who possess the nature of manifestation, [established] by those abiding in mortal conditions during the rites of consecration and sacrifice. || 295 ||
And having first established the deities of saṃsāra, one should then place the image of the Blessed One either in the temple or upon that very seat. (296)
He who, out of delusion, installs [the image] together with the original form (bimba) indeed experiences terrible fear, which brings about faults both in this world and the next. 297.
The image does not receive supreme worship from those who propitiate it; likewise, the agent [who commissioned it] shall not obtain the highest fruit. 298.

Regarding the installation ceremony (*pratiṣṭhāyajña*) of deities of the *vibhava* class, one should not—without following the prescribed sequence—arbitrarily perform rites characterized by different mantras and tantras together with those who abide solely by mortal dharma. Furthermore, it is said that in a temple where deities have already been installed, or on their very seat, the re-installation of another image of the Lord equal to the former, along with that [original] image, brings about defects; this is stated in the passage beginning with "having a different mantra, ritual, and form" and ending with "one shall not obtain the supreme fruit. (294–298)

In the case of an image, when it is placed upon an elevated pedestal that is free from the requirement of [an underlying] substratum, the simultaneous installation of the manifest deities does not cause any contradiction. (299)
Neither at another time, nor for another person,
nor the installation of another form is prescribed upon the seat of the Blessed One, except in the case of a transposition of positions.

The simultaneous installation of the deities of the various manifestations (*vibhava*) upon a single pedestal is not contradictory; however, he states in two verses beginning with "arcāyām" that at another time, the installation of one [deity] while another is already installed, or the installation of a different form (*mūrti*), is not prescribed. By the phrase "without transposition" (*vyatyayaṃ vinā*), it is implied that at the time of the initial installation, if there was a transposition of the positions and so forth, it is now prescribed that they be installed again according to their proper order. (299–300)
Just as worship is prescribed for the deities who possess the requisites of existence within a mandala,
it is not so prescribed for their placement upon a single pedestal.

Regarding all the previously mentioned twenty-four deities who provide the requisites for existence, it is said [in verse 301] with the word "yathā" (just as) that their arrangement within a single mandala, as previously described, does not prescribe their arrangement upon a single pedestal.
Even one who performs the ritual in a different sequence, or separately upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā),
should likewise perform the circumambulation of the deities counter-clockwise on the left and right sides.
Indeed, by means of that sacrifice known as Pratiṣṭhā, accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
his lofty fame was established by him quite spontaneously.

That which was previously established is superior to the measurement; that which is diminished by the southern [measurement] is rejected. Only that which was previously established and is greater than that [subsequent measurement] is praised for the present day.
He does not desire equality with others in terms of status, conduct, or wealth;
even when seated upon a high throne, he is always devoid of pride.
But one who is devoid of pride causes the destruction of the happiness of the sons of those who make the image, as well as of the image-maker, the embodied devotee, and the consecrator. (306)
The placement on the left may be equal, less, or greater;
having understood this, one should construct the layout separately according to one's capacity. (307)

For the sake of accomplishment and liberation, worship in a temple of the deity must be performed by installing the images separately in every possible way; thus he says with the words beginning "bhinna" (differentiated), etc. (verses 302–308).
The gateway, the surrounding wall with its various parts, the base platform, and the temple of the deity; || 308 ||
Where the image of the Blessed One, together with its pedestal, is joined so that devotees may properly perform circumambulation preceded by offerings and incense. (309)
Know that sacred abode of the deity to be equal to Śvetadvīpa;
this settlement is the primary one, whereas any other is indeed secondary.
From the primary [site] comes the attainment of the full fruit; from the secondary [site], the fruit is of that same kind.

With three verses beginning with "pratolī," he describes how the primary status belongs to that place which contains the temple of the Lord together with its gateway (pratolī) and the pedestal along with the image of the Lord where circumambulation is possible, while the status of being secondary belongs to a place where there is no opportunity for such circumambulation. (308–311)
The forms of the primordial goddesses that were previously described are established in their proper places.
The deities residing in the image should never be worshipped by Brahmins without a pedestal;
in the home they reside on a pedestal, in the temple image they reside in the leaf [of the lotus], and outside they reside in the vessel.

Indeed, this form of Paravāsudeva mentioned previously must always be propitiated by Brāhmaṇas for both worldly prosperity and liberation. It is stated that the worship of these images should be performed by Brāhmaṇas in their own homes without a maṇḍala; furthermore, regarding the maṇḍala, he explains the division of the places for that worship and so forth in two verses beginning with "samyak sthā". Thus, it is implied that the worship of those images in a temple (ālaya) should also be performed by Brāhmaṇas. (311–313)
Whether with their vehicles or without their vehicles, whether outside or within one's own house. || 313 ||
"Those [deities] are not to be worshipped by kings and others in an image except within a mandala.

He states "along with their vehicles" (savāhana) to mean that for Kṣatriyas and others, worship must be performed in both cases, yet in the case of an image, worship is to be performed only within a mandala, not in the image itself. || 313-314 ||
All these [images] are established in the form of Garuḍas by Brāhmaṇas and kings within the sacred image.
Indeed, they should always be worshipped everywhere, beginning with one's own home; likewise, all others [the goddesses] up to the Vaiśyas should be worshipped by the most excellent among men. 315.
Together with the various divisions of Śakti and Īśa, Śakti and Īśa themselves are without vehicles.

It is said that the forms mounted upon Suparṇa (Garuḍa) are to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas either in their own homes or elsewhere, within images—in all cases, indeed—within the icons. Thus [ends the commentary on verses] 314–315.
The Bimba stone, along with the Brahmanas and others, should always be worshipped individually and separately. 316.
Indeed, [the Lord] should be worshipped constantly in His own hermitage (āśrama) while standing in the midst of His circle of kinsmen;

likewise, those whose forms are mounted upon Garuḍa and Tārkṣya, together with the various manifestations of His opulent forms (vibhavamūrti), are to be worshipped everywhere in their images along with the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. However, he states in the verse beginning with "evam" (315–316) that the image of Śaktīśa alone, without one mounted on a vehicle, should not be worshipped at home by Brahmins and the other castes.
And by means of a form that is neither terrifying nor gentle, for the sake of people who are unenlightened. || 317 ||
When the face of the Blessed One, which causes terror to the three worlds, is seen in a painting,
those who seek only auspiciousness bestow good fortune, whereas [the same image] brings misfortune when located in the home.
She has been especially excluded from the grounds of mansions and palaces by the wealthy, who dwell in the heights of enjoyment and are currently longing for spiritual success.
Because it lacks luster, an image made of clay or stone should not be kept in the house, nor one made of wood,
except for those who have renounced the world, who are peaceful, and who are constantly devoted to liberation.
And arising from that, all external [lights] should indeed be performed within those [channels] at that very time;
for the moon, the sun, and the rest constantly produce great radiance therein. 321.

Just as an image with a fierce form is not to be worshipped in the home [if it lacks a mild form], likewise, images made of stone, clay, or wood are not to be worshipped by householders without an image made of paint or metal; and he states the reason for this, beginning with the words "svāśrame" and ending with "candrasūryādayo 'niśam. (317–321)
O Mahāmati, [this applies] from the single form up to all forms,
as well as to other forms and the multitude of their manifestations.
But for the sake of the welfare and propitiation of all those other manifestations who remain wherever they may be, at all times— 323.
The Praṇava, accompanied by the word of salutation (namas), is for the purpose of worshipping the seat;
and the four well-known mantras are those consisting of the four-fold self.
But that fool who, being ignorant, performs the worship of the mobile image and its attendants otherwise, without the mantra and without the secret ritual, [attains no fruit]. 325.
In the home, a fault arises for one who is ignorant of the mantra.

Now, regarding the worship of the Paravyūha, Vibhava, and Bimba forms situated in sacred fields and other locations—whether manifesting spontaneously or otherwise—he states, beginning with the words "And if... (ā ceti), in four and a half verses, that these may generally be worshipped with the *praṇava*, or with the fourfold mantras known as Vāsudeva and the others, or with the mantra called *jitantā*; and he further declares the transgression incurred by worshipping without a mantra.

Of the Supreme Vāsudeva who is of a single form; of all forms, namely the forms such as Vyūha-Vāsudeva and others; of other forms, namely Keśava and others; and of the group of manifestations (*prādurbhāva*), meaning the group of *vibhava* incarnations such as Padmanābha and others, as well as other manifestations—that is, other *vibhavas*. The detailed exposition of this, however, should be seen as discussed in the ninth chapter. (322–326)
And that which belongs to one who has attained the moving image, even without the general mantras. || 326 ||
Or one may perform the worship of the deity known as Viśeṣa with the Vāśeṣa mantra; otherwise, the impurity arising from that [impure substance] will quickly produce defects for him. 327.
Having understood this, one must always remain vigilant and devoted to one's duties,
especially by one who is intent upon the householder stage of life.

With two and a half verses beginning with "vinā," [the author] states the prohibition against worshipping movable images in the home using various specific mantras for particular forms, rather than the general ones. "General mantras" means pervasive mantras; that is to say, the *praṇava*, the eight-syllabled, the twelve-syllabled, the six-syllabled, and the mantra known as *jitantā*, since these are common to all forms. (326–328)

Likewise, in the case of defects beginning with the breaking of the earth (kṣmābhaṅga) and ending with the loss of the dhava syllable, the pentad beginning with the Praṇava should be employed as an introductory supplement (upoddhāra). 329.
During the performance of fire-offerings and worship, or during the rites of creation and destruction,
one should raise the banner and all other [emblems] when an earthquake occurs.
O Mahāmati, having likewise arranged [the components] up to the base-stone (ādhāropala), the image (bimba) should be placed above the divisions of the wheel and the palace.
Indeed, when the pedestal is destroyed, the image is likewise destroyed;
therefore, whatever one wishes to remove, that very thing should first be sacrificed.
Having gratified [the deity] in sequence with honey, clarified butter, guggulu resin, milk, curd, parched grain, and so forth,
one should perform oblations of sesame seeds by the count of one hundred thousand.
Having recited the flood of mantras from the heart, one should project them into that [space];
there, all the powers of consciousness (cicchaktayaḥ) take on a radiant form like a net. 334.
Those who have been previously obstructed enter; one should then bring back the flood of mantras and cause all those consisting of the Ṛgveda to recite, saying "Arise! to those who know that.
At the commencement of the rite and at its conclusion, one should indeed [worship] the Supreme Prakṛti separately with the four Saṃjñā-mantras beginning with Aniruddha. || 336 ||

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should thereafter [perform it] with all the syllables of that name in reverse order, preceded and followed by the Praṇava (Oṃ), in the eight directions as previously described.

Furthermore, oblations for the temple should be offered with Gāyatrī mantras as well as those dedicated to Vāsudeva and the other [deities]; then, at the conclusion of the homa, one should do so together with them.
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) along with its ancillaries for himself by means of the vehicle-mantra,
he should likewise touch the vehicles themselves as Brahman.
Having thus moved [the weapon] with his heart while muttering the mantra, he should then withdraw it;
or, having placed it upon a celestial chariot (vimāna) or a war-chariot (ratha), he should cast it into fathomless waters.
Thereafter, one should indeed recite the mantra of Saṃjñā for the purpose of expiation;
one thousand or half of that [number] should be offered as oblations for the sake of universal peace.
As before, he should satisfy everyone with gold and other gifts according to his capacity;
he should gratify all, beginning with the preceptor, with food, drink, and other offerings. (342)
Those with joyful minds should declare, "It is indeed flawless," using the twelve-syllable mantra;
furthermore, one should perform the re-establishment of both that which was removed and that which was performed.
The Guru, who is always composed of the four forms through mantras possessing general characteristics and accompanied by the Praṇava, is truly identical with the Blessed One. 344.

For those who know Brahman, there exists in reality no mantra other than that which begins with the Praṇava, nor any fourfold nature (cāturātmya) distinct from it; rather, the mantra itself is the very form of the deity. 345.

The *prapañca*, the *praṇava*, and the mantra of the fourfold Self of the God [are to be used]. Now, regarding the procedure for the restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*) of temples, pedestals, images, and so forth, when defects such as subsidence of the ground arise, he explains [it] starting from "In the event of defects such as the breaking of the ground" up to "of the fourfold Self of the God. The "five beginning with the *praṇava*" means the five pervasive mantras, such as the *praṇava* and the eight-syllabled [mantra], and so on; or alternatively, it refers to the previously mentioned pentad of mantras known as Vāsudeva and the others, ending with Saṃjñāmin.

Here, by the phrase "like a net," the intended meaning is understood as follows: just as when a net is spread out in the middle of a forest for the purpose of catching deer, all the deer enter therein; likewise, when the mantra is projected from one's own heart into the images (*bimba*) and so forth, all the mantras residing there enter into them. The instruction "one should cast it into deep water" refers to non-human images, because it is stated that self-manifested (*svayamvyakta*) and other such images should not be abandoned, as they are to be joined with the flow [of the mantra]. Many considerations regarding this should be observed as elaborated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, the *Parameśvara*, and other works. (329–343)
Having thus understood that past karma culminates in both establishing and overturning [the state], || 346 ||
But he who, preceded by sacrifice according to the rules and without the shifting of the image, [offers] with devotion again the splendor and the pedestal of the divine shrines and so forth; 347.
One should fashion a banner, a bright temple, a pedestal, a halo, and a base-piṇḍikā, marked at the top with lotuses and other designs made from fine metal, stone, or wood. || 348 ||
It was well-fastened with single and multiple layers of iron and other materials,
richly endowed with the splendor of the sun, moon, and fire, and exceedingly beautiful.
Having established eternal fame in the world together with his lineage,
he shall surely attain at the end a station characterized by union [with the divine].

Thus, with four and a half verses beginning with "evam," he states the fruit for one who performs the consecration, restoration of ruins, and so forth, preceded by knowledge of the scriptures. (346–350)
Those who fashion and provide for the Lord armlets and other ornaments, enriched with the luster of various jewels and made of gold and other precious materials; 351.
Having all washed away their impurities, they assume a purifying body and become endowed with perfect knowledge, by which they do not return to worldly existence.
For one's own benefit and for the cessation of all suffering, [one should meditate] here from the tip of the big toe to the ankle, up to the knees, or as far as the shoulders. (353)
He who, with great devotion and according to his own capacity, casts upon the image of Acyuta armor made of gold and other materials, enriched with gems, pearls, and corals; 354.
He goes to the supreme abode along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
[The author] describes the fruit for one who offers various ornaments made of jewels, gem-studded armor, and so forth, to the Blessed One, by means of the verses beginning with "nānā" (351–355).
O Blessed One, those armlets, anklets, and other ornaments that were fastened upon your physical form—
He who, out of delusion, deprives [the Lord] of them, has his fixed abode in the Vīci hell;
the fruit for one who steals the ornaments of the Blessed One is stated as "clinging" (lagna). || 355-356 ||
[He is the one] for those authorized Brahmins who are devoted to the five times (pañcakāla). || 356 ||
And also for those twice-born ones who know the Pañcarātra, who desire spiritual perfection, whose lineages are unbroken, and whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (357)
Or for ascetics, those observing vows, Snātakas, and Brahmachārins; or for devotees and others whose souls are intent on purification and similar practices. || 358 ||
Having constructed it properly for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord, he presents it,
complete with halls and other sanctuaries, and provided with stone-built and baked-brick structures.
It was filled with both cultivated and wild grains, provided with excellent means of subsistence, and attended by merchants, householders, laborers, and guards. (360)
He obtains infinite fruit for as long as the moon and stars exist;
he shall attain eternal stability in this world and imperishable fame. || 361 ||
The fruit for one who bestows agrahāras and other gifts upon the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) is stated by the verses beginning with "yaḥ" and so forth. (356–361)

One who desires the completion of the sacrifice should place before the vicinity of the pedestal a beautiful and charming woman, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, who is capable of providing enjoyment and pleasure. (362)
Or, for the sake of external propitiation, the performer of rituals who offers sacrifices to Brahman is liberated from the three debts known as those to humans, ancestors, and gods. || 363 ||
In the center, it should be marked with a Garuḍa treading upon a discus and a lotus;
or else, it may be square, circular like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or provided with a path.
He who with devotion constructs a sacrificial altar outside the abode of Acyuta goes to the station of Acyuta in celestial chariots possessing the luster of the moon. || 365 ||
He who indeed bestows upon the Lord a pleasure grove enclosed by a wall, endowed with various flowers and fruits, and filled with ponds and trees; || 366 ||
Endowed with lotus-filled reservoirs and accompanied by Māraṅga and Khasa,
he enjoys pleasures in the Nandana grove and then goes to the abode of Acyuta.
He who [gives] the earth filled with crops, or endowed with fragrance, or a field surrounded on all sides by waterfalls; || 368 ||
Having reached the eternal time, he restrains himself from the source of the world;
he shall go to the well-white island, where he dwells like the Blessed One.

Having honored a herd of cows together with a preeminent bull for the purpose of the mantras used during the ritual bath and enjoyment, one who indeed offers the Vaiṣṇava image [attains the fruit]. || 370 ||
Having been freed from his faults before long, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
[he who gives] an elephant, a chariot, a noble horse, and a well-characterized lamp-stand. (371)
Fans, yak-tail whisks, umbrellas, musical instruments, and troupes of courtesans;
auspicious garments, divine eye-ornaments, and celestial jewels.
A canopy, a Vaijayantī banner, a collection of variegated leafy creepers,
a sweet-sounding bell, and an auspicious incense burner.
A golden pitcher, a mirror, a water-jar, a large fragrant stone, and other various grains previously mentioned; 374.
He who gives with devotion to Hari shall attain His world—[he who], while bearing a vessel of lamps, gazes upon the face of the All-pervading Lord. (375)

Or else, one may fashion a large lamp or a yantra in the form of a tortoise or other such creatures, situated upon a bed of reeds and sacrificial grass, and adorned with a variegated casket. || 376 ||
O Mahāmati, he who with faith bestows various seats of true scripture upon the God of gods attains that very station. || 377 ||

He describes the fruits of offering [these things]—such as a noble throne, an altar for offerings, villages, groves, fields, cattle, elephants, chariots, horses, and so forth, as well as articles for worship such as lamp-stands and the like—by means of the verses beginning with "useful for enjoyment" (bhogopayoginīm) and so on. (362–377)
Whatever is offered with devotion, placing the Source of the Universe at the forefront, shall become inexhaustible for those intent on His worship. (378)
Thus addressed by the God of gods out of a desire to bestow grace upon all, O brahmins, the wielder of the plough remained established in the worldly ways of dharma.
Through the grace of the Creator of the World, I have attained that which leads to the perfection of liberation;
I have now revealed it exactly as it is before all of you. (380)

This supreme merit, which removes sin, purifies, and bestows the two-fold accomplishments (siddhis), should be spoken to those of noble disposition whose souls are delighted by the true nature of reality. 381.
Of those devotees who are vigilant, who serve the Lotus-Eyed One, and who long for sacrifice, the attainment of liberation, good fame, and the company of the virtuous; 382.

[This applies] especially to those desiring enjoyments, those who are not devotees, those whose minds delight in verbal quibbles and the like, those who approach [the teaching] through unrighteous means, and particularly the nihilists. || 383 ||
"He who protects those who are unworthy and bestows [wealth] upon those who are worthy—such a person is honorable in my eyes; may it be well with you all, I am departing. (384)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation," in the Śrīsātvatasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.

"This scripture was taught by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva to Saṃkarṣaṇa for the sake of favoring all beings; having received it through the grace of the Blessed One, I have revealed it to you exactly as it is.

This should be disclosed to those who are believers (āstikas) and kept secret from those who are non-believers (nāstikas). He who performs such disclosure and concealment becomes highly esteemed by me. May there be infinite well-being for you both in this world and the next. "Thus I depart," the Blessed Lord Nārada said to the sages. Thus [he] spoke. (379–384)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Sātvatatantrabhāṣya*, composed by Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa, son of the venerable Yogānandabhaṭṭācārya, who was an ornament of the Mauñjyāyana lineage and a worshipper of the lotus feet of the Lord of Yadugiri.
